docs.title: Role Structure
docs.text:
Every reusable role follows a standardized directory layout to ensure discoverability and consistency across the infrastructure codebase.

roles/
├── <role-name>/
│   ├── defaults/           # lowest priority variable values
│   │   └── main.yml        # default versions, features, package versions
│   ├── dependencies/       # roles that must be installed before this one
│   │   └── main.yml        # version-compatible dependency declarations
│   ├── files/              # static files deployed as-is (no templating)
│   │   └── ...             # checksummed binaries, configs, scripts
│   ├── handlers/           # handlers notified by role tasks
│   │   └── main.yml        # services, daemons, restart actions
│   ├── metadata/           # role versioning and Galaxy metadata
│   │   └── galaxy.yml      # name, description, author, company, min_ansible_version
│   ├── README.md           # role documentation: purpose, variables, examples
│   ├── tasks/              # ordered list of tasks
│   │   └── main.yml        # the core role logic
│   ├── templates/          # Jinja2-templated configuration files
│   │   └── ...             # .j2 files deployed to destination
│   ├── tests/              # testing infrastructure
│   │   ├── test.yml        # integration test playbook
│   │   └── inventory.yml   # test inventory (localhost by default)
│   └── tests/
│       └── molecule/       # Molecule testing framework directory
│           ├── convergence/
│           ├── molecule.yml
│           ├── setup/
│           ├── playbook.yml
│           └── verify/

docs.title: Minimal Required Files
docs.text:
Each role must include at minimum:

  • tasks/main.yml — the role's task list
  • README.md — documentation with variable descriptions and usage examples
  • metadata/galaxy.yml — role metadata for Galaxy publishing and dependency resolution

All other directories are optional but encouraged for complete roles.

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text: Roles declare dependencies in dependencies/main.yml. This file lists other roles that must be applied before the current role's tasks execute.

docs.title: Dependency Declaration
docs.text:
# dependencies/main.yml
galaxy_info:
  author: Your Name
  company: Your Company
  description: Role that configures NTP
  company_url: https://yourcompany.com
  min_ansible_version: "2.14"

  galaxy_tags:
    - ntp
    - time
    - system

dependencies:
  - role: community.general.timezone
    version: ">=3.0.0"
  - role: hostname
    version: ">=1.2.0"

docs.title: Dependency Best Practices
docs.text:
• Explicit version constraints — always pin dependency versions using version: to prevent breaking changes from upstream updates
  • Directional dependencies — if Role A depends on Role B, ensure the dependency is declared in Role A's dependencies/main.yml, not Role B's
  • Avoid circular dependencies — validate the dependency graph with ansible-galaxy role inspect-tags before merging
  • Self-sufficient roles — each role should function correctly even if dependencies are absent, with graceful degradation or clear error messages

docs.title: Dependency Validation
docs.text:
# Inspect a role's dependency tree
ansible-galaxy role inspect-tags --role-path roles/ntp --tags

# Lint dependencies
ansible-lint --offline --enable-plugins galaxy-tags roles/ntp

docs.title: Variable Design
docs.text: Variables are the primary mechanism for customizing role behavior. Consistent variable design ensures roles are predictable and composable.

docs.title: Variable Priority Order (highest to lowest)
docs.text:
1. vars/ directory — role-internal variables, rarely overridden
  2. default/main.yml — lowest priority; can be overridden by user
  3. vars/main.yml — medium priority; overrides defaults
  4. extra_vars / variable_files — highest priority; user-controlled override

docs.title: Variable Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Prefix role-specific variables with the role name to avoid collisions (e.g., ntp::servers, containerd::registry_mirrors)
  • Use lowercase_with_underscores for all variable names
  • Document every public variable in the role's README.md
  • Mark internal variables with an underscore prefix (e.g., _internal_cache_key) to signal they are not part of the public API

docs.title: Variable Defaults
docs.text:
# defaults/main.yml
ntp::servers:
  - "0.pool.ntp.org"
  - "1.pool.ntp.org"
  - "2.pool.ntp.org"
ntp::timezone: "UTC"
containerd::log_level: "info"

docs.title: Variable Documentation
docs.text:
Each variable in README.md should include:

  • Description: What the variable configures
  • Default: The default value (if any)
  • Required: Whether the variable must be provided
  • Type: String, list, boolean, integer, or JSON object
  • Example: A concrete usage example

docs.title: Idempotency Patterns
docs.text: Ansible roles must be fully idempotent — repeated execution must converge to 0 changed tasks.

docs.title: Core Idempotency Rules
docs.text:
1. Prefer modules over shell/command — built-in modules are idempotent by design
  2. Guard all shell commands — use changed_when with a meaningful condition, or creates/removes for file operations
  3. Never use bare command — only ansible.builtin.command with changed_when: false when the command is inherently idempotent (e.g., sysctl -w)
  4. Use check mode extensively — ansible-playbook --check --diff must pass before any production run

docs.title: Common Pattern Examples
docs.text:
Correct — module-based (idempotent):

- name: Ensure containerd registry mirror is configured
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: hosts.toml.j2
    dest: /etc/containerd/certs.d/{{ item }}/hosts.toml
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: "0644"
  loop: "{{ containerd_registries }}"
  notify: restart containerd

Correct — guarded shell command:

- name: Set sysctl parameter
  ansible.builtin.sysctl:
    name: "{{ item.key }}"
    value: "{{ item.value }}"
    state: present
  loop: "{{ sysctl_settings }}"

Incorrect — unguarded shell command:

- name: Set sysctl (will always report changed)
  ansible.builtin.shell: sysctl -w {{ item.key }}={{ item.value }}
  loop: "{{ sysctl_settings }}"

docs.title: Idempotency Verification Workflow
docs.text:
# 1. Syntax check
ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging/hosts.yml site.yml --syntax-check

# 2. Lint
ansible-lint playbooks/ roles/

# 3. Dry-run (check mode)
ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging/hosts.yml site.yml --check --diff

# 4. First run — record output
ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging/hosts.yml site.yml

# 5. Second run — must show 0 changed (idempotency validation)
ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging/hosts.yml site.yml

# Expected recap:
PLAY RECLOSED
ok=X   changed=0   unreachable=0   failed=0

docs.title: Role Testing Procedures
docs.text: Each role must include a test suite to validate functionality, idempotency, and compatibility.

docs.title: Molecule Testing Framework
docs.text: Modern roles use Molecule for testing Ansible roles against multiple platforms and distributions.

docs.title: Molecule Directory Structure
docs.text:
roles/<name>/tests/molecule/
├── convergence/
├── molecule.yml          # scenario configuration
├── playbook.yml          # playbook to execute role tasks
├── setup/
│   └── __init__.py       # post-create setup scripts
├── verify/
│   └── __init__.py       # post-state verification scripts
└── inventory.yml         # test inventory (localhost by default)

docs.title: Minimum molecule.yml Configuration
docs.text:
dependency:
  name: galaxy
  role: ../..

driver:
  name: docker

platforms:
  - name: instance1
    image: docker.io/centos:9
    cpus: 2
    memory: 4GB

provisioner:
  name: ansible
  playbook: playbook.yml

verifier:
  name: testinfra

scenario:
  name: default

dependency:
  name: galaxy

docs.title: Test Playbook Example
docs.text:
# playbook.yml
- name: Converge the role
  hosts: all
  become: true
  roles:
    - role: <role-name>
      # role-specific variables
      ntp::servers:
        - "0.pool.ntp.org"

docs.title: Running the Test Suite
docs.text:
# From the role directory
molecule test

# Individual phases
molecule converge    # run the playbook
molecule verify      # run verification tests
molecule check       # run ansible-lint and syntax check
molecule destroy     # clean up test instances

docs.title: Traditional Test Playbooks (Molecule-less)
docs.text:
Roles without Molecule still require a test playbook:

# tests/test.yml
- name: Test role idempotency
  hosts: localhost
  become: true
  roles:
    - role: <role-name>
      # variables as needed

  tasks:
    - name: Verify idempotency — first run
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "First run recap: {{ ansible_run_stats }}"

    - name: Verify idempotency — second run
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Second run recap: {{ ansible_run_stats }}"

# Run twice:
# ansible-playbook -i tests/inventory.yml tests/test.yml
# # second run must show 0 changed

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria for Role Acceptance
docs.text:
A role is considered production-ready when:

  • [ ] All tasks use Ansible modules (no bare shell/command without idempotency guards)
  • [ ] changed_when is set on every non-module task
  • [ ] Molecule tests pass against at least one Linux distribution (Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky/Alma, AlmaLinux)
  • [ ] Idempotency validation: second consecutive run reports 0 changed tasks
  • [ ] README.md documents all public variables with defaults and examples
  • [ ] metadata/galaxy.yml has correct name, version, and dependencies
  • [ ] Lint passes: ansible-lint with no errors or warnings
  • [ ] Syntax check passes: ansible-playbook --syntax-check
  • [ ] Role can be installed via ansible-galaxy install <role-name>

docs.title: Release and Versioning
docs.text:
Roles follow Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH):

  • MAJOR — incompatible API changes; bump when breaking changes are introduced
  • MINOR — new functionality, backward-compatible additions; bump for new variables/tasks
  • PATCH — bug fixes, internal changes, no new public-facing behavior

docs.title: Version Bumping
docs.text:
# Using galaxy-tag plugin
ansible-galaxy role init <role-name>  # creates skeleton with version 0.1.0

# After changes, bump patch
ansible-galaxy version bump --type patch

# Or manually edit metadata/galaxy.yml
galaxy_info:
  version: "2.3.1"

docs.title: Galaxy Publishing
docs.text:
# Tag and push a release
git tag v2.3.1
git push origin v2.3.1

# Publish to Ansible Galaxy
ansible-galaxy role publish <role-name>

docs.title: AWX
docs.text:
AWX is the optional web UI, RBAC layer, and scheduler in front of the Ansible control repository (ansible/README.md). It does not replace the repository: the playbooks, inventories, and group vars stay in Git, and AWX runs them.

Version: not pinned. No AWX release is recorded in compatibility/version-matrix.md, so no version is asserted here. Add a row with a source URL and check date before deploying, and mirror the images offline.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use AWX when more than one team needs to run automation without SSH access to the automation server, or when jobs must run on a schedule with an audit trail. A single platform team running playbooks from the automation server does not need it — automation/ansible/index.md is sufficient and has fewer moving parts.

docs.title: Deployment shape
docs.text:
Decision Choice Reason Runtime Kubernetes (Operator) in the management cluster Reuses the platform's HA, backup, and ingress instead of a second VM stack Database PostgreSQL inside the cluster, backed up with Velero AWX state is job history and credentials, not cluster state Exposure Ingress with TLS, identity through Keycloak Same SSO path as the rest of the platform (ADR-0031) Credentials AWX credential objects sourced from Vault at job start No long-lived secrets in AWX's database where avoidable

Images must be copied to the internal registry before deployment; AWX pulls several images (web, task, EE) and the default execution environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Management cluster running: management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md.
  2. Internal registry with the AWX images and an execution environment image that contains the pinned Ansible and Python versions (compatibility/version-matrix.md).
  3. A PostgreSQL instance or the operator's bundled database, with backup coverage (lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md).
  4. Keycloak client registration if SSO is required (management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md).

docs.title: Operating rules
docs.text:
• Projects are synced from Git; "manual" projects are not permitted, because they make the running configuration unverifiable.
  • Inventories are sourced from the repository, not typed into the UI, for the same reason.
  • Job templates map one-to-one to playbooks in site.yml's import graph.
  • Credentials are attached to job templates, never to ad-hoc jobs run by users.
  • Job output is retained long enough to cover an audit window; the retention value is a site decision, recorded in the deployment values.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl -n awx get pods
kubectl -n awx logs deploy/awx-operator-controller-manager --tail=50
# A test job must complete against a staging inventory before production use.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Effect Recovery AWX unavailable Scheduled jobs stop; playbooks can still be run from the automation server Restore the AWX namespace from Velero, or run the playbook manually Execution environment image missing from the mirror Jobs fail at start Mirror the image; do not point AWX at a public registry Database loss Job history and AWX-local credentials lost Restore from Velero; re-create credentials from Vault SSO misconfiguration Users cannot log in Local admin account remains as break-glass, stored offline

docs.title: 7.1 Repository structure
docs.text:
One GitLab group per logical domain, separate projects for separate ownership. Rule: one project = one owner = one change-review path.

GitLab project Contents Owner Visibility docs-architecture architecture/, decisions/ Platform Architect Internal docs-requirements requirements/, compatibility/ Platform Architect Internal docs-operations troubleshooting/, lifecycle/, network-matrix/ SRE Internal infra-ansible ansible/ (roles, collections, inventories) DevOps Internal infra-os-config OS baselines, sysctl, security hardening, repos DevOps + SecOps Internal infra-kubespray kubespray/ (inventories, group vars, overrides) Platform Internal infra-gitlab-ci automation/gitlab-ci/ (pipeline templates) DevOps Internal infra-storage storage/ceph, storage/rook-ceph (CRs, config) Storage Internal infra-k8s-addons kubernetes/ (ingress, csi, security policies) Platform Internal mgmt-rancher management-cluster/rancher Platform Internal mgmt-argocd management-cluster/argocd (app-of-apps) Platform Internal mgmt-keycloak management-cluster/keycloak (realm export, clients) SecOps Internal sec-policies security/ (Gatekeeper, Kyverno, Falco, baseline) SecOps Internal sec-vault secrets-management/ (policies, roles, PKI layout) SecOps Restricted sec-scanning Trivy/Grype/Syft/Cosign policy + reports SecOps Internal obs-monitoring monitoring/ (Prometheus, rules, dashboards, Grafana JSON) SRE Internal obs-logging logging/ SRE Internal infra-vault Vault config, policies SecOps Restricted infra-gitlab GitLab runner config, backup scripts DevOps Restricted gpu-infra gpu-ai/ (drivers, operator, scheduling) AI/Platform Internal gpu-models model manifests, versions, checksums (no weights) AI Internal apps-<team> application GitOps repos (one per team) Teams Internal site-<env> environment-specific overlays (hosts, CIDRs, endpoints) Platform Restricted

Environment overlay pattern: base content in the domain project, environment-specific values in site-<env>. Never fork base content per environment.

docs.title: 7.2 Pipeline stages
docs.text:
Stages run in order; each is a gate.

# Stage Job Tooling Gate 1 source branch policy, signed commits, template check GitLab protected branch, MR required 2 lint YAML lint, markdown lint yamllint, markdownlint must pass 3 ansible syntax check + lint ansible-lint, ansible-playbook --syntax-check must pass 4 helm helm lint + helm template helm must pass 5 manifest kubeconform / kubeval + policy dry-run kubeconform, Gatekeeper dry-run must pass 6 policy OPA/conftest policy checks, Kyverno test conftest, kyverno CLI must pass 7 security secret scan, dependency scan, image scan, SBOM gitleaks, trivy, syft, grype no HIGH/CRITICAL, no secrets 8 artifact verify checksums, verify signatures, produce SBOM cosign, sha256sum must pass 9 staging apply to staging cluster ansible + Argo CD health checks pass 10 integration post-deploy tests from tests/ bats/shell + k6 pass 11 approval MR approval gate, production job manual GitLab approvals 2 approvals + owner 12 production apply to production ansible + Argo CD sync — 13 post-check health, drift, SLO dashboards prometheus queries, argocd app list pass 14 drift nightly scheduled diff of live vs Git ansible --check --diff, Argo CD diff report only, no auto-fix

Validation is fully separate from production execution: no production credentials are present in the pipeline until the approval stage, and the production job runs from a protected tag, never from a branch.

docs.title: 7.3 Runner architecture
docs.text:
Runner type Use Isolation Notes Shell executor on automation server Ansible lint, syntax check Host-level Cheap, low risk tasks only Docker executor image build, unit tests Container Default for CI Kubernetes executor integration tests, Helm tests Pod Needs cluster agent token; keep separate namespace VM runner (dedicated) heavy builds VM Optional

Rules: - Runners never have cluster-admin. Namespace-scoped service accounts with a dedicated ci namespace. - No runner on a Kubernetes control-plane node. - Runner images pinned by digest. - Concurrency limits to protect the artifact registry and cluster API. - Protected variables for production secrets; masked and hidden in job logs.

docs.title: 7.4 Configuration ownership
docs.text:
Object Owner tool Not owned by OS packages, sysctl, users, firewall, repos Ansible any in-cluster controller Node labels/taints, kubelet config, CNI, CSI, K8s version Kubespray manual kubectl Add-ons (ingress, metrics, cert-manager, ESO, Gatekeeper) Argo CD Helm CLI by hand Application manifests Argo CD (per team repo) platform repo Cluster lifecycle (create/delete/upgrade) Kubespray / Rancher Fleet Argo CD Secrets values Vault Git, Helm values, env files Certificates Vault PKI / cert-manager manual openssl Policy Git (sec-policies) applied by Argo CD runtime kubectl edits

Conflict rule: if two tools would reconcile the same field, one is the owner and the other is forbidden from writing it. Recorded per component in the component guide (section D/E).

docs.title: 7.5 Secrets in CI
docs.text:
• GitLab CI variables marked masked + protected for production values.
  • Preferred: OIDC/JWT authentication from GitLab CI job to Vault, exchanging the job's ID token for a Vault token with a narrow policy — avoids static CI tokens. Compatibility and edition constraints are recorded in secrets-management/vault/gitlab-integration.md.
  • Vault agent sidecar for the runner if the GitLab edition does not support the chosen OIDC flow.
  • ansible-vault only for bootstrap-time offline secrets, with the key file stored outside Git (Vault + offline copy).
  • Never: secrets in Git, in images, in pipeline artifacts, in ordinary job logs, in set -x output.

docs.title: 7.6 Approval gates
docs.text:
Change class Approvals Who Docs/comment only 1 Any maintainer Add-on or policy change (staging+prod) 2 Platform + SecOps OS baseline, Ansible role change 2 DevOps + SecOps K8s version upgrade 2 + change window Platform lead + owner Storage class / Ceph change 2 + change window Storage + owner Network/firewall change 2 Network + SecOps Secrets/PKI policy change 2 SecOps only

Protected branches: main (protected, no direct push), release/* (tagged, deploy source), hotfix/* (time-boxed).

docs.title: GitLab CI pipeline
docs.text: Reference pipeline. Adapt the stage list to the environment; keep the ordering and the separation between validation and production execution.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
.gitlab-ci.yml              # top-level, includes the shared template
ci/
├── templates/
│   ├── validate.yml       # stages 1-8 (validation only)
│   ├── deploy-staging.yml # stage 9-10
│   └── deploy-prod.yml    # stage 11-13
└── scripts/
    ├── drift-report.sh
    └── post-deploy-check.sh

docs.title: Top-level pipeline
docs.text:
include:
  - project: platform/gitlab-ci
    ref: v1.0.0
    file: /ci/templates/validate.yml

stages:
  - source
  - lint
  - validate
  - policy
  - security
  - artifact
  - staging
  - integration
  - approval
  - production
  - postcheck
  - drift

variables:
  HELM_VERSION: "3.22.0"
  KUBECONFORM_VERSION: "v0.7.0"
  TRIVY_VERSION: "0.76.1"
  COSIGN_VERSION: "v3.1.4"
  KUBE_VERSION_TARGET: "v1.36.5"
  HARBOR: harbor.internal
  # Secrets are NEVER in this file. They are protected, masked CI/CD variables
  # or Vault-issued short-lived credentials.

default:
  interruptible: true
  tags: [docker, linux]

docs.title: Stage 1-2: source and lint
docs.text:
source:validate-branch:
  stage: source
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
  script:
    - |
      if [ "$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE" = "merge_request_event" ]; then
        git fetch origin "$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME"
        git diff --name-only origin/"$CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME"...HEAD
      fi

lint:yaml:
  stage: lint
  image: registry.internal/tools/yamllint:1.35.1
  script:
    - yamllint -c .yamllint.yml .

lint:markdown:
  stage: lint
  image: registry.internal/tools/markdownlint:0.42.0
  script:
    - markdownlint -c .markdownlint.yml --ignore node_modules .

docs.title: Stage 3: Ansible validation
docs.text:
validate:ansible-syntax:
  stage: validate
  image: registry.internal/tools/ansible:2.19.2
  script:
    - ansible-playbook --syntax-check -i ansible/inventory/staging/hosts.ini ansible/site.yml
    - ansible-lint -p ansible/
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"

validate:ansible-idempotency:
  stage: validate
  script:
    # Dry run against the staging inventory; catches task-level errors without touching prod
    - ansible-playbook -i ansible/inventory/staging/hosts.ini ansible/site.yml --check --diff

docs.title: Stage 4: Helm and manifest validation
docs.text:
validate:helm:
  stage: validate
  image: registry.internal/tools/helm:3.22.0
  script:
    - |
      for chart in $(find . -name Chart.yaml -printf '%h\n'); do
        helm lint "$chart"
        helm template "$(basename "$chart")" "$chart" > /dev/null
      done

validate:manifests:
  stage: validate
  image: registry.internal/tools/kubeconform:v0.7.0
  script:
    - |
      find . -name '*.yaml' -not -path './.git/*' | while read -r f; do
        kubeconform -strict -summary -kubernetes-version "${KUBE_VERSION_TARGET}" "$f"
      done

docs.title: Stage 5: policy validation
docs.text:
validate:policy:
  stage: policy
  image: registry.internal/tools/conftest:0.56.0
  script:
    - conftest test --policy .conftest/ .

validate:kyverno:
  stage: policy
  image: registry.internal/tools/kyverno:v1.19.2
  script:
    - |
      for p in security/kyverno/policies/*.yaml; do
        kyverno apply "$p" --resource security/kyverno/test-resources/ --policy-report
      done

Gatekeeper constraints are validated with opa test against their Rego unit tests, which live next to the constraint.

docs.title: Stage 6: security scanning
docs.text:
security:secret-scan:
  stage: security
  image: registry.internal/tools/gitleaks:v8.28.0
  script:
    - gitleaks detect --source . --redact --report-format json --report-path gitleaks.json
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths: [gitleaks.json]

security:dependency-scan:
  stage: security
  image: registry.internal/tools/trivy:0.76.1
  script:
    - trivy fs --scanners vuln,secret,license --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 .

security:image-scan:
  stage: security
  image: registry.internal/tools/trivy:0.76.1
  script:
    - trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

security:sbom:
  stage: security
  image: registry.internal/tools/syft:v1.55.0
  script:
    - syft "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA" -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
  artifacts:
    paths: [sbom.json]

The Trivy vulnerability database is refreshed monthly in the connected staging environment and mirrored into the internal registry (harbor.internal/security/trivy-db). The scan runs with --skip-db-update so it never reaches out.

docs.title: Stage 7: artifact verification
docs.text:
artifact:verify-signature:
  stage: artifact
  image: registry.internal/tools/cosign:v3.1.4
  script:
    - cosign verify --key security/cosign/cosign.pub "$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE@$CI_IMAGE_DIGEST"
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

docs.title: Stage 8: deployment to staging
docs.text:
deploy:staging:
  stage: staging
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://argocd.internal/applications
  script:
    - ansible-playbook -i ansible/inventory/staging/hosts.ini ansible/site.yml
    - |
      # Argo CD syncs the app; the pipeline only triggers and waits
      kubectl -n argocd annotate application "$APP_NAME" \
        argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=hard --overwrite

docs.title: Stage 9: integration tests
docs.text:
integration:tests:
  stage: integration
  script:
    - bash tests/acceptance/run.sh --suite integration --env staging
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths: [tests/results/]

docs.title: Stage 10: approval gate
docs.text:
approval:production:
  stage: approval
  when: manual
  allow_failure: false
  environment:
    name: production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG

when: manual on a protected environment is the approval gate. The environment is protected, so only the named approvers can trigger it.

docs.title: Stage 11-12: production execution
docs.text:
deploy:production:
  stage: production
  environment:
    name: production
  resource_group: production-cluster   # prevents concurrent production runs
  script:
    - ansible-playbook -i ansible/inventory/production/hosts.ini ansible/site.yml
    - kubectl -n argocd annotate application "$APP_NAME" argocd.argoproj.io/refresh=hard --overwrite

postcheck:health:
  stage: postcheck
  script:
    - bash tests/acceptance/run.sh --suite smoke --env production

docs.title: Stage 13: drift detection
docs.text:
drift:detect:
  stage: drift
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
  script:
    - bash ci/scripts/drift-report.sh
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths: [drift-report.json]

The drift job reports; it never fixes. Automatic remediation belongs to Argo CD (selfHeal) for declared state, and to Ansible for node state.

docs.title: Vault integration in CI
docs.text:
Preferred: OIDC/JWT authentication from the GitLab job to Vault.

variables:
  VAULT_ADDR: "https://vault.internal:8200"
  VAULT_AUTH_PATH: "jwt"
  VAULT_ROLE: "gitlab-ci"

vault:login:
  script:
    - export VAULT_TOKEN="$(vault write -field=token auth/jwt/login role="$VAULT_ROLE" jwt="$CI_JOB_JWT_V2")"
    - vault kv get -field=password secret/ci/deploy

CI_JOB_JWT_V2 is the GitLab-provided job token. The Vault JWT auth method must trust GitLab's JWKS, which requires an outbound fetch from Vault to GitLab — in an air-gapped environment, configure the JWKS URL as the internal GitLab URL, or upload the JWKS to Vault.

Fallback: AppRole with a short TTL, where the runner holds the role id and retrieves the secret id from Vault using a bootstrapping credential. This reintroduces a long-lived credential on the runner and is the weaker option — use it only if OIDC cannot be made to work.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Validation jobs never have production credentials.
  2. Production jobs run from a protected tag, never from a branch.
  3. resource_group serializes production deployments.
  4. Every job's output is scanned; set -x is off in jobs that handle secrets.
  5. Artifacts never contain secrets.
  6. The pipeline is the only path to production. Manual kubectl changes are drift and are reverted by selfHeal.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Validate structural and semantic consistency across the documentation repository. These checks ensure that all files adhere to the same formatting rules, version references, and cross-reference patterns.

docs.title: Checks Included
docs.text:
• Duplicate content detection: Identify overlapping topics across markdown files using keyword and heading similarity analysis
  • Version drift detection: Verify that pinned versions and check dates are identical where content overlaps
  • ** formatting compliance**: Check that markdown files follow the repository's style conventions (headings, tables, links)
  • Link pattern validation: Ensure all internal links follow expected patterns; anchors must resolve to headings or explicit <a name> tags

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Run all consistency checks
python3 scripts/validate_catalog.py

# Check for duplicates
grep -irl "keyword" automation/**/*.md | sort | uniq -d > duplicate-candidates.txt

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Verify that every cross-reference in the documentation resolves correctly — both the target file exists and any in-page anchors are valid.

docs.title: Checks Included
docs.text:
• File existence: Every link target must exist in the repository — documentation example pattern, do not create path/to/file.md
  • Anchor validity: Every #anchor reference must correspond to a heading or explicit <a name="..."> in the target file
  • Broken link detection: Catch dead anchors and missing files before they reach readers
  • Relative path correctness: Ensure all internal links use correct relative paths from the repository root

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Run the link checker
python3 scripts/check_links.py

# Expected: 0 broken link(s) in /workspace/project/github/public-repository/cloud-native-guide

docs.title: Anchor Resolution
docs.text: The scripts/check_links.py tool detects: - Missing file references: used as documentation example only — do not create a file named nonexistent.md - Missing anchors: used as documentation example only — no heading generates the anchor #missing-anchor - Explicit anchor mismatches: used as documentation example only — anchor #anchor-name does not exist in the target file

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Scan the entire repository for broken relative links and dead in-page anchors. This is the primary gate before any merge or publication.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Walks all .md files in the repository
  • Extracts Markdown link syntax ][(url)]
  • Skips external URLs (http/https/mailto/tel)
  • Checks relative file existence
  • Validates in-page anchors against generated heading slugs
  • Reports each broken link with its source file path

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
<relative-path>: missing file <target>
<relative-path>: missing anchor <target>

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
python3 scripts/check_links.py
# Reports: N broken link(s) in <repository-root>
# Exit code: 1 if problems found, 0 if clean

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Validate configuration files (YAML, JSON, HCL) used throughout the repository for correctness, required fields, and schema compliance.

docs.title: Checks Included
docs.text:
• Schema validation: Verify configuration files conform to expected JSON/YAML schemas
  • Required field presence: Ensure all mandatory fields are present
  • Value range checks: Validate that numeric values (ports, sizes, counts) are within acceptable ranges
  • Type checking: Verify that values are the expected types (string, integer, boolean, list)
  • Cross-config consistency: Ensure configuration values are consistent across multiple files

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Example: Validate YAML config files
python3 -c "
import yaml, sys, os
base = '/workspace/project/github/public-repository/cloud-native-guide'
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(base):
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in {'.git', 'node_modules', '__pycache__'}]
    for f in files:
        if f.endswith('.yaml') or f.endswith('.yml'):
            path = os.path.join(root, f)
            try:
                with open(path) as fh:
                    data = yaml.safe_load(fh)
                # Add specific validation rules here
            except Exception as e:
                print(f'{path}: YAML parse error: {e}')
"

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Integrate validation tools into the CI/CD pipeline so that every pull request passes all consistency, link, and configuration checks before merging.

docs.title: Recommended GitHub Actions Workflow
docs.text:
name: Validation Gates

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  consistency-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Run link check
        run: python3 scripts/check_links.py
      - name: Run catalog validation
        run: python3 scripts/validate_catalog.py
      - name: Check for duplicates
        run: |
          grep -irl "keyword" automation/**/*.md | sort | uniq -d > duplicate-candidates.txt
          if [ -s duplicate-candidates.txt ]; then
            echo "Duplicate candidates found — review required"
            exit 1
          fi

  config-validation:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Validate YAML configs
        run: python3 -c "
import yaml, os
base = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
for root, dirs, files in os.walk(base):
    dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs if d not in {'.git', 'node_modules', '__pycache__'}]
    for f in files:
        if f.endswith('.yaml') or f.endswith('.yml'):
            path = os.path.join(root, f)
            try:
                with open(path) as fh:
                    data = yaml.safe_load(fh)
            except Exception as e:
                print(f'{path}: YAML parse error: {e}')
"

  # Fail the PR if any check fails
    if: failure()

docs.title: Failure Conditions
docs.text:
• scripts/check_links.py returns exit code 1 (broken links found)
  • scripts/validate_catalog.py reports missing docs, bad placeholders, or stale data
  • Duplicate content candidates are detected without review
  • Any YAML/JSON configuration fails schema validation

DevOps Automator: This documentation ensures automated validation is embedded in the development workflow. All changes must pass the link-check gate before merging. Regularly run these checks to catch drift, duplicates, and configuration errors early.

docs.title: Terraform — Ansible integration
docs.text: Terraform provisions the VM; Ansible configures it. Terraform outputs the VM IPs; Ansible reads them as inventory.

docs.title: Symptom: Ansible cannot reach the new VM
docs.text:
Likely cause: Terraform output not consumed by Ansible inventory, or the guest is not yet booted when Ansible runs.

Fix: Generate the Ansible inventory from Terraform output (or from a static hosts file updated by Terraform via local_exec/null_resource). Wait for SSH readiness before running Ansible.

Self-check: ansible all -m ping from the automation host reaches every new VM.

docs.title: Symptom: Ansible configures a VM that Terraform is still changing
docs.text:
Likely cause: Terraform and Ansible run in parallel instead of sequence.

Fix: Sequence: terraform apply → wait → ansible-playbook. Never run both against the same VM concurrently.

Self-check: terraform plan shows no changes before Ansible runs; Ansible reports 0 changed on a second run.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — sequential provision then configure. Add dynamic inventory plugins (e.g. community.vmware.vmware_vm_inventory) and parallel batch provisioning when those patterns are used.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Terraform drift detection: terraform plan drift, remediation, state locking, state migration.

Cross-references automation/terraform/vsphere.md, automation/terraform/state-management.md.

docs.title: B. Drift detection
docs.text:
Drift is detected by comparing Terraform state with actual infrastructure:

# Plan without applying — shows drift
terraform plan -out=tfplan.binary

# Show plan details
terraform show tfplan.binary

# Detect drift in all resources
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode

# Exit codes:
# 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = changes/drift detected

docs.title: C. Remediation
docs.text:
When drift is detected:

  1. Review the drift — is it intentional?
  2. If intentional, import the resource into state
  3. If unintentional, apply to reconcile
  4. Document the decision
# Import drifted resource into state
terraform import aws_instance.web i-0123456789

# Apply to reconcile drift
terraform apply -auto-approve

docs.title: D. State locking
docs.text:
State locking prevents concurrent modifications:

# Force unlock (only if lock is stale)
terraform force-LOCK <lock-id>

docs.title: E. State migration
docs.text:
State migration when moving between backends:

# Migrate state from local to S3
terraform init -migrate-state

# Pull state for backup
terraform state pull > terraform.tfstate.backup

# Push state after manual edit
terraform state push terraform.tfstate

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:
• automation/terraform/vsphere.md — vSphere Terraform

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This procedure documents Terraform state migration operations: backend migration, state locking, and state import. These operations are essential when moving Terraform state between backends, preventing concurrent modifications, or adopting existing infrastructure into Terraform management.

docs.title: 1.1 Migrate State from Local to S3
docs.text:
# Initialize with S3 backend (first time)
terraform init -backend=s3 -backend-config="bucket=my-tf-state" -backend-config="key=terraform-state" -backend-config="region=us-east-1"

# Migrate existing local state to S3
terraform init -migrate-state -backend=s3 -backend-config="bucket=my-tf-state" -backend-config="key=terraform-state" -backend-config="region=us-east-1"

docs.title: 1.2 Migrate State from Local to GCS
docs.text:
# Initialize with GCS backend
terraform init -backend=gcs -backend-config="bucket=my-tf-state" -backend-config="prefix=terraform"

# Migrate existing local state to GCS
terraform init -migrate-state -backend=gcs -backend-config="bucket=my-tf-state" -backend-config="prefix=terraform"

docs.title: 1.3 Migrate State Between Cloud Backends
docs.text:
# Phase 1: Pull state from source backend
terraform state pull > tfstate.backup

# Phase 2: Initialize with destination backend
terraform init -backend=NEW_BACKEND -backend-config="..."

# Phase 3: Push state to destination backend
terraform state push tfstate.backup

docs.title: 1.4 Manual Backend Transition
docs.text:
When switching backends without terraform init -migrate-state:

# 1. Export state from current backend
terraform state pull > tfstate.exported

# 2. Initialize new backend
terraform init -backend=NEW_BACKEND -backend-config="..."

# 3. Import state into new backend
terraform import terraform.state tfstate.exported
# Or: copy the state file directly and run terraform init

docs.title: 2.1 Understanding State Locking
docs.text: Terraform uses state locking to prevent concurrent operations from corrupting the state file. When terraform apply, terraform plan, or other state-modifying commands run, Terraform acquires a lock on the state file. If a lock is held from a crashed operation, subsequent operations will fail with a "state locked" error.

docs.title: 2.2 Check Lock Status
docs.text:
# Check if state is currently locked
terraform force-unlock 2>&1 || echo "No lock found or lock is valid"

docs.title: 2.3 Force Unlock (Use with Caution)
docs.text:
Only use force-unlock if you are certain the previous operation did not complete and the state is consistent. Force unlocking while another operation is in progress can corrupt the state.

# List locked operations
terraform force-unlock

# Or with specific lock ID
terraform force-unlock <lock-id>

docs.title: 2.4 Manual Lock Management
docs.text:
If the lock file is stale (e.g., from a crashed run without cleanup), manually remove the lock:

# Remove the lock file (platform-dependent)
# For S3 backend: remove the .tfstate.lock file from the bucket
# For local backend: remove .terraform.tfstate.lockfile

# Then re-run the operation
terraform apply

docs.title: 2.5 Recover from Lock Errors
docs.text:
# Wait for any in-progress operation to complete, then re-run
# Or force-unlock only if you've verified state consistency

docs.title: 3.1 Import Existing Resource into Terraform
docs.text:
# Import an existing AWS EC2 instance into Terraform state
terraform import aws_instance.web i-0123456789abcdef0

# After import, run terraform plan to verify
terraform plan

# Review and update the configuration as needed

docs.title: 3.2 Import Existing Resource with Specific Address
docs.text:
# Import and assign to a specific resource address
terraform import -index 0 aws_instance.web i-0123456789abcdef0

# Or import with explicit target name
terraform import 'aws_instance.web[i-0123456789abcdef0]' i-0123456789abcdef0

docs.title: 3.3 Import Resource Using Resource ID
docs.text:
# Import using full resource identifier
terraform import aws_instance.web i-0123456789abcdef0

# Verify in state
terraform state list

docs.title: 3.4 Import Multiple Resources
docs.text:
# Import multiple resources at once
terraform import aws_instance.web1 i-0123456789abcdef0
terraform import aws_instance.web2 i-0456789abcdef01

# Verify all imported
terraform state list

docs.title: 3.5 Post-Import Verification
docs.text:
# List all resources in state
terraform state list

# Show full state
terraform show

# Run plan to check for drift
terraform plan

docs.title: Terraform — VM provisioning overview
docs.text: Terraform provisions VMs across virtualization platforms. vSphere is the primary platform; the same pattern applies to other providers (libvirt, Proxmox, oVirt, OpenStack) where a provider plugin exists.

docs.title: Supported platforms
docs.text: Platform Terraform provider Notes VMware vSphere hashicorp/vsphere Primary platform. Template clone + customization spec. libvirt / KVM dmacvicar/libvirt Local lab and CI runners. QEMU/KVM on Linux hosts. Proxmox bpg/proxmox Alternative hypervisor for on-prem labs. oVirt / RHEV terraform-provider-ovirt RHEV-based virtualization. OpenStack terraform-provider-openstack Private cloud with Nova.

docs.title: Symptom: Provider not found at terraform init
docs.text:
Likely cause: required_providers block missing or pinned to an unavailable version.

Fix: Add a required_providers block and run terraform init to install the provider.

Self-check: terraform init completes with Providers are fully installed.; terraform providers lists the expected provider.

docs.title: Symptom: Template not found
docs.text:
Likely cause: The vSphere template path or name does not match, or the datacenter/folder is wrong.

Fix: Use the full inventory path (/DC01/vm/template/ubuntu-2404) and confirm the template exists in vCenter.

Self-check: terraform plan lists the template as the source for vsphere_virtual_machine.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — provider selection and template cloning. Add multi-region vCenter, storage-policy-based placement, and VM affinity rules when those patterns are used.

docs.title: Terraform — vSphere VM example
docs.text:
Minimal Terraform configuration that clones a template, sets hardware, network, and customizes the guest. All versions pinned; no latest tags.

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.9.0, < 1.10.0"
  required_providers {
    vsphere = {
      source  = "hashicorp/vsphere"
      version = ">= 2.4.0, < 3.0.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "vsphere" {
  user           = var.vsphere_user
  password       = var.vsphere_password
  vsphere_server = var.vsphere_server
}
# Trust the vCenter CA certificate on the host where Terraform runs so the
# provider verifies the vCenter TLS certificate. Add the CA certificate to the
# system trust store (e.g. /etc/ssl/certs on Linux) before running terraform.
# Do not disable TLS verification to bypass a self-signed or internal CA.

variable "vsphere_user"   { type = string }
variable "vsphere_password" { type = string, sensitive = true }
variable "vsphere_server" { type = string }

variable "vm_name"        { type = string }
variable "vm_template"    { type = string }   # e.g. /DC01/vm/template/ubuntu-2404
variable "vm_datacenter"  { type = string }
variable "vm_cluster"     { type = string }
variable "vm_datastore"   { type = string }
variable "vm_network"     { type = string }   # e.g. /DC01/network/VM Network
variable "vm_cpu"         { type = number, default = 4 }
variable "vm_memory"      { type = number, default = 8192 }
variable "vm_disk_gb"     { type = number, default = 100 }

data "vsphere_datacenter" "dc" {
  name = var.vm_datacenter
}

data "vsphere_compute_cluster" "cluster" {
  name          = var.vm_cluster
  datacenter_id = data.vsphere_datacenter.dc.id
}

data "vsphere_datastore" "ds" {
  name          = var.vm_datastore
  datacenter_id = data.vsphere_datacenter.dc.id
}

data "vsphere_network" "net" {
  name          = var.vm_network
  datacenter_id = data.vsphere_datacenter.dc.id
}

data "vsphere_virtual_machine" "template" {
  name          = var.vm_template
  datacenter_id = data.vsphere_datacenter.dc.id
}

data "vsphere_resource_pool" "pool" {
  name          = "Resources"
  datacenter_id = data.vsphere_datacenter.dc.id
}

resource "vsphere_virtual_machine" "vm" {
  name             = var.vm_name
  resource_pool_id = data.vsphere_resource_pool.pool.id
  datastore_id     = data.vsphere_datastore.ds.id
  num_cpus         = var.vm_cpu
  memory           = var.vm_memory
  guest_id         = data.vsphere_virtual_machine.template.guest_id
  scsi_type        = data.vsphere_virtual_machine.template.scsi_type

  network_interface {
    network_id   = data.vsphere_network.net.id
    adapter_type = data.vsphere_virtual_machine.template.network_adapter_type
  }

  disk {
    label            = "disk0"
    size             = var.vm_disk_gb
    eagerly_scrub    = false
    thin_provisioned = true
  }

  clone {
    template_uuid = data.vsphere_virtual_machine.template.id
  }

  # Guest customization: static IP, DNS, hostname. Applied on first boot.
  # Requires VMware Tools in the template.
  customization {
    timeout        = 0
    dns_suffix     = var.vm_dns_suffix
    dns_server_list = [var.vm_dns_server]
    ipv4_gateway   = var.vm_ipv4_gateway
    wait_for_guest_ip_timeout = 0

    network_interface {
      ipv4_address  = var.vm_ipv4_address
      ipv4_netmask  = var.vm_ipv4_netmask
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Symptom: Customization fails (guest IP never appears)
docs.text:
Likely cause: VMware Tools not installed in the template, or the customization spec conflicts with the guest OS network config.

Fix: Install open-vm-tools / VMware Tools in the template; use DHCP or match the guest's existing network config.

Self-check: terraform apply output shows the VM's ip_address after wait_for_guest_ip_timeout.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — single VM from template with static customization. Add VM tags, storage policies, resource pools with limits, and anti-affinity rules when those patterns are used.

docs.title: Terraform — VM provisioning on vSphere and virtualization platforms
docs.text:
Terraform provisions VMs on vSphere and other virtualization platforms; Ansible (see automation/ansible/) configures them after provisioning. One tool owns each layer:

Layer Tool Responsibility VM create / destroy / resize Terraform vSphere provider, VM hardware, network, disk, template clone OS and service config after boot Ansible base OS, users, ssh, sudo, repos, runtime, identity Secrets Vault looked up at execution time, never in Git

docs.title: Symptom: VM provisioned but not reachable
docs.text:
Likely cause: vSphere template has no cloud-init / no customization spec, or the VM network is on the wrong portgroup.

Fix: Set network and customization in the Terraform resource; confirm the template has an IP source (DHCP or static via customization spec).

Self-check: terraform show lists the VM with the expected network_interface and ip_address; ping the guest from the automation host.

docs.title: Symptom: Terraform plan always shows drift
docs.text:
Likely cause: A value set in vSphere directly (e.g. vCPU manually changed) diverges from the Terraform state.

Fix: Never edit VM settings in vSphere outside Terraform. Re-run terraform apply after correcting state, or terraform import to adopt an existing VM.

Self-check: terraform plan reports No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — VM provisioning lifecycle only. Add VM snapshots, clones from existing VMs (not templates), and VM-to-VM migration when those patterns are used.

docs.title: Kernel requirements (Kubespray release-2.32, docs/operations/kernel-requirements.md)
docs.text:
OS Kernel Meets >=4.19 Platform note Oracle Linux 9 5.14 Yes Preferred Oracle Linux release for this platform Oracle Linux 8 4.18 No Below the 4.19 recommendation. Usable, but the platform standard is OL9 Ubuntu 24.04 6.6 Yes Preferred Ubuntu release Ubuntu 22.04 5.15 Yes Supported RHEL/Rocky/Alma 9 5.14 Yes

For Kubernetes >= 1.32, the recommended 4.x LTS kernel is 4.19; any 5.x or 6.x is supported. cgroups v2 needs >= 4.15 (5.8+ recommended). If a node's kernel is below the requirement, kubeadm_ignore_preflight_errors: [SystemVerification] can be set, but that is a documented deviation, not a default.

docs.title: Vault licensing (verified 2026-10-17)
docs.text:
• HashiCorp announced the change from MPL 2.0 to BSL 1.1 on 2023-08-10 (https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/hashicorp-adopts-business-source-license).
  • The Vault LICENSE file states: "Licensed Work: Vault, Version 1.15.0 or later. The Licensed Work is (c) 2024 IBM Corp." — so every Vault release from 1.15.0 onward is BSL 1.1, with the licensor now IBM.
  • Change Date: four years from the first public distribution of each version, at which point that version becomes MPL 2.0.
  • Additional Use Grant: production use is permitted provided the use is not a "competitive offering" as defined. Internal enterprise use is not a competitive offering.
  • Consequence for this platform: internal use is permitted under the BSL grant. Redistribution to third parties as a hosted service is not. Legal must confirm the interpretation for the site's specific use.
  • OpenBao is the MPL-licensed alternative if legal rejects the BSL. The deployment model in secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md is portable; only Consul integration and Vault-Enterprise-only features are not.

docs.title: Version pinning policy
docs.text:
• Production uses exact versions. No latest tags, no floating Git references, no unpinned Helm charts.
  • Container images are deployed by digest wherever the platform supports it.
  • Every pin has a row in this file, a source URL, and a check date.
  • A version bump is an MR that updates this file, the artifact matrix, and the component guide in the same change.
  • Upgrading a component to a version that is not in this file requires the compatibility checks in the "Component-to-component compatibility constraints" table first.

docs.title: ADR-0001 — Oracle Linux and Ubuntu Server standardization
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Both are required by the master prompt. Full standardization on one distro would reduce test surface but conflicts with the stated requirement and with hardware/support realities (GPU driver availability, enterprise support contracts).

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Support both with a shared control plane, but keep OS-specific playbooks separate.
    1. Standardize on one distro and mirror it elsewhere.
    1. Standardize on one and drop the other.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Support both. Common automation is factored into shared roles; distro-specific behaviour lives in separate role directories with distinct package names, paths, security modules, and service managers.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Boring: one control plane, two well-tested variants.
  • Twice the OS test surface.
  • SELinux vs AppArmor both need policy work.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Security posture differs: SELinux is more granular and blocks more by default (container runtimes need explicit labeling); AppArmor is path-based, more permissive by default, easier to break silently.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 LTS and Oracle Linux 8/9 (both have long support windows; exact supported releases must be confirmed against Kubespray's supported-OS list at the pinned release).

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A node built for one distro is not portable to the other without a rebuild. Nodes are disposable and rebuilt by Ansible, so a rebuild is a routine operation, not an incident.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Standardization on a single distro would halve OS-level test effort, but drops a mandated platform and risks unsupported hardware paths. The mitigation is a shared-role factoring discipline.

docs.title: ADR-0002 — Kubernetes control-plane topology
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Control-plane size drives API availability, etcd quorum, and cost. Master prompt asks for 5 as preferred reference, 3 as minimum production.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. 3 control-plane nodes with stacked etcd.
    1. 5 control-plane nodes with stacked etcd.
    1. 3 control-plane nodes with dedicated etcd on 3 separate nodes.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: 3 control-plane nodes with stacked etcd for the first environment; 5 documented as the reference production topology for larger sites. Revisit when sustained API load or a third failure domain justifies it.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• 3 nodes tolerate 1 control-plane failure.
  • 5 nodes tolerate 2, but 5 stacked etcd members on 5 nodes still lose quorum at 3 failures.
  • 5 nodes cost more and lengthen every maintenance window.
  • Fewer nodes to patch, drain, and replace, and lower etcd write-latency exposure. 5 nodes are justified only by API load or by a real third failure domain.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Each control-plane node runs kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, etcd, and the CNI agent. etcd members are colocated on control-plane nodes: a node loss takes one member and one API replica together.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: 5 stacked-etcd members in 3 failure domains is possible but raises quorum sensitivity to correlated failures; dedicated etcd is cleaner but adds 3+ nodes.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: etcd is the state store for all cluster state. Loss of quorum stops all API writes immediately; running pods keep their state.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Kubespray supports both topologies; dedicated etcd requires a separate inventory group and more careful host preparation. A later migration from stacked to dedicated etcd means etcd data migration, not a simple role change.

docs.title: ADR-0003 — etcd placement
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: etcd holds all cluster state. Its failure characteristics dominate cluster recovery.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Stacked on control-plane nodes.
    1. Dedicated hosts.
    1. Dedicated managed service (out of scope offline).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Stacked on control-plane nodes in the first environment. Dedicated etcd hosts become mandatory when the site has separate failure domains for control-plane and storage-heavy workloads, or when etcd disk latency threatens API latency.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Fewer nodes, lower cost.
  • etcd gets dedicated fast local disks.
  • Best isolation, highest cost.
  • Stacking is the standard, supported, simplest path. Dedicated etcd pays off when disks or failure domains justify it.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: etcd traffic is sensitive to disk latency and network jitter. Colocating etcd with the API server means a slow disk degrades both.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: 3 or 5 members spread across the failure domains available. 3 members tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Total etcd quorum loss halts all cluster writes. Restore is from a snapshot; recovery time is dominated by snapshot size and restore bandwidth.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating from stacked to dedicated etcd is a data migration performed by the Kubespray workflow with the dedicated-etcd inventory; it is not a role flip.

docs.title: ADR-0004 — Load balancing for control plane and ingress
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: kube-apiserver, Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, and ingress all need stable virtual IPs that fail over. The requirement is an active/active pair of Linux edge nodes running Nginx or HAProxy with Keepalived, deployed with Docker Compose. Superseded in detail by ADR-0028, which defines the tiered design; this record states the boundary between the edge and the in-cluster load balancing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Hardware F5/HA pair.
    1. Keepalived (VRRP) on a pair of nodes.
    1. HAProxy in a small dedicated pair.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Keepalived VRRP on two dedicated edge nodes for the control-plane API VIP, with an HAProxy or NGINX layer in front for TLS termination and upstream health checks. Hardware F5 only if the site already owns one. The full external load balancer design, including the active/active tiers, is in ADR-0028 and network-matrix/external-load-balancer.md.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• VRRP failover is in the second range, not instant.
  • HAProxy is explicit and scriptable.
  • Hardware gives the best support path.
  • A single VRRP-owned VIP is active/standby, so the active/active requirement is met above the VIP layer, not by VRRP itself.
  • Keepalived is a small, well-understood dependency and can be managed by Ansible. Hardware is preferred where it exists.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: VRRP depends on multicast or unicast peer configuration on the network segment; a switched network with multicast filtering needs unicast peers. HAProxy and keepalived both need health checks against the real backends. The edge is the only host exposed to the untrusted segment, so it runs a minimal image set and allows only 80 and 443 inbound.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: VRRP protocol 112 (IP protocol), keepalived health-check ports, HAProxy frontend/backend ports, and the management-only stats port. Verify against the installed versions.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A VIP with no working failover is worse than no VIP: it hides a single point of failure behind a stable address. A split-brain VIP (both nodes think they are master) causes intermittent failures.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating from keepalived to HAProxy or to hardware is a config change, not a data migration. Moving from tier 1 to the active/active tier 2 needs router ECMP or BGP for the second VIP, as described in ADR-0028.

docs.title: ADR-0005 — Container runtime
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Kubespray supports containerd, Docker, and CRI-O. The runtime must match the offline image distribution design and the GPU stack.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. containerd.
    1. Docker (via cri-dockerd).
    1. CRI-O.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: containerd. It is the upstream default, has native registry mirror/TLS configuration, and is the runtime the NVIDIA Container Toolkit integrates with.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Native image pull policy, no daemon socket privilege.
  • Docker adds a socket and a shim layer.
  • CRI-O is fine but less common in offline images.
  • containerd is the boring, supported default with the cleanest offline-mirror story.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: containerd is the component that holds the registry trust and mirror configuration, so it is also the security-relevant choice for offline operation.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: containerd API/registry config paths and the CRI plugin version. Verify against the pinned Kubespray release and the containerd release notes.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A broken containerd config takes down image pulls on the node, but running containers keep running until they need to restart.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Switching runtimes means rebuilding nodes. Kubespray supports it but it is a node-level operation, not a live migration.

docs.title: ADR-0006 — CNI selection
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: CNI defines pod networking, network policy, and integration with load balancing and service meshes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Calico.
    1. Cilium.
    1. Flannel.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Cilium. eBPF datapath, Hubble observability, L7 network policy, native integration with MetalLB, and no kube-proxy dependency, which removes a class of iptables scaling problems.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• eBPF performance, L7 policy, Hubble, kube-proxy-free.
  • Calico is mature with more third-party integrations.
  • Flannel has no network policy.
  • Cilium gives the most capability with the least extra infrastructure, and Hubble materially helps troubleshooting. Calico remains the fallback if kernel constraints bite.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Cilium's eBPF datapath needs a compatible kernel and, for some features, specific kernel versions. It creates a wider kernel-compatibility envelope than Calico.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Cilium agent and operator ports, Hubble relay/metrics, the agent's health and metrics ports. Verify against the pinned Cilium release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A CNI failure takes down pod-to-pod connectivity for everything on the node, and can make existing pods unreachable. This is one of the highest-blast-radius components.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Swapping CNI requires draining and recreating pods (pod IP and connectivity change), and re-validating network policy. There is no in-place conversion.

docs.title: ADR-0007 — Ingress controller and Gateway API
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: L7 traffic entry, TLS termination, and routing. The community ingress-nginx project (kubernetes/ingress-nginx) was retired in March 2026 with no further releases or security fixes, so the previously default choice is no longer adoptable. The successor options are F5's NGINX Ingress Controller (nginx/kubernetes-ingress), F5's NGINX Gateway Fabric (Gateway API native), and Traefik.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. F5 NGINX Ingress Controller (nginx/kubernetes-ingress).
    1. F5 NGINX Gateway Fabric.
    1. Traefik.
    1. Retain the retired kubernetes/ingress-nginx.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: F5 NGINX Ingress Controller as the L7 controller, with Gateway API objects adopted for new applications and Ingress retained for compatibility. Re-evaluate toward NGINX Gateway Fabric when Gateway API becomes the only API in use across the estate.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• F5-maintained with a commercial support path; mature TLS handling; NGINX dataplane; supports both Ingress and Gateway API.
  • NGINX Gateway Fabric is Gateway API native and is the vendor's forward path, but it requires converting every Ingress resource before it can serve them.
  • Traefik is simpler and label-driven but has a smaller enterprise support ecosystem.
  • Retaining the retired controller leaves the platform with no security fixes and a read-only repository; the steering committee has stated that doing so leaves users vulnerable.
  • The NGINX dataplane and the F5 support path are the deciding factors, not inertia: the NGINX Ingress Controller is a different project from the retired ingress-nginx and is actively maintained by F5.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: The controller must be hardened: no unnecessary NGINX modules, explicit worker and connection limits, and admission webhooks that do not permit arbitrary configuration injection from untrusted namespaces. The retired project was explicitly criticised for the snippets annotation allowing arbitrary NGINX directives, so the replacement must not reintroduce that surface.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: NGINX Ingress Controller controller, webhook, and metrics ports; Gateway API CRDs are client-side only. For NIC 5.7.0 the officially tested Kubernetes range is 1.30-1.37, with Helm chart 2.8.0 and operator 3.8.0. NGINX Gateway Fabric 2.8.0 is conformant with Gateway API 1.6.3 and requires Kubernetes 1.32+. Verify against the pinned release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Ingress controller failure affects all external traffic to the cluster, but internal ClusterIP traffic is unaffected. A Gateway API implementation failure has the same blast radius.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Moving from Ingress to Gateway API is incremental: both can coexist and a Gateway controller can run alongside the Ingress one on a separate address. The Kubernetes SIG Network ingress2gateway tool converts existing Ingress resources to Gateway API, but it is a conversion utility, not an end-to-end migration, so the converted output must be reviewed and tested. Changing the controller is a helm swap with a brief traffic interruption.

docs.title: ADR-0008 — Ceph deployment model
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Ceph can be deployed by cephadm on dedicated hosts, by Rook-Ceph inside Kubernetes, or by containerized Ceph under Podman/Docker.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. cephadm on dedicated storage hosts.
    1. Rook-Ceph inside Kubernetes.
    1. Containerized Ceph under Podman/Docker.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Two supported models, used for different purposes: Rook-Ceph inside the Application Cluster for cluster-local storage, and cephadm on dedicated storage hosts for shared capacity consumed by multiple clusters through the external CSI driver. Containerized Ceph under Docker/Podman is explicitly NOT a supported model here — it is neither cephadm nor Rook and carries no upgrade or support path.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• cephadm is the vendor-supported path with clean lifecycle.
  • Rook gives K8s-native CRDs and CSI integration.
  • Containerized Ceph is unsupported operationally.
  • Using only cephadm for everything means the Application Cluster depends on an external storage cluster for basic PVCs, which is a deliberate choice with a deliberate cost in complexity. Supporting both models covers both needs but doubles the operational surface, so it is accepted only with distinct documentation, monitoring, and upgrade runbooks.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: cephadm owns the whole lifecycle including upgrade orchestration; Rook adds an operator layer between K8s and cephadm-style daemons, which shifts the upgrade sequence (Ceph first, then Rook, then CSI).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Ceph MON/OSD/MDS/RGW ports, the CSI driver needs to reach MON and OSD. Rook's operator and CSI images must be mirrored offline.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A Ceph failure that takes out the storage network affects both models. Running Ceph in Kubernetes adds a coupling: a cluster-wide network or CNI failure can take storage with it.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Rook to cephadm is a migration of the whole cluster, not a config change. cephadm to Rook is likewise. Plan the Ceph version before committing to either path.

docs.title: ADR-0009 — Service mesh adoption
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The master prompt asks for a mesh evaluation, and the requirement to explain benefits and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Adopt Istio now.
    1. Adopt Linkerd now.
    1. Defer until a threshold is met.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Defer. No mesh in the initial platform. Adopt only when a documented threshold is met: >=30 services requiring mTLS, cross-team traffic policy requirements, and >=2 application clusters. Istio is the first candidate, Linkerd the lighter alternative.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Istio has the largest feature set and ecosystem.
  • Linkerd is lighter and simpler.
  • No mesh means fewer artifacts, less CPU, fewer upgrades.
  • Native Kubernetes networking plus NetworkPolicy covers the current requirement. Adopting a mesh before it is needed adds operational cost with no benefit.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: A mesh adds a sidecar (or ambient) data path, its own control plane, CRDs, and a large artifact set that must all be mirrored offline. It also creates new failure modes: a bad DestinationRule can blackhole traffic.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Istio/Linkerd control plane, sidecar, and gateway ports, plus the Envoy/xDS ports. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Mesh misconfiguration can break service-to-service traffic cluster-wide. The blast radius is larger than any other add-on, and it is silent until traffic is affected.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Removing a mesh later means removing sidecars from every workload and cleaning up CRDs; it is disruptive but not a data migration.

docs.title: ADR-0010 — Management Cluster design and what runs inside it
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The master prompt asks which platform services run in the Management Cluster and which stay outside.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Everything platform-related in the Management Cluster.
    1. Everything outside, on dedicated hosts.
    1. Split by criticality.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Split by criticality. The Management Cluster runs Rancher, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and platform dashboards. It does NOT run Vault, GitLab, the registry, or the artifact repositories — those run on dedicated infrastructure outside Kubernetes so that a cluster loss cannot remove the secrets, source, or images needed to rebuild it.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Cluster-scoped visibility and control in one place.
  • Independent services are more work to run.
  • Split avoids the circular dependency of rebuilding a cluster from tools inside it.
  • Keeping the restore-critical services outside the cluster is what makes the rebuild path work. The cost is running a few more plain services on dedicated hosts.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Running Vault inside the cluster it protects is the classic circular dependency: losing the cluster can lock you out of the secrets needed to restore it.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: All platform service ports are in the network matrix. Cross-cluster traffic rules: Management -> Application on 6443, Argo CD -> Vault on 8200, and Application -> Harbor on 443.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Management Cluster loss does not stop running workloads. It stops new deployments (Argo CD sync), cluster registration, and dashboards. This is the intended blast radius.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Moving a service out of the Management Cluster later is a deployment change; moving Vault out is a data migration with an unseal procedure.

docs.title: ADR-0011 — Rancher versus alternatives
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Multi-cluster management is required; Rancher is the named candidate.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Rancher.
    1. Cluster API with a management platform.
    1. Plain kubectl plus a config repo.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Rancher as the primary multi-cluster management plane, with Cluster API evaluated later if the fleet exceeds roughly five clusters or if declarative cluster lifecycle becomes a hard requirement.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Familiar UI, cluster lifecycle, Fleet GitOps, mature RBAC, provisioning integrations.
  • Cluster API is the upstream standard and strongly declarative.
  • kubectl alone has no lifecycle story.
  • Rancher gives the most usable day-2 experience with the least new machinery. Cluster API is the better long-term standard but is not needed at the current fleet size.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Rancher requires its own cluster to run and has license tiers with feature differences that must be checked for the intended use. Cluster API introduces a bootstrap-provider dependency (ClusterClass or CAPD/CAPM3).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Rancher server/agent and webhook ports, plus 6443 to managed clusters. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Rancher loss does not affect workloads or Argo CD sync inside each cluster. It removes cluster registration and Fleet-based provisioning.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Switching from Rancher to Cluster API is a re-platforming of the management layer; clusters themselves survive because Argo CD and the workload state are independent.

docs.title: ADR-0012 — Ansible GUI platform
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Ansible is primary; a GUI is evaluated for approval workflows and audit.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. AWX.
    1. Semaphore UI.
    1. Rundeck.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: AWX. It is the closest to the Ansible Automation Platform's open-source core, has built-in RBAC, job approval, scheduling, and audit logging, and consumes the same roles and inventories. Semaphore UI is the lighter alternative. Rundeck is not recommended because it introduces a second job model that is not Ansible-native.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• AWX has the strongest audit and approval story.
  • Semaphore is simpler and lighter.
  • Rundeck is a general job runner, not an Ansible UI.
  • AWX provides the audit trail the change-management model requires, which is the deciding factor.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: AWX is stateful (PostgreSQL) and therefore needs its own backup and restore path, and it becomes a control-plane component for change management.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: AWX web port, PostgreSQL port, and callback/websocket traffic between AWX and target hosts. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: AWX loss blocks GUI-driven changes but does not block direct ansible-playbook runs from the automation server, nor Argo CD deployments.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating to Semaphore is a UI swap; the roles and inventories carry over. Migrating to AWX later means re-importing inventories and job templates.

docs.title: ADR-0013 — GitLab runner architecture
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: CI must not endanger the clusters or the registries it deploys to.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Shell runner on the automation server.
    1. Docker runner on the automation server.
    1. Kubernetes runner inside the cluster.
    1. Dedicated VM runner.

docs.title: Decision
