docs.text: Docker executor on the automation server for build and unit stages, plus a Kubernetes executor in a dedicated ci namespace with namespace-scoped service accounts for integration and deploy stages. No shell executor for anything that touches a cluster, and never a runner on a control-plane node.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Isolation without a second virtualization layer.
  • Real pod isolation for cluster jobs.
  • A VM runner isolates the host.
  • Docker on the automation server is the simplest isolation that still protects the host. The cluster runner is scoped and separated so a CI job cannot reach production namespaces.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: A cluster runner needs an agent token with cluster-scoped power; a misconfigured CI job can then read the whole cluster. The ci namespace and a scoped service account reduce that.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Runner -> GitLab 443, runner -> GitLabLab API, runner -> K8s API 6443, runner -> Harbor 443. All in the network matrix.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A compromised runner that holds a cluster-admin token can read every Secret in the cluster. Keep runner tokens short-lived where possible and scope them.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Changing runner type means re-registering runners and updating job tags. Low risk, small operational cost.

docs.title: ADR-0014 — GitOps strategy and division of labour with Ansible
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Multiple tools must not fight over the same configuration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Argo CD manages everything including cluster add-ons.
    1. Argo CD manages add-ons and applications; Ansible manages OS and cluster lifecycle.
    1. Argo CD for add-ons only; applications deployed by CI.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Argo CD manages Kubernetes-declared state: platform add-ons and application manifests. Ansible owns the operating system, node configuration, Kubespray cluster lifecycle, and external services. GitLab owns source control, validation, approvals, and pipeline execution. Each object has exactly one reconciler.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Single writer per object avoids drift fights.
  • Clear mental model for operators.
  • More tools to learn.
  • One writer per object is the only way multi-tool estates stay stable. The boundary between node-level and cluster-level state is the natural line.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Overlapping ownership causes Argo CD to revert manual changes and Ansible to overwrite Helm-managed state. The ownership table in the CI design doc is normative.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Argo CD -> GitLab 443, Argo CD -> K8s API 6443, Argo CD -> Vault 8200 (if using plugin-based secret management).

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Argo CD loss stops automated sync but does not stop running workloads. Ansible-driven changes continue.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Moving an object to a different owner is a one-time change in the Argo CD exclusion list or the Ansible role, plus a Git move.

docs.title: ADR-0015 — Identity integration layer
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Operators and applications need directory-backed identity, but Linux nodes must stay independent of a directory service.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. SSSD join every node to AD or LDAP (the original plan).
    1. Authentication for humans happens in the platform's identity-aware services (Rancher, Keycloak, Harbor, GitLab, Vault, Argo CD), while nodes keep local accounts only.
    1. Both: OS-level join plus application-level federation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Identity is integrated at the application layer only. Linux nodes keep local administrative accounts plus an offline break-glass key; no SSSD, realmd, Kerberos membership or AD join on the host. Rancher, Keycloak, Harbor, GitLab, Argo CD and Vault authenticate through OIDC or LDAP federation against the customer directory, and Keycloak brokers the protocols so each service speaks one dialect.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• A directory outage cannot block local node recovery, because the node never depended on it.
  • One integration point per service, expressed in its own configuration and owned by its own GitOps repository.
  • No UID/GID mapping on hosts, so Ceph OSD directory ownership cannot be disturbed by a directory change.
  • Group-to-role mapping is explicit per service instead of being implied by host membership.
  • Joining every node to the directory couples host recovery to a service the operator may not control during an outage, and it buys nothing for workloads: Kubernetes authorization comes from the API server's OIDC/LDAP integration, not from host membership. Application-level federation gives the same audit trail with a smaller blast radius.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Account lifecycle is now per service: removing a user requires that each integration is revoked, and there is no single host-level switch. Users still need a local account if they must log in to a node, and the break-glass account is shared operational emergency access rather than per-person accountability.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Outbound from the management plane to the directory: LDAPS 636 (or 389 with StartTLS), HTTPS 443 for OIDC discovery. The directory never needs inbound access to the cluster.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A directory outage blocks new interactive logins to the platform UI but does not stop running workloads, and does not affect node access or SSH recovery. Local accounts and the break-glass key remain the last resort.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating from OS-level SSSD to application-level federation removes work from the host baseline and adds it to each service integration. The reverse path (adding SSSD later) remains available per cluster without touching the platform services.

docs.title: ADR-0016 — Vault deployment model
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Secrets must survive the loss of the cluster they protect.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Inside the Management Cluster.
    1. Inside a dedicated separate Kubernetes cluster.
    1. On dedicated Linux hosts.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: On dedicated Linux hosts, 3 nodes, integrated Raft storage. Unseal material held offline. Vault is never deployed inside the Management Cluster.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Independent of every cluster failure.
  • No admission or scheduling problems.
  • Manual HA management, no Helm chart.
  • Host deployment is the only model that has no circular dependency with the cluster. The cost is a small amount of manual HA configuration that Ansible absorbs.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Running Vault in-cluster means a cluster outage can lock you out of the secrets needed to restore it. The unseal path would depend on the same infrastructure that failed.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: 8200 (API), 8201 (cluster, raft), 8202 (HA redirect/clustering), plus the unseal/KMS endpoint. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Vault down means: no new secret issuance, no rotation, no certificate renewal. Running workloads are unaffected unless they read secrets at startup. Applications that need renewed secrets will fail on the next renewal cycle unless they can tolerate the outage.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating Vault from hosts into a cluster is a supported but non-trivial move involving the storage backend and the unseal configuration. Keep the host deployment as the long-term state.

docs.title: ADR-0017 — PKI and certificate ownership
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: TLS is required everywhere, offline, with renewal.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. cert-manager with an internal CA.
    1. cert-manager with Vault PKI.
    1. External enterprise CA with an ACME/EST bridge.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: cert-manager as the Kubernetes-side issuer and renewer, backed by Vault PKI for the internal CA, with the root CA key stored offline. Enterprise CA integration is supported if the site owns one, via a documented bridge.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• One renewal engine in the cluster.
  • Vault PKI keeps the CA key inside the secrets manager.
  • An enterprise CA centralizes policy across non-K8s systems.
  • Vault PKI plus cert-manager gives automated renewal with the CA key protected, and Vault is already required for secrets. The trust distribution burden is real and is handled by the OS baseline.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: An internal CA means trust must be distributed to every client (OS trust store, container images, Java keystores). Missing trust distribution is the most common cause of offline TLS failures. If a Vault outage stops issuance, renewals fail at the CA layer and that path needs to be documented.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Vault 8200, cert-manager webhook 6443, ACME/EST port as configured. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: CA unavailability stops issuance and renewal. Existing certificates keep working until expiry, so expiry alerting is mandatory.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Root CA rotation is a multi-step process with no instant cutover: issue a new intermediate, move issuance, wait for leaves to expire, revoke the old intermediate. It is not a single command.

docs.title: ADR-0018 — Monitoring platform and long-term metrics
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Prometheus is mandatory; long-term retention and cross-cluster views need a decision.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Prometheus only.
    1. Prometheus + Thanos.
    1. Prometheus + VictoriaMetrics.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Prometheus Operator with kube-prometheus-stack, and Thanos sidecar for long-term retention and cross-cluster queries once retention exceeds about 30 days or more than one cluster is monitored. VictoriaMetrics is the alternative if cost becomes a driver.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Thanos is the ecosystem standard and integrates with kube-prometheus-stack.
  • VictoriaMetrics uses less resource and stores more per byte.
  • Prometheus alone is simplest but retains only as long as local disk allows.
  • Thanos is the boring choice that matches the existing operator stack.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Thanos adds object-storage coupling and a sidecar per Prometheus. VictoriaMetrics is a different operational model with its own consistency semantics.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Prometheus 9090, node_exporter 9100, kube-state-metrics 8080, Alertmanager 9093, Thanos sidecar/UI ports. Verify per exporter release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Monitoring outage does not affect workloads. Losing the object storage breaks long-term queries and Thanos compaction but not live metrics.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Switching from Thanos to VictoriaMetrics means re-pointing the query layer and re-importing historical data. Do it while the data volume is still small.

docs.title: ADR-0019 — Centralized logging backend
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Central logs are needed for audit, troubleshooting, and security detection.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Loki + Fluent Bit.
    1. OpenSearch + Fluent Bit/Logstash.
    1. Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Loki with Fluent Bit as the default backend, with OpenSearch added only where full-text search across log content is a hard requirement (audit investigation, compliance). Elasticsearch is avoided in favour of OpenSearch on licensing grounds, subject to a licence review.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Loki is far cheaper and label-based, and it fits Kubernetes metadata well.
  • OpenSearch gives full-text, SQL, and alerting on content.
  • Elasticsearch is the most capable but the most resource-hungry and licence-encumbered.
  • Loki is the pragmatic default for Kubernetes-native logs. OpenSearch is added as a targeted capability rather than a platform-wide default.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Loki's label model is index-like: high-cardinality labels (pod UID, request id) destroy performance. Label cardinality must be a design constraint, not a discovery.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Fluent Bit forwarder to the backend, Loki 3100, OpenSearch 9200, Logstash 5044, and Fluent Bit OTLP 4317/4318. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Log ingestion failure does not affect workloads unless a workload writes to stdout/blocked logging, which must be avoided with bounded buffers.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating from Loki to OpenSearch means re-indexing historical logs. Keep the Fluent Bit output layer abstracted so the backend can change without touching nodes.

docs.title: ADR-0020 — Security policy engine
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Admission control and runtime detection are required.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. OPA Gatekeeper only.
    1. Kyverno only.
    1. Both, with a defined split.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Both, with a defined split: OPA Gatekeeper for constraint validation expressed in Rego (complex cross-resource rules, quotas, allowed-registries), Kyverno for image and resource policies that teams can write directly in YAML without learning Rego.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Rego is powerful and testable.
  • Kyverno policies are readable by application teams.
  • One engine means one webhook and one failure mode.
  • The split avoids forcing every team to learn Rego while keeping the power of Rego for platform-wide constraints. It is accepted with the cost of two webhooks explicitly documented.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Two admission engines mean two webhooks on the API path and two failure policies. A misconfigured webhook can block all deployments. Both must be deployed in audit mode first, then switched to enforce, and both must be excluded from the platform's own namespaces.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Webhook ports (typically 443 via the apiserver), Gatekeeper controller and manager ports, Kyverno admission/background/cleanup/report ports. Verify per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A broken admission webhook can block all writes to the cluster. FailurePolicy must be configured deliberately: Fail for security namespaces, Ignore for the platform namespaces, with a documented exception process.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Removing one engine means deleting its constraints and webhook configuration, then re-validating that the remaining engine covers the policies that were dropped.

docs.title: ADR-0021 — GPU worker architecture and isolation
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: GPU workers are expensive and have distinct failure modes.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Shared general worker pool with GPU nodes added to it.
    1. Dedicated GPU worker pool with taints and labels.
    1. Dedicated GPU hosts outside Kubernetes.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Dedicated GPU worker pool: GPU nodes form their own node pool with a nvidia.com/gpu taint, their own network segment, and their own resource quota. Non-GPU workloads cannot land there by default; GPU workloads require an explicit toleration.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• No noisy-neighbour impact on CPU/memory workloads.
  • Isolated failure and upgrade domain.
  • Explicit capacity accounting for GPU hours.
  • Dedicated GPU pools are the standard practice for inference fleets and keep the AI capacity predictable.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Dedicated pools consume some scheduling efficiency: a GPU node with a free GPU but no tolerating pod sits idle. Mitigated with a controlled burst policy allowing a non-GPU workload class to tolerate the GPU taint.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: GPU node -> API 6443, DCGM exporter 9400, model store 443, node-to-node NVLink/PCIe is local traffic, and the NVIDIA container runtime talks to the driver locally.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A GPU node loss removes that capacity and may interrupt in-flight inference requests. Clients must handle connection resets and retry.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Converting a general node into a GPU node is a hardware change and a node rebuild. Keeping a small, separately-managed general pool for burst removes the scheduling dead time.

docs.title: ADR-0022 — GPU sharing strategy
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: One physical GPU serving several tenants needs an isolation decision.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. MIG.
    1. Time-slicing.
    1. MPS.
    1. Exclusive allocation only.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: MIG for production multi-tenancy, exclusive allocation for maximum throughput, and time-slicing strictly limited to development and burst use. MPS is not adopted by default.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• MIG gives hardware-level memory isolation with predictable capacity.
  • Exclusive gives full throughput and no interference.
  • Time-slicing is zero-setup but has no isolation.
  • MIG is the only option that delivers hard VRAM isolation, which the master prompt explicitly requires for multi-tenant GPU sharing. Time-slicing is retained only where the isolation requirement is knowingly waived, and it is labelled as such everywhere it appears.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: MIG requires a supported GPU SKU and a fixed profile set. MIG reconfiguration requires draining the GPU, which is disruptive. Time-slicing has no VRAM isolation at all: one tenant can exhaust memory and kill another tenant's process. MPS shares a single process address space, so a fault in one tenant can affect the others.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: MIG resource names are published by the device plugin (for example a resource per MIG profile) and must be read from the live node rather than assumed.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Time-slicing contention is invisible in the API: a pod scheduled successfully can still fail at runtime with an out-of-memory error caused by a neighbour.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: MIG is not reversible into a single full GPU without a drain and reconfigure cycle, and only on MIG-capable hardware.

docs.title: ADR-0023 — LLM inference platform
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Serving engine selection drives VRAM sizing, throughput targets, and the artifact footprint.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. vLLM only.
    1. Triton only.
    1. Multiple engines.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: vLLM as the primary production engine, llama.cpp for small or aggressively quantized models and CPU fallback, Triton only if non-LLM model types enter the estate, and NIM evaluated against licence and offline artifact size before any use.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• vLLM has the best throughput and continuous batching for LLMs.
  • llama.cpp runs tiny models on small hardware with GGUF.
  • Triton is multi-framework but heavier to run.
  • NIM removes tuning effort but adds licence terms.
  • vLLM covers the primary use case with the best throughput. The others are justified by specific constraints, not by preference.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Each engine brings its own model formats, quantization, memory behaviour, and metrics. Supporting several means supporting several artifact sets offline. A model converted for one engine is not directly usable in another.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Inference API port (for example 8000 for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint), DCGM exporter 9400, model store access 443, and the metrics port per engine.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Engine failure affects inference availability only. Autoscaling on queue depth and GPU utilisation is required, and pre-loading models on the node-local NVMe cache avoids cold-start latency.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Engine migration requires model conversion and re-benchmarking. Model conversion is a lossy operation for some quantization schemes.

docs.title: ADR-0024 — Offline repository and registry design
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The environment has no internet, so the distribution architecture is a hard constraint.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. One Nexus for everything.
    1. Harbor for images plus Nexus for packages.
    1. GitLab registry plus Nexus.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Harbor for OCI images and Helm charts (OCI), Nexus for rpm/deb/PyPI/npm/helm-hosted/raw formats, GitLab for source and CI, and Ceph RGW S3 (or MinIO) for AI model weights. One system of record per artifact type, with no duplication.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Harbor has image-specific features: scanning, replication, retention, immutability, provenance.
  • Nexus covers the long tail of package formats well.
  • GitLab registry duplicates Harbor without adding value.
  • Splitting by artifact type avoids one system doing everything badly, and it keeps the image-specific governance (scan, sign, retain) in the tool that understands images.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Multiple systems mean multiple auth schemes and multiple backup jobs. The client configuration burden is real: containerd, apt, dnf, pip, Helm, Git, and Ansible each need pointing at the internal source, and TLS trust must be distributed.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Harbor 443 (and 5000 for the registry component), Nexus 443/8081, GitLab 443, RGW 7480, plus the manager ports for the stateful backing services. All in the network matrix.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Registry outage blocks new deployments but not running workloads, provided images are cached on the nodes. A missing transitive dependency discovered mid-deployment is the most likely failure mode, and it is why a full staging dry run is required before production.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Migrating a format from one repository system to another is a re-import plus client reconfiguration. Keeping the mapping in the artifact matrix makes that a scripted operation.

docs.title: ADR-0025 — Vault recovery and avoidance of circular dependencies
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The restore path must work when the cluster, the identity provider, and the network are all in a bad state.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Vault inside the Management Cluster, unsealed with a KMS inside the same cluster.
    1. Vault on dedicated hosts with offline Shamir shares.
    1. Vault with a cloud KMS auto-unseal.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Vault on dedicated hosts with offline Shamir key shares (or an external HSM/KMS that is not in the cluster). Restore order is fixed: Vault first, then identity, then the Management Cluster, then Application Clusters. Argo CD is never the only path to restore a cluster it manages.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• The unseal path does not depend on anything that can be lost in the incident.
  • The restore path is not circular.
  • Manual unseal is slower than auto-unseal but has no infrastructure dependency.
  • The whole point of the architecture is that a total loss is recoverable with a documented sequence of manual steps and offline material. Every other design choice is subordinate to that.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Manual unseal needs a documented, practiced procedure with a quorum of custodians. It is a human process during an incident, which is exactly when human processes fail. Auto-unseal needs a KMS outside the cluster, which adds a dependency but removes the human step.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Vault 8200 for the API, 8201/8202 for cluster communication, plus the KMS endpoint if auto-unseal is used.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: An extended Vault outage stops secret renewal. Certificates expiring during the outage, and applications that read secrets only at startup, are the two hard failure modes to test.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Restoring a Vault cluster from a snapshot requires the storage snapshot plus the unseal material plus the root token, and they must come from different places. Vault backup and Kubernetes backup are separate procedures; a Velero backup does not include Vault data in this model.

docs.title: ADR-0026 — Kubespray multi-version support
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A single pinned Kubespray release is a single point of failure. It pins one Kubernetes, etcd, containerd, CNI and Helm set, and when that release ages out, or when a site needs a Kubernetes version it cannot deploy, the whole estate is blocked on one upgrade. Kubespray maintains parallel release branches, each with its own pinned component versions and its own Ansible and Python compatibility window.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Support exactly one Kubespray release, the newest.
    1. Support three Kubespray releases.
    1. Support five Kubespray releases in parallel, each fully deployable and offline-capable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Support five Kubespray release branches in parallel: release-2.28 through release-2.32. Each release gets its own checkout, its own Python virtualenv, its own inventory directory, and its own mirrored artifact set. A cluster is bound to the release that built it, and that binding is recorded in the inventory.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Covers five consecutive Kubernetes minor versions, so a cluster that must stay on an older version is still deployable and still rebuildable.
  • A release leaves the supported set only when a fifth successor exists, which keeps the set at five.
  • Each release is a complete configuration, so a rebuild on an older pinned combination is possible.
  • Five virtualenvs, five artifact trees and five inventories is a real maintenance cost, and the offline mirror size grows accordingly.
  • Mixing component versions across releases is not supported, so the inventory must not be shared between them.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Each release's artifacts must be mirrored and pull-verified independently, because the image sets differ per Kubernetes and containerd version. A release that is not mirrored cannot be used to rebuild a cluster, which defeats the purpose of keeping it supported.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Five Kubespray checkouts, five virtualenvs with different Ansible versions, five inventory trees, five files_repo trees, and five Harbor projects. The artifact matrix gains one row set per release.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A cluster moves one Kubernetes minor at a time, using the next-newer release's inventory and virtualenv. Rebuilding a cluster on an older release is a matter of pointing at that release's checkout, inventory and venv, with the same group vars.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: The supported set is reduced when a Kubernetes version inside it reaches end of life, or when a critical CVE in a pinned Kubernetes version forces an early exit. Either case is recorded as an ADR amendment with the reason and the date.

docs.title: ADR-0027 — Ingress controller portfolio and deprecation policy
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: One ingress controller is a single point of failure and a single point of lock-in. The community ingress-nginx project was retired in March 2026, which showed concretely what happens when a controller's project ends: deployments keep running on a frozen version with no security fixes and no upgrade path. A portfolio with an explicit lifecycle gives the platform a rehearsed escape route and a second implementation for failover and for Gateway API migration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. One controller, replaced when its project is retired.
    1. A portfolio with no lifecycle rules.
    1. A bounded portfolio of at most three deployed controllers, each with a stage, a replacement, and a removal date.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: A bounded portfolio of at most three deployed controllers, each assigned one of five stages (Candidate, Supported, Deprecated, Removed, Retired upstream), with a dated deprecation schedule and a mandatory replacement named before a controller is deployed. F5 NGINX Ingress Controller and F5 NGINX Gateway Fabric are Supported; Envoy Gateway is Supported as the Gateway API native failover target; everything else is a Candidate. Upstream retirement forces Deprecated immediately, and a critical CVE forces an urgent removal plan.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• A second implementation on a separate address gives a rehearsed failover path and a safe place to land Gateway API traffic.
  • A named replacement and a removal date mean a deprecation is a plan, not a surprise.
  • A cap of three keeps the offline artifact footprint and the operational surface bounded.
  • Three controllers means three sets of images, CRDs, certificates, addresses, admission webhooks and skills.
  • A controller held in the Deprecated stage still consumes address space, artifacts, and attention.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Each controller runs in its own namespace with its own admission webhook and a namespace-scoped failure policy, so one controller's webhook outage does not block writes for another. The annotation-driven configuration surface must stay disabled: the retired project was explicitly criticised for allowing arbitrary NGINX directives through an annotation, and the replacement must not reintroduce that. A wildcard certificate is issued per controller, so a compromised controller cannot serve a valid certificate for another controller's address.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Per controller: 2-4 images, 1 chart, up to 3 CRDs, 1-2 MetalLB addresses, 2 DNS records, 1 ConfigMap and 1 policy. The Gateway API CRDs are shared. Failure is signalled by a DNS or load-balancer target change, not by a controller feature, and a load-balancer health-check-driven change is preferred over DNS because of the TTL.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Migrating a controller is a staged traffic move, not a big bang: new applications go to the replacement immediately, existing applications move on their next deployment, and the remaining ones are migrated on a deadline. Removal is blocked while any traffic share remains, and a controller is never removed before its replacement has served a full business cycle. The Kubernetes SIG Network ingress2gateway tool assists with the conversion, but it is a utility and its output must be reviewed and tested.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: A controller is never deployed without a named replacement and a removal date, and no controller stays Deprecated for more than three months without a recorded exception. The deprecation schedule is anchored to upstream dates where they exist, such as the Envoy Gateway release end-of-life dates.

docs.title: ADR-0028 — External load balancer architecture
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform needs a stable, highly available address for the Kubernetes API, the Rancher agent, the Argo CD controller, the CI runners, and the client-facing ingress. The requirement is an active/active pair of Linux nodes running Nginx or HAProxy with Keepalived, deployed with Docker Compose. The tension is that Keepalived implements VRRP, and VRRP elects one master per virtual router id, so a single VIP under VRRP is active/standby by protocol, not by configuration.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. One VIP with Keepalived VRRP, active/standby.
    1. One VIP with the dataplane running active/active on both nodes behind it.
    1. Two VIPs, one per node, with upstream ECMP or BGP balancing between them, plus DNS/GSLB for client-facing names.
    1. A hardware or cloud load balancer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Tiered design. The dataplane (HAProxy for L4 and active health checks, Nginx for L7 policy and TLS) runs on both edge nodes, containerised with Docker Compose, on the host network, binding the wildcard address with net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1 so the socket is held whether or not the node currently owns a VIP. Keepalived manages the addresses with unicast peers. Active/active is delivered at tier 2: each node owns its own VIP and the router balances between them with ECMP or BGP; tier 3 adds DNS with health checks for client-facing names the router cannot balance. Tier 1, a single VRRP-owned VIP, is retained as the fallback when the router cannot balance, and is documented as active/standby rather than active/active.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• The dataplane is always up and serving on both nodes, so the VIP movement is a routing change, not a service start.
  • Both nodes carry traffic, so losing one halves capacity instead of removing it.
  • The edge is stateless and rebuilt by Ansible from committed configuration, so it is reconciled by GitOps at the node level.
  • Two tiers of upstream dependency: the router must support ECMP or BGP for tier 2, and DNS must support health-checked records for tier 3.
  • VRRP failover is roughly three seconds, and in-flight connections on the failing node reset; the drain window mitigates but does not eliminate it.
  • Nginx and HAProxy in the same path doubles the component count and the failure surface for no benefit.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: The edge is the only host exposed to the untrusted segment, so it runs a minimal image set with no shell access, and the host firewall allows only 80 and 443 inbound. VRRP uses unicast peers because the DMZ segment is assumed to filter multicast; multicast must be confirmed with the network team before use. The dataplane binds the wildcard address and never the VIP, so an address move does not require a container restart, and the VRRP auth_pass and the TLS key are written by Ansible from Vault rather than committed to Git. A keepalived track_script health check stops a node with a broken dataplane from taking an address. SO_REUSEPORT on the Nginx listeners gives per-host worker sharding only; it is not cross-node balancing.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: The dataplane binds 80, 443, and the local health port 8443, plus the management-only stats port 8404 on the management address. Keepalived needs IP protocol 112 and the unicast peer port 112 between the edge nodes. The container runtime needs NET_ADMIN, NET_BROADCAST, NET_RAW, and SYS_MODULE for keepalived. Images and configuration are mirrored offline; the edge images are nginx 1.31.8, haproxy 3.2.26, and keepalived 2.4.3, with the Compose file and the configuration in Git.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: The edge is stateless, so losing both nodes loses only the edge. Losing one node in tier 2 leaves the surviving node serving its own VIP and the router converging on it. Losing the router's balancing capability in tier 2 degrades to whichever node the router still considers healthy, so the router's health-check configuration is part of the edge's failure model.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Moving from tier 1 to tier 2 requires the network team to add ECMP or BGP for the two VIPs; the edge configuration itself is unchanged apart from a second VIP in keepalived. Moving from tier 2 to a hardware load balancer means pointing the router at it and retiring the edge nodes. The dataplane configuration is portable between Nginx and HAProxy for the L4 role, so the choice is not a one-way door.

docs.title: ADR-0029 — Cephadm dedicated storage model
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Ceph can run either as the storage layer of the application cluster (Rook-Ceph, operator-managed, pods on worker nodes) or on dedicated hosts outside Kubernetes (cephadm, systemd-managed daemons). The choice sets the blast radius between storage and workloads and determines whether storage can outlive a cluster rebuild.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. Rook-Ceph inside the application cluster.
    1. cephadm on dedicated storage hosts outside Kubernetes.
    1. External storage appliance (out of scope for the offline reference design).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: cephadm on dedicated storage hosts is the reference design: OSDs and MON/MGR daemons run on hosts that are not Kubernetes nodes, and the application cluster consumes the cluster through the Ceph CSI driver. Rook-Ceph is documented as the alternative for sites without dedicated hosts, where storage must share the worker nodes.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Storage failure does not consume worker capacity and does not depend on the Kubernetes control plane being healthy.
  • Ceph upgrades are scheduled independently of Kubernetes upgrades, so neither becomes a coupled change window.
  • Dedicated hosts cost more than reusing worker capacity, and they add a second provisioning and patching surface.
  • Two upgrade runbooks to maintain when a site chooses Rook instead.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Dedicated storage hosts sit on the storage network only and are reached over SSH from the management network. Cephx keys and the dashboard TLS certificate are issued per cluster and stored in Vault, never in Git. Host firewall permits MON 3300/6789 and OSD 6800-7300 from cluster peers only. The hosts run no container workloads other than the Ceph daemons, so the exposed surface is the daemon set plus SSH.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Three or more storage hosts with at least three MONs across failure domains, one OSD per physical disk, and a separate storage network. Images come from the internal registry mirror. The application cluster needs the Ceph CSI driver and a provisioned pool plus a client key with the minimum capability set for that pool.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Losing one host leaves data available while Ceph recovers; losing enough OSDs to drop below min_size makes the affected pool read-only rather than corrupt. Loss of MON quorum stops pool and key operations but does not stop existing I/O. Loss of the storage network forces OSDs down, which is why the storage network is a separate failure domain from the workload network.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Moving from cephadm to Rook-Ceph means standing up a second cluster and migrating data with RBD mirroring or application-level copy; there is no in-place conversion. The reverse move is the same. Choosing cephadm first is the lower-risk order because the storage layer survives application-cluster rebuilds.

docs.title: ADR-0030 — No service mesh initially
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A service mesh adds mTLS, retries, traffic shifting, and per-request policy, at the cost of a control plane and a sidecar or node proxy on every workload path. The reference design must decide whether that belongs in the first deployment or waits for a requirement that justifies it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. No mesh: native Kubernetes networking plus NetworkPolicy and ingress.
    1. Istio ambient mode (ztunnel per node, waypoint only where L7 policy is needed).
    1. Istio sidecar mode (Envoy injected into every pod).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: No mesh in the first deployment. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy provides namespace and pod isolation, ingress provides TLS termination, and the platform's own components handle identity at the application layer. Istio ambient is the documented next step, adopted when a concrete requirement appears: cross-namespace mTLS with workload identity, canary traffic shifting, or per-request authorization that NetworkPolicy cannot express.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Zero additional control plane, zero proxy on the data path, and one less upgrade to sequence against Kubernetes.
  • NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 only, so L7 policy and workload-identity mTLS stay unsolved until a mesh is added.
  • Ambient mode keeps the sidecar cost off the pod but still adds ztunnel to every node and a waypoint for L7.
  • Sidecar mode is the most capable and the most invasive; it is not the first choice for an air-gapped estate with mixed application teams.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Without a mesh, service-to-service traffic inside the cluster is unencrypted unless the application does it. The mitigation is namespace isolation plus a documented rule that cross-namespace traffic is allowed only through an ingress or an explicit NetworkPolicy. Adopting ambient mode later adds mTLS without application changes, which is the reason ambient is preferred over sidecar when the requirement arrives.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: NetworkPolicy requires a CNI that enforces it; Calico and Cilium both do, and the choice is recorded in the CNI decision. Istio ambient needs a Kubernetes version and kernel (eBPF) supported by the pinned Istio release, plus its own images mirrored offline. No application change is required to adopt ambient later.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: A mesh control-plane outage in sidecar mode affects only new connections, not established ones; in ambient mode a ztunnel failure affects the node's pod traffic. Without a mesh, the failure mode is simpler: policy is enforced by the CNI, and a CNI failure is already a cluster-level incident.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Adopting ambient later is additive: install the control plane, enroll namespaces, then move L7 policy to waypoints. There is no data migration. Retiring a mesh means removing enrollment and falling back to NetworkPolicy, which must still be maintained as the baseline even while a mesh is present.

docs.title: ADR-0031 — Identity integration with LDAP AD federation
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (provisional pending Phase 1 review)
  • Date: 2026-10-22
  • Deciders: Platform Architect / SecOps / SRE
  • Supersedes / superseded by: none

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Enterprise sites have an existing directory (Active Directory or LDAP). The question is where that directory is consumed: on the Linux hosts, or only by the platform's application-layer identity provider. ADR-0015 already forbids joining Linux hosts to the directory, so this record fixes the application-layer pattern.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: See requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md (R-01..R-14, D-01..D-14).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
1. No directory integration: local accounts everywhere.
    1. Keycloak as the identity broker, federating LDAP/AD, with Rancher, Harbor, GitLab, Argo CD, and Vault trusting Keycloak.
    1. Each platform component configured directly against AD/LDAP, with no broker.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Keycloak as the single broker. It federates the site's LDAP or AD, and every platform component trusts Keycloak over OIDC or SAML. Linux hosts keep local accounts plus an offline break-glass account, per ADR-0015. Direct per-component directory configuration is rejected because it multiplies credentials, groups, and outage dependencies across components.

docs.title: Rationale and trade-offs
docs.text:
• One place to map directory groups to platform roles, and one place to revoke access.
  • Components stay usable if the directory is unreachable, because Keycloak caches sessions and can fall back to a local admin account.
  • Keycloak becomes a critical service: if it is down, new logins fail across the platform, so it needs its own HA pair and backup.
  • Group mapping is per-component work regardless of the broker, so the broker reduces credential sprawl, not mapping effort.

docs.title: Security and operational implications
docs.text: Keycloak stores no directory passwords; it validates them against the directory over LDAPS and stores only federation metadata and sessions. The LDAPS certificate and the bind account credential live in Vault and are injected at deploy time. Admin access to Keycloak itself is a separate realm with its own strong authentication, because compromising the broker compromises every trusting component. Break-glass local accounts on the hosts remain the recovery path when both the directory and Keycloak are unavailable.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: An LDAPS-reachable directory endpoint and a read-only bind account. Keycloak runs in the management cluster with a backed-up database (PostgreSQL) and its own ingress hostname. Each integrated component needs a client registration in Keycloak and its own group-to-role mapping. The offline mirror must carry the Keycloak and PostgreSQL images.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Directory outage: existing Keycloak sessions continue, new federated logins fail, local break-glass still works. Keycloak outage: new logins across the platform fail; existing tokens remain valid until expiry, so token lifetime bounds the blast radius. Loss of the Keycloak database means re-creating clients and mappings, not loss of directory data.

docs.title: Migration considerations
docs.text: Starting with no integration and adding Keycloak later is additive: deploy Keycloak, register clients, then switch each component's auth provider in a maintenance window. Moving from per-component directory configuration to the broker means re-creating clients and group mappings, which is why the broker is chosen first.

docs.title: 9.1 GPU worker reference architecture
docs.text:
+--------------------------------------------------+
| GPU Worker Node                                   |
|  CPU: 2x socket, NUMA-aware, AVX-512              |
|  RAM: >= 512 GB (H200) / >= 256 GB (H100)         |
|  Disks: 2x NVMe 3.84TB (model cache + container  |
|         runtime), 1x boot disk                    |
|  NIC: 2x 25/100GbE (RDMA/RoCE for multi-GPU)     |
|  GPU: 4-8x H100 SXM 80GB or H200 141GB           |
|                                                  |
|  [GPU Operator]  driver + toolkit + device plugin|
|        |                                         |
|  [DCGM Exporter] -> Prometheus                   |
|        |                                         |
|  [vLLM / llama.cpp] -> OpenAI-compatible API     |
+--------------------------------------------------+

Isolation from general workers: dedicated taints, dedicated node pool, dedicated network segment, separate resource quota. Reason: GPU nodes are expensive, have different failure modes (ECC, thermal, driver), and are a noisy-neighbour risk for CPU/memory-constrained workloads.

docs.title: 9.2 Hardware and software compatibility
docs.text:
Exact versions are maintained in compatibility/version-matrix.md and gpu-ai/drivers/compatibility-matrix.md. The chain that must line up:

NVIDIA driver (branch) -> CUDA runtime -> NVIDIA Container Toolkit -> containerd -> GPU Operator -> k8s-device-plugin

Rule: the NVIDIA Container Toolkit must be compatible with the installed driver. The GPU Operator upgrades driver + toolkit + operator together and can transiently break running GPU pods during upgrade — plan a GPU node drain for operator upgrades.

MIG: only on supported GPUs and only on specific SKUs. Verify per model: H100 SXM and H100 PCIe support MIG; H200 supports MIG. A100 supports MIG on specific SKUs. Consumer GPUs do not. The exact profile list per GPU must be read from the official NVIDIA documentation — recorded with the check date in gpu-ai/sharing/mig-profiles.md.

docs.title: 9.3 GPU sharing decision matrix
docs.text:
Mechanism Isolation VRAM partitioning Reconfigure downtime Overhead Multi-tenant Inference fit Recommendation Exclusive (whole GPU per pod) Full N/A None None One pod per GPU High-throughput serving Production default MIG Hardware-level, hard Yes, fixed profiles Yes (drain + reconfigure) Low Strong Latency-sensitive multi-tenant Production, multi-tenant Time-slicing None No (shared VRAM pool) None Medium-high (context switching) Weak Dev, burst, batch Dev only MPS Same process address space No None Low Weak Low-latency shared inference Limited use

Hard facts to hold: time-slicing does not provide VRAM isolation — one tenant's memory pressure can OOM another tenant's process. MIG provides hardware-level partition but each MIG instance is a separate GPU partition with a fixed memory slice; it cannot be combined with time-slicing of the same parent GPU in a useful way (time-slicing across MIG instances is possible but pointless for isolation goals). Multiple physical GPUs do not combine into one device with unified VRAM: they are separate devices, connected by NVLink/PCIe, and used either for model parallelism (sharded weights) or independent replicas. vLLM tensor parallelism splits one model across GPUs; it does not create a single larger GPU.

docs.title: 9.4 GPU scheduling
docs.text:
Labels and taints:

# Applied by Ansible to GPU nodes
nodeLabels:
  nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"
  nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.k8s.io/operator: "true"
  nvidia.com/gpu.product: "H100-80GB-HBM3"   # exact value from `nvidia-smi -L` + operator discovery
nodeTaints:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu
    value: "true"
    effect: NoSchedule

Workload side:

resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1

MIG-mode scheduling uses the MIG resource name published by the device plugin, e.g. nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb — the exact resource names must be read from the live node (kubectl describe node shows advertised resources), not assumed.

Isolation model: - Namespace-level quota on nvidia.com/gpu. - PriorityClass for interactive inference vs batch. - Gang scheduling for multi-GPU jobs (Volcano/Kueue) — required to avoid partial allocation deadlock.

docs.title: 9.5 LLM serving platform
docs.text:
Engine Throughput Latency Batching Quantization VRAM need Ops complexity Offline Best fit vLLM High Good Continuous + chunked prefill AWQ/GPTQ/FP8/FP16 High (sharded across GPUs) Medium Yes Primary production serving llama.cpp Low-Med Low Basic GGUF (Q4/Q5/Q8/K-quants) Low Low Yes Edge, small models, CPU fallback Triton Medium-High Good Dynamic + model ensemble Per-backend Medium High Yes Multi-framework estate NIM High (pre-optimized) Good Vendor-managed Vendor-defined Medium-High Low (if license permits) Image must be mirrored Fast deploy, license permitting

Selection: vLLM primary. llama.cpp for small/quantized models and CPU fallback. Triton only if non-LLM model types enter the estate. NIM evaluated against license and offline artifact size.

Serving API: OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/models. Put an API gateway (NGINX + auth) in front; do not expose the vLLM port directly to the DMZ.

docs.title: 9.6 Multi-GPU inference
docs.text:
• Tensor parallelism: one model sharded across N GPUs. All N GPUs must be on the same node, connected by NVLink for acceptable performance; PCIe-only cross-socket works but with significant latency. Requires one pod requesting N GPUs.
  • Pipeline parallelism: layers split across GPUs; higher latency, better for very large models where tensor parallelism is memory-constrained.
  • Data parallelism / replicas: independent models on independent GPUs. Best throughput scaling, no inter-GPU communication.
  • Inter-node: RDMA/RoCE + InfiniBand required for acceptable cross-node model parallelism. Design the fabric accordingly or keep model-parallel workloads node-local.

Network requirement: for H100 SXM 8-GPU nodes with NVSwitch, intra-node is fine; cross-node model parallelism must be sized on measured fabric bandwidth, not on nominal line rate.

docs.title: 9.7 Model artifact distribution
docs.text: Concern Approach Storage Ceph RGW S3 (or MinIO) on the storage segment; models are large objects, not registry artifacts Mirroring Connected staging pulls from Hugging Face (or vendor CDN), records exact revision SHA, pushes to internal RGW Integrity SHA256 of each file recorded in gpu-models repo manifest; verify at load time Versioning Model = <org>/<model>:<revision-sha>; never "latest" Pull path Init container pulls from RGW, verifies checksum, populates a node-local NVMe cache (hostPath or local PV) Cache Per-node cache on NVMe; image-based distribution of weights is an alternative when the model is small or the fleet is uniform Auth Workload Identity to RGW (SigV4) with a per-team IAM-ish policy; credentials from Vault via External Secrets Licensing Some models carry usage licenses; record them in the model manifest and enforce approval before mirroring

docs.title: 9.8 GPU observability
docs.text:
Metric Source Utilization, memory, temp, power, ECC, PCIe errors DCGM exporter Driver/health, operator reconciliation GPU Operator metrics Container allocation, device plugin state device plugin metrics + kubelet state Inference throughput, req/s, tokens/s vLLM /metrics Time to first token, inter-token latency vLLM metrics Model load time, KV-cache usage vLLM metrics OOM events, restarts Kubernetes + DCGM

Dashboards: gpu-ai/monitoring/dashboards/. Alerts: OOM, ECC errors, sustained high temp, device plugin crash, low utilization with pending requests, KV-cache pressure.

docs.title: 9.9 AI security
docs.text:
• Model artifacts verified by checksum and stored in an access-controlled bucket; write-once.
  • Serving images scanned (Trivy), signed (Cosign), and pulled by digest.
  • API auth via OIDC tokens validated at the gateway; per-tenant quota and rate limits.
  • GPU access controlled by namespace quota and taint tolerance; no default access.
  • Audit: inference request metadata logged (model, tokens, tenant, latency), never prompt contents by default — add content logging only if a policy requires it, with explicit data-handling rules.
  • Network: inference API only reachable from the DMZ gateway and approved cluster networks; model store only from GPU nodes.

docs.title: NVIDIA driver, CUDA and GPU Operator compatibility
docs.text: Check date: 2026-10-17. Source: NVIDIA official documentation.

docs.title: Driver branch lifecycle
docs.text:
From https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/drivers/latest/driver-lifecycle.html:

Branch type Purpose Cadence Support length New Feature Branch (NFB) Early adopters, new CUDA APIs ~quarterly Not supported for production Production Branch (PB) Qualified for enterprise/data center GPUs Twice a year 1 year of bug and security updates Long Term Support Branch (LTSB) Production, longer cycle At least once per hardware architecture 3 years

docs.text:
From https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/drivers/latest/supported-drivers-and-cuda-toolkit-versions.html:

Note: R535 and R610 are at or past their EOL. For this platform the candidate branches are R580 (LTSB, to June 2028) and R595 (Production, to March 2027).
