docs.title: Minimum driver for MIG
docs.text:
From the NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide:

GPU CUDA version Minimum driver A100 / A30 CUDA 11 R525 (>= 525.53) or later H100 / H200 CUDA 12 R450 (>= 450.80.02) or later B200 CUDA 12 R570 (>= 570.133.20) or later RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell CUDA 12 R575 (>= 575.51.03) or later GB300 (DGX Station) CUDA 13 R595 (>= 595.58.03) or later

The MIG minimum is a floor, not a target. Use a current production or LTSB branch.

docs.title: Component matrix
docs.text: Component Version Source Status GPU Operator 26.7.2 https://github.com/NVIDIA/gpu-operator/releases VERIFIED k8s-device-plugin v0.20.1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/k8s-device-plugin/releases VERIFIED NVIDIA Container Toolkit v1.20.1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/nvidia-container-toolkit/releases VERIFIED Driver branch R580 or R595 NVIDIA driver matrix VERIFIED for the branch set, UNVERIFIED for the exact patch to deploy Driver patch 595.71.05 NVIDIA release notes VERIFIED as the latest listed release; not yet pinned CUDA toolkit (container) 13.x with R595, 12.x with R580 NVIDIA driver matrix VERIFIED for the branch mapping

docs.title: GPU Operator version pairing
docs.text:
The GPU Operator upgrades the driver, the container toolkit, the device plugin, and DCGM together. The driver and toolkit versions it ships must be compatible with each other.

Procedure before every operator upgrade: 1. Read the operator release notes for the target version and list the driver.version and toolkit.version it ships. 2. Confirm the toolkit release notes for that version state compatibility with the driver version. 3. Confirm the operator's supported Kubernetes versions cover the cluster version. 4. Mirror the new driver, toolkit, and operator images into Harbor before the upgrade. 5. Drain one GPU node first, upgrade it, verify nvidia-smi and a test pod, then continue.

docs.title: Kernel and driver coupling
docs.text:
The NVIDIA kernel module is built against the running kernel. A kernel update without a matching module makes the GPU invisible. On a managed node the GPU Operator rebuilds the module as part of the driver deployment, but the rebuild takes time and the node must be drained.

Rule: never upgrade the kernel on a GPU node without a planned drain, and never uncordon it before nvidia-smi returns a valid result.

docs.title: Offline artifacts
docs.text: Artifact Destination Notes NVIDIA driver runfile / RPM nexus.internal/rpm-nvidia Pin the exact patch version; keep the matching kernel-module package for each kernel version in the fleet CUDA toolkit container harbor.internal/platform/cuda Multi-GB; mirror per version NVIDIA Container Toolkit nexus.internal/rpm-nvidia + harbor.internal/platform/nvidia-container-toolkit The toolkit ships a container toolkit and a nvidia-ctk binary; the operator consumes the container GPU Operator chart harbor.internal/charts/gpu-operator Pin the chart version GPU Operator images harbor.internal/platform/gpu-operator driver, toolkit, device plugin, dcgm-exporter, k8s-device-plugin, and the operator itself DCGM Exporter harbor.internal/platform/dcgm-exporter Pin the version matching the operator release

docs.title: Validation after any driver change
docs.text:
# On the node
nvidia-smi                       # must list the expected GPUs
nvidia-smi -q | grep -i "driver version"
lsmod | grep nvidia

# In a pod
kubectl run gputest --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version> \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu":"true"},"containers":[{"name":"gputest","image":"harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version>","command":["nvidia-smi"],"resources":{"limits":{"nvidia.com/gpu":1}}}]}}' \
  -- nvidia-smi

Expected: nvidia-smi inside the pod lists the same GPU count as on the host, and the driver version matches the host driver version.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Dedicated NVIDIA GPU worker nodes for AI training and LLM inference: hardware preparation, driver installation, GPU Operator, scheduling, and day-2 operations.

docs.title: B. Hardware baseline
docs.text:
Component Requirement (H100 SXM) Requirement (H200 SXM) CPU 2x 24+ core, AVX-512 2x 24+ core, AVX-512 RAM 256 GB+ 512 GB+ Boot disk 2x 960 GB SSD (RAID1) 2x 960 GB SSD (RAID1) Data disk 2x 3.84 TB NVMe (model cache + runtime) 2x 3.84 TB NVMe GPU 4-8x H100 80GB SXM 4-8x H200 141GB SXM Interconnect NVSwitch intra-node, 8x 400Gb/s IB or 8x 200Gb/s RoCE inter-node Same NIC 2x 100 GbE 2x 100 GbE Power 2x 3.0 kW+ per node, PDU A/B Higher per GPU Cooling Direct liquid cooling for high-density SXM Same

BIOS settings that matter: - Above 4G decoding: enabled - IOMMU: enabled (needed for passthrough or isolation) - NUMA: one NUMA node per GPU (for H100/H200 SXM systems, 1 GPU per NUMA node is the vendor layout) - ACS enabled, if available, for IOMMU grouping - Resizable BAR: enabled - SR-IOV/IOMMU: enabled if virtualizing

Physical: confirm the GPU topology with nvidia-smi topo -m before scheduling anything. It determines which GPUs are NVLink-connected and therefore which multi-GPU topologies are usable.

docs.title: C. OS preparation
docs.text:
The GPU nodes use the same OS baseline as every other node (operating-systems/), plus:

# NVIDIA driver prerequisites
dnf install kernel-devel-$(uname -r) kernel-headers-$(uname -r) gcc make pciutils
# or on Ubuntu
apt install -y linux-headers-$(uname -r) build-essential pciutils

# Verify the kernel version matches the modules
uname -r
ls /lib/modules/

The NVIDIA kernel module must be built against the running kernel. A kernel update without a matching module build means the GPU is invisible until the driver is rebuilt or a prebuilt kmod is installed for that kernel.

docs.title: D. Driver installation
docs.text:
Path A — the GPU Operator (recommended): the operator manages the driver, the container toolkit, the device plugin, DCGM, and the operator's own monitoring, and can upgrade them together.

Path B — manual driver install (for troubleshooting or a driver the operator does not ship):

# NVIDIA driver (data center, production branch)
dnf install -y nvidia-driver:<branch>   # Oracle Linux
# or
apt install -y nvidia-driver-<branch>   # Ubuntu

nvidia-modprobe -u -c=0
nvidia-smi

The exact package name and branch for the pinned version must come from the NVIDIA official download page — record the check in gpu-ai/drivers/compatibility-matrix.md.

docs.title: E. NVIDIA Container Toolkit
docs.text:
# Install the toolkit from the internal repository
dnf install -y nvidia-container-toolkit   # or apt

# Configure containerd to use the NVIDIA runtime
nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=containerd --config=/etc/containerd/config.toml
systemctl restart containerd

Verify:

# Run a test container from the internal registry
ctr -n k8s.io run --rm --net-host \
  --with-nvidia-runtime \
  harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version> \
  nvidia-smi

docs.title: F. GPU Operator
docs.text:
Installed by Argo CD into the gpu-operator namespace.

# values.yaml (relevant)
driver:
  enabled: true
  version: "<pinned>"
  repository: harbor.internal/platform/nvidia
toolkit:
  enabled: true
  version: "<pinned>"
  repository: harbor.internal/platform/nvidia
devicePlugin:
  enabled: true
  version: "<pinned>"
  repository: harbor.internal/platform/nvidia
dcgmExporter:
  enabled: true
  version: "<pinned>"
  repository: harbor.internal/platform/nvidia
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: true
operator:
  env:
    USE_GPU_OPERATOR: "true"
    CLUSTER_TYPE: "kubernetes"
  initContainer:
    image: harbor.internal/platform/nvidia/cuda

The operator needs privileged DaemonSets and host mounts. It must be excluded from Pod Security Standards enforcement and from restrictive admission policies.

The operator's node selector targets the GPU pool:

nodeSelector:
  nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"

docs.title: G. Node labelling and scheduling
docs.text:
The operator adds nvidia.com/gpu.present=true automatically. Ansible adds the pool labels and the taint:

nodeLabels:
  node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu: "true"
  accelerator: nvidia
nodeTaints:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu
    value: "true"
    effect: NoSchedule

A workload requests a GPU through the extended resource name, which the device plugin publishes. For exclusive allocation:

resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1

For MIG, the published resource names are per MIG profile. Read them from the live node rather than assuming them:

kubectl describe node <gpu-node> | grep -A 40 "Allocatable"

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Node is ready and advertises GPUs
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu
kubectl describe node <gpu-node> | grep nvidia.com/gpu

# Device plugin is running
kubectl -n gpu-operator get pods | grep device-plugin

# A pod sees the GPU
kubectl run gputest --rm -it --image=harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version> \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu":"true"},"containers":[{"name":"gputest","image":"harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version>","command":["nvidia-smi"],"resources":{"limits":{"nvidia.com/gpu":1}}}]}}' -- nvidia-smi

docs.title: I. Day-2 operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Node drain for maintenance kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data — this stops the GPU pods; the operator's daemonsets stay Driver upgrade The operator upgrades the driver in place. GPU pods restart; use a drain first. Plan a window Kernel upgrade Requires a matching driver module. Drain, upgrade, rebuild the module, verify nvidia-smi before uncordoning Replace a failed GPU Replace the physical card, drain, rebuild the node, re-apply the operator, verify nvidia-smi MIG reconfigure Drain the node, run nvidia-mig-parted or the MIG manager to reconfigure, verify the new resource names Add GPUs to a node Power down, install, drain, reboot, verify topology with nvidia-smi topo -m

docs.title: J. Known traps
docs.text:
1. Kernel mismatch after an OS upgrade — the GPU disappears. Fix: rebuild the module or install the matching kmod before uncordoning the node.
  2. nvidia.com/gpu vs MIG resources — a workload requesting nvidia.com/gpu on a MIG-configured node will not schedule. Request the specific MIG resource.
  3. Operator upgrade restarts GPU pods — a driver upgrade is not zero-disruption. Use a drain plus a maintenance window.
  4. The container toolkit and the driver must match — a toolkit upgrade alone can break container GPU access.
  5. MIG reconfiguration requires the GPU to be idle — a running GPU pod blocks it.
  6. nvidia-smi topo -m shows PCIe-only for some GPU pairs — those GPUs are not usable for efficient model parallelism.

docs.title: K. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - GPU nodes in their own node pool with a taint, so general workloads cannot land there. - Node drain before any driver, kernel, or card change. - nvidia-smi verified after every driver or kernel change, before the node returns to service. - The exact driver, toolkit, CUDA, and operator versions pinned in gpu-ai/drivers/compatibility-matrix.md and mirrored offline.

Strongly recommended: - Model cache on local NVMe to avoid pulling weights on every pod start. - Health check on every inference pod that reports model load time and GPU memory. - Record the GPU topology in the asset register, not only in the node description. - A rolling node upgrade procedure, one GPU node at a time, with inference capacity headroom for the loss of one node.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Serving large language models on the GPU worker pool: engine selection, model distribution, multi-GPU configuration, API exposure, autoscaling, and observability.

docs.title: B. Engine selection
docs.text:
Criterion vLLM llama.cpp Triton NIM Throughput (large model) Highest Low High High (pre-optimized) Latency Low with continuous batching Low Good Low Batching Continuous + chunked prefill Basic Dynamic, multi-model Vendor-managed Quantization AWQ, GPTQ, FP8, FP16 GGUF (Q4/Q5/Q8, K-quants) Per-backend Vendor-defined VRAM need High Low Medium Medium-high Multi-GPU Tensor/pipeline parallel Layer split Ensemble Per deployment Ops complexity Medium Low High Low (if licensed) Offline Yes (weights + image) Yes Yes Yes if image mirrored and licence permits Best fit Production LLM serving Small models, CPU, edge Mixed model estate Fast deploy

Decision: vLLM primary. llama.cpp for small/quantized models and CPU fallback. Triton only if non-LLM model types enter the estate. NIM only after a licence review and an offline artifact size check.

docs.title: C. Model distribution
docs.text: Models are large S3 objects, not container images. They live in Ceph RGW (or MinIO) in the models/ bucket.

docs.title: Mirror procedure (connected staging)
docs.text:
# Record the exact revision, never "latest"
export HF_REPO=<org>/<model>
export HF_REV=<commit-sha>

huggingface-cli download "$HF_REPO" \
  --revision "$HF_REV" \
  --local-dir "./models/$(echo $HF_REPO | tr '/' '-')" \
  --include "*.safetensors" "*.json" "*.model" "*.txt"

# Checksums for verification at load time
find ./models -type f -exec sha256sum {} \; > model-checksums.txt

# Push to the internal object store
aws --endpoint-url https://rgw.internal s3 sync ./models s3://models/<org>/<model>/<rev>/

The manifest (model name, revision, files, checksums, licence, VRAM requirement, context length) is committed to the gpu-models GitLab project. Weights are not.

docs.title: Pull at runtime
docs.text:
An init container pulls and verifies:

initContainers:
  - name: fetch-model
    image: harbor.internal/platform/model-fetcher:<pinned>
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
      - |
        set -e
        aws --endpoint-url "$S3_ENDPOINT" s3 cp \
          "s3://models/$MODEL_PATH/config.json" /models/config.json
        # ... remaining files
        sha256sum -c /models/checksums.txt
    env:
      - name: MODEL_PATH
        value: "org/model/rev"
      - name: S3_ENDPOINT
        value: "https://rgw.internal"
    volumeMounts:
      - name: model-cache
        mountPath: /models
    envFrom:
      - secretRef:
          name: model-store-credentials   # from Vault via External Secrets

Alternative for a uniform fleet: bake the weights into a container image. Simple, but the image becomes several tens of gigabytes and every model change means a new image. Use the image path only for small models or a single-model fleet.

docs.title: Local NVMe cache
docs.text:
volumes:
  - name: model-cache
    hostPath:
      path: /mnt/models
      type: DirectoryOrCreate

Each node keeps a copy on local NVMe. A DaemonSet warms the cache before the inference pods start. The cache key is the model revision, so a rollout to a new revision pulls once per node.

docs.title: D. vLLM deployment
docs.text:
Single GPU:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: vllm-llama
  namespace: ai
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: vllm-llama}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: vllm-llama}
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu: "true"
      tolerations:
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Equal
          value: "true"
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: vllm
          image: harbor.internal/platform/vllm:<pinned>
          args:
            - "--model=/models/model"
            - "--served-model-name=llama"
            - "--port=8000"
            - "--tensor-parallel-size=1"
            - "--gpu-memory-utilization=0.90"
            - "--max-model-len=8192"
            - "--trust-remote-code=false"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
              memory: 120Gi
            requests:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
              memory: 60Gi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
            initialDelaySeconds: 120
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
            initialDelaySeconds: 300
            periodSeconds: 30
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: model-cache, mountPath: /models}
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: {name: model-store-credentials}
      volumes:
        - name: model-cache
          hostPath: {path: /mnt/models, type: DirectoryOrCreate}

Key parameters: - --gpu-memory-utilization — the fraction of VRAM vLLM may claim. Leave headroom for KV cache growth and for co-tenants. 0.90 is typical for a dedicated GPU. - --max-model-len — context length. Larger costs KV cache memory. Set it to the real requirement; an oversized value silently reduces concurrency. - --tensor-parallel-size — number of GPUs for one model replica. Must match nvidia.com/gpu: N. - --trust-remote-code=false — keep it off unless a specific model requires it, and review the model code when it is on.

docs.title: E. Multi-GPU inference
docs.text:
Two distinct things, often confused:

Model parallelism — one model spread across several GPUs. vLLM's --tensor-parallel-size N shards the weights and the attention heads across N GPUs inside a single pod. It requires N GPUs on the same node. A pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 4 with --tensor-parallel-size 4 does this.

Data parallelism — independent model replicas, each on its own GPU. This is just replicas: N with --tensor-parallel-size 1 and the scheduler spreading them across nodes. It scales throughput without any inter-GPU communication and is the preferred path unless a single model does not fit on one GPU.

What multi-GPU does NOT do: it does not create a single device with unified VRAM. A 4x H100 80GB setup with tensor parallelism gives 320 GB of aggregate memory for one model, and the model still must be sharded — the engines cooperate over NVLink, and each layer's activation still lives on its own GPU.

Cross-node model parallelism needs RDMA/RoCE. With plain TCP the all-reduce communication dominates and throughput collapses. Design the fabric accordingly or keep model-parallel workloads node-local.

docs.title: Memory sizing
docs.text:
weights_bytes ≈ params × bytes_per_param
KV_cache_bytes ≈ 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × dtype_bytes

Measure with vllm startup logs, which report the weight size and the KV cache blocks allocated. Use those numbers, not the formula, for capacity planning.

docs.title: F. API exposure
docs.text:
The inference port is never exposed directly. An API gateway handles authentication, rate limiting, and routing:

client -> NGINX (TLS, OIDC token validation, rate limit) -> vLLM service -> GPU nodes

upstream vllm_backend {
    least_conn;
    server vllm-llama.ai.svc.cluster.local:8000;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name llm.internal;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/tls.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/tls.key;

    location / {
        auth_request /oauth2_verify;
        limit_req zone=llm burst=20 nodelay;
        proxy_pass http://vllm_backend;
        proxy_read_timeout 600s;
        proxy_buffering off;
    }
}

Token validation with Keycloak:

location = /oauth2_verify {
    internal;
    proxy_pass https://keycloak.internal/realms/ai/protocol/openid-connect/token;
    proxy_pass_request_body off;
    proxy_set_header Content-Length "";
    proxy_set_header X-Original-URI $request_uri;
}

docs.title: G. Autoscaling
docs.text:
Signal Use Queue depth / pending requests Primary for LLM serving (KEDA on a queue metric) GPU KV-cache utilization Secondary — high utilization with pending requests means saturation Request latency (TTFT) Guardrail, not a scale-up signal on its own GPU utilization Misleading: a batched server can show high utilization and still be queueing

KEDA ScaledObject:

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: vllm-llama
  namespace: ai
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: vllm-llama
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 8
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
        metricName: vllm:num_requests_waiting
        threshold: "5"
        query: "sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{namespace='ai'})"

Cooldown must exceed the model load time. A scale-up that starts a pod which takes 5 minutes to load the model does not help a latency-sensitive request. Keep minReplicaCount at a level that covers the expected load, and scale out for bursts.

docs.title: H. Observability
docs.text:
vLLM exposes Prometheus metrics on /metrics. The important ones:

Metric Meaning Alert vllm:num_requests_waiting Queue depth Scale signal vllm:num_requests_running Concurrent requests Capacity vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc KV cache utilization Saturation vllm:request_success_total Counter Error rate vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds (histogram) End-to-end latency SLO vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds (histogram) TTFT SLO vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds (histogram) Inter-token latency SLO vllm:model_load_time_seconds Model load Slow load

TTFT and inter-token latency are the metrics a user feels. Track p95 and p99, not averages.

DCGM covers the hardware side: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED, DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_FREE, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP, DCGM_FI_DEV_POWER_USAGE, DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_XID_ERRORS, DCGM_FI_DEV_ECC_ERRORS.

docs.title: I. Benchmarking
docs.text:
# Throughput and latency
vllm bench serve \
  --backend vllm \
  --model llama \
  --dataset-name sharegpt \
  --dataset-path ./sharegpt.json \
  --host 10.50.0.11 --port 8000 \
  --num-prompts 200 \
  --save-result --result-dir ./results

# Reproducible run
vllm bench serve --backend vllm --model llama \
  --num-prompts 200 --seed 42 --save-result --result-dir ./results

Record: model, revision, quantization, GPU model and count, tensor-parallel size, batch settings, input/output length distribution, concurrency, and the resulting throughput, TTFT p50/p95/p99, and ITL p50/p95/p99. Without that metadata the result is not comparable.

Before and after any change (quantization, new engine, different GPU), re-run the same benchmark and compare. gpu-ai/inference/benchmarking.md holds the procedure and the result template.

docs.title: J. Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix OOM at startup Model plus KV cache plus runtime exceed VRAM Lower --gpu-memory-utilization, lower --max-model-len, use quantization, more GPUs OOM under load Concurrency exceeds KV cache capacity Lower --max-model-len, raise --gpu-memory-utilization carefully, or scale out Pod stays Pending No GPU capacity, or the resource name does not match (MIG) kubectl describe pod; check advertised resources on the node Container starts, nvidia-smi fails Toolkit/runtime mismatch or a missing device plugin kubectl -n gpu-operator logs; re-run nvidia-ctk runtime configure Model load timeout Weights not cached, pulling from object storage at start Pre-warm the node-local cache TTFT spikes Cold cache, no prefix caching, or GPU contention Enable prefix caching, check co-tenancy, verify the model is on local NVMe High ITL GPU saturated, or a slow tokenization path Scale out, or check the CPU contention on the node

docs.title: K. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Serve by digest, from a signed image. - Never expose the inference port directly to the DMZ. - Request the exact advertised resource (including MIG profiles). - Keep inference pods off nodes with other GPU tenants unless isolation is intentional.

Strongly recommended: - Keep minReplicaCount high enough for the steady-state load, and use autoscaling for bursts only. - Cache models on local NVMe. - Record every benchmark with full metadata. - Test the OOM behaviour deliberately before production: know what happens when a tenant exceeds its MIG profile.

docs.title: GPU monitoring
docs.text:
GPU metrics come from DCGM Exporter, scraped by the platform Prometheus and rendered in Grafana. This is the observability layer for the GPU estate; the scheduling model is in gpu-ai/scheduling/index.md.

Design context: gpu-ai/gpu-ai-architecture.md §9.5 and the monitoring summary.

docs.title: Data path
docs.text:
GPU node (DCGM Exporter :9400) -> Prometheus (scrape) -> Grafana / Alertmanager

DCGM Exporter is deployed by the GPU Operator as a DaemonSet on GPU nodes. It is not a per-application exporter: one instance per node serves every GPU on that node.

docs.title: Versions and ports
docs.text: Item Value Source DCGM Exporter 4.8.4 compatibility/version-matrix.md GPU Operator 26.7.2 compatibility/version-matrix.md Scrape port TCP 9400 network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md row 43

docs.title: Metrics that matter
docs.text: Signal Use Utilization Idle GPUs are the most expensive waste in the estate Framebuffer memory used Distinguishes real capacity pressure from transient spikes Temperature and power Thermal throttling shows up here before it shows up as latency ECC errors (correctable and uncorrectable) Uncorrectable errors mean the device must be drained PCIe replay and link errors Host or riser fault, not a GPU fault XID errors Driver-level faults; map the XID code to the NVIDIA table before acting

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
• GPU OOM events (container killed with an OOM reason on a GPU node).
  • Uncorrectable ECC error — page the on-call; drain the node.
  • Sustained temperature above the vendor throttle threshold.
  • Device plugin crash or DCGM Exporter down on a GPU node.
  • GPU allocated but utilization near zero for a sustained window (waste, and often a stuck job).
  • Pods pending with a GPU request while GPUs are free (scheduling defect, not capacity).

Thresholds are site values. Record them with the alert rules so a change is a reviewed diff, not a UI edit.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
Store dashboard JSON in gpu-ai/monitoring/dashboards/ and provision them from Git (Grafana provisioning or the Grafana Operator). A dashboard edited in the UI is lost on rebuild.

Minimum set: 1. Fleet view — GPUs per node, utilization, memory, temperature. 2. Node detail — per-device metrics, XID and ECC counters. 3. Workload view — GPU requests vs allocation, pending GPU pods, namespace quota usage.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl -n gpu-operator get pods -l app=nvidia-dcgm-exporter
curl -s http://<gpu-node>:9400/metrics | grep -c '^DCGM_FI_'
kubectl -n monitoring get servicemonitor | grep -i dcgm

A scrape target that is up but returns zero DCGM_FI_* series means the exporter is running without device access — check the driver container, not Prometheus.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Effect Recovery DCGM Exporter down No GPU metrics or alerts from that node; workloads unaffected Restart the DaemonSet pod; check driver container Prometheus scrape misconfigured Metrics missing fleet-wide Fix the ServiceMonitor; the exporter is still serving on :9400 Alert threshold drift Real incidents do not page, or noise hides them Keep thresholds in Git with the rules Dashboard edited in UI Change lost on rebuild Re-apply from dashboards/

docs.title: GPU scheduling
docs.text:
GPU nodes are dedicated, tainted, and labelled so that only GPU workloads land on them. The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs the driver, container toolkit, device plugin, and DCGM exporter; scheduling then depends on the resource the device plugin advertises.

Design context: gpu-ai/gpu-ai-architecture.md §9.4.

docs.title: Node preparation
docs.text:
Applied by Ansible to every GPU node:

nodeLabels:
  nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"
  nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.k8s.io/operator: "true"
  nvidia.com/gpu.product: "H100-80GB-HBM3"   # exact value from `nvidia-smi -L` + operator discovery
nodeTaints:
  - key: nvidia.com/gpu
    value: "true"
    effect: NoSchedule

The product label must be read from the node, not assumed: the device plugin publishes the model string it discovers.

docs.title: Workload request
docs.text:
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1

A pod that requests a GPU but tolerates no taint stays Pending. That is the intended failure: it makes a missing toleration visible instead of silently scheduling onto a GPU node.

docs.title: Isolation model
docs.text:
Mechanism Use Namespace quota on nvidia.com/gpu Caps each team's total devices PriorityClass Interactive inference above batch Gang scheduling (Volcano or Kueue) Multi-GPU jobs; without it, partial allocation can deadlock MIG Hardware partitioning on supported GPUs only; resource names come from the live node Time-slicing Oversubscription, no VRAM isolation — one tenant can OOM another

MIG resource names are not portable across GPU models or profiles. Read them from kubectl describe node and record them per cluster; do not copy a name from another site.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
Component Pin Source NVIDIA GPU Operator 26.7.2 compatibility/version-matrix.md DCGM Exporter 4.8.4 compatibility/version-matrix.md

The GPU Operator version determines the driver and DCGM versions it deploys. Changing it is a node-level change with a drain.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -l nvidia.com/gpu.present=true
kubectl describe node <gpu-node> | grep -A5 "Allocatable"     # nvidia.com/gpu: N
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator
kubectl run gpu-test --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=<internal-registry>/cuda-vectoradd --limits=nvidia.com/gpu=1

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Effect Recovery Device plugin not running Node advertises no GPU; GPU pods stay Pending Restart the operator pod on that node; check the driver container logs Driver mismatch after node upgrade Device plugin crash-loops Pin the driver to the operator release; re-run the GPU role Taint removed by drift Non-GPU pods consume GPU nodes Re-apply labels and taints from the gpu Ansible role MIG configuration changed Advertised resource names change; existing requests no longer match Drain, reconfigure, and update workload requests

docs.title: MIG and GPU sharing
docs.text: Check date: 2026-10-17. Profile data from the NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide (https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/latest/supported-mig-profiles.html).

docs.title: The three sharing mechanisms are not equivalent
docs.text:
Property MPS Time-slicing MIG Partition type Logical Logical Physical Max partitions 48 Unlimited 7 Performance isolation No No Yes, by percentage (not partitioning) Memory protection No No Yes Memory bandwidth QoS No No Yes Error isolation No No Yes Cross-partition interop Always (IPC) IPC Limited IPC Reconfigure Dynamic On process launch When the GPU is idle

The load-bearing line: time-slicing provides no memory protection and no memory bandwidth QoS. One tenant's memory pressure can OOM another tenant's process inside the same GPU, and a tenant saturating the memory bandwidth degrades the other tenant. MPS is worse in one respect: it is a single process address space, so a fault in one tenant can affect the others.

MIG is the only mechanism that delivers hardware-level memory isolation. That is why it is the production choice in this platform (ADR-0022).

docs.title: Supported GPUs
docs.text:
From the NVIDIA MIG User Guide supported-GPUs table:

Product Architecture Compute capability Memory Max instances H100-SXM5 Hopper 9.0 80 GB 7 H100-PCIE Hopper 9.0 80 GB 7 H100-SXM5 Hopper 9.0 94 GB 7 H100-PCIE Hopper 9.0 94 GB 7 H100 on GH200 Hopper 9.0 96 GB 7 H200-SXM5 Hopper 9.0 141 GB 7 H200 NVL Hopper 9.0 141 GB 7 A100-SXM4 Ampere 8.0 40 GB / 80 GB 7 A100-PCIE Ampere 8.0 40 GB / 80 GB 7 A30 Ampere 8.0 24 GB 4 B200 Blackwell 10.0 180 GB 7 GB200 Blackwell 10.0 186 GB 7

MIG starts at the Ampere generation (compute capability 8.0+). Consumer GPUs do not support MIG.

docs.title: What MIG does and does not give
docs.text:
Gives: - Hard memory isolation: an instance cannot address memory outside its slice. - Memory bandwidth QoS: each slice has its own memory controllers and DRAM paths. - Fault isolation: a hang in one instance does not take down the others. - A schedulable resource per instance, published by the device plugin.

Does not give: - Shared VRAM between instances. Two MIG instances cannot be combined into one larger device. - More total memory than the physical GPU. - Zero reconfiguration cost. Reconfiguration requires the GPU to be idle.

docs.title: Multi-GPU is not unified memory
docs.text:
Multiple physical GPUs on a node are separate devices. They are connected by NVLink or PCIe, and used in one of two ways:

  • Model parallelism — one model sharded across the GPUs (vLLM --tensor-parallel-size N). Requires N GPUs in one pod, on one node, with the GPUs NVLink-connected for acceptable performance.
  • Independent replicas — each GPU runs its own copy of the model. This is replicas: N with --tensor-parallel-size 1.

There is no configuration where two H100s behave as one 160 GB device. Total aggregate VRAM is available to a sharded model, but the model is split layer by layer and the engines communicate over NVLink; VRAM is not pooled.

docs.title: Kubernetes resource names
docs.text:
The device plugin publishes one resource per MIG profile. The exact names are published per node and must be read from the live node, not assumed:

kubectl describe node <gpu-node> | sed -n '/Allocatable/,/^Events/p'

Typical shape: nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb, nvidia.com/mig-2g.20gb, nvidia.com/mig-3g.40gb, nvidia.com/mig-4g.40gb, nvidia.com/mig-7g.80gb for H100 80GB. The +me (media extension) profiles are published separately, for example nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb+me.

Requesting the plain nvidia.com/gpu resource on a MIG-configured node will not schedule: on a MIG-mode GPU the device plugin no longer advertises a whole-GPU resource. This is a common and confusing failure.

docs.title: MIG configuration procedure
docs.text:
# On the node (GPU must be idle)
nvidia-smi -q | grep -i "MIG Mode"
# Current: Disabled -> enable
sudo nvidia-mig-mode -m 1

# Apply a profile
sudo nvidia-mig-parted -i 0 -m 1g.10gb

# Verify
nvidia-smi -L
nvidia-smi mig -lgip

The GPU Operator manages MIG configuration declaratively:

# gpu-operator values
mig:
  enabled: true
  strategy: mixed
  # or a single profile for all GPUs

strategy: mixed lets the device plugin expose multiple profile sizes on the same GPU, which is more flexible but makes the node's advertised resource set harder to reason about. single gives one profile size per GPU, which is simpler to schedule against. For production multi-tenancy, one profile size per GPU is easier to operate.

docs.title: Reconfiguration
docs.text:
MIG reconfiguration requires the GPU to be idle — no processes, no clients. In Kubernetes that means draining the node and evicting every GPU pod:

kubectl drain <gpu-node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
# reconfigure
kubectl uncordon <gpu-node>

An in-place reconfiguration of a live profile (for example 1g.20gb to 1g.10gb) also requires the GPU to be idle.

docs.title: Scheduling with MIG
docs.text:
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1

Combined with a per-tenant namespace quota:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: gpu-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: "4"
    limits.nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: "4"

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
# The node advertises the MIG resources
kubectl get node <gpu-node> -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep nvidia

# A pod gets exactly its slice
kubectl run migtest --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version> \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"nodeSelector":{"node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu":"true"},"containers":[{"name":"migtest","image":"harbor.internal/platform/cuda:<version>","command":["nvidia-smi","-L"],"resources":{"limits":{"nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb":1}}}]}}' \
  -- nvidia-smi -L

Hard-isolation test (mandatory acceptance test G-02): in a 1g.10gb instance, allocate more than 10 GB. The allocation must fail with an out-of-memory error, and the co-tenant instance must remain unaffected and continue serving.

docs.title: Identity integration
docs.text:
Decision (ADR-0015): integrate identity at the application layer. Linux nodes are not joined to a directory.

No SSSD, realmd, Kerberos membership or samba-style join on any host. Nodes keep local administrative accounts plus one offline break-glass credential. Nothing in the host baseline depends on the directory being reachable.

docs.title: Why not on the hosts
docs.text:
Reason Consequence of joining Recovery independence An unreachable domain controller blocks sudo or login exactly when you need it Blast radius One directory change affects every node, including the ones running Ceph and etcd It buys nothing for workloads Kubernetes authorization comes from the API server's OIDC/LDAP integration, not from host membership UID/GID mapping AD UIDs can collide with local ones and change ownership on Ceph OSD directories Audit Per-service audit logs are richer than a shared host login record

The cost is explicit: account lifecycle is per service. Removing a person means revoking them in every integration below, not disabling one host account.

docs.title: Targets and protocols
docs.text:
Service Integration Protocol Group → role mapping Rancher AD or LDAP auth provider LDAPS 636 / StartTLS 389 Rancher global role per group Keycloak User federation against AD/LDAP LDAPS 636 Realm roles, group→role mapper Harbor OIDC (via Keycloak) HTTPS 443 Project role per group GitLab LDAP (or OIDC via Keycloak) LDAPS 636 / HTTPS Group sync, role per group Argo CD OIDC (via Keycloak) HTTPS 443 RBAC policy per group claim Vault OIDC (via Keycloak) or LDAP auth HTTPS 443 / LDAPS 636 Vault policy per group Kubernetes API OIDC (via Keycloak) HTTPS 443 RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding per group

Keycloak is the broker. Prefer OIDC from every service to Keycloak and one federation from Keycloak to the directory: one place to change the directory endpoint, one place to see failed logins, and services that only speak OIDC stay simple.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Break-glass first. Confirm a local account with sudo and an offline SSH key works on every node. Test it with the directory link down. Without this, the rest is a lockout waiting to happen.
  2. Keycloak realm and federation. Set the LDAP/AD user federation, import groups, and create the realm roles. Test with a real federated user before wiring anything else.
  3. Keycloak clients. One OIDC client per service, with an explicit redirect URI and a group claim mapper. No wildcard redirects.
  4. Service by service, in this order: Argo CD (so the manifests for the rest are under GitOps), Rancher, Harbor, GitLab, Vault, then the Kubernetes API server.
  5. Remove the local superuser path from each service only after the federated path is verified for a normal user and for an administrator.

docs.title: Rancher
docs.text:
# Rancher UI: Users & Authentication -> Auth Provider -> Active Directory / OpenLDAP
# Server: ldaps://dc.internal:636
# Service account: a read-only bind account, not a domain admin
# User search base / group search base: scope them to the platform OU
# Group schema: name + DN, then map groups to global roles

Verify: log in as a federated user, confirm the role comes from the group, then confirm the local admin account still works. Rancher keeps a local admin regardless of the provider state — leave it, with its password in Vault, and record who may use it.

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text:
# Federation (UI: User Federation -> ldap), or declarative:
kcadm.sh create components -r platform -s name=corp-ad -s provider=ldap \
  -s 'config.vendor=ad' -s 'config.connectionUrl=ldaps://dc.internal:636' \
  -s 'config.usersDn=OU=Platform,DC=corp,DC=internal' \
  -s 'config.bindDn=CN=svc-keycloak,OU=Service,DC=corp,DC=internal' \
  -s 'config.bindCredential=@/run/secrets/kc-bind' \
  -s 'config.editMode=READ_ONLY' -s 'config.usernameLDAPAttribute=sAMAccountName' \
  -s 'config.uuidLDAPAttribute=objectGUID' -s 'config.groupObjectClasses=group'

Rules:

  • editMode=READ_ONLY. The directory is the source of truth; Keycloak never writes back.
  • Bind credential comes from Vault, never from a values file in Git.
  • A local realm with two emergency accounts, credentials offline, separate from the federated realm. A directory outage must not lock out the platform administrators.
  • Group membership drives roles. Do not hand-assign roles to federated users.

docs.title: The rest
docs.text:
Service Configuration point Verification Harbor Administration → Authentication → OIDC, client id/secret from Vault, "automatic onboarding" off, group admin mapping A federated user lands in the group's project with the expected role GitLab omniauth/ldap block in gitlab.rb, group sync enabled A group member sees the project and cannot see another group's Argo CD oidc.config + policy.csv with g, <group>, role:readonly-style rules A federated read-only user cannot sync Vault auth/oidc role bound to a group claim + policy Token issued with exactly the expected policy set Kubernetes --oidc-issuer-url, --oidc-client-id, --oidc-groups-claim on the API server kubectl auth can-i --list as a federated user matches the RoleBinding

The Kubernetes API server flags are set in the Kubespray group vars (kube_apiserver_oidc_*), so a change goes through the inventory, not through a live edit.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text:
Failure Effect Recovery Directory unreachable New UI logins fail; running workloads continue; node SSH unaffected Local break-glass account, then fix the link Keycloak unavailable Every OIDC service rejects new sessions; existing tokens last until expiry Restore Keycloak from backup; local service admin accounts are the interim path Group renamed in the directory Roles silently disappear or widen, depending on the mapping Alert on login failures by group; keep mappings in Git and review on directory changes Bind account password rotated Federation stops with an authentication error in Keycloak logs Rotation procedure updates the Vault path and the Keycloak component together

Alert on: failed federated logins per service, a bind failure, and a drop to zero successful logins during working hours — the last one catches a broken mapping before the ticket arrives.

docs.title: What replaces the old host-level procedure
docs.text: identity/sssd-realmd.md was removed. If a cluster genuinely needs host-level directory login (a regulatory requirement, or a shared jump host), implement it as an explicit per-cluster exception with SSSD, and record it in an ADR addendum. It is not part of the baseline and the site does not generate it.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Two operating models, both supported, with a documented migration path between them.

Model Description When to use Standalone Local accounts, local sudo, SSH keys Small sites, isolated labs, break-glass only Directory-integrated SSSD against AD or LDAP, local break-glass retained Production

Both models keep a local emergency account on every node. Directory integration never removes it.

docs.title: B. Package differences
docs.text:
Oracle Linux Ubuntu SSSD dnf install sssd sssd-tools apt install sssd sssd-ad sssd-tools realmd dnf install realmd apt install realmd Kerberos krb5-user (krb5-workstation on OL) krb5-user AD provider sssd-ad (part of the AD DC package on OL) sssd-ad Config /etc/sssd/sssd.conf same Cache /var/lib/sss/db/ same Services sssd, sssd-be, sssd-kcm same

Ubuntu splits the AD support into sssd-ad; on Oracle Linux it is usually in the base sssd package. Verify with dnf provides / apt-cache search on the target release.

docs.title: C. Standalone model
docs.text:
# Create a group and user
groupadd -r sre
useradd -m -G sse -s /bin/bash sre-user

# Sudo
echo "%sre ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" > /etc/sudoers.d/90-sre
visudo -c /etc/sudoers.d/90-sre
chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-sre

# SSH key
install -d -m 0700 -o sre-user -g sre-user /home/sre-user/.ssh
install -m 0600 -o sre-user -g sre-user authorized_keys /home/sre-user/.ssh/

Account lifecycle is managed by Ansible from Git. The password is never stored; the account is key-only.

docs.title: Realmd join (AD)
docs.text:
dnf install -y realmd
realmd discover
realm join --user=join-account EXAMPLE.COM

realm join requires DNS SRV records for the domain controller to be resolvable. In an offline environment, verify the SRV lookups work before attempting the join:

dig SRV _ldap._tcp.example.com
dig SRV _kerberos._tcp.example.com

If the SRV records are not resolvable, the join fails with a DNS error. Fix DNS first.

docs.title: SSSD configuration (AD)
docs.text:
# /etc/sssd/sssd.conf
[sssd]
services = nss, pam, sshd
domains = EXAMPLE.COM
cache_credentials = true
entry_cache_timeout = 3600
# 8h = 8 hours of offline login before the password cache is exhausted
offline_credentials_expiration = 8h
re-enable_logins = true

[domain/EXAMPLE.COM]
ad_domain = example.com
id_provider = ad
auth_provider = ad
ldap_schema_extensions = idns
access_provider = ad
subdomains = ALL
# Required for nested groups and for the AD "SSH" tab
ldap_id_mapping = schema_only
use_fully_qualified_names_for_forever = true
enumerate = false

# /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (LDAP provider alternative)
[domain/example.com]
id_provider = ldap
auth_provider = ldap
ldap_uri = ldaps://ldap1.example.com ldaps://ldap2.example.com
ldap_search_base = dc=example,dc=com
ldap_id_attrs = uid
ldap_uuid_attribute = entryUUID

Key settings and their consequences:

Setting Effect Risk if wrong cache_credentials = true Passwords cached for offline login A revoked AD account can still log in until the cache expires offline_credentials_expiration How long the cache works offline Too long extends the revocation window enumerate = false Avoids a full domain enumeration at start getent passwd will not list domain users; use id <user> instead ldap_id_mapping = schema_only Uses the AD schema for SID mapping Required for POSIX groups from AD use_fully_qualified_names_for_forever = true user@domain form works permanently Without it, some lookups fail after a change

docs.title: UID/GID mapping
docs.text:
AD assigns a SID; Linux needs a UID/GID. With ldap_schema_extensions = idns and ldap_id_mapping = schema_only, SSSD derives the UID from the SID via the AD schema, so the mapping is stable and reversible.

Collision risk: a local account with UID 1000 and an AD user mapping to UID 1000 will produce the wrong home directory. SSSD's default range starts at 100000, so the risk is low unless local accounts are created with high UIDs. Keep local accounts below 1000 and the emergency account at a fixed low UID.

docs.title: SSH integration
docs.text:
dnf install -y openssh-server
# SSSD provides the sshd integration module
systemctl restart sshd

With services = nss, pam, sshd, SSSD answers AuthorizedKeysCommand for domain users. Public keys come from the AD user's attributes, so the key distribution is in the directory.

docs.title: Sudo with domain groups
docs.text:
# /etc/sudoers.d/90-domain-sre
%sre-admins@example.com ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL

Test the group resolution before relying on it:

getent group sre-admins
id sre-user@example.com
sudo -l -U sre-user@example.com

A missing group in sssd.conf is the usual cause of "the user can log in but has no privileges".

docs.title: E. Break-glass
docs.text:
On every node, regardless of the model:

useradd -m -s /bin/bash -u 999 emergency
passwd -l emergency                       # key only
install -d -m 0700 /home/emergency/.ssh
# key installed from the offline escrow
usermod -aG wheel emergency                # OL
usermod -aG sudo emergency                 # Ubuntu

The emergency SSH key is stored on offline media and in the Vault. It is not in Git. The account must be able to log in with the directory down, which means its key must be in authorized_keys and not depend on SSSD.

Test it: stop SSSD (systemctl stop sssd) and log in as emergency.

docs.title: F. Directory outage behaviour
docs.text:
Situation Effect DC unreachable, cached credentials exist Login continues for up to offline_credentials_expiration DC unreachable, no cache Login fails; emergency account still works SSSD service down Same as DC unreachable AD account disabled in AD The cached password may still work until the cache expires Group membership changed in AD SSSD picks it up within entry_cache_timeout; running sessions are unaffected

The revocation window is the security trade-off of offline login. It is a deliberate, documented decision, and the cache timeout must be set deliberately rather than left at the default.

docs.title: G. Migration path
docs.text:
Standalone -> directory-integrated: 1. Create the AD users/groups. 2. Set enumerate = false, join the host. 3. Create local ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for the emergency account before joining. 4. Run sssctl user-checks <user> to verify the identity path. 5. Test sudo group resolution. 6. Remove the standalone local accounts (keep emergency).

Directory-integrated -> standalone (reversal, rare): 1. Create the local accounts from the AD export. 2. Move /home if the UIDs differ, or keep the homes and accept the UID change with chown -R. 3. Disable the sssd service. 4. Keep the break-glass account throughout.

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Identity resolution
getent passwd sre-user@example.com
getent group sre-admins
id sre-user@example.com

# SSSD health
sssctl domain-list
sssctl user-checks sre-user@example.com
sssctl auth-check sre-user@example.com

# Offline login simulation
systemctl stop sssd
# attempt login with a cached credential; then restart sssd
systemctl start sssd

# Break-glass
sudo -u emergency sudo -n true

docs.title: I. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - The emergency account exists on every node, key-only, tested with the directory down. - SSSD cache TTLs set deliberately, not left at default. - Domain sudo groups verified with sudo -l -U before use. - UID ranges kept disjoint between local and domain accounts.

Strongly recommended: - enumerate = false to avoid a slow full-domain enumeration at boot. - Service accounts for automation with their own scoped keys, not personal accounts. - Central group management in AD, not per-host sudoers edits. Per-host sudoers edits are drift. - Monitor the SSSD service and the SSSD cache directory; a stale cache looks like a healthy system.

docs.title: Cluster Acceptance Tests
docs.text: This document defines the cluster acceptance tests for Kubernetes deployment validation. Each test section corresponds to a critical cluster component that must be verified before a deployment is considered production-ready.

docs.title: Control-plane Health
docs.text: Ensure the control-plane components are healthy and responsive.

docs.title: API Server
docs.text:
• SLI: curl -k https://<apiserver>:6443/healthz returns ok
  • Command: curl -k https://<apiserver>:6443/healthz
  • Reference: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md § Validation

docs.title: Controller Manager
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=controller-manager
  • Command: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=controller-manager --field-selector=status=Running
  • Expected: All controller-manager pods Running

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=scheduler
  • Command: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=scheduler --field-selector=status=Running
  • Expected: All scheduler pods Running

Cross-references: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md, decisions/ADR-0002-*

docs.title: etcd Quorum
docs.text: Ensure the etcd cluster has healthy quorum and all members are reachable.

docs.title: etcd Member Health
docs.text:
• SLI: etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
  • Command: kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key endpoint health --cluster
  • Expected: All members report healthy
  • Reference: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md § Validation

docs.title: etcd Member List
docs.text:
• SLI: etcdctl member list
  • Command: kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key member list
  • Expected: Member count matches control-plane node count
  • Reference: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md § Validation

docs.title: etcd Snapshot
docs.text:
• SLI: etcdctl snapshot status <latest>
  • Command: kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot status <latest>
  • Expected: Snapshot is valid and accessible
  • Reference: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md § Backup

Cross-references: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md

docs.title: Node Readiness
docs.text: Ensure all nodes report Ready status and have correct resource state.

docs.title: Node Status
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl get nodes
  • Command: kubectl get nodes --ignore-not-found
  • Expected: All nodes Ready status
  • Reference: kubernetes/node-lifecycle.md

docs.title: Node Resource Availability
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl describe nodes <node-name> | grep -E 'Conditions|Memory|CPU'
  • Command: for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name); do kubectl describe $node | grep -E 'Conditions:|Allocated resources'; done
  • Expected: All nodes have Condition=True for Ready
  • Reference: kubernetes/node-lifecycle.md

docs.title: Node Label Compliance
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
  • Command: kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane --no-headers | wc -l
  • Expected: Control-plane nodes labeled correctly
  • Reference: kubernetes/control-plane/index.md § Topology

Cross-references: kubernetes/node-lifecycle.md, kubernetes/control-plane/index.md

docs.title: Network Connectivity
docs.text: Ensure pod networking, service resolution, and cross-node traffic flow.

docs.title: DNS Resolution
docs.text:
• SLI: dig +short <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local
  • Command: kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --rm -i --rm=forever --overrides='{"spec': {"namespace": "default"}}' --command -- dig +short kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
  • Expected: Correct IP resolves
  • Reference: kubernetes/networking/cilium.md § Cilium CNI

docs.title: Service-to-Service Connectivity
docs.text:
• SLI: kubectl run nettest --image=networktools --restart=Never --rm -i --rm=forever -- <command>
  • Command: kubectl run nettest --image=busybox --restart=Never --rm=forever --rm=forever --overrides='{"spec": {"network": "cluster"}}' -- nslookup <svc>
  • Expected: Services resolve and connect
  • Reference: kubernetes/networking/cilium.md

docs.title: Cross-Node Pod Traffic
docs.text:
• SLI: Pod A → pod B on different node
  • Command: kubectl run traffic-test --image=busybox --restart=Never --rm -i --rm=forever --rm=forever --overrides='{"spec": {"nodeSelector": {"kubernetes.io/hostname": "<node-b>"}}}' -- ping <pod-cid>
  • Expected: Cross-node pod traffic flows
  • Reference: kubernetes/networking/cilium.md

docs.title: MTU Verification
docs.text:
• SLI: ping -M do -s 1472 <peer> from each node
  • Command: for node in $(kubectl get nodes -o name | cut -d'/' -f2); do ping -M do -s 1472 $node; done
  • Expected: No fragmentation, DF bit set
  • Reference: kubernetes/networking/cilium.md § MTU verification

docs.title: NetworkPolicy Enforcement
docs.text:
• SLI: Deny-all policy + allowed exception
  • Command: Apply deny-all NetworkPolicy, then test allowed/denied flows
  • Expected: Denied flows fail, allowed flows succeed
  • Reference: kubernetes/networking/network-policy-examples.md

Cross-references: kubernetes/networking/cilium.md, kubernetes/networking/network-policy-examples.md, network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md

docs.title: Test Summary
docs.text:
Test Area Key Metric Threshold Control-plane Health API server healthz ok etcd Quorum Member health All healthy Node Readiness Node Ready status All True Network Connectivity DNS resolution Correct IP

Note: These acceptance tests must be executed against a running Kubernetes cluster. Run the procedures documented in each section and record evidence in tests/acceptance/<test-id>/ per the acceptance test framework.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document admission policy implementation: OPA Gatekeeper constraints, Kyverno policies, validation failure actions.

Cross-references security/pod-security-standards.md, kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §Admission control.

docs.title: B. OPA Gatekeeper
docs.text:
OPA Gatekeeper enforces policies via ConstraintTemplates and Constraints:

# Constraint template for required labels
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredlabels
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredLabels
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.io
      rego: |
        package k8srequiredlabels

        violation[{"msg": msg, "details": {}}] {
          label := input.review.object.metadata.labels[required_label]
          not label
          msg := sprintf("You must set a %v label", [required_label])
        }

---
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: require-app-label
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
  parameters:
    required_label: app
    message: "Pods must have an app label"

docs.title: C. Kyverno
docs.text:
Kyverno policies are Kubernetes-native:

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: require-run-as-non-root
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must run as non-root"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - (securityContext):
                  runAsNonRoot: true

docs.title: D. Validation failure actions
docs.text: Action Behavior Enforce Block the request Warn Allow the request, emit warning Audit Allow the request, record audit event

docs.title: E. Cross-references
docs.text:
• security/pod-security-standards.md — Pod Security Standards
  • kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §Admission control — Admission control overview
  • kubernetes/control-plane/index.md — Control plane

docs.title: Multiple application clusters
docs.text: One management cluster, several application clusters. Each application cluster has its own control plane, its own pod and service CIDRs, its own Ceph (or none), and its own Argo CD registration. What they share is the management plane, the registry and the identity provider.

docs.title: When more than one
docs.text:
Reason Split by Failure domain Site A / Site B, separate power and network Environment Production / staging / development Tenant or regulation A cluster per regulated workload, separate audit scope Kubernetes version A cluster pinned to the previous minor while it drains

Do not split because a namespace feels crowded. Namespaces, quotas and NetworkPolicies handle that without a second control plane.

docs.title: What must differ per cluster
docs.text:
Setting Why it must be unique clusterName It is the kubectl context, the DNS suffix (cluster.local stays, but the name is the identity) Pod CIDR Overlapping pod CIDRs cannot be routed between clusters Service CIDR Same reason; overlapping services break cross-cluster DNS API VIP One VIP per control plane Ceph cluster Two Ceph clusters may share hardware only with separate MONs and CRUSH roots Argo CD registration One Secret or cluster entry per cluster, named by cluster

What may be shared: the registry, the NTP and DNS servers, the identity provider, the edge load balancer (different VIPs or SNI hosts), the backup target.

docs.title: How the configurator models it
docs.text:
The Application cluster page configures the first cluster fully. Each extra cluster is added with the + Add application cluster button, which appends a card holding that cluster's name, pod and service CIDRs, node counts and node sizing. Every card is independent; Remove deletes it. The first card starts with non-overlapping CIDRs derived from the main cluster (10.32.0.0/16 and 10.33.0.0/16 by default), and the numbers are editable.

From those cards the site generates:

  • additional-clusters.yaml — one record per cluster with name, counts and CIDRs;
  • argocd-cluster-secrets.yaml — one Argo CD cluster Secret per entry, labelled argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster, with the API server placeholder to fill from that cluster's admin.conf;
  • the runbook lists the repeat procedure: run deploy.sh again with CLUSTER=<name> and that cluster's nodes.tsv.

The first cluster remains the default context. Every extra cluster needs its own inventory, its own k8s-cluster.yml (different CIDRs) and its own nodes.tsv.

docs.title: Order of work
docs.text:
1. Build cluster A completely and register it in Argo CD.
  2. Build cluster B with its own CIDRs and its own inventory; do not copy cluster A's k8s-cluster.yml and edit the name — the CIDRs come with it.
  3. Register B in Argo CD with its own Secret.
  4. Create one ApplicationSet per cluster (or one Application per cluster) so a bad sync in B cannot roll out to A.
  5. Verify cross-cluster DNS only if you actually need it. Otherwise keep the clusters independent; cross-cluster service discovery is a product decision, not a default.

docs.title: Failure isolation rules
docs.text:
• No shared etcd. Ever.
  • No shared Ceph MON quorum between clusters that must survive independently.
  • The management cluster must not depend on any application cluster for DNS, registry or identity.
  • Backups go to a target that survives the loss of the cluster, and the restore is tested per cluster, not once for all of them.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document node lifecycle procedures for Kubernetes clusters managed by Kubespray: add worker, add control-plane, remove worker, replace worker, reset node, drain/cordon.

Cross-references kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §Node lifecycle, kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §Inventory, lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md §Node upgrade sequence.

docs.title: B. Node types
docs.text: Type Groups Purpose Control-plane [control-plane], [etcd] API server, scheduler, controller-manager, stacked etcd Worker [k8s-node] Application pods GPU worker [k8s-node], [gpu-node] GPU-accelerated workloads

docs.title: 1. Add to inventory
docs.text:
[k8s-node]
k8s-w-3 ansible_host=10.20.0.23 ip=10.20.0.23

docs.title: 2. Add OS and container runtime
docs.text: The node must have: - OS installed from internal mirror (Oracle Linux or Ubuntu) - containerd 2.3.7 installed from internal repository - SSH access for the Ansible user - NTP/synchronized time

docs.title: 3. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes k8s-w-3
kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-w-3

docs.title: 1. Add to inventory
docs.text:
[control-plane]
k8s-cp-4 ansible_host=10.20.0.14 ip=10.20.0.14

[etcd]
k8s-cp-4

docs.title: 2. Add OS and container runtime
docs.text: Same requirements as worker, plus etcd data directory storage (local SSD/NVMe).

docs.title: 3. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-4

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes k8s-cp-4
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-cp-4
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-4 -- etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

One control-plane node at a time — never add all control-plane nodes simultaneously during a rebuild.

docs.title: 1. Drain the node
docs.text: kubectl drain k8s-w-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

docs.title: 2. Remove from inventory
docs.text: Remove the node from [k8s-node] in inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini.

docs.title: 3. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

docs.title: 4. Verify
docs.text: kubectl get nodes | grep k8s-w-3  # Should return nothing

docs.title: F. Replace worker
docs.text:
Replace = drain + remove + rebuild + re-add:

  1. Drain: kubectl drain k8s-w-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  2. Remove from inventory
  3. Rebuild the host (Terraform + Ansible, or manual reinstall)
  4. Re-add to inventory with same or new name
  5. Run Kubespray: cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3
  6. Verify: node is Ready

docs.title: G. Reset a node
docs.text:
Use Kubespray's reset.yml playbook:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini reset.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

Warning: reset.yml removes Kubernetes from the node. Only use on nodes that will be rebuilt or decommissioned. Never run rm -rf /etc/kubernetes manually — use reset.yml instead.

After reset, the node can be re-added with cluster.yml.

docs.title: Cordon (mark unschedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl cordon k8s-w-3

Use before maintenance or when a node is unhealthy.

docs.title: Uncordon (mark schedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl uncordon k8s-w-3

Use after maintenance is complete and the node is healthy.

docs.title: I. Node failure scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Procedure Node temporarily offline Cordon, investigate, uncordon when fixed Node permanently lost Remove from inventory, replace with new node Control-plane node lost (1 of 3) API available through remaining nodes; rebuild and rejoin Control-plane node lost (2 of 3) etcd loses quorum; restore from snapshot before adding new node etcd disk failure Replace disk, restore etcd from snapshot, rejoin node

docs.text:
• kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §I — Node lifecycle
  • kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §D — Inventory grouping rules
  • lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md §E — Node upgrade sequence
