docs.title: Node resource reservation
docs.text:
A Kubernetes node is not only for pods. The kubelet, the container runtime, the CNI agent, the CSI node plugin, the log shipper and the monitoring agent all run on the same CPU and memory. If none of it is reserved, a busy workload can evict the kubelet's own dependencies and take the node down with it.

Reservation has three parts:

Part Flag What it protects System reserved --system-reserved OS daemons, udev, sshd, the container runtime Kube reserved --kube-reserved kubelet, CNI, CSI node plugin, device plugins Eviction thresholds --eviction-hard The point where the kubelet starts killing pods instead of the node

docs.title: Values the configurator sets
docs.text:
Value Default Meaning reservedSystemCpu 500m CPU kept for the OS and its daemons reservedSystemMem 1Gi RAM kept for the OS and its daemons reservedKubeCpu 500m CPU kept for kubelet, CNI, CSI node plugin reservedKubeMem 1Gi RAM kept for kubelet, CNI, CSI node plugin evictionHardMem 100Mi Free memory below which the kubelet evicts pods evictionHardNodefs 10% Free node filesystem below which pods are evicted

Sizing rule: reserve 10% of CPU and 15% of RAM on a worker; on a control-plane node reserve 1 vCPU and 2 GiB. The numbers above are a floor for an 8 vCPU / 32 GiB node, not a universal answer.

docs.title: How it reaches the node
docs.text:
Kubespray writes kubelet flags from kubelet_custom_flags. The generated k8s-cluster.yml carries:

kubelet_custom_flags:
  - "--system-reserved=cpu={{value.reservedSystemCpu}},memory={{value.reservedSystemMem}}"
  - "--kube-reserved=cpu={{value.reservedKubeCpu}},memory={{value.reservedKubeMem}}"
  - "--eviction-hard=memory.available<{{value.evictionHardMem}},nodefs.available<{{value.evictionHardNodefs}}"

Verify on the node, not in the playbook output:

kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/<node>/proxy/configz" | python3 -m json.tool | grep -A5 -i reserved
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A6 "Allocated resources"

Allocatable must be lower than Capacity. If the two are equal, the reservation did not apply and the kubelet silently kept its defaults.

docs.title: What not to do
docs.text:
• Do not reserve more than 20% of a node. The scheduler then reports capacity the cluster does not have and pods stay Pending while the node looks empty.
  • Do not set --kube-reserved without a matching --kube-reserved-cgroup unless the cgroup exists; the kubelet logs a warning and continues without enforcing it.
  • Do not rely on eviction thresholds instead of requests and limits. Eviction is the last resort, not the capacity plan.

docs.title: GPU nodes
docs.text: A GPU node carries the device plugin, the driver container and the DCGM exporter. Reserve one extra CPU and 2 GiB on top of the numbers above; nvidia.com/gpu is not compressible and cannot be overcommitted, so CPU pressure is what actually breaks a GPU node.

docs.title: Windows worker nodes
docs.text: Kubespray can join Windows Server nodes to a Linux control plane. The support is real but narrower than Linux: the CNI, the storage and the workload model all change.

docs.title: What works, what does not
docs.text:
Capability Windows worker Note Calico CNI Yes The supported path. BGP or VXLAN, Windows nodes in their own block Cilium CNI Partial Requires Cilium with the Windows daemon set and strict tunnel mode; not the default here HostProcess containers Yes The Windows equivalent of a privileged pod CSI: Ceph RBD No RBD maps a Linux kernel device; Windows has no ceph-csi node plugin CSI: SMB / Azure Files Yes Only if the storage backend provides an SMB CSI driver GPU (DirectX / CUDA) Yes, separately Needs the NVIDIA Windows driver and the Windows GPU device plugin Linux-only workloads No A Deployment with a Linux image will not schedule on Windows

Consequence for this platform: a Windows node pool is for .NET Framework, IIS and Windows containers. Stateful workloads that need Ceph stay on Linux.

docs.title: Enabling it in the configurator
docs.text:
The Application cluster page has a Windows node group: count, vCPU, RAM, disk. When the count is above zero:

  • the inventory gains a [windows] group and adds it to [k8s-cluster:children];
  • the sizing table gains a Windows row;
  • the generated windows-vars.yaml sets the Kubernetes version, the CNI and the container runtime for the group;
  • the runbook adds the Windows prerequisites step.

Calico is required when Windows nodes exist. If Cilium is selected, the runbook warns and the generated vars keep kube_network_plugin: calico for the Windows group — a mixed CNI cluster is not a supported configuration.

docs.title: Prerequisites on each Windows node
docs.text:
1. Windows Server 2022 (or 2019 with the current cumulative update).
  2. The Containers feature and the container runtime (containerd 1.7+ or the Mirantis runtime that matches the Kubespray release).
  3. WinRM over HTTPS, or SSH, reachable from the Ansible host.
  4. The node in the same L2/L3 path as the Linux nodes for the CNI overlay; no NAT between them.
  5. The internal registry reachable and the CA installed in the Windows certificate store.
  6. nssm or a native service wrapper so the kubelet and kube-proxy survive a reboot.

Kubespray's Windows playbook expects ansible_connection: winrm, ansible_winrm_transport: ntlm (or certificate), and an account in the local Administrators group.

docs.title: Version alignment
docs.text: The Windows node must run the same Kubernetes minor version as the control plane. Kubespray installs kubernetesVersion from the release it is pinned to; do not let a Windows node lag a minor behind. The generated windows-vars.yaml pins kube_version so a mixed cluster cannot drift.

docs.title: End-user cluster access
docs.text: How a developer or operator connects to the cluster from their own machine, on Linux or Windows. This is the hand-over document: the platform team produces one kubeconfig per user or per group, the user installs two tools and runs one command.

docs.title: What the user needs
docs.text:
Tool Why Linux Windows kubectl The API client Package or a single binary from dl.k8s.io winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl, or the binary kubelogin OIDC token refresh (exec plugin in the kubeconfig) kubelogin from the Azure/kubelogin releases winget install -e --id Azure.kubelogin helm (optional) Only if the user deploys charts Package or binary winget install -e --id Helm.Helm

Do not hand a user a kubeconfig that embeds a client certificate with cluster-admin rights. The platform issues short-lived OIDC tokens; the kubeconfig only names the issuer and the client id.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
# kubectl, pinned to the cluster minor version
curl -fsSLO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/{{version.kubernetes}}/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
install -m 0755 kubectl ~/.local/bin/kubectl

# kubeconfig from the platform team, then merge, never overwrite
mkdir -p ~/.kube
cp ~/Downloads/{{value.clusterName}}-{{value.env}}.yaml ~/.kube/config.d/{{value.clusterName}}.yaml
chmod 600 ~/.kube/config.d/{{value.clusterName}}.yaml
export KUBECONFIG="$HOME/.kube/config:$HOME/.kube/config.d/{{value.clusterName}}.yaml"

kubectl config use-context {{value.clusterName}}
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl get nodes

If KUBECONFIG is set, kubectl config view shows the merged result. Merging is additive; copying a new file over ~/.kube/config deletes every other cluster the user had.

docs.title: Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
winget install -e --id Kubernetes.kubectl
winget install -e --id Azure.kubelogin

# kubeconfig
$dir = "$env:USERPROFILE\.kube"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$dir\config.d" | Out-Null
Copy-Item "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\{{value.clusterName}}-{{value.env}}.yaml" "$dir\config.d\{{value.clusterName}}.yaml"
$env:KUBECONFIG = "$dir\config;$dir\config.d\{{value.clusterName}}.yaml"

kubectl config use-context {{value.clusterName}}
kubectl auth whoami

kubelogin must be on PATH. If the kubeconfig's exec command is kubelogin and PowerShell cannot find it, the error is executable kubelogin not found — reopen the terminal after winget install, then check Get-Command kubelogin.

docs.title: OIDC login
docs.text:
The kubeconfig contains an exec block, not a token:

users:
  - name: {{value.clusterName}}-oidc
    user:
      exec:
        apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1
        command: kubelogin
        args: ["get-token", "--login", "devicecode", "--issuer-url", "{{value.keycloakHost}}/realms/platform", "--client-id", "kubectl", "--scopes", "openid,groups"]

The first command opens a browser and a device code. The token is cached under ~/.kube/cache/oidc-login/; it is refreshed silently until the refresh token expires. A revoked user fails at the next refresh, not at the next command — that is the delay to explain to the user.

docs.title: Service account token, when a human is not in the loop
docs.text:
For CI and automation, do not copy a kubeconfig with a user's identity. Create a service account and request a short-lived token:

kubectl -n {{value.appNamespace}} create serviceaccount ci-deploy
kubectl -n {{value.appNamespace}} create rolebinding ci-deploy \
  --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount={{value.appNamespace}}:ci-deploy

# Short-lived token (1 hour), returned as JSON, never stored in Git
kubectl -n {{value.appNamespace}} create token ci-deploy --duration=1h

The token is a bearer credential. Put it in the CI secret store, never in a repository, never in a shell history. For a long-lived integration, create a Secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token only when the platform explicitly allows it — bound tokens are the default for a reason.

docs.title: Export and import a token
docs.text:
# Export on the machine that has cluster-admin
kubectl -n {{value.appNamespace}} create token ci-deploy --duration=24h > /tmp/ci-token.json
scp /tmp/ci-token.json user@workstation:~/ci-token.json
shred -u /tmp/ci-token.json

# Import on the workstation
TOKEN=$(python3 -c 'import json,sys;print(json.load(open("ci-token.json"))["status"]["token"])')
kubectl --server="https://{{value.apiServerIp}}:6443" \
  --certificate-authority="$HOME/.kube/ca.crt" \
  --token="$TOKEN" get nodes

--certificate-authority needs the cluster CA. Export it from the admin machine: kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d > ca.crt.

docs.title: Verify and troubleshoot
docs.text:
Symptom Cause Fix x509: certificate signed by unknown authority The internal CA is not in the kubeconfig or the OS trust store Use certificate-authority-data in the kubeconfig; install the CA in the OS store Unauthorized Token expired or the user was removed from the group Re-run the login; check the group claim in Keycloak executable kubelogin not found Plugin not on PATH Install it, reopen the terminal, Get-Command kubelogin connection refused on the API VIP The user is outside adminCidr or the edge does not forward 6443 Check the network matrix; use the VPN Forbidden on one namespace RBAC, not authentication kubectl auth can-i --list -n <namespace>

The generated user-access.md fills this document with the plan's cluster name, API address and issuer URL. The repository remains the authority for the procedure.

docs.title: Kubernetes Add-ons
docs.text: Optional add-ons deployed on top of the Kubespray cluster. Each add-on is installed via Helm chart from the internal Helm repository, with values air-gapped to internal registries.

docs.title: Add-ons in this platform
docs.text: Add-on Chart Purpose cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager Certificate issuance and management (Let's Encrypt, internal CA, Vault PKI) External DNS kubernetes-sigs/external-dns DNS records for Services and Ingresses Descheduler kubernetes-sigs/descheduler Evict pods to rebalance the cluster VPA kubernetes/autoscaler Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations Metrics Server kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server Resource metrics for HPA and VPA Trivy Operator aquasecurity/trivy-operator Vulnerability and config scans as CRDs OpenTelemetry Operator open-telemetry/opentelemetry-operator Collector, instrumentation, traces

docs.title: Symptom: Add-on pod CrashLoopBackOff
docs.text:
Likely cause: Image not mirrored to the internal registry, or values point to docker.io / quay.io instead of the internal registry.

Fix: Update image.repository in the Helm values to registry.internal:5000/<image>, then helm upgrade --install.

Self-check: kubectl get pods -n <addon-ns> shows all pods Running.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — add-on install and image mirroring only. Add add-on lifecycle, upgrades, and multi-environment promotion when those patterns are used.

docs.title: cert-manager
docs.text:
cert-manager provisions and renews TLS certificates for ingress and service workloads only. Kubernetes internal PKI (API server, kubelet, front-proxy, etcd) is owned by Kubespray and is out of scope for cert-manager.

Two issuance paths exist:

  • Public ACME (Let's Encrypt): requires outbound internet connectivity and a reachable ACME challenge endpoint (HTTP-01 or DNS-01). Optional, not a dependency, and unsuitable for air-gapped clusters.
  • Internal CA / Vault PKI: the air-gapped path. Vault PKI provides CA signing; cert-manager requests and renews leaf certificates. See secrets-management/pki/index.md for the full PKI workflow, and kubernetes/ingress/nginx-ingress.md for the internal-ca ClusterIssuer example.

Responsibility boundary:

Component Responsibility Vault PKI Provides internal CA/intermediate signing capability; CA key never stored in Git cert-manager Requests and renews leaf certificates; writes TLS Secrets Platform Distributes internal CA trust to workloads and clients

docs.title: Symptom: Certificate stuck in Pending
docs.text:
Likely cause: Issuer not ready, or ACME challenge not reachable (public ACME path only).

Fix: 

kubectl get certificate -A
kubectl get issuer,clusterissuer -A
kubectl describe certificate <name> -n <ns>

Self-check: kubectl get certificate <name> -n <ns> shows READY: True.

docs.title: Symptom: cert-manager webhook cannot start
docs.text:
Likely cause: cert-manager webhook needs a certificate from itself (chicken-and-egg on first install).

Fix: Install cert-manager with --set installCRDs=true first, then apply issuers, then enable the webhook. Or use the Helm chart which handles ordering.

docs.title: Air-gapped deployment notes
docs.text:
• Use the internal CA/Vault PKI path; public ACME is not usable without internet connectivity.
  • Mirror the cert-manager Helm chart and images to the internal registry (registry.internal:5000/...).
  • Install CRDs before issuers; cert-manager writes certificates into Kubernetes Secrets automatically.

See secrets-management/pki/index.md for the complete root CA, intermediate CA, and cert-manager ClusterIssuer bootstrap order. The internal-ca ClusterIssuer example is in kubernetes/ingress/nginx-ingress.md.

docs.title: Descheduler
docs.text: Descheduler evicts pods so the cluster can rebalance (e.g. after new nodes join or when node utilization is uneven).

docs.title: Symptom: Pods not evicted despite uneven utilization
docs.text:
Likely cause: Descheduler not running, or the eviction policy does not match the imbalance.

Fix: 

kubectl get descheduler -A
kubectl describe descheduler -n <ns>
kubectl get events -n <ns> | grep -i descheduler

Self-check: Run in DryRun: true mode first and confirm events list evictions without actually evicting.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — Descheduler install and dry-run verification. Add production eviction, profile selection, and scheduling integration when those patterns are used.

docs.title: External DNS
docs.text: External DNS publishes DNS records for Services and Ingresses to the internal DNS server. It is a cluster-scoped component that reads Kubernetes resources and writes to the DNS control plane. Kubernetes RBAC and DNS-provider authorization are separate concerns: RBAC governs what ExternalDNS may read from the API server; DNS credentials govern what it may write to the DNS server.

docs.title: RBAC and permissions
docs.text:
ExternalDNS runs with cluster-scoped RBAC by default (rbac.create: true). It requires Kubernetes read/list/watch permissions on Ingress, Service, and (optionally) HTTPRoute resources for each enabled source. Gateway API (HTTPRoute) permissions are required only when the Gateway API source is enabled; do not add them otherwise.

The chart supports namespace-scoped operation (namespaced: true), which creates Role/RoleBinding instead of ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding. Namespace-scoped mode limits ExternalDNS to resources in one namespace and avoids cluster-scoped RBAC for Gateway sources. Choose cluster-wide mode when ExternalDNS manages records across multiple namespaces; choose namespace-scoped when a single application team owns a dedicated namespace.

docs.title: RFC2136 configuration (air-gapped)
docs.text:
In an air-gapped site the only supported providers are RFC2136 against the internal DNS or the CoreDNS etcd provider. Public providers (Route 53, Cloudflare, etc.) require internet connectivity and are not usable offline.

provider:
  name: rfc2136
env:
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_HOST
    value: "10.10.0.53"
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_PORT
    value: "53"
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_ZONE
    value: "internal.example.com."
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_TSIG_KEYNAME
    value: "externaldns-key"
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_TSIG_SECRET_ALG
    value: "hmac-sha256"
  - name: EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_TSIG_SECRET
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: externaldns-tsig-secret
        key: tsig-secret
domainFilters: ["internal.example.com"]
policy: upsert-only
registry: txt
txtOwnerId: "{{clusterName}}"
  • EXTERNAL_DNS_RFC2136_TSIG_SECRET is sensitive and must never appear in Git or Helm values. It is injected only through the verified env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef structure above, referencing a Kubernetes Secret produced by External Secrets Operator from Vault KV v2.
  • Host, port, zone, key name, and algorithm are non-sensitive configuration and may remain as plain value entries.
  • The chart exposes env as a standard Kubernetes environment-variable list. envFrom and extraEnv are not supported by chart 1.23.0.

docs.title: Secret delivery (Vault KV → ExternalSecret → K8s Secret)
docs.text:
Store the TSIG secret in Vault KV v2, then use External Secrets Operator to sync it into a Kubernetes Secret referenced by secretKeyRef. See secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md for the ClusterSecretStore and ExternalSecret patterns. The Vault secret path is distinct from Vault PKI certificate issuance; do not confuse KV credentials with PKI intermediates.

Chart version: external-dns 1.23.0 (application v0.23.0). See compatibility/version-matrix.md.

docs.title: Air-gap deployment
docs.text:
• Mirror the external-dns Helm chart and container image to registry.internal:5000/....
  • At runtime, ExternalDNS must reach the RFC2136 DNS server (e.g. 10.10.0.53) over TCP/UDP port 53. An internet-isolated cluster is not the same as a DNS control plane that is unreachable: Kubernetes can be air-gapped while the internal DNS remains reachable.
  • Mirror chart and images per offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md.

docs.title: DNS safety and production behavior
docs.text:
• domainFilters restricts ExternalDNS to the zones it may touch. A missing or over-broad filter lets ExternalDNS create or delete records outside its intended scope.
  • registry: txt uses TXT ownership records. txtOwnerId must be unique per cluster; two clusters sharing an owner ID delete each other's records.
  • Start with policy: upsert-only. ExternalDNS creates and updates records but never deletes. Run for at least one week before switching.
  • policy: sync adds deletion. It requires --rfc2136-axfr (zone transfer) on the ExternalDNS command, and the DNS server must authorize AXFR from ExternalDNS Pod addresses using the TSIG identity. Without AXFR, sync behaves like create-only and never deletes stale records.
  • A wrong zone or missing domainFilters can delete records ExternalDNS does not own. Validate in upsert-only first.

docs.title: Secret rotation
docs.text: TSIG secret rotation follows: Vault KV update → ESO refresh (on refreshInterval) → Kubernetes Secret update → ExternalDNS Deployment rollout restart. Environment variables are read at process start; they do not update inside an already-running ExternalDNS process. After the K8s Secret changes, trigger kubectl rollout restart deployment externaldns -n <ns> (or the namespace ExternalDNS runs in).

docs.title: Monitoring and troubleshooting
docs.text:
• kubectl get deployment external-dns -n <namespace> — verify the ExternalDNS Deployment exists and is available.
  • kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=external-dns -n <namespace> — inspect ExternalDNS pods.
  • kubectl describe deployment external-dns -n <namespace> — inspect Deployment events and configuration.
  • kubectl logs -n <namespace> -l app.kubernetes.io/name=external-dns --tail=100 — inspect record creation failures.
  • nslookup <service>.<zone> from inside the cluster — confirm the record resolves.
  • The metrics endpoint is on port 7979; do not invent metric names.

docs.title: Related documentation
docs.text:
• Secret delivery: secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md
  • Version pins: compatibility/version-matrix.md
  • Air-gap artifacts: offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md

docs.title: Metrics Server
docs.text: Metrics Server provides resource metrics (CPU/memory) for HPA and VPA.

docs.title: Symptom: HPA cannot scale (no metrics)
docs.text:
Likely cause: Metrics Server not deployed, or kubelet is not exposing the metrics endpoint.

Fix: 

kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -A

Self-check: kubectl top nodes returns metrics for all nodes.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — Metrics Server install and basic verification. Add HPA integration, custom metrics, and resource quotas when those patterns are used.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry Operator
docs.text: OpenTelemetry Operator deploys the OTel Collector for traces, metrics, and logs.

docs.title: Symptom: No traces exported
docs.text:
Likely cause: Collector not deployed, or the exporter endpoint is unreachable.

Fix: 

kubectl get opentelemetrycollector -A
kubectl logs -n opentelemetry -l app.kubernetes.io/component=collector --tail=100

Self-check: The OTel Collector pod is Running and traces appear in the backend (Tempo/Jaeger).

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — OTel Operator install and collector health. Add instrumentation auto-injection, trace sampling, and log routing when those patterns are used.

docs.title: Trivy Operator
docs.text: Trivy Operator runs vulnerability and configuration scans as Kubernetes CRDs.

docs.title: Symptom: No vulnerability reports
docs.text:
Likely cause: Trivy Operator cannot reach the Trivy DB, or the image is not mirrored.

Fix: 

kubectl get trivyoperator -A
kubectl get vulnerabilityreport -A
kubectl logs -n trivy-operator -l app.kubernetes.io/name=trivy-operator --tail=100

Self-check: kubectl get vulnerabilityreport -A returns reports for scanned images.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — Trivy Operator install and report verification. Add air-gapped DB mirror, automated remediation, and admission control integration when those patterns are used.

docs.title: VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler)
docs.text: VPA recommends or applies CPU/memory requests based on observed usage.

docs.title: Symptom: VPA recommendations not shown
docs.text:
Likely cause: VPA not deployed, or the target Deployment has no resource requests set.

Fix: 

kubectl get vpa -A
kubectl describe vpa <name> -n <ns>

Self-check: kubectl describe vpa <name> shows recommendation with CPU/memory values.

Ponytail: Scope ceiling — VPA install and recommendation verification. Add Auto mode (with pod restarts), HPA coexistence, and exclusion rules when those patterns are used.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the high-availability Kubernetes deployment architecture for production platforms: multi-control-plane setup, etcd quorum, API server load balancing, worker node patterns, and HA validation procedures.

Cross-references: kubernetes/control-plane/ha-topology.md, architecture/03-failure-domains.md, infrastructure-provisioning-docs/terraform-iks.md, and site/cluster-status.md.

docs.title: B.1. Multi-control-plane setup
docs.text:
Configuration Control-plane nodes etcd placement Failure tolerance Recommended use 3-node 3 Stacked on each CP node 1 node Development, small production 5-node 5 Stacked on each CP node 2 nodes Reference production topology

Both configurations use stacked etcd — etcd members run on the same nodes as kube-apiserver. This is the Kubespray default and the simplest operational model.

Rule: A node in the [control-plane] inventory group with stacked etcd must also be listed in the [etcd] group. Never list a host in both [control-plane] and [k8s-node].

docs.title: B.2. Node placement and failure domains
docs.text:
Control-plane nodes must be spread across independent failure domains:

  • 3-node: 3 separate failure domains (e.g., 3 availability zones, 3 racks, or 3 physical sites)
  • 5-node: 5 separate failure domains, or 3 zones with 2+2+1 distribution

Control-plane nodes must not run application workloads. Taints are applied to prevent scheduling, and a NoSchedule taint is enforced via admission controller.

docs.title: B.3. etcd quorum and failure scenarios
docs.text:
Failure Effect etcd quorum Recovery 1 CP node lost (3-node) API available through remaining 2 members Intact (2/3) Rebuild node, rejoin with cluster.yml --limit <host> 1 CP node lost (5-node) API available through remaining 4 members Intact (4/5) Rebuild node, rejoin with cluster.yml --limit <host> 2 CP nodes lost (3-node) etcd loses quorum, all API writes stop Lost (1/3) Restore quorum from etcd snapshot 2 CP nodes lost (5-node) etcd quorum intact at 3 members Intact (3/5) Rebuild nodes one at a time Slow etcd disk API latency rises, leader elections flap Intact Replace disk; etcd is not tunable around bad hardware

Never restart all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes API server quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: C.1. Front-end load balancer
docs.text:
API server access is fronted by a load balancer (MetalLB, HAProxy, or cloud external LB) in the management subnet:

                    +-------------------+
                    | External LB /     |
                    | MetalLB speaker   |
                    | (VIP: 10.20.0.10) |
                    +-------------------+
                              |
        +---------------------+---------------------+
        |                     |                     |
+-------+-----------------+---------+   +-------+-----------+--------+--------+
| CP node 1 |         CP node 2      |   | CP node 3 |       CP node 4  | CP node 5 |
| kube-apiserver |            |  | kube-apiserver |  | kube-apiserver | kube-apiserver |
| stacked etcd  |            |  | stacked etcd  |  | stacked etcd  | stacked etcd  |
+-----------+--------------+  +-----------+  +-------+-----------+--------+--------+

The load balancer health-checks the API server port (6443/TCP) on each control-plane node and removes failed nodes from the pool.

docs.title: C.2. Load balancer configuration
docs.text:
• Protocol: TCP port 6443 for API server, TCP port 2379-2380 for etcd peer communication (if exposed)
  • Health check: TCP connect to 6443, optionally /readyz endpoint
  • Session persistence: None required (API server is stateless between requests)
  • Algorithm: Round-robin or least-connections
  • Timeouts: Health check timeout 10s, connection drain 30s

docs.title: C.3. DNS and VIP
docs.text:
• Virtual IP (VIP) configured on the load balancer
  • DNS kubernetes.<cluster-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local → VIP
  • Split-horizon DNS for internal/external access
  • TLS termination at the load balancer; re-encrypt to API server

docs.title: D.1. Node categories
docs.text: Node type Purpose Taints Autoscaling General workers Application workloads None HPA, KHA GPU workers AI/ML workloads nvidia.com/gpu role Device plugin + HPA Infrastructure workers Platform add-ons, no app pods node-role.kubernetes.io/infra:NoSchedule Manual Edge workers Perimeter workloads node-role.kubernetes.io/edge:NoSchedule Manual

docs.title: D.2. Node taint topology
docs.text:
# Control-plane taint (prevents workload scheduling)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  name: k8s-cp-1
spec:
  taints:
  - key: "CriticalAddonsOnly"
    effect: "NoSchedule"

docs.title: D.3. Worker node sizing
docs.text:
• Minimum 2 worker nodes per availability zone
  • Node labels for topology spread constraints
  • kubernetes.io/hostname and beta.kubernetes.io/arch labels set automatically

docs.title: E.1. Pre-deployment validation
docs.text:
# Verify control-plane node connectivity
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane

# Verify etcd cluster health
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# Verify etcd member list matches inventory
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  member list

# Verify API server readiness
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

# Verify load balancer health
<check-lb-health.sh>

docs.title: E.2. Post-deployment validation
docs.text:
# All control-plane nodes Ready and Ready status
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane -o wide

# All control-plane pods running
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=control-plane

# API server availability through LB
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://<VIP>:6443/readyz

# etcd quorum verification
etcdctl member list \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  -w table

# Pod scheduling on control-plane nodes (should be zero)
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.unschedulable}'

# Network policy connectivity test
kubectl run test-net --rm -i --restart=Never --image=busybox -- /bin/sh -c "curl -s http://<service>:<port>"

docs.title: E.3. HA failure scenario testing
docs.text: Scenario Expected outcome Validation 1 CP node power loss API continues through remaining nodes kubectl get nodes shows 2/3 or 4/5 CP nodes Ready 1 CP node network partition API failover to healthy nodes Load balancer removes partitioned node etcd member loss (1 of 3) Cluster continues with reduced quorum etcdctl member list shows remaining members healthy etcd member loss (2 of 5) Cluster continues with 3/5 quorum etcdctl endpoint health all healthy Load balancer node failure API failover to remaining CP nodes curl to VIP returns 200 from remaining node

docs.title: E.4. Upgrade validation order
docs.text:
1. Upgrade one control-plane node with cluster.yml --limit <host>
  2. Verify node is Ready and etcd member is healthy
  3. Verify API server availability through load balancer
  4. Repeat for remaining control-plane nodes
  5. Verify worker nodes still schedule pods
  6. Run full HA validation suite (Section E.2)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Kubernetes clusters rely on X.509 certificates for mutual TLS authentication between components. This document covers the complete certificate lifecycle: issuance, renewal, rotation, and emergency procedures.

docs.title: Root CA Rotation
docs.text:
1. Generate new root key and CSR 

    openssl genrsa -out new-root-ca.key 4096
openssl req -new -key new-root-ca.key -out new-root-ca.csr \
  -subj "/CN=kubernetes-root-CA"

  2. Sign intermediate CA (if used) 

    openssl x509 -req -in new-root-ca.csr -CA existing-intermediate-ca.pem \
  -CAkey existing-intermediate-ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out new-intermediate-ca.pem -days 3650

  3. Distribute new CA bundle to all nodes

  4. Update ConfigMaps containing CA certificates
  5. Rotate kubelet client certificates signed by new CA
  6. Rotate etcd peer and client certificates
  7. Rotate front-proxy certificates

  8. Rotate service account signing keys

  9. Validate cluster health after rotation 

    kubectl cluster-info --kubeconfig=kubeconfig-with-new-ca

docs.title: Intermediate CA Rotation
docs.text: Follow the same process as root CA rotation, but maintain the root CA trust anchor.

docs.title: Automatic Renewal (recommended)
docs.text:
Kubelet can automatically rotate its serving certificate via the --rotate-certificates flag (default: true in kubeadm-managed clusters).

# kubelet configuration snippet
kubeconfig: /etc/kubernetes/kubeconfig
clientcafile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
autoRotateCertificates: true

docs.title: Manual Renewal
docs.text:
1. Check certificate expiration 

    openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubernetes/kubelet-client-current.pem -text -noout | grep -A2 "Validity"

  2. Generate new kubelet client certificate 

    openssl genrsa -out kubelet-client.key 2048
openssl req -new -key kubelet-client.key -out kubelet-client.csr \
  -subj "/CN=kubelet-client-kubernetes-node-XXXXXXXXXXXX"

# Sign with cluster CA
kubectl certificate sign --cluster=kubernetes \
  --cert=ca.crt --key=ca.key \
  --request=kubelet-client.csr \
  --kubeconfig=kubeconfig \
  --duration=2160h

  3. Distribute and restart kubelet 

    cp kubelet-client.pem /var/lib/kubernetes/kubelet-client-current.pem
systemctl restart kubelet

docs.title: Certificate Components
docs.text: Certificate Type CN Usage peer etcd-peer etcd peer communication client etcd-client etcd API client communication legacy-client etcd-legacy Deprecated: legacy kubelet etcd access

docs.title: Rotation Procedure
docs.text:
1. Generate new etcd certificates 

    # Generate peer key and CSR
openssl genrsa -out etcd-peer.key 2048
openssl req -new -key etcd-peer.key -out etcd-peer.csr \
  -subj "/CN=etcd-peer"

# Generate client key and CSR
openssl genrsa -out etcd-client.key 2048
openssl req -new -key etcd-client.key -out etcd-client.csr \
  -subj "/CN=etcd-client"

# Sign certificates
kubectl certificate sign --cluster=kubernetes \
  --cert=ca.crt --key=ca.key \
  --request=etcd-peer.csr \
  --kubeconfig=kubeconfig \
  --duration=2160h --name=etcd-peer

kubectl certificate sign --cluster=kubernetes \
  --cert=ca.crt --key=ca.key \
  --request=etcd-client.csr \
  --kubeconfig=kubeconfig \
  --duration=2160h --name=etcd-client

  2. Distribute certificates to etcd members 

    cp etcd-peer.pem /etc/etcd/peer/peer.pem
cp etcd-client.pem /etc/etcd/client/client.pem
# Distribute CA certificate if rotated
cp ca.crt /etc/etcd/ca/ca.crt

  3. Restart etcd services 

    systemctl restart etcd

  4. Verify etcd health 

    etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=https://localhost:2379

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Front-proxy certificates protect the Kubernetes API server access via the front-proxy endpoint (default: :8080). These control who can interact with the cluster via kubectl --request-header-urlPrefix=.

docs.title: Rotation Procedure
docs.text:
1. Generate new front-proxy key and CSR 

    openssl genrsa -out front-proxy.key 2048
openssl req -new -key front-proxy.key -out front-proxy.csr \
  -subj "/CN=front-proxy-client"

  2. Sign with appropriate extensions 

    kubectl certificate sign --cluster=kubernetes \
  --cert=ca.crt --key=ca.key \
  --request=front-proxy.csr \
  --kubeconfig=kubeconfig \
  --duration=2160h --name=front-proxy-client \
  --extfile=<(printf "subjectAltName=DNS:front-proxy-client,IP:127.0.0.1")

  3. Distribute to front-proxy components 

    cp front-proxy.pem /etc/kubernetes/front-proxy/front-proxy-client.pem
# Update kubeconfig for kubectl access
cp front-proxy.kubeconfig /etc/kubernetes/front-proxy/kubeconfig

  4. Restart kube-apiserver (if serving front-proxy cert) 

    systemctl restart kube-apiserver

docs.title: Token Signing Key Rotation
docs.text:
1. Check current key expiration 

    # List signing keys
kubectl get configmap/tka -n kube-system -o yaml

  2. Rotate token signing key 

    # Create new signing key
openssl genrsa -out tsig-key.pem 2048

# Create CA certificate for signing
openssl req -new -x509 -key tsig-key.pem -out tsig-key.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=token-signing-key"

# Create ConfigMap with new key
kubectl create configmap tka --from-file=tsig-key.pem \
  --from-file=tsig-key.crt -n kube-system --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

  3. Rotate aggregated API server signing keys similarly, updating the relevant ConfigMaps.

docs.title: API Server Certificate with SANs
docs.text:
Ensure the API server certificate includes the front-proxy SAN: 

# When generating API server cert
openssl req -new -key apiserver.key -out apiserver.csr \
  -subj "/CN=kubernetes"

# Add SANs
openssl x509 -req -in apiserver.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \
  -out apiserver.crt -days 365 \
  -extfile <(printf "subjectAltName=DNS:kubernetes,DNS:kubernetes.default,DNS:kubernetes.default.svc,DNS:kubernetes.default.svc.cluster,DNS:kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local,IP:10.96.0.1")

docs.title: Trigger Emergency Rotation
docs.text:
When a certificate is compromised or expiring outside the normal rotation window:

  1. Immediate actions
  2. Identify all affected components and their certificates
  3. Generate new certificates with short validity (24-48 hours for emergency)

  4. Document the reason for emergency rotation

  5. Accelerated distribution

  6. Use configuration management tools (Ansible, Terraform) for mass distribution
  7. Validate each component starts with new certificates before decommissioning old ones

  8. Monitor for authentication failures during transition

  9. Post-rotation verification 

    # Verify all plane connectivity
kubectl cluster-info
etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=https://localhost:2379

# Check kubelet status
kubectl get nodes

# Verify front-proxy access
kubectl get nodes --request-header-urlPrefix=

  10. Update monitoring and alerting

  11. Update certificate expiration metrics
  12. Set short-term alerts for newly-rotated certificates
  13. Document the rotation in the change log

docs.title: Revocation Workflow
docs.text:
If a certificate is compromised:

  1. Revoke the certificate using your internal PKI
  2. Update CRL distribution points if using CRL-based revocation
  3. Accelerate rotation using the emergency procedure above
  4. Investigate the compromise and fix the root cause before returning to normal rotation

docs.title: Renewal Schedule and Monitoring
docs.text: Certificate Type Default Validity Renewal Trigger Monitoring Metric API Server 1 year 30 days before expiry kube_ap_server_certificate_expiry_seconds Kubelet 1 year 30 days before expiry kubelet_certificate_expiry_seconds etcd peer 1 year 30 days before expiry etcd_peer_certificate_expiry_seconds etcd client 1 year 30 days before expiry etcd_client_certificate_expiry_seconds Front-proxy 1 year 30 days before expiry front_proxy_certificate_expiry_seconds SA token key 1 year 30 days before expiry service_account_token_key_age

docs.title: Automated Monitoring Example
docs.text:
# Prometheus alert for certificate expiry
alert: CertificateExpiryWarning
expr: (kubelet_certificate_expiry_seconds - time()) < 2592000
for: 10m
labels:
  severity: warning
annotations:
  summary: "Kubelet certificate expiring within 30 days"
  description: "Kubelet certificate will expire in less than 30 days. Renewal required."

docs.title: Control plane and etcd
docs.text: The control plane runs the Kubernetes API server, controller manager, scheduler, and — in the reference topology — a stacked etcd member on each control-plane node. Kubespray owns installation and upgrades; this document records the decisions and the operational boundaries.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Decision Value Record Control-plane nodes 3 for the first environment, 5 documented as the reference production topology decisions/ADR-0002-* etcd placement Stacked on control-plane nodes decisions/ADR-0003-* Failure tolerance 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure; 5 tolerate 2 ADR-0002, ADR-0003 Upgrade order Control plane first, one node at a time kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md

Inventory grouping follows Kubespray: a node in [control-plane] with stacked etcd must also be in [etcd] (kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md).

docs.title: What lives where
docs.text:
Path Content Owner /etc/kubernetes/pki API server, kubelet, front-proxy, and etcd certificates Kubespray /etc/kubernetes/manifests Static pod manifests for API server, controller manager, scheduler, etcd Kubespray /var/lib/etcd etcd data directory etcd /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf Admin kubeconfig (never distributed to users) Kubespray

Kubernetes internal PKI is Kubespray's, not cert-manager's. cert-manager issues ingress and service certificates only (secrets-management/pki/index.md).

docs.title: Sizing and placement
docs.text:
• Control-plane nodes are not workers: no application pods, taints applied.
  • etcd is latency-sensitive. Local SSD or NVMe, and no shared storage.
  • Control-plane nodes spread across failure domains (architecture/03-failure-domains.md).
  • API server access is restricted to the management subnet (network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=control-plane
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl member list

All members must report healthy; a member list shorter than the inventory means a member was lost and must be replaced before the next failure.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
etcd snapshots are separate from Velero. Velero does not back up etcd, and a cluster restore without an etcd snapshot restores workloads onto a different control plane.

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db

Move the snapshot off the node and verify it (etcdctl snapshot status). The cadence and retention are recorded with the backup policy in lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Failure Effect Recovery One control-plane node lost API available through the remaining members; etcd quorum intact at 3 nodes Rebuild the node, rejoin with cluster.yml --limit <host> Two of three control-plane nodes lost etcd loses quorum, all API writes stop; running pods keep running Restore quorum from a snapshot; do not attempt partial writes Slow etcd disk API latency rises, leader elections flap Replace the disk; etcd is not tunable around bad hardware Certificate expiry API server or kubelet TLS fails cluster.yml certificate renewal workflow in kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md

docs.title: Auto-Test Kubernetes Control-Plane Scaling
docs.text: This document covers the procedures for testing Kubernetes control-plane scaling, including node add/remove and auto-scaling configuration validation. It is intended for automated testing and operational verification.

docs.title: 1. Check etcd cluster health
docs.text:
# Run on any control-plane node
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

Expected: All members report healthy

docs.title: 2. Check etcd member list
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

Expected: Member count matches inventory. A member list shorter than the inventory means a member was lost and must be replaced before the next failure.

docs.title: 3. etcd quorum rules
docs.text:
Control-plane nodes Tolerated failures Quorum size 3 nodes 1 failure 2/3 5 nodes 2 failures 3/5

Never restart all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes API server quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: 4. etcd snapshot verification (automated test)
docs.text:
# Verify latest snapshot is healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-*.db \
  --write-out=table

Expected output shows health: "true".

docs.title: 1. /healthz endpoint
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/healthz?verbose'

Expected: 200 OK with healthy component statuses

docs.title: 2. /readyz endpoint
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

Expected: All components Ready — API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd

docs.title: 3. API server availability through load balancer
docs.text:
curl -k https://<load-balancer-vip>:6443/healthz
curl -k https://<load-balancer-vip>:6443/readyz

docs.title: C. Controller-Manager Status
docs.text:
# Check controller-manager pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=controller-manager

# Describe controller-manager
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod -l component=controller-manager

# Check controller-manager metrics
kubectl -n kube-system get --raw '/readyz' | grep -i controller

Expected: All controller-manager pods are Ready and running

docs.title: Common issues
docs.text:
• Certificate expiry causing TLS hand failures
  • CPU starvation on control-plane nodes
  • etcd latency causing leader election flaps

docs.title: D. Scheduler Status
docs.text:
# Check scheduler pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=scheduler

# Describe scheduler
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod -l component=scheduler

# Check scheduler metrics
kubectl -n kube-system get --raw '/readyz' | grep -i scheduler

Expected: Scheduler pod is Ready and accepting scheduling decisions

docs.title: Common issues
docs.text:
• Resource constraints preventing pod scheduling
  • Node selector/affinity misconfiguration
  • Insufficient resources on target nodes

docs.title: a. Add to inventory
docs.text:
[control-plane]
k8s-cp-4 ansible_host=10.20.0.14 ip=10.20.0.14

[etcd]
k8s-cp-4

docs.title: b. Add OS and container runtime
docs.text:
• OS installed from internal mirror (Oracle Linux or Ubuntu)
  • containerd installed from internal repository
  • SSH access for the Ansible user
  • NTP/synchronized time
  • etcd data directory storage: local SSD or NVMe (no shared storage)

docs.title: c. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-4

docs.title: d. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes k8s-cp-4
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-cp-4
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-4 -- etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

Rule: Add one control-plane node at a time. Never add all control-plane nodes simultaneously during a rebuild.

docs.title: a. Drain the node
docs.text: kubectl drain k8s-cp-4 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

docs.title: b. Remove from inventory
docs.text: Remove the node from [control-plane] and [etcd] in inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini.

docs.title: c. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-4

docs.title: d. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes | grep k8s-cp-4  # Should return nothing
kubectl -n kube-system get etcd-member-list  # Verify quorum intact

Never remove more than one control-plane node at a time without ensuring quorum remains intact.

docs.title: a. Add to inventory
docs.text:
[k8s-node]
k8s-w-3 ansible_host=10.20.0.23 ip=10.20.0.23

docs.title: b. Add OS and container runtime
docs.text:
• OS installed from internal mirror
  • containerd 2.3.7 installed from internal repository
  • SSH access for the Ansible user
  • NTP/synchronized time

docs.title: c. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

docs.title: d. Verify
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes k8s-w-3
kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-w-3

docs.title: a. Drain the node
docs.text: kubectl drain k8s-w-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

docs.title: b. Remove from inventory
docs.text: Remove the node from [k8s-node] in inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini.

docs.title: c. Run Kubespray
docs.text: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

docs.title: d. Verify
docs.text: kubectl get nodes | grep k8s-w-3  # Should return nothing

docs.title: Cordon (mark unschedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl cordon k8s-w-3

Use before maintenance or when a node is unhealthy.

docs.title: Uncordon (mark schedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl uncordon k8s-w-3

Use after maintenance is complete and the node is healthy.

docs.title: 1. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
docs.text:
HPA is configured per-workload based on CPU and memory utilization:

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: app-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: app-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80

docs.title: 2. Cluster-Autoscaler
docs.text:
The cluster-autoscaler monitors pod pending times and adds/removes worker nodes automatically:

# Check cluster-autoscaler status
kubectl -n kube-system get deployment cluster-autoscaler -o yaml

# Scale the node group min/max size
kubectl -n kube-system patch deployment cluster-autoscaler -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"cluster-autoscaler","resources":{"limits":{"cpu":"500m","memory":"512Mi"}}]}}}}'

# Node group scaling (managed by cloud provider or on-prem provisioner)
# See infrastructure-specific documentation for node group configuration

Node group autoscaling rules: - Min replicas: 2 (high availability) - Max replicas: based on infrastructure capacity and SLO error budget - Scale-down delay: 10 minutes to avoid flapping - Cooldown period: 5 minutes between scale events

docs.title: 3. Manual Scaling Override
docs.text:
To manually override auto-scaling during a window:

# Scale deployment manually
kubectl scale deployment app-deployment --replicas=5

# HPA resumes control on next metrics reconciliation

docs.title: G. Error Budget and SLO Considerations
docs.text:
• Node additions that increase API server load must not push latency p99 above the 300ms SLO target.
  • HPA/VPA reactions are rate-limited; manual intervention may be required for rapid scaling.
  • Cluster-autoscaler scale-out is blocked if the error budget is >80% consumed.
  • Scale-in is blocked if pending pods exceed the available capacity threshold.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document certificate rotation for Kubespray-deployed Kubernetes clusters: kube-apiserver, kubelet, etcd, front-proxy, and service account certificates.

Cross-references kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §Certificate renewal, kubespray/certificate-lifecycle.md, kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Certificate expiry.

docs.title: B. Certificate types managed by Kubespray
docs.text: Certificate Managed by Location Rotation method kube-apiserver Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt cluster.yml kubelet Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet.crt cluster.yml front-proxy-client Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/front-proxy-client.crt cluster.yml etcd server/client Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ cluster.yml service account Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/sa.key, sa.crt cluster.yml OIDC CA Manual (owner-operated) /etc/kubernetes/pki/oidc-ca.crt Manual replacement

docs.title: C. Kubespray certificate renewal
docs.text:
Kubespray manages Kubernetes internal PKI. Certificates are renewed by running cluster.yml:

# Renew all certificates managed by Kubespray
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b

# Renew certificates on specific nodes only
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit <node>

Kubespray regenerates certificates on each run if they are expired or approaching expiry. The renewal is automatic — no manual certificate generation is required.

docs.title: Rotation procedure
docs.text:
1. Update cluster.yml if certificate parameters changed
  2. Run cluster.yml -b on all control-plane nodes
  3. Run cluster.yml -b on all worker nodes
  4. Verify: kubectl get nodes shows all Ready
  5. Verify: kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all ok

docs.title: D. etcd certificate rotation
docs.text:
etcd certificates are managed by Kubespray as part of the control plane. Rotation follows the same cluster.yml procedure:

# Rotate etcd certificates on one control-plane node at a time
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-1

# Verify etcd health after rotation
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-1 -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

One control-plane node at a time — never rotate etcd certificates on all control-plane nodes simultaneously.

docs.title: E. Certificate expiration detection
docs.text:
Kubespray does not proactively alert on certificate expiration. Monitor:

# Check kube-apiserver certificate expiry
kubectl -n kube-system get secret <apiserver-cert-secret> -o yaml | \
  grep 'tls.crt:' | head -1 | awk '{print $2}' | base64 -d | \
  openssl x509 -noout -enddate

# Check all certificates on a node
find /etc/kubernetes/pki -name '*.crt' -exec sh -c 'echo "{}:"; openssl x509 -in "{}" -noout -enddate' \;

# Check etcd certificate expiry
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  certificate list

docs.title: F. OIDC CA certificate (manual rotation)
docs.text:
The OIDC CA certificate is not managed by Kubespray. Follow the manual rotation procedure in kubespray/certificate-lifecycle.md §D:

  1. Replace oidc-ca.crt on one control-plane node
  2. Restart kube-apiserver static pod
  3. Verify node health
  4. Repeat for remaining control-plane nodes, one at a time

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document certificate lifecycle management for Kubespray-deployed Kubernetes clusters. Cross-references kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §Certificate renewal, kubespray/certificate-lifecycle.md, and kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Certificate expiry.

docs.title: Certificate types managed by Kubespray
docs.text: Certificate Managed by Location Rotation method kube-apiserver Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt cluster.yml kubelet Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/kubelet.crt cluster.yml front-proxy-client Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/front-proxy-client.crt cluster.yml etcd server/client Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ cluster.yml service account Kubespray PKI /etc/kubernetes/pki/sa.key, sa.crt cluster.yml OIDC CA Manual (owner-operated) /etc/kubernetes/pki/oidc-ca.crt Manual replacement

docs.title: Kubespray certificate renewal
docs.text:
Kubespray manages Kubernetes internal PKI. Certificates are renewed by running cluster.yml:

# Renew all certificates managed by Kubespray
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b

# Renew certificates on specific nodes only
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit <node>

Kubespray regenerates certificates on each run if they are expired or approaching expiry. The renewal is automatic — no manual certificate generation is required.

docs.title: Rotation procedure
docs.text:
1. Update cluster.yml if certificate parameters changed
  2. Run cluster.yml -b on all control-plane nodes
  3. Run cluster.yml -b on all worker nodes
  4. Verify: kubectl get nodes shows all Ready
  5. Verify: kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all ok

docs.title: etcd certificate rotation
docs.text:
etcd certificates are managed by Kubespray as part of the control plane. Rotation follows the same cluster.yml procedure:

# Rotate etcd certificates on one control-plane node at a time
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-1

# Verify etcd health after rotation
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-1 -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

One control-plane node at a time — never rotate etcd certificates on all control-plane nodes simultaneously.

docs.title: kubelet certificate renewal
docs.text:
kubelet certificates are regenerated by Kubespray during cluster.yml execution. For manual renewal or rotation outside the standard workflow:

  1. Ensure the kubelet static pod is running on the target node
  2. Run cluster.yml -b --limit <node> to regenerate the kubelet client certificate and key
  3. Restart the kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet or kubelet --rotate-certificates
  4. Verify: kubectl get nodes shows the node Ready
  5. Repeat for each node, one at a time

docs.title: service account key rotation
docs.text:
service account keys are managed by Kubespray and regenerated on cluster.yml run. To rotate service account keys:

  1. Update service-account-keys in cluster.yml if key parameters changed
  2. Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b
  3. Regenerate any secrets referencing the old service account key
  4. Verify: kubectl get secret <secret-name> -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.key}' returns the new key
  5. Restart workloads that depend on the previous key if they fail to authenticate

docs.title: front-proxy certificate rotation
docs.text:
front-proxy-client certificates are regenerated by Kubespray during cluster.yml execution. To rotate front-proxy certificates:

  1. Verify the front-proxy client configuration: front-proxy-client.crt and front-proxy-client.key in /etc/kubernetes/pki/
  2. Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b
  3. Verify: kubectl auth can-i --help works without errors
  4. Verify: API server logs show no front-proxy TLS errors

docs.title: Internal CA (Kubespray-managed)
docs.text:
The internal Kubernetes CA is managed by Kubespray. CA rotation is performed as part of the cluster.yml workflow:

  1. Update CA parameters in cluster.yml if the CA key or validity period changes
  2. Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b on all control-plane nodes
  3. Verify all certificates are regenerated with the new CA
  4. Rotate user-facing trust stores if the CA change affects external consumers

CA rotation is destructive — existing certificates signed by the old CA will stop working. Plan CA rotation during a maintenance window with sufficient error budget.

docs.title: External CA (e.g., cert-manager, external PKI)
docs.text: The external CA is not managed by Kubespray. Follow the owner-operated procedure in kubespray/certificate-lifecycle.md §F for OIDC CA rotation principles, adapted for the specific external CA.

docs.title: When to use emergency renewal
docs.text:
• Certificate expiry within less than the standard rotation window
  • Compromised private key
  • Unexpected CA failure
  • Premature certificate revocation

docs.title: Emergency renewal procedure
docs.text:
1. Assess impact: Determine which services and workloads will be affected
  2. Rotate affected certificates: Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b to regenerate all certificates managed by Kubespray
  3. Rotate compromised keys manually if Kubespray automation cannot reach affected nodes:
  4. Generate new key pair: openssl genrsa -out <name>.key 2048
  5. Generate new CSR: openssl req -new -key <name>.key -out <name>.csr
  6. Sign with appropriate CA: openssl x509 -req -in <name>.csr -CA <ca.crt> -CAkey <ca.key> -CAcreateserial -out <name>.crt -days 365
  7. Deploy new key/cert to the affected nodes
  8. Verify: Confirm all affected services are healthy (kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods, API connectivity)
  9. Post-incident: Review root cause and update monitoring to provide earlier warning

docs.title: Emergency rollback
docs.text:
If emergency renewal introduces issues:

  1. Restore previous certificates from backup
  2. Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b to re-establish the prior PKI state
  3. Verify service restoration
  4. Document the incident and update procedures to prevent recurrence

docs.title: Monitoring and detection
docs.text:
Proactively monitor certificate expiration:

# Check kube-apiserver certificate expiry
kubectl -n kube-system get secret <apiserver-cert-secret> -o yaml | \
  grep 'tls.crt:' | head -1 | awk '{print $2}' | base64 -d | \
  openssl x509 -noout -enddate

# Check all certificates on a node
find /etc/kubernetes/pki -name '*.crt' -exec sh -c 'echo "{}:"; openssl x509 -in "{}" -noout -enddate' \;

# Check etcd certificate expiry
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  certificate list

# Alert when certificates have less than 30 days remaining
# (configured in your monitoring system, e.g. Prometheus alerting)

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the etcd backup procedure: snapshot frequency, retention, off-node storage, verification, and restore procedure.

etcd stores all Kubernetes cluster state. Losing etcd means losing the entire cluster. Regular, verified backups are mandatory.

Cross-references kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §etcd, lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md §etcd quorum lost.

docs.title: B. Backup frequency and retention
docs.text: Item Value Snapshot frequency Every 4 hours (configurable) Retention 7 daily snapshots, 4 weekly snapshots, 1 monthly snapshot Off-node copy Within 15 minutes of snapshot completion Verification Every snapshot verified with etcdctl snapshot status

docs.title: 1. Take etcd snapshot
docs.text:
Run on one etcd member (control-plane node):

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db

docs.title: 2. Verify snapshot
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db \
  --write-out=table

Expected output shows health: "true".

docs.title: 3. Copy off-node
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system cp etcd-<node>:/var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db \
  /backups/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db

Store off-node in object storage (Ceph RGW) or offline media.

docs.title: 1. Stop etcd on the affected member
docs.text:
# Delete the static pod manifest to stop etcd
rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# Wait for the pod to terminate
sleep 30

docs.title: 2. Restore from snapshot
docs.text:
# Copy snapshot to the node
cp /backups/etcd/snapshot-<date>.db /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-<date>.db

# Restore
etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot-<date>.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/restored

# Replace the data directory
mv /var/lib/etcd/member /var/lib/etcd/member.old
mv /var/lib/etcd/restored/member /var/lib/etcd/member

docs.title: 3. Restart etcd
docs.text:
# Recreate the static pod manifest
cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml.bak /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# kubelet automatically picks up the change

docs.title: 4. Verify restore
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  member list

All members must report healthy.

docs.title: E. Retention and cleanup
docs.text:
# Keep 7 daily snapshots
ls -t /backups/etcd/*.db | tail -n +8 | xargs rm

# Keep 4 weekly snapshots (Sundays)
# Keep 1 monthly snapshot (1st of month)

docs.title: F. Automation
docs.text:
The snapshot procedure is automated via a CronJob or systemd timer on the Automation Management Server:

# Example CronJob (applied by Argo CD)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: etcd-snapshot
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  schedule: "0 */4 * * *"  # Every 4 hours
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: etcd-snapshot
            image: harbor.internal/platform/kubespray:v2.32.0
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              etcdctl snapshot save /backup/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db \
                --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
                --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
                --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
                --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379
              etcdctl snapshot status /backup/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document etcd operational procedures for production Kubernetes clusters: backup, restore, snapshot management, compaction, defragmentation, and member management. etcd stores all Kubernetes cluster state. Operational proficiency with etcd is essential for reliability and recovery.

Cross-references kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup, kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-backup.md §Backup procedure, kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-restore.md §Restore procedure, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §etcd.

docs.title: 1. Etcd snapshot workflow
docs.text:
Take snapshots regularly. The backup procedure (etcd-backup.md) defines frequency and retention, but the operational snapshot commands are documented here.

Take a snapshot on one etcd member (control-plane node):

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db

Verify a snapshot:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db \
  --write-out=table

Expected output shows health: "true".

docs.title: 2. Snapshot retention
docs.text:
• Keep at least 7 daily snapshots
  • Keep 4 weekly snapshots (Sundays)
  • Keep 1 monthly snapshot (1st of month)
  • Rotate and prune old snapshots per the retention policy in lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md

Prune old snapshots:

# Keep 7 daily snapshots
ls -t /backups/etcd/*.db | tail -n +8 | xargs rm

# Keep 4 weekly snapshots (Sundays)
# Keep 1 monthly snapshot (1st of month)

docs.title: 1. Why compaction matters
docs.text: etcd retains all revision history in the WAL (Write-Ahead Log). Without compaction, the WAL grows unboundedly, consuming disk space and degrading performance. Compaction prunes the WAL up to a specified revision.

docs.title: 2. Trigger compaction after snapshot
docs.text:
Always compaction after taking a snapshot to keep the WAL small:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  compaction <revision>

Use the latest snapshot revision or a known good revision:

# After snapshot, get the revision from snapshot status output
# Then compact up to that revision
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  compaction $(etcdctl snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F-%H%M).db \
    --write-out=json | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['revision'])")

docs.title: 3. Compaction best practices
docs.text:
• Run compaction after every snapshot
  • Do not compact to revisions that lose needed history
  • Monitor disk usage of the WAL directory (/var/lib/etcd/member/wal/)
  • If disk is filling up, compaction is behind — increase snapshot frequency

docs.title: 1. Why defragmentation matters
docs.text: Compaction frees logical space in the WAL, but the physical database file may still be sparse or bloated. Defragmentation rewrites the database, reclaiming physical disk space and improving performance.

docs.title: 2. Defragmentation workflow
docs.text:
Run defragmentation during a maintenance window when etcd is healthy and under low load:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  defrag

docs.title: 3. Defragmentation best practices
docs.text:
• Run on one member at a time
  • Do NOT run during a snapshot or compaction
  • Monitor disk space before and after
  • After defragmentation, verify member health:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster
  • Verify member list:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

docs.title: 4. Automated defragmentation
docs.text: Consider scheduling defragmentation weekly or monthly as part of routine toil reduction, especially for clusters with high write throughput.

docs.title: 1. Add a member
docs.text:
etcdctl member add <member-name> \
  --peer-urls=https://<member-ip>:2380 \
  --member-zone=<zone> \
  --member-site=<site> \
  --member-role=learner \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://<member-ip>:2380

Verify:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

docs.title: 2. Remove a member
docs.text:
Step 1: Remove the member from the cluster:

etcdctl member remove <member-id>

Step 2: Remove the etcd static pod manifest from the node (if applicable):

rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# Wait for the pod to terminate
sleep 30

Step 3: Rejoin the cluster (if using Kubespray inventory update):

# Update the inventory to exclude the removed member
# Re-run Kubespray to redeploy etcd without the member

Verify quorum after removal:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

docs.title: 3. Move a member to a new node
docs.text:
1. Add the new node as an etcd member
  2. Remove the old member
  3. Verify the cluster operates with the new member before deleting the old node

docs.title: 4. Member list verification
docs.text:
Regularly verify the member count matches the control-plane inventory:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

A member count shorter than the inventory indicates a lost member that must be replaced before the next failure.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document etcd restore procedure: snapshot restore, quorum recovery, member replacement, validation.

etcd stores all Kubernetes cluster state. Restoring etcd recovers the cluster to the point of the last snapshot.

Cross-references kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup, kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-backup.md, lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md §etcd quorum lost, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §etcd.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source etcd snapshot available kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-backup.md etcd binary on the node Installed by Kubespray etcd certificates /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ etcd stopped on the target node Static pod removed

docs.title: 1. Stop etcd on the affected member
docs.text:
# Delete the static pod manifest to stop etcd
rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# Wait for the pod to terminate
sleep 30

# Verify etcd is stopped
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=etcd --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>

docs.title: 2. Back up existing data directory
docs.text:
# Move existing data directory aside
mv /var/lib/etcd/member /var/lib/etcd/member.backup-$(date +%F)

docs.title: 3. Restore from snapshot
docs.text:
# Copy snapshot to the node
cp /backups/etcd/snapshot-<date>.db /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-<date>.db

# Restore
etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot-<date>.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/restored

# Replace the data directory
mv /var/lib/etcd/member /var/lib/etcd/member.old
mv /var/lib/etcd/restored/member /var/lib/etcd/member

docs.title: 4. Restart etcd
docs.text:
# Recreate the static pod manifest
kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart daemonset/etcd
# or manually recreate the static pod manifest

# Wait for etcd to start
sleep 30

docs.title: 5. Verify restore
docs.text:
# Check etcd endpoint health
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# Check etcd members
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  member list

# Check cluster API
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

All etcd members must report healthy.

docs.title: D. Quorum recovery
docs.text:
If etcd quorum is lost (less than majority of members available):

  1. Identify the member with the most recent data
  2. Restore etcd on that member from snapshot
  3. Start etcd on that member first (single-member cluster temporarily)
  4. Add remaining members one at a time
  5. Verify quorum is restored
# Add a member back to the cluster
etcdctl member add <new-member> \
  --peer-urls=https://<new-member-ip>:2380 \
  --member-zone=<zone>

docs.title: E. Member replacement
docs.text:
To replace a failed etcd member:

  1. Remove the failed member from the cluster
  2. Provision a new host with the same IP
  3. Restore etcd from snapshot on the new host
  4. Add the new host as an etcd member
  5. Verify cluster health
