docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the high-availability control plane topology for the platform: 3 or 5 control-plane nodes, stacked etcd, failure domain distribution, VIP/load balancing, and node loss recovery.

Cross-references kubernetes/control-plane/index.md, architecture/03-failure-domains.md, kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md, and network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md.

docs.title: B. Topology options
docs.text:
Option Control-plane nodes etcd placement Failure tolerance Use case 3-node 3 Stacked on each CP node 1 node First environment, development/staging 5-node 5 Stacked on each CP node 2 nodes Reference production topology

Both options use stacked etcd — etcd members run on the same nodes as the control plane components. This is the Kubespray default and the simplest operational model.

docs.title: C. Node placement and failure domains
docs.text:
Control-plane nodes must be spread across failure domains:

  • 3-node: 3 separate failure domains (e.g., 3 availability zones or 3 racks)
  • 5-node: 5 separate failure domains, or 3 zones with 2+2+1 distribution

Control-plane nodes are not workers — no application pods are scheduled on them. Taints are applied to prevent workload scheduling.

docs.title: D. Load balancing and VIP
docs.text:
API server access is fronted by a load balancer (MetalLB or external LB) in the management subnet:

                    +-------------------+
                    |  External LB /    |
                    |  MetalLB speaker  |
                    |  (VIP: 10.20.0.10)|
                    +-------------------+
                             |
        +--------------------+--------------------+
        |                    |                    |
   +----+----+         +----+----+         +----+----+
   | CP node 1 |       | CP node 2 |       | CP node 3 |
   | kube-apiserver |  | kube-apiserver |  | kube-apiserver |
   | stacked etcd  |  | stacked etcd  |  | stacked etcd  |
   +----+----+         +----+----+         +----+----+

The load balancer health-checks the API server port (6443/TCP) on each control-plane node and removes failed nodes from the pool.

docs.title: E. Inventory grouping
docs.text:
Kubespray inventory for stacked etcd:

[control-plane]
k8s-cp-1 ansible_host=10.20.0.11 ip=10.20.0.11
k8s-cp-2 ansible_host=10.20.0.12 ip=10.20.0.12
k8s-cp-3 ansible_host=10.20.0.13 ip=10.20.0.13

[etcd]
k8s-cp-1
k8s-cp-2
k8s-cp-3

[k8s-cluster:children]
control-plane
etcd

Rule: A node in [control-plane] with stacked etcd must also be in [etcd]. Never list a host in two k8s-node groups.

docs.title: F. etcd quorum and failure scenarios
docs.text:
Failure Effect etcd quorum Recovery 1 CP node lost (3-node) API available through remaining 2 members Intact (2/3) Rebuild node, rejoin with cluster.yml --limit <host> 1 CP node lost (5-node) API available through remaining 4 members Intact (4/5) Rebuild node, rejoin with cluster.yml --limit <host> 2 CP nodes lost (3-node) etcd loses quorum, all API writes stop Lost (1/3) Restore quorum from etcd snapshot 2 CP nodes lost (5-node) etcd quorum intact at 3 members Intact (3/5) Rebuild nodes one at a time Slow etcd disk API latency rises, leader elections flap Intact Replace disk; etcd is not tunable around bad hardware

Never restart all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes API server quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: G. Certificate lifecycle
docs.text:
Kubernetes internal PKI (API server, kubelet, front-proxy, etcd certificates) is managed by Kubespray, not cert-manager:

  • Certificates are renewed by Kubespray's cluster.yml certificate renewal workflow
  • cert-manager issues ingress and service certificates only (secrets-management/pki/index.md)
  • OIDC integration requires kube_oidc_ca_file (CA that signed Keycloak TLS cert) on every control-plane node (kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md Section L)

Certificate expiry causes API server or kubelet TLS failure. Renew via cluster.yml before expiry.

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Control-plane nodes are Ready
kubectl get nodes -l node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane

# Control-plane pods running
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l tier=control-plane

# etcd cluster healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# etcd members all present
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  member list

# API server readiness
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

All etcd members must report healthy. A member list shorter than the inventory means a member was lost and must be replaced before the next failure.

docs.title: I. Upgrade order
docs.text:
Control plane first, one node at a time:

  1. Upgrade one control-plane node with cluster.yml --limit <host>
  2. Verify node is Ready and etcd member is healthy
  3. Repeat for the next control-plane node
  4. Then upgrade worker nodes

Kubernetes supports only one minor version skew in each direction — do not skip minors.

docs.title: F. Replace worker
docs.text:
Replace = drain + remove + rebuild + re-add:

  1. Drain: kubectl drain k8s-w-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  2. Remove from inventory
  3. Rebuild the host (Terraform + Ansible, or manual reinstall)
  4. Re-add to inventory with same or new name
  5. Run Kubespray: cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3
  6. Verify: node is Ready

docs.title: Cordon (mark unschedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl cordon k8s-w-3

Use before maintenance or when a node is unhealthy.

docs.title: Uncordon (mark schedulable)
docs.text:
kubectl uncordon k8s-w-3

Use after maintenance is complete and the node is healthy.

docs.title: Add taint to control-plane nodes (default)
docs.text: Control-plane nodes have the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule taint applied by Kubespray. This prevents application pods from being scheduled on control-plane nodes unless they have a matching toleration.

docs.title: Add a dedicated taint for specialized workloads
docs.text: kubectl taint node k8s-cp-5 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule

docs.title: Add matching toleration to pod spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: gpu-workload
      image: gpu-image:latest
  tolerations:
    - key: dedicated
      operator: Equal
      value: gpu
      effect: NoSchedule

docs.title: Remove a taint
docs.text: kubectl taint node k8s-cp-5 dedicated:NoSchedule-

docs.title: Golden signals to monitor
docs.text: Signal Tool Alert condition Latency kubectl top node, Prometheus Node response time > 500ms sustained Traffic Prometheus node_network_receive_bytes_total Sudden drop > 90% Errors kubelet logs, Prometheus kubelet_volume_errors_total Disk error rate spikes Saturation Prometheus node_cpu_seconds_total, node_memory_Active_bytes CPU > 80% or memory > 85% for 5m

docs.title: Health check commands
docs.text:
# Node status
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Node conditions
kubectl describe node k8s-w-3 | grep -A 10 "Conditions:"

# Node allocatable
kubectl get nodes k8s-w-3 -o jsonpath='{.status.allocatable}'

# Kubelet status
systemctl status kubelet

# Node heartbeat
kubectl get nodes --request-timeout=5s

# Disk usage on node
ssh k8s-w-3 "df -h /var/lib/kubelet/pods"

docs.title: Node drain safety checks
docs.text:
Before draining, verify:

  • No critical pods are DaemonSet-managed
  • Pods are not stuck in Terminating state
  • DaemonSet pods will be rescheduled to other nodes
  • Pod disruption budgets (PDBs) allow eviction
kubectl drain k8s-w-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force

docs.title: Node reset (Kubespray)
docs.text:
Use Kubespray's reset.yml playbook to remove Kubernetes from a node:

ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini reset.yml -b --limit k8s-w-3

Warning: reset.yml removes Kubernetes from the node. Only use on nodes that will be rebuilt or decommissioned. Never run rm -rf /etc/kubernetes manually — use reset.yml instead.

After reset, the node can be re-added with cluster.yml.

docs.title: 1. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
docs.text:
HPA is configured per-workload based on CPU and memory utilization:

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: app-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: app-deployment
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80

docs.title: 2. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)
docs.text: VPA is configured for stateful workloads that benefit from automatic resource adjustment. See addons/vpa.md for deployment and operation procedures.

docs.title: 3. Cluster-Autoscaler
docs.text:
The cluster-autoscaler monitors pod pending times and adds/removes worker nodes automatically:

# Check cluster-autoscaler status
kubectl -n kube-system get deployment cluster-autoscaler -o yaml

# Scale the node group min/max size
kubectl -n kube-system patch deployment cluster-autoscaler -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"cluster-autoscaler","resources":{"limits":{"cpu": "500m","memory": "512Mi"}}]}}}}'

# Node group scaling (managed by cloud provider or on-prem provisioner)
# See infrastructure-specific documentation for node group configuration

Node group autoscaling rules: - Min replicas: 2 (high availability) - Max replicas: based on infrastructure capacity and SLO error budget - Scale-down delay: 10 minutes to avoid flapping - Cooldown period: 5 minutes between scale events

docs.title: 4. Manual Scaling Override
docs.text:
To manually override auto-scaling during a window:

# Scale deployment manually
kubectl scale deployment app-deployment --replicas=5

# HPA resumes control on next metrics reconciliation

docs.title: I. Error Budget and SLO Considerations
docs.text:
• Node additions that increase API server load must not push latency p99 above the 300ms SLO target.
  • HPA/VPA reactions are rate-limited; manual intervention may be required for rapid scaling.
  • Cluster-autoscaler scale-out is blocked if the error budget is >80% consumed.
  • Scale-in is blocked if pending pods exceed the available capacity threshold.

docs.title: Multiple ingress controllers — portfolio and deprecation plan
docs.text: Check date: 2026-10-17. Gateway API conformance data is from the Gateway API implementation reports (https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/docs/implementations/list/), which are the authoritative statement of what each implementation supports.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text:
A single ingress controller is a single point of failure and a single point of lock-in. A portfolio of controllers lets the platform:

  • Serve different traffic classes with different implementations (for example a Gateway API-native controller for new services, an Ingress controller for the long tail).
  • Keep a second implementation running on a separate address so the primary can be upgraded or failed over without a full outage.
  • Escape a controller's deprecation without a big-bang migration, because the next controller is already deployed and taking a share of the traffic.
  • Use conformance reports as an objective measure of which implementation to prefer.

The cost is real: each controller is a set of images to mirror, a set of CRDs, a certificate, an address in the load-balancer pool, a configuration surface, and a skill requirement. The portfolio is bounded deliberately.

docs.title: Lifecycle model
docs.text:
Every controller in the portfolio moves through five stages. The stage is a property of the controller in the platform, not of the upstream project.

Stage Deployment New apps Upgrades in Artifact mirroring Exit condition Candidate Not installed No No No Evaluated and rejected, or promoted to Supported Supported Installed, taking traffic Yes Yes Yes Upstream EOL, or the platform's usage drops below the threshold Deprecated Installed, frozen at its pinned version No No Yes, the pinned version only 3 months after the stage change, or immediately if a critical CVE appears Removed Uninstalled n/a n/a No The traffic has been migrated and the runbook is retired Retired upstream Same as the stage it was in, but with a hard deadline No No Only the pinned version, and only for continuity Upstream stopped releasing: the platform sets its own deadline and treats the controller as Deprecated on that date

Two hard rules:

  1. Upstream retirement forces Deprecated. A controller whose project is retired (as kubernetes/ingress-nginx was in March 2026) becomes Deprecated on the retirement date, regardless of what stage it was in. There is no upgrade path, so the platform must treat it as frozen.
  2. A critical CVE in a Deprecated controller forces immediate removal planning. The controller stays deployed to keep traffic flowing, but the removal plan becomes urgent and the exception is recorded with an owner and a date.

docs.title: The portfolio
docs.text: Controller Stage Role Gateway API Conformance (v1.5 reports) Upstream status Deprecation trigger F5 NGINX Ingress Controller (nginx/kubernetes-ingress) Supported Primary L7. Serves Ingress and Gateway API Yes NGINX Gateway Fabric v2.6.0: 29/35 extended features Active, F5 supported. NIC 5.7.0 supports k8s 1.30-1.37 Upstream EOL, or Gateway API coverage of the estate reaches 100% and NGINX Gateway Fabric takes the load F5 NGINX Gateway Fabric Supported Gateway API native. New services Yes, primary v2.6.0: 29/35 (v2.5.0: 26/35) Active. Fabric 2.8.0 conforms to Gateway API 1.6.3, k8s 1.32+ Never, while NGINX remains the vendor's strategic direction. Deprecated only if F5 changes direction Envoy Gateway Supported Gateway API native. Second opinion and failover target Yes v1.8.0: 33-34/35 Active, CNCF. v1.9 EOL 2027-02-14; v1.8 EOL 2026-11-08 Upstream EOL, or the platform adopts a service mesh that provides the same function (ADR-0009) Traefik Candidate Not installed. Evaluated for teams that want label-driven configuration Yes v3.7: 14/35 Active, v3.7.16 Remains a candidate unless a team requires it Cilium as a Gateway API implementation Candidate Not installed as a controller. Cilium already provides the datapath Yes Cilium v1.20.0-pre.2: 25/35 Active, part of the CNI already deployed Never. Attractive because it removes a separate data path, but the conformance coverage is lower than the dedicated controllers Istio ingress gateway Candidate Tied to the service-mesh decision Yes Istio 1.30.5: 31/35 Active Follows the mesh decision (ADR-0009): deprecated the moment a mesh is adopted, because the mesh provides ingress kgateway Candidate Not installed Yes v2.3.7: 32/35 Active Remains a candidate HAProxy Ingress, Contour, Emissary, Kong, APISIX, Varnish Candidate Not installed Varies Low Active Remain candidates. None clears the bar for a second deployment today

docs.title: Deprecation schedule
docs.text:
Dates are anchored to the triggers, not to a fixed calendar. Where an upstream date exists, it is used.

Controller Latest known upstream EOL Platform stage on that date Platform removal target kubernetes/ingress-nginx (community) Retired 2026-03 Deprecated immediately (already retired upstream) 2026-12, after migration to the F5 controller or NGINX Gateway Fabric Envoy Gateway v1.8 2026-11-08 Deprecated on that date unless upgraded to v1.9 2027-02 (after the v1.9 EOL) Envoy Gateway v1.9 2027-02-14 Deprecated unless a newer version is adopted 2027-05 F5 NGINX Ingress Controller Not scheduled Supported Only when Gateway API covers the whole estate F5 NGINX Gateway Fabric Not scheduled Supported Only if F5 changes direction Ceph Squid (storage, tracked because Rook depends on it) ~2026-10-31 Deprecated 2027-01

docs.title: Concrete deprecation procedure
docs.text:
When a controller enters the Deprecated stage:

  1. Freeze. The version is pinned. No upgrades in, no new applications. The chart and images stay in the internal registry at the pinned version.
  2. Announce. A dated notice in the platform changelog naming the controller, the replacement, the removal date, and the owner.
  3. Migrate. Move traffic in slices, not all at once:
  4. New applications go to the replacement immediately.
  5. Existing applications move when they are next deployed, not as a separate project.
  6. A deadline-driven bulk migration is scheduled for the remaining applications.
  7. Measure. Track the traffic share still on the deprecated controller. Removal is blocked until it is zero and the address has been released.
  8. Remove. Uninstall the controller, remove its CRDs, release its VIP from the MetalLB pool, remove its DNS record, and delete its artifacts from the internal registry. Update the network matrix and the artifact matrix in the same change.
  9. Record. Update this file, the ADR, the version matrix, and the EOL watchlist.

docs.title: Traffic sharing and failover
docs.text:
Two controllers run on separate addresses, never behind the same VIP:

  DMZ LB
    ├── VIP-A  ->  NGINX Ingress Controller   (primary)
    └── VIP-B  ->  Envoy Gateway             (secondary / failover)

Each has its own certificate and its own entry in the MetalLB pool and the DNS records. Failover is a DNS or load-balancer target change, executed by the network team, not by a controller feature.

The secondary takes traffic only when: - The primary is being upgraded. - The primary has a defect. - A share of new applications is deliberately routed to it to prove the path.

A DNS-based failover is slow (TTL-bound). For a platform where the ingress is on the critical path, prefer a load-balancer health-check-driven target change over DNS.

docs.title: Admission and policy interaction
docs.text:
Each controller has its own admission webhook, and each webhook is a cluster-wide dependency. The policy:

  • Each controller runs in its own namespace with its own webhook configuration.
  • The webhook's failurePolicy is Fail for the namespaces that controller serves, and Ignore elsewhere.
  • The webhook's namespaceSelector restricts it to the namespaces it owns, so a failure in one controller does not block writes for another controller's namespaces.
  • The admission webhooks of two controllers must not both claim the same resource in the same namespace without a documented precedence rule. Where both would apply, the newer controller takes the namespace and the older one is excluded by the namespace selector.

docs.title: Certificate strategy
docs.text: One wildcard certificate per controller, issued by cert-manager from the internal CA, presented by the controller that owns the address. The certificate is not shared between controllers: a compromised controller must not be able to serve a valid certificate for the other's address.

docs.title: Offline footprint
docs.text:
Each controller adds:

Item Per controller Container images 2-4 (controller, webhook, agent, dataplane) Helm chart 1 CRDs 0-3 (Gateway API CRDs are shared) CRD upgrades Shared, but the controller version constrains which Gateway API release it supports MetalLB IPs 1-2 (one VIP, one failover VIP) DNS records 2 (one per VIP) Configuration surface One ConfigMap, one policy, one set of annotations

A three-controller portfolio is roughly 12 images and 3 charts. That is the practical ceiling for an air-gapped estate, and the reason the portfolio is capped at three deployed controllers.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. At most three controllers are deployed at any time. The fourth is a candidate until one of the three is removed.
  2. Every controller has a named replacement and a removal date before it is deployed.
  3. No controller stays in the Deprecated stage for longer than three months without a recorded exception.
  4. Upstream retirement immediately forces Deprecated.
  5. Removal is blocked while any traffic share remains.
  6. A controller is never removed without its replacement having served production traffic for a full business cycle.

docs.title: L7 ingress — F5 NGINX Ingress Controller and Gateway API
Why this is not the ingress-nginx you may know
docs.text:
The community project kubernetes/ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026. SIG Network and the Security Response Committee announced the retirement on 2025-11-11, and the Kubernetes Steering Committee followed with a statement on 2026-01-29. After the retirement there are no further releases, no bug fixes, and no security updates; the repositories are read-only and remain available for reference. Existing deployments keep running and the artifacts remain available, but a new deployment on that controller starts with no security support.

The replacement in this platform is F5's NGINX Ingress Controller (nginx/kubernetes-ingress). It is a different project from the retired one: same NGINX dataplane, different codebase, different maintainer (F5), different chart, different admission model.

Verified compatibility (F5 technical specifications, check date 2026-10-17):

NIC version Kubernetes tested Helm chart Operator NGINX / NGINX Plus 5.7.0 1.30 - 1.37 2.8.0 3.8.0 1.31.7 / R37.2.0.1 5.6.3 1.30 - 1.37 2.7.3 3.7.3 1.31.6 / R37.1.1.2 5.5.4 1.29 - 1.36 2.6.4 3.6.5 1.31.3 / R37.0.3.1

F5 supports the most recent release, and provides support to customers for any version released within two years of the current release.

F5's other product, NGINX Gateway Fabric, is the Gateway API-native path: version 2.8.0 is conformant with Gateway API 1.6.3 and requires Kubernetes 1.32+. It is the vendor's forward direction, and the platform moves to it when Gateway API is the only API in use across the estate (ADR-0007).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
external client
        |
  DMZ load balancer (keepalived/HAProxy) --VIP--> nginx-ingress service
        |                                                   |
  TLS termination at the controller                      MetalLB VIP
        |
  HTTPRoute / Ingress -> Service -> pods

Two exposure models:

Model Description Use Inside the cluster The controller's Service is type: LoadBalancer; MetalLB assigns a VIP The cluster edge is behind the site load balancer Outside the cluster The controller runs in hostNetwork or with a static loadBalancerIP and the site load balancer forwards to it Where the site load balancer owns the VIP and health checks

Pick one per cluster and document it. Running both means two ingress paths and two sets of certificates.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
helm repo add nginx-ingress https://nginx.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install nic nginx-ingress/nginx-ingress \
  --version 2.8.0 \
  --namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace \
  --set controller.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/nginx-ingress/controller \
  --set controller.admissionWebhooks.enabled=true \
  --set controller.admissionWebhooks.patch.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/nginx-ingress/admission-webhook \
  --set controller.admissionWebhooks.patch.image.digest="" \
  --set controller.service.type=LoadBalancer \
  --set controller.config.ingress-class=nginx \
  --set controller.metrics.enabled=true \
  --set controller.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled=true

Offline: the chart and all three images (controller, admission webhook, and any sidecar) must be mirrored into the internal registry. The chart pulls the image repository from values, so the internal path is set explicitly rather than relying on a mirror.

docs.title: Gateway API
docs.text:
Gateway API CRDs are client-side and versioned separately from the controller:

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.6.3/standard-install.yaml

Install the standard channel, not experimental, unless a specific experimental feature is required. The experimental channel installs CRDs with a shorter support commitment.

The controller needs to be told to watch Gateway API resources:

controller:
  config:
    enable-gateway-api: "true"
    gateway-class: nginx

docs.title: Configuration model hardening
docs.text:
The retired project was explicitly criticised for the snippets annotation, which allowed arbitrary NGINX directives to be injected through an Ingress annotation — a direct configuration-injection path. The replacement must not reintroduce that surface.

Mandatory: - snippets annotation support disabled. Confirm the controller version's default and pin the value explicitly. - server-snippet, stream-snippet, and lua-shared-dicts disabled unless a documented, reviewed use case exists. - The admission webhook validates and mutates Ingress, HTTPRoute, and VirtualServer resources. Its failure policy must be Fail for application namespaces. - The controller runs as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem where the version supports it. - The controller's ConfigMap is owned by the platform team. Application teams do not edit it.

controller:
  config:
    enable-snippets: "false"
    enable-server-snippets: "false"
    enable-stream-snippets: "false"
    allow-snippet-annotations: "false"

Confirm the exact key names for the pinned version before relying on them.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
# cert-manager + Vault PKI issuer (canonical per ADR-0017)
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: internal-ca
spec:
  vault:
    server: https://vault.internal:8200
    path: pki/sign/platform
    auth:
      kubernetes:
        role: cert-manager
        mountPath: /v1/auth/kubernetes
        serviceAccountRef:
          name: cert-manager-vault-issuer

Vault PKI holds and protects the CA signing key; cert-manager authenticates to Vault via Kubernetes auth using a projected ServiceAccount token for ServiceAccount cert-manager-vault-issuer (no long-lived token Secret), and requests/renews certificates; Vault performs certificate signing. The root CA key remains offline.

Certificate trust is distributed to workloads and clients through the OS baseline and container images (see operating-systems/host-configuration.md).

A bootstrap/self-signed CA Issuer may be used temporarily only while the Vault PKI path is being built; it must be removed once the Vault Issuer is operational. It is not a supported production path.

ClusterIssuer namespace semantics (cert-manager v1.21): serviceAccountRef has no namespace field. The referenced ServiceAccount resolves in cert-manager's configured --cluster-resource-namespace — cert-manager is only an example and only if that is the configured value. The dedicated ServiceAccount cert-manager-vault-issuer, its Role, and its RoleBinding must be created in the configured ClusterResourceNamespace. The RoleBinding subject must identify the actual cert-manager controller ServiceAccount and its actual controller namespace (which may differ from the ClusterResourceNamespace). Verify the effective ClusterResourceNamespace from the cert-manager controller deployment arguments or configuration, as it is not necessarily the Helm release namespace.

cert-manager v1.21 TokenRequest RBAC: cert-manager v1.21 no longer grants the controller ServiceAccount permission to create tokens for itself by default. When serviceAccountRef.name points to a ServiceAccount, you must create:

  • A dedicated ServiceAccount for Vault certificate issuance (cert-manager-vault-issuer in the configured ClusterResourceNamespace).
  • A narrow Role allowing create on serviceaccounts/token for that ServiceAccount only, in the ClusterResourceNamespace.
  • A RoleBinding allowing the cert-manager controller ServiceAccount (in its actual namespace) to use that Role, in the ClusterResourceNamespace.
  • A Vault Kubernetes-auth role (cert-manager) bound to that ServiceAccount and its namespace, with pki/sign/platform signing permissions.

Example (substitute namespace and ServiceAccount name as needed; the namespace shown is the configured ClusterResourceNamespace, not assumed to always be cert-manager):

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: cert-manager-vault-issuer
  namespace: <cluster-resource-namespace>
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: cert-manager-vault-token-request
  namespace: <cluster-resource-namespace>
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["serviceaccounts/token"]
  resourceNames: ["cert-manager-vault-issuer"]
  verbs: ["create"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: cert-manager-vault-token-request
  namespace: <cluster-resource-namespace>
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: <controller-serviceaccount-name>
  namespace: <controller-namespace>
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: cert-manager-vault-token-request
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

Vault audience: cert-manager automatically includes the Vault server address from spec.vault.server and the issuer-specific audience vault://internal-ca (the form vault://<cluster-issuer-name> for a ClusterIssuer) in the projected ServiceAccount JWT via the Kubernetes TokenRequest API. Do not describe https://kubernetes.default.svc as cert-manager's default audience.

Kubernetes API audience is conditional: When Vault uses a configured token_reviewer_jwt, cert-manager does not need to add the Kubernetes API audience merely for that reason. When Vault runs outside Kubernetes and reuses the cert-manager JWT for TokenReview, with token_reviewer_jwt omitted, the JWT must additionally include the actual Kubernetes API server audience. In that case, configure serviceAccountRef.audiences with the API server audience discovered from the cluster — do not use a hardcoded universal value. The automatically generated Vault server and issuer-specific audiences are preserved; serviceAccountRef.audiences adds audiences rather than replacing them.

Safe audience discovery: Obtain a short-lived token with kubectl create token and inspect its aud claim to discover the Kubernetes API audience. Do not print or persist a live token in documentation or logs.

Vault role audience: For a dedicated ClusterIssuer Vault role using Kubernetes auth, the issuer-specific audience vault://internal-ca must match the Vault role's audience restriction (the Kubernetes auth role field is audience; bound_audiences is for JWT auth roles). The actual ClusterIssuer name must match the audience configured in Vault. Keep bound_service_account_names and bound_service_account_namespaces aligned with the dedicated ServiceAccount and its actual ClusterResourceNamespace.

ServiceAccount token projection: cert-manager uses its own ServiceAccount (in the controller namespace) to request a short-lived, projected JWT from the Kubernetes API server and presents it to Vault. Configure an RBAC rule allowing cert-manager to request tokens, and a Vault Kubernetes-auth role (cert-manager) bound to that ServiceAccount with pki/sign/platform signing permissions. Token audiences follow the Vault role configuration; no manually provisioned token Secret is required.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get pods
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get svc
kubectl get gatewayclass
kubectl get gateway,httproute -A

# From outside
curl -vk https://<ingress-vip>/ -H 'Host: app.internal'

# Certificate
openssl s_client -connect <ingress-vip>:443 -servername app.internal </dev/null

Expected: the controller pods are Ready, the Service has a VIP, and the certificate chain validates against the internal CA.

docs.title: Migration from the retired ingress-nginx
docs.text:
For an estate that already runs the retired controller:

  1. Inventory: kubectl get ingress -A and list the annotations in use. The retired controller's annotation set is large; each one needs an equivalent or a deliberate decision to drop it.
  2. Convert to Gateway API with the SIG Network tool:
ingress2gateway print --providers=nginx --input-file=ingress.yaml > gateway-api-resources.yaml

The tool is a conversion utility, not an end-to-end migration. Review every converted resource and test it. It covers the common annotations, not all of them. 3. Run the new controller alongside the old one on a different address, as the Gateway API migration guide recommends, and validate before switching traffic. 4. Switch the DNS record or the load balancer target. 5. Remove the old controller only after the new one has served production traffic for a full business cycle.

The Kubernetes project published a specific warning about this migration: "a seemingly correct translation can still cause outages if it does not consider Ingress-NGINX's quirks." The five surprising behaviours are described in https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/02/27/ingress-nginx-before-you-migrate/. Read that document before converting anything.

docs.title: Known traps
docs.text:
1. The two projects share a name and nothing else. kubernetes/ingress-nginx (retired) and nginx/kubernetes-ingress (F5, active) have different chart names (ingress-nginx vs nginx-ingress), different namespaces, different admission webhooks, and different image paths. A copy-paste from an old playbook will install the retired one.
  2. The admission webhook is a cluster-wide dependency. If it is unavailable and its failure policy is Fail, every Ingress mutation is blocked. Confirm the failure policy per namespace group.
  3. Gateway API CRDs are a separate upgrade. Updating the controller does not update the CRDs. A controller that expects a newer CRD version fails at reconciliation.
  4. enable-snippets defaults change between versions. Pin it explicitly; do not rely on the default.
  5. The NGINX Plus variants are a different product. The OSS build is what this platform uses. NGINX Plus features (JWT, WAF, active health checks) are licensed and not available in the OSS image.
  6. Retiring the old controller changes the certificate story. If the old controller managed certificates through cert-manager in a shared namespace, the migration must move that ownership.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - The F5 controller (nginx/kubernetes-ingress), never the retired community project. Verify the chart source before every install. - snippets and the related annotation-driven configuration surfaces disabled. - The admission webhook with failurePolicy: Fail for application namespaces, Ignore for the platform's own namespaces. - Certificates from cert-manager with the CA in Vault. - The controller pinned to an exact chart version, with the image digest pinned in the offline registry.

Strongly recommended: - Gateway API for all new applications, Ingress only for what still needs it. - A dedicated ingress-nginx namespace owned by the platform team; application namespaces only get IngressClass and policy. - The controller's Service as type: LoadBalancer with a static loadBalancerIP from the MetalLB pool for the platform endpoints (Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, Grafana). - Prometheus scraping of the controller's metrics endpoint, with an alert on the admission webhook's rejection rate. - A migration plan toward NGINX Gateway Fabric written down before the Gateway API migration starts.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document the Kubernetes node upgrade procedure for clusters managed by Kubespray. This procedure covers node draining, kubeadm and kubelet upgrades, CNI compatibility verification, rollback, and validation steps. Cross-references kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §Node lifecycle, lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md §D — Upgrade order.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Kubespray release pinned in kubespray/VERSION kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §M Inventory and group vars in Git kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §M etcd snapshot taken before upgrade Section F below New kube_version verified against compatibility matrix compatibility/version-matrix.md CNI plugin version compatible with target Kubernetes version compatibility/version-matrix.md Ansible version compatible with target Kubespray release compatibility/version-matrix.md

docs.title: C. Upgrade constraints
docs.text:
• Upgrade one node at a time; never upgrade all nodes simultaneously
  • Control-plane nodes must be upgraded before worker nodes
  • Kubernetes supports only one minor version skew in each direction. Do not skip minors.
  • The kubeadm version must be compatible with the target Kubernetes version.
  • CNI and CSI may need separate upgrades. Plan them explicitly.
  • Rollback of a Kubernetes minor version is not supported. Take a snapshot before starting.
  • Drain each node only after verifying no critical pods are stuck in Terminating state.

docs.title: D. Upgrade order
docs.text:
1. Upgrade control-plane nodes one at a time (Section E — control-plane)
  2. Upgrade worker nodes one at a time (Section E — worker)
  3. Verify cluster health (Section G)
  4. Update kubespray/VERSION and group vars to the new release

docs.title: E. Node upgrade sequence (one at a time)
Control-plane nodes
docs.text:
# 1. Update kube_version in group_vars/k8s_cluster/k8s-cluster.yml
# 2. Commit the change to Git
# 3. Run Kubespray for one control-plane node
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-1

# 4. Verify node is Ready
kubectl get nodes k8s-cp-1

# 5. Verify etcd member is healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-1 -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# 6. Repeat for the next control-plane node

Never upgrade all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes etcd quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: Worker nodes
docs.text:
# 1. Drain the worker
kubectl drain k8s-w-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# 2. Run Kubespray for one worker node
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-1

# 3. Uncordon the worker
kubectl uncordon k8s-w-1

# 4. Verify node is Ready and pods are running
kubectl get nodes k8s-w-1
kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-w-1

# 5. Repeat for the next worker node

docs.title: F. etcd snapshot before upgrade
docs.text:
# Take snapshot on one etcd member
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

# Verify snapshot
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

# Move snapshot off the node
kubectl -n kube-system cp etcd-<node>:/var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db \
  /tmp/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: kubeadm control-plane upgrade (control-plane nodes)
docs.text:
# On each control-plane node, upgrade kubeadm and the control-plane components
sudo kubeadm upgrade apply v<VERSION> \
  --config=/etc/kubernetes/kubeadm-config.yaml

# Verify the upgrade
kubectl get nodes
kubectl version --short

docs.title: kubelet upgrade
docs.text:
# On all nodes (control-plane and worker)
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y kubelet=<VERSION>-00
sudo systemctl restart kubelet

# Verify kubelet version
kubelet --version

After kubelet upgrade, verify that all pods are running and the node reports the correct version.

docs.title: H. CNI compatibility verification
docs.text:
After upgrading Kubernetes nodes, verify CNI plugin compatibility:

# Check CNI plugin version compatibility
kubectl get cni -n kube-system

# Verify pod networking is functional
kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pods -o wide

# Check CNI status
kubectl describe cnf -n kube-system <cni-plugin-name>

If the CNI plugin requires a separate upgrade:

  1. Upgrade the CNI plugin DaemonSet to the version compatible with the new Kubernetes version
  2. Verify networking continues to function
  3. Confirm no CNI-related pod errors in logs

docs.title: I. Rollback
docs.text:
Kubernetes minor-version rollback is not supported. If an upgrade fails:

  1. Restore etcd from the pre-upgrade snapshot (Section F)
  2. Revert group_vars and kubespray/VERSION to the previous values
  3. Re-run Kubespray on affected nodes using the previous release
  4. Verify cluster health (Section G)

Important: Take an etcd snapshot before starting any upgrade. Without a snapshot, rollback is impossible.

docs.title: J. Validation steps
docs.text:
After completing the upgrade of all nodes, run the following validations:

# All nodes Ready
kubectl get nodes

# All system pods running
kubectl -n kube-system get pods

# etcd cluster healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# API server ready
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

# Version matches target
kubectl version --short

# CNI networking functional
kubectl run test-pod --image=nginx --restart=Never
kubectl get pods -o wide

# No CNI-related errors
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=<cni-plugin> | grep -i "error\|fail"

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document BGP peering and eBPF datapath considerations for the platform network. Cilium uses eBPF for pod networking and service load balancing; MetalLB uses BGP for external load balancer peering.

docs.title: B. BGP (MetalLB)
docs.text: MetalLB speaks BGP to edge routers to announce service IPs. The platform uses BGP peering on port 179/TCP.

docs.title: BGP configuration
docs.text: Item Value BGP peer port 179/TCP MetalLB speaker DaemonSet on edge LB nodes BGP router ID Node IP ASN Per-environment (internal ASN) Peer ASN Edge router ASN

docs.title: BGP ports
docs.text: Refer to network-matrix/port-requirements.md — Edge LB node ↔ MetalLB peers on 179/TCP.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Effect Recovery BGP session down Edge LB stops announcing service IPs; external traffic blackholes Check BGP peer config, router ACLs, session state MetalLB speaker not running No service IP announcement Restart speaker daemonset Route not accepted by router Service IP unreachable externally Check route filters, prefix lists, AS_PATH

docs.title: C. eBPF (Cilium)
docs.text: Cilium's eBPF datapath replaces iptables-based kube-proxy with XDP/TC-attached BPF programs.

docs.title: eBPF requirements
docs.text: Item Requirement Kernel >= 4.19 (5.4+ recommended) Mounts bpffs at /sys/fs/bpf, debugfs Privileges NET_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE BTF Optional, required for some features

docs.title: eBPF failure scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Effect Recovery Kernel too old Cilium agent fails to start Upgrade kernel or use Calico fallback bpffs not mounted eBPF programs cannot load Mount bpffs: mount bpffs /sys/fs/bpf -t bpf BTF missing Some eBPF features unavailable Install kernel debuginfo packages eBPF verifier rejects program Cilium datapath broken Check kernel version, reduce program complexity

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Check bpffs mounted
mount | grep bpf

# Check Cilium status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium
cilium status

# Check eBPF programs loaded
cilium bpf lb list
cilium bpf policy list

# Check Hubble
cilium hubble status

docs.title: D. Cross-references
docs.text:
• kubernetes/networking/cilium.md — Cilium CNI deployment
  • decisions/ADR-0006-cni-selection.md — CNI selection (Cilium)
  • network-matrix/port-requirements.md — Port 179/TCP for BGP
  • network-matrix/cloud-native-dmz.md — DMZ architecture

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document covers BGP peering configuration for Kubernetes networking using MetalLB in BGP mode. MetalLB provides load-balancer IP addresses for type: LoadBalancer services in bare-metal Kubernetes clusters by speaking BGP to edge routers.

docs.title: MetalLB BGP Mode
docs.text:
MetalLB operates in two modes:

  • L2 mode: Uses ARP to assign the VIP on the local segment. No router configuration required.
  • BGP mode: Announces the VIP via BGP peering with configured routers. Required for routed segments.

BGP mode configuration requires:

  • IPAddressPool defining the VIP range
  • BGPAdvertisement defining the peering peers
  • Router ACLs permitting TCP port 179
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: default-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 10.61.0.10-10.61.0.30

apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: default-bgp
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - default-pool
  peers:
    - my-asn: 64500
      peer-asn: 64500
      peer-address: 10.20.0.1
      peer-port: 179
      my-router-id: 10.20.0.11
      password:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: bgp-credentials
          key: password

docs.title: BGP Peer Selection
docs.text:
Peer selection determines which routers MetalLB will establish BGP sessions with. Key considerations:

Factor Requirement Peer ASN Must match the router's ASN Peer address Must be reachable from the node's network namespace My router ID Typically the node's BGP-facing IP Password/secret Stored in a Kubernetes secret if not plain-text Port Default 179/TCP, configurable per-peer

Multiple peers can be configured for high availability. MetalLB will attempt to peer with each in order, and will failover if a session drops.

docs.title: Peer Configuration Fields
docs.text: Field Description Required my-asn Local ASN for this BGP speaker Yes peer-asn Peer router's ASN Yes peer-address Router's BGP listen address Yes peer-port TCP port for BGP session No (default 179) my-router-id Router ID for BGP sessions Recommended password / password-secret Authentication password Optional, depends on router

docs.title: Route Advertisement
docs.text: Route advertisement is the process by which MetalLB announces the service VIP over BGP. The BGPAdvertisement resource controls this behavior.

docs.title: Single vs Multiple Peers
docs.text:
• Single peer: One BGP session. If it drops, all VIPs are withdrawn.
  • Multiple peers: HA setup. MetalLB advertises to all peers; router converges on the best path.

docs.title: Route Withdrawal
docs.text:
When a LoadBalancer service is deleted, MetalLB withdraws the associated routes. This happens via:

  1. Withdraw from all configured peers
  2. Wait for router to withdraw its announcement
  3. Service EXTERNAL-IP becomes pending until reconfigured

docs.title: Advertisement Liveness
docs.text: MetalLB periodically checks that routes are still advertised. If a peer becomes unreachable, the routes are withdrawn and re-advertised when connectivity is restored.

docs.title: BGP Session Health
docs.text: Monitor BGP session health using MetalLB's built-in metrics and logs.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Metric Purpose metallb_bgp_sessions Current BGP session states (established, openconfirm, openmessage, etc.) metallb_bgp_routes_advertised Number of routes currently advertised metallb_bgp_routes_withdrawn Number of routes withdrawn

docs.title: Checking Session State
docs.text:
# View speaker logs for BGP session events
kubectl -n metallb-system logs ds/speaker -f | grep -i "bgp\|session\|peer"

# Check BGPAdvertisement status
kubectl -n metallb-system get bgpadvertisement default-bgp -o yaml

# View MetalLB IP pool and advertisement status
kubectl -n metallb-system get ipaddresspool,ippools,l2advertisements,bgpadvertisements

docs.title: Healthy Session Indicators
docs.text:
• Sessions transition to Established state
  • Regular KEEPALIVE messages exchanged
  • Routes being advertised and withdrawn as expected
  • No log errors about TCP connections or authentication

docs.title: Unhealthy Session Signs
docs.text:
• Session stuck in Idle, Connect, or OpenConfirm states
  • TCP connection failures (port 179 blocked by firewall)
  • Authentication mismatches (password/secret mismatch)
  • Route reflector misconfiguration
  • AS_PATH or prefix-list filtering on the router

docs.title: 1. BGP Session Fails to Establish
docs.text:
Symptoms: Service EXTERNAL-IP stays pending; logs show connection timeouts.

Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Router ACL blocking TCP 179 Allow traffic from node IPs to router peer-address:179 Wrong peer-address in BGPAdvertisement Verify the router's BGP listen IP; check node routing table ASN mismatch Confirm my-asn and peer-asn match router configuration Password/auth mismatch Check password vs secret key; ensure base64 encoding if applicable Node not reachable from router Verify return path; test with telnet <peer-address> 179

docs.title: 2. Routes Not Accepted by Router
docs.text:
Symptoms: VIP assigned but externally unreachable; router logs show "prefix filtered" or "AS_PATH too long".

Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Prefix-list filtering routes Add the IP pool range to the router's advertised prefix-list AS_PATH policy rejecting routes Adjust AS_PATH prepend or acceptance policy on the router Maximum-prefix limit exceeded Increase or disable the router's maximum-prefix threshold Route reflector client misconfig Ensure MetalLB speakers are configured as clients if using a route reflector

docs.title: 3. Session Drops Intermittently
docs.text:
Symptoms: BGP session flaps; traffic blackholes during reconvergence.

Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Link instability between node and router Check physical/cable, SFP modules, switch logs Router resource exhaustion (CPU/memory) Scale router resources; optimize BGP routing table MTU mismatch path MTU discovery issues Ensure consistent MTU across link; adjust if needed keepalive/holdtimers mismatch Align keepalive and holdtime between MetalLB and router

docs.title: 4. VIP Not Reachable After Failover
docs.text:
Symptoms: After a node loss, the VIP becomes unreachable.

Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Single peer without HA Configure multiple BGP peers for session diversity Router not converging fast enough Tune router's BGP timers; reduce withdraw/advertise delay ARP cache stale on clients Clear ARP caches; BGP mode avoids this vs L2 mode

docs.title: 5. MetalLB Speaker Not Announcing
docs.text:
Symptoms: No BGP routes visible; speaker pod restarting.

Causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Speaker DaemonSet not scheduled on edge nodes Use node selectors/affinities to place speaker on edge LB nodes Insufficient IP addresses in pool Expand the IPAddressPool address range RBAC preventing speaker from advertising Ensure service account has metallb.io/speaker permissions IP conflict in the pool range Verify no other entity uses addresses from the pool range

docs.title: Commands Summary
docs.text:
# Install MetalLB with BGP
helm repo add metallb https://metallb.github.io/metallb/charts
helm install metallb metallb/metallb \
  --namespace metallb-system --create-namespace \
  --version 0.16.1

# Create IP pool
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: default-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 10.61.0.10-10.61.0.30
EOF

# Create BGP advertisement with peers
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: default-bgp
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - default-pool
  peers:
    - my-asn: 64500
      peer-asn: 64500
      peer-address: 10.20.0.1
      peer-port: 179
      my-router-id: 10.20.0.11
      password:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: bgp-credentials
          key: password
EOF

# Check BGP status
kubectl -n metallb-system get bpga
kubectl -n metallb-system logs ds/speaker | grep -E "BGP|session|peer"

# Test traffic flow
kubectl -n default expose deployment nginx --port=80 --type=LoadBalancer
kubectl -n default get svc nginx
curl http://<EXTERNAL-IP>

docs.title: A. XDP (eXpress Data Path)
docs.text:
XDP is the fastest packet processing hook in the Linux kernel, positioned at the network driver's TX ring entry point. Cilium leverages XDP to provide wire-speed networking with sub-microsecond latency.

Feature Details Hook point XDP_DATA, at driver level, before the kernel network stack Program type XDP_PROG_TYPE_XDP — attached via bpftool or Cilium agent Capability Drop, redirect, pass-through, generic offload eBPF program format Compiled to BPF bytecode, verified by kernel verifier Cilium usage Packet filtering, port redirect, load distribution across CPUs

docs.title: XDP Flow
docs.text:
NIC driver → XDP hook (program loaded by Cilium) → kernel network stack →

XDP programs in Cilium typically implement: - Allow/deny filtering based on BPF maps (IDs, labels) - Port redirect — redirect intercepted traffic to a userspace proxy (CiliumEnvoy) - Load distribution — hash-based distribution across CPUs using bpf_lxc_load_hash

docs.title: XDP Attachment
docs.text:
# Load and attach XDP program
sudo bpftool prog load xdp_kern.o /sys/fs/bpf/xdp0 attach xdp

# Via Cilium agent (automatic)
cilium agent run — XDP programs are programs loaded and attached by the agent

docs.title: B. Load Balancing
docs.text: Cilium's layer 4 load balancer operates in eBPF, replacing kube-proxy's iptables-based approach. It programs BPF maps for destination NAT and load distribution.

docs.title: LB Modes
docs.text: Mode Description Pros Cons l4-nat NAT destination IP to backend pods Simple, no pod CIDR routing needed Loses original destination IP l4-fair Per-flow NAT with hash-based distribution Preserves client IP better Still NAT, moderate CPU l4-transparent Transparent proxy, no DNAT Full original IP preservation Requires IPVS or eBPF redirect

docs.title: LB Architecture
docs.text:
Client → Cilium LB eBPF program → Backend pod (selected by hash)

The LB eBPF program maintains: - Endpoint maps — maps service VIP → ready endpoints - Connection tracking — ensures stickiness for existing flows - Health checks — probe endpoints via Hubble or integrated checks

docs.title: LB Configuration
docs.text:
# CiliumService LB configuration
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumService
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 443
      protocol: TCP
  sessionAffinity: "source-ip"

docs.title: LB Commands
docs.text:
# List LB entries
cilium bpf lb list

# Show service load balancing details
kubectl get ciliumservices -A

docs.title: C. Routing
docs.text: Cilium implements two primary routing modes: native routing (no encapsulation) and tunnel routing (VXLAN). The mode is selected based on whether the underlay network can route the pod CIDR.

docs.title: Native Routing
docs.text:
• Condition: Underlay network has routes for the pod CIDR pointing at node IPs
  • Mechanism: eBPF programs attached to XDP/TC redirect traffic based on destination IP prefix
  • MTU: Physical MTU (no encapsulation overhead)
  • Requirement: Router/switch must have pod CIDR routes

docs.title: Tunnel Routing (VXLAN)
docs.text:
• Condition: Underlay cannot route pod CIDR, or multi-cluster connectivity needed
  • Mechanism: VXLAN encapsulation, VTEP tunnel endpoints in the kernel
  • MTU: Physical MTU - 50 (VXLAN header overhead)
  • Encapsulation: UDP port 4789

docs.title: Route Resolution
docs.text: Pod IP → eBPF routing lookup → Node IP (native) or VXLAN tunnel (encapsulated)

docs.title: Routing Commands
docs.text:
# Check routing mode
cilium status --verbose

# Show BPF programs related to routing
cilium bpf endpoint list

# Verify native routing
ip route show <pod-cidr>

docs.title: D. NAT
docs.text: Cilium provides several NAT modes for service exposure and pod connectivity. The NAT mode is configured per-cluster and affects both service load balancing and pod egress.

docs.title: Service NAT (l4-nat mode)
docs.text:
• Destination NAT: VIP → backend pod IP:port
  • Source NAT: Optional masquerade for pod egress
  • Masquerade: bpf.masquerade=true — uses eBPF for fast MASQUERADE, avoids iptables overhead

docs.title: Egress NAT
docs.text:
• Default: No egress NAT; pods use pod IP directly
  • With masquerade: All pod egress goes through the node's external IP
  • Use case: When pod IP space cannot be routed on the underlay

docs.title: NAT Configuration
docs.text:
# BPF masquerade setting
--set bpf.masquerade=true

# Verify masquerade
cilium bpf nat list
iptables -t nat -L -n -v

docs.title: NAT Performance
docs.text:
• eBPF NAT: Near-line speed, minimal CPU overhead compared to iptables
  • Connection tracking: Stored in BPF maps, not kernel conntrack table
  • Scale: Millions of concurrent connections possible with sufficient BPF map size

docs.title: Key Metrics
docs.text: Metric Target Measurement Packet processing latency < 10µs per hop perf stat, bpftrace CPU overhead per Gbps < 1% eBPF overhead pidstat, mpstat Connection setup rate > 1M conn/s haproxy, custom benchmark BPF map lookup latency < 1µs bpftool map dump

docs.title: Performance Tuning
docs.text: Tuning knob Effect Recommended value BPF map size Affects lookup performance, memory usage map_entries ≥ expected concurrent connections × 2 XDP mode XDP_PASS, XDP_DROP, XDP_REDIRECT Use XDP_REDIRECT for LB, XDP_DROP for deny Program complexity Verifier rejection risk, runtime performance Keep XDP programs under 4KB BPF instructions CPU pinning Ensures LB programs run on dedicated cores Pin Cilium agent pods to separate CPU set

docs.title: Common Performance Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. XDP attachment failure — Ensure kernel supports XDP on the device; check dmesg for attachment errors
  2. BPF verifier rejects program — Reduce instruction count, use BTF for type safety
  3. BPF map contention — High concurrency on a single map; shard maps by CPU/core
  4. MTU mismatches — VXLAN: physical MTU - 50; native: physical MTU; verify with ping -M do -s <size> <dest>
  5. CPU saturation — eBPF programs run in interrupt context; monitor softirq and si steal

docs.title: Verification Commands
docs.text:
# Check BPF program loads and CPU attachment
cilium bpf lb list

# Show XDP program stats
sudo bpftool prog info /sys/fs/bpf/xdp0

# Monitor eBPF performance
perf stat -e cpu-clock,cache-references,cache-misses sudo cilium bpf lb list

# Check map sizes and utilization
cilium bpf map list

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Cilium provides pod networking, network policy, service load balancing, and observability, using eBPF in the kernel instead of iptables.

  pod A (node 1)  --eBPF-->  node 1 host stack  --underlay-->  node 2 host stack --eBPF--> pod B
        |                                                                |
     Cilium agent (DaemonSet, one per node)                     Cilium agent
        |                                                                |
   CiliumEnvoy (L7 proxy, per node)                            Hubble relay + UI

Modes used here: - Routing mode: native (no encapsulation) when the network can route the pod CIDR; tunnel (VXLAN) otherwise. - kube-proxy replacement: kubeProxyReplacement: strict, so iptables is not used for service handling.

docs.title: B. Requirements
docs.text:
Item Requirement Kernel >= 4.19 (5.4+ recommended); the pinned release requires 4.19+ cgroups v1 or v2; v2 recommended Mounts bpffs, debugfs; Cilium mounts them if the host allows Privileges The agent needs NET_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE (for certain features), and host mounts BTF Optional; required for some eBPF features

Cilium's eBPF datapath narrows the kernel compatibility envelope compared to Calico. Confirm the node kernel against the Cilium release's requirements before deploying.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• Helm chart: harbor.internal/charts/cilium (chart 1.20.3, app 1.20.3).
  • Images: cilium/cilium, cilium/operator-generic, cilium/hubble-relay, cilium/hubble-ui, cilium/certgen, cilium/envoy, and the quay.io/cilium/* variants of the same.
  • The Cilium chart tarball and index.yaml must also be in the internal file mirror, because the Kubespray offline guide specifically requires helm.cilium.io/index.yaml and the chart tarball.

docs.title: D. Installation
docs.text:
Through Kubespray, the release sets kube_network_plugin: cilium and installs the chart itself. The offline override is in group_vars/all/offline.yml (see kubespray/group-vars-template.md).

Standalone installation (used when the cluster is not built by Kubespray):

helm install cilium cilium/cilium \
  --version 1.20.3 \
  --namespace kube-system \
  --set kubeProxyReplacement=strict \
  --set k8sServiceHost=10.20.0.100 \
  --set k8sServicePort=6443 \
  --set ipam.mode=kubernetes \
  --set ipv4.enabled=true \
  --set ipv6.enabled=false \
  --set tunnel=disabled \
  --set bpf.masquerade=true \
  --set hubble.relay.enabled=true \
  --set hubble.ui.enabled=true \
  --set image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set operator.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set operator.image.useDigest=false \
  --set hubble.relay.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set hubble.ui.backend.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set hubble.ui.frontend.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set envoy.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set certgen.image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cilium \
  --set image.useDigest=false

tunnel=disabled is native routing. Use tunnel: vxlan if the network cannot route the pod CIDR.

docs.title: E. Network policy
docs.text:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: payments
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  egress:
    - toEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": kube-system
            "k8s:app.kubernetes.io/name": kube-dns
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "53"
              protocol: UDP
            - port: "53"
              protocol: TCP

L7 policy (requires CiliumEnvoy):

apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-api-only
  namespace: payments
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  ingress:
    - fromEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            app: web
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "443"
              protocol: TCP

docs.title: F. Observability
docs.text:
cilium status --verbose
cilium connectivity test
cilium bpf lb list
cilium bpf endpoint list

# Hubble
cilium hubble list
cilium hubble observe --namespace payments

The Hubble UI is exposed through an Ingress or a LoadBalancer Service.

docs.title: G. Validation
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium
cilium status
# expect: KubeProxyReplacement: True, KubeProxyReplacementError: none

# Connectivity
cilium connectivity test
# expect: all probes pass

# Cross-node pod traffic
kubectl run a --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep 300 &
kubectl run b --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- ping -c3 <a-pod-ip>

# Policy enforcement
# an allowed flow succeeds, a denied flow fails

docs.title: H. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Upgrade Helm upgrade through Argo CD; a canary node pool first. The agent restarts, which briefly interrupts pod connectivity on that node Add a node Label and taint per the platform standard; Cilium's agent DaemonSet schedules onto it automatically Replace a node Drain, rebuild, uncordon. The new agent rebuilds its state from the operator Change the MTU mtu in the Helm values; the agent restarts and pods on that node lose connectivity briefly Debug a flow cilium policy trace <src> <dst> and cilium hubble observe Recover from a stuck agent kubectl -n kube-system delete pod -l k8s-app=cilium on that node

docs.title: I. Known traps
docs.text:
1. kube-proxy replacement requires the API endpoint. Without k8sServiceHost and k8sServicePort, the agent cannot reach the API server and never becomes ready.
  2. Native routing requires external routes. The router or switch must have a route for the pod CIDR pointing at the node addresses. Without it, cross-node pod traffic fails while same-node traffic works.
  3. A default-deny egress policy breaks DNS. Always allow DNS to kube-dns before enabling a deny policy.
  4. MTU mismatch. With VXLAN, the pod MTU is the physical MTU minus 50. With native routing, it equals the physical MTU.
  5. Hubble relay and UI are optional but have their own images. In an offline environment, a missing UI image leaves the relay pod in ImagePullBackOff even when the datapath is fine.
  6. The operator must be able to write the Cilium CRDs and to reach the API server. A broken operator means the agent never reconciles.

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - kubeProxyReplacement: strict with the API endpoint set. - Explicit ipam.mode=kubernetes and a documented pod CIDR. - The Hubble relay and UI images mirrored, or the features disabled entirely. - A network policy per namespace, deployed in audit mode first.

Strongly recommended: - Native routing where the network team can add the pod CIDR route; it removes the encapsulation overhead and the MTU problem. - bpf.masquerade=true for better masquerade performance. - A dedicated CiliumNetworkPolicy per application namespace, owned by the application team in their own GitOps repository. - Hubble metrics exported to Prometheus for flow-level observability.

docs.title: Kubernetes Networking: CNI, DNS, Ingress, and Load Balancing
CNI Plugin Options
docs.text: Plugin Description Key Features Typical Use-Case Calico Widely adopted CNI using BPF fast-path. - Scales to thousands of nodes- Supports IPv4/IPv6- NetworkPolicy CRDs- Can run on bare metal, cloud, on-prem General-purpose clusters, multi-cloud, where simple networking is needed Cilium CNI based on eBPF for observability and security. - L7 traffic awareness- Transparent encryption- Kubernetes-native NetworkPolicy enhanced- Integration with Hubble for visibility Performance-sensitive workloads, need L7 observability, zero-trust networking Flannel Simple overlay CNI using VXLAN. - Minimal configuration- Supports etcd-backed subnet allocation- Works on all CNI-compatible runtimes Small clusters, labs, or environments where eBPF/BPF is not available

docs.title: DNS Configuration
docs.text:
Kubernetes DNS is provided by CoreDNS by default. CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in the kube-system namespace and resolves:

  • Service DNS: my-service.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local
  • Pod DNS: my-pod.my-namespace.pod.local
  • External DNS: Forwards external names via upstream resolvers

docs.title: Customizing CoreDNS
docs.text:
• Add plugins in Corefile ConfigMap (kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml)
  • Enable forwarder for external zones
  • Configure cache TTLs, health probes, and query logging

SRE tip: Monitor CoreDNS query latency and error rate as part of the cluster Latency SLO. A spike in DNS errors can masquerade as application latency.

docs.title: Ingress Controllers
docs.text:
An Ingress resource exposes HTTP/HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services. The Ingress controller satisfies the request.

Controller Description Key Features NGINX The de facto standard Ingress controller. - Mature, wide ecosystem- Supports TLS, rewrite, redirect- Can run as DaemonSet or Deployment GCE / ALB / NLB Cloud-provider-specific controllers. - Native integration with cloud load balancers- ExternalIP handling- Native support for cloud IAM Traefik Modern Ingress controller with dynamic config. - Single binary, automatic cert retrieval via Let's Encrypt- Middleware chaining- Good for dynamic environments

docs.title: Minimal Ingress Example
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: http-service
            port:
              number: 80

docs.title: Service Type LoadBalancer
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: my-app
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
  • On cloud providers, an external IP (or hostname) is provisioned automatically.
  • On on-premises, use MetalLB to assign an IP from a configured range.

docs.title: MetalLB (bare-metal load balancer)
docs.text:
MetalLB implements the Kubernetes LoadBalancer and IPAddress APIs using ARP announcements (Layer 2) or BGP (Layer 3).

# ConfigMap example for MetalLB IP address pool
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  namespace: metallb-system
  name: config
data:
  config: |
    address-pools:
    - name: default
      protocol: layer2
      addresses: ["192.168.100.240/28"]

docs.title: Network Policy Design
docs.text: NetworkPolicies restrict traffic flow between pods. They are opt-in: if no NetworkPolicy exists, all traffic is allowed.

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text: Pattern Example Allow only specific ingress ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: allow-frontend spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: web ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: app: frontend ``` Allow egress to external DNS ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: allow-dns-egress spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: web egress: - to: - ipBlock: ip: 8.8.8.8/32 ``` Deny all ingress by default Create a catch-all policy deny-all with spec.ingress: [] in namespaces where you want to lock down traffic.

docs.title: Design Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Define a default-deny NetworkPolicy in namespaces that require strict isolation.
  • [ ] Allow necessary ingress from trusted labels or namespaces.
  • [ ] Allow egress for container images, package managers, and external APIs.
  • [ ] Test policies with kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> and kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces.
  • [ ] Audit with kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o yaml to ensure no accidental allow-all.
  • [ ] Align policies with the Error Budget SLO: overly restrictive policies can increase failure rates during deployments.

docs.title: CoreDNS forwarding
docs.text: Cluster DNS answers two different question sets: service names inside the cluster, and everything else. The second set is forwarded upstream. In an air-gapped site the upstream is the internal DNS, and the forward path is the difference between a cluster that resolves harbor.internal and one that silently times out on every image pull.

docs.title: What the configurator sets
docs.text:
Value Default Meaning corednsForwarders 10.10.0.53 10.10.0.54 Upstream resolvers, space separated corednsForwardPolicy sequential Try the first, then the next. random spreads load but hides a broken server corednsCacheTtl 30 Cache TTL in seconds

Kubespray renders the upstream list from upstream_dns_servers in k8s-cluster.yml. The generated coredns-configmap.yaml is the same intent expressed as a Corefile patch, for clusters whose CoreDNS is managed outside Kubespray (or after a manual change).

docs.title: The Corefile
docs.text:
.:53 {
    errors
    health {
        lameduck 5s
    }
    ready
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
        pods insecure
        fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
        ttl 30
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . 10.10.0.53 10.10.0.54 {
        policy sequential
        max_concurrent 1000
    }
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}

loop is not optional. Without it, a CoreDNS that forwards to itself (or to a resolver that points back at it) answers every query with a loop error and the whole cluster loses DNS.

docs.title: Domain-specific forwarding
docs.text:
Some zones must not go to the general resolver: an AD domain, a partner network, a legacy zone with its own servers. Add a server block; the most specific zone wins:

corp.internal:53 {
    errors
    cache 30
    forward . 10.10.0.20 10.10.0.21 {
        policy sequential
    }
}

Do not forward cluster.local anywhere. If a stub domain collides with the cluster domain, rename the cluster domain in the Kubespray vars (cluster_name) before the cluster exists; renaming it after is a rebuild.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap coredns -o yaml | grep -A8 "forward"
kubectl run dnstest --rm -it --image={{value.registryHost}}/library/busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup harbor.internal
kubectl run dnstest --rm -it --image={{value.registryHost}}/library/busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

Both must answer. If the first works and the second does not, the kubernetes plugin or the cluster domain is wrong; if the second works and the first does not, the forward path is wrong.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause All external names time out, cluster names work Upstream unreachable, or the node resolver is not the upstream SERVFAIL for one zone only That zone's forward block points at a dead server Intermittent 5s latency on every new name policy random with one broken upstream; switch to sequential CoreDNS pods OOM after a cache change TTL too high for the query volume; cache memory is proportional to names × TTL

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document CoreDNS forwarding: upstream resolvers, stub domains, conditional forwarding, split-horizon DNS for offline.

Cross-references network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md, network-matrix/coredns-forwarding.md, offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md.

docs.title: B. CoreDNS configuration
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors
        health
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
            pods insecure
            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
            ttl 30
        }
        # Upstream resolvers for non-cluster domains
        forward . 10.20.0.53 10.20.0.54 {
            except cluster.local
        }
        # Stub domains for service discovery
        stubdomains:
          svc.cluster.local:
            - 10.20.0.53
            - 10.20.0.54
        prometheus :9153
        forward . /etc/resolv.conf
        cache 30
        loop
        reload
        loadbalance
    }

docs.title: C. Upstream resolvers
docs.text: Environment Upstream Source Online 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 Internet Offline 10.20.0.53, 10.20.0.54 Internal DNS Air-gapped /etc/resolv.conf Host DNS

docs.title: D. Split-horizon DNS (offline)
docs.text:
In offline environments, CoreDNS forwards non-cluster queries to internal DNS servers that resolve from the local mirror:

forward . 10.20.0.53 {
    except cluster.local
}

docs.title: E. Conditional forwarding
docs.text:
Conditional forwarding for service discovery across clusters:

stubdomains:
  svc.east.cluster.local:
    - 10.50.0.53
  svc.west.cluster.local:
    - 10.60.0.53
