docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: This document covers Ingress TLS configuration for Kubernetes clusters using Ingress resources, cert-manager, and Let's Encrypt. It addresses certificate management, TLS termination, custom certificate deployment, and HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect policies.

docs.title: B. Requirements
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster with an Ingress controller installed (e.g., NGINX, Cilium, Contour).
  • cert-manager v1.11+ installed and configured.
  • A DNS domain reachable from the cluster (for Let's Encrypt challenges).
  • Appropriate RBAC permissions for cert-manager to create ClusterIssuer/Issuer resources.
  • Node-level access to port 80 and 443 for ACME challenges.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• cert-manager chart: harbor.internal/charts/cert-manager (v1.11.0).
  • Images: cert-manager/controller, cert-manager/webhook, cert-manager/ca-controller, cert-manager/cainjector.
  • ClusterIssuer resources must be mirrored in the internal chart repository.
  • If using external-dns, ensure it mirrors DNS records for propagated domains.

docs.title: 1. Install cert-manager
docs.text:
helm repo add jet https://charts.jetstack.io
helm repo update jet

helm install cert-manager jet/cert-manager \
  --namespace cert-manager --create-namespace \
  --version 1.11.0 \
  --set image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/cert-manager \
  --set node-drainer.enabled=false

docs.title: 2. Create the cert-manager namespace
docs.text: kubectl create namespace cert-manager

docs.title: a) Let's Encrypt production (ACME DNS-01 challenge)
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: admin@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-key
    solvers:
    - dns01:
        provider: azure
        resourceGroup: my-rg
        subscriptionID: my-sub-id

docs.title: b) Let's Encrypt staging (for testing)
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-staging.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: admin@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging-key
    solvers:
    - dns01:
        provider: azure
        resourceGroup: my-rg
        subscriptionID: my-sub-id

docs.title: c) Self-signed CA for internal/custom certificates
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: selfsigned
spec:
  selfSigned: {}

docs.title: E. TLS Termination
docs.text:
Ingress resources terminate TLS at the Ingress controller. The flow is:

  1. Client initiates an HTTPS connection to the Ingress VIP.
  2. The Ingress controller presents the TLS certificate.
  3. TLS is decrypted and the cleartext HTTP request is forwarded to the backend service.

docs.title: 1. Automatic TLS with cert-manager
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: payment-api-ingress
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - payments.example.com
    secretName: tls-payments
  rules:
  - host: payments.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: payment-api
            port:
              number: 443

docs.title: 2. Manual TLS with a pre-provisioned secret
docs.text:
# Create a TLS secret from existing certificates
kubectl create secret tls tls-manual \
  --key=key.pem \
  --cert=cert.pem \
  --namespace payments

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: internal-api-ingress
  namespace: internal
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "selfsigned"
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - internal-api.example.com
    secretName: tls-manual
  rules:
  - host: internal-api.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: internal-api
            port:
              number: 8080

docs.title: 1. Deploying a custom CA bundle
docs.text:
# Create a ConfigMap with the CA bundle
kubectl create configmap custom-ca \
  --from-file=ca.crt=/path/to/internal-ca.crt \
  -n cert-manager

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: internal-ca-bundle
  namespace: cert-manager
data:
  ca.crt: |
    -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    MIIDazCCAl+gAwIBAgIUCg+y... (truncated)
    -----END CERTIFICATE-----

docs.title: 2. Reference the CA in a ClusterIssuer
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: internal-ca
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: internal-ca-bundle
    rootKeySelector: {}
    rootCertificateSelector: {}

docs.title: 3. Issue a certificate for an internal host
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: internal-api-cert
  namespace: internal
spec:
  secretName: tls-internal-api
  issuerRef:
    name: internal-ca
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  commonName: internal-api.example.com
  dnsNames:
  - internal-api.example.com
  sans:
  - api-gateway.internal.example.com
  renewable: false

docs.title: 1. Global redirect via Ingress annotation
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-ingress
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    # Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-to: https://$host$request_uri
    # OR for Contour/Envoy:
    # ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-frontend
            port:
              number: 80

docs.title: 2. Explicit HTTP redirect route
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: redirect-ingress
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    # Redirect anything under /old-path to the HTTPS equivalent
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-to: https://$host/new-path$request_uri
spec:
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /old-path
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-frontend
            port:
              number: 80
  - host: web.example.com
    https:
      paths:
      - path: /new-path
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-frontend
            port:
              number: 443

docs.title: 3. Catch-all HTTP redirect to HTTPS
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: secure-ingress
  namespace: payments
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    # Alternatively, use a dedicated redirect Ingress with no backend
spec:
  defaultBackend:
    service:
      name: web-frontend
      port:
        number: 80
  rules:
  - host: web.example.com
    http:
      paths: []  # Explicitly disable HTTP paths
    https:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-frontend
            port:
              number: 443

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Check that the Ingress has TLS configured
kubectl get ingress -A -o yaml

# Verify the certificate is issued and valid
kubectl describe certificate -A

# Check cert-manager status
kubectl -n cert-manager get pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=cert-manager

# Test the TLS connection
openssl s_client -connect payments.example.com:443 -servername payments.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | head -20

# Verify the error budget impact
# If using SLOs: ensure TLS failures are counted as errors

docs.title: I. Known traps
docs.text:
1. ClusterIssuer vs Issuer scope — Use ClusterIssuer for cluster-wide TLS; use Issuer for namespace-scoped certificates.
  2. Propagation delay — ACME certificate issuance can take 1–5 minutes after the Ingress is updated; cert-manager does not auto-reconcile on every Ingress change.
  3. Rate limits — Let's Encrypt enforces per-domain and global rate limits. Use the staging server for development and testing.
  4. Secret mounting — cert-manager creates the TLS secret referenced in tls.secretName; do not manually manage this secret if cert-manager is the sole issuer.
  5. Default backend — Ensure the Ingress defaultBackend serves a valid page or redirect; otherwise clients may hit a 404 on HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect.
  6. DNS propagation — For DNS-01 challenges, ensure the DNS provider's propagation delay is accounted for before expecting the certificate to become ready.
  7. TLS version/cipher mismatch — Verify the Ingress controller supports the desired TLS version (1.2/1.3) and that cert-manager's issued certificates negotiate the expected protocol.

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
MetalLB provides a load-balancer implementation for type: LoadBalancer Services on bare metal, using either L2 (ARP) or BGP. Without it, a LoadBalancer Service stays pending forever outside a cloud environment.

  Service (type: LoadBalancer) -> MetalLB assigns an IP from the pool
      |
  speaker (DaemonSet) announces the IP:
     L2 mode: ARP replies on the LAN segment
     BGP mode: BGP peering with the router

docs.title: B. Requirements
docs.text:
• A dedicated IP range that is not used for anything else and is routable to the nodes.
  • Layer 2 (same VLAN) for L2 mode, or BGP peering with the router for BGP mode.
  • The nodes must be able to announce and receive the traffic.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• Helm chart: harbor.internal/charts/metallb (chart 0.16.1, app v0.16.1).
  • Images: metallb/controller and metallb/speaker, both v0.16.1.

docs.title: D. Installation
docs.text:
helm repo add metallb https://metallb.github.io/metallb/charts
helm install metallb metallb/metallb \
  --namespace metallb-system --create-namespace \
  --version 0.16.1 \
  --set image.repository=harbor.internal/platform/metallb

L2 mode (simplest):

apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: default-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 10.61.0.10-10.61.0.30
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: default-l2
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - default-pool

BGP mode (needs router peering):

apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: default-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 10.61.0.10-10.61.0.30
---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: BGPAdvertisement
metadata:
  name: default-bgp
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  ipAddressPools:
    - default-pool
  peers:
    - 10.20.0.1          # the router's BGP peer address

# Helm values for BGP
peers:
  - my-asn: 64500
    peer-asn: 64500
    peer-address: 10.20.0.1
    peer-port: 179
    my-router-id: 10.20.0.11
    password: "<from Vault>"
    password-secret:
      name: bgp-credentials
      key: password

BGP uses TCP port 179 and requires a router that peers with the node addresses. L2 mode needs no router change but requires the client and the VIP to be on the same VLAN.

docs.title: E. Integration
docs.text: Integration Mechanism LoadBalancer Services The controller assigns an IP from the pool and programs the speaker Ingress The ingress controller requests a LoadBalancer Service, or the VIP is configured statically ExternalDNS Publishes an A record for the assigned IP Cilium Cilium's loadBalancer.mode=hybrid handles the traffic forwarding; MetalLB provides the address

docs.title: F. Validation
docs.text:
# A LoadBalancer Service gets an address
kubectl -n default expose deployment nginx --port=80 --type=LoadBalancer
kubectl -n default get svc nginx
# NAME    TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP      PORT(S)
# nginx   LoadBalancer   10.61.0.10       80/TCP

# From a client on the same segment
curl http://10.61.0.10

# The speaker is announcing
kubectl -n metallb-system logs ds/speaker --tail=50
kubectl -n metallb-system get ippools,ipaddresspools,l2advertisements

Expected: the Service shows an EXTERNAL-IP from the pool and the client reaches it.

docs.title: G. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Add an IP to the pool Edit the IPAddressPool; new Services can use it, existing assignments are unaffected Remove an IP Remove it from the pool only after checking no Service holds it: kubectl get svc -A -o json and look for the address Move a Service's IP Delete the Service and recreate it; MetalLB reassigns Switch L2 to BGP Apply the BGPAdvertisement, remove the L2Advertisement, and configure the router peer Failover L2 mode: the new leader answers the ARP requests after a short delay. BGP mode: the router converges on the withdraw and re-advertise

docs.title: H. Known traps
docs.text:
1. The VIP must be on a segment the clients can reach. An IP from a different VLAN works only with BGP and a correct router configuration.
  2. L2 mode on a routed VLAN fails. ARP requests do not cross a router. Use BGP or put the clients on the same segment.
  3. IPAddressPool changes do not move existing assignments. A Service keeps its IP until it is deleted.
  4. A single-advertisement setup has a single point of failure. The leader speaks for the whole pool. For HA, run BGP with multiple peers or accept the failover delay.
  5. The MetalLB service account needs speaking permissions. The chart handles this; a custom RBAC override breaks it.

docs.title: I. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - A dedicated, documented IP range, not carved out of the pod CIDR or the node subnet. - A corresponding DNS record managed by ExternalDNS, so nothing depends on a hard-coded IP. - The pool sized for the number of Services that need external addresses, plus headroom.

Strongly recommended: - BGP where the network team can peer, because it survives a routed segment and gives a faster, cleaner failover. - Static loadBalancerIP on the Services that must have a stable address (the ingress controller, Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak). - Monitor metallb_ippool_assignments_total and alert when the pool is nearly exhausted.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Example Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources for the platform. Cilium is the CNI and supports standard NetworkPolicy plus Cilium-specific extensions.

docs.title: B. Default deny-all
docs.text:
Apply to every namespace as a baseline:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress

docs.title: C. Allow DNS
docs.text:
All pods need DNS resolution:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector: {}
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

docs.title: D. Allow ingress from specific namespace
docs.text:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-frontend
  namespace: backend
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: frontend
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080

docs.title: E. Cilium-specific: L7 policy
docs.text:
Cilium supports L7 (HTTP) policy beyond standard NetworkPolicy:

apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: l7-http-policy
  namespace: backend
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - fromEntities:
    - cluster
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "8080"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "/healthz"

docs.title: F. Verification
docs.text:
# Check NetworkPolicy exists
kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace>

# Test connectivity is blocked
kubectl run test --rm -i --tty --image=registry.internal/tools/curl:1.0 -- curl -v http://backend:8080

# Test connectivity is allowed
kubectl run test --rm -i --tty --image=registry.internal/tools/curl:1.0 -- curl -v http://backend:8080/healthz

# Check Cilium policy enforcement
cilium policy list

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document Kubernetes PriorityClass and PriorityConfiguration for pod scheduling precedence, preemption policies, and resource quota integration. Cross-references kubernetes/scheduling/resource-reservation.md §Priority classes.

docs.title: B. PriorityClass definition
docs.text:
A PriorityClass is a cluster-level object that assigns a priority to pods. Higher-priority pods are scheduled ahead of lower-priority pods and preempt them when necessary.

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: critical-pods
value: 1000000000
globalDefault: false
description: "Critical business workloads — scheduled before all other priorities"
Field Required Description value yes Integer priority value. Higher values = higher precedence. Range: -2147483648 to 2147483647 globalDefault no If true, assigns this priority to all pods without an explicit priorityClassName description no Human-readable description (visible in kubectl describe)

docs.title: Recommended priority values
docs.text: Priority class name Value Use case system-node-critical 2000000000 K8s system pods (kube-proxy, DNS, etc.) system-cluster-critical 2000000000 Cluster networking, storage controllers critical-pods 1000000000 Business-critical workloads high-priority 1000000 Important but preemptable workloads normal-pods 0 Default / best-effort workloads

docs.title: C. Preemption policies
docs.text:
When the scheduler cannot find a feasible node for a pod, it may preempt (terminate) lower-priority pods to make room. Preemption is controlled per PriorityClass via the preemptionPolicy field.

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: critical-pods
value: 1000000000
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
globalDefault: false
description: "Preempts lower-priority pods when scheduling"

docs.title: PreemptionPolicy options
docs.text: Policy Behavior PreemptLowerPriority (default) Preempts pods with lower priorityClassValue; does not preempt pods with equal or higher priority NeverPreemptLowerPriority Never preempts lower-priority pods; the pod will remain in a Pending state if no node can satisfy it

docs.title: Controlling preemption with clusterSettings
docs.text:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterSettings
metadata:
  name: scheduler
spec:
  defaultPreemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority

docs.title: D. Resource quota integration
docs.text:
Priority classes interact with resource quotas to determine which pods can be scheduled. When a namespace has a ResourceQuota, the scheduler considers:

  1. Total allocatable resources across all pods in the namespace
  2. Priority order when admitting new pods
  3. Preemption decisions based on priority differences

docs.title: Example: Namespace with resource quota and priority classes
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: critical-workloads
annotations:
  scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/critical-pods: "true"
---
apiResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: critical-quota
  namespace: critical-workloads
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "50"
    memory: "100Gi"
    pods: "20"
    requests.cpu: "40"
    requests.memory: "80Gi"

docs.title: Interaction summary
docs.text: Scenario Behavior High-priority pod exceeds quota Admission denied unless preemption removes lower-priority pods Low-priority pod in namespace with high-priority traffic May be preempted to satisfy the high-priority pod globalDefault: true PriorityClass All pods without explicit priorityClassName get this priority

docs.title: E. Default priority class configuration
docs.text:
Set a globalDefault PriorityClass to apply a baseline priority to all pods that do not specify priorityClassName. This ensures no pod falls below a minimum precedence.

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: true
description: "Baseline priority for all pods without explicit priority class"

Best practice: Do not set globalDefault: true for very high values (e.g., >1000000) as it can cause unexpected preemption behavior. Instead, explicitly set priorityClassName on critical pods.

docs.title: F. Example PriorityClass YAML
docs.text:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: critical-pods
value: 1000000000
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
description: "Critical business workloads — preempts lower-priority pods to ensure availability"

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-critical-app
spec:
  priorityClassName: critical-pods
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "512Mi"
        limits:
          cpu: "1"
          memory: "1Gi"

docs.title: G. Preemption victim selection guidance
docs.text:
When the scheduler decides which pods to preempt, it follows these rules:

  1. Select lowest total value first — Among all pods in the scheduling queue, prefer preempting pods with the lowest priorityClassValue
  2. Minimize preempted pods — Preempt the minimum number of pods needed to satisfy the higher-priority pod
  3. Respect preemptionPolicy — Pods with NeverPreemptLowerPriority are never selected; pods with PreemptLowerPriority can be selected only if their value is lower than the incoming pod's value
  4. Consider pod disruption budgets (PDBs) — Prefer preempting pods that have PDB minAvailable > 0 or no PDB at all
  5. Avoid starving system-critical pods — System pods (system-node-critical, system-cluster-critical) are never preempted even if their value is lower

docs.title: Visual flow
docs.text:
High-priority pod arrives → Scheduler checks resources →
No fit → Check preemption candidates →
  ▼
  Lowest priority value first →
  ▼
  PDB compliance check →
  ▼
  Preempt and reschedule

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document kubelet resource reservation, pod priority classes, QoS classes, topology spread constraints.

Cross-references kubernetes/control-plane/node-lifecycle.md, kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Sizing and placement.

docs.title: B. Kubelet resource reservation
docs.text:
Resource reservation reserves CPU and memory for Kubernetes system daemons:

# kubelet config
kubeletConfig:
  systemReserved:
    cpu: "100m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  kubeReserved:
    cpu: "100m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  evictionHard:
    memory.available: "500Mi"
    nodefs.available: "10%"
    nodefs.inodesFree: "5%"

docs.title: C. Priority classes
docs.text:
Priority classes determine pod scheduling precedence:

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
description: "High priority for critical workloads"

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: cluster-critical
value: 2000000000
globalDefault: false
description: "Critical cluster system pods"

docs.title: D. QoS classes
docs.text:
Kubernetes assigns QoS classes based on resource requests and limits:

QoS class Requirements OOM score Guaranteed All containers have equal requests and limits -998 Burstable At least one container has request != limit -998 to -999 BestEffort No requests or limits -1000

docs.title: E. Topology spread constraints
docs.text:
Topology spread constraints distribute pods across failure domains:

spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: myapp

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Layered controls for the cluster and the workloads on it: admission, runtime detection, image provenance, host baseline, network policy, and audit.

docs.title: B. Control layers
docs.text: Layer Tool Enforcement point Failure mode Image supply chain Trivy, Syft, Cosign CI pipeline and admission (Kyverno verifyImages) Unsigned image slips in Admission Pod Security Standards, OPA Gatekeeper, Kyverno kube-apiserver webhook Webhook down blocks writes (or is ignored) Runtime Falco Node kernel Sensor crash loses detection Secrets Vault, External Secrets Workload startup and renewal Secret rotation stalls Network CiliumNetworkPolicy, Cilium L7 policy CNI datapath Policy gap = lateral movement Host CIS baseline, SELinux/AppArmor, hardened SSH Node Compromise of the node Audit Kubernetes audit log, auditd apiserver + node Log loss = no evidence

docs.title: C. Pod Security Standards
docs.text:
Three profiles: privileged, baseline, restricted. Apply at namespace level.

# Cluster-wide defaults
kubectl label --overwrite ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-system pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged
kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-public pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged

The kube-system and kube-public namespaces stay at privileged because CNI and control-plane components require it. Every other namespace is restricted. Workloads needing less are in their own namespace with the correct label, not with a cluster-wide exemption.

Enforce the restricted profile meaning: - allowPrivilegeEscalation: false - runAsNonRoot: true - seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault or Localhost - capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] - no hostPath, no hostNetwork, no hostPID, no privileged

Enforce with an admission policy, not just the label — the label is only an audit signal by itself.

docs.title: D. OPA Gatekeeper
docs.text:
Two constraint templates are used: one blocking privileged pods, one restricting image registries. Both are deployed in audit mode first, then switched to enforce.

apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sPSPPrivilegedContainer
metadata:
  name: block-privileged
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
  parameters:
    exemptNamespaces: ["kube-system", "gatekeeper-system"]

apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sAllowedRepos
metadata:
  name: allowed-repos
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
  parameters:
    repos:
      - "harbor.internal/*"
      - "!harbor.internal/library/*"

Gatekeeper values that must be set deliberately:

# Helm values
replicas: 3
audit:
  replicas: 2
  auditInterval: 60
constraintTemplates:
  replicaCount: 3
validatingWebhookFailurePolicy: Fail        # for security namespaces

validatingWebhookFailurePolicy is the critical setting: Fail blocks writes when Gatekeeper is down, Ignore lets writes through. The recommendation is Fail for application namespaces and Ignore for the platform's own namespaces, with the exception process documented.

Verification that the failure policy is scoped per namespace uses the namespaceSelector in the webhook configuration, not a global value.

docs.title: E. Kyverno
docs.text:
Kyverno covers the policies teams write themselves. Use it for image verification and resource mutation.

apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-image-digest
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: require-digest
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Images must be pinned by digest and come from harbor.internal"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "harbor.internal/*@sha256:*"

docs.title: F. Falco
docs.text:
Falco watches kernel events. Default rules are noisy; ship a tuned ruleset.

# values.yaml (relevant parts)
driver: modern_ebpf
tty: false
auditLog: true
priority: notice
falcoctl:
  enabled: true
  config:
    rules:
      - custom-rules.yaml

Tuning rules to keep: writes to /etc, /usr/bin, /var/lib/ceph; shell spawned inside a container; unexpected setuid; Kubernetes API token reads from a container; outbound connection to a known-bad address. Remove the noisy default rules that fire on every package manager or container start.

A test rule:

- rule: Test file write to /etc
  desc: Write to /etc in any container
  condition: container and evt.type=open and open.flags=O_WRONLY and fd.name startswith /etc
  output: "Suspicious file write in container (user=%user.name container=%container.name file=%fd.name)"
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [test]

docs.title: G. Image supply chain
docs.text:
Stage Tool Command Scan Trivy trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL <image> SBOM Syft syft <image> -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json Sign Cosign cosign sign --key cosign.key <image>@sha256:... Verify Cosign cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image>@sha256:...

Pipeline order: build -> scan -> SBOM -> sign -> push to Harbor -> deploy by digest.

Deploy by digest, not by tag. A tag can be repointed; a digest cannot.

spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: harbor.internal/platform/app@sha256:abc123...

docs.title: H. Host baseline
docs.text:
CIS benchmark scripts are available for both distributions. Run them in audit mode first, then remediate.

# Oracle Linux
dnf install -y aqua-sec-cis 2>/dev/null || true   # or use the CIS-CAT tarball from the internal repo

# Ubuntu
apt install -y cis 2>/dev/null || true

The scoring baseline is recorded in security/host-baseline.md together with the deviations that are accepted and why (for example, password authentication on the console for the break-glass account, which is an accepted, monitored deviation).

docs.title: I. Audit
docs.text:
Kubernetes audit policy — Metadata level by default:

apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages:
  - RequestReceived
rules:
  - level: None
    users: ["system:kube-proxy", "system:node:agent"]
    verbs: ["watch"]
    resources: ["endpoints", "services", "endpointslices"]
  - level: None
    users: ["system:serviceaccount:kube-system:generic-garbage-collector"]
    verbs: ["get"]
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets"]
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "configmaps"]
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: "authentication.k8s.io"
        resources: ["tokenreviews"]

RequestResponse on secrets is included only if there is a strong requirement to audit secret access, and it means secret values land in the audit log. Treat that as a secret-at-rest decision: encrypt the audit log, restrict access, and consider the omitStages option.

Audit log destination: write to a local file, ship off-host quickly, and keep it out of the cluster's own failure domain.

docs.title: J. Validation
docs.text: See requirements/validation-strategy.md family C. The mandatory subset: privileged pod denied, Gatekeeper constraint enforced, Falco test alert raised, CRITICAL image blocked in CI, Cosign verification passes for signed and fails for unsigned, no secrets found in Git, TLS scan clean, break-glass login works with the IdP down.

docs.title: K. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Admission controllers in audit mode before enforce, with the violation report reviewed. - Explicit validatingWebhookFailurePolicy per namespace group, and a documented exception path. - Images deployed by digest. - Namespaces labelled for Pod Security Standards, with kube-system exempted explicitly and narrowly. - Secrets never in Git, images, or logs.

Strongly recommended: - Separate namespaces per team, with quotas and network policies per team. - Restrict pods/exec and pods/portforward via RBAC; they are equivalent to shell on the node. - Alert on audit-log pipeline failure, not only on audit-log content. - Quarterly re-run of the CIS scan and a re-review of accepted deviations.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This runbook documents Kubernetes operational troubleshooting procedures for control plane diagnostics, node issues, etcd quorum loss, API server failures, scheduler issues, and a diagnostic command reference. Follow the universal first-response sequence before proceeding to component-specific procedures.

docs.title: Universal First-Response Sequence
docs.text:
Run this before any component-specific procedure. It eliminates most misdiagnoses.

# 1. Is the problem in my session or in the system?
date; timedatectl  # skew?

# 2. Is the target reachable at all?
ping -c 3 <target-ip>        # layer 3
nc -zv <target> <port>       # layer 4
curl -vk https://<target>    # layer 5/7

# 3. Is the service actually running?
systemctl status <unit> --no-pager
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30

# 4. Is it the cluster, or the workload?
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl describe node <node>

docs.title: Universal Rules
docs.text:
1. Root cause before remediation. Restarting a component hides the symptom and loses the evidence. Collect the evidence first.
  2. One change at a time. Each change is a new hypothesis.
  3. Check the version matrix. Most "impossible" failures are a version incompatibility.
  4. Check the network matrix. Most "the service is down" reports are a firewall rule.
  5. Preserve the evidence. Copy logs before restarting anything.
  6. Never run a destructive command without explicit authorization.
  7. Record the resolution in the relevant runbook, with the command that actually fixed it.

docs.title: Diagnostic Commands by Layer
docs.text: Layer Command Healthy state Name resolution dig +short <name> The expected IP Reverse dig -x <ip> The expected hostname Time chronyc tracking Leap status normal, offset < 100 ms Reachability ping -c3 <ip> 0% loss Port nc -zv <ip> <port> Connection succeeded TLS openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername <name> Verify return code 0, correct chain Service systemctl is-active <unit> active Container kubectl get pod -o wide Running, 0 restarts Events kubectl describe pod No recent warnings Logs kubectl logs <pod> --previous The previous container's output (for crash loops) Cluster kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' All checks ok Storage kubectl get pvc Bound Admission kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations Expected configs present

docs.title: When to Escalate
docs.text:
Escalate to a second engineer when:

  • The evidence contradicts the runbook (the runbook is then wrong and must be corrected).
  • A destructive action is required and the authorization is ambiguous.
  • The failure spans two components and the boundary is unclear.
  • The same symptom returns after a documented remediation.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• kubectl commands fail with "connection refused" or "timeout"
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns failures
  • Control plane pods crash-looping
  • etcd quorum loss detected

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• API server static pod not created by kubelet
  • etcd unreachable from control plane
  • Certificate expired or wrong
  • Scheduler not scheduling
  • Controller-manager not running
  • Cloud provider integration issues

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check control plane pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-scheduler
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=controller-manager

# Check API server reachability
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check etcd member health
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# Check scheduler status
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-scheduler | tail -20

# Check controller-manager status
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=controller-manager | tail -20

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• All control plane pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all checks ok
  • etcd endpoint health: all endpoints healthy
  • Scheduler: accepting and scheduling pods
  • Controller-manager: all controllers healthy

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart control plane components: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix etcd connectivity (see etcd quorum loss section below)
  • Rotate expired control plane certificates
  • Verify cloud provider credentials and connectivity
  • Check kubelet logs for control plane registration issues

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting API server pod makes cluster temporarily unreachable
  • Restarting control plane components can cause brief availability outage
  • Certificate rotation can break existing client connections

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A | head -10

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Node not ready or ReportingStatus="False"
  • Kubelet not communicating with API server
  • High resource usage (CPU, memory, disk)
  • Container runtime failures
  • Network plugin errors

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• kubelet service stopped or failing
  • Node network configuration issues
  • Container runtime (Docker/containerd) not running
  • Disk pressure or memory pressure
  • CNI plugin misconfiguration

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check node status
kubectl get nodes <node-name>

# Check kubelet service
systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
journalctl -u kubelet -f --no-pager | tail -30

# Check container runtime
systemctl status containerd --no-pager
crictl ps -a

# Check node conditions
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A 10 Conditions

# Check kubelet logs
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50

# Check CNI plugin status
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-flannel
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-flannel

# Check disk and memory
df -h /
free -h

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• Node status: Ready
  • Kubelet service: active
  • Container runtime: running
  • All node conditions: True (MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, Ready)
  • CNI plugins: Running, 0 restarts

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart kubelet: systemctl restart kubelet
  • Restart container runtime: systemctl restart containerd
  • Address resource pressure: delete pods, expand disk
  • Reapply CNI configuration if misconfigured
  • Rejoin node to cluster if disconnected

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Restarting kubelet can cause pod evictions on the node
  • Rejoining a node can cause IP conflicts
  • Expanding disk requires careful partitioning

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes <node-name>
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -A 10 Conditions

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• API server errors: etcd cluster is unhealthy
  • kubectl commands timeout or fail
  • Unable to create/update/delete resources
  • Cluster operates in read-only mode

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• Lost etcd members (reboot, network partition)
  • etcd disk full
  • etcd configuration drift
  • Unexpected member removal

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check etcd member health
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# Check etcd member list
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

# Check etcd quorum
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  quorum status

# etcd endpoint status
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint status -w table

# Check etcd logs
journalctl -u etcd --no-pager | tail -30

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• All etcd members: healthy
  • Quorum: achieved (majority of members responding)
  • Member count: matches control-plane inventory
  • Disk usage: below threshold (typically < 80%)

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
Step 1: Identify lost members 

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list

Step 2: Add replacement member (if available) 

etcdctl member add <member-name> \
  --peer-urls=https://<member-ip>:2380 \
  --member-zone=<zone> \
  --member-site=<site> \
  --member-role=learner \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://<member-ip>:2380

Step 3: Remove lost member 

etcdctl member remove <member-id>

Step 4: Re-run Kubespray to redeploy etcd without the lost member 

# Update inventory to exclude removed member
# Re-run Kubespray to redeploy etcd

Step 5: Verify quorum after remediation 

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting a member without replacement loses quorum permanently
  • etcd data loss if not enough members remain
  • Certificate issues if member IPs change

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• kubectl commands fail with "connection refused" or "timeout"
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns failures
  • API server pod crash-looping
  • Authentication/authorization failures
  • Admission webhooks rejecting all requests

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• API server static pod not created by kubelet
  • etcd unreachable from API server
  • Certificate expired or wrong
  • Admission webhook configuration pointing to wrong service
  • etcd quorum lost

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Is API server running?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-apiserver

# Is etcd reachable?
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check API server certificate
kubectl -n kube-system secret <apiserver-cert-secret> -o yaml

# Check admission webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration

# Test authentication
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods

# Check API server audit log
kubectl get --raw='/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/configmaps/kube-apiserver-audit-settings' -o yaml

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• API server pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all checks ok
  • kubectl auth whoami returns authenticated user
  • etcd endpoint health: all endpoints healthy
  • Admission webhooks: configured and responding

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart API server: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix etcd connectivity (see etcd quorum loss section)
  • Rotate expired API server certificates
  • Fix admission webhook service references
  • Restore etcd quorum (see etcd troubleshooting)

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting API server pod makes cluster temporarily unreachable
  • Fixing admission webhooks can block all cluster operations if done wrong
  • Certificate rotation can break existing client connections

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A | head -5

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Pods not scheduled to nodes
  • Scheduler pod crash-looping
  • Pods stuck in Pending state
  • Node affinity/anti-affinity not respected
  • Taints not being handled correctly

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• Scheduler not running or unhealthy
  • All nodes have taints that prevent pod scheduling
  • Insufficient resources (CPU, memory) on nodes
  • Node selectors don't match pod requirements
  • Pod disruption budgets blocking scheduling
  • Volume provisioning failures

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check scheduler pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-scheduler
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-scheduler | tail -20

# Check pending pods and reasons
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -o wide
kubectl describe pod <pending-pod-name> -n <namespace> | grep -A 20 "Warning.*Scheduled\|Warning.*Taint"

# Check node conditions and resources
kubectl get nodes -o json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
for node in data['items']:
    name = node['metadata']['name']
    conditions = [c['type'] + ': ' + c['status'] for c in node['status']['conditions']]
    addresses = [a['address'] for a in node['status']['addresses']]
    print(f'{name}: conditions={conditions} addresses={addresses}')
"

# Check taints
kubectl get nodes -o json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
for node in data['items']:
    name = node['metadata']['name']
    taints = node['status'].get('taints', [])
    print(f'{name}: taints={taints}')
"

# Check resource limits
kubectl get nodes -o json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
for node in data['items']:
    name = node['metadata']['name']
    cpu = node['status']['capacity'].get('cpu', 'N/A')
    memory = node['status']['capacity'].get('memory', 'N/A')
    print(f'{name}: cpu={cpu} memory={memory}')
"

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• Scheduler pod: Running, 0 restarts
  • No pods stuck in Pending indefinitely
  • Nodes have appropriate resources for scheduled pods
  • Taints are intentionally applied and documented
  • Pods schedule to appropriate nodes based on requirements

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart scheduler: delete scheduler static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Remove unintended taints from nodes: kubectl taint nodes <node-name> <key>:<effect>-
  • Add more nodes or increase resource limits
  • Fix pod resource requests/limits to match available resources
  • Review and adjust pod disruption budgets
  • Ensure volume plugins are functioning for persistent volumes

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Removing taints can cause pods to schedule to inappropriate nodes
  • Restarting scheduler can cause brief scheduling disruption
  • Adding nodes requires network and storage integration

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending | head -5
kubectl get nodes -o json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
data = json.load(sys.stdin)
for node in data['items']:
    name = node['metadata']['name']
    taints = node['status'].get('taints', [])
    print(f'{name}: taints={taints}')
"
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep -v Running | head -10

docs.title: Core kubectl commands
docs.text: Purpose Command Example Check all pods kubectl get pods -A kubectl get pods -A Describe resource kubectl describe <resource> <name> kubectl describe pod my-pod -n default Check events kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp Ready check kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' Health check kubectl get --raw='/healthz' kubectl get --raw='/healthz' API server introspection kubectl get --raw='/apis/' kubectl get --raw='/apis/' Node status kubectl get nodes kubectl get nodes Node conditions kubectl describe node <name> kubectl describe node master-1 Logs (current) kubectl logs <pod> kubectl logs my-pod Logs (previous) kubectl logs <pod> --previous kubectl logs my-pod --previous Exec into container kubectl exec <pod> -c <container> kubectl exec my-pod -c my-container -- sh Port forward kubectl port-forward <pod> <local>:<remote> kubectl port-forward my-pod 8080:80

docs.text: Purpose Command Example Member health etcdctl endpoint health --cluster etcdctl endpoint health --cluster Member list etcdctl member list etcdctl member list Quorum status etcdctl quorum status etcdctl quorum status Snapshot save etcdctl snapshot save /path/to/snap.db etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/snap-$(date +%F).db Snapshot status etcdctl snapshot status /path/to/snap.db etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/snap-$(date +%F).db Defragmentation etcdctl defrag etcdctl defrag --rev 12345 Member add etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=... etcdctl member add new-mem --peer-urls=https://10.0.0.1:2380 Member remove etcdctl member remove <id> etcdctl member remove df2e8a12

docs.title: System commands
docs.text: Purpose Command Example Time sync check timedatectl timedatectl Network reachability ping -c 3 <ip> ping -c 3 10.0.0.1 Port check nc -zv <ip> <port> nc -zv 10.0.0.1 6443 DNS resolution dig +short <name> dig +short api.example.com TLS check openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername <name> openssl s_client -connect 10.0.0.1:443 -servername api.example.com Kubelet status systemctl status kubelet --no-pager systemctl status kubelet --no-pager Container runtime systemctl status containerd --no-pager systemctl status containerd --no-pager Crictl list pods crictl ps -a crictl ps -a

docs.text: Component Log path API server /var/log/pods/kube-system/kube-apiserver-* Scheduler /var/log/pods/kube-system/kube-scheduler-* Controller-manager /var/log/pods/kube-system/kube-controller-manager-* Kubelet /var/log/kubelet.log or journalctl etcd /var/log/etcd.log or journalctl Container runtime /var/log/containers/ or journalctl
