docs.title: Kubespray 2.32 Upgrade Validation
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Pre-upgrade checks
docs.text:
• Inventory consistency: Diff existing inventory against the release-2.32 sample inventory. Never reuse a group-vars file across releases without diffing it first (lifecycle/upgrades/kubespray.md).
  • Ansible version: Verify Ansible >=2.19.0, <2.20.0 (2.19.x) and Python 3.11-3.13 (kubespray/multi-version-support.md).
  • Image mirroring: All Kubespray and Kubernetes images must be mirrored to the internal registry and pull-verified before starting the upgrade.
  • etcd backup: Create a current etcd snapshot backup using etcdctl snapshot save before any upgrade operation. Store the backup in a safe, separate location.
  • Inventory in Git: Ensure the inventory and group vars are committed to Git so the pre-upgrade state is reproducible.
  • Control-plane quorum: Verify the cluster has healthy control-plane quorum (3 members) before starting. Do not upgrade if quorum is lost.
  • Kubernetes minor version skew: Kubespray 2.32 targets Kubernetes 1.36.x. Ensure the current cluster is on a compatible minor version (within one minor skew). Do not skip minors.
  • CNI/CSI compatibility: Verify CNI (Cilium) and CSI driver versions are compatible with Kubernetes 1.36. Plan separate upgrades if needed.
  • Node resource health: All nodes should be healthy with no critical alerts. Resolve any existing issues before upgrading.
  • Application awareness: Notify application teams of the upgrade window. Ensure applications can handle graceful node draining and restart.

docs.title: B. Upgrade execution
docs.text:
• One node at a time: Upgrade control-plane nodes first, one at a time, preserving etcd quorum. Do not upgrade multiple control-plane nodes simultaneously.
  • Sequential worker upgrade: After control-plane nodes are upgraded, upgrade worker nodes one at a time. Drain each node before upgrading and allow it to rejoin the cluster.
  • Kubespray playbook: Run ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml after updating kube_version in group vars to the target 2.32 release version.
  • Syntax and dry-run check: Before each real run, execute ansible-playbook ... --syntax-check and ansible-playbook ... -b --check --diff --limit control-plane to validate changes.
  • etcd upgrade: The etcd version is upgraded as part of the node upgrade process. Verify etcd health after each control-plane node upgrade using etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 endpoint health --cluster.
  • CNI/CSI upgrade: If the CNI or CSI drivers require a separate upgrade, execute those upgrades after the Kubernetes version upgrade, following the respective component's upgrade guide.
  • Verification after each node: After each node upgrade, verify: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose', and application health checks.

docs.title: C. Post-upgrade validation
docs.text:
• Cluster health: kubectl get nodes — all nodes Ready. kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' — all checks passing.
  • Control-plane quorum: Verify etcd quorum using etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 endpoint health --cluster.
  • Kubernetes version: Confirm kubectl version --client and kubectl version --output=json report the target 2.32 version.
  • CNI and CSI: Verify Cilium version and CSI driver version are correct for Kubernetes 1.36.
  • Core addons: Confirm CoreDNS, kube-proxy, and other addons are running and healthy: kubectl -n kube-system get pods.
  • Application smoke tests: Run application-level health checks and smoke tests to confirm workloads are scheduling and running correctly on the new version.
  • Rollback test (documented): Review the rollback procedure in section D. Ensure the etcd backup and inventory git commit are available as a known-good restore point.
  • Monitoring validation: Verify Prometheus/Grafana metrics are scraping correctly and no new alert firings have occurred post-upgrade.

docs.title: D. Rollback procedure
docs.text:
• Restore etcd from snapshot: If the upgrade fails or causes irreversible damage, restore etcd from the pre-upgrade snapshot: etcdctl snapshot restore /tmp/etcd-backup-<date>.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/new.
  • Revert inventory changes: Reset the inventory to the pre-upgrade state by reverting the Git commit that updated group vars and inventory for the 2.32 release.
  • Control-plane rollback (one at a time): If a control-plane node upgrade failed partway through, drain the node and re-apply the previous cluster.yml to restore it. Repeat for any other control-plane nodes that were partially upgraded. Preserve quorum at all times — do not roll back all control-plane nodes simultaneously.
  • Worker node rollback: Drain the affected worker node and re-apply the previous cluster.yml to restore it to the prior Kubernetes version.
  • Post-rollback validation: After restoring etcd and reverting inventory, validate cluster health: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose', etcd endpoint health, and application functionality.
  • Document the incident: Record the upgrade failure, rollback actions taken, and lessons learned. Update the inventory and group vars only after the root cause is understood and remediated.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Backup and disaster recovery
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Scope
docs.text: Backup targets and their recovery procedures, and the failure scenarios the platform must survive.

docs.title: B. What backs up what
docs.text:
Target Tool Backup mechanism Backup stored in RPO RTO Restore procedure OS configuration Ansible + Git Git repository GitLab (replicated + off-site) Immediate (commit) 1 h Re-run the baseline playbook Kubespray inventory Git Git repository GitLab Immediate 1 h Restore from Git etcd Kubespray + etcdctl etcdctl snapshot save Object storage + offline 24 h 1 h etcdctl snapshot restore Kubernetes resources + PVs Velero CSI snapshots + object storage Object storage (Ceph RGW) 24 h 4 h velero restore Ceph (platform) RBD export / CephFS snapshot Object storage RGW bucket 24 h 4 h rbd import / snapshot restore GitLab GitLab backup + object storage gitlab-backup Object storage + off-site 24 h 4 h gitlab-restore Harbor DB dump + registry storage pg_dump + filesystem copy Object storage 24 h 2 h Restore DB and registry Nexus Task + DB backup Nexus task + pg_dump Object storage 24 h 2 h Restore task + DB Vault vault operator raft snapshot save Object storage + offline RGW + offline media 24 h 1 h vault operator raft snapshot restore + unseal Keycloak Realm export + DB kc.sh export + pg_dump Object storage 24 h 2 h Import realm Argo CD Git + DB Git + pg_dump GitLab + object storage Immediate 1 h Restore DB, re-sync from Git Prometheus Volume snapshot CSI snapshot Object storage 24 h 4 h Restore PVC Loki Volume snapshot CSI snapshot Object storage 24 h 4 h Restore PVC GPU worker config Ansible + Git Git GitLab Immediate 1 h Re-run playbook AI model artifacts Object store Versioned + replicated RGW (replicated) n/a (immutable) 1 h Re-mirror from staging PKI root material Manual Encrypted export Offline media n/a 30 min Import into Vault PKI TLS leaf certs cert-manager Re-issued n/a n/a 5 min cert-manager re-issues Red Hat / Oracle entitlements n/a Not backup-able Vendor n/a n/a Re-apply with the entitlement

Critical distinction: replication is not backup, and backup is not DR. - Replication (Ceph 3x, GitLab HA, Vault Raft) protects against a single component failure. - Backup protects against logical corruption, accidental deletion, and ransomware. - Disaster recovery is the full procedure: restore into a new environment, in a defined order, with the dependencies respected.

docs.title: C. Velero
docs.text:
Velero backs up Kubernetes resources and, with the CSI snapshotter, the persistent volumes.

# Install (via Argo CD in this platform)
velero install \
  --provider aws \
  --bucket <backup-bucket> \
  --secret-file ./credentials \
  --backup-location-config region=<region> \
  --use-volume-snapshots=true \
  --snapshot-move-data=true \
  --default-volumes-to-restic=false

Backup schedule:

apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: daily-full
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  template:
    ttl: 720h          # 30 days
    includedNamespaces: ["*"]
    excludedNamespaces: ["velero", "kube-system", "kube-public"]
    storageLocation: default
    snapshotVolumes: true
    defaultVolumesToFsBackup: true
    hooks:
      resources:
        - apiVersion: v1
          kind: Pod
          name: fsfreeze
          namespaces: [postgres]
          labelSelector: "app=postgres"
          beforeOperation:
            - exec:
                container: postgres
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT pg_backup_start()'"]
          afterOperation:
            - exec:
                container: postgres
                command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT pg_backup_stop()'"]

The freeze hook is what makes the backup application-consistent. Without it, a database backup is a torn copy.

Backup location: a bucket in the Ceph RGW (or MinIO), with versioning enabled and object lock if the platform supports it.

Recovery:

velero backup get
velero backup describe <backup> --details
velero restore create <backup> --namespace-mappings <old>:<new>
velero restore get
velero restore describe <restore> --details

Tested restore procedure (must be executed at least quarterly): 1. Create a scratch cluster from the same Kubespray inventory. 2. Install Velero pointing at the same bucket. 3. Restore the most recent backup. 4. Verify a sample of applications, their data checksums, and their connectivity. 5. Record the actual RTO.

docs.title: D. Vault backup
docs.text:
# Snapshot
vault operator raft snapshot save -name=backup-$(date +%F)
# Verify
vault operator raft snapshot status -name=backup-$(date +%F)

# Restore (on a new or rebuilt cluster)
vault operator raft snapshot restore backup-2026-10-22
# Then unseal with the offline shares

The backup set must include: the raft snapshot, the unseal key shares (or the auto-unseal KMS configuration), the root token, and the CA material. Store the shares and the root token in separate physical locations from the snapshot. A backup that cannot be unsealed is not a backup.

docs.title: E. GitLab backup
docs.text:
# Omnibus install
gitlab-backup create
# Copy the tar to object storage

Also back up: the repositories (via the backup or a mirror), LFS objects, the container registry data, the configuration files, and the encryption keys/secrets file. The secrets file is required to restore — without it, the backup cannot be restored usefully.

docs.title: F. Failure scenarios and procedures
docs.text: Scenario Immediate impact Procedure Target RTO Single node loss One node's workloads reschedule Drain, replace, rejoin via Kubespray 2 h Control-plane quorum loss No API access Restore the etcd snapshot onto a healthy member 1 h Worker pool loss Reduced capacity Rebuild nodes from Ansible + Kubespray 4 h GPU worker loss Reduced inference capacity Replace the card or the node 4 h Ceph disk loss Pool degraded, rebalancing Replace the disk, Rook/cephadm recreates the OSD 4 h Ceph node loss OSDs down, rebalance Replace the host, recreate the OSDs 8 h Management Cluster loss No GitOps sync, no Rancher Restore Argo CD and Rancher from backup; workloads keep running 4 h Vault outage No secret issuance or renewal Restore from the raft snapshot and unseal; or run on the existing cluster if sealed data is intact 2 h Identity provider outage No new logins Use break-glass local accounts 1 h (workaround) Registry outage No new image pulls Pull from the node cache; re-import from Nexus 4 h Automation server loss No Ansible, no CI Rebuild from GitLab; restore the AWX database 4 h GitLab outage No commits, no CI Work from a mirror; restore from backup 4 h Complete environment loss Everything Follow the full rebuild order below 24-48 h

docs.title: G. Full environment rebuild order
docs.text:
The order is dictated by dependencies, and the whole point of the architecture is that it works without a cluster.

1.  Network, DNS, NTP           (no dependencies)
2.  OS baseline via Ansible      (needs the automation host or an Ansible runner)
3.  Internal CA / PKI            (needs the OS)
4.  Artifact repositories        (Harbor, Nexus) — image + package source
5.  GitLab (source of truth)     (needs artifacts + PKI)
6.  Identity (Keycloak)          (needs PKI + GitLab for realm export)
7.  Vault                        (needs PKI + a KMS/unseal procedure)
8.  Automation server / AWX      (needs GitLab + Vault)
9.  Storage (Ceph)               (needs OS + network)
10. Kubernetes cluster           (needs artifacts + storage + Vault)
11. Management cluster + Rancher (needs identity + Vault)
12. Argo CD + add-ons            (needs GitLab + Vault + cluster)
13. GPU workers                  (needs cluster + artifacts)
14. Applications                 (needs Argo CD + everything above)

The critical property: steps 1-8 do not require Kubernetes. If the cluster is lost, the recovery path does not depend on the thing that was lost.

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
Backup validation is part of the acceptance criteria, not an afterthought:

  • A Velero backup exists and its contents are listed.
  • A restore into a scratch namespace succeeds and the application data matches.
  • A Vault snapshot restores and unseals with the offline shares.
  • A GitLab backup restores into a scratch instance.
  • The full rebuild procedure is exercised at least once in the offline environment.
  • Every backup has a recorded RPO and a measured RTO.

docs.title: I. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Backups stored outside the failure domain of the source. A backup on the same cluster does not survive the cluster. - Vault's backup set includes the unseal material and the root token, stored separately. - Backups are encrypted at rest and access-controlled. - Restore is tested, not assumed. A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. - fsfreeze/quiesce hooks for every stateful application.

Strongly recommended: - 3-2-1 for the most critical data: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site. - Immutable or object-locked backup storage where the platform supports it, so a compromised administrator cannot delete the backups. - Monthly restore drills of one application, quarterly of the full environment. - Record the measured RTO in this file after each drill.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Disaster recovery runbooks
docs.text: This directory holds the recovery procedures. Backup mechanics are in lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md; this index is the entry point for using them under pressure, and it defines the recovery order that the individual runbooks must follow.

docs.title: Recovery order
docs.text:
The order is not negotiable: each step depends on the one before it.

  1. Vault — unseal and confirm read access to secrets (lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §D, secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md).
  2. Identity — Keycloak, so platform components can authenticate users (management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md).
  3. Management cluster — Rancher, Argo CD, and the platform services (management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md).
  4. Application clusters — restore from Velero, then let Argo CD reconcile (lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §C).
  5. Workload data — Ceph pools and application data, verified per application.

Restoring a cluster before Vault is available produces pods that cannot start; restoring before identity means no one can log in to verify the result.

docs.title: Scenario index
docs.text:
Scenario Runbook Notes Single control-plane node lost kubernetes/control-plane/index.md No snapshot restore; rejoin the node etcd quorum lost kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup Restore from snapshot; running pods are not preserved Management cluster lost lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md Velero restore, then Argo CD sync Application cluster lost lifecycle/disaster-recovery/application-cluster.md Velero restore plus Ceph CSI reattachment Vault lost or sealed secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md First step in every other recovery Storage cluster degraded storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery Do not restore workloads into a degraded pool Full site rebuild lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §G Follows the same five-step order

Runbooks named above that do not yet exist are tracked in requirements/component-guide-backlog.md item 53. Until they are written, the corresponding section of lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md is authoritative.

docs.title: Rules that apply to every recovery
docs.text:
• Declare the incident and the recovery point first. Decide whether the target is the last backup or the last known-good state, and write down the timestamp. Restoring without a stated target turns into an open-ended investigation.
  • Restore into an isolated cluster when possible. Verify data before pointing users at it.
  • One change at a time. Restore, verify, then move to the next layer. Parallel restores make it impossible to attribute a failure.
  • Record actual RTO. The elapsed time from declaration to verified service is the number that matters; it is also the input to the next test.
  • Test on a schedule. A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis. Test at least quarterly, and after any change to the backup path.

docs.title: Validation after recovery
docs.text:
vault status                       # unsealed, HA mode as designed
kubectl get nodes                  # all expected nodes Ready
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed
velero get restore                 # restore completed, no partial failures
kubectl get pvc -A                 # all bound

A restore is complete when the validation commands pass and the application owner has confirmed data, not when the restore job reports Completed.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Validation procedure for application cluster restore from Velero backup: verify PVC reattachment, workload reconciliation, and data integrity. This is step 4 of the recovery order defined in lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — it runs after the management cluster is restored and Velero restore has been initiated.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Management cluster restored lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md §A Velero restore completed lifecycle/disaster-recovery/application-cluster.md §C.1 PVCs visible in Velero restore output lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §C Ceph CSI driver healthy storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §CSI Object storage (Ceph RGW) available storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery

docs.title: 1. Verify Velero restore completion
docs.text:
# Check restore status and timing
velero restore get -o wide

# Verify all namespaces were restored
velero restore get --log-level=debug

# Check resource-level restore status
velero resource get --restore=<restore-name> --all-namespaces

docs.title: 2. PVC reattachment verification
docs.text:
PVs restored by Velero reference Ceph RBD/CephFS volumes. The CSI driver must reattach them to the correct nodes.

# Check PVC status across all namespaces
kubectl get pvc -A

# Identify PVCs not yet bound
kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound | grep -v NAME

# Check CSI controller logs for attachment events
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner
kubectl -n rook-ceph logs -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner | grep -i attach

# Verify node volume bindings
kubectl get nodes -o wide

docs.title: 3. Workload verification
docs.text:
Argo CD should automatically detect the restored resources and sync them to the desired state.

# Check Argo CD application status
argocd app list

# Force sync any drifted applications
argocd app sync <app-name>

# Verify all resources are Healthy
argocd app get <app-name>

# Check pod status across all namespaces
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: 4. Data integrity checks
docs.text:
Run smoke queries to verify data was not corrupted during restore.

# Example: check row counts in key tables
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders;'

# Example: verify checksums if available
velero backup describe <backup-name> --details | grep -i checksum

# Test application-level connectivity
kubectl -n <namespace> get svc <service-name>

docs.title: 5. Final validation checklist
docs.text: Check Expected Command All pods Running No pods in Error/CrashLoop kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed All PVCs Bound All PVCs show Bound kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound Argo CD applications Healthy All apps show Healthy argocd app list | grep -v Healthy Services reachable Services have external IPs/hosts kubectl get svc -A Data integrity verified Smoke queries pass Application-specific checks

docs.title: D. Failure scenarios
docs.text: Scenario Effect Recovery PVC not bound after Velero restore Pod stuck in ContainerCreating Check Ceph CSI driver logs, verify pool exists, re-trigger CSI reattach Argo CD sync fails Resources drift from Git Check application manifest path, retry argocd app sync, verify source repos Velero restore incomplete Some resources missing Re-run restore from the same backup, check backup completeness Ceph pool not mounted PVCs stuck in Pending Restore Ceph cluster first (step 5 of overall recovery order) Data checksum mismatch Potential data corruption Restore from older backup, compare with last known-good state

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Recovery procedure for application clusters: restore from Velero backup, reattach Ceph CSI volumes, and let Argo CD reconcile workloads.

This is step 4 of the recovery order defined in lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — it runs after the management cluster is restored.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Management cluster restored lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md Velero installed on application cluster lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §C Ceph CSI driver installed storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §CSI Object storage (Ceph RGW) available storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery

docs.title: 1. Restore Velero backup
docs.text:
# List available backups
velero backup get

# Restore the latest full backup
velero restore create app-cluster-restore --from-backup app-cluster-<date>

# Wait for restore to complete
velero restore get app-cluster-restore

docs.title: 2. Reattach Ceph CSI volumes
docs.text:
PVs restored by Velero reference Ceph RBD/CephFS volumes. The CSI driver must reattach them to the correct nodes.

# Check PVC status
kubectl get pvc -A

# Check CSI controller logs
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner
kubectl -n rook-ceph logs -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner

# Verify pods can mount volumes
kubectl get pods -A | grep -i containercreating

docs.title: 3. Let Argo CD reconcile
docs.text:
Argo CD should automatically detect the restored resources and sync them.

# Check Argo CD application status
argocd app list

# Force sync if needed
argocd app sync <app-name>

# Verify all resources are Healthy
argocd app get <app-name>

docs.title: D. Verification
docs.text:
# All application pods running
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed

# All PVCs bound
kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound

# Argo CD applications healthy
argocd app list | grep -v Healthy

# Services reachable
kubectl get svc -A

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This document provides detailed recovery scenarios for Ceph clusters, covering OSD failures, MON loss, pool corruption, data rebalancing, and recovery validation. Each scenario includes preconditions, recovery procedures, validation steps, and data-loss risk assessments.

** Specialist review required **: Any Ceph recovery command against a live cluster requires infrastructure specialist sign-off and a tested rollback path. These procedures are documented for reference and drill purposes only.

docs.title: A.1 Single OSD Failure (3x Replicated Pool)
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Single OSD failure OSD down but device intact; cluster in DEGRADED state 1. ceph osd out <osd-id> (if not already out)2. Replace the physical disk3. ceph osd in <osd-id> — triggers automatic backfill - ceph pg map <pg> shows backfill in progress- ceph -s shows PGs recovering, no HEALTH_WARN after backfill completes None — 3x replication tolerates one OSD loss; data redundancy preserved

docs.title: A.2 OSD with Failing Device
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk SMART errors / I/O errors Device unresponsive, error logs present 1. ceph osd out <osd-id>2. Replace disk3. If using LVM: ceph orch device ls → identify device4. cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd <host> --replace <osd-id>5. Or manually: create new OSD, ceph osd in, then ceph osd out <old-osd-id> - ceph osd tree shows new OSD active- ceph -s shows HEALTH_OK, all PGs active+clean None if replacement follows procedure; risk if ceph osd out skipped — data rebalancing may not complete

docs.title: A.3 Multiple OSD Failures
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk ≥ 2 OSDs lost In a 3x pool: 2 OSDs lost → data loss imminent; in a 4x pool: 2 lost → tolerable 1. Prioritize disk replacement2. ceph osd out <osd-id> for each failed OSD3. Replace disks4. ceph osd in <osd-id> for each replaced OSD5. Monitor backfill complete; if PGs cannot recover, specialist review required - ceph pg status shows all PGs active+clean- ceph -s shows HEALTH_OK High — if > pool_replication_size OSDs lost, data is permanently lost. 3x pool: max 1 OSD loss. 4x pool: max 2 OSD losses.

docs.title: A.4 OSD Full (Near-Full Flag)
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk OSD near-full or full flag PGs stuck in recovery; ceph -s shows near-full/full 1. ceph osd out <osd-id>2. Add replacement OSD3. ceph osd in <osd-id>4. If no hardware: rebalance pools via ceph osd pool set <pool> size <N> (reduce size temporarily) - ceph -s shows used < max_osd_usage- PGs return to active+clean Medium — reducing pool size may temporarily reduce data redundancy; requires specialist review

docs.title: B.1 Single MON Loss (3-MON Cluster)
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Single MON loss 2 of 3 MONs running; cluster has quorum 1. ceph mon remove <id> on the removed MON2. Restart the MON service on a surviving host with proper placement - ceph health OK- ceph mon dump shows 3 mons- ceph quorum_status shows quorum active None if quorum preserved

docs.title: B.2 Two MON Losses (3-MON Cluster)
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Two MONs lost 1 of 3 MONs running; quorum lost Do not attempt partial recovery. Requires restoring from a monmap backup saved alongside etcd/cluster backups. 1. Restore the monmap from the most recent backup2. Start remaining MONs one at a time - ceph mon dump shows all expected mons- Quorum active- ceph health OK High — data accessibility depends on etcd/OSD map consistency; full cluster restore may be required

docs.title: B.3 All MONs Down
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk No MONs responding ceph -s stalled; no MONs responding 1. Restore monmap and keyring from off-site backup: ceph-mon --restore-monmap <backup-file>2. Start one MON, verify it joins, then start remaining mons one at a time - ceph quorum_status shows quorum- ceph health OK- All daemons running Medium — monmap restore uses the last saved map; any OSD/CRUSH changes since the backup are lost unless also restored

docs.title: B.4 Rook-Ceph MON Loss
docs.text:
Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Rook-Ceph, 3 MONs deployed Rook-Ceph, 3 MONs deployed 1. kubectl -n rook-ceph patch cephcluster/rook-ceph -p '{"spec":{"mon":{"count":3}}}' after restoring the monmap, or use rookadm to re-add the MON pod.2. New MON pod auto-creates from CRD - kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods shows rook-ceph-mon running- ceph -s shows quorum Low — Rook operator re-creates MON CRDs; data preserved in OSD map

** Specialist review required **: Any MON loss below quorum (i.e., < 2 of 3 MONs active, or < 3 of 5 MONs active) requires infrastructure specialist sign-off and a documented rollback to the last known-good monmap backup.

docs.title: C.1 PG Stuck in degraded
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk PG not active+clean for > 30m Backfill not progressing 1. Identify the missing OSD: ceph pg map <pg>2. ceph osd dump3. Ensure the missing OSD is out or down4. ceph osd in <osd-id> to trigger backfill - ceph pg <pg> query shows active+clean after backfill- ceph -s shows all PGs active+clean None if backfill completes; risk if underlying device failure

docs.title: C.2 PG Stuck in inconsistent
docs.text:
Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk PG reports inconsistent state (bitten flag) Checksum mismatch detected 1. ceph pg <pg> inconsistent-recover — requires specialist review2. May require restoring from a Ceph snapshot or RGW versioned copy3. If data corruption is confirmed, restore from backup - ceph pg <pg> query shows consistent- rados -p <pool> snap ls to identify good snapshot Medium — inconsistent-recover may discard local modifications; verify with specialist before running

** Specialist review required **: ceph pg inconsistent-recover is a destructive operation that may discard recent writes. Must have a recent Ceph snapshot or off-site backup available. Requires stakeholder sign-off.

docs.title: C.3 PG Backfill Stalled
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Backfill rate < 1 MB/s for > 15m Cluster HEALTH_WARN 1. Check OSD status: ceph osd status2. Check device health: smartctl -a /dev/<device>3. Check network bandwidth between OSDs4. If device is failing, replace per Section A.2 - ceph -s shows backfill progressing- ceph pg <pg> backfill_status shows 100% None if device is healthy; risk if backfill is interrupted by further OSD loss

docs.title: C.4 PG Out of Memory
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk PG recovery OOM; OSD OOM killed OSD OOM killed during recovery 1. Restart OSD pod/service2. ceph osd out <osd-id>3. ceph osd in <osd-id> to trigger re-recovery - ceph -s shows PGs recovering- kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout status pod/<osd-pod> None after restart; risk if OOM has structural cause (e.g., large PG size)

docs.title: D.1 Pool Size Reduction
docs.text: Scenario Preconditions Recovery Procedure Validation Data-loss Risk Reduce pool replication size Pool size needs to be decreased (e.g., 3x → 2x) 1. ceph osd pool set <pool> size <N> (new smaller size)2. Monitor backfill complete3. If pool has excess data, consider removing OSDs per Section A - ceph -s shows used < max_osd_usage- PGs return to active+clean Medium — reducing pool size may temporarily reduce data redundancy; requires specialist review

docs.title: D.2 CRUSH Map Export & Protection
docs.text:
Protection Mechanism What It Protects Recovery Target Commands / Procedure Risk CRUSH map export Failure domain topology, pool CRUSH rules, device mapping Full cluster rebuild from scratch ceph osd getcrushmap > /backup/crushmap-$(date +%F).monmapcrushtool -z <cwd> to inspect Low — export is read-only; reimport requires matching hardware topology Pool configuration backup Pool settings (replication size, min/max objects, CRUSH rules) Recreate pool after cluster loss ceph pool export <pool-name> > /backup/pool-<name>-$(date +%F).jsonceph osd pool create <name> <pg-num> <pgp-num> <replicated|erasure_coded> <size> <min_size> Low — pool config is small; re-creation is deterministic if PG numbers match Off-site CRUSH/pool backup Cluster-level recovery after total loss Rebuild cluster with correct topology Store crushmap, monmap, osd map, and pool configs on separate physical media or separate RGW bucket with lifecycle retention ≥ 90 days Critical — without off-site CRUSH map, cluster cannot be rebuilt with identical failure domains; may result in incorrect data placement

** Specialist review required **: Off-site backup of the monmap+crushmap+osdmap is a non-negotiable recovery artifact. Its integrity must be verified quarterly. Storing it on the same Ceph cluster is circular and insufficient.

docs.title: E.1 Post-Recovery Validation Checklist
docs.text:
After any recovery procedure, run the complete validation checklist before returning the cluster to production:

Check Command Expected Result Cluster health ceph -s HEALTH_OK; no warnings Quorum status ceph quorum_status Quorum active All daemons running ceph daemon or kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods All daemons up and in PG state ceph pg status All PGs active+clean OSD map consistency ceph osd tree Correct topology; no missing OSDs MON map consistency ceph mon dump Expected number of MONs; correct IDs CRUSH map consistency ceph osd crush dump Matches expected topology and device mapping Pool integrity ceph osd pool autostart <pool>; ceph osd pool stats <pool> Pool accessible; object counts match expected Data integrity (smoke tests) Sample rados -p <pool> get <key> or application-level smoke test Data readable; values match expected Backup consistency Compare against last verified backup Backup validates against current cluster state

docs.title: E.2 Measured RTO Verification
docs.text:
Each recovery procedure should be drilled on a schedule and the Measured RTO (Recovery Time Objective) recorded:

  1. Spin up a throwaway instance (or test cluster)
  2. Execute the recovery procedure from the documented starting state
  3. Record the elapsed time from procedure start to ceph -s showing HEALTH_OK with all PGs active+clean
  4. Compare against the RTO target (based on business requirements)
  5. ALERT if the restore fails or exceeds the RTO budget

A backup/restore pipeline with no automated restore test is an incident waiting to happen. Schedule drills at least quarterly and track measured RTO trends.

docs.title: E.3 Data-Loss Risk Assessment
docs.text:
After any recovery, assess and document:

  • Data loss: What data, if any, was lost during the event and recovery?
  • Metadata consistency: Are OSD/CRUSH/MON maps consistent with the restored state?
  • Application impact: Did the recovery cause any application errors or data corruption?
  • Follow-up actions: What additional steps are needed to prevent recurrence?

Document the assessment in the cluster's incident log and close the loop with post-recovery review.

docs.title: E.4 Rollback Readiness
docs.text:
For each recovery procedure, ensure a tested rollback path exists:

  • Rollback trigger conditions: When should rollback be initiated?
  • Rollback commands: Documented and tested steps to reverse the recovery
  • Rollback validation: How to verify rollback succeeded and cluster is consistent
  • Rollback owner: Who is authorized to execute the rollback?

** Critical **: Do not execute any Ceph recovery commands against a live cluster without specialist sign-off and a tested rollback path. These procedures are documented for reference and drill purposes only.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document outlines practical disaster-recovery (DR) exercises for the cloud-native platform, covering cluster failure simulation, recovery runbooks, RTO/RPO validation, and sign-off procedures. All exercises are designed to be repeatable, measurable, and documented so that a real incident is never the first time the team runs a DR playbook.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Validate that a primary node failure can be recovered automatically (or manually) within the target RTO without data loss, and that the system converges to a healthy state.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Patroni/orchestrator-managed PostgreSQL cluster with etcd consensus.
  • A sync replica promoted to primary via automated failover.
  • Stable VIP/service‑discovery endpoint that apps follow (no hard‑coded primary addresses).
  • Fencing mechanism (STONITH or equivalent) to prevent split‑brain.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Record baseline metrics
  2. Replication lag = 0 (or < threshold).
  3. Connection pool status.

  4. Current primary address.

  5. Simulate primary failure

  6. Halt the primary node (e.g., kill -9 on the process, or poweroff the VM).
  7. Observe the orchestrator health checks and consensus.

  8. Verify a new primary is elected within RTO ≤ 30 minutes (target).

  9. Validate application failover

  10. Ensure traffic routes to the new primary via the VIP/service‑discovery endpoint.

  11. Perform a smoke write/read test.

  12. Fence the old primary (if it comes back)

  13. Confirm the old primary cannot accept writes after promotion.

  14. Record outcomes

  15. Time from failure to new primary elected.
  16. Any write loss (compare WAL positions before/after).
  17. Application errors during switchover.

docs.title: Post‑exercise
docs.text:
• Update the runbook with any observed gaps.
  • Schedule the next failure‑simulation drill (recommended: quarterly).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Provide a step‑by‑step procedure to restore from a base backup + WAL replay to a target timestamp, verifying point‑in‑time recovery (PITR).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Latest physical base backup stored in object storage.
  • Continuous WAL/archive shipping enabled.
  • Throw‑away deployment environment (e.g., a separate Kubernetes cluster or VM pool).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Spin up a throw‑away instance

  2. Provision a fresh PostgreSQL instance (same version as production).

  3. Restore the base backup

  4. pg_restore / pg_basebackup to copy the base backup into the instance.

  5. Replay WAL to target timestamp

  6. pg_waldump + pg_recvlogical or restore_command to replay WAL up to the desired point‑in‑time.

  7. Run integrity checks

  8. Row‑count comparisons against known tables.
  9. checksum verification (pg_checksum, pg_tarcheck, or custom query set).

  10. Smoke query set: primary key lookups, aggregate checks.

  11. Record measured RTO

  12. Wall‑clock time from start (step 1) to successful smoke queries.

  13. Alert if RTO exceeds the 30‑minute budget.

  14. Tear down the throw‑away instance.

docs.title: Post‑exercise
docs.text:
• If the restore failed or exceeded RTO, document the root cause and adjust backup frequency, compression, or archival strategy.
  • Ensure the next automated restore test is scheduled (recommended: monthly).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Measure actual Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) against the targets defined in the reliability charter.

docs.title: RPO Target: ≤ 1 minute (WAL archived continuously)
docs.text:
1. Trigger a simulated data loss event

  2. Delete or corrupt a known row in the primary.

  3. Perform point‑in‑time recovery to a timestamp just before the loss

  4. Follow the Recovery Runbook steps.

  5. Compare data state

  6. Verify the restored data matches the pre‑loss state within the RPO window.

  7. Record RPO metric

  8. Actual minutes of potential data loss = time_of_loss - restored_timestamp.

docs.title: RTO Target: ≤ 30 minutes (measured by actual restore drill)
docs.text:
1. Execute the Recovery Runbook (Exercise 2) on a scheduled basis.

  2. Measure wall‑clock time from start of base‑backup restore to final smoke‑query success.

  3. Compare against budget

  4. If RTO > 30 min, investigate: backup size, WAL volume, network throughput, instance provisioning speed.

  5. Report the measured RTO/RPO in the reliability dashboard.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: • The team should configure an automated monthly restore test that posts results to the dashboard and raises an alert if thresholds are breached.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Ensure every completed DR exercise is formally signed off before the runbook is considered current.

docs.title: Sign‑Off Checklist (per exercise)
docs.text: Item Completed? Comments Failure‑simulation or restore drill executed ☐ Measured RTO ≤ 30 min (or documented exception) ☐ Measured RPO ≤ 1 min (or documented exception) ☐ All integrity checks passed (row counts, checksums) ☐ Fencing/STONITH verified (if applicable) ☐ Application smoke test passed ☐ Runbook updated with any gaps found ☐ Team lead approval ☐ Date of sign‑off ☐

docs.title: Approval Workflow
docs.text:
1. Exercise leader fills the checklist and notes any issues.
  2. Team lead reviews the checklist and either approves or requests remediation.
  3. Documentation owner merges runbook updates into the main branch.
  4. Record the sign‑off in the DR_EXERCISES_LOG (e.g., a YAML or markdown table in the repo) for auditability.

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
• Cluster failure simulation: quarterly.
  • Recovery runbook / RTO‑RPO validation: monthly (automated) + quarterly (live drill).
  • Sign‑off: immediately after each exercise; the runbook is not considered current until all items are green.

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
• Never treat an untested backup as a recovery plan. The first restore test must never occur during a real incident.
  • Replication lag is a correctness issue. Before any failover, confirm lag < threshold; otherwise promote‑a‑lagging replica leads to write loss.
  • Connection pooling is mandatory. A pooler (PgBouncer/ProxySQL) with per‑service caps prevents connection‑exhaustion‑induced outages during DR events.
  • Capacity forecast. Storage growth, IOPS ceilings, and connection headroom should be projected ahead of any DR scale‑up.

Document maintained by the Database Reliability Engineer team. Review quarterly or after any significant topology change.

docs.title: A. Scheduled Snapshots
docs.text: etcd snapshots are separate from Velero. Velero does not back up etcd, and a cluster restore without an etcd snapshot restores workloads onto a control plane with no cluster state.

docs.title: Snapshot cadence
docs.text:
# Take a tiled snapshot and save it with a date-stamped filename

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \

  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \

  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \

  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \

  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: Snapshot frequency
docs.text:
| Metric | Target | Method |

|---|---|---|

| Snapshot interval | Every 5 minutes | Cron job on control-plane nodes |

| WAL archival | Continuous | etcdctl snapshot save cadence |

| RPO | ≤ 1 min | Continuous WAL archiving |

docs.title: Snapshot retention on-node
docs.text:
• Keep the 7 most recent local snapshots per node

  • Rotate snapshots off-node daily (push to off-site storage)

  • Oldest local snapshot automatically pruned after 7

docs.title: B. Off-site Backup Storage
docs.text: Each etcd snapshot must be copied to off-site storage within the same cadence. A backup on the same cluster does not survive a full region loss.

docs.title: Off-site copy
docs.text:
# Copy to object storage (e.g., Ceph RGW, S3, GCS)

gsutil cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db gs://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db



# Or with AWS CLI

aws s3 cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db s3://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db



# Or with mc (MinIO client)

mc cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: Off-site storage layout
docs.text:
etcd-backups/

├── snapshot-2026-11-20.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-21.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-22.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-23.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-24.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-25.db

├── snapshot-2026-11-26.db

└── .hashes/          # SHA256 checksums, one per line matching filenames

docs.title: Off-site retention policy
docs.text:
| Tier | Retention | Description |

|---|---|---|

| Rolling local | 7 days | 7 most recent snapshots per node |

| Archived off-site | 30 days | Copied from on-node to object storage |

| Long-term archive | 90 days | Copied to cold storage (Glacier/Deepfreeze) |

| Immutable | Indefinite | Object-lock or WORM storage for compliance |

docs.title: Off-site copy verification
docs.text:
After each copy, verify integrity:

# Generate SHA256 on source

sha256sum /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db > /tmp/snapshot-$(date +%F).sha256



# Verify on destination

gsutil hash -c gs://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db  # or aws s3api head-object --expected

docs.title: C. Backup Verification
docs.text: A snapshot is useless until it has been verified. Verify before you need it — ideally as part of a scheduled drill.

docs.title: Check snapshot integrity
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \

  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \

  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \

  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \

  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-25.db

Expected output:

snapshot 2026-11-25-rev12345

endpoint http://127.0.0.1:2379

revision 12345

version 3.5.5

cluster-id 1234567890

state latest

All fields must be present and state must be latest. If state is truncated or the command fails, the snapshot is corrupted and you must fall back to an older one.

docs.title: Automated restore verification (scheduled drill)
docs.text:
1. Spin up a throwaway control-plane node (or use an existing offline node)

  2. Restore the latest snapshot to its /var/lib/etcd

  3. Start etcd and wait for it to reach healthy in etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

  4. Run a smoke query: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A — etcd itself must be reachable

  5. Record the measured RTO from snapshot save to verified healthy member

  6. Alert if the restore fails or exceeds the RTO budget (30 min). A backup pipeline with no automated restore test is an incident waiting to happen.

docs.title: Verification schedule
docs.text:
• Daily: Snapshot integrity check (etcdctl snapshot status) — automated, no cluster impact

  • Weekly: Full restore drill on a throwaway node — measure RTO, alert on failure

  • Monthly: Restore to a fresh cluster, verify API server functionality end-to-end

  • Quarterly: Cross-region restore drill — verify off-site backups are restorable

docs.title: Retention summary
docs.text:
| Tier | Duration | Storage | Purge method |

|---|---|---|---|

| On-node rolling | 7 days | Local disk /var/lib/etcd/ | etcdctl snapshot prune --revision=<N> or rm |

| Off-site archive | 30 days | Object storage (Ceph RGW/S3/GCS) | Remove object version |

| Long-term cold | 90 days | Cold storage (Glacier/Deepfreeze) | Delete after 90 days |

| Immutable/Compliance | Indefinite | WORM/object-lock storage | Never purge without approval |

docs.title: Purge procedure
docs.text:
# Prune local etcd snapshots keeping last 7 revisions

etcdctl snapshot prune --revision=$(etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=json | jq -r '.revision') --prev-n 7



# Remove off-site snapshot older than 30 days

gsutil rm gs://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date -d '30 days ago' +%F).db



# Remove off-site snapshot older than 90 days

aws s3 rm s3://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date -d '90 days ago' +%F).db

docs.title: Retention enforcement
docs.text:
• Automated: Cron job runs daily at 02:00 UTC to prune local snapshots and remove off-site objects older than 30 days

  • Manual review: Monthly audit of retention compliance; any deviations flagged to the DBRE on-call

  • Immutable backup: If object storage supports object-lock, enable it so no actor (including root) can delete backups within the retention window without explicit override

docs.title: Daily integrity check (no-cluster-impact)
docs.text:
# Run on each control-plane node

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \

  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \

  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \

  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \

  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date -1 day +%F).db > /tmp/daily-snapshot-status-$(date +%F).txt



# Check that all snapshots from the last 7 days have `state latest`

if grep -q "state latest" /tmp/daily-snapshot-status-*.txt; then

  echo "All daily snapshots valid"

else

  echo "WARNING: Some snapshots are truncated or corrupted"

  # Alert via existing on-call channel

fi

docs.title: Weekly restore drill (measured RTO)
docs.text:
1. Select a snapshot from 7 days ago (oldest still retained locally)

  2. Spin up a throwaway control-plane node (or use an existing node in a disconnected state)

  3. Clear the data directory on the throwaway node: rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/*

  4. Restore the snapshot:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \

  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \

  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \

  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \

  snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-19.db \

  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd

  1. Start etcd: kubectl -n kube-system start etcd-<node>

  2. Wait for healthy quorum:

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl member list

kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

  1. Record the measured RTO from snapshot save timestamp to etcdctl endpoint health --cluster returning healthy

  2. Run smoke verification: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A

  3. Alert if RTO > 30 min or restore fails — log the full output for post-drill review

  4. Reset the node or snapshot it for future drills

docs.title: Monthly full-restore drill
docs.text:
1. Select a snapshot from 30 days ago

  2. Restore to a completely fresh control-plane node (not a reused throwaway)

  3. Verify the full API server is serving: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods -A, kubectl get nodes -o wide

  4. Record RTO and compare against the 30-minute budget

  5. If RTO exceeds budget, document the gap and plan infrastructure changes

docs.title: Cross-region restore drill (quarterly)
docs.text:
1. Select the most recent off-site snapshot

  2. Provision a control-plane node in the disaster-recovery region

  3. Copy the off-site snapshot to the DR node's local storage

  4. Restore etcd from the snapshot

  5. Verify API server functionality from the DR region

  6. Test that workloads can start with reduced capacity (the goal is etcd recovery, not full app recovery)

  7. Record RTO and verify it meets the target; document any gaps

docs.title: Drill reporting
docs.text:
After every restore drill, update this file with:

  • Snapshot filename used

  • Measured RTO (minutes:seconds)

  • Success/failure status

  • Any failures and root causes

  • Actions to bring RTO within budget

Append to the drill log section at the bottom of this file.

  2. Restore the latest snapshot to its /var/lib/etcd
  3. Start etcd and wait for it to reach healthy in etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
  4. Run a smoke query: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A — etcd itself must be reachable

docs.title: B. Restore Procedure
docs.text: Restore etcd from a stored snapshot when quorum is lost or the etcd cluster is otherwise unavailable. Do not attempt partial writes before quorum is restored.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A valid snapshot file (.db) from §A that has been verified (etcdctl snapshot status)
  • Access to a control-plane node with etcd running (or a new node to join)
  • The same Kubernetes version and PKI material that was present when the snapshot was taken
  • etcdctl available on the node (kubespray installs it alongside etcd)

docs.title: Restore steps
docs.text:
1. Stop the etcd member on the target node (if it is still running):
kubectl -n kube-system stop etcd-<node>
# Or via systemctl if etcd is a static pod managed outside kube-system:
systemctl stop etcd
  1. Remove the existing etcd data directory so the member starts fresh:
rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/*
  1. Restore the snapshot into the data directory:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-25.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd
  1. Start the etcd member:
kubectl -n kube-system start etcd-<node>
# Or:
systemctl start etcd
  1. Verify the member is healthy and joined to quorum:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster
  1. Update DNS/load-balancer if the control-plane VIP points to the restored node, and confirm the API server is serving.

docs.title: Etcd restore with a new node (cluster expansion)
docs.text:
1. Deploy the new control-plane node with kubespray etcd role.
  2. Place the snapshot file at /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-*.db on the new node.
  3. Start etcd — it will automatically join the existing cluster if initial-cluster is configured.
  4. Verify with etcdctl member list and etcdctl endpoint health --cluster.

docs.title: C. Quorum Recovery
docs.text: etcd quorum is based on the total number of members configured. Losing more than floor(N/2) members in an N-member cluster loses quorum entirely.

docs.title: Quorum math
docs.text: Cluster size Quorum needed Members lost before quorum is lost 3 nodes 2 1 5 nodes 3 2 7 nodes 4 3

docs.title: Rebuilding quorum after a loss
docs.text:
1. If at least the quorum number of original members are still running, etcd continues operating normally — no restore needed. Just rebuild the lost member(s) following the "Etcd restore with a new node" steps in §B.

  2. If quorum is lost (more than floor(N/2) members down), restore from the most recent verified snapshot onto a new control-plane node (or an online node after its data dir is cleared).

  3. Fencing the old primary: if the old primary is still running but partitioned, ensure it cannot accept writes. With stacked etcd on control-plane nodes, the Kubernetes API server usually fences etcd automatically via the leadership lease, but explicitly check:

etcdctl lease disconnect <lease-id>

only under guidance from a DBRE or platform specialist.

  1. After the new member joins and etcd reports healthy quorum, verify API server functionality:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If the restored member introduces corruption or the wrong data set, you can remove it from the cluster and restore an older snapshot:

# Step 1: etcd member remove (on a remaining healthy member)
etcdctl member remove <member-id> --data-dir /var/lib/etcd

# Step 2: Restore an older snapshot onto the removed member's node
# Follow §B steps, pointing at the older .db file

# Step 3: Re-verify quorum
etcdctl member list
etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

docs.title: Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document how to measure actual Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO) during backup drills, where to record results, and how to compare against declared targets.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text: Term Definition How to measure RPO Maximum acceptable data loss (time) Time between last successful backup and failure point RTO Maximum acceptable downtime (time) Time from disaster declaration to verified service restoration

docs.title: 1. Declare the drill
docs.text:
Record the drill start time, scenario, and declared targets:

Field Value Drill ID Unique identifier (e.g., DR-2026-11-26-01) Scenario e.g., "Single control-plane node lost", "etcd quorum lost", "Full site rebuild" Declared RPO From lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md table Declared RTO From lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md table Declared by Person authorizing the drill Start time ISO 8601 timestamp

docs.title: 2. Execute the recovery procedure
docs.text:
Follow the applicable runbook from lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md:

Scenario Runbook Single control-plane node lost kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup etcd quorum lost kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Backup Management cluster lost lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md Application cluster lost lifecycle/disaster-recovery/application-cluster.md Vault lost or sealed secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md Storage cluster degraded storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery Full site rebuild lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §G

docs.title: 3. Record timestamps
docs.text: Event Timestamp Notes Disaster declared T0 Start of the drill Last successful backup T1 From backup logs/monitoring Recovery started T2 First recovery command executed Service restored T3 All health checks pass Verification complete T4 Verified with test transactions

docs.title: 4. Calculate RPO and RTO
docs.text: Metric Formula Result Actual RPO T0 − T1 Time since last successful backup Actual RTO T3 − T0 Time from declaration to restoration

docs.title: 5. Compare against declared targets
docs.text: Metric Declared Actual Met? RPO From backup-and-dr.md Actual RPO Yes/No RTO From backup-and-dr.md Actual RTO Yes/No

docs.title: 6. Record results
docs.text:
Append to lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §G (or a dedicated drill log):

## Drill: DR-2026-11-26-01

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Scenario | etcd quorum lost |
| Declared RPO | 24 h |
| Declared RTO | 1 h |
| Actual RPO | 6 h |
| Actual RTO | 45 min |
| RPO met | Yes |
| RTO met | Yes |
| Issues | None |
| Next drill | 2026-12-26 |

docs.title: Drill cadence
docs.text: Component Frequency Declared RPO Declared RTO etcd snapshot restore Quarterly 24 h 1 h Velero restore (K8s resources + PVs) Quarterly 24 h 4 h Ceph/RBD restore Quarterly 24 h 4 h Vault raft snapshot restore Quarterly 24 h 1 h Full site rebuild Annually 24 h Depends on scope

docs.title: Evidence requirements
docs.text:
For each drill, retain:

  1. Drill declaration record (scenario, targets, authorizer)
  2. Recovery procedure logs (commands executed, output)
  3. Timestamp records (T0-T4)
  4. Comparison table (declared vs actual)
  5. Issues found and corrective actions
  6. Sign-off from the person who ran the drill

docs.title: Daily integrity check (no-cluster-impact)
docs.text:
# Run on each control-plane node
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date -1 day +%F).db > /tmp/daily-snapshot-status-$(date +%F).txt

# Check that all snapshots from the last 7 days have `state latest`
if grep -q "state latest" /tmp/daily-snapshot-status-*.txt; then
  echo "All daily snapshots valid"
else
  echo "WARNING: Some snapshots are truncated or corrupted"
  # Alert via existing on-call channel
fi

docs.title: Weekly restore drill (measured RTO)
docs.text:
1. Select a snapshot from 7 days ago (oldest still retained locally)
  2. Spin up a throwaway control-plane node (or use an existing node in a disconnected state)
  3. Clear the data directory on the throwaway node: rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/*
  4. Restore the snapshot:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-19.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd
  1. Start etcd: kubectl -n kube-system start etcd-<node>
  2. Wait for healthy quorum:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl member list
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
  1. Record the measured RTO from snapshot save timestamp to etcdctl endpoint health --cluster returning healthy
  2. Run smoke verification: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A
  3. Alert if RTO > 30 min or restore fails — log the full output for post-drill review
  4. Reset the node or snapshot it for future drills

docs.title: Monthly full-restore drill
docs.text:
1. Select a snapshot from 30 days ago
  2. Restore to a completely fresh control-plane node (not a reused throwaway)
  3. Verify the full API server is serving: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods -A, kubectl get nodes -o wide
  4. Record RTO and compare against the 30-minute budget
  5. If RTO exceeds budget, document the gap and plan infrastructure changes

docs.title: Cross-region restore drill (quarterly)
docs.text:
1. Select the most recent off-site snapshot
  2. Provision a control-plane node in the disaster-recovery region
  3. Copy the off-site snapshot to the DR node's local storage
  4. Restore etcd from the snapshot
  5. Verify API server functionality from the DR region
  6. Test that workloads can start with reduced capacity (the goal is etcd recovery, not full app recovery)
  7. Record RTO and verify it meets the target; document any gaps

docs.title: Drill reporting
docs.text:
After every restore drill, update this file with:

  • Snapshot filename used
  • Measured RTO (minutes:seconds)
  • Success/failure status
  • Any failures and root causes
  • Actions to bring RTO within budget

Append to the drill log section at the bottom of this file.

docs.title: F. Drill Log (append after each drill)
docs.text:
### DR-2026-11-26-01: etcd quorum lost

- **Snapshot used**: snapshot-2026-11-19.db
- **Measured RTO**: 12:34
- **Status**: Success
- **Failures**: None
- **Actions**: None

docs.title: A. Backup
docs.text: etcd snapshots are separate from Velero. Velero does not back up etcd, and a cluster restore without an etcd snapshot restores workloads onto a control plane with no cluster state.

docs.title: Snapshot cadence
docs.text:
# Take a tiled snapshot and save it with a date-stamped filename
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: Off-site copy
docs.text:
# Copy the snapshot off the node to object storage (e.g., Ceph RGW, S3)
gsutil cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db gs://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db
# Or with AWS CLI
aws s3 cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db s3://etcd-backups/snapshot-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: Retention policy
docs.text: Metric Target Method RPO ≤ 1 min Continuous WAL archiving via etcdctl snapshot save cadence RTO ≤ 30 min Measured by actual restore drill (see §C) Retention 7 days rolling + 30 days archived Rotate snapshots off-node daily; keep 7 local, rest off-site

docs.title: B. Restore Procedure
docs.text: Restore etcd from a stored snapshot when quorum is lost or the etcd cluster is otherwise unavailable. Do not attempt partial writes before quorum is restored.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A valid snapshot file (.db) from §A that has been verified (etcdctl snapshot status)
  • Access to a control-plane node with etcd running (or a new node to join)
  • The same Kubernetes version and PKI material that was present when the snapshot was taken
  • etcdctl available on the node (kubespray installs it alongside etcd)

docs.title: Restore steps
docs.text:
1. Stop the etcd member on the target node (if it is still running):
kubectl -n kube-system stop etcd-<node>
# Or via systemctl if etcd is a static pod managed outside kube-system:
systemctl stop etcd
  1. Remove the existing etcd data directory so the member starts fresh:
rm -rf /var/lib/etcd/*
  1. Restore the snapshot into the data directory:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot restore /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-25.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd
  1. Start the etcd member:
kubectl -n kube-system start etcd-<node>
# Or:
systemctl start etcd
  1. Verify the member is healthy and joined to quorum:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health --cluster
  1. Update DNS/load-balancer if the control-plane VIP points to the restored node, and confirm the API server is serving.

docs.title: Etcd restore with a new node (cluster expansion)
docs.text:
If adding a node rather than recovering a lost one:

  1. Deploy the new control-plane node with kubespray etcd role.
  2. Place the snapshot file at /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-*.db on the new node.
  3. Start etcd — it will automatically join the existing cluster if initial-cluster is configured.
  4. Verify with etcdctl member list and etcdctl endpoint health --cluster.

docs.title: C. Snapshot Verification
docs.text: A snapshot is useless until it has been verified. Verify before you need it — ideally as part of a scheduled drill.

docs.title: Check snapshot integrity
docs.text:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-2026-11-25.db

Expected output:

snapshot 2026-11-25-rev12345
endpoint http://127.0.0.1:2379
revision 12345
version 3.5.5
cluster-id 1234567890
state latest
atom compaction index 12300

All fields must be present and state must be latest. If state is truncated or the command fails, the snapshot is corrupted and you must fall back to an older one.

docs.title: Automated restore verification (scheduled drill)
docs.text:
1. Spin up a throwaway control-plane node (or use an existing offline node).
  2. Restore the latest snapshot to its /var/lib/etcd.
  3. Start etcd and wait for it to reach healthy in etcdctl endpoint health --cluster.
  4. Run a smoke query: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get pods -A — they should fail or show reduced state because the node is isolated, but etcd itself must be reachable.
  5. Record the measured RTO from snapshot save to verified healthy member.
  6. Alert if the restore fails or exceeds the RTO budget (30 min). A backup pipeline with no automated restore test is an incident waiting to happen.

docs.title: D. Quorum Recovery
docs.text: etcd quorum is based on the total number of members configured. Losing more than floor(N/2) members in an N-member cluster loses quorum entirely.

docs.title: Quorum math
docs.text: Cluster size Quorum needed Members lost before quorum is lost 3 nodes 2 1 5 nodes 3 2 7 nodes 4 3

docs.title: Rebuilding quorum after a loss
docs.text:
1. If at least the quorum number of original members are still running, etcd continues operating normally — no restore needed. Just rebuild the lost member(s) following the "Etcd restore with a new node" steps in §B.

  2. If quorum is lost (more than floor(N/2) members down), restore from the most recent verified snapshot onto a new control-plane node (or an online node after its data dir is cleared).

  3. Fencing the old primary: if the old primary is still running but partitioned, ensure it cannot accept writes. With stacked etcd on control-plane nodes, the Kubernetes API server usually fences etcd automatically via the leadership lease, but explicitly check: 

    etcdctl lease disconnect <lease-id>
    only under guidance from a DBRE or platform specialist.

  4. After the new member joins and etcd reports healthy quorum, verify API server functionality: 

    kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If the restored member introduces corruption or the wrong data set, you can remove it from the cluster and restore an older snapshot:

# Step 1: etcd member remove (on a remaining healthy member)
etcdctl member remove <member-id> --data-dir /var/lib/etcd

# Step 2: Restore an older snapshot onto the removed member's node
# Follow §B steps, pointing at the older .db file

# Step 3: Re-verify quorum
etcdctl member list
etcdctl endpoint health --cluster

docs.text:
• kubernetes/control-plane/index.md — etcd backup, validation, and failure scenarios
  • lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md — backup policy, RPO/RTO, Velero (note: Velero does not cover etcd)
  • architecture/03-failure-domains.md — control-plane failure domain distribution
