docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the full site rebuild procedure: restore the entire platform from backups into a new environment, following the defined recovery order.

This is the most severe disaster scenario — every component must be restored in the correct dependency order.

Cross-references lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md §Recovery order and all individual runbooks.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Vault raft snapshot available lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §Vault Unseal keys (3 of 5 shares) Offline storage, key holders GitLab repository accessible (replicated + off-site) lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §GitLab Object storage (Ceph RGW) available storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery New hardware ready (bare metal or VMs) automation/terraform/vsphere.md OS images mirrored to internal registry offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md Kubespray checkout mirrored internally kubespray/multi-version-support.md

docs.title: C. Rebuild order (non-negotiable)
docs.text:
Each step depends on the one before it. Do not skip steps.

Step Component Runbook Depends on 1 Vault secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md — 2 Identity (Keycloak) management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md Vault 3 Management cluster lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md Vault, Identity 4 Application clusters lifecycle/disaster-recovery/application-cluster.md Management cluster 5 Workload data (Ceph pools) storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery Application clusters

docs.title: Step 1: Rebuild Vault
docs.text:
1. Provision new Vault hosts (Terraform + Ansible)
  2. Install Vault from internal registry
  3. Unseal Vault with 3 of 5 shares
  4. Restore from raft snapshot
  5. Verify: vault status shows unsealed, vault kv list secret/platform/ works

docs.title: Step 2: Rebuild Identity (Keycloak)
docs.text:
1. Provision Keycloak hosts
  2. Install Keycloak from internal registry
  3. Configure Keycloak OIDC clients (from Vault secrets)
  4. Import realm configuration from backup
  5. Verify: curl https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform/.well-known/openid-configuration returns valid JSON

docs.title: Step 3: Rebuild Management Cluster
docs.text:
1. Provision management cluster nodes (3 control-plane + 3 infra workers)
  2. Install OS from internal mirror
  3. Deploy Kubespray cluster (release-2.32)
  4. Restore Rancher from Velero backup
  5. Restore Argo CD from Git + DB
  6. Restore Harbor, Nexus, GitLab
  7. Verify: kubectl get nodes shows all Ready, Rancher API reachable

docs.title: Step 4: Rebuild Application Clusters
docs.text:
1. Provision application cluster nodes
  2. Install OS from internal mirror
  3. Deploy Kubespray cluster (release-2.32)
  4. Register clusters with Rancher (generate new registration tokens)
  5. Restore from Velero backup
  6. Reattach Ceph CSI volumes
  7. Let Argo CD reconcile workloads
  8. Verify: kubectl get pods -A shows all Running, Argo CD applications Healthy

docs.title: Step 5: Restore Workload Data
docs.text:
1. Verify Ceph cluster health: ceph health shows HEALTH_OK
  2. Restore Ceph pools from backup (RBD import, CephFS snapshot restore)
  3. Verify PVCs bind successfully
  4. Verify application data is accessible

docs.title: E. Verification checklist
docs.text:
# 1. Vault
vault status | grep "Sealed.*false"
vault kv list secret/platform/

# 2. Identity
curl -sf https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform/.well-known/openid-configuration

# 3. Management cluster
kubectl get nodes
kubectl -n cattle-system get deployment rancher
kubectl -n argocd get deployment argocd-server

# 4. Application clusters
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed
kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound
argocd app list | grep -v Healthy

# 5. Storage
ceph health
kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound

docs.title: E. Rollback
docs.text: A full site rebuild has no rollback — if the rebuild fails at any step, restore from the most recent backup and retry. Document the failure point and corrective action.

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:
• lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — Recovery order (step 5)
  • lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md — Backup mechanics and RPO/RTO
  • secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md — Vault recovery (step 1)
  • management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md — Identity recovery (step 2)
  • lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md — Management cluster recovery (step 3)
  • lifecycle/disaster-recovery/application-cluster.md — Application cluster recovery (step 4)
  • storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery — Ceph recovery (step 5)

docs.title: A. Velero Backup Configuration
docs.text: Velero is the primary mechanism for backing up Kubernetes resources and PVCs. Without it, a cluster loss means complete workload data loss.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Install Velero with an object storage bucket (Ceph RGW, S3, or GCS)
velero install \
  --provider aws \
  --bucket velero-backups \
  --secret-file <credentials-file> \
  --backup-location-config region=us-east-1 \
  --snapshot-location-config region=us-east-1 \
  --use-restic

docs.title: Backup Criteria
docs.text: Resource Included Excluded Notes Namespaces All kube-system, openshift-marketplace Exclude noisy namespaces PVCs All persistent volumes Ephemeral inline volumes Only bound PVs are backed up Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets All — Resources are restored as manifests ClusterRoles, RBAC Excluded — Restored from cluster spec, not backup PV metadata Included PV data PV data is in the underlying storage snapshot

docs.title: RPO and RTO targets
docs.text:
• RPO: ≤ 5 minutes (Velero periodic backup interval)
  • RTO: ≤ 30 minutes (measured from backup restore drill; includes Velero restore + CSI reattachment + Argo CD sync)

docs.title: Velero backup schedule
docs.text:
# Create a Velero scheduled backup every 5 minutes
velero schedule create daily-backup \
  --schedule "every 5 minutes" \
  --include-namespaces "*" \
  --exclude-namespaces "kube-system,openshift-marketplace" \
  --label-selector app.integrations/backup=true \
  --ttl 24h0m0s

docs.title: Restic integration for pod files
docs.text: Restic is required for backing up container volumes that are not managed by a CSI driver. Ensure each namespace has the label app.integrations/backup=true if you want Restic-backed inclusion.

docs.title: B. Snapshot Strategies
docs.text: Velero snapshots alone only capture PVC metadata. The underlying block/storage snapshots provide the point-in-time data consistency.

docs.title: CSI driver snapshots (Ceph RBD, Ceph FS, EBS, GCSF, etc.)
docs.text:
# Trigger a manual volume snapshot via Velero
velero snapshot create manual-snapshot \
  --volume <pvc-name> \
  --snapshot-location <location-name>

docs.title: Snapshot cadence
docs.text: Tier Frequency Method Retention On-node rolling Every 5 min etcdctl snapshot (separate from Velero) 7 most recent per node Off-site archive Within 1 cycle Copy to object storage 30 days Long-term cold After 30 days Cold storage (Glacier/Deepfreeze) 90 days Immutable/compliance Indefinite WORM/object-lock storage Never purge without approval

docs.title: Off-site copy verification
docs.text:
After each copy, verify integrity:

# Generate SHA256 on source
sha256sum /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-$(date +%F).db > /tmp/snapshot-$(date +%F).sha256

# Verify on destination (Ceph RGW example)
# The object storage must support hash verification;
# otherwise compare the downloaded file against the source checksum

docs.title: Snapshot retention policy
docs.text:
# Prune local Velero snapshots older than 7 days
velero snapshot list -o wide | grep older-than 7d | xargs velero snapshot delete

# Remove off-site objects older than 30 days (using gsutil)
gsutil -m rm gs://velero-backups/snapshot-$(date -d '30 days ago' +%F).db

docs.title: Restore order
docs.text:
1. Vault — unseal and confirm secrets read access
  2. Identity — Keycloak authentication
  3. Management cluster — Rancher, Argo CD, platform services
  4. Application cluster — Velero restore + PVC reattachment
  5. Workload data — Ceph pools and application data verification

docs.title: Velero restore (application cluster)
docs.text:
# List available backups
velero backup list

# Restore from a specific backup
velero restore create --from-backup <backup-name>

# Wait for restore to complete
velero restore describe --restore <restore-name> -o wide

docs.title: PVC reattachment verification
docs.text:
After Velero restore, PVCs reference the original PV. The CSI driver must reattach them to the correct nodes.

# Check PVC status across all namespaces
kubectl get pvc -A

# Identify PVCs not yet bound
kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound | grep -v NAME

# Check CSI controller logs for attachment events
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner
kubectl -n rook-ceph logs -l app=csi-rbd-provisioner | grep -i attach

# Verify node volume bindings
kubectl get nodes -o wide

docs.title: Workload verification
docs.text:
Argo CD should automatically detect the restored resources and sync them to the desired state.

# Check Argo CD application status
argocd app list

# Force sync any drifted applications
argocd app sync <app-name>

# Verify all resources are Healthy
argocd app get <app-name>

# Check pod status across all namespaces
kubectl get pods -A

docs.title: Data integrity checks
docs.text:
Run smoke queries to verify data was not corrupted during restore.

# Example: check row counts in key tables
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- psql -U postgres -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders;'

# Example: verify checksums if available
velero backup describe <backup-name> --details | grep -i checksum

# Test application-level connectivity
kubectl -n <namespace> get svc <service-name>

docs.title: Final validation checklist
docs.text: Check Expected Command All pods Running No pods in Error/CrashLoop kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running | grep -v Completed All PVCs Bound All PVCs show Bound kubectl get pvc -A | grep -v Bound Argo CD applications Healthy All apps show Healthy argocd app list | grep -v Healthy Services reachable Services have external IPs/hosts kubectl get svc -A Data integrity verified Smoke queries pass Application-specific checks

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Recovery procedure for the management cluster: Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, GitLab, Harbor, Vault, and the platform services that run on it.

This is step 3 of the recovery order defined in lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — it runs after Vault and Identity are restored, before application clusters.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Vault unsealed and readable secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md Identity (Keycloak) restored management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md GitLab repository accessible lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §GitLab Object storage (Ceph RGW) available storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery

docs.title: C. Recovery order within the management cluster
docs.text:
1. Vault — already restored (step 1 of overall order)
  2. Keycloak — already restored (step 2 of overall order)
  3. Rancher — restore from Velero backup, then re-register clusters
  4. Argo CD — restore from Git + DB, then sync applications
  5. Harbor — restore DB and registry storage
  6. Nexus — restore task + DB
  7. Platform services — Argo CD sync from GitLab

docs.title: D. Rancher recovery
docs.text:
# 1. Restore Rancher from Velero
velero restore create rancher-restore --from-backup rancher-<date>

# 2. Verify Rancher is running
kubectl -n cattle-system get deployment rancher
kubectl -n cattle-system rollout status deployment/rancher

# 3. Re-register management clusters
# Generate new cluster registration tokens in Rancher UI
# Apply the registration manifests to each managed cluster

# 4. Verify fleet is reconciling
kubectl -n cattle-fleet-system get deployment fleet-controller

docs.title: E. Argo CD recovery
docs.text:
# 1. Restore Argo CD from Velero
velero restore create argocd-restore --from-backup argocd-<date>

# 2. Verify Argo CD is running
kubectl -n argocd get deployment argocd-server
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deployment/argocd-server

# 3. Re-sync all applications from GitLab
argocd app sync <app-name>
# or sync all:
argocd app list | awk 'NR>1 {print $1}' | xargs -I {} argocd app sync {}

docs.title: F. Harbor recovery
docs.text:
# 1. Restore Harbor database
kubectl -n harbor exec deploy/harbor-core -- pg_dump -U postgres \
  -f /tmp/harbor-backup-$(date +%F).sql

# 2. Restore registry storage from object storage
# Copy registry data from RGW bucket back to Harbor PVC

# 3. Restart Harbor
kubectl -n harbor rollout restart deployment/harbor-core
kubectl -n harbor rollout restart deployment/harbor-registry

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document how to measure actual Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO) during backup drills, where to record results, and how to compare against declared targets.

Referenced by lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md and lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md.

docs.title: B. Definitions
docs.text: Term Definition How to measure RPO Maximum acceptable data loss (time) Time between last successful backup and failure point RTO Maximum acceptable downtime (time) Time from disaster declaration to verified service restoration

docs.title: 1. Declare the drill
docs.text:
Record the drill start time, scenario, and declared targets:

Field Value Drill ID Unique identifier (e.g., DR-2026-11-26-01) Scenario e.g., "Single control-plane node lost", "etcd quorum lost", "Full site rebuild" Declared RPO From lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md table Declared RTO From lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md table Declared by Person authorizing the drill Start time ISO 8601 timestamp

docs.title: 2. Execute the recovery procedure

Follow the applicable runbook from lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md:

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the Kubernetes minor-version upgrade procedure using Kubespray. Referenced by kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md Section J (Upgrades).

This procedure covers the upgrade-order checklist, etcd upgrade, CNI/CSI considerations, and rollback path.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Kubespray release pinned in kubespray/VERSION kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §M Inventory and group vars in Git kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md §M etcd snapshot taken before upgrade Section F below New kube_version verified against compatibility matrix compatibility/version-matrix.md Ansible version compatible with target Kubespray release compatibility/version-matrix.md

docs.title: C. Upgrade constraints
docs.text:
• Kubernetes supports only one minor version skew in each direction. Do not skip minors.
  • The kubeadm version must be compatible with the target Kubernetes version.
  • etcd is upgraded as part of the node upgrade.
  • CNI and CSI may need separate upgrades. Plan them explicitly.
  • Rollback of a Kubernetes minor version is not supported. Take a snapshot before starting.

docs.title: D. Upgrade order
docs.text:
1. Take etcd snapshot (Section F)
  2. Upgrade control-plane nodes one at a time (Section E)
  3. Upgrade worker nodes one at a time (Section E)
  4. Verify cluster health (Section G)
  5. Update kubespray/VERSION and group vars to the new release

docs.title: E. Node upgrade sequence (one at a time)
Control-plane nodes
docs.text:
# 1. Update kube_version in group_vars/k8s_cluster/k8s-cluster.yml
# 2. Commit the change to Git
# 3. Run Kubespray for one control-plane node
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-cp-1

# 4. Verify node is Ready
kubectl get nodes k8s-cp-1

# 5. Verify etcd member is healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-k8s-cp-1 -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# 6. Repeat for the next control-plane node

Never upgrade all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes etcd quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: Worker nodes
docs.text:
# 1. Drain the worker
kubectl drain k8s-w-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

# 2. Run Kubespray for one worker node
ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b --limit k8s-w-1

# 3. Uncordon the worker
kubectl uncordon k8s-w-1

# 4. Verify node is Ready and pods are running
kubectl get nodes k8s-w-1
kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=k8s-w-1

# 5. Repeat for the next worker node

docs.title: F. etcd snapshot before upgrade
docs.text:
# Take snapshot on one etcd member
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

# Verify snapshot
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  snapshot status /var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

# Move snapshot off the node
kubectl -n kube-system cp etcd-<node>:/var/lib/etcd/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db \
  /tmp/snapshot-pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db

docs.title: G. Post-upgrade verification
docs.text:
# All nodes Ready
kubectl get nodes

# All system pods running
kubectl -n kube-system get pods

# etcd cluster healthy
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-<node> -- etcdctl \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# API server ready
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

# Version matches target
kubectl version --short

docs.title: H. Rollback
docs.text:
Kubernetes minor-version rollback is not supported. If an upgrade fails:

  1. Restore etcd from the pre-upgrade snapshot (Section F)
  2. Revert group_vars and kubespray/VERSION to the previous values
  3. Re-run Kubespray on affected nodes
  4. Verify cluster health (Section G)

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document the Kubespray upgrade procedure. kubespray-deployment.md references this file for diffing group-vars across releases. Covers inventory diffing, Ansible version compatibility, control-plane upgrade sequencing, and etcd upgrade considerations.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Pin the Kubespray release in kubespray/VERSION; never track master
  • Keep inventory and group vars in Git; cluster must be reproducible from repo
  • Mirror every image the deploy uses, verified by pull test in offline environment
  • Record Ansible and Python versions in automation/ansible/requirements.txt
  • Run --check --diff on control-plane before any real run

docs.title: C. Inventory diffing procedure
docs.text:
Kubespray variables change between releases. Never reuse a group-vars file across a Kubespray release without diffing it against the new release's inventory/sample.

# Diff existing inventory against new release sample
diff -ru inventory/<cluster>/group_vars/ <new-kubespray>/inventory/sample/group_vars/

# Review all differences before applying
# Update group_vars to match new release expectations

docs.title: D. Ansible version compatibility
docs.text:
Kubespray release-2.32 requires Ansible >=2.19.0, <2.20.0 (2.19.x) and Python 3.11-3.13.

# Verify Ansible version
ansible --version

# Verify Python version
python3 --version

# Check requirements.txt
cat automation/ansible/requirements.txt

Never mix Ansible versions across Kubespray releases. Each release gets its own Python virtualenv.

docs.title: E. Control-plane upgrade sequence
docs.text:
One control-plane node at a time — preserve quorum:

  1. On one control-plane node, apply updated inventory and group_vars
  2. Run Kubespray deploy: ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml
  3. Verify node is healthy: kubectl get nodes and kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
  4. Repeat for the next control-plane node

Do not restart all control-plane nodes simultaneously — this removes API server quorum and makes the cluster unreachable.

docs.title: F. etcd upgrade considerations
docs.text:
etcd is deployed as static pods managed by kubelet. Upgrade etcd by:

  1. Update etcd_version in group_vars
  2. Run Kubespray deploy for control-plane nodes one at a time
  3. Verify etcd health: etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 endpoint health --cluster
  4. Verify quorum: kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

docs.title: G. Rollback
docs.text:
Kubespray does not provide automated rollback. Before upgrading:

  1. Backup etcd: etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup-<date>.db
  2. Backup inventory: git commit inventory/<cluster>/
  3. Test upgrade on a single control-plane node first

If upgrade fails, restore etcd from snapshot and revert inventory changes.

docs.title: Upgrade procedures
docs.text:
Previous step

Format for every component upgrade: source -> target, compatibility, pre-validation, offline artifact preparation, backup, dependency and upgrade order, canary, execution, post-checks, rollback feasibility, downtime, risks, success criteria.

docs.title: Rules that apply to every upgrade
docs.text:
This document is the authority; the site renders a configurable walkthrough of it. Each flow in catalog/upgrades.json maps to a section here and carries the same gates, the same order, and the rollback statement. If the two disagree, fix the catalog — the site must not become a second source of truth.

  1. Never skip a minor version. Kubernetes supports one minor of skew; Ceph and Istio have explicit supported upgrade paths.
  2. Pin, do not float. The target version is added to compatibility/version-matrix.md with a source URL and a check date before the upgrade starts.
  3. Mirror first, upgrade second. Every artifact for the target version is in the internal registry and pull-verified before any node is touched.
  4. Backup before the change. Not "a backup exists" — a backup that has been verified.
  5. One node at a time for node-level components, with a health check between nodes.
  6. Know the rollback before the upgrade. If the rollback is not possible, say so explicitly in the change record and get approval for the risk.
  7. Canary first. Every upgrade runs on a staging copy of the production inventory first.

docs.text: Component Upgrade path Reversible? docs.title: Helm 3 to Helm 4
docs.text:
Helm 3 is in support mode: the final Helm 3 feature release was 2026-09-09, and security fixes end 2027-02-10 (https://helm.sh/blog/helm-v3-end-of-life). Helm 4 is the current stable line.

  1. Read the Helm 4 release notes and the HIP-0012 migration notes for the pinned target version.
  2. Install the Helm 4 binary alongside Helm 3 on the automation server and in the CI image. Do not replace in place.
  3. Run every chart install, upgrade, template, and lint operation with Helm 4 against the full chart set. Helm 4 is expected to be compatible with the majority of existing Helm 3 charts, but "expected" is not "verified": run it.
  4. Fix the charts that fail. Each fix is an MR in the owning chart repository.
  5. Switch the CI image and the automation scripts to Helm 4.
  6. Keep the Helm 3 binary available until 2027-02-10, because Kubespray release-2.32 ships Helm 3.22.0 internally.

Rollback: the Helm 3 binary is kept, so a rollback is a path change. The risk is in the charts: if a chart was modified to work with Helm 4, confirm it still works with Helm 3 before removing the old binary.

docs.title: Kubernetes minor upgrade
docs.text:
Source and target: consecutive minor versions only. Both must be in the Kubespray release's supported range.

  1. Compatibility: read the Kubespray release notes for the target Kubernetes version; confirm the kubeadm version required. Confirm the CNI, CSI, and ingress chart versions support the target Kubernetes version (see compatibility/version-matrix.md).
  2. Pre-validation: kubectl get nodes -o wide all Ready, etcd healthy, no pods in CrashLoopBackOff, no pending CSI volumes.
  3. Offline artifacts: mirror the kubeadm binaries, the control-plane images, and any new CNI or CSI images. Pull-verify them.
  4. Backup: Velero backup plus an etcd snapshot.
  5. Order: control-plane nodes one at a time, then workers. Kubespray does this sequentially; the control plane is upgraded first.
  6. Canary: run the same upgrade on a staging cluster with the production inventory.
  7. Execution: change kube_version in the group vars, commit, then ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini cluster.yml -b.
  8. Post-checks: kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods -A, kubectl --version, the CSI driver pod version, the ingress controller version, and a functional smoke test per application.
  9. Rollback: not supported by Kubernetes. The recovery path is the backup restore.
  10. Downtime: control-plane API availability is maintained by the HA setup; workloads do not restart. Worker pods restart on their node's turn.
  11. Risks: an incompatible CNI or CSI version is the most common failure; a webhook that does not support the new API version blocks writes.
  12. Success: all nodes Ready at the new version, all pods running, application checks pass.

docs.title: Ceph upgrade (cephadm)
docs.text:
Order is fixed: monitor -> manager -> OSD -> MDS -> RGW.

  1. Confirm the source and target are adjacent in the Ceph release sequence and that the path is documented in the target release's upgrade notes.
  2. Confirm the target Ceph version is supported by the pinned Rook release if the same cluster is also consumed by Rook.
  3. Snapshot: cephadm shell -- ceph mon dump and the OSD map, plus a RBD/CephFS backup.
  4. Upgrade the manager first: cephadm shell -- ceph orch upgrade start cephadm.
  5. Then the monitors, one at a time: cephadm shell -- ceph orch upgrade start mon.
  6. Then the OSDs: cephadm shell -- ceph orch upgrade start osd. The orchestrator restarts OSDs one at a time and waits for the cluster to return to HEALTH_OK between them.
  7. Then the MDS and RGW.
  8. Post-checks: ceph -s HEALTH_OK, ceph versions shows the target on every daemon, a workload read/write test on RBD and CephFS.
  9. Rollback: not possible across a major version. Within a minor version, reinstalling the previous package is possible but not a supported rollback path.
  10. Risks: an interrupted upgrade leaves the cluster in a mixed-version state. Ceph supports mixed versions only within a narrow window.

docs.title: Rook upgrade
docs.text:
Order: operator -> Ceph -> CSI.

  1. Read the target Rook release notes for the supported Ceph version and the supported Kubernetes versions. Both are hard constraints.
  2. Mirror the new operator, CSI, and Ceph images.
  3. Upgrade the operator via Argo CD.
  4. Change cephVersion.image to the target Ceph version and apply.
  5. Wait for the Rook orchestrator to complete the daemon upgrade.
  6. Verify ceph -s and that existing PVCs still mount.
  7. Rollback: reverting the operator to the previous version is possible; reverting Ceph across a major version is not.

docs.title: GPU operator and driver upgrade
docs.text:
1. Read the target operator release notes: the shipped driver version, the shipped toolkit version, and the supported Kubernetes versions.
  2. Mirror the driver, toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, and operator images.
  3. Drain one GPU node. Verify no GPU pods remain (kubectl get pods -A --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>).
  4. Upgrade the operator via Argo CD. The operator upgrades the driver on the node.
  5. Verify on the node: nvidia-smi, lsmod | grep nvidia, and the driver version matching the target.
  6. Verify in a pod: run nvidia-smi in a test pod on that node.
  7. Uncordon and repeat for the next node.
  8. Rollback: reinstall the previous driver package and re-apply the previous operator. The driver rollback is straightforward; a workload pinned to a CUDA feature removed in the new driver is not.

docs.title: Secret and certificate rotation
docs.text:
Not a version upgrade, but the same discipline applies.

Item Trigger Procedure Reversible Vault unseal key Share rotation Generate a new key, re-unseal, vault operator generate-root No Vault root token Compromise or policy vault operator generate-root, revoke the old No CA intermediate Planned rotation Issue a new intermediate from the root, switch issuance, wait for leaf expiry, revoke the old No Leaf certificate Expiry or compromise cert-manager re-issues; for a manual certificate, openssl + reload Yes Repository credential Rotation schedule Update in the repository, then in the client config Yes K8s client certificate Expiry Kubespray renews; kubeadm certs renew Yes

docs.title: After every upgrade
docs.text:
• Update compatibility/version-matrix.md with the new version, the source URL, and the check date.
  • Update offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md status for the affected artifacts.
  • Re-run the affected acceptance tests.
  • Record the actual downtime and any deviation from this procedure in the change record.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: One pipeline for node logs, Kubernetes control plane, container stdout/stderr, storage, identity, secrets, CI, registry, security, and AI workloads. Redaction is a pipeline property, not a per-application hope.

docs.title: B. Architecture
docs.text:
nodes: journald / auditd -> Fluent Bit (DaemonSet + host agent) -> Fluent Bit forwarder
                                                       |
                                     +---------------+----------------+
                                     |                                |
                                  Loki                          OpenSearch (optional)
                                     |                                |
                                 Grafana                     OpenSearch Dashboards

Fluent Bit is deployed twice per node: - A DaemonSet for container logs (reads /var/log/containers and /var/log/pods). - A host-level agent (DaemonSet with hostPath, or a systemd unit) for journald, auditd, and kern.log.

Both must redact before forwarding. Container logs and node logs are separate streams so that a container cannot spoof a host log entry.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• Fluent Bit image and Helm chart: harbor.internal/platform/fluent-bit.
  • Loki chart and image: harbor.internal/charts/loki, harbor.internal/platform/loki.
  • OpenSearch: optional, harbor.internal/platform/opensearch.
  • Log shipper config lives in Git, applied by Argo CD.

docs.title: D. Installation
docs.text:
Loki Helm values (values.yaml):

loki:
  auth_enabled: false
  server:
    http_listen_port: 3100
  storage:
    filesystem:
      chunks_directory: /loki/chunks
      rules_directory: /loki/rules
  limits_config:
    retention_period: 720h        # 30 days
    ingestion_rate_mb: 16
    ingestion_burst_size_mb: 32
    max_label_names_length: 512
    max_label_value_length: 2048
  ruler:
    storage:
      local:
        directory: /loki/rules
    rule_path: /loki/rules-temp
    ring:
      kvstore:
        store: inmemory
    enable_api: true
  pattern_ingester:
    enabled: true

Fluent Bit DaemonSet (key parts):

serviceAccount: fluent-bit
hostNetwork: true
securityContext:
  privileged: false
  capabilities:
    drop: [ALL]
    add: [CHOWN]
volumes:
  - name: varlog
    hostPath: {path: /var/log, type: Directory}
  - name: varlibdockercontainers
    hostPath: {path: /var/lib/docker/containers, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
  - name: containers
    hostPath: {path: /var/log/containers, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
  - name: pods
    hostPath: {path: /var/log/pods, type: DirectoryOrCreate}

Output configuration (Loki):

[OUTPUT]
    Name loki
    Match *
    Host loki-gateway.monitoring.svc
    Port 3100
    Labels job=fluent-bit,namespace=${K8S_NAMESPACE_NAME},pod=${K8S_POD_NAME},container=${K8S_CONTAINER_NAME}
    Retry_Limit False
    Line_Format json

docs.title: E. Redaction — mandatory
docs.text:
Redaction happens in the Fluent Bit filter stage, before any output. Two layers:

  1. Key/value redaction — a modify/lua filter that drops or masks keys whose name matches a secret pattern:
password, passwd, secret, token, apikey, api_key, authorization, private_key, client_secret, credential, bearer
  1. Value pattern redaction — regex filters for well-known credential shapes:
- Bearer [A-Za-z0-9\-._~+/]+=*
- eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}   # JWT
- -----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----[\s\S]*?-----END [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----
- (AKIA|ASIA)[0-9A-Z]{16}                                            # AWS access key id
- xox[baprs]-[A-Za-z0-9-]{10,}                                       # Slack token
- glpat-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}                                           # GitLab PAT
- sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}                                                # OpenAI-style key

Rule: redact by default. A log field that is known to contain a secret must be explicitly allow-listed, and that allow-list entry is reviewed.

Additional controls: - Never enable Kubernetes audit log level RequestResponse — it records request bodies containing secrets. Use Metadata level, or Request with a scrub policy. - auditd rules that record file writes must exclude the secret paths (Vault data, TLS keys). - Log ingestion is over TLS to the backend, with authentication. Without auth, anyone with network access to the backend can read all logs.

docs.title: F. Log model
docs.text:
Stream Labels Notes Container stdout/stderr namespace, pod, container, job, cluster The core stream. Label cardinality is bounded by pod count Node system log hostname, unit, severity No pod labels; keeps queries cheap auditd hostname, event type Security evidence; separate retention K8s audit user, verb, resource, namespace, response code Do not include request bodies Ceph hostname, daemon type From the Ceph hosts, not the container stream GitLab CI project, pipeline, job, runner From the GitLab application logs, not the container stream

Retention: container logs 30 days, node logs 30 days, audit logs 1 year, CI logs 90 days. Apply per-stream retention in the backend, not per-collector.

docs.title: G. Storage sizing
docs.text:
Estimate before deploying:

daily_volume = avg_lines_per_sec * avg_line_bytes * 86400
compressed_volume ≈ daily_volume * 0.25 (JSON/labels compress well, but index overhead adds back)
retention_storage = compressed_volume * retention_days * 1.3 (index + WAL overhead)

Worked example: 2000 lines/s, 500 bytes/line -> 86 GB/day uncompressed -> roughly 22-30 GB/day with compression and index -> 30 days retention ≈ 0.9 TB. Verify against the actual backend after one week of real traffic and correct the estimate.

Guardrails: - Cap ingestion rate per tenant to protect the backend (Loki ingestion_rate_mb). - Alert when the backend's disk crosses 70% and 85%. - Do not index full log content in Loki. Use OpenSearch for content search.

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Log reaches the backend
kubectl -n logging exec ds/fluent-bit -- sh -c 'echo test | cat'
kubectl -n logging port-forward svc/loki 3100:3100
curl -s "http://localhost:3100/loki/api/v1/query_range?query={namespace=\"default\"}" | jq '.data.result | length'

# Redaction works
kubectl exec deploy/test-app -- sh -c 'echo "password=supersecret123"'
# Then search for "supersecret123" in the backend -> must return no results

The redaction test is a mandatory acceptance test (requirements/validation-strategy.md, family C/F).

docs.title: I. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix No logs Fluent Bit DaemonSet not running, or the host path is not mounted kubectl -n logging logs ds/fluent-bit; check hostPath types Logs for some pods only Label filter mismatch, or a container writes to a file instead of stdout Check the collector's tail pattern Backend 429 Ingestion rate exceeded Raise the limit, or reduce the stream Loki OOM Excessive label cardinality or unbounded query Check max_label_names_length; reduce labels Secrets visible in logs Redaction filter not applied to that stream Add the filter, purge affected data, rotate the exposed credential

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Redaction before forwarding, with a test that proves it. - TLS plus authentication between the collector and the backend. - Audit logs retained separately and for longer than application logs. - No RequestResponse audit level.

Strongly recommended: - Keep the label set small and fixed per stream. - Use an OpenSearch sidecar only where content search is a hard requirement. - Ship audit logs off-host as soon as they are generated, so a compromised node cannot delete its own evidence. - Alert on log ingestion rate, not only on backend health — a silent collector looks identical to a quiet cluster.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document access management: RBAC, roles, bindings, service accounts, OIDC integration with Keycloak.

Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md, management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md, kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §RBAC.

docs.title: B. RBAC model
docs.text: Role Scope Capabilities Admin Cluster Full access Member Project Read/write resources Viewer Cluster/Project Read-only Restricted Project Read-only, no exec/secrets

docs.title: C. Service accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts are created per application and scoped to a namespace:

# ServiceAccount example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: app-ns
automountServiceAccountToken: true

docs.title: D. OIDC integration with Keycloak
docs.text:
Management cluster integrates with Keycloak for centralized identity:

# Configure OIDC provider
rancher auth configure oidc \
  --issuer https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform \
  --client-id rancher \
  --client-secret <secret>

# Map Keycloak groups to Rancher roles
rancher group create --name developers --oidc-group developers
rancher role-template binding create --role project-member --group developers --project app-prod

docs.title: E. Authentication flows
docs.text:
• User authentication: Keycloak OIDC provides login tokens consumed by Rancher/Headlamp
  • Service-to-service authentication: Mutual TLS + JWT verification for internal APIs
  • Machine authentication: Service account tokens with automatic rotation

docs.title: F. Authorization boundaries
docs.text:
• Cluster-level roles: admin, cluster-admin
  • Project-level roles: project-member, project-viewer, restricted
  • Namespace-level restrictions: via Role/RoleBinding scoped to application namespaces

docs.title: G. Cross-references
docs.text:
• management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md — Rancher deployment
  • management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md — Keycloak deployment
  • kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §RBAC — Kubernetes RBAC
  • management-cluster/alternatives.md — management plane options

Management Cluster Access Management: RBAC roles scoped by scope, Keycloak OIDC for user auth, service accounts for app auth, automated token rotation

docs.title: Management plane: Rancher and its alternatives
docs.text: Rancher is the default management plane in this platform: it registers clusters, projects and users, and it is the one place an operator sees every cluster. It is not the only option, and it is not required for a cluster to work. This document states when each alternative is the right answer.

docs.title: The comparison
docs.text: Option What it is Strength Cost Rancher Cluster manager + UI + auth proxy + Fleet GitOps One console for many clusters, mature RBAC, works with the existing Keycloak A control plane of its own, a large API surface, its own upgrade cadence Headlamp + Argo CD CNCF UI for one cluster + GitOps Small, no cluster registry, RBAC stays in Kubernetes No multi-cluster console; each cluster is opened separately KubeSphere Full platform UI with multi-cluster Integrated observability and DevOps UI Heavy, opinionated, duplicates Prometheus/Argo CD No UI (kubectl + Argo CD) CLI and Git only Least to operate, least to secure Every read is a command; no shared console for an audit view

docs.title: When to choose what
docs.text:
• Rancher — more than three clusters, a platform team, and a requirement for one console with per-user cluster access. The default in the configurator.
  • Headlamp + Argo CD — one or two clusters, a small team, and a policy that the UI must not hold the only copy of cluster state. The configurator option headlamp renders this.
  • KubeSphere — already standardized on it, or a requirement for a built-in DevOps console.
  • No UI — a regulated environment where the console itself is an attack surface. Helm and Argo CD still work.

docs.title: What does not change
docs.text: The management cluster is separate from the application clusters in every option. Identity stays at the application layer (ADR-0015): Rancher, Headlamp and Argo CD all federate with Keycloak; no Linux node joins the directory. The management cluster still runs Keycloak, Harbor, GitLab, Argo CD and Vault, whichever UI is chosen.

docs.title: Headlamp deployment shape
docs.text:
Headlamp runs as a Deployment in the management cluster with a ServiceAccount and a ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin only if the deployment is single-tenant. For multi-user use, run it with OIDC and let each user bring their own token:

config:
  oidc:
    clientID: headlamp
    issuerURL: {{value.keycloakHost}}/realms/platform
    scopes: "openid profile email groups"
  inCluster: false
serviceAccount:
  create: false

Generated as headlamp-values.yaml when the option is selected. It is a UI, not a control plane: if it is down, kubectl and Argo CD continue.

docs.title: Migration between options
docs.text:
Rancher → Headlamp: register nothing; install Headlamp in the management cluster, keep Argo CD, and remove Rancher only after every user has a kubeconfig path that does not go through Rancher. The Rancher-generated kubeconfig embeds a proxy URL; once Rancher is gone, that file stops working.

Rancher → none: keep the clusters registered in Argo CD, hand out OIDC kubeconfigs, and document the kubectl path as the primary interface. This is the lowest-dependency end state.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
ApplicationSets enable scalable, dynamic application creation in Argo CD. Instead of managing individual Application manifests, a single ApplicationSet definition generates multiple Applications based on defined generators and templates. This document covers the core patterns for building, managing, and onboarding applications using ApplicationSets.

Cross-references: management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md, management-cluster/argocd/application-sync.md, management-cluster/argocd/drift-detection.md.

docs.title: B. ApplicationSet generators
docs.text: ApplicationSets support multiple generator types to produce the list of target Applications. Choosing the right generator depends on the fleet structure and update cadence.

docs.title: 1. list generator
docs.text:
Static, declarative element list. Best for small, stable fleets that change infrequently.

generators:
  - list:
      elements:
        - service: payments
          tier: gold
        - service: ledger
          tier: gold
        - service: notify
          tier: silver

docs.title: 2. git generator
docs.text:
Watches a Git repository for a directory structure. Each subdirectory under the configured path becomes an Application. Ideal for directory-of-services layouts where each service has its own k8s manifests folder.

generators:
  - git:
      repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
      revision: main
      directories:
        - path: k8s/*

docs.title: 3. cluster generator
docs.text:
Targets applications deployed to specific clusters. Useful when the same Application configuration must be rendered across multiple Kubernetes clusters.

generators:
  - cluster:
      name: cluster-1
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc

docs.title: 4. matrix generator
docs.text:
Cartesian product of element lists. Each combination of elements produces one Application. Useful for combining multiple dimensions (e.g., services × tiers × regions).

generators:
  - matrix:
      elements:
        - service: payments
        - service: ledger
        - tier: gold
        - tier: silver

docs.title: 5. random generatör
docs.text:
Produces a random set of Applications. Each Application receives a random generatorName and generatorKind in its metadata. Useful for canary or A/B testing fleets.

generators:
  - random:
      count: 5

docs.title: 6. fillgenerator generator
docs.text:
Fills a range of sequential numbers or strings. Commonly used with template to generate Applications with indexed names.

generators:
  - fillgenerator:
      start: 1
      end: 10
      step: 1

docs.title: C. Template application spec
docs.text:
The template field defines the spec for each generated Application. Only the fields that differ between Applications need to be included; shared configuration is typically set at the AppProject level.

template:
  metadata:
    name: '{{service}}'
    labels:
      app: '{{service}}'
      tier: '{{tier}}'
  spec:
    project: team-payments
    source:
      repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
      targetRevision: main
      path: 'k8s/{{service}}'
    destination:
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: '{{service}}'
    syncPolicy:
      automated:
        prune: true
        selfHeal: true
      syncOptions:
        - CreateNamespace=true

Key template functions: {{variable}} references are resolved from generator elements. Unknown variables resolve to empty strings; guard templates against missing values using Go template default function or conditional logic.

docs.title: D. Target revision management
docs.text:
The targetRevision field controls which git ref the generated Applications track. This is critical for fleet-wide version alignment and rollback strategies.

Value Behavior main Tracks the default branch; Applications update when the branch tip advances. A specific branch name (e.g., release-1.8) All generated Applications track that branch; updates require a branch push. $patch Updates to the patch version of the current main commit; useful for hotfix pipelines. $auto Auto-detects the default branch and tracks it; the most common default.

Best practice: Pin targetRevision: main for continuous deployment pipelines. Use a named branch (e.g., release-1.8) for release trains. Avoid $patch unless the CI pipeline explicitly manages patch bumps.

docs.title: E. Sync policies
docs.text:
ApplicationSets inherit sync policy behavior, but per-Application sync policies can override the generator-level defaults. The syncPolicy in the template applies to every generated Application.

template:
  spec:
    syncPolicy:
      automated:
        prune: true
        selfHeal: true
      syncOptions:
        - CreateNamespace=true
      retry:
        limit: 5
        backoff: {duration: 15s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 5m}

Sync policy fields: - automated.prune: Delete resources no longer present in Git. - automated.selfHeal: Auto-sync when the Application detects drift. - automated.syncOptions: Additional options such as CreateNamespace or ServerSideApply. - retry.limit: Maximum sync retry attempts. - retry.backoff: Exponential backoff configuration. - syncOptions: One-time sync options passed to the Argo CD sync API.

Per-application override: To change sync behavior for a specific generated Application, edit that Application's spec directly via argocd app set or by modifying the generated Application manifest in Git.

docs.title: F. ApplicationSet-based application onboarding
docs.text: Onboarding new applications via ApplicationSets reduces the manual workload of creating individual Application manifests. The onboarding pattern depends on the generator type.

docs.title: 1. Git-based onboarding (git generator)
docs.text:
1. Add a new subdirectory under the watched path (e.g., k8s/new-service/).
  2. Ensure the directory contains valid k8s manifests or a Helm chart.
  3. Argo CD automatically creates an Application for the new directory on the next sync.
  4. The Application name is derived from the directory name; customize using the name template field if needed.

docs.title: 2. List-based onboarding (list generator)
docs.text:
1. Edit the ApplicationSet's spec.generators[0].list.elements array to add a new element.
  2. Commit the change to the ApplicationSet manifest.
  3. Argo CD reconciles and creates the new Application on the next sync.
  4. The Application name follows the template.metadata.name pattern (e.g., new-service).

docs.title: 3. Cluster generator onboarding
docs.text:
1. Ensure the target cluster is reachable from the Argo CD repo-server.
  2. Add a new cluster generator entry with the cluster name and server URL.
  3. Generated Applications receive the cluster's context; override destination.server in the template if needed.

docs.title: 4. Matrix generator onboarding
docs.text:
1. Add new elements to any of the matrix dimension lists.
  2. The Cartesian product expands automatically; no need to re-list combinations.
  3. Verify the generated Application count matches matrix.size in the Argo CD UI.

docs.title: 5. Verifying onboarding
docs.text:
# List all applications generated by an ApplicationSet
argocd app list -l argocd.argoproj.io/application-set-name=microservices

# Describe a specific generated application
argocd app get payments-api -n argocd

# View the generated Application manifest
argocd app view payments-api --output yaml

Onboarding checklist: - [ ] Generator configuration is correct for the target fleet structure. - [ ] Template spec includes all required fields: source.repoURL, destination.server, destination.namespace, syncPolicy. - [ ] targetRevision is set appropriately for the deployment model (main, release branch, $patch). - [ ] syncPolicy.automated is configured per reliability requirements (prune, selfHeal). - [ ] AppProject has destination and resource whitelists that allow the new Application's namespace and resource types. - [ ] Run argocd app list to confirm the new Application appeared after the commit. - [ ] Run argocd app sync <name> --dry-run to verify the Application is readable by Argo CD.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Argo CD application sync: sync waves, pruning, self-heal, drift detection, rollback procedures.

Cross-references management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md, management-cluster/argocd/drift-detection.md, management-cluster/argocd/gitops-boundaries.md.

docs.title: B. Application sync
docs.text:
# Manual sync
argocd app sync <application>

# Sync with prune
argocd app sync <application> --prune

# Sync with self-heal
argocd app sync <application> --self-heal

# Rollback to previous version
argocd app rollback <application> <revision>

docs.title: C. Sync waves
docs.text:
Sync waves control the order of resource creation:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: platform
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
  source:
    directoryRecurse: true
    kustomize:
      namePrefix: platform-
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: platform

Sync waves are set via annotation: 

metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"

docs.title: D. Drift detection
docs.text:
Argo CD detects drift between desired and actual state:

# Check for drift
argocd app diff <application>

# Auto-sync on drift
argocd app set <application> --sync-policy automated

docs.title: E. Rollback procedures
docs.text:
# List revisions
argocd app history <application>

# Rollback to specific revision
argocd app rollback <application> <revision>

# Verify rollback
argocd app get <application>

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:
• management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md — Argo CD deployment
  • management-cluster/argocd/drift-detection.md — Drift detection
  • management-cluster/argocd/gitops-boundaries.md — GitOps boundaries

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Argo CD reconciles Kubernetes state against Git. It is the single writer for every Kubernetes-declared object except the Kubespray-managed ones (see ADR-0014).

GitLab repo ---> Argo CD repo-server ---> application-controller ---> K8s API
                      |                             |
                 ApplicationSet              Argo CD UI / API

docs.title: B. Installation
docs.text:
Managed by Argo CD itself (bootstrap is a one-time exception) and thereafter by Argo CD.

kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deployment/argocd-server --timeout=300s
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d

HA configuration (Argo CD HA docs, pinned version): - argocd-server, argocd-repo-server, argocd-application-controller with replicas: 2+ - Redis with a sentinel or a managed HA Redis - PostgreSQL as the backend (never SQLite in production) - A separate argocd-application-controller per cluster for large fleets, with sharding

docs.title: C. Project model
docs.text:
One AppProject per team:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: team-payments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  description: Payments team applications
  sourceRepos:
    - https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
  destinations:
    - namespace: payments
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Namespace
  namespaceResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ""
      kind: ConfigMap
    - group: ""
      kind: Secret
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
    - group: ""
      kind: Service
    - group: networking.k8s.io
      kind: Ingress
  namespaceResourceBlacklist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Pod
    - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRole
    - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRoleBinding

Restricting destinations prevents a team from deploying into the platform namespaces.

docs.title: D. Application and ApplicationSet
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: team-payments
  source:
    repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s/api
    helm:
      valueFiles: [values-production.yaml]
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff: {duration: 15s, factor: 2, maxDuration: 5m}

ServerSideApply=true matters at scale: client-side apply has a size limit and loses field ownership for some types.

ApplicationSet for a fleet of identical services:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: microservices
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - service: payments
            tier: gold
          - service: ledger
            tier: gold
          - service: notify
            tier: silver
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{service}}'
    spec:
      project: team-payments
      source:
        repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
        targetRevision: main
        path: 'k8s/{{service}}'
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: '{{service}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}

Git generator variant for a directory-of-services layout:

  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: k8s/*

docs.title: E. Offline configuration
docs.text:
Need Configuration Internal GitLab repoURL points at the internal GitLab Internal image registry image rewrite rule in argocd-cm, or the images are already named with the internal registry in Git Internal Helm chart repo helm.repoURL points at the internal OCI registry in Harbor Repository credentials Argo CD repository secret in the argocd namespace, value from Vault via External Secrets TLS trust for the internal CA Mounted into the repo-server pods (see below)

Image rewrite rule (argocd-cm):

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  application.resourceTrackingMethod: annotation
  application.instanceLabelKey: argocd.argoproj.io/instance
  resource.customizations.health.lua: |
    hs = {}
    if obj.status ~= nil then
      if obj.status.phase == "Running" then hs.status = "Healthy"
      ...
    end
    hs = {status = "Progressing", message = "Waiting"}
    return hs
  # Rewrite upstream image names to the internal registry
  # (implemented via a config-management-plugin or a sidecar in this platform)

The standard way to rewrite images is a Config Management Plugin running as an Argo CD sidecar. It is a small plugin image that the repo-server executes. Because the offline environment cannot fetch the upstream image at deploy time, the plugin (or the Git repo itself) must reference the internal registry. The simplest and most auditable approach: the Git repo already contains the internal registry path, produced by the CI pipeline at build time. The plugin approach is used when the same Git repo must serve both connected and offline environments.

TLS trust for the internal CA in Argo CD:

# In the repo-server Deployment
volumeMounts:
  - name: ca
    mountPath: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
    subPath: ca-certificates.crt
volumes:
  - name: ca
    configMap:
      name: argocd-ca
      items:
        - key: ca-certificates.crt
          path: ca-certificates.crt

docs.title: F. OIDC / SSO
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  oidc.config: |
    name: Keycloak
    issuer: https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform
    clientID: argocd
    clientSecret: $oidc-keycloak:oidc.clientSecret
    requestedScopes: openid,profile,email,groups
    groupMappingEnabled: "true"
    groupsClaim: groups
    # Map Keycloak groups to Argo CD roles
    groupMapping:
      "platform-admins": role:admin
      "platform-operators": role:admin
      "developers": role:readonly
    scopes: |
      - group:platform-admins
      - group:platform-operators

The clientSecret is referenced as a Vault secret, not inline. Argo CD resolves $namespace:key references against secrets in the Argo CD namespace.

Argo CD's built-in RBAC is coarse (admin, edit, readonly). For per-project permissions, use the Argo CD RBAC ConfigMap with project-scoped policies, or the Keycloak group mapping above.

docs.title: G. Validation
docs.text:
# Application health
argocd app list
argocd app get payments-api
argocd app history payments-api

# Diff between Git and the cluster
argocd app diff payments-api

# Sync manually
argocd app sync payments-api

# From inside the cluster
kubectl -n argocd get applications
kubectl -n argocd describe application payments-api

Expected healthy state: Sync Status: Synced, Health Status: Healthy, no OutOfSync on a quiet system.

docs.title: H. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Promote a version Merge to main; Argo CD syncs automatically Roll back argocd app rollback <app> <history-id> or revert the Git commit Pause an app argocd app set <app> --sync-policy=none — during an incident this prevents Argo CD from reverting a hotfix Add a resource Add it to Git; Argo CD adopts or creates it Delete a resource Remove it from Git; with prune: true Argo CD deletes it — confirm the resource is not stateful Refresh a secret argocd app get <app> --refresh

docs.title: I. Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix OutOfSync with no diff Resource modified outside Argo CD With selfHeal: true it reverts; investigate the manual change ComparisonError Repo unreachable, or the CA is not trusted by the repo-server Check repo-server logs and the CA mount Failed to load target state Wrong path, or the manifest is invalid argocd app get shows the error Sync fails with a webhook error An admission controller is blocking the resource See troubleshooting/admission.md Image pull error after sync The image name does not resolve internally Rewrite rule or CI-side rewrite Secret not populated The ExternalSecret has not synced, or the Vault path is wrong Check the ExternalSecret and the ClusterSecretStore App stuck Progressing A resource is healthy-checked as Progressing (a Deployment with a missing readiness probe) Fix the health check in the app manifest

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - prune: true and selfHeal: true for application workloads, and an explicit review for anything stateful. - AppProject per team with a restricted destination and resource whitelist. - ServerSideApply=true for large applications. - Repository credentials from Vault via External Secrets, never in the Application manifest. - Pin the Argo CD version and mirror the images.

Strongly recommended: - The App-of-apps pattern: one root Application that creates the platform Applications, so the platform bootstraps itself. - A sync window per project to avoid a fleet-wide sync at the same moment. - Health checks customised per resource type in argocd-cm. - Argo CD notifications for sync failures, wired to Alertmanager.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Argo CD drift detection: detection frequency, notification, manual sync vs auto-sync, conflict resolution.

Cross-references management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md, management-cluster/argocd/application-sync.md, management-cluster/argocd/gitops-boundaries.md.

docs.title: B. Drift detection frequency
docs.text:
Argo CD detects drift at configurable intervals:

# Application spec with drift detection
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: platform
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10

Drift detection happens every 3 minutes by default. The interval is controlled by the Argo CD status.processors and reconciliationTimeout settings.

docs.title: C. Notification on drift
docs.text:
Drift notifications are sent via:

Channel Configuration Argo CD UI Application shows OutOfSync status Webhook argocd-notifications with Slack/Teams Email argocd-notifications email template

docs.title: D. Manual sync vs auto-sync
docs.text:
Mode When to use Manual sync Production clusters where changes require approval Auto-sync Development/staging clusters where rapid iteration is preferred Self-heal only Detect and alert on drift, but don't auto-remediate 
# Enable auto-sync with self-heal
argocd app set <application> --sync-policy automated --self-heal

# Enable auto-sync with prune
argocd app set <application> --sync-policy automated --prune

# Disable auto-sync (manual only)
argocd app set <application> --sync-policy none

docs.title: E. Conflict resolution
docs.text:
When drift is detected:

  1. Review the diff: argocd app diff <application>
  2. Decide: accept drift (update Git) or reconcile (sync from Git)
  3. If accepting drift: update Git manifest, commit, push
  4. If reconciling: argocd app sync <application>

docs.title: Fleet vs Argo CD Decision Matrix
Use Cases
docs.text:
| Situation | Recommended Tool | Rationale |

|---|---|---|

| Cluster registration and lifecycle (provisioning, deprovisioning, labeling, tainting) | Fleet | Fleet manages the Rancher cluster lifecycle: registration tokens, kubeconfig distribution, and cluster-level configuration. Applications are deployed afterward via Argo CD. |

| Baseline add-on deployment (monitoring, logging, ingress, policy, cert-manager) | Fleet | Fleet GitRepo resources deploy cluster-scoped add-ons to every managed cluster consistently. |

| Application workload deployment (team services, Helm charts, K8s manifests) | Argo CD | Argo CD owns application namespaces and deployment objects. ApplicationSets drive multi-environment spreads. |

| Multi-tenant fleet of clusters (10+ clusters, per-team isolation) | Fleet + Argo CD (combined) | Fleet handles cluster-level concerns; Argo CD handles per-application GitOps within each cluster. See the ownership table in automation/gitlab-ci/gitlab-ansible-design.md §7.4. |

| Canary / blue-green deployments | Argo CD | Argo CD application sync policies support automated canary, blue-green, and rolling strategies with health-based promotion. |

| Application-level rollback | Argo CD | argocd app rollback operates against the Application resource history. |

| GitOps for platform-level resources (ClusterRoleBindings, CRDs, namespace templates) | Fleet (or Argo CD via app-of-apps) | Fleet can push baseline CRDs; the app-of-apps pattern in management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md §G uses Argo CD for platform bootstrap. |

| Migration from one management plane to another | Fleet + Argo CD (coordinated) | See migration criteria below. |

docs.title: Ownership Boundaries
docs.text:
| Resource Type | Owner | Tool | Notes |

|---|---|---|---|

| Cluster registration token | Fleet | Rancher | Short-lived; rotates automatically. |

| kubeconfig distribution | Fleet | Rancher | Embeds Rancher server URL and CA. |

| Baseline add-ons (monitoring, logging, ingress, policy) | Fleet | Fleet GitRepo | Deployed to monitoring, logging, ingress-nginx, gatekeeper-system, cert-manager namespaces. |

| Application deployments | Argo CD | Argo CD Application | Per-team AppProject with restricted destinations. |

| Namespace creation | Fleet | Fleet | Baseline namespaces created by add-ons. |

| Application namespace resources | Argo CD | Argo CD Application | All workload objects (Deployments, Services, etc.). |

| RBAC for applications | Argo CD | Argo CD Application + AppProject | Project-scoped policies via Keycloak group mapping. |

| Network policies (baseline) | Fleet | Fleet GitRepo | Applied to infrastructure namespaces. |

| Pod Security Standards (baseline) | Fleet | Fleet GitRepo | Applied via Gatekeeper/OPA constraints. |

| Application-level NetworkPolicies | Argo CD | Argo CD Application | Per-workload policies. |

| Never deploy an application workload via Fleet. Never deploy baseline add-ons via Argo CD. | — | — | Ownership inversion causes drift and merge conflicts. |

Normative reference: the ownership table in automation/gitlab-ci/gitlab-ansible-design.md §7.4 is authoritative.

docs.title: Migration Criteria
docs.text:
Migrate from Argo CD to Fleet (or vice versa) when the following conditions are met:

| Direction | Trigger | Action |

|---|---|---|

| Argo CD → Fleet | Workload deployment logic needs to be cluster-registration-aware, or you want to co-locate application manifests with baseline add-ons in a single Git repo. | 1. Convert Application/ApplicationSet resources to Fleet GitRepo/Application CRs. 2. Remove Argo CD Application resources for the same workloads. 3. Update AppProject destinations to align with Fleet-added namespaces. 4. Verify no resource is owned by both tools per the ownership table. |

| Fleet → Argo CD | You need advanced deployment strategies (canary, blue-green) or per-application rollback that Fleet does not natively support. | 1. Migrate baseline add-on GitRepos to Argo CD app-of-apps or Helm releases. 2. Convert application workloads to Argo CD Applications. 3. Remove Fleet GitRepo resources for application paths. 4. Re-register clusters via Argo CD repo connections if Fleet is decommissioned. |

| Fleet → Argo CD (management plane switch) | Replacing Rancher with an alternative management plane (Headlamp + Argo CD, KubeSphere, or no UI). | 1. Follow migration steps in management-cluster/alternatives.md §Migration between options. 2. Register clusters with the new plane. 3. Keep Argo CD Application resources pointing at the new cluster endpoints. 4. Remove Fleet resources only after every user has a kubeconfig path that does not go through the old plane. |

| Argo CD → Fleet (consolidation) | Fleet already manages cluster registration and baseline add-ons, and you want to unify under a single controller. | 1. Import existing Argo CD Applications into Fleet as Application CRs (if Fleet supports it) or recreate them via Git. 2. Remove Argo CD Application resources. 3. Update any ApplicationSet generators to Fleet-compatible formats. 4. Validate that check_links.py reports 0 broken links across the repo. |

docs.title: Argo CD Server
docs.text:
# Create the Argo CD namespace
kubectl create namespace argocd

# Install Argo CD using the official manifest
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Wait for the server to become ready
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deployment/argocd-server --timeout=300s

# Retrieve the initial admin password
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret \
  -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d

docs.title: High Availability Setup
docs.text:
For production deployments, deploy Argo CD with HA configuration:

  • argocd-server, argocd-repo-server, argocd-application-controller with replicas: 2
  • Redis with a sentinel or a managed HA Redis instance
  • PostgreSQL as the backend database (never SQLite in production)
  • A separate argocd-application-controller per cluster for large fleets, with sharding

docs.title: Application Projects
docs.text:
Create an AppProject for each team or group to organize applications and restrict destinations:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: team-payments
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  description: Payments team applications
  sourceRepos:
    - https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
  destinations:
    - namespace: payments
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  clusterResourceWhitelist: []
  namespaceResourceWhitelist: []
  clusterResourceBlacklist:
    - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRole
    - group: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRoleBinding
  namespaceResourceBlacklist:
    - group: ""
      kind: Pod

Restricting destinations prevents a team from deploying into platform namespaces.

docs.title: ConfigMap Settings
docs.text:
Configure the Argo CD ConfigMap (argocd-cm) for site-wide settings:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: argocd-cm
  namespace: argocd
data:
  application.resourceTrackingMethod: annotation
  application.instanceLabelKey: argocd.argoproj.io/instance
  # OIDC configuration is configured via the argocd-cm ConfigMap
  oidc.config: |
    name: Keycloak
    issuer: https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform
    clientID: argocd
    clientSecret: $oidc-keycloak:oidc.clientSecret
    requestedScopes: openid,profile,email,groups
    groupMappingEnabled: "true"
    groupsClaim: groups
    groupMapping:
      "platform-admins": role:admin
      "platform-operators": role:admin
      "developers": role:readonly
    scopes:
      - group:platform-admins
      - group:platform-operators

The clientSecret is referenced using the $namespace:key syntax, which Argo CD resolves against secrets in the argocd namespace.

docs.title: TLS for Internal CA
docs.text:
Mount the internal CA certificate into the repo-server pods so Argo CD can trust internal Git hosts:

# In the repo-server Deployment
volumeMounts:
  - name: ca
    mountPath: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt
    subPath: ca-certificates.crt
volumes:
  - name: ca
    configMap:
      name: argocd-ca
      items:
        - key: ca-certificates.crt
          path: ca-certificates.crt

docs.title: Creating an Application
docs.text:
Define an Argo CD Application to represent a Kubernetes workload:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: team-payments
  source:
    repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
    targetRevision: main
    path: k8s/api
    helm:
      valueFiles: [values-production.yaml]
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff:
        duration: 15s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 5m

docs.title: ApplicationSet for Fleet Management
docs.text:
Use ApplicationSet to manage a fleet of identical services:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: microservices
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - list:
        elements:
          - service: payments
            tier: gold
          - service: ledger
            tier: gold
          - service: notify
            tier: silver
  template:
    metadata:
      name: '{{service}}'
    spec:
      project: team-payments
      source:
        repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
        targetRevision: main
        path: 'k8s/{{service}}'
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: '{{service}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}

docs.title: Git Generator for Directory-of-Services Layout
docs.text:
generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/apps/payments
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: k8s/*

docs.title: Offline Configuration
docs.text:
• Internal GitLab: repoURL points at the internal GitLab instance
  • Internal image registry: Images already named with the internal registry in Git, or use argocd-cm resource customizations
  • Repository credentials: Argo CD repository secret in the argocd namespace, sourced from Vault via External Secrets
  • TLS trust for internal CA: Mounted into repo-server pods as described above

docs.title: Controlling Sync Order
docs.text:
Sync waves control the order in which resources are created across multiple applications. Set the sync wave via annotation:

metadata:
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"

docs.title: Example: Platform Application with Sync Wave
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: platform
  namespace: argocd
  annotations:
    argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "0"
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
  source:
    directoryRecurse: true
    kustomize:
      namePrefix: platform-
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: platform

docs.title: Sync Wave Hierarchy
docs.text:
• Lower wave numbers sync first (wave "0" before wave "1", etc.)
  • Applications at the same wave sync in parallel
  • Sync waves prevent resource ordering issues when one application depends on resources created by another
  • Use cases: placing core infrastructure applications at wave "0", followed by dependent services at higher wave numbers

docs.title: Setting Sync Waves via CLI
docs.text:
# Set sync wave for an application
argocd app set <application> --annotation argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave="1"

# View current sync wave annotation
argocd app get <application> --metric annotation.argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave

docs.title: Check Application Status
docs.text:
# List all applications
argocd app list

# Get detailed status of a specific application
argocd app get payments-api

# View sync history
argocd app history payments-api

# Diff between Git and cluster state
argocd app diff payments-api

docs.title: Healthy State Expectations
docs.text:
• Sync Status: Synced
  • Health Status: Healthy
  • No OutOfSync on a quiet system

docs.title: From Inside the Cluster
docs.text:
# List applications managed by Argo CD
kubectl -n argocd get applications

# Describe a specific application
kubectl -n argocd describe application payments-api

docs.title: Promote a Version
docs.text: Merge to main; Argo CD syncs automatically (respecting sync wave order).

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
# Roll back to a previous revision
argocd app rollback <application> <revision>

docs.title: Pause an Application
docs.text:
# Prevent Argo CD from auto-syncing during an incident
argocd app set <app> --sync-policy=none

docs.title: Add or Delete a Resource
docs.text:
• Add it to Git; Argo CD adopts or creates it
  • Remove it from Git; with prune: true Argo CD deletes it — confirm the resource is not stateful

docs.title: Refresh a Secret
docs.text: argocd app get <app> --refresh

docs.title: H. Best Practices
docs.text:
• prune: true and selfHeal: true for application workloads (explicit review for stateful resources)
  • AppProject per team with restricted destinations and resource whitelists
  • ServerSideApply=true for large applications
  • Repository credentials from Vault via External Secrets, never inline in Application manifests
