  • A sync window per project to avoid fleet-wide sync at the same moment
  • Health checks customized per resource type in argocd-cm
  • Argo CD notifications for sync failures, wired to Alertmanager

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Keycloak is the identity broker for the platform. Applications integrate with it via OIDC; the directory service (AD or LDAP) is the upstream source for some realms.

  browser / kubectl / CI
        |
  keycloak.internal:8443 (or 443 behind the site proxy)
        |
  +-------------------+
  | realm: platform   |  -> applications (Rancher, Argo CD, Grafana, Harbor, Vault, GitLab)
  | realm: ai         |  -> inference API gateway
  | realm: external   |  -> AD / LDAP upstream
  +-------------------+
        |
  PostgreSQL (external, shared with other stateful services)

docs.title: B. Deployment
docs.text:
Keycloak runs in the Management Cluster, but the database is external (PostgreSQL on the platform database host) so a cluster loss does not take the identity store with it. The identity provider is a restore dependency, so it must not live only inside the thing it protects (ADR-0025 reasoning applied to identity).

# values.yaml (subset)
replicas: 2
image:
  repository: harbor.internal/platform/keycloak/keycloak
  tag: "26.8.1"
dbchecker:
  image:
    repository: harbor.internal/platform/keycloak/keycloak
extraEnv: |
  - name: KC_HOSTNAME
    value: keycloak.internal
  - name: KC_HTTP_ENABLED
    value: "true"
  - name: KC_PROXY_HEADERS
    value: xforwarded
  - name: KC_HEALTH_ENABLED
    value: "true"
  - name: KC_DB
    value: postgres
  - name: KC_DB_URL_HOST
    value: postgres.platform-db.internal
  - name: KC_DB_URL_DATABASE
    value: keycloak
  - name: KC_DB_USERNAME
    value: keycloak
  - name: KC_DB_PASSWORD
    value: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  - name: JAVA_OPTS_APPEND
    value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70.0"
command:
  - "/opt/keycloak/bin/kc.sh"
  - "start"
  - "--http-enabled=true"
  - "--hostname-strict=false"

The database password comes from an ExternalSecret, never from the values file.

docs.title: C. Realms
docs.text:
Realm Purpose Upstream platform Operators and developers of the platform AD/LDAP federation, plus a local breakglass realm for emergency accounts ai Service accounts and tenant identities for the inference API Local external Federates to AD/LDAP and exposes it to the other realms AD/LDAP

Federation setup for AD (in the external realm):

# In the external realm, add an LDAP provider
kc.sh config ldap --hostname=ldap.internal --port=636 --protocol=ldaps \
  --truststore-path=... --truststore-password=... \
  --bind-dn="cn=svc-keycloak,ou=services,dc=example,dc=com" \
  --bind-credential="$BIND_PASSWORD" \
  --users-query="(&(objectClass=person)(sAMAccountType=805306368)(uid={0}))" \
  --username-attribute=uid \
  --first-name-attribute=givenName \
  --last-name-attribute=sn \
  --email-attribute=mail \
  --group-query="(&(objectClass=group)(member={0}))" \
  --groups-attribute=memberOf

Bind credential is a service account password, stored in Vault and fetched at configuration time.

docs.title: D. Clients
docs.text:
Client Type Redirect URI Notes rancher Confidential https://rancher.internal/oidc/authorize groups and uid claims required argocd Confidential https://argocd.internal/auth/callback Same grafana Confidential https://grafana.internal/login/generic_oauth email and groups required harbor Confidential https://harbor.internal/c/oidc/callback gitlab Confidential https://gitlab.internal/users/auth/oidc/callback argocd-ci Confidential none Client credentials, for CI ai-gateway Confidential https://llm.internal/callback Token validation for inference

Every client is confidential with a client secret stored in Vault. Public clients are avoided entirely — there is no case here that needs one.

Protocol mapper for groups (required by Rancher and Argo CD):

  • Mapper type: Group membership
  • Claim name: groups
  • Full path: off
  • Add to ID token: on
  • Add to access token: on

Protocol mapper for uid:

  • Mapper type: User Attribute
  • User attribute: uid
  • Claim name: uid
  • Add to ID token: on

docs.title: E. Roles and group mapping
docs.text:
Keycloak group Platform role Grants platform-admins Administrator Everything platform-operators Operator Cluster and platform operations, no secret values developers Developer Own namespaces only auditors Auditor Read-only access to logs and audit data team-<name> Team member The team's namespace and its Argo CD project

Group membership is authoritative in the directory. Do not manage groups in Keycloak for federated users.

docs.title: F. Session and token settings
docs.text:
Setting Value Reason SSO session idle 30 min Limits the exposure window of an unattended workstation SSO session max 10 h Bounds the re-authentication burden Access token lifespan 5 min Short-lived access tokens limit the blast radius of a leaked token Refresh token lifespan 30 min Offline sessions off No persistent sessions on shared workstations Revoke refresh token on A logout invalidates the refresh token too Brute force detection on Protects against password guessing

Access tokens are short-lived on purpose. Every application that caches an access token must handle expiry, or it will present an expired token and get a 401 during normal operation. This is the most common OIDC integration bug.

docs.title: G. Offline operation
docs.text:
Keycloak does not need the internet. It needs:

  • The database (local PostgreSQL).
  • The CA certificate for the internal TLS endpoints.
  • The AD/LDAP endpoint for federated realms. If the directory is down, Keycloak itself keeps running and issues tokens for local users; federated logins fail.

Break-glass: a local realm with a small number of emergency accounts, whose credentials are held offline. Keep this separate from the federated realms so a directory outage does not lock out the administrators.

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Discovery document
curl -k https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .

# Token issue with a client-credentials grant
curl -sk -X POST \
  https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform/protocol/openid-connect/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials \
  -d client_id=argocd-ci \
  -d client_secret="$SECRET" | jq -r .access_token

# Groups claim present
curl -sk -X POST ... | jq -r '.access_token' | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .groups

Expected: the ID token contains groups and uid for a federated user.

docs.title: I. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Add a client kc.sh create clients or the admin console; the secret goes to Vault immediately Rotate a client secret Create a new secret, update the consumer, verify, then remove the old one Export a realm kc.sh export --realm platform --users skip --directory /backup/keycloak Import a realm kc.sh import --realm platform --file /backup/keycloak/platform-realm.json Backup PostgreSQL dump plus the realm export; the export is for review and for a rebuild, the dump is the recovery source Upgrade Read the release notes for the Keycloak version, back up the database, upgrade, run the automatic migration, verify the realm import

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - The database outside the cluster. - Client secrets in Vault, rotated on a schedule and immediately on suspected exposure. - The groups and uid claims verified in the ID token before any application integrates. - A local break-glass realm with offline-held credentials. - Short access token lifetimes, with every application prepared for expiry.

Strongly recommended: - A dedicated realm per trust boundary, so a compromise in one does not reach the others. - Federation rather than user sync, so the directory stays the single source of truth. - Alert on the Keycloak health endpoint and on authentication failure rates. - Alert on the certificate expiry of the Keycloak endpoint.

docs.title: Platform services
docs.text: Purpose: Make the platform observable and operated — monitoring, logging, GitOps, and platform add-ons (Harbor, Nexus, GitLab, Velero).

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Purpose Document Prometheus + Alertmanager Metrics collection and alerting monitoring/prometheus.md Log shipping Centralized logs from nodes and clusters monitoring/prometheus.md (§logging) Argo CD GitOps — sync manifests from internal GitLab management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md Harbor Container image registry + vulnerability scanning addons/platform-addons.md Nexus Artifact cache (Helm, PyPI, npm, Maven) addons/platform-addons.md GitLab Source control + pipelines automation/ Velero Cluster backup/restore (to Ceph) lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md

docs.title: Scrape targets
docs.text:
Prometheus scrapes: - Kubernetes components (kubelet, API server, scheduler, controller-manager) - Ceph MGR endpoint :9283 - Node exporters on every host - Edge load balancers

Alertmanager routes critical alerts: node down, disk full, etcd quorum lost.

docs.title: GitOps
docs.text: Argo CD auto-syncs every platform component from config/ in the internal GitLab. Use the platform GitLab project for platform manifests, apps for workloads.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document access management: RBAC, roles, bindings, service accounts, OIDC integration with Keycloak.

Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md, management-cluster/keycloak/keycloak.md, kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §RBAC.

docs.title: B. RBAC model
docs.text: Role Scope Capabilities Admin Cluster Full access Member Project Read/write resources Viewer Cluster/Project Read-only Restricted Project Read-only, no exec/secrets

docs.title: C. Service accounts
docs.text:
Service accounts are created per application and scoped to a namespace:

# ServiceAccount example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: app-ns
automountServiceAccountToken: true

docs.title: D. OIDC integration with Keycloak
docs.text:
Rancher integrates with Keycloak for centralized identity:

# Configure OIDC provider
rancher auth configure oidc \
  --issuer https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform \
  --client-id rancher \
  --client-secret <secret>

# Map Keycloak groups to Rancher roles
rancher group create --name developers --oidc-group developers
rancher role-template binding create --role project-member --group developers --project app-prod

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document cluster lifecycle: registration, upgrade, decommission, backup, restore via Rancher API.

Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md, management-cluster/rancher/fleet-integration.md, lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md.

docs.title: B. Cluster registration
docs.text:
New downstream clusters register with Rancher via cluster registration token:

# Generate registration token
rancher cluster-token create <cluster-name>

# Join cluster nodes
curl -sLf https://ranchermirror.internal/rancher/v3/cluster-registration-token | \
  bash -s -- --etcd --controlplane --worker

docs.title: C. Cluster upgrade
docs.text:
Upgrades follow Fleet or Rancher's built-in upgrade mechanism:

# Fleet-based upgrade (preferred)
kubectl apply -f fleet/cluster-upgrade.yaml

# Rancher API upgrade
rancher cluster upgrade <cluster-id> --kubernetes-version v1.36.5

docs.title: D. Cluster decommission
docs.text:
# Delete workloads
kubectl delete namespace -l cluster=<name>

# Drain and delete cluster via Rancher API
rancher cluster delete <cluster-id>

# Verify deletion
rancher cluster list | grep <name>

docs.title: E. Backup and restore
docs.text:
Management cluster backup follows lifecycle/disaster-recovery/management-cluster.md. Downstream clusters are backed up via Velero:

# Backup downstream cluster
velero backup create <cluster-name>-backup --include-namespaces all

# Restore downstream cluster
velero restore create --from-backup <cluster-name>-backup

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document cluster onboarding: importing existing clusters, provisioning new clusters, cluster registration, and validation procedures. Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md, management-cluster/rancher/cluster-lifecycle.md, management-cluster/rancher/fleet-integration.md.

docs.title: In-cluster registration
docs.text:
The Rancher agent is deployed inside the target cluster. The target cluster must be reachable from Rancher.

# In the Application Cluster
kubectl -n cattle-system create secret generic cattle-cluster-agent \
  -n cattle-system --from-literal="token=<token>" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/rke2-k3s.yaml   # for RKE2

For a Kubespray-built (kubeadm) cluster, use the rke2 agent manifest only if the cluster is RKE2. For kubeadm clusters, Rancher supports the "import existing" flow with the agent applied by hand:

# Import existing cluster via agent manifest
kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/agent.yaml

The exact manifest path must be confirmed against the pinned Rancher release before use.

docs.title: Out-of-cluster registration
docs.text:
Rancher deploys the agent using kubeconfig. Use this when firewalls prevent Rancher from reaching the target cluster's API.

# Generate registration token in Rancher UI
# Or via API: rancher cluster-token create <cluster-name>

# Join cluster nodes
curl -sLf https://ranchermirror.internal/rancher/v3/cluster-registration-token | \
  bash -s -- --etcd --controlplane --worker

docs.title: Kubespray deployment
docs.text:
New clusters are provisioned using Kubespray with the same OS baseline as the management cluster. Three workers is the default; one is acceptable for a lab and gives no rollout headroom for the Rancher upgrade itself.

# Generate hosts inventory
python3 contrib/inventory_builder.py -i <inventory_name> --etcd --control-plane --worker

# Apply Kubespray
ansible-playbook -i <inventory> site.yml --tags=rke-cluster

docs.title: RKE2 cluster provisioning
docs.text:
# RKE2 install via systemd
systemctl enable rke2
systemctl start rke2

# Verify cluster status
rke2ctl get-cluster-token
kubectl get nodes

docs.title: K3s cluster provisioning
docs.text:
# K3s install
curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -

# Verify cluster status
kubectl get nodes

docs.title: Registration models
docs.text: Model How Use In-cluster registration The agent is deployed inside the target cluster by Rancher The target cluster is reachable from Rancher Out-of-cluster registration Rancher deploys the agent using kubeconfig Firewalls prevent Rancher from reaching the target cluster's API

docs.title: Registration token flow
docs.text:
# 1. Generate token in Rancher UI or API
rancher cluster-token create <cluster-name>

# 2. Join cluster nodes with token
curl -sLf https://ranchermirror.internal/rancher/v3/cluster-registration-token | \
  bash -s -- --etcd --controlplane --worker

docs.title: Agent-based import for kubeadm clusters
docs.text:
# Apply the Rancher agent manifest
kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/agent.yaml

Confirm the exact manifest path against the pinned Rancher release before use.

docs.title: Rancher is up
docs.text:
# Check Rancher pods
kubectl -n cattle-system get pods

# Health check
curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

docs.title: Managed cluster registration and nodes visible
docs.text: # Rancher UI: Cluster Management -> the cluster -> Nodes

docs.title: From the Rancher API
docs.text:
curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  https://rancher.internal/v3/clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, state}'

Expected: state: "active" and the node count matching the cluster.

docs.title: Post-onboarding verification
docs.text:
# Verify Fleet integration
kubectl get gitrepo -n fleet-default

# Verify baseline add-ons are synced
kubectl get bundle -n fleet-default

# Check cluster resources
kubectl -n cattle-system get clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, phase, health}'

docs.title: Rancher cluster upgrade procedure
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Pre-upgrade validation
docs.text:
• Confirm the current Rancher version and embedded Kubernetes version (RKE2/K3s).
  • Review the Rancher upgrade guide for breaking changes and deprecations.
  • Verify the error budget: if the current SLO consumption is above 50% with less than 30 days remaining, defer the upgrade.
  • Take a etcd snapshot of the management cluster.
  • Ensure a full backup of the GitOps repositories (Fleet bundles, Argo CD applications).
  • Validate that all managed clusters are in active state and healthy.
  • Check that no pending upgrades or failed rollouts exist in the Fleet baseline.

docs.title: B. RKE2/K3s version selection
docs.text:
• Choose the target Kubernetes version compatible with the Rancher release being upgraded to (Rancher v2.8 → K3s v1.27+ / RKE2 v1.27+).
  • Confirm that the node OS baseline (Ubuntu 22.04 / RHEL 9) supports the target K8s version.
  • Record the desired K8s version in inventory/hosts-mgmt.ini under the [mgmt] section: 
    [mgmt]
mgmt-01 ansible_host=10.0.0.1
mgmt-02 ansible_host=10.0.0.2
mgmt-03 ansible_host=10.0.0.3
kubernetes_version=v1.27.3
  • Run kubespary/cluster-upgrade-prep.sh (if available) to pre-stage the new K8s binaries on all nodes.
  • Verify that the RKE2/K3s agent version in Rancher matches the target K8s version; update the agent manifest if needed.

docs.title: C. Control plane upgrade
docs.text:
• Drain one control‑plane node (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir).
  • Upgrade K8s on the control‑plane node via Kubespray rolling upgrade: 
    ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts-mgmt.ini kubespray/roles/kubernetes.yml --tags=kube-apiserver
  • Wait for the node to re‑join and become Ready.
  • Repeat for each control‑plane node (3 total), draining one at a time and respecting the 5‑minute cooldown between nodes.
  • After the last control‑plane node is upgraded, verify the cluster version: 
    kubectl version --client=false | grep ServerVersion

docs.title: D. Worker node upgrade
docs.text:
• For each worker node group:
  • Drain the node.
  • Upgrade the K8s runtime and binaries using the Kubespray inventory version set in step B.
  • Verify the node rejoins and becomes Ready.
  • Run the Fleet reconciliation to re‑sync node metadata: 
    fleetctl check node <node-name>
  • If using node pools managed by the node-pool-management.md procedure, follow that workflow instead of manual drain/upgrade.
  • After all workers in a group are upgraded, confirm the cluster-wide K8s version matches the target.

docs.title: E. Post‑upgrade verification
docs.text:
• Run the health check endpoint: 
    curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health
  • Verify Rancher UI loads and shows the upgraded K8s version under Cluster Management → System.
  • Confirm all managed clusters are still registered and their nodes report the correct version: 
    curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  https://rancher.internal/v3/clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, state, nodes}'
  • Execute the Fleet sync check: 
    fleetctl check --targets all
  • Review the etcd metrics for any spike in latency or failed proposals immediately after the upgrade.
  • If using monitoring, confirm that SLO error‑budget consumption has not spiked (e.g., latency p99 within target).

docs.title: F. Rollback procedures
docs.text:
• Rollback window: Within 2 hours of upgrade completion, before the error budget is significantly consumed.
  • Control plane: To rollback a single control‑plane node, re‑apply the previous Kubespray tags (kubespray/roles/kubernetes.yml --tags=kube-apiserver) with the prior kubernetes_version. Drain the node, apply the older version, and uncordon.
  • Worker nodes: Re‑run the Kubespray playbook with the previous kubernetes_version on the affected worker(s). Drain, downgrade, uncordon.
  • Rancher Helm chart: If the Rancher upgrade itself caused issues, helm rollback -n cattle-system rancher <revision> can revert the Rancher Helm release.
  • After any rollback, re‑verify the health check, cluster state, and SLO metrics. Document the rollback in the incident tracker and schedule a post‑mortem to identify the root cause.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Fleet integration with Rancher: cluster registration, baseline add-ons through Git, GitOps workflow, and Fleet vs Argo CD ownership boundaries.

Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md §Fleet, management-cluster/argocd/argocd.md, automation/gitlab-ci/gitlab-ansible-design.md.

docs.title: B. Fleet vs Argo CD ownership
docs.text:
Rancher manages the lifecycle of application clusters. Fleet and Argo CD have complementary but distinct roles:

Component Responsibility Owns Fleet Cluster registration, baseline add-ons, cluster-level configuration Rancher cluster resources, namespace resources, baseline add-ons Argo CD Application workloads, application-level GitOps Application namespaces, application deployments

Rule: Fleet and Argo CD must never both own the same object. The ownership table in automation/gitlab-ci/gitlab-ansible-design.md is normative.

docs.title: C. Fleet architecture
docs.text:
Rancher Server (management cluster)
  ├── Fleet Controller
  │     ├── GitRepo resources (cluster registration)
  │     ├── ClusterRegistration resources
  │     └── Baseline add-on bundles
  └── Kubernetes API
        ├── Managed clusters (registered via Fleet)
        └── Baseline add-ons (deployed to each cluster)

Fleet runs in the management cluster (cattle-fleet-system namespace) and manages: - Cluster registration tokens and kubeconfigs - Baseline add-ons (monitoring, logging, ingress, policy) - Cluster-level configuration (labels, taints, annotations)

docs.title: 1. Generate registration token
docs.text:
In Rancher UI: Cluster Management → Add Cluster → Custom → Generate registration command.

The registration command includes: - Server URL (Rancher API endpoint) - Token (short-lived, rotates automatically) - CA certificate (Rancher server TLS)

docs.title: 2. Register cluster via Fleet
docs.text:
Create a Fleet ClusterRegistration resource:

apiVersion: fleet.cattle.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterRegistration
metadata:
  name: <cluster-name>
  namespace: fleet-default
spec:
  base64ca: <base64-encoded-CA>
  serverUrl: https://<rancher-url>
  labels:
    environment: production
    tier: application

docs.title: 3. Verify registration
docs.text:
kubectl -n fleet-local get clusters
kubectl -n fleet-local get clusterregistrations
kubectl get nodes  # On the managed cluster

docs.title: E. Baseline add-ons
docs.text:
Baseline add-ons are deployed to every managed cluster via Fleet GitRepo resources:

Add-on Purpose Fleet target Monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) Cluster observability monitoring namespace Logging (Fluent Bit/Loki) Log aggregation logging namespace Ingress (NGINX) External traffic entry ingress-nginx namespace Policy (Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper) Security policy enforcement gatekeeper-system namespace Cert-manager Certificate management cert-manager namespace

Each add-on is a separate Fleet GitRepo pointing to a directory in the GitLab repository:

apiVersion: fleet.cattle.io/v1alpha1
kind: GitRepo
metadata:
  name: baseline-monitoring
  namespace: fleet-default
spec:
  repo: git@gitlab.internal:platform/baseline-addons.git
  branch: main
  paths:
    - monitoring/
  targetNamespace: monitoring

docs.title: F. GitOps workflow
docs.text:
1. Provision cluster: Terraform creates VMs, Ansible configures OS
  2. Register cluster: Fleet ClusterRegistration resource
  3. Deploy baseline add-ons: Fleet GitRepo resources deploy monitoring, logging, ingress, policy
  4. Deploy applications: Argo CD syncs application workloads from GitLab
  5. Monitor and reconcile: Fleet and Argo CD continuously reconcile drift

docs.title: G. Ownership boundaries
docs.text:
Resource type Owner Tool Cluster registration token Fleet Rancher kubeconfig distribution Fleet Rancher Baseline add-ons (monitoring, logging, ingress, policy) Fleet Fleet GitRepo Application deployments Argo CD Argo CD Application Namespace creation Fleet Fleet (baseline namespaces) Application namespace resources Argo CD Argo CD Application RBAC for applications Argo CD Argo CD Application Network policies Fleet (baseline) Fleet GitRepo Pod Security Standards Fleet (baseline) Fleet GitRepo

Never deploy an application workload via Fleet. Never deploy baseline add-ons via Argo CD.

docs.title: H. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Cluster not showing in Rancher Registration token expired Generate new token, re-register Baseline add-ons not deploying Fleet GitRepo sync error Check fleet get gitrepo status Application drift not detected Argo CD not syncing Check argocd app sync status Fleet and Argo CD conflict Both owning same object Remove one owner per ownership table

docs.title: Rancher HA Installation
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Rancher HA provides high availability for the Rancher server across three control-plane nodes. The deployment uses an external PostgreSQL database, embedded ETCD (on each control-plane node), and a load balancer for frontend access.

  admin workstation
        |
  Rancher VIP (DNS + HAProxy)
        |
  3 x Rancher control-plane nodes
    ETCD embedded (multi-node cluster)
    PostgreSQL external (dedicated RDS instance)
    Rancher server pods (replicated x3)
  Management Cluster (3 control-plane + 3 infra workers)

docs.title: B. Deployment model
docs.text:
HA requirement: Rancher HA requires a minimum of 3 control-plane nodes. Each node runs the Rancher server pod and participates in the embedded ETCD cluster. An external PostgreSQL database is required for the Rancher system catalog.

Node count, vCPU, RAM and disk are inputs, not constants: the site generates hosts-mgmt.ini from the management worker count. Three control-plane nodes is the minimum for HA; one is acceptable for a lab and gives no rollout headroom for the Rancher upgrade itself.

The management cluster is built with Kubespray, like every other cluster, so it is reproducible from the same inventory and the same OS baseline.

docs.title: C. Prerequisites
docs.text: Component Requirement Kubernetes v1.25+ with three control-plane nodes ETCD Embedded, multi-node cluster (3 nodes minimum) PostgreSQL External database, version 12+ Load balancer DNS + HAProxy or cloud LB, TLS termination OS Ubuntu 22.04 / Rocky Linux 9 on all nodes Ports 443 (TCP), 80 (TCP), 5432 (TCP), 2379-2380 (ETCD)

docs.title: D. Server installation (Kubespray HA)
docs.text:
Build the management cluster with Kubespray configured for three control-plane nodes.

# Clone Kubespray and checkout the release
git clone https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubespray.git
cd kubespray
git checkout release-2.26

# Create virtual environment
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Generate inventory from existing or create new
ansible-inventory -i inventory/hosts -y > inventory.json

# Scale to 3 control-plane nodes
# Edit inventory to set count of etcd and control-plane nodes to 3
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml site.yml --become --become-user root

After Kubespray completes, verify three control-plane nodes are ready:

kubectl get nodes -A | grep -E "control-plane|etcd"

docs.title: E. External PostgreSQL database setup
docs.text: Rancher HA requires an external PostgreSQL database. Do not use the embedded database.

docs.title: 1. Provision RDS or self-hosted PostgreSQL
docs.text:
# Example: self-hosted PostgreSQL on the management cluster
kubectl create namespace cattle-system

# Create a PostgreSQL deployment with external access
cat > postgres.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres-external
  namespace: cattle-system
spec:
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
      targetPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: cattle-system
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:15
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_DB
              value: rancher
            - name: POSTGRES_USER
              value: rancher
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              value: <strong-password>
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
          volumeMounts:
            - name: postgres-data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: postgres-pvc
      volumes:
        - name: postgres-data
          emptyDir: {}
EOF

kubectl apply -f postgres.yaml

docs.title: 2. Create the Rancher system database
docs.text:
# Connect and create the database
psql "postgresql://rancher:<password>@<postgres-host>:5432/rancher" -c \
  "CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS cattle;"

docs.title: 3. Verify connectivity
docs.text: PGPASSWORD=<password> psql -h <postgres-host> -U rancher -d rancher -c "SELECT 1;"

docs.title: F. TLS certificates
docs.text: Rancher HA uses TLS certificates terminated at the load balancer. Generate certificates using cert-manager or provided scripts.

docs.title: 1. Generate certificates with cert-manager
docs.text:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
  namespace: cattle-system
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: admin@example.com
    privateKeySize: 4096
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingressClassName: nginx

docs.title: 2. Create the TLS secret for Rancher
docs.text:
# Generate a signed certificate for rancher.internal
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:4096 \
  -keyout /etc/rancher/cert.key \
  -out /etc/rancher/cert.crt \
  -subj "/CN=rancher.internal"

# Create the Kubernetes secret
kubectl -n cattle-system create secret tls rancher-tls \
  --cert=/etc/rancher/cert.crt \
  --key=/etc/rancher/cert.key

docs.title: 3. Configure Rancher to use the TLS secret
docs.text:
# values.yaml
tls:
  source: secret
  existingSecret: rancher-tls

docs.title: 4. Alternative: Terminate TLS at load balancer
docs.text: Configure HAProxy or cloud load balancer to terminate TLS before forwarding to Rancher nodes. The internal Rancher communication uses self-signed certificates signed by the embedded ETCD cluster.

docs.title: 1. DNS setup
docs.text:
; DNS records for Rancher HA
$ORIGIN internal.
rancher    IN  A     <lb-node-1-ip>
           IN  A     <lb-node-2-ip>
           IN  A     <lb-node-3-ip>
_rancher   IN  SRV   0 0 443 rancher.internal.

docs.title: 2. HAProxy configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
global
  log /dev/log local0
  log /dev/log local1 notice
  maxconn 2000

defaults
  mode http
  option dontlognull
  timeout connect 5000ms
  timeout client 50000ms
  timeout server 50000ms

frontend http_front
  bind *:80
  redirect scheme https if !{ ssl_f }

frontend https_front
  bind *:443 ssl crt /etc/rancher/cert.pem
  option forwardfor
  default_backend rancher_backend

backend rancher_backend
  mode http
  balance roundrobin
  option httpchk HEAD /v3/health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: rancher.internal
  http-check expect status 200
  server rancher1 rancher.internal:443 ssl verify none
  server rancher2 rancher.internal:443 ssl verify none
  server rancher3 rancher.internal:443 ssl verify none

docs.title: 3. Cloud load balancer (AWS ALB/NLB)
docs.text: Configure TLS listener and target group pointing to the three Rancher control-plane nodes. Enable health check on /v3/health.

docs.title: H. Rancher HA Helm installation
docs.text:
Add the Rancher chart repository and install with HA values.

helm repo add rancher-stable https://releases.rancher.com/server-charts/stable
helm repo update

cat > values-ha.yaml << 'EOF'
hostname: rancher.internal
replicas: 3
ingress:
  enabled: true
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    source: secret
    existingSecret: rancher-tls
privateRegistry: harbor.internal
rancherImage: harbor.internal/platform/rancher/rancher
systemDefaultRegistry: harbor.internal
useBundledSystemChart: true
bootstrapPassword: ""            # from External Secrets, not inline
extraEnv:
  - name: CATTLE_SYSTEM_DB_TYPE
    value: "postgresql"
  - name: CATTLE_SYSTEM_DB_URL
    value: "postgresql://rancher:<password>@<postgres-host>:5432/rancher?sslmode=require"
  - name: CATTLE_ETCD_SERVERS
    value: "https://etcd-1.internal:2379,https://etcd-2.internal:2379,https://etcd-3.internal:2379"
EOF

helm install rancher rancher-stable/rancher \
  --namespace cattle-system --create-namespace \
  --values values-ha.yaml

docs.title: 1. Verify Rancher pods are running
docs.text:
kubectl -n cattle-system get pods

Expected: 3 Rancher server pods, all in Running state.

docs.title: 2. Verify ETCD cluster health
docs.text:
# Check ETCD member status on each node
for node in etcd-1 etcd-2 etcd-3; do
  ssh $node "etcdctl member list \
    -w endpoints=https://localhost:2379 \
    --cacert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.crt \
    --key /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/peer.key"
done

docs.title: 3. Test Rancher UI via load balancer
docs.text:
curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

Expected: {"status":"healthy"}.

docs.title: 4. Verify database connectivity
docs.text:
kubectl -n cattle-system exec -it <rancher-pod> -- \
  pg_isready -h <postgres-host> -U rancher -d rancher

docs.title: 5. Verify load balancer traffic distribution
docs.text:
# Check each Rancher node receives requests
for i in 1 2 3; do
  curl -k -s https://rancher.internal/v3/health | head -1
done

docs.title: 6. Expected validation output
docs.text:
$ kubectl -n cattle-system get pods
NAME                              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
rancher-7d8f9b6c9-x8mlp           2/2     Running   0          10m
rancher-7d8f9b6c9-pd9jl           2/2     Running   0          10m
rancher-7d8f9b6c9-q9bhm           2/2     Running   0          10m
$ curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

docs.title: Rancher Node Pool Management
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Node pools control the lifecycle of node groups within the management cluster and application clusters. Proper node pool management ensures capacity availability, enables rolling upgrades without downtime, and prevents workloads from being scheduled on nodes undergoing maintenance. This document covers the full node pool lifecycle: creation, scaling, auto-scaling, taints/labels, drain/cordon, and upgrade strategies.

docs.title: 1. Identify the purpose
docs.text:
• Baseline worker pool: General-purpose nodes running application workloads.
  • Dedicated pool: Nodes with specialized hardware (GPU, storage) or security requirements.
  • Upgrade pool: Nodes targeted for a rolling upgrade batch.

docs.title: 2. Create via Rancher UI
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Cluster Management → target cluster → Nodes → Node Pools → Add node pool.
  2. Specify a Name (e.g., general, gpu, upgrade-batch-1).
  3. Select the Instance type, OS image, and Root disk size.
  4. Set the Initial replica count (minimum 2 for high availability).
  5. Click Create.

docs.title: 3. Create via kubectl / rancher-cli (GitOps)
docs.text:
# Example: add a general worker pool via the Rancher API
curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  -X POST "https://rancher.internal/v3/cluster-api-providers/capa/aws/nodepools" \
  -d '{
    "name": "general",
    "labels": {"node-role.kubernetes.io/general": ""},
    "taints": [{"key": "node-type", "value": "general", "effect": "NoSchedule"}],
    "capacity": "on-demand",
    "instance_type": "m5.large",
    "desired_capacity": 4,
    "max_capacity": 8,
    "min_capacity": 2
  }'

docs.title: 4. RKE2-specific: add node pool with rke2
docs.text:
# Create a node pool using the Rancher agent manifest
kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/rke2-k3s.yaml
# Then in the Rancher UI, the new nodes will appear under the cluster's node pools.

docs.title: 5. Verification
docs.text:
# List all node pools in the cluster
kubectl -n cattle-system get nodepools -A

# Confirm the new pool is present and its desired/replica counts
kubectl -n cattle-system describe nodepools <pool-name>

docs.title: 1. Manual scaling (Rancher UI)
docs.text:
1. Go to Cluster Management → target cluster → Nodes → Node Pools.
  2. Click the ⋮ menu → Edit on the target pool.
  3. Adjust the Desired replica count.
  4. Save changes. The ASG (Auto Scaling Group) will reconcile within the provider's reconciliation interval.

docs.title: 2. Manual scaling (CLI)
docs.text:
# Scale a node pool desired count
kubectl -n cattle-system scale nodepool <pool-name> --replicas=6

# Verify
kubectl -n cattle-system get nodepools <pool-name> -o yaml | grep -E "desired|replicas"

docs.title: 3. Scaling rationale
docs.text: Scenario Action Adding capacity for a new feature flag Increase desired by the expected workload size Removing underutilized nodes Decrease desired; verify drain completes first Preparing for an upgrade Scale up the upgrade pool before draining the old batch

docs.title: 4. Cloud provider auto-scaling group bounds
docs.text:
When scaling via the underlying ASG, verify min_capacity, desired_capacity, and max_capacity are set appropriately:

# Describe the ASG linked to the node pool
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups \
  --filter "Name=tag:Name,Values=<pool-name>*" \
  --query "AutoScalingGroups[0].{Min: MinSize, Desired: DesiredCapacity, Max: MaxSize}"

docs.title: 1. Enable cluster-autoscaler
docs.text:
The Cluster Autoscaler works with the ASG to grow/shrink node pools based on pod scheduling needs.

# Deploy the Cluster Autoscaler (Rancher-managed cluster example)
helm repo add rancher-stable https://releases.rancher.com/server-charts/stable
helm install cluster-autoscaler rancher-stable/cluster-autoscaler \
  --namespace cattle-system \
  --set awsRegion=us-east-1 \
  --set nodeGroupSelector=nodepool-name=<pool-name> \
  --set scaleDown.enabled=true \
  --set scaleDown.unneededTime=6m \
  --set scaleDown.skipNodesWithLocalStorage=true

docs.title: 2. Auto-scaling configuration
docs.text:
Configure the Cluster Autoscaler deployment with these parameters:

Parameter Recommended value Description --scale-down-unneeded-time 6m Nodes unneeded for 6 minutes are candidates for scale-down --scale-down-skips-nodes-with-local-storage true Prevents losing ephemeral local data --node-group-auto-discovery tag Auto-discovers node groups by tag --scale-down-after-transition 5m Wait 5m after a scale-up before considering scale-down

docs.title: 3. Pod disruption budget (PDB) considerations
docs.text:
Ensure PDBs allow nodes to be removed:

# Example PDB that allows 1 unavailable during scale-down
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: app-pdb
  namespace: app-ns
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app

docs.title: 4. Auto-scaling troubleshooting
docs.text:
# Check Cluster Autoscaler logs
kubectl -n cattle-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler

# Manual node addition/removal is blocked if the autoscaler is active.
# To manually add a node, temporarily disable the autoscaler or use a
# separate ASG not managed by the autoscaler.

docs.title: 1. Purpose of taints
docs.text:
• NoSchedule: Pods without a matching toleration are not scheduled onto the node.
  • PreferNoSchedule: Pods without a matching toleration are preferred not to be scheduled, but may still be placed if no other node is available.
  • NoExecute: Pods already running on the node are evicted if they don't have a matching toleration; also blocks new scheduling.

docs.title: 2. Common taint patterns
docs.text: Taint Use case key=value:NoSchedule Dedicated pools (GPU, storage, isolated workloads) key=value:NoExecute Draining nodes for upgrade; taint-added automatically during drain node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule Control-plane nodes only (Rancher sets this automatically)

docs.title: 3. Add/remove taints via Rancher UI
docs.text:
1. Go to Cluster Management → target cluster → Nodes.
  2. Click the ⋮ menu on the target node → Edit taints.
  3. Add a new taint with Key, Value, and Effect.
  4. Click Save.

docs.title: 4. Add/remove taints via CLI
docs.text:
# Add a taint to a node
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> key=value:NoSchedule

# Remove a specific taint (keep others)
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> key=value:NoSchedule-

# Remove all taints
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> -

# List current taints
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep Taints

docs.title: 5. Common label patterns
docs.text: Label Typical value Purpose node-role.kubernetes.io/<role> `` Identifies the node role nodepool-name/<name> <pool-name> Links node to its pool cluster-name/<cluster> <cluster> Identifies the cluster ownership failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone <zone> AZ awareness for scheduler

docs.title: 6. Bulk label/taint application on node pool creation
docs.text: When creating a node pool, apply labels and taints at the pool level so all nodes inherit them automatically. This avoids per-node operations and ensures consistency across scale-out events.

docs.title: 1. Cordon a node (prevent new scheduling)
docs.text:
# Mark node as unschedulable
kubectl cordon <node-name>

# Verify
kubectl describe node <node-name> | grep -i schedulable
# Output: ...
#        Schedulable: true  # becomes "false" after cordon

docs.title: 2. Drain a node (evict pods safely)
docs.text:
# Drain with PDB awareness and graceful deletion
kubectl drain <node-name> \
  --ignore-daemonsets \
  --delete-emptydir-data \
  --timeout=300s \
  --grace-period=30

Flags explained:

Flag Purpose --ignore-daemonsets Skips DaemonSet pods (they are recreated elsewhere) --delete-emptydir-data Removes emptyDir volumes --timeout Maximum time to wait for pod eviction --grace-period Seconds of grace given to each pod before force-delete

docs.title: 3. Drain during node pool upgrade
docs.text:
The standard upgrade pattern is:

# 1. Cordon the node (optional, if using --delete-emptydir-data)
kubectl cordon <node-name>

# 2. Drain the node (evicts pods respecting PDBs)
kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --timeout=300s

# 3. (Optional) If the node comes back, taint it for the upgrade
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> key=upgrade-effect:NoSchedule

# 4. After upgrade completes, remove the taint
kubectl taint nodes <node-name> key=upgrade-effect:NoSchedule-

docs.title: 4. Re-enable scheduling after drain
docs.text:
# Mark node as schedulable again
kubectl uncordon <node-name>

docs.title: 5. Bulk cordon/drain via node pool
docs.text:
Since cordon/drain operate on individual nodes, use the node pool as a loop:

# List nodes in a pool and cordon each
kubectl get nodes -l nodepool-name=<pool-name> -o name | while read -r node; do
  kubectl cordon "$node"
done

docs.title: 1. Rolling upgrade (recommended)
docs.text:
The safest approach for production clusters: upgrade one node pool at a time, maintaining enough capacity for workloads throughout.

# Step 1: Scale up the new node pool (or create a new pool with the target version)
kubectl -n cattle-system scale nodepool <pool-name> --replicas=2

# Step 2: Taint the new nodes so existing workloads are not disrupted
kubectl taint nodes -l nodepool-name=<pool-name> version=upgraded:NoSchedule

# Step 3: Drain and upgrade old nodes one at a time
for node in $(kubectl get nodes -l nodepool-name=<pool-name> -o name); do
  kubectl drain "$node" --ignore-daemonsets --timeout=300s
  # Node is removed from the pool; new node with updated OS/image joins
done

# Step 4: Scale down to desired count
kubectl -n cattle-system scale nodepool <pool-name> --replicas=<desired>

docs.title: 2. Canary upgrade (for risky OS / kernel updates)
docs.text:
1. Create a new node pool with the target OS/image version.
  2. Set a small desired capacity (e.g., 1-2 nodes).
  3. Deploy a canary workload that exercises the new environment.
  4. If the canary passes, scale up the new pool and drain the old one.
  5. If the canary fails, roll back by deleting the new pool.

docs.title: 3. Blue-green at the node-pool level
docs.text: Phase Action Blue Existing node pool running the current version Green New node pool spun up on the target version Shift traffic Gradually move workloads to the green pool (via PDBs, re-deploys, or service ingress changes) Retire blue Drain and delete the old node pool

docs.title: 4. Upgrade rollback
docs.text:
If an upgrade fails mid-stream:

# Identify the last known-good node pool configuration
kubectl -n cattle-system get nodepools -o yaml > /tmp/before-upgrade.yaml

# Re-apply the previous desired count and taints
kubectl -n cattle-system scale nodepool <pool-name> --replicas=<previous-count>

# Restore taints that were in effect before the upgrade
kubectl taint nodes -l nodepool-name=<pool-name> <previous-taints>

docs.title: 5. Post-upgrade verification
docs.text:
# Confirm all nodes report the expected OS version / Rancher agent version
kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -E "VERSION|AgentVersion"

# Run the health check from rancher.md §G
curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

# Verify fleet sync is healthy after the node pool change
fleetctl get clusters -o wide

docs.title: 6. Upgrade checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Backup etcd and critical cluster records
  • [ ] Confirm sufficient capacity in the remaining node pools
  • [ ] Verify PDBs allow drain of target nodes
  • [ ] Taint new nodes before draining old ones
  • [ ] Execute drain one node at a time; wait for pod reconciliation
  • [ ] Confirm no NotReady nodes remain longer than the cluster-autoscaler grace period
  • [ ] Run integration smoke test against the upgraded nodes
  • [ ] Document the upgrade in the change log

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Rancher management cluster
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Rancher manages the lifecycle of the Application Clusters and provides the operator view of the estate.

  admin workstation
        |
   Rancher VIP (DMZ)
        |
  Management Cluster (3 control-plane + 3 infra workers)
    rancher server x3
    cattle-cluster-agent (runs in each managed cluster)
    fleet agent (in each managed cluster)

docs.title: B. Deployment model
docs.text:
Its own cluster, its own inventory, its own capacity. Rancher, Keycloak, Argo CD, Harbor and Vault run on a management cluster that is built with the same Kubespray release but a different inventory file, and sized independently from the application clusters it manages. Sharing worker nodes with a workload cluster means a workload can starve the console you need to fix it, and a management-cluster upgrade then shares a maintenance window with production.

Node count, vCPU, RAM and disk are inputs, not constants: the site generates hosts-mgmt.ini from the management worker count and the first management address (catalog/catalog.json, page p3). Three workers is the default; one is acceptable for a lab and gives no rollout headroom for the Rancher upgrade itself.

Rancher runs on its own dedicated cluster, not on an Application Cluster. Rationale: ADR-0010 and ADR-0011. If Rancher shares a cluster with workloads, a workload failure domain becomes a management failure domain.

The Rancher cluster is built with Kubespray, like every other cluster, so it is reproducible from the same inventory and the same OS baseline.

docs.title: C. Installation
docs.text:
Rancher is installed with the official Helm chart, applied by Argo CD into the Management Cluster.

# values.yaml
hostname: rancher.internal
replicas: 3
ingress:
  enabled: true
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    source: letsEncrypt
privateRegistry: harbor.internal
rancherImage: harbor.internal/platform/rancher/rancher
systemDefaultRegistry: harbor.internal
useBundledSystemChart: true
bootstrapPassword: ""            # from External Secrets, not inline

helm repo add rancher-stable https://releases.rancher.com/server-charts/stable
helm install rancher rancher-stable/rancher \
  --namespace cattle-system --create-namespace \
  --values values.yaml

Bootstrap password:

kubectl -n cattle-system get secret rancher-bootstrap-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

The password is changed on first login and the bootstrap secret is then deleted. In GitOps, the value comes from Vault via External Secrets and the rendered Secret is never committed.

docs.title: D. Cluster registration
docs.text:
Two registration models:

Model How Use In-cluster registration The agent is deployed inside the target cluster by Rancher The target cluster is reachable from Rancher Out-of-cluster registration Rancher deploys the agent using kubeconfig Firewalls prevent Rancher from reaching the target cluster's API 
# In the Application Cluster
kubectl -n cattle-system create secret generic cattle-cluster-agent \
  -n cattle-system --from-literal="token=<token>" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/rke2-k3s.yaml   # for RKE2

For a Kubespray-built (kubeadm) cluster, use the rke2 agent manifest only if the cluster is RKE2. For kubeadm clusters, Rancher supports the "import existing" flow with the agent applied by hand:

kubectl apply -f https://releases.rancher.com/rancher-agent/v2.15/agent.yaml

The exact manifest path must be confirmed against the pinned Rancher release before use.

docs.title: E. Identity
docs.text:
Rancher is configured against Keycloak with OIDC.

# Rancher global setting (via the UI or the API)
oidc:
  issuer: https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform
  clientId: rancher
  clientSecret: <from vault>
  redirectUri: https://rancher.internal/oidc/authorize?client_id=rancher&redirect_uri=https://rancher.internal/oidc/auth
  scope: "openid profile email groups"
  userSearchBase: "ou=users,dc=example,dc=com"
  groupSearchBase: "ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com"
  uidField: "uid"
  groupsField: "memberOf"
  idpCert: <CA cert>

Keycloak client requirements: - A dedicated client rancher with client credentials off and standard flow on. - The groups claim must be present in the ID token. Add a protocol mapper in Keycloak: - Mapper type: Group membership - Claim name: groups - Full path: off - Add to ID token: on - The uid claim must be present. Add a mapper for uid if the user attribute is not the default.

Group-to-role mapping in Rancher:

Keycloak group Rancher role platform-admins admin platform-operators admin (limited to the platform project) app-developers project-member in the team projects

docs.title: F. Fleet (GitOps for downstream clusters)
docs.text:
Fleet manages cluster registration and baseline add-ons through Git. It is complementary to Argo CD:

Fleet Argo CD Scope Clusters and the add-ons every cluster must have Applications and their configuration Repository mgmt-rancher project Per-team application projects Sync model Bundle-based Application/ApplicationSet Used here for cluster registration, CNI baseline, node metadata Everything else

Fleet bundle:

apiVersion: fleet.cattle.io/v1alpha1
kind: GitRepo
metadata:
  name: platform-baseline
  namespace: fleet-default
spec:
  repo: https://gitlab.internal/platform/fleet-baseline.git
  branch: main
  paths:
    - bundle.yaml

apiVersion: fleet.cattle.io/v1alpha1
kind: Bundle
metadata:
  name: platform-baseline
  namespace: fleet-default
spec:
  targets:
    - clusterSelector:
        matchLabels:
          env: production

Rule: Fleet and Argo CD must never both own the same object. The ownership table in automation/gitlab-ci/gitlab-ansible-design.md is normative.

docs.title: G. Validation
docs.text:
# Rancher is up
kubectl -n cattle-system get pods
curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

# The managed cluster is registered and its nodes are visible
# Rancher UI: Cluster Management -> the cluster -> Nodes

From the Rancher API:

curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  https://rancher.internal/v3/clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, state}'

Expected: state: "active" and the node count matching the cluster.

docs.title: H. Operations
docs.text:
Task Procedure Add a cluster Create the cluster with Kubespray, then import it into Rancher with the registration token Remove a cluster Delete in Rancher, then decommission the nodes Upgrade Rancher Helm upgrade via Argo CD. Check the release notes for the CRD changes first Rotate the Rancher TLS certificate cert-manager re-issues; the Rancher pod picks up the new secret Rotate the OIDC client secret Update in Keycloak and in the Rancher global setting; the order matters — update Rancher first if it re-reads at request time, Keycloak second

Failure behaviour: Rancher loss does not affect running workloads or Argo CD sync inside each cluster. It removes cluster registration and the UI.

docs.title: I. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Rancher on its own dedicated cluster. - OIDC via Keycloak, with a dedicated client and the groups and uid claims verified before go-live. - The bootstrap password never in Git; the secret deleted after first login. - A local break-glass admin path documented (Rancher supports a local admin password in addition to OIDC — confirm the exact mechanism for the pinned release).

Strongly recommended: - Rancher limited to the platform project for operators, so an operator cannot manage unrelated clusters. - Project-scoped RBAC for each application team. - Alert on Rancher availability, and on the Rancher operator's own reconciliation errors.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Rancher RBAC: Projects, Namespaces, and Multi-Tenancy
Overview
docs.text: This document describes Rancher's RBAC model for managing access across projects, namespaces, and resource quotas. It covers role templates, global vs project-scoped roles, and multi-tenancy patterns for platform teams.

docs.title: Rancher Project Roles
docs.text:
Rancher provides three default project roles that control what members can do within a project:

Role Scope Capabilities Admin Project Full access including user management, project settings, and all resources Member Project Read/write access to most resources, cannot manage project settings or users Viewer Project Read-only access to project resources and metadata

docs.title: Custom Role Templates
docs.text:
Platform teams can create custom role templates using the Rancher API or kubectl against the management-cluster. Role templates define precise permissions and can be bound to groups or users.

# Custom role template example
apiVersion: v3.rancher.io/v1
kind: RoleTemplate
metadata:
  name: restricted-developer
spec:
  description: "Restricted developer role - no cluster-scoped resources"
  targets:
    - targetKind: Project
      targetName: project-name
  permissions:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
      verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
    - apiGroups: ["apps"]
      resources: ["deployments"]
      verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]

docs.title: Kubernetes RBAC Within Projects
docs.text:
Inside each Rancher project, standard Kubernetes RBAC applies within project namespaces. This allows granular control over which applications and operators can access which namespaces.

# Namespace-level Role
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: namespace-reader
  namespace: app-production
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "services", "ingresses"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

docs.title: Service Account Scoping
docs.text: Service accounts should be scoped to specific namespaces to limit blast radius. Use project-level service account projections to avoid cross-project leakage.

docs.title: Resource Quotas
docs.text:
Resource quotas enforce per-project resource limits and prevent namespace-level overconsumption.

# Resource quota example
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: project-quota
  namespace: project-name
spec:
  hard:
    cpu: "4"
    memory: "8Gi"
    pods: "20"
    services: "10"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: "4Gi"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: "8Gi"

docs.title: Global Roles
docs.text:
Global roles apply across all projects in the Rancher management cluster. Use sparingly for cluster-wide operations.

Role Type When to Use cluster-admin Cluster infrastructure, add-on deployment, disaster recovery cluster-reader Observability, monitoring, audit tools Custom global roles API server access, certificate rotation, Velero backup

docs.title: Project-Scoped Roles
docs.text:
Project-scoped roles apply only within their specific project. This is the default and recommended approach for application teams.

Role Type When to Use project-admin Platform teams managing a specific project project-member Application developers within a project project-viewer Auditors, compliance teams

docs.title: Migration Pattern
docs.text:
When moving from global to project-scoped roles:

  1. Identify all global role bindings
  2. Create equivalent project role templates
  3. Bind to specific projects instead of cluster-wide
  4. Verify no functional gaps
  5. Decommission global bindings

docs.title: Pattern 1: Shared Infrastructure, Isolated Workloads
docs.text:
• Single Rancher management cluster
  • Multiple projects for different teams/departments
  • Resource quotas enforce isolation
  • Network policies prevent cross-project traffic

docs.title: Pattern 2: Dedicated Management Clusters per Tenant
docs.text:
• Separate management clusters for each tenant/org
  • Centralized identity provider (Keycloak/OIDC)
  • Federation for cross-tenant visibility
  • Higher operational overhead

docs.title: Pattern 3: Fleet-Driven Multi-Tenancy
docs.text:
• Use Rancher Fleet for cluster management
  • Applications deployed as GitOps via Argo CD
  • Project boundaries enforced via namespace templates
  • Role templates deployed as Git manifests
# Fleet role template deployment example
apiVersion: fleets Rancher/v1
kind: GitConfig
metadata:
  name: rbac-templates
spec:
  repo:
    url: https://github.com/org/rancher-configs
    branch: main
  paths:
    - management-cluster/rancher/rbac-role-templates/

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Prefer project-scoped roles over global roles for application teams
  2. Use role templates to codify permissions in Git, enabling review and change tracking
  3. Enforce resource quotas on every project to prevent resource exhaustion
  4. Implement namespace segregation within projects for different application environments
  5. Audit role bindings quarterly to remove unused or overly permissive roles
  6. Use OIDC group mapping (Keycloak → Rancher roles) for centralized identity management
  7. Document role purpose in the template metadata for future maintainers

docs.title: Rancher Server Health
docs.text:
# Check Rancher pods status
kubectl -n cattle-system get pods

# Verify Rancher API endpoint
curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health

# Check Rancher API via CLI
curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  https://rancher.internal/v3/clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, state}'

Expected: state: "active" for all clusters, healthy pod counts matching the deployment replicas.

docs.title: Management Cluster Node Health
docs.text:
# kubespray-built management cluster node status
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Verify etcd endpoints are responsive
kubectl -n cattle-system exec deployment/rancher -- curl -sk https://127.0.0.1:2379/health

docs.title: etcd Cluster Health
docs.text:
# etcd snapshot and health check
kubectl -n cattle-system exec -it $(kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- etcdctl endpoint health

# etcd snapshot management
kubectl -n cattle-system exec -it $(kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') -- etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-snapshot.db --cluster-id=<cluster-id>

# Verify etcd backup integrity
etcdctl snapshot restore /tmp/etcd-snapshot.db --with-revision=<revision>
etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-snapshot.db

docs.title: Workload and Cluster Health
docs.text:
# Check all cluster resources
kubectl get management-cluster -A

# Application cluster status via Rancher API
curl -sk -u "$RANCHER_TOKEN:$RANCHER_TOKEN" \
  https://rancher.internal/v3/clusters | jq '.data[] | {name, state, nodes}'

# Fleet application health
kubectl -n fleet-default get applications -A

# Check fleet pipeline status
kubectl -n cattle-fleet-system get pipelines -A

docs.title: Keycloak OIDC Health
docs.text:
# Keycloak pod status
kubectl -n keycloak get pods

# Keycloak health check
curl -k https://keycloak.internal/realms/platform/status

# Rancher OIDC configuration validation
kubectl -n cattle-system describe secret rancher-oidc-config 2>/dev/null || echo "OIDC config not found via secret"

docs.title: Automated Backup Workflow
docs.text:
# Trigger etcd backup
BACKUP_DIR=/backup/etcd
TIMESTAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
SNAPSHOT_NAME="etcd-backup-${TIMESTAMP}.db"

kubectl -n cattle-system exec -it $(kubectl -n cattle-system get pods -l app=etcd -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') \
  -- etcdctl snapshot save ${BACKUP_DIR}/${SNAPSHOT_NAME} --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd

# Validate backup against source
etcdctl snapshot restore ${BACKUP_DIR}/${SNAPSHOT_NAME} --name=restored-test --with-revision=$(etcdctl endpoint status -w table | grep revision | tail -1 | awk '{print $3}')
etcdctl snapshot status ${BACKUP_DIR}/${SNAPSHOT_NAME}

# Clean up old backups (keep last 7 days)
find ${BACKUP_DIR} -name "etcd-backup-*.db" -mtime +7 -delete

docs.title: Backup Verification Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] etcd snapshot created successfully without errors
  • [ ] Snapshot restoration test performed in isolated environment
  • [ ] Restoration produces cluster with matching etcd revision
  • [ ] Backup artifacts stored in immutable location
  • [ ] Backup schedule documented and tested quarterly
  • [ ] etcd defragmentation schedule recorded
  • [ ] Backup size and retention policy reviewed monthly

docs.title: Rancher UI Not Reachable
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health times out Ingress not deployed / TLS certificate expired kubectl -n cattle-system get ingress, check cert-manager certificates 502 Bad Gateway from ingress Rancher pod not healthy kubectl -n cattle-system rollout status deployment/rancher, restart if stuck UI loads but components fail OIDC misconfiguration Verify Keycloak client settings, check Rancher global OIDC config

docs.title: Cluster Registration Failures
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy Agent pod stuck in Pending Target cluster resources exhausted Scale up target cluster nodes, check resource quotas Registration token expired Token TTL exceeded Generate new token: rancher cluster-token create <name> Cluster shows provisioning status Network connectivity issues Verify firewall rules, ensure Rancher can reach cluster API endpoint

docs.title: Fleet GitOps Not Syncing
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy Applications stuck in Pending Git repository inaccessible helm repo update, verify Git remote URL, check SSH keys Pipeline jobs failing Fleet controller resource issue kubectl -n cattle-fleet-system rollout restart deployment/fleet-controller Drift detected between Git and cluster Manual changes outside Git Run kubectl apply -f fleet/cluster-baseline.yaml, investigate drift causes

docs.title: etcd Performance Degradation
docs.text: Symptom Cause Remedy High etcd CPU utilization Excessive watch pressure Review fleet application sync frequency, reduce watch batch sizes etcd member lagging Network partition or slow disks Check etcd member health, upgrade storage class, run etcd defrag Frequent leader elections Disk latency or split brain Verify etcd storage performance, check for network instability

docs.title: Daily Operations
docs.text:
• [ ] Verify Rancher UI reachable via curl -k https://rancher.internal/v3/health
  • [ ] Check Rancher pod status: kubectl -n cattle-system get pods
  • [ ] Confirm cluster agents connected and visible in Rancher UI
  • [ ] Review fleet application sync status
  • [ ] Check for any alert notifications in Rancher

docs.title: Weekly Operations
docs.text:
• [ ] Validate etcd backup creation and integrity
  • [ ] Review etcd snapshot retention and clean old backups
  • [ ] Inspect logs for recurring warnings or errors
  • [ ] Verify Keycloak OIDC token refresh functioning
  • [ ] Check node resource utilization on management cluster

docs.title: Monthly Operations
docs.text:
• [ ] Perform etcd restoration test in staging environment
  • [ ] Review and update registration token TTL settings
  • [ ] Audit RBAC permissions across clusters and projects
  • [ ] Update Rancher Helm chart to latest stable version
  • [ ] Verify backup storage costs and retention compliance
  • [ ] Test disaster recovery procedure end-to-end

docs.title: Quarterly Operations
docs.text:
• [ ] Full disaster recovery drill: backup → restore → validation
  • [ ] Upgrade Rancher to next supported minor version
  • [ ] Re-rotate all secrets (Rancher bootstrap password, OIDC client secrets)
  • [ ] Review and update infrastructure as code templates
  • [ ] Assess cluster sizing against current workload demands
  • [ ] Security scan of container images and cluster dependencies

docs.title: Rancher Cluster Loss
docs.text:
1. Re-deploy Rancher on new dedicated management cluster (Kubespray + Helm)
  2. Restore etcd from latest validated backup
  3. Re-import all managed clusters using registration tokens
  4. Re-configure Keycloak OIDC integration
  5. Restore Fleet Git repositories from Git hosting backup
  6. Sync applications via Argo CD and Fleet

docs.title: Single Cluster Failure
docs.text:
1. For application cluster: use cluster delete/re-create flow in Rancher
  2. For management cluster: redeploy from infrastructure-as-code templates
  3. Verify etcd data consistency post-recovery
  4. Validate all cross-cluster references and fleet pipelines

docs.title: Rancher Workload Scheduling
docs.text: Previous step | [Next step](../../kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md]

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Rancher and Kubernetes workload scheduling mechanisms: resource requests/limits, node affinity, pod affinity/anti-affinity, topology spread constraints, and priority classes. These controls determine where pods are placed, how they compete for resources, and how critical workloads are prioritized during resource contention.

Cross-references management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md §Architecture, kubernetes/scheduling/priority-classes.md §Priority classes, kubernetes/scheduling/resource-reservation.md §QoS classes.

docs.title: B. Resource requests and limits
docs.text:
Resource requests and limits determine the QoS class and influence scheduling decisions.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "512Mi"
        limits:
          cpu: "1"
          memory: "1Gi"
Resource Requests Limits Effect CPU Guaranteed scheduling slot; vCPU charged at runtime Capped at limit; excess throttled on cpu.cfs_quota Requests = minimum guaranteed; Limits = maximum consumption Memory Guaranteed memory available at admission OOM killed if exceeded; no throttling Requests determine QoS class; Limits determine OOM boundary

docs.title: QoS class derivation
docs.text: QoS class CPU requests/limits Memory requests/limits Typical use Guaranteed All containers have equal requests and limits All containers have equal requests and limits Critical stateful workloads Burstable At least one container has request != limit At least one container has request != limit Most application workloads BestEffort No requests or limits No requests or limits Batch/job workloads

docs.title: C. Node affinity
docs.text: Node affinity schedules pods based on node labels. Use it to constrain workloads to specific node groups (e.g., GPU nodes, bare-metal, zoned infrastructure).

docs.title: Node affinity types
docs.text: Type Syntax Behavior Required during scheduling (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) nodeSelectorTerms[0].matchExpressions[0].operator In Pod will not schedule unless at least one term matches; enforced at pod creation Preferred during scheduling (preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) nodeSelectorTerms[0].weightedPreferredSchedulingTerms[0].weight Soft preference; scheduler tries to find a matching node but falls back

docs.title: Example: required node affinity
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: kubernetes.io/arch
                operator: In
                values: ["amd64", "arm64"]
              - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                operator: In
                values: ["us-west-2a", "us-west-2b"]

docs.title: Example: preferred node affinity
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 80
          preference:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: node-type
                operator: In
                values: ["gpu"]
        - weight: 60
          preference:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                operator: In
                values: ["us-west-2a"]

docs.title: D. Pod affinity and anti-affinity
docs.text: Pod affinity/anti-affinity control scheduling based on labels of other pods already running on a node. Use affinity to co-locate related workloads (e.g., frontend + backend) and anti-affinity to separate them.

docs.title: Affinity types
docs.text: Type Operator Behavior Required (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) In Pod will not schedule unless the condition is met Preferred (preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) Weight + label selector Soft preference with weight (0-100) Not (requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution) Not In Pod will not schedule if any label matches

docs.title: Example: pod affinity (co-locate)
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values: ["backend"]
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone

docs.title: Example: pod anti-affinity (separate)
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    podAntiAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - labelSelector:
            matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values: ["database"]
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone

docs.title: Soft preferred affinity
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  affinity:
    podAffinity:
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 100
          preference:
            labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
                - key: app
                  operator: In
                  values: ["cache"]
            topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/hostname

docs.title: E. Topology spread constraints
docs.text: Topology spread constraints distribute pods across failure domains (nodes, zones, hosts) to improve availability and fault tolerance.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      affinity: {}
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: my-app

docs.title: maxSkew options
docs.text: Value Description Integer Maximum difference between the highest and lowest pod counts across topology nodes Fraction Percentage-based skew (alpha feature, not recommended for production)

docs.title: whenUnsatisfiable options
docs.text: Option Behavior DoNotSchedule Pods are not scheduled if the constraint cannot be satisfied ScheduleAnyway Pods are scheduled regardless; skew may occur MostSuitable (default) Scheduler picks the most suitable node among candidates

docs.title: Example: multi-zone spread
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: my-app

docs.title: Example: spread across nodes (host-level)
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: my-app

docs.title: F. Priority classes
docs.text: Priority classes assign a priority to pods, influencing scheduling order and preemption behavior. Higher-priority pods are scheduled ahead of lower-priority pods and can preempt them when resources are insufficient.

docs.title: Built-in priority classes
docs.text: Name Value Description system-node-critical 2000000000 K8s system pods (kube-proxy, DNS, device plugins) system-cluster-critical 2000000000 Cluster networking, storage controllers

docs.title: Custom priority class example
docs.text:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: critical-pods
value: 1000000000
globalDefault: false
description: "Critical business workloads — scheduled before all other priorities"

docs.title: Preemption policy
docs.text:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: critical-pods
value: 1000000000
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
globalDefault: false
description: "Preempts lower-priority pods when scheduling"

docs.title: Policy options
docs.text: Policy Behavior PreemptLowerPriority (default) Preempts pods with lower priorityClassValue; does not preempt pods with equal or higher priority NeverPreemptLowerPriority Never preempts lower-priority pods; the pod will remain in Pending state if no node can satisfy it

docs.title: Global default
docs.text:
Set a globalDefault PriorityClass to apply a baseline priority to all pods that do not specify priorityClassName. Best practice: Do not set globalDefault: true for very high values (e.g., >1000000) as it can cause unexpected preemption behavior. Instead, explicitly set priorityClassName on critical pods.

apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority
value: 1000000
globalDefault: true
description: "Baseline priority for all pods without explicit priority class"

docs.title: Usage in pod spec
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-critical-app
spec:
  priorityClassName: critical-pods
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "500m"
          memory: "512Mi"
        limits:
          cpu: "1"
          memory: "1Gi"

docs.title: G. Cross-references
docs.text:
• management-cluster/rancher/rancher.md — Rancher deployment and architecture
  • kubernetes/scheduling/priority-classes.md — Kubernetes priority classes and preemption
  • kubernetes/scheduling/resource-reservation.md — QoS classes and kubelet resource reservation
  • Kubernetes scheduler documentation — Official scheduler reference
  • Kubernetes topology spread constraints — Official topology spread docs

docs.title: H. Best practices
docs.text:
• Set resource requests equal to actual minimum usage; over-requesting wastes cluster capacity and can cause scheduling failures.
  • Use node affinity for hardware-specific or regulatory constraints (GPU, compliance zones, bare-metal).
  • Prefer pod anti-affinity for stateful services to avoid co-locating replicas on the same node.
  • Apply topology spread constraints across zones to protect against zone-level failures; use maxSkew: 1 as a starting point.
  • Assign priority classes to critical system and business workloads; avoid globalDefault: true for high values.
  • Combine multiple scheduling mechanisms for complex placement: e.g., node affinity + topology spread constraints for multi-zone dedicated infrastructure.
  • Verify scheduling with kubectl describe pod <pod-name> --field-selector=status.phase=Pending to understand why a pod is not scheduling.
