docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document monitoring alert validation procedures, including alert testing, silences, inhibition rules, troubleshooting firing alerts, and capacity visibility. All procedures integrate with the Prometheus + Alertmanager stack and follow the SRE reliability framework guidelines from the engineering SRE specialist.

docs.title: B.1. Unit-testing rules with promtool
docs.text:
# Validate individual rules
promtool check rules /path/to/alert-rules.yml

# Validate recording rules
promtool check rules /path/to/recording-rules.yml --output json

# Validate full PrometheusRule CR
promtool check crds

docs.title: B.2. Integration-testing via CI
docs.text:
• CI pipeline runs promtool check rules on every PR merge to monitoring/.
  • Fails the build if any rule has syntax errors, missing for: durations, or invalid Expr.

docs.title: B.3. Manual alert trigger
docs.text:
# Fire an alert manually for testing notification routing
kubectl -n monitoring exec deployment/alertmanager -- \
  amtool alert add \
    --alertname=TestAlert \
    --severity=warning \
    --annotation=summary="Manual test alert" \
    --annotation=description="Testing alert routing and silences"

docs.title: B.4. Verifying alert delivery
docs.text:
# Check that a test alert reached its receiver
kubectl -n monitoring logs deployment/alertmanager | grep -i "TestAlert"

# Verify webhook payload
curl -s http://localhost:9093/api/v2/alerts | jq '.[] | select(.alertname=="TestAlert")'

docs.title: C.1. Creating silences
docs.text:
# UI: Alertmanager UI → Silences → New silence
# Define matchers, startsAt, endsAt, and a descriptive comment.

# API: Create a silence via curl
curl -X POST http://alertmanager:9093/api/v2/silences \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "startsAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "endsAt": "2026-01-01T02:00:00Z",
    "createdBy": "maintenance",
    "comment": "Node reboot for firmware update",
    "matchers": [
      {"name": "alertname", "value": "NodeCPUUsageHigh", "isRegex": false},
      {"name": "cluster", "value": "prod", "isRegex": false}
    ]
  }'

# API: Delete a silence
curl -X DELETE http://alertmanager:9093/api/v2/silences \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "matchers": [
      {"name": "alertname", "value": "NodeCPUUsageHigh"},
      {"name": "cluster", "value": "prod"}
    ]
  }'

docs.title: C.2. Silence lifecycle
docs.text: Step Action Owner Frequency Create Define matchers + endsAt SRE on-call As needed Review Check silences still relevant SRE lead Weekly Cleanup Delete expired silences SRE on-call After each maintenance window

docs.title: C.3. Listing and inspecting silences
docs.text:
# List all active silences
kubectl -n monitoring exec deployment/alertmanager -- \
  amtool silence list

# Show silence details by ID
amtool silence info <silence-id>

docs.title: D.1. Purpose
docs.text: Inhibition rules suppress redundant alerts so a single root-cause alert (e.g., ClusterDown) suppresses lower-severity node/container alerts for the same cluster.

docs.title: D.2. Example inhibition rule set
docs.text:
inhibit_rules:
  # ClusterDown suppresses NodeCPUUsageHigh, MemoryUsageHigh, DiskUsageHigh
  - source_match:
      severity: 'critical'
      alertname: 'ClusterDown'
    target_match:
      severity: 'warning'
      alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
    equal: ['cluster']
  - source_match:
      severity: 'critical'
      alertname: 'ClusterDown'
    target_match:
      severity: 'warning'
      alertname: 'MemoryUsageHigh'
    equal: ['cluster']
  - source_match:
      severity: 'critical'
      alertname: 'ClusterDown'
    target_match:
      severity: 'warning'
      alertname: 'DiskUsageHigh'
    equal: ['cluster']

  # NodeCPUUsageHigh suppresses DiskUsageHigh at warning level (same cluster)
  - source_match:
      severity: 'warning'
      alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
    target_match:
      severity: 'info'
      alertname: 'DiskUsageHigh'
    equal: ['cluster']

docs.title: D.2. Verifying inhibition rules
docs.text:
# Generate test alert data
echo '{"alerts": [{"labels": {"alertname": "ClusterDown", "severity": "critical", "cluster": "prod"}, "status": "firing"}]}' | \
  kubectl -n monitoring exec deployment/alertmanager -- \
    amtool inhibit -

# Expected: NodeCPUUsageHigh, MemoryUsageHigh, DiskUsageHigh from cluster=prod are suppressed

docs.title: D.3. Inhibition best practices
docs.text:
• Keep equal labels minimal: cluster + alertname when needed.
  • Avoid chained inhibition (A → B → C) — it creates suppression ambiguity.
  • Document each rule's intent in the rule comment and this file.
  • Validate with amtool inhibit in CI.

docs.title: E.1. Initial diagnosis
docs.text:
# List firing Prometheus alerts
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheusrules -o json | \
  jq '.items[]?.status?.ruleStatus?.[]?.status == "firing"' | grep true

# Show all firing alerts with labels
kubectl -n monitoring get alerts --all-namespaces -o wide

# Check Alertmanager routing status
amtool alert list

docs.title: E.2. Common failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Alert not firing despite condition true for: duration not met Adjust for: in rule or check Prometheus scrape interval Alert firing but no notification sent Receiver misconfiguration Verify routing rules; check receiver secrets Multiple identical alerts firing Missing inhibition rules Add inhibition rule with correct equal: labels Alert silenced unexpectedly Active silence with matching matchers List silences; update endsAt or remove silence Alert routing to wrong receiver Label mismatch in routing rule Adjust match: labels; verify group_by Alert firing every repeat_interval repeat_interval set too low Increase repeat_interval; add wait for first notification

docs.title: E.3. Runbook references
docs.text:
• Each alert in monitoring/prometheus-alert-rules.md must link to a runbook in troubleshooting/.
  • Runbooks follow the template: troubleshooting/<alertname>.md.
  • If no runbook exists, create one before deploying the alert.

docs.title: E.4. Escalation path
docs.text:
1. On-call SRE (0-15 min): Check firing alerts, silences, and inhibition.
  2. SRE lead (15-30 min): Review recent changes; correlate with deployment history.
  3. Platform team (30+ min): Investigate Prometheus/Alertmanager infrastructure issues.

docs.title: F.1. Golden signals to monitor
docs.text: Pillar Metric Alert SLO target Latency histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) p99 latency > 300ms 99% under 300ms Traffic rate(http_requests_total[5m]) Traffic spike > 200% baseline N/A (observability) Errors rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]) Error rate > 1% < 1% (error budget) Saturation 100 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100) Memory > 85% < 85% utilization

docs.title: F.2. Capacity dashboards
docs.text:
• Grafana dashboards in monitoring/grafana-dashboards.md display real-time capacity.
  • Dashboards are versioned in Git and applied by Argo CD.
  • Key dashboards: node-capacity, cluster-resources, ceph-pool-usage.

docs.title: F.3. Capacity alert thresholds
docs.text:
# Example: Node memory capacity alert
- alert: NodeMemoryCapacityHigh
  expr: 100 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100) > 85
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Node memory usage high on {{ $labels.instance }}"
    description: "Memory usage at {{ $value }}% for 10m. Review workloads or scale up."

docs.title: F.4. Capacity planning workflow
docs.text:
1. Collect: Pull 30-day trends from Prometheus TSDB (prometheus query or Grafana).
  2. Forecast: Project resource needs 30/60/90 days forward using linear regression.
  3. Validate: Compare forecast against SLO error budget consumption.
  4. Act: If forecasted utilization > 80% at 30d, file a capacity ticket; if > 90%, schedule immediate resize.
  5. Review: Post-action review to confirm forecast accuracy and update assumptions.

docs.title: F.5. Capacity alert acknowledgment
docs.text:
# Acknowledge a capacity alert in Alertmanager
amtool alert acknowledge <alert-id> --comment "Investigating capacity issue"

# Declare alert resolved once issue is fixed
amtool alert resolve <alert-id> --comment "Capacity resolved after scaling"

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document the Prometheus alerting rules and Alertmanager routing configuration. Alerts fire from Prometheus and are routed by Alertmanager to receivers (email, webhook, chat).

docs.title: B. Alert severity levels
docs.text: Severity Meaning Response time Example Critical Service outage or data loss risk Immediate (15 min) etcd down, API server unreachable Warning Degraded performance or capacity risk Within 1 hour Node CPU > 85%, disk > 80% Info Informational, no immediate action Next business day New version available, deprecated API

docs.title: C. Alert rule categories
docs.text: Category Rules covered Example alert Cluster API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd KubeAPIDown Node kubelet, node_exporter, CPU, memory, disk NodeCPUUsageHigh Storage Ceph, Rook-Ceph, ceph-csi, PVC CephOsdDown, PVCNotBound Platform Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, GitLab, Harbor, Vault ArgoCDApplicationNotHealthy GPU NVIDIA GPU utilization, driver, thermals NVIDIA GPUTemperatureHigh Ingress NGINX ingress, MetalLB, external LB IngressBackendDown

docs.title: D. Alertmanager routing
docs.text:
Alerts are routed by Alertmanager based on severity, cluster, and service:

  • Critical → PagerDuty, Slack #critical-alerts
  • Warning → Slack #warnings-alerts
  • Info → Slack #info-alerts

docs.title: E. Verification
docs.text:
# Verify Alertmanager is reachable
kubectl -n monitoring get svc alertmanager

# Verify alerting rules are loaded
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheusrules

# Check firing alerts
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheusrules -o yaml | grep -A5 state: firing

docs.title: E. Cross-references
docs.text:
• monitoring/prometheus.md — Prometheus and Alertmanager architecture
  • monitoring/grafana-dashboards.md — Grafana dashboards

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the Alertmanager configuration including receiver definitions, routing rules, inhibition rules, silence management, and notification templates. Alertmanager receives alerts from Prometheus and routes them to the appropriate receivers based on alert severity, alertname, and custom labels. All configuration is stored in Git and applied by Argo CD.

This document integrates with:

  • monitoring/prometheus.md — Prometheus and Alertmanager architecture
  • monitoring/alerting-rules.md — Cluster-wide alert severity definitions and routing
  • monitoring/prometheus-alert-rules.md — Prometheus alerting rules, recording rules, and notification routing
  • monitoring/slo-sla.md — SLOs and error budgets that alert severity maps to

docs.title: B. Alertmanager architecture
docs.text:
Prometheus --> |Alerts| --> Alertmanager --> |Routes| --> Receivers
       |                      |
       |                      +--> Inhibition rules (suppress duplicates)
       +--> Silences (suppress temporarily)

docs.title: C. Receiver definitions
docs.text: Receivers define where alerts are sent. Receiver names are referenced in routing rules.

docs.title: Email receiver
docs.text:
receivers:
- name: 'email-admins'
  email_configs:
  - to: 'sre-admins@example.com'
    from: 'alertmanager@example.com'
    smarthost: 'smtp.example.com:25'
    hello: 'alertmanager.example.com'
    subject: 'Alert: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }} — {{ .Status }}'
    body: |
      {{ if .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
      Summary: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
      {{ end }}
      {{ if .CommonAnnotations.description }}
      Description: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}
      {{ end }}
      {{ if .Alerts }}
      Alerts:
      {{- range .Alerts }}
      - {{ .Labels.severity }}: {{ .Annotations.description }} ({{ .StartsAt }})
      {{- end }}
      {{ end }}

docs.title: Slack receivers (by severity)
docs.text:
receivers:
- name: 'slack-critical'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#critical-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookCritical }}'
    send_resolved: true
    title: '{{ .CommonLabels.alertname }} — {{ .Status }}'
    text: |
      *Summary*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
      *Description*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}
      *Severity*: critical
      *Alertname*: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}
      *Cluster*: {{ .CommonLabels.cluster }}
      *Service*: {{ .CommonLabels.service }}

- name: 'slack-warning'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#warnings-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookWarning }}'
    send_resolved: true
    title: '{{ .CommonLabels.alertname }} — {{ .Status }}'
    text: |
      *Summary*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
      *Description*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}
      *Severity*: warning
      *Alertname*: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}
      *Cluster*: {{ .CommonLabels.cluster }}
      *Service*: {{ .CommonLabels.service }}

- name: 'slack-info'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#info-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookInfo }}'
    send_resolved: true
    title: '{{ .CommonLabels.alertname }} — {{ .Status }}'
    text: |
      *Summary*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
      *Description*: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}
      *Severity*: info
      *Alertname*: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}
      *Cluster*: {{ .CommonLabels.cluster }}
      *Service*: {{ .CommonLabels.service }}

docs.title: PagerDuty receiver
docs.text:
receivers:
- name: 'pagerduty-critical'
  pagerduty_configs:
  - service_key: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.PagerDutyKey }}'
    description: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}'
    severity: critical
    client: 'alertmanager'
    client_url: 'https://example.com'

docs.title: Webhook receiver
docs.text:
receivers:
- name: 'webhook-incident'
  webhook_configs:
  - url: 'https://internal.example.com/api/v1/alerts'
    send_resolved: true
    http_config:
      bearer_token: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.IncidentWebhookToken }}'
      tls_config:
        insecure_skip_verify: false

docs.title: D. Routing rules
docs.text:
Routing directs alerts to receivers based on label matching. Rules are evaluated top-down; the first matching rule wins.

route:
  receiver: 'slack-info'
  group_by: ['alertname', 'cluster', 'service']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 24h

  # Route critical alerts to PagerDuty
  routes:
  - match:
      severity: 'critical'
    receiver: 'pagerduty-critical'
    continue: true

  # Route warning alerts to Slack warnings
  - match:
      severity: 'warning'
    receiver: 'slack-warning'

  # Route info alerts to Slack info
  - match:
      severity: 'info'
    receiver: 'slack-info'

  # Default fallback
  - match: {}
    receiver: 'slack-info'

Routing logic:

  • group_by: How alerts are grouped into a single notification
  • group_wait: Wait this long before sending the first notification for a group
  • group_interval: How often to repeat notifications for the same group
  • repeat_interval: How often to repeat the notification if the alert remains firing
  • receiver: Default receiver if no match is found
  • routes: Nested routes evaluated after the initial match; continue: true allows falling through to child routes

docs.title: E. Inhibition rules
docs.text:
Inhibition rules suppress redundant alerts. For example, a ClusterDown alert should suppress all lower-severity alerts from the same cluster.

inhibit_rules:
- source_match:
    severity: 'critical'
    alertname: 'ClusterDown'
  target_match:
    severity: 'warning'
    alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
  equal: ['cluster']

- source_match:
    severity: 'critical'
    alertname: 'ClusterDown'
  target_match:
    severity: 'warning'
    alertname: 'MemoryUsageHigh'
  equal: ['cluster']

- source_match:
    severity: 'warning'
    alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
  target_match:
    severity: 'info'
    alertname: 'DiskUsageHigh'
  equal: ['cluster']

Inhibition logic:

  • source_match: The alert that, when firing, triggers suppression
  • target_match: The alerts that get suppressed
  • equal: Labels that must match between source and target (alerts are only suppressed if all equal labels match)

docs.title: F. Silence management
docs.text: Silences suppress alerts for a defined duration, useful during maintenance windows or known issues.

docs.title: Creating silences
docs.text:
# UI: Alertmanager UI → Silences → New silence

# API:
curl -X POST http://alertmanager:9093/api/v2/silences \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "startsAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "endsAt": "2026-01-01T02:00:00Z",
    "createdBy": "maintenance",
    "comment": "Node reboot for firmware update",
    "matchers": [
      { "name": "alertname", "value": "NodeCPUUsageHigh", "isRegex": false },
      { "name": "cluster", "value": "prod", "isRegex": false }
    ]
  }'

docs.title: UI operations
docs.text:
• New silence: Define matchers, start/end time, and comment
  • Edit silence: Modify duration or matchers of an existing silence
  • Delete silence: Remove a silence to re-enable alerts

docs.title: Silencing via PrometheusRule (annotation)
docs.text:
Silences are managed externally through the Alertmanager UI or API. They are not defined in PrometheusRule objects, but alerts can be annotated to opt-out of silencing:

metadata:
  annotations:
    alertmanager.openshift.io/skipSilence: "true"

docs.title: G. Notification templates
docs.text:
Alertmanager uses Go templates for notification formatting. Available data context:

Variable Description .CommonLabels All label key-value pairs from the alert .CommonAnnotations All annotation key-value pairs from the alert .Alerts List of alerts in the group .Status "firing" or "resolved" .GroupLabels Labels grouping the alerts .GroupKey Key for the alert group .CommonTimestamp Timestamp of the status change .ExternalURL URL base for links to Alertmanager

docs.title: Example template snippet
docs.text:
Summary: {{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}
Description: {{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}
Alert: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}
Severity: {{ .CommonLabels.severity }}
Cluster: {{ .CommonLabels.cluster }}
Starts at: {{ .CommonTimestamp }}

docs.title: H. Example alertmanager.yml
docs.text:
global:
  resolve_timeout: 5m
  slack_api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookCritical }}'
  pagerduty_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.PagerDutyKey }}'

route:
  receiver: 'slack-info'
  group_by: ['alertname', 'cluster', 'service']
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 24h
  routes:
  - match:
      severity: 'critical'
    receiver: 'pagerduty-critical'
    continue: true
  - match:
      severity: 'warning'
    receiver: 'slack-warning'
  - match:
      severity: 'info'
    receiver: 'slack-info'

inhibit_rules:
- source_match:
    severity: 'critical'
    alertname: 'ClusterDown'
  target_match:
    severity: 'warning'
    alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
  equal: ['cluster']

receivers:
- name: 'pagerduty-critical'
  pagerduty_configs:
  - service_key: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.PagerDutyKey }}'
    severity: critical

- name: 'slack-warning'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#warnings-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookWarning }}'
    send_resolved: true

- name: 'slack-info'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#info-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookInfo }}'
    send_resolved: true

- name: 'email-admins'
  email_configs:
  - to: 'sre-admins@example.com'
    from: 'alertmanager@example.com'
    smarthost: 'smtp.example.com:25'
    subject: 'Alert: {{ .CommonLabels.alertname }}'
    body: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.summary }}'

docs.title: I. Verification
docs.text:
# Verify Alertmanager configuration is valid
amtool validate config alertmanager.yml

# Verify Alertmanager is reachable
kubectl -n monitoring get svc alertmanager

# Verify alerting rules are loaded
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheusrules

# Check firing alerts
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheusrules -o yaml | grep -A5 state: firing

# Check routes and receivers
amtool route alerts --config=alertmanager.yml < alert.json

# Check inhibition
amtool inhibit alertmanager.yml < alert.json

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory:

  • All Alertmanager configuration lives in Git, applied by Argo CD. Never edit Alertmanager directly in the cluster.
  • Validate configuration with amtool validate config in CI.
  • Keep receiver names consistent across all configuration files.
  • Use continue: true in routing only when intentional fan-out is needed.
  • Document inhibition rules to prevent alert storms.

Strongly recommended:

  • Use send_resolved: true for Slack receivers to get resolution notifications.
  • Group alerts by alertname, cluster, and service to keep notifications focused.
  • Set appropriate repeat_interval to avoid notification fatigue.
  • Store receiver secrets (API keys, webhook URLs) in External Secrets or Vault, not in plain YAML.
  • Run a canary Alertmanager in the Management Cluster for testing.
  • Every alert must link to a runbook in troubleshooting/.

Anti-patterns to avoid:

  • Overly specific matchers that make routing brittle — prefer label-based matching.
  • for: 0s on Prometheus rules — always include a duration before firing.
  • Too many inhibition rules — keep them focused on the most disruptive duplicates.
  • Silences that are never cleaned up — set endsAt explicitly and review periodically.
  • Notification templates without annotations — receivers will have no useful context.

docs.title: B. Dashboard categories
docs.text: Dashboard Scope Datasource Description Cluster health MON status, quorum, overall health Prometheus Ceph cluster health overview, monitor quorum status, OSD map summary OSD performance OSD I/O latency, throughput, commit time Prometheus Per-OSD commit latency, I/O bytes/sec, ops/sec, device health PG status PG health distribution, state, peering Prometheus PG status distribution, degraded/missing/undersized counts, PG peering progress Capacity planning Pool usage, OSD capacity, warning thresholds Prometheus Pool byte usage, OSD used %, cluster capacity, forecast based on growth rate

docs.title: 1. Cluster Health Dashboard
docs.text:

  • ceph_osd_in — Percentage of OSDs that are in (active member of cluster)
  • ceph_mon_up — Percentage of MONs that are up

docs.title: 2. OSD Performance Dashboard
docs.text:

  • ceph_osd_io_bytes_total — I/O bytes per second (read + write)
  • ceph_osd_ops — Operations per second (read + write)
  • ceph_osd_queue_depth — Pending I/O queue depth per OSD
  • ceph_osd_object_count — Number of objects per OSD

docs.title: 3. PG Status Dashboard

  • ceph_pg_incomplete — Count of incomplete PGs

docs.title: 4. Capacity Planning Dashboard

  • ceph_pool_bytes_total — Total bytes per pool
  • ceph_osd_used — Used bytes per OSD
  • ceph_df — Cluster-wide capacity (used % of total)
  • ceph_pool_target_size — Target pool size
  • ceph_pool_size — Pool size factor (replication factor or EC scheme)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Provision Grafana dashboards as code using JSON files, configuration files, and Argo CD. This approach replaces manual dashboard creation with reproducible, version-controlled workflows.

docs.title: Dashboard JSON Management
docs.text: Dashboards are stored as JSON files in the repository and applied via Argo CD to the mgmt-argocd namespace. Each dashboard JSON file follows a naming convention that reflects its purpose and category.

docs.title: Example: Listing dashboard JSON files
docs.text:
# Find all Grafana dashboard JSON files in the monitoring directory
find ./monitoring -name "*.json" | sort

# Validate a dashboard JSON file syntax
kubectl get secret -n monitoring grafana-dashboards -o jsonpath='{.data.dashboards}' | base64 --decode | python3 -m json.tool > /dev/null && echo "Valid JSON" || echo "Invalid JSON"

docs.title: Example: Dashboard JSON structure overview
docs.text:
{
  "dashboard": {
    "id": null,
    "uid": "example-uid",
    "title": "Example Dashboard",
    "timezone": "browser",
    "panels": [],
    "templating": {
      "list": []
    }
  },
  "folder": "Example",
  "overwrite": true
}

docs.title: Dashboard Provisioning Files
docs.text: Provisioning files declare which dashboards should be loaded into Grafana and how they are configured. These are processed by Grafana's dashboard provisioning API on startup.

docs.title: Example: Dashboard provisioning directory structure
docs.text:
monitoring/provisioning/dashboards/
├── cluster-overview.json
├── node-metrics.json
├── storage.json
└── platform-services.json

docs.title: Example: Provisioning dashboard via Argo CD Application
docs.text:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: mgmt-grafana
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  source:
    repoURL: https://gitlab.example.com/obs-monitoring/obs-monitoring
    targetRevision: main
    path: dashboards
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: monitoring
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true

docs.title: Data Source Configuration
docs.text: Data sources must be configured before dashboards can render metrics. Provisioning supports Prometheus and other supported datasources.

docs.title: Example: Prometheus data source provisioning file
docs.text:
apiVersion: 1
kind: datasource
metadata:
  name: Prometheus
  uid: prometheus-example
type: prometheus
access: proxy
url: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
version: 1

docs.title: Example: Verifying datasource configuration
docs.text:
# List all Grafana data sources
kubectl -n monitoring get grafanadatasource -o yaml

# Verify a specific datasource is reachable
curl -s http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090/api/v1/query?query=up | python3 -m json.tool

docs.title: Variable Templates
docs.text: Dashboards use templating variables to make them reusable across clusters, namespaces, and environments. Variables are defined in the dashboard JSON or via provisioning ConfigMaps.

docs.title: Example: Dashboard variable for cluster selection
docs.text:
{
  "type": "query",
  "name": "cluster",
  "label": "Cluster",
  "datasource": "Prometheus",
  "query": "label_values(kubernetes_pod_info{cluster!=\"\"}, cluster)",
  "refresh": 5
}

docs.title: Example: Variable for namespace filtering
docs.text:
{
  "type": "query",
  "name": "namespace",
  "label": "Namespace",
  "datasource": "Prometheus",
  "query": "label_values(kubernetes_namespace_info)",
  "refresh": 5,
  "multi": true
}

docs.title: Example: Using variables in panel queries
docs.text:
Prometheus query with variable:

rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{cluster="$cluster",namespace="$namespace"}[1m])

docs.title: Dashboard as Code Workflows
docs.text: The dashboard as code lifecycle follows: edit JSON → commit → Argo CD sync → verification.

docs.title: Example: Workflow steps
docs.text:
# 1. Edit a dashboard JSON file
vim monitoring/provisioning/dashboards/node-metrics.json

# 2. Commit and push the change
git add monitoring/provisioning/dashboards/node-metrics.json
git commit -m "Update node metrics dashboard: add CPU panel"
git push origin main

# 3. Wait for Argo CD to apply the change
kubectl -n argocd wait application mgmt-grafana --for=condition=Healthy --timeout=300s

# 4. Verify the dashboard is provisioned
kubectl -n monitoring get grafanadashboard node-metrics -o jsonpath='{.metadata.name}'

# 5. Run link and syntax validation
python3 scripts/check_links.py monitoring/grafana-dashboard-provisioning.md

docs.title: Example: Rolling back a dashboard change
docs.text:
# Revert to previous commit
git revert HEAD

# Or restore from Argo CD source
kubectl -n monitoring get grafanadashboard -o yaml | base64 --decode > previous-version.json

docs.title: Example: Dashboard version tracking
docs.text:
# Tag a dashboard version after Argo CD sync
git tag -a "dashboards-v1.2.0" -m "Release node-metrics v1.2.0 after Argo CD sync"
git push origin "dashboards-v1.2.0"

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Hubble provides network visibility and observability for Cilium-managed clusters. It exposes L3-L7 networking data via eBPF, enabling flow inspection, security policy verification, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Accessing Hubble
docs.text:
# Port-forward Hubble UI (port 12000)
kubectl -n kube-system port-forward deployment/hubble-ui 12000:12000

# Access at http://localhost:12000

# Or use CLI
kubectl hubble observe
kubectl hubble top

docs.title: Hubble Commands
docs.text: Command Description kubectl hubble status Check Hubble connectivity and status kubectl hubble ls List observed flows kubectl hubble watch Watch flows in real-time kubectl hubble resolve <pod> Resolve pod IP to node kubectl hubble ls --oflow <pod> Show outbound flows from pod kubectl hubble ls --iflow <pod> Show inbound flows to pod

docs.title: Health Checks
docs.text:
# Verify Hubble components are running
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=hubble

# Check Hubble relay
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=hubble-relay

# Verify eBPF dataplane
kubectl exec -n kube-system daemonset/cilium -- hubble status

docs.title: Common Hubble Issues
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Fix No flows displayed Hubble not enabled or relay disconnected Enable Hubble: cilium hubble enable; check relay connectivity Partial flows eBPF load limitations or kernel version Verify kernel version supports required eBPF features; check Cilium pod logs Hubble UI not loading Port-forward conflict or service not exposed Ensure port 12000 is free; use hubble ui service exposure

docs.title: Flow Log Configuration
docs.text: Flow logs capture network traffic metadata for Cilium-managed pods. They are exported via eBPF and can be shipped to external systems.

docs.title: Enable Flow Logs
docs.text:
# Via CiliumConfig
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumConfig
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  flowLog:
    enabled: true
    aggregation:
      timeout: 30s
    formats:
      - json
    destinations:
      - type: kafka
        broker: kafka.internal:9092
        topic: cilium-flow-logs
      - type: syslog
        address: syslog.internal:514

docs.title: Flow Log Fields
docs.text: Field Description timestamp Flow start timestamp (RFC3339) src_ip Source pod IP dst_ip Destination pod/IP or service VIP src_port Source port dst_port Destination port protocol IP protocol (tcp/udp/icmp) packets Number of packets in flow bytes Number of bytes in flow action Allow/deny (based on policy) source_namespace Pod namespace destination_namespace Target namespace

docs.title: Troubleshooting Flow Logs
docs.text: Issue Check Resolution No flow logs appearing Flow log not enabled in CiliumConfig Enable flowLog.enabled: true; verify Cilium restart Logs missing fields Aggregation timeout too short Increase aggregation.timeout; verify flow completeness Cannot consume logs Kafka/Syslog destination misconfigured Verify broker connectivity; check TLS certs; test with kubectl exec High cardinality Too many label combinations Tighten aggregation rules; reduce label set

docs.title: Verifying Flow Logs
docs.text:
# Check flow log pod
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app=flow-logs

# View recent flow logs from Kafka
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l app=flow-logs -c kafka

# Verify flow log endpoint
curl -s http://localhost:9999/flowlogs | head -20

docs.title: Golden Signals for Network Health
docs.text:
• Latency — End-to-end request duration (p99 < 300ms)
  • Errors — Connection refused, timeout, policy denied (rate < 0.1%)
  • Traffic — Requests per second, flow volume per namespace
  • Saturation — eBPF map memory, flow table entries, connection tracking

docs.title: Layer 3: Reachability
docs.text:
# Pod-to-pod connectivity
kubectl exec -it <src-pod> -- ping -c3 <dst-pod-ip>

# Service reachability
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nc -zv <service> <port>

# Cross-node connectivity
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- ip route get <dst-ip>

docs.title: Layer 4: Port & Protocol
docs.text:
# TCP connect test
kubectl exec -it <src-pod> -- nc -zv <dst-service> <port>

# UDP test
kubectl exec -it <src-pod> -- nc -u -zv <dst-service> <port>

# Port forwarding for inspection
kubectl port-forward svc/<service> <local-port>:<port>

docs.title: Layer 5/7: Application Layer
docs.text:
# HTTP(S) health check
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl -sf http://<service>/healthz

# TLS verification
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- openssl s_client -connect <service>:<port> -servername <hostname>

# DNS resolution
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- getent host <service>

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document the Prometheus alerting rules, recording rules, and Alertmanager configuration used across the Kubernetes and Ceph clusters. Alerts fire from Prometheus and are routed by Alertmanager to receivers (email, webhook, Slack). All rules are stored as PrometheusRule custom resources in Git and applied by Argo CD.

docs.title: Prometheus rule types
docs.text: Rule type File extension Purpose AlertingRule .yml / .yaml Fires when an expressed condition is true for a sustained duration RecordingRule .yml / .yaml Pre-computes expensive queries for use in dashboards and other rules

docs.title: Alerting rule structure
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: example-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: example-group
    interval: 30s
    rules:
    - alert: ExampleAlert
      expr: node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="system"} > 300
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: critical
      annotations:
        summary: "High CPU usage on {{ $labels.instance }}"
        description: "CPU usage has been above 300 seconds for 5 minutes.\nValue: {{ $value }}s\nInstance: {{ $labels.instance }}"

docs.title: Key fields
docs.text: Field Description expr PromQL expression that evaluates to boolean for Duration the expression must be true before firing labels Static labels added to the alert (e.g., severity) annotations Human-readable text rendered in notifications interval How often the rule is evaluated (default 1m)

docs.title: Recording rule structure
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: recording-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: recording-group
    interval: 1m
    rules:
    - record: job:node_cpu_seconds:sumrate
      expr: rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="system"}[1m])

Recording rules pre-compute queries that are expensive or used repeatedly, reducing dashboard query latency and ensuring consistent metrics across visualizations.

docs.title: C. Alert severity levels
docs.text:
Severity Code Response time Typical use critical critical Immediate (15 min) Service outage, data loss risk, PagerDuty warning warning Within 1 hour Degraded performance, capacity risk info info Next business day Informational, no immediate action needed none none Suppressed Used for testing or suppressed alerts

Severity is set via the labels.severity field in the rule and is the primary factor in Alertmanager routing.

docs.title: D. Notification routing
docs.text: Alertmanager routes alerts based on labels, particularly severity, alertname, and custom labels such as cluster and service.

docs.title: Routing tree example
docs.text:
groups:
- name: 'example'
  interval: 1m
  rules:
  - receiver: 'pagerduty-critical'
    match:
      severity: 'critical'
    continue: true
  - receiver: 'slack-warning'
    match:
      severity: 'warning'
  - receiver: 'slack-info'
    match:
      severity: 'info'
receivers:
- name: 'pagerduty-critical'
  pagerduty_configs:
  - service_key: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.PagerDutyKey }}'
- name: 'slack-warning'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#warnings-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookWarning }}'
- name: 'slack-info'
  slack_configs:
  - channel: '#info-alerts'
    api_url: '{{ .Chart.Secrets.SlackWebhookInfo }}'

docs.title: Inhibition rules
docs.text:
Inhibition rules suppress redundant alerts. For example, a ClusterDown alert inhibits all lower-severity alerts from the same cluster:

- source_match:
    severity: 'warning'
    alertname: 'NodeCPUUsageHigh'
  target_match:
    severity: 'critical'
    alertname: 'ClusterDown'
  equal: ['cluster']

docs.title: E. Alert silencing
docs.text: Silences suppress alerts for a defined duration, useful during maintenance windows or known issues.

docs.title: Creating a silence
docs.text:
# UI: Alertmanager UI → Silences → New silence
# API:
curl -X POST http://alertmanager:9093/api/v2/silences \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "startsAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "endsAt": "2026-01-01T02:00:00Z",
    "createdBy": "maintenance",
    "comment": "Node reboot for firmware update",
    "matchers": [
      { "name": "alertname", "value": "NodeCPUUsageHigh", "isRegex": false },
      { "name": "cluster", "value": "prod", "isRegex": false }
    ]
  }'

docs.title: Silencing rules in PrometheusRule (via Alertmanager)
docs.text: Silences are managed externally through the Alertmanager UI or API; they are not defined in PrometheusRule objects.

docs.title: F. Common alert patterns for Kubernetes
Availability alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition KubeAPIDown up{job="kubernetes-apiserver"} == 0 API server not reachable KubeStateMetricsNoData count by (job) (kube_deployment_status_replicas{job="kube-state-metrics"}) == 0 No metrics received for 10m NodeNotReady kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready", status="true"} == 0 Node not ready

docs.title: Node alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition NodeCPUUsageHigh 100 - (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[1m]) * 100) > 85 CPU usage > 85% for 10m NodeMemoryUsageHigh 100 - (node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100) > 85 Memory usage > 85% NodeDiskPressure node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"} < 20% * node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"} Disk < 20% available

docs.title: Pod/Container alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition PodRestarted increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[5m]) > 3 Pod restarted > 3 times in 5m ContainerCrashLoop kube_pod_container_status_phase{phase="CrashLoopBackoff"} == 1 Container in crash loop PodDown up{pod!=""} == 0 for 5m Pod not running

docs.title: Network alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition IngressBackendDown count by (ingress) (nginx_ingress_up{backend!=""} == 0) Ingress backend unreachable MetalLBPoolUnavailable lb_set{pool!=""} == 0 MetalLB pool has no available members

docs.title: G. Common alert patterns for Ceph
Ceph cluster health
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition CephHealthError ceph_health_status == 1 Ceph reports non-healthy status CephOSDDown ceph_osd_up == 0 One or more OSDs down CephPGDegraded ceph_pg_degraded > 0 PGs in degraded state CephPGRecoveryStuck ceph_pg_recovery_acting > 0 and ceph_pg_recovery_queue > 1000 Recovery queue stuck

docs.title: Ceph OSD alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition CephOSDFull ceph_osd_full > 0 OSD(s) at or near capacity CephOSDNearFull ceph_osd_nearfull > 0 OSD(s) near full threshold CephOSDHeartbeatLost increase(ceph_osd_heartbeat_lost[5m]) > 0 OSD heartbeat lost

docs.title: Ceph pool alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition CephPoolNearFull ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total > 0.85 Pool > 85% used CephPoolFull ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total >= 1.0 Pool 100% used

docs.title: Ceph mon/manager alerts
docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition CephMonDown ceph_mon_up == 0 Monitor daemon down CephMgrDown ceph_mgr_up == 0 Manager daemon down

docs.title: H. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory:

  • All rules and dashboards live in Git, applied by Argo CD. Never kubectl apply a rule by hand.
  • Validate rules in CI with promtool check rules.
  • Inhibit duplicates at the cluster level — a single ClusterDown alert should suppress all node-level alerts for that cluster.
  • Prometheus storage on a real PVC with a size limit, not emptyDir.
  • Scrape credentials and receiver secrets come from Vault via External Secrets, not from a values file.

Strongly recommended:

  • Keep the scrape label set small; pod, namespace, container, job are enough. Adding pod_uid or request IDs destroys performance.
  • Record rules for expensive queries so dashboards do not recompute them.
  • Run a canary Prometheus in the Management Cluster scraping both clusters as a second line of visibility.
  • Alert on "no data" separately from "bad data" — a Prometheus that cannot scrape produces silence, not an alert.
  • Every alert must link to a runbook in troubleshooting/.

Anti-patterns to avoid:

  • Overly specific PromQL that matches only a single pod by pod_uid — makes silencing and scaling difficult.
  • for: 0s on alerts — fires instantly on any single scrape failure; always include a for duration.
  • Recording rules with high cardinality group-by labels — can blow up the TSDB.
  • Alerts without annotations — notifications will have no useful context.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Cluster-wide monitoring system with single-node and multi-node deployments. Covers scrape pipelines, long-term storage, and high-availability patterns used across the platform.

docs.title: Single-node deployment
docs.text:
• One Prometheus instance per cluster, deployed via the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart.
  • Resources: 500m CPU / 2Gi requests, 2 CPU / 4Gi limits.
  • Storage: PVC with ceph-block storage class, 15d retention, 80GB size limit.
  • Run kubectl -n monitoring get pods and kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090 to verify.

docs.title: Multi-node / sharded deployment
docs.text:
• Prometheus scales by sharding targets across instances via prometheusSpec.replicas.
  • Each replica owns a hash of the target; no central coordinator needed.
  • Replicas do not share state; long-term storage is handled by Thanos sidecar.
  • Use prometheusSpec.serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false to ensure cross-namespace ServiceMonitors are discovered.

docs.title: Built-in scrape targets
docs.text: Component Exporter Discovery method Nodes node-exporter DaemonSet, K8s node label selectors Control plane apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd K8s service discovery Cluster add-ons kube-state-metrics K8s SD Ceph ceph-exporter Static config or Ceph endpoints GPU dcgm-exporter ServiceMonitor with dcgm-exporter labels Git infra harbor-exporter, nexus-exporter, gitlab-exporter Static config

docs.title: Service Discovery
docs.text:
• K8s service discovery: Prometheus picks up Service objects with annotations prometheus.io/scrape: "true" and prometheus.io/port / prometheus.io/path.
  • ServiceMonitor (Prometheus Operator): Preferred method. Define ServiceMonitor CRs that select Services by labels; the operator generates the required scrape_config automatically.
  • Relabeling: Use metric_relabel_configs and source_relabel_configs to drop/rename labels, limit cardinality (keep pod, namespace, job only), and drop pod_uid.

docs.title: Remote write / storage
docs.text:
• Local storage: Default; TSDB on local PVC. Retention configured via prometheusSpec.retention (e.g., 15d) and prometheusSpec.retentionSize (e.g., 80GB).
  • Remote write: Configure remoteWrite in the Prometheus spec to ship metrics to Thanos sidecar or Thanos object storage.
  • Typical URL: http://thanos-sidecar. monitoring.svc:9093/api/v1/write
  • Compression: snappy
  • Write timeout: 30s
  • Remote read: remoteRead points to the Thanos query endpoint for historical queries across clusters.

docs.title: Long-term storage (Thanos)
docs.text:
• Thanos sidecar runs alongside Prometheus, uploading encrypted blocks to object storage (Ceph S3-compatible).
  • Thanos querier provides global view across clusters.
  • Verify with thanos query and view retention timeline in the Thanos UI.

docs.title: D. Retention
docs.text:
• Short-term: Local TSDB on PVC. Default 15d retention, adjustable via Helm value prometheusSpec.retention.
  • Size cap: retentionSize (e.g., 80GB) enforces a hard limit; when exceeded, the oldest chunks are deleted.
  • Long-term: Thanos uploads compressed blocks to object storage after compaction. Retention there is effectively unlimited, governed by object-store lifecycle policies.
  • Compaction: Runs every 2h by default; monitor prometheus_tsdb_compaction_seconds_total for failures.

docs.title: Active-Passive (replica-based)
docs.text:
• Multiple Prometheus replicas via prometheusSpec.replicas > 1.
  • Each replica scrapes a disjoint subset of targets (sharded by target hash).
  • No active-active sync; if one replica fails, others continue with reduced coverage.
  • Failover is manual: delete the failed pod, the operator reschedules it.

docs.title: Cross-cluster visibility
docs.text:
• Deploy a canary Prometheus in the Management Cluster that scrapes both clusters.
  • Use Thanos federation or query across clusters for unified dashboards.
  • Alternatively, use prometheusSpec.remoteWrite to forward all metrics to a central Thanos bucket.

docs.title: Alertmanager coupling
docs.text:
• Prometheus HA requires matching Alertmanager deployment.
  • Use alertmanagerSpec with replicas: 3 and clusterName: <unique>.
  • Inhibit rules and routing configs live in Git; changes are applied by Argo CD.

docs.title: F. Validation
docs.text:
# Check active targets
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090 &
curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | jq '.data.activeTargets[] | {job: .labels.job, health: .health}'

# Verify retention and TSDB health
kubectl -n monitoring exec deployment/kube-prometheus-prometheus -c prometheus -- promtool check tsdb

# Long-term storage check
thanos object stats <bucket-name> | head -20

# Scrape failure troubleshooting
kubectl -n monitoring get prometheus -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.selectorDuration}'

docs.text: Alert name PromQL expression Condition CephMonDown ceph_mon_up == 0 Monitor daemon down CephMgrDown ceph_mgr_up == 0 Manager daemon down

docs.title: H. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory:

  • All rules and dashboards live in Git, applied by Argo CD. Never kubectl apply a rule by hand.
  • Validate rules in CI with promtool check rules.
  • Inhibit duplicates at the cluster level — a single ClusterDown alert should suppress all node-level alerts for that cluster.
  • Prometheus storage on a real PVC with a size limit, not emptyDir.
  • Scrape credentials and receiver secrets come from Vault via External Secrets, not from a values file.

Strongly recommended:

  • Keep the scrape label set small; pod, namespace, container, job are enough. Adding pod_uid or request IDs destroys performance.
  • Record rules for expensive queries so dashboards do not recompute them.
  • Run a canary Prometheus in the Management Cluster scraping both clusters as a second line of visibility.
  • Alert on "no data" separately from "bad data" — a Prometheus that cannot scrape produces silence, not an alert.
  • Every alert must link to a runbook in troubleshooting/.

Anti-patterns to avoid:

  • Overly specific PromQL that matches only a single pod by pod_uid — makes silencing and scaling difficult.
  • for: 0s on alerts — fires instantly on any single scrape failure; always include a for duration.
  • Recording rules with high cardinality group-by labels — can blow up the TSDB.
  • Alerts without annotations — notifications will have no useful context.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document the Prometheus recording rules used across the Kubernetes, Ceph, and Rancher clusters. Recording rules pre-compute expensive PromQL queries for use in dashboards, alerts, and other queries. All rules are stored as PrometheusRule custom resources in Git and applied by Argo CD.

This file is dedicated to recording rules; see monitoring/prometheus-alert-rules.md for alerting rules and monitoring/prometheus-architecture.md for the overall Prometheus deployment architecture.

docs.title: Prometheus rule types
docs.text: Rule type File extension Purpose AlertingRule .yml / .yaml Fires when an expressed condition is true for a sustained duration RecordingRule .yml / .yaml Pre-computes expensive queries for use in dashboards and other rules

docs.title: Recording rule structure
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: recording-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: recording-group
    interval: 1m
    rules:
    - record: job:node_cpu_seconds:sumrate
      expr: rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="system"}[1m])

Key fields:

Field Description expr PromQL expression to pre-compute record Name of the new vector time-series to record interval How often the rule is evaluated (default 1m)

Recording rules pre-compute queries that are expensive or used repeatedly, reducing dashboard query latency and ensuring consistent metrics across visualizations.

docs.title: Kubernetes metrics
docs.text: Record name PromQL expression Description kube:node:cpu:sumrate rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="system"}[1m]) Node CPU usage in seconds per second (summed across all nodes) kube:node:memory:available node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes Available memory bytes per node kube:pod:restart:count increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[5m]) Pod container restarts in last 5 minutes kube:namespace:count count by (namespace) (kube_namespace_status_phase) Number of namespaces in each phase kube:ingress:up count by (ingress) (nginx_ingress_up) Ingress availability status kube:persistentvolume:bound count by (pv) (kube_persistentvolume_status{phase="Bound"}) Bound persistent volumes

docs.title: Ceph metrics
docs.text: Record name PromQL expression Description ceph:osd:up ceph_osd_up Whether OSDs are up (1 = up, 0 = down) ceph:pg:degraded ceph_pg_degraded Number of PGs in degraded state ceph:pool:bytes:used:ratio ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total Pool usage ratio (0-1) ceph:health:status ceph_health_status Ceph cluster health status (0 = healthy, 1 = error) ceph:osd:heartbeat:lost increase(ceph_osd_heartbeat_lost[5m]) Lost OSD heartbeats in last 5 minutes ceph:mon:up ceph_mon_up Whether Ceph monitors are up

docs.title: Rancher metrics
docs.text: Record name PromQL expression Description rancher:cluster:count count by (cluster) (rancher_cluster_active) Number of active Rancher clusters rancher:service:cpu:sumrate rate(rancher_service_cpu_seconds_total[1m]) Rancher service CPU usage rancher:workload:phase rancher_workload_phase{workload!=""} Workload phase status (running, stopped, etc.) rancher:endpoint:health count by (endpoint) (rancher_endpoint_health) Rancher endpoint health status

docs.title: Common aggregation patterns
docs.text: Pattern PromQL example Use case Rate per second rate(node_cpu_seconds_total[1m]) CPU utilization trends Increase over interval increase(node_cpu_seconds_total[5m]) Total CPU seconds elapsed Sum across labels sum by (cluster) (node_cpu_seconds_total) Cluster-level totals Count distinct count by (namespace) (kube_pod) Number of pods per namespace Histogram quantiles histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) Latency p95 In-rate irange(node_cpu_seconds_total[1m]) Instant rate over 1m

docs.title: Grouping strategies
docs.text:
• By cluster: sum by (cluster) (...) — aggregate across all clusters in a fleet
  • By namespace: sum by (namespace) (...) — isolate per-namespace metrics
  • By service: sum by (service) (...) — service-level aggregation
  • Without cardinality: Remove high-cardinality labels (pod_uid, container_id) from recording rules to avoid TSDB bloat

docs.title: Template: Kubernetes node overview
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: kubernetes-node-recording-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: kubernetes-node
    interval: 1m
    rules:
    - record: kube:node:cpu:sumrate
      expr: rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="system"}[1m])
    - record: kube:node:memory:available
      expr: node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes
    - record: kube:node:disk:available
      expr: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"}

docs.title: Template: Ceph cluster health
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: ceph-recording-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: ceph
    interval: 1m
    rules:
    - record: ceph:osd:up
      expr: ceph_osd_up
    - record: ceph:pg:degraded
      expr: ceph_pg_degraded
    - record: ceph:pool:bytes:used:ratio
      expr: ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total
    - record: ceph:health:status
      expr: ceph_health_status

docs.title: Template: Rancher cluster overview
docs.text:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: rancher-recording-rules
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  groups:
  - name: rancher
    interval: 1m
    rules:
    - record: rancher:cluster:count
      expr: count by (cluster) (rancher_cluster_active)
    - record: rancher:service:cpu:sumrate
      expr: rate(rancher_service_cpu_seconds_total[1m])
    - record: rancher:workload:phase
      expr: rancher_workload_phase{workload!=""}

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Run promtool check rules <rule-file>.yaml against every PrometheusRule to catch syntax errors and cardinality issues.
  • Verify recorded series appear in Prometheus with vector( recording_rule_name ) queries.
  • Check TSDB growth after deploying new recording rules; high cardinality will increase storage costs.

docs.title: Review cycle
docs.text: Activity Frequency Owner Review rule expressions for deprecated PromQL Quarterly SRE team Re-run promtool check rules after any change On every PR PR author Prune recording rules unused for > 90 days Semi-annual Platform team Update documentation when rules change On every change SRE team

docs.title: Deployment flow
docs.text:
1. Add or edit .yaml files in monitoring/ directory
  2. Open a PR against the cloud-native-guide repo
  3. Ensure CI passes promtool check rules validation
  4. Argo CD automatically applies merged changes to the cluster
  5. Verify recorded series in Prometheus UI after deployment
  6. Update this documentation if rule names or expressions change

docs.title: Rollback procedure
docs.text:
1. If a new recording rule causes TSDB bloat or errors, revert the PrometheusRule change in Git.
  2. Argo CD will sync back to the previous state within the sync interval.
  3. Monitor prometheus_tsdb_errors_total for any spike indicating a bad rule.
  4. File a follow-up task to rewrite the rule with corrected cardinality.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Cluster, node, storage, platform service, and GPU metrics with a single scrape pipeline, plus alert routing.

docs.title: B. Architecture
docs.text:
kube-prometheus-stack (Prometheus Operator)
  Prometheus  -> scrape targets (node_exporter, kube-state-metrics, exporters)
  Alertmanager -> routes -> receivers (email, webhook, chat)
  Grafana  -> dashboards, datasources
  Thanos sidecar -> object storage (long-term, optional)

The stack runs in the Management Cluster, and the Application Cluster's Prometheus is scraped by the Management Prometheus, or each cluster runs its own Prometheus with Thanos for global queries. Decision: each cluster runs its own Prometheus; Thanos provides the global view.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• Chart: kube-prometheus-stack from harbor.internal/charts/.
  • Images: prometheus, alertmanager, node-exporter, kube-state-metrics, pushgateway, thanos, grafana, and the kube-prometheus-stack adapter images. All in offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md.
  • Grafana dashboards: JSON dashboards are stored in the obs-monitoring GitLab project and applied by Argo CD, not baked into a container image. That keeps dashboards versioned and reviewable.

docs.title: D. Installation
docs.text:
Argo CD Application (in mgmt-argocd):

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: kube-prometheus-stack
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: platform
  source:
    repoURL: https://gitlab.internal/platform/obs-monitoring.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: kube-prometheus-stack
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values.yaml
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: monitoring
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

Key Helm values (values.yaml):

grafana:
  enabled: true
  adminPassword: ""            # from ExternalSecret, not inline
  dashboards:
    enabled: false             # dashboards applied from Git instead
prometheus:
  prometheusSpec:
    retention: 15d
    retentionSize: 80GB
    serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 2Gi}
      limits: {cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi}
    storageSpec:
      volumeClaimTemplate:
        spec:
          storageClassName: ceph-block
          accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
          resources: {requests: {storage: 200Gi}}
alertmanager:
  alertmanagerSpec:
    storage:
      volumeClaimTemplate:
        spec:
          storageClassName: ceph-block
          accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
          resources: {requests: {storage: 20Gi}}

serviceMonitorSelectorNilUsesHelmValues: false is required so ServiceMonitors in other namespaces are scraped — a common cause of "no metrics" in a multi-cluster setup.

docs.title: E. Integration
docs.text: Integration Mechanism Nodes node-exporter DaemonSet Kubernetes objects kube-state-metrics Control plane apiserver + scheduler + controller-manager + etcd endpoints, scraped via the K8s SD Ceph ceph-exporter (or the Ceph mgr prometheus module) GPU DCGM exporter ServiceMonitor Vault Vault telemetry/exporter GitLab, Harbor, Nexus, Keycloak their own metrics endpoints Alert routing Alertmanager config in Git, receivers from External Secrets

docs.title: F. Validation
docs.text:
kubectl -n monitoring get pods
kubectl -n monitoring port-forward svc/kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090
curl -s http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets | jq '.data.activeTargets[] | {job: .labels.job, health: .health}'

Expect every job to report health: "up". A job with zero targets is a ServiceMonitor selector problem, not a connectivity problem.

Alert test:

# Fire a test alert
kubectl -n monitoring exec sts/kube-prometheus-prometheus -c prometheus -- \
  wget -qO- 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/alerts'

Category Example alert Condition Availability APIServerDown up{job="apiserver"} == 0 Availability NodeNotReady kube_node_status_condition{condition="Ready",status="true"} == 0 Availability etcdNoLeader etcd_server_has_leader == 0 Availability TargetDown up == 0 for 10m Capacity NodeMemoryPressure condition True Capacity PVCNearFull kubelet_volume_stats_available_bytes / kubelet_volume_stats_capacity_bytes < 0.15 Capacity DiskWillFillIn4Hours standard node-exporter filesystem rule Capacity PrometheusTSDBCompactionsFailing rate(prometheus_tsdb_compactions_failed_total[3h]) > 0 Storage CephHealthError ceph_health_status == 1 Storage CephOSDDown ceph_osd_up == 0 Storage CephPoolNearFull ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total > 0.85 Storage CephPGDegraded ceph_pg_degraded > 0 Certificates CertificateExpiringSoon probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry - time() < 14*24*3600 Certificates CertificateExpiringIn7Days same with 7 days, page Backup VeleroBackupFailed velero_backup_status_backup_success == 0 Backup NoRecentBackup time() - velero_backup_last_success_timestamp > 86400*2 Authentication VaultAuthFailureSpike rate(vault_route_auth_login[5m]) with failure labels Authentication SSHFailedLogins from logs (log-based rule) Security GatekeeperConstraintViolation gatekeeper_validation_error_count increase Security FalcoAlert falco_alerts_total increase Upgrade risk NodeReadinessDegraded during maintenance kube_node_status_condition per node GPU DCGM GPU errors DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_XID_ERRORS GPU GPU memory pressure DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED / DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_FREE + USED > 0.95 GPU GPU temperature DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_TEMP > 85 AI Inference OOM vLLM metric for OOM/retries AI TTFT regression vLLM histogram quantile above threshold

Adding pod_uid or request ids destroys performance. - Record rules for expensive queries so dashboards do not recompute them. - Run a canary Prometheus in the Management Cluster scraping both clusters as a second line of visibility. - Alert on "no data" separately from "bad data" — a Prometheus that cannot scrape produces silence, not an alert.

docs.title: Cloud-native DMZ — edge segmentation and traffic policy
docs.text: One exposed segment. Everything else is unreachable from outside.

docs.title: Segments
docs.text: Segment CIDR What lives there DMZ 10.60.0.0/24 Edge LB nodes only: keepalived + HAProxy/Nginx via Docker Compose. VIP 10.60.0.10/24. Management 10.10.0.0/24 Ops workstation, Ansible server, Vault, GitLab, HAProxy stats (8404), SSH. Control plane 10.20.0.0/24 Kubespray control plane with stacked etcd; kube-apiserver 10.20.0.100. Storage (public) 10.40.0.0/24 Ceph MON/OSD/MDS/RGW public network. Storage (cluster) 10.41.0.0/24 Ceph replication/rebalance between OSDs. GPU 10.50.0.0/24 GPU workers, DCGM exporter 9400, model store.

docs.title: Edge dataplane
docs.text:
Two nodes (lb-node-1, lb-node-2), identical stack:

  • keepalived — VRRP instance VI_EDGE, VIP 10.60.0.10, unicast peers (10.60.0.1 ↔ 10.60.0.2) because the DMZ VLAN filters multicast 224.0.0.18; auth_pass rendered by Ansible from Vault; health script checks local HAProxy and lowers priority on failure. See ../manifests/external-lb/keepalived.conf.
  • HAProxy — binds 0.0.0.0:443 (TCP) → Nginx 127.0.0.1:8443 (L7 ingress tier) and 0.0.0.0:6443 (TCP) → kube-apiserver 10.20.0.100:6443 with /readyz check. The dataplane binds the wildcard address, not the VIP, so a VRRP failover needs no container restart. See ../manifests/external-lb/haproxy.cfg.
  • Stats — 10.60.0.1:8404 on the management address only. Never bound to the DMZ address.

docs.title: What crosses the DMZ
docs.text:
Direction Flow Ports Firewall location In Clients / ops workstation → edge LB VIP 443, 22 dmz fw In Edge LB peer → edge LB peer IP proto 112 (VRRP) dmz fw Out Edge LB → kube-apiserver (via itself) 6443 dmz fw Out Edge LB → MetalLB peers (BGP, if used) 179 dmz fw In Everything else to the DMZ — dropped

Nothing terminates directly on the DMZ except the edge:

  • vLLM inference port 8000 is never exposed to the DMZ; clients reach it through the DMZ gateway only (gpu-ai/inference/llm-serving.md).
  • HAProxy stats never listen on the DMZ address.
  • MetalLB is an in-cluster L4 LB; it is not DMZ-exposed.

Services reachable through the DMZ VIP (clients address the VIP, never the backends): Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, Grafana, L7 ingress (F5 NGINX IC / NGINX Gateway Fabric / Envoy Gateway), LLM inference via the API gateway. Their backends run in the cluster or management segments.

docs.title: Role-specific firewall behavior
docs.text:
Role Adds Removes Management cluster 443 from dmz — DMZ edge 443 from outside Everything else

Full ruleset skeleton: network-matrix/firewall-rules-generation.md; per-flow matrix: network-matrix/port-requirements.md.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
# From an allowed source (ops workstation / DMZ client)
nmap -Pn -p 22,443,6443 <edge-vip>
# Expect: 22, 443 open; 6443 open only via the edge proxy check below

# From a denied source
nmap -Pn -p 22,443,6443 <edge-vip>
# Expect: filtered

# Ruleset loaded on each node
nft list ruleset
firewall-cmd --list-all   # firewalld hosts only

# Edge health
docker logs edge-keepalived
curl -k https://<vip>:6443/readyz      # expect 200
curl -s http://<lb-mgmt>:8404/         # from management: expect stats page
curl -s http://<vip>:8404/             # from DMZ: expect failure

Both nmap results are recorded as evidence for acceptance test B-10.

docs.title: Rules never to break
docs.text:
1. Stats bound to 10.60.0.1:8404 (management) only — never the DMZ address.
  2. Edge image set is minimal, no shell; VRRP auth_pass and TLS keys written by Ansible from Vault.
  3. Unicast VRRP peers unless the network team confirms multicast 224.0.0.18 end to end on the DMZ VLAN.
  4. vLLM port 8000 never reachable directly from the DMZ.
  5. One firewall implementation per host — nftables or firewalld, never both.
