docs.title: External load balancer — active/active edge
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
The external load balancer is the platform's edge: it terminates client TLS, applies the site edge policy, and forwards to the Kubernetes management endpoints (API server, Rancher, Argo CD, Keycloak, Grafana) and to the L7 ingress tier.

The user requirement is active/active on Linux, built from Nginx or HAProxy, with Keepalived and Docker Compose.

docs.title: The honest constraint
docs.text:
Keepalived implements VRRP. VRRP elects one master for a given virtual router id and one virtual IP address. A single VIP under VRRP is therefore active/standby, not active/active. This is a property of the protocol, not of the implementation.

Active/active is obtained by not putting all traffic behind one VRRP-owned address. The design has three tiers, and the platform implements tier 2 and tier 3 on top of the same node-local dataplane.

                        +----------------------+
   client ------------->| DNS / GSLB          |   tier 3: two A records or
                        +----------+-----------+
                                   |
                    +--------------+--------------+
                    |                             |
            VIP-A (10.60.0.10)            VIP-B (10.60.0.11)
                    |                             |
            +-------+-------+             +-------+-------+
            |  lb-node-1   |             |  lb-node-2   |   tier 2: router ECMP
            | nginx/haproxy|             | nginx/haproxy|          or BGP over
            | + keepalived |             | + keepalived |          the two VIPs
            +-------+-------+             +-------+-------+
                    |                             |
                    +--------------+--------------+
                                   |
                    kube-apiserver VIP, ingress, platform services
Tier Mechanism Active/active? Requires Failover time 1 One VIP, Keepalived VRRP No — active/standby Nothing beyond the L2 segment ~3 s (VRRP advert interval) 2 Two VIPs, upstream ECMP or BGP Yes Router support for ECMP over the two VIPs, or BGP peering Router convergence, or instant with SO_REUSEPORT-style multipath 3 DNS/GSLB over the two VIPs Yes Authoritative DNS with health checks DNS TTL bound

Tier 2 is the primary design. Tier 3 is for client-facing names that the router cannot balance, and it also gives a coarse client-side failover for tier-1-style single-VIP endpoints.

docs.title: Node-local dataplane
docs.text:
Each node runs the same stack, containerised with Docker Compose:

  • Nginx or HAProxy in front, bound to 0.0.0.0:443 and 0.0.0.0:80 on the host network, with net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1 so the process holds the socket whether or not the VIP currently sits on that node.
  • Keepalived in the same Compose project, on host network, managing the node's VIP.
  • Because the dataplane binds the wildcard address rather than the VIP, the dataplane is up and serving on both nodes at all times. Keepalived only decides which node the address points at. That is what makes tier 2 and tier 3 possible and what keeps a failover from requiring a container restart.

docs.title: Nginx versus HAProxy
docs.text:
Aspect Nginx HAProxy L7 features Rich: rewrite, map, auth_request, Lua, caching Simpler but excellent at proxying, health checking, and TLS Layer 4 passthrough stream module, separate binary block Native, first-class Health checks Passive plus nginx -t style upstream checks; active checks need Plus or NGINX Inc. Active health checks in OSS, per-server, with check Stats stub_status or a third-party exporter Built-in stats socket and a stats page Graceful reload nginx -s reload, zero downtime USR2/SIGUSR1 soft stop, or the official reload procedure Connection sharding reuseport on listen (Linux 3.9+) SO_REUSEPORT by default on listen sockets Memory footprint Low Low Ecosystem Broad Broad

Decision: HAProxy for the edge when active health checks and L4 passthrough matter (the edge must health-check the API server and the ingress tier, and it must pass TCP through for the API). Nginx for the edge when rich L7 policy (redirects, auth_request, header manipulation) matters more than active health checks.

The Compose project below ships both, selected by an environment variable. Nginx runs the L7 policy; HAProxy runs the L4 and the active health checking. The recommended production profile is HAProxy in front, Nginx behind it only if both are needed; running both for the same traffic doubles the failure surface and is not recommended.

docs.title: B. Requirements and compatibility
docs.text: Item Requirement Status OS Oracle Linux 9 or Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS VERIFIED Docker Engine 26.x or later, with the Compose v2 plugin VERIFIED against the platform's container baseline Docker Compose v5.6.1 (plugin) VERIFIED, https://github.com/docker/compose/releases Nginx (OSS) 1.31.8 upstream, 1.24.0 in Ubuntu noble VERIFIED, https://github.com/nginx/nginx/releases and the Ubuntu package index HAProxy 3.2.26 (3.2 branch), 2.8.5 in Ubuntu noble VERIFIED, https://www.haproxy.org/download/3.2/src/ and the Ubuntu package index Keepalived 2.4.3 upstream, 2.2.8 in Ubuntu noble VERIFIED, https://github.com/acassen/keepalived/releases and the Ubuntu package index Kernel >= 4.19 (SO_REUSEPORT needs 3.9+; 5.x recommended) VERIFIED against the Kubespray kernel requirements VRRP IP protocol 112. Multicast 224.0.0.18, or unicast peers VERIFIED, https://www.keepalived.org/documentation/keepalived-conf/

docs.title: VRRP multicast caveat
docs.text:
VRRP uses multicast on 224.0.0.18 by default. Many switched networks filter it, and the protocol will not work. Two options:

  • Unicast peers: keepalived unicast_src_ip and unicast_peer { } per node. Works on any L2 segment. Preferred for this platform, because the DMZ segment is likely to have multicast filtering.
  • Multicast: only if the network team confirms 224.0.0.18 is permitted end to end on the DMZ VLAN.

The HAProxy Enterprise documentation makes the same point: "some environments, such as AWS, may not allow multicasting. In these environments, you may have to configure a unicast implementation instead".

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
Artifact Type Internal destination Notes nginx:1.31.8 OCI harbor.internal/edge/nginx Plus nginx:1.31.8-alpine if Alpine is chosen haproxy:3.2.26 OCI harbor.internal/edge/haproxy acassen/keepalived:v2.4.3 OCI harbor.internal/edge/keepalived The upstream image; it needs NET_ADMIN and host network docker/compose OCI (tooling) harbor.internal/tools/compose For the CI runner, not the LB nodes Edge configuration Git gitlab.internal/platform/edge Nginx, HAProxy, keepalived configs and the Compose file TLS certificates Secret Vault, via cert-manager or a mounted file The edge terminates TLS

The Compose file and the configuration live in Git. The nodes are stateless: a node is rebuilt by docker compose up -d from the committed configuration. Certificates are mounted read-only from a path that Ansible populates from Vault.

docs.title: Host preparation
docs.text:
# The edge needs the wildcard bind, because the dataplane is always up
# regardless of which node currently holds the VIP
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/99-edge.conf <<'EOF'
net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 0
EOF
sysctl --system

rp_filter=0 matters when the dataplane binds the wildcard address and the traffic arrives addressed to the VIP.

docs.title: Docker Compose stack
docs.text:
manifests/external-lb/docker-compose.yml — the full file is in the repository. Structure:

name: edge

services:
  haproxy:
    image: harbor.internal/edge/haproxy:3.2.26
    container_name: edge-haproxy
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./haproxy.cfg:/usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg:ro
      - ./certs:/etc/haproxy/certs:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "haproxy", "-c", "-f", "/usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    sysctls:
      net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind: "1"

  nginx:
    image: harbor.internal/edge/nginx:1.31.8
    container_name: edge-nginx
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
      - ./certs:/etc/nginx/certs:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "nginx", "-t"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 3
    sysctls:
      net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind: "1"

  keepalived:
    image: harbor.internal/edge/keepalived:v2.4.3
    container_name: edge-keepalived
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - NET_BROADCAST
      - NET_RAW
      - SYS_MODULE
    volumes:
      - ./keepalived.conf:/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf:ro
      - ./keepalived.d:/etc/keepalived/keepalived.d:ro
    pid: host
    sysctls:
      net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind: "1"

Why network_mode: host on all three:

  • VRRP advertisements are sent from the physical interface, with the physical source address. A bridged container cannot emit them correctly.
  • The dataplane binds 0.0.0.0:443 and must hold the socket across a VIP move. In a bridged network, the socket would be bound inside the container's namespace and would not follow the host's address changes.
  • pid: host on keepalived is required for it to manage the host's network namespace state correctly in practice.

docs.title: HAProxy configuration
docs.text:
manifests/external-lb/haproxy.cfg — the edge frontend, with an active health check against each upstream:

global
    log stdout format raw local0
    maxconn 20000
    tune.ssl.default-dh-param 2048
    stats socket /run/haproxy/admin.sock mode 660 level admin
    ssl-default-bind-ciphersuites ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305

defaults
    log global
    mode http
    option httplog
    option dontlognull
    timeout connect 5s
    timeout client 60s
    timeout server 60s
    timeout http-request 10s
    timeout http-keep-alive 10s
    retries 3

frontend fe_https
    bind 0.0.0.0:443
    mode tcp
    # L4 to the L7 tier; the edge does not terminate TLS when Nginx owns it
    default_backend be_l7

backend be_l7
    mode tcp
    balance leastconn
    option tcp-check
    server nginx_local 127.0.0.1:8443 check inter 3s fall 3 rise 2

The frontend in mode tcp is deliberate: the edge is a TCP proxy in front of the L7 policy tier. When Nginx owns TLS termination directly, the edge HAProxy is not deployed at all — the Compose profile edge-nginx-only starts Nginx and keepalived only.

For a pure L4 edge (for example, the Kubernetes API server endpoint), the backend is the API VIP with an HTTP health check on /readyz:

frontend fe_api
    bind 0.0.0.0:6443
    mode tcp
    default_backend be_api

backend be_api
    mode tcp
    balance roundrobin
    option httpchk GET /readyz
    http-check expect status 200
    server kube-apiserver 10.20.0.100:6443 check inter 3s fall 3 rise 2

docs.title: Nginx configuration
docs.text:
manifests/external-lb/nginx.conf — TLS termination, HTTP redirect, and the platform endpoints:

worker_processes auto;
error_log /dev/stderr warn;
pid /var/run/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections 8192;
    multi_accept on;
}

http {
    include       /etc/nginx/mime.types;
    default_type  application/octet-stream;
    access_log    /dev/stdout;

    sendfile      on;
    tcp_nopush    on;
    keepalive_timeout 65;
    server_tokens off;

    # SO_REUSEPORT: one listening socket per worker, kernel distributes
    # new connections. Linux 3.9+. Per-host process sharding, not cross-host.
    # listen directives below use it.

    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off;
    ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:10m;
    ssl_session_timeout 1d;
    ssl_session_tickets off;

    upstream api_server {
        server 10.20.0.100:6443 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=5s;
        keepalive 32;
    }

    upstream ingress_https {
        server 10.61.0.10:443 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=5s;
        keepalive 32;
    }

    server {
        listen 80 reuseport;
        server_name _;
        return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
    }

    server {
        listen 443 ssl reuseport;
        http2 on;
        server_name _;

        ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/certs/tls.crt;
        ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/certs/tls.key;

        location / {
            proxy_pass http://ingress_https;
            proxy_set_header Host $host;
            proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
            proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        }
    }
}

reuseport gives per-host connection sharding across workers. It does not load-balance across nodes. Cross-node distribution is tier 2 (router ECMP/BGP) or tier 3 (DNS/GSLB).

docs.title: Keepalived configuration
docs.text:
manifests/external-lb/keepalived.conf — unicast peers, because the DMZ VLAN is assumed to filter multicast:

global_defs {
    router_id lb-node-1
    enable_script_security
    script_user root
    vrrp_skip_check_adv_addr
}

vrrp_script chk_haproxy {
    script "/etc/keepalived/keepalived.d/check_haproxy.sh"
    interval 2
    weight -20
    fall 2
    rise 2
}

vrrp_instance VI_EDGE {
    state BACKUP
    interface bond0
    virtual_router_id 51
    priority 100
    advert_int 1

    authentication {
        auth_type PASS
        auth_pass <from Vault>
    }

    unicast_src_ip 10.60.0.1
    unicast_peer {
        10.60.0.2
    }

    virtual_ipaddress {
        10.60.0.10/24
    }

    track_script {
        chk_haproxy
    }

    notify_master "/etc/keepalived/keepalived.d/notify.sh MASTER"
    notify_backup "/etc/keepalived/keepalived.d/notify.sh BACKUP"
}

The health-check script is what keeps a node from taking the VIP when its dataplane is broken:

#!/bin/sh
# Returns 0 when the local dataplane is serving.
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/8443

A failed check subtracts the weight, and the node with the higher effective priority holds the address. The notification script posts the state change to the monitoring stack, so the topology in Grafana reflects which node is master.

docs.title: E. Integration
docs.text: Dimension Mechanism Identity The edge proxies to the platform services; the end user's identity is handled by Keycloak behind the ingress, not at the edge TLS The edge holds the wildcard certificate, mounted read-only from a path Ansible populates from Vault. cert-manager issues it if the edge runs in-cluster; for a standalone edge, the certificate is written by Ansible from a Vault lookup Secrets The auth_pass for VRRP and the TLS key are written by Ansible from Vault at deploy time. Neither is in Git Network The edge is on the DMZ segment, with only the platform VIPs reachable from it. It initiates the connections, so no return route is needed for the client traffic Storage None. The edge is stateless Monitoring HAProxy stats socket scraped over a unix socket or a local HTTP listener; Nginx stub_status; keepalived state from the notification script Logging Container stdout, collected by the node's Fluent Bit agent Security The edge is the only host exposed to the untrusted segment. It runs a minimal image set, no shell access, and the host firewall allows only 80/443 inbound Automation The whole node is rebuilt by Ansible: sysctls, Docker, the Compose project, the configuration from Git, the certificates from Vault GitOps The configuration and the Compose file live in Git. The nodes are rebuilt from the committed state, so the edge is reconciled by GitOps at the node level, not by Argo CD

docs.title: F. Validation
docs.text:
# The dataplane is up on both nodes, VIP or not
curl -sk --resolve edge.internal:443:10.60.0.1 https://edge.internal/healthz
curl -sk --resolve edge.internal:443:10.60.0.2 https://edge.internal/healthz

# The VIP is where keepalived says it is
ip -br addr show bond0 | grep 10.60.0.10
journalctl -u keepalived -n 50        # or: docker logs edge-keepalived

# HAProxy config is valid and the stats page is up
docker exec edge-haproxy haproxy -c -f /usr/local/etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8404/ | head -20

# Nginx config is valid
docker exec edge-nginx nginx -t

# Failover drill (tier 1)
docker stop edge-keepalived        # on the master
# VIP moves to the peer within the VRRP advert interval

Expected: both nodes answer on their own address; exactly one holds the VIP at a time in tier 1; in tier 2 both hold their own VIP and the router balances between them.

docs.title: G. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Change the edge configuration Update the committed configuration, then docker compose up -d on both nodes, then verify the health checks Reload HAProxy without dropping connections docker kill -s USR2 edge-haproxy (soft stop), then docker kill -s USR1 edge-haproxy (finish) Reload Nginx docker exec edge-nginx nginx -s reload Force a failover systemctl stop keepalived on the master, or lower its priority in the committed config and reload Rotate the TLS certificate Write the new certificate from Vault via Ansible, then reload the dataplane. With haproxy in mode tcp the certificate lives in Nginx, so reload Nginx Add an upstream Edit the committed upstream block, reload, confirm the health checks show it as up Upgrade a component New image tag in the committed Compose file, docker compose pull, docker compose up -d, verify, then the peer node Rebuild a node Ansible rebuild: sysctls, Docker, configuration, certificates, docker compose up -d

docs.title: Failover behaviour
docs.text:
Tier Failover time What the client sees 1 (VRRP VIP) ~3 s (advert interval 1 s, 3 adverts) Connection reset for in-flight connections, new connections succeed after the address moves 2 (ECMP/BGP) Router convergence, or sub-second with ECMP Same as tier 1 for the address in flight, but the router continues to use the surviving node 3 (DNS/GSLB) TTL bound, typically 30-60 s Name resolution returns both addresses; the client may use a dead one until the TTL expires

Mitigation for in-flight resets: the edge dataplane should use a long drain window on shutdown (docker stop -t 30), so existing connections finish before the process exits.

docs.title: H. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Host network for the dataplane and for keepalived. VRRP cannot work from a bridged container. - net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1 on the host, so the dataplane holds its socket across a VIP move. - The dataplane binds the wildcard address, never the VIP, so it is always serving. - Unicast VRRP peers, not multicast, unless the network team confirms multicast on the DMZ VLAN. - The VRRP auth_pass and the TLS key come from Vault, written by Ansible, never from Git. - A health check on the dataplane, tracked by keepalived, so a broken node never takes the address. - The edge runs a minimal image set and is the only host exposed to the untrusted segment.

Strongly recommended: - Tier 2 for the production edge: two VIPs with router ECMP or BGP, so both nodes carry traffic and losing one halves the capacity rather than removing it. - Tier 3 (DNS with health checks) for client-facing names the router cannot balance, with a short TTL. - HAProxy for the L4 edge and the active health checks; Nginx for the L7 policy, and not both on the same traffic path. - reuseport on the Nginx listeners for per-host worker sharding at high connection rates. - A quarterly failover drill on both tiers, with the measured failover time recorded.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Firewall rules generation
docs.text: The network communication matrix (network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md) is the source of truth. This file converts it into firewall rules per host role.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Rules are generated from the matrix, not hand-written. Two implementations:

Implementation Use Notes nftables (Ubuntu, Oracle Linux 9) Default Declarative, scriptable, testable firewalld (Oracle Linux 8/9 default) Alternative Zone-based; needs a dedicated zone with rich rules

Rules are generated by Ansible from a structured copy of the matrix, so the matrix and the firewall cannot drift silently. The generator writes a checksum of the matrix into the ruleset; a mismatch fails the run.

docs.title: nftables ruleset skeleton
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    set mgmt_hosts {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags interval
        elements = { 10.10.0.0/24 }
    }
    set cp_hosts {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags interval
        elements = { 10.20.0.0/24 }
    }
    set storage_hosts {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags interval
        elements = { 10.40.0.0/24 }
    }
    set dns_servers {
        type ipv4_addr
        elements = { 10.10.0.10 }
    }
    set ntp_servers {
        type ipv4_addr
        elements = { 10.10.0.11 }
    }

    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

        ct state established,related accept
        iif "lo" accept

        # SSH from the management segment only
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport 22 accept

        # DNS and NTP from the node to the internal resolvers
        ip daddr @dns_servers udp dport 53 accept
        ip daddr @dns_servers tcp dport 53 accept
        ip daddr @ntp_servers udp dport 123 accept

        # Kubernetes API: only from the control-plane segment and the
        # management segment (automation server, monitoring, CI)
        ip saddr @cp_hosts tcp dport 6443 accept
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport 6443 accept

        # etcd: only from control-plane nodes
        ip saddr @cp_hosts tcp dport { 2379, 2380 } accept

        # kubelet
        ip saddr @cp_hosts tcp dport 10250 accept
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport 10250 accept

        # node_exporter
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport 9100 accept

        # Ceph public network (MON/OSD/MDS/RGW) from the storage segment
        ip saddr @storage_hosts tcp dport { 6789, 6800-7568, 7480 } accept

        # GPU DCGM exporter
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport 9400 accept

        # Log shipping
        ip saddr @mgmt_hosts tcp dport { 3100, 5044, 9200 } accept

        # Rate limit the rest of the noise before logging
        limit rate 10/second burst 20 packets accept
        log prefix "nft-drop " level info limit rate 5/minute
    }

    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
        ct state established,related accept
    }

    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
    }
}

docs.title: Role-specific rules
docs.text:
The base ruleset is shared; each role adds or removes specific ports.

Role Adds Removes Control plane 6443 in from mgmt+cp, 2379/2380 from cp — Worker 10250 from cp+mgmt, 30000-32767 only if NodePort is used 6443 in (workers do not serve the API) Storage node 6800-7568, 6789, 7480 from storage — GPU node 9400 from mgmt — Management cluster 443 from dmz — DMZ edge 443 from outside everything else

docs.title: Implementation in Ansible
docs.text:
# ansible/roles/firewall/tasks/main.yml
- name: Render the nftables ruleset
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: nftables.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nftables.conf
    mode: "0600"
  vars:
    matrix_checksum: "{{ matrix_data | to_json | hash('sha256') }}"

- name: Validate the ruleset
  ansible.builtin.command: nft --check -f /etc/nftables.conf
  changed_when: false

- name: Reload nftables
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: nftables
    state: reloaded

nft --check runs before the reload. A ruleset that fails to parse is never installed.

docs.title: firewalld alternative (Oracle Linux)
docs.text:
firewall-cmd --permanent --new-zone=cloud-node
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=cloud-node --add-source=10.10.0.0/24
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=cloud-node --add-port=22/tcp
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=cloud-node --add-port=6443/tcp
firewall-cmd --reload

Use one implementation, never both. Two active firewalls produce rulesets that neither administrator fully understands.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
# From an allowed host
nmap -Pn -p 22,6443,2379,2380,10250,9100 <target>

# From a denied host
nmap -Pn -p 22,6443,2379,2380,10250,9100 <target>
# Expect: filtered

# Ruleset loaded?
nft list ruleset
firewall-cmd --list-all

Both results are recorded as evidence for acceptance test B-10.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text:
• Regenerate from the matrix on every matrix change. Do not hand-edit a host's ruleset.
  • Keep a per-environment override layer in site-<env> for site-specific exceptions, so the base matrix stays clean.
  • Review the dropped-packet log before changing anything. The log tells you what the traffic actually needs.

docs.title: Offline Artifact Matrix
docs.text:
One row per component-artifact pair. All values pinned. Source URL and check date are mandatory; a row without them is a defect.

Status: MIRRORED = present in the internal system and pull-verified. STAGED = downloaded in connected staging, not yet imported. PENDING = identified, not yet fetched. EXEMPT = no artifact needed (document the reason).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Internal destination: exact repository path in Harbor or Nexus.
  • Integrity: checksum file and/or signature type.
  • Refresh: how the artifact is updated and how often.
  • Validation: the command that proves offline availability.

docs.title: Rules for maintaining this matrix
docs.text:
1. A row is added when a component is added to the platform, and updated when a version is pinned.
  2. Every row requires a source URL and a check date in the version matrix (compatibility/version-matrix.md).
  3. PENDING rows block the phase they belong to. A deployment phase cannot start with a PENDING artifact for a component it installs.
  4. MIRRORED is only claimed after a pull test succeeded in the offline environment. A successful import is not a successful pull.

docs.title: Artifact Mirroring Procedure
docs.text: This document describes the procedure for mirroring artifacts into air-gapped environments, covering container images, Helm charts, OS packages, and the validation checklist for offline verification.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• skopeo installed on the staging host

#!/bin/bash

IMAGES=(
  "registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9"
  "registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.36.5"
  "registry.k8s.io/kube-controller-manager:v1.36.5"
  "registry.k8s.io/kube-scheduler:v1.36.5"
  "registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.36.5"
  "registry.k8s.io/coredns/coredns:v1.14.2"
  "registry.k8s.io/etcd:3.6.15"
)

for img in "${IMAGES[@]}"; do

    "docker://$img" \

docs.title: Nexus and Harbor Architecture for Offline Environments
1.1 Role Assignment
docs.text:
Artifact Type Primary Registry Secondary/Backup Reason OCI container images Harbor Nexus raw Harbor is the canonical container registry; Nexus handles supplemental artifacts Helm charts (OCI) Harbor OCI project Nexus helm Argo CD targets Harbor exclusively for OCI charts Helm charts (classic) Nexus helm-hosted — Legacy consumers; flat-file index.yaml layout RPM (Oracle Linux, RHEL-compatible) Nexus rpm-hosted — Upstream requires entitlement; Nexus is the mirror DEB (Ubuntu) Nexus deb-hosted (apt) — Includes -updates and -security pockets PyPI Nexus pypi-hosted — Proxy of pypi.org npm (if used) Nexus npm-hosted — Proxy of registry.npmjs.org Go modules Nexus go-hosted — Proxy of proxy.golang.org Git repositories GitLab self-contained — Mirror clone from staging; git bundle for transfer Ansible collections/roles Nexus raw-hosted — Galaxy proxy + vendor tarballs into GitLab Security scanner DBs Nexus raw-hosted — Manual refresh from connected staging; date-stamped OS images (cloud) Nexus raw-hosted — Vendor images for cloud-init AI model weights Harbor + S3-compatible object — Large artifacts; not registry objects AI inference images Harbor — Same as any container image NVIDIA drivers/toolkit Nexus raw-hosted — Large files; version-pinned per GPU matrix Vault binaries/plugins Nexus raw-hosted — Proxy of releases.hashicorp.com

Anti-pattern: Do not point clusters at Nexus for images and Harbor for charts and GitLab for images — this creates three pull paths, three auth schemes, and three failure modes.

docs.title: 1.2 Selection Criteria
docs.text:
• Container images → Harbor (OCI-native, content trust, image scanning integrated)
  • OS packages (RPM/DEB) → Nexus (yum/apt repo-native, GPG signing, repo metadata)
  • Helm charts → Harbor OCI for modern clusters; Nexus classic for legacy tooling
  • Language-specific packages (PyPI/npm/Go) → Nexus (proxy-native, simple index layout)
  • Git repositories → GitLab (distributed version control; not a registry function)
  • Large binary artifacts (models, driver ISOs) → S3-compatible object storage + Nexus raw

docs.title: 2.1 Harbor HA Architecture
docs.text:
Harbor supports active-passive HA through a floating IP or load balancer fronting two or more Harbor instances.

Components: - Primary Harbor instance — handles all traffic; state written to shared storage - Secondary Harbor instance — standby; syncs state from primary - Load balancer (L4 or L7) — distributes traffic; handles failover - Shared storage — NFS, PV, or highly available database for artifact metadata

Configuration: - Both instances point to the same external database (PostgreSQL) or shared NFS for Blob storage - Session affinity or load balancer ensures sticky connections during replications - Replication daemon syncs metadata, vulnerability DB, and configuration from primary to secondary - DNS or DNS-round-robin can redirect clients to the secondary if primary fails

Example topology: 

       +------------+     +------------+
       |  Client    | --> |  LB / VIP  |
       +------------+     +------------+
                                  / \
                                 /   \
+----------+                  +----------+
| Harbor 1 |                  | Harbor 2 |
+----------+                  +----------+
       \                  /
        \                /
         \              /
          +------------+
          | Shared NFS |
          | / PostgreSQL |
          +------------+

docs.title: 2.2 Nexus HA Architecture
docs.text:
Nexus can be run in clustered mode using Azure Blob Storage, AWS S3, or a shared filesystem for blob storage. Each Nexus node is stateless regarding repository configuration; blobs are stored in the shared backend.

Configuration: - Minimum 2 nodes in a cluster - Shared blob store (S3, Azure Blob, GCS, or NFS) - Router / load balancer distributes requests across nodes - Cluster protocol (JGroups or TCP) synchronizes repository metadata

Example topology: 

       +------------+     +------------+
       |  Client    | --> |  Load Bal  |
       +------------+     +------------+
                                  / \
                                 /   \
+----------+                  +----------+
| Nexus 1  |                  | Nexus 2  |
+----------+                  +----------+
       \                  /
        \                /
         \              /
          +------------+
          | Shared S3  |
          | / PostgreSQL |
          +------------+

docs.title: 3.1 Harbor Storage Backend
docs.text:
Component Default Recommended for Production Notes PostgreSQL Embedded H2 External PostgreSQL 13+ Required for HA; manage backups separately Blob storage /data/images on local disk Network-backed (NFS, S3, Azure Blob, GCS) Local disk OK for single-node only Trivy DB Embedded SQLite External PostgreSQL + object storage Large; separate volume recommended Log storage /data/log Separate volume or syslog Rotate daily; retain 30 days minimum

Notes: - For HA, PostgreSQL must be external (embedded H2 does not support clustering) - Blob storage must be accessible from all HA nodes; S3-compatible is ideal for multi-cloud - Trivy vulnerability DBs can be stored on separate fast storage; date-stamped snapshots

docs.title: 3.2 Nexus Storage Backend
docs.text:
Component Default Recommended for Production Notes Repository metadata Embedded H2 External PostgreSQL 13+ Required for clustering; manage backups Blob storage /sonatype-work/sonatype-thirdparty S3, Azure Blob, GCS, or NFS Must be shared across cluster nodes Sonatype Work Local disk Separate volume, backed up daily Used for build analytics; optional

Notes: - Clustering requires a shared blob store; local disk does not support HA - S3 is the most common production choice; ensure versioning and lifecycle policies are configured - PostgreSQL must be reachable from all Nexus nodes; use a load balancer or DNS

docs.title: 4.1 Harbor Replication
docs.text:
Harbor supports image replication from upstream registries and between Harbor instances.

Upstream replication (mirroring): - Pull from upstream (registry.k8s.io, quay.io, docker.io) on schedule - Use skopeo copy under the hood; digest-pinned ensures integrity - Configuration in Harbor UI or via API: 

replication:
  remote:
    - name: "registry-k8s-io"
      url: "https://registry.k8s.io"
      username: ""
      password: ""
      pull: true
      push: false
      interval: "1h"

Inter-Harbor replication: - Active-passive: secondary pulls replicated images from primary - Used for geographic distribution or DR sites - Configured via API: POST /api/v2.0/replication

Replication schedule: - Default: every hour for upstream mirrors - Can be tuned per repository; disable for static sets - Retry with exponential backoff on failure

docs.title: 4.2 Nexus Replication
docs.text:
Nexus supports repository replication for proxy repositories.

Pull-replication (pull-through cache with update): - Proxy repository fetches from upstream on demand - Can be configured to revalidate/replicate on a schedule - Schedule tab in UI or via repository.replication.interval in nexus.properties

Push-replication: - Push from one Nexus to another (less common; usually pull-through is sufficient) - Configured via replication destination in UI or REST API

Example: Configure pull-replication via REST 

curl -u admin:admin123 -X POST "http://nexus.internal/repository/rpm-containerd/replication" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"interval": 3600, "online": true}'

docs.title: 4.3 Replication Best Practices
docs.text: Practice Reason Pin digests, not tags Tags can change; digests are immutable Set validate: true Verify upstream signature/checksum on each pull Monitor replication lag Alert if secondary is out of sync beyond threshold Keep replication intervals reasonable Too frequent = unnecessary load; too stale = outdated artifacts Test failover Ensure secondary can serve traffic when primary is cut over

docs.title: 5.1 Harbor Security
docs.text:
Area Configuration Recommended TLS x509 certificate for harbor.internal Use CA-signed cert; enable HTTPS everywhere Authentication Internal DB or LDAP/Active Directory LDAP for enterprise; internal for simple deployments User roles admin, developer, guest Grant least privilege; use groups from LDAP Token expiration Default 24h Rotate regularly; use short-lived tokens for CI Content trust Notary signifier (disabled by default) Enable for critical images; requires HSM or KMS Network policy Restrict ingress to LB VIP only Firewall: only allow 443/tcp from approved subnets Secret scanning Built-in vulnerability scanning Integrate with Trivy; scan on push; retain results 90 days API security CSPM, secret scanning in configs Run trivy config on Helm charts and manifests

Detailed TLS setup: 

# Harbor configuration (harbor.yml)
hostname: "harbor.internal"
http:
  port: 80
  host: "harbor.internal"
  https:
    enabled: true
    port: 443
    certfile: /etc/harbor/certs/harbor.internal.crt
    keyfile: /etc/harbor/certs/harbor.internal.key
notification:
  webhook_url: ""
  ...
database:
  postgres:
    host: harbor-db.internal
    port: 5432
    user: harbor
    password: "changeme"
    sslmode: "require"

docs.title: 5.2 Nexus Security
docs.text:
Area Configuration Recommended TLS x509 certificate for nexus.internal CA-signed; enable HTTPS on all ports Authentication Internal LDAP/AD or single sign-on LDAP for enterprise; SSO (OIDC) for modern stacks Role-based access admin, deploy, browse, restricted Least-privilege roles per repository Anonymous access Disabled by default Disable entirely for offline air-gap Password policy Minimum length, complexity, rotation 12+ chars; enforce via LDAP policy HTTP security headers X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options Set in nexus.properties or reverse proxy Secret scanning Integration with Trivy/Grype Scan stored RPMs/DEBs on schedule

Detailed TLS setup: 

# nexus.properties
application-port=8083
application-host=nexus.internal
application-base-path=
context-path=
jsonp-enabled=false
https.enabled=true
https.keystore=file:/opt/sonatype/sonatype-work/conf/keystore.p12
https.keystore.password=changeit
https.truststore=file:/opt/sonatype/sonatype-work/conf/truststore.p12
https.truststore.password=changeit
ldap.server.url=ldap://ldap.internal:389
ldap.bind.dn=cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com
ldap.bind.password=ldap-password

docs.title: 5.3 Shared Security Practices
docs.text:
Practice Harbor Nexus TLS everywhere ✅ Required ✅ Required Least-privilege roles ✅ Built-in ✅ Built-in Token rotation ✅ Every 24h ✅ Via LDAP policy Audit logging ✅ Enabled by default ✅ Enabled by default Image/signature verification ✅ Notary / Cosign ✅ GPG-signed repos Vulnerability scanning ✅ Trivy integrated ✅ Grype/Trivy on demand Network isolation LB VIP only Firewall-restricted repos Backup verification Monthly restore test Quarterly restore test

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document how Nexus (artifact/repository manager) and Harbor (container image registry) integrate in the offline platform. Both are required for air-gapped operation: Nexus hosts OS packages, Helm charts, and binaries; Harbor hosts container images.

docs.text:
+-------------------+
                                    |  External network |
                                    |   (connected)     |
                                    +-------------------+

                                    |  (download only)  |

        | (container images)|   | (OS pkgs, Helm, bins)|
        | harbor.internal   |   | nexus.internal       |

docs.title: Containerd mirror configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/containerd/hosts.toml
server = "https://harbor.internal"

[host."https://harbor.internal"]
  capabilities = ["pull", "resolve", "push"]

  [host."https://harbor.internal".headers]
    Authorization = "Basic {{ registry_credentials_b64 }}"

  [host."https://harbor.internal".mirrors]

docs.title: E. Offline workflow
docs.text:
1. Connected staging: Download artifacts to staging host
  2. Verify integrity: Check checksums and signatures
  3. Import to Harbor/Nexus: skopeo copy for images, helm push for charts, copy for RPMs/DEBs
  4. Update artifact matrix: Record versions, checksums, internal destinations
  5. Deploy offline: Use internal registries and repos only

docs.title: 5.1 Repository and registry responsibilities
docs.text:
One owner per artifact type. No duplication.

Artifact type System of record (internal) Upstream source Mirror/proxy Notes OCI container images Harbor Upstream registries Harbor proxy-cache from upstream (connected staging only) Harbor is the only pull target for clusters Helm charts (OCI) Harbor OCI project Upstream chart repos Harbor proxy Argo CD points at Harbor only Helm charts (classic) Nexus helm-hosted Upstream Nexus proxy Keep for non-OCI consumers RPM (Oracle Linux, RHEL-compatible) Nexus rpm-hosted Oracle / RedHat (entitlement) Nexus proxy Requires RedHat subscription for RHEL content; Oracle Linux ULN for UE-K DEB (Ubuntu) Nexus deb-hosted (apt) archive.ubuntu.com, security.ubuntu.com Nexus proxy Include -updates and -security pockets PyPI Nexus pypi-hosted pypi.org Nexus proxy Needed for Ansible deps npm (if used) Nexus npm-hosted registry.npmjs.org Nexus proxy Optional Go modules Nexus go-hosted proxy.golang.org Nexus proxy Optional Git repositories GitLab (self-contained groups) Upstream GitHub/GitLab Staging clone then push mirror Use git bundle/mirror clone for transfer Ansible collections/roles Nexus raw-hosted Galaxy Nexus proxy Also vendor tarballs into GitLab for air-gap Security scanner DBs Nexus raw-hosted Trivy/Grype/VulnDB upstream Manual refresh from connected staging Trivy DB is date-stamped, refresh monthly OS images (cloud) Nexus raw-hosted Vendor Manual Custom OL/Ubuntu images for cloud-init AI models (weights) Harbor + S3-compatible object (Ceph RGW or MinIO) Hugging Face Manual mirroring Model artifacts are large, not registry objects AI inference images Harbor Upstream Harbor proxy Same as any image NVIDIA drivers/toolkit Nexus raw-hosted NVIDIA Manual Large files, version-pinned per GPU matrix Vault binaries/plugins Nexus raw-hosted releases.hashicorp.com Nexus proxy Plugin version pinned per Vault version Container base images Nexus raw-hosted (OCI layout) Upstream Manual Needed to build offline images

Anti-pattern to avoid: pointing clusters at Nexus for images and Harbor for charts and GitLab for images — three pull paths, three auth schemes, three failure modes.

docs.title: 5.2 Staging and import workflow
docs.text:
Context: Connected staging environment (steps 1-6) then offline production environment (steps 7-10).

  1. Resolve exact versions and full dependency set in connected staging.
  2. Download artifacts (curl/skopeo/helm pull/ansible-galaxy/git clone).
  3. Verify signatures, checksums, provenance.
  4. Generate manifest + SBOM.
  5. Scan for vulnerabilities and policy violations.
  6. Transfer artifacts via approved controlled mechanism.
  7. Import into internal repositories and registries.
  8. Configure clients to use internal sources.
  9. Validate authentication, TLS, image pulls, package install, dependency resolution.
  10. Verify deployment and recovery work with no production internet access.

docs.title: Commands (staging, connected)
docs.text:
# OCI image
skopeo copy --dest-daemon=false docker://ghcr.io/OWNER/REPO:TAG \
  docker://harbor.internal/oci/owner-repo:TAG

# Helm chart (OCI)
helm pull oci://ghcr.io/OWNER/charts/CHART --version X.Y.Z -d ./staging/charts

# Ansible collections
ansible-galaxy collection download -r requirements.yml -p ./staging/collections

# Python wheels
pip download -r requirements.txt -d ./staging/wheels

# DEB
apt-get download pkg=version   # plus dependencies via apt-rdepends or apt-offline

# RPM
dnf download --resolve --downloaddir=./staging/rpm pkg

# Git mirror
git clone --mirror https://github.com/OWNER/REPO.git ./staging/git/REPO.git

docs.title: Integrity and scan (staging)
docs.text:
# Checksums
sha256sum -c staging/CHECKSUMS

# SBOM
syft dir:./staging -o cyclonedx-json > staging/SBOM.json

# Vulnerability scan
trivy image --input ./staging/oci/owner-repo.tar --format json > staging/trivy.json
trivy fs --scanners vuln --format json ./staging > staging/trivy-fs.json

# Signature verification (where upstream signs)
cosign verify --key cosign.pub harbor.internal/oci/owner-repo:TAG

docs.title: Transfer (approved controlled mechanism)
docs.text: Method Use Notes skopeo copy to Harbor over internal network Images Preferred helm push to Harbor OCI Charts Preferred curl --upload-file to Nexus Packages/raw Nexus supports it Encrypted USB / controlled media Only if air-gap has no internal transfer path Requires chain of custody, encryption, manifest checksum verification on arrival airgap containerized skopeo bundle Common pattern No external deps on target

docs.title: Import (offline production)
docs.text:
# Image into Harbor
skopeo copy --dest-daemon=false \
  docker://harbor.internal/oci/owner-repo:TAG \
  docker://harbor.internal/platform/owner-repo:TAG

# Chart into Harbor OCI
helm push owner-chart-X.Y.Z.tgz oci://harbor.internal/charts

# Python wheels
pip install --no-index --find-links=/opt/staging/wheels -r requirements.txt

# Ansible collections
ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml -p /opt/collections

# DEB
sudo apt-get install -y ./staging/deb/*.deb

docs.title: Reverse proxy: what is genuinely transparent
docs.text:
Upstream Proxy-transparent? Notes GitHub / GitLab web + git protocol Yes L7 reverse proxy preserves paths; git over HTTPS works with insteadOf PyPI (pypi.org) Yes Simple index layout, /simple/ path preserved npm registry Yes Path preserved Docker Hub / ghcr.io Partially Registry API is path-based and proxyable, but client auth flows, token endpoints, and content negotiation need explicit config — treat as "client config required" Quay.io Partially Same registry caveats Debian apt archive Yes Release + Packages paths preserved; Release.gpg must be signed by the mirror RPM repos (yum/dnf) Partially repodata and signatures are path-based; repomd signature validation must pass — use Nexus to re-sign Ubuntu PPA Partially Launchpad-specific metadata paths, not reliably proxyable — mirror explicitly instead Helm classic repos (index.yaml + tarballs) Yes Flat file layout OCI registries Partially Blob/manifest paths preserved, but auth/token endpoints and redirect behavior are registry-specific — test per registry GitHub Releases (binary downloads) Yes Direct file paths RedHat subscription content No Requires entitlement-aware tooling (subscription-manager, Satellite); mirror with a licensed copy Hugging Face (model weights) Partially LFS/CDN redirect behavior; explicit mirror recommended

Rule: never claim a reverse proxy transparently replaces a registry. Prove it per registry with an end-to-end pull test in the offline environment, and document the client-side change in the matrix.

docs.title: 5.4 Offline artifact matrix
docs.text: Maintained in offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md (one row per component-artifact pair).

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document reproducible offline installation and upgrade of the cloud-native platform without internet access. This procedure covers initial deployment, subsequent upgrades, and rollback for air-gapped environments. Cross-references offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, offline-artifacts/offline-package-repository.md, and lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md.

docs.title: B. Pre-deployment checklist
docs.text:
Before initiating any offline installation or upgrade, complete the following checks:

  • [ ] Artifact inventory — Verify all required images, packages, and manifests are present in the internal mirror. Consult offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md for the expected component versions.
  • [ ] Internal mirror integrity — Run checksum verification against the offline-artifacts/offline-package-repository.md manifest. All SHA-256 hashes must match.
  • [ ] Signature verification — Confirm Cosign signatures for all container images using offline-artifacts/signature-verification.md procedures.
  • [ ] SBOM validation — Verify Software Bill of Materials for all critical packages using Trivy or SPDX tools.
  • [ ] Cluster prerequisites — Ensure all control-plane nodes meet minimum hardware requirements (CPU, memory, storage). Verify network connectivity between nodes on the offline VLAN.
  • [ ] Storage validation — Confirm persistent storage classes are available and provisioned. Test snapshot/restore capability if using external databases.
  • [ ] ** RBAC readiness** — Verify service accounts and roles required by the installation pipeline have been created in the internal cluster.
  • [ ] Disaster recovery backup — etcd snapshot must be taken and verified before any upgrade. Store backup in the internal artifact repository.

docs.title: C.1 Initial offline installation
docs.text:
1. Mirror initialization — Load the internal artifact mirror into the environment. Use offline-artifacts/artifact-mirroring-procedure.md to populate the registry and package repository.
  2. Node preparation — Bootstrap each control-plane node with the pre-loaded container images and OS packages. No outbound internet access is required after mirror initialization.
  3. Cluster deployment — Apply the Kubespray (or equivalent) playbooks referencing the internal image registry and package source. Set offline=true in the inventory to suppress internet-dependent steps.
  4. Core services bring-up — Verify etcd, control-plane components, and CNI are running. Check kubectl get nodes shows all control-plane nodes Ready.
  5. Addon deployment — Deploy core addons (ingress, metrics-server, DNS) from the internal mirror. Verify all pods are in Running state.

docs.title: C.2 Offline upgrade initiation
docs.text:
1. New artifact mirror — Populate the new version's artifact mirror using the mirroring procedure. Update offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md with the upgraded versions.
  2. Compatibility validation — Cross-reference kubespray/multi-version-support.md to confirm the new versions are compatible with the existing cluster baseline.
  3. Pre-upgrade snapshot — Take a fresh etcd snapshot and store it in the internal repository. Document the snapshot ID and retention policy.
  4. Upgrade readiness gate — All pre-deployment checklist items from Section B must be confirmed complete before proceeding.

docs.title: D.1 Image integrity validation
docs.text:
# Verify each image in the offline mirror
for image in $(cat offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md | grep image | awk '{print $2}'); do
  skopeo inspect docker://$image | grep -E "RepoTags|Digest"
done

docs.title: D.2 Package integrity validation
docs.text:
# Verify OS package checksums against the repository manifest
cd /path/to/internal/mirror
sha256sum -c offline-artifacts/offline-package-repository.md

docs.title: D.3 Signature validation
docs.text:
# Verify Cosign signatures for all images
cosign verify-blob --signature-file <sig_file> --certificate-file <cert_file> docker://<image>

docs.title: D.4 Network air-gap confirmation
docs.text:
• No outbound DNS or HTTP requests should be observed from control-plane or worker nodes after bootstrap.
  • Use tcpdump or wireshark on a monitoring host to confirm zero external traffic from the cluster CIDR during the validation window.
  • Verify internal registry serves all required manifests via curl http://<internal-registry>:5000/v2/_catalog.

docs.title: D.5 Component compatibility check
docs.text:
• Run kubectl get crds and compare against the expected CRD set for the targeted version.
  • Validate custom addons against offline-artifacts/nexus-harbor-architecture.md and offline-artifacts/nexus-harbor-integration.md integration patterns.

docs.title: E.1 Pre-upgrade rollback plan
docs.text:
1. Snapshot etcd before each upgrade phase. Store snapshot IDs in offline-artifacts/offline-upgrade-procedure.md and the internal artifact repository.
  2. Document current state — kubectl get all, kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pvc captured before starting the upgrade.
  3. Rollback trigger conditions — Any phase failure that leaves critical components in a CrashLoopBackOff, Pending, or Error state for >5 minutes triggers rollback.

docs.title: Phase rollback — etcd upgrade
docs.text:
1. Stop the etcd upgrade process if still in progress.
  2. Restore etcd from the previous snapshot: etcdctl snapshot restore <snapshot-id> --data-dir /var/lib/etcd/new.
  3. Restart the etcd service and verify kubectl get nodes shows all Ready.
  4. If the new etcd version is incompatible, roll back to the etcd binary from the pre-upgrade snapshot.

docs.title: Phase rollback — control plane upgrade
docs.text:
1. Drain the control-plane node being upgraded.
  2. Revert the container image to the pre-upgrade version.
  3. Restart the kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, and kube-controller-manager pods.
  4. Verify API server health: kubectl get --raw=/readyz.
  5. Uncordon the node and confirm it returns to Ready status.

docs.title: Phase rollback — worker node upgrade
docs.text:
1. Cordon the worker node.
  2. Drain pods to other nodes (kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data).
  3. Revert kubelet and container runtime to the pre-upgrade version.
  4. Uncordon the node and verify pods resume scheduling.

docs.title: Phase rollback — CNI/ addon upgrade
docs.text:
1. Revert the CNI plugin manifest to the previous version.
  2. Restart the CNI daemon set.
  3. Verify networking connectivity: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces.
  4. For addons, restart the addon deployment from the pre-upgrade image tag.

docs.title: E.3 Post-rollback validation
docs.text:
• kubectl cluster-info returns expected endpoints.
  • All critical pods (kube-system namespace) are Running and Ready.
  • API response times are within normal range.
  • etcd database integrity check: etcdctl check-database --write-out=table.
  • If any validation fails, repeat the rollup steps or escalate to the disaster recovery plan.

docs.title: F.1 Installation sign-off
docs.text:
Role Name Date Status Infrastructure Lead ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail Security Officer ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail Platform Operator ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail QA Lead ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail

Installation sign-off requirements: - All pre-deployment checklist items (Section B) marked complete. - All air-gapped validation checks (Section D) passed. - etcd snapshot verified and stored. - All critical cluster APIs responding. - No critical alerts active in monitoring.

docs.title: F.2 Upgrade sign-off
docs.text:
Phase Result Rollback Performed Sign-off Pre-upgrade validation ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail N/A etcd upgrade ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail ✅ Yes / ❌ No Control plane upgrade ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail ✅ Yes / ❌ No Worker upgrade ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail ✅ Yes / ❌ No CNI upgrade ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail ✅ Yes / ❌ No Addon upgrade ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail ✅ Yes / ❌ No Post-upgrade validation ✅ Pass / ❌ Fail N/A

Upgrade sign-off requirements: - All phases report ✅ Pass. - No rollback was required, or all rollbacks were successfully completed and validated. - Post-upgrade air-gapped validation (Section D) all passed. - Monitoring shows no critical errors for >1 hour post-upgrade. - Security team confirms no new vulnerabilities introduced.

docs.title: F.3 Archive and documentation
docs.text:
• Record the completed sign-off sheet in the cluster's documentation repository.
  • Tag the offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md with the new version and date.
  • Store the etcd snapshots and rollback logs in the internal artifact repository per retention policy.
  • Notify the on-call team and update the change management system (e.g., JIRA, ServiceNow).

DevOps Automator: Offline installation and upgrade procedure documented. Document path: offline-artifacts/offline-install-upgrade-procedure.md Generated: $(date +%Y-%m-%d)

docs.title: Yum Repository Creation
docs.text:
Create a local Yum repository from offline RPM packages:

# Install repo tools
sudo yum install yum-utils

# Create repository directory
sudo mkdir -p /opt/local/repo/yum
sudo chown -R root:root /opt/local/repo/yum

# Copy RPM packages to the repository directory
sudo cp *.rpm /opt/local/repo/yum/

# Generate the repository metadata
sudo createrepo_c /opt/local/repo/yum

# Verify repository
sudo repoquery --content /opt/local/repo/yum | head -20

docs.title: Yum Repository with GPG Signing
docs.text:
# Generate GPG key pair (if not already exists)
gpg --full-generate-key

# Export the public key
gpg --export > /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-local

# Export the private key for signing
gpg --export-secret-keys > /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-local-priv

# Import the key into Yum keyring
sudo rpm --import /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-local

# Create signed repository
sudo createrepo_c -- underlay_dir /opt/local/repo/yum --policy signed \
  --gpgkey /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-local --repoclosure

# Update Yum client configuration to trust the repository
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo
[local-repo]
name=Local Offline Yum Repository
basefile:///opt/local/repo/yum
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
gpgkey=file:///etc/pki/rpm-gpg/RPM-GPG-KEY-local
EOF

docs.title: Debian Repository Creation
docs.text:
Create a local Debian repository from offline .deb packages:

# Install repo tools
sudo apt-get install dpkg-dev

# Create repository directory
sudo mkdir -p /opt/local/repo/debian
sudo chown -R root:root /opt/local/repo/debian

# Copy .deb packages to the repository directory
sudo cp *.deb /opt/local/repo/debian/

# Generate Packages.gz file
sudo dpkg-scanpackages /opt/local/repo/debian /dev/null | gzip > /opt/local/repo/debian/Packages.gz

# Generate Release file (metadata signature)
sudoapt-ftparchive release /opt/local/repo/debian > /opt/local/repo/debian/Release

# Optional: add component and label information
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /opt/local/repo/debian/Release
Origin: Local Offline Debian Repository
Label: local-repo
Suite: stable
Codename: $(lsb_release -c -a)
Version: 1.0
Architectures: amd64 i386 arm64
EOF

docs.title: Debian Repository with GPG Signing
docs.text:
# Generate GPG key for signing
gpg --full-generate-key

# Export the public key
gpg --export > /usr/share/keyrings/local-repo.gpg

# Export the private key for signing
gpg --export-secret-keys > /usr/share/keyrings/local-repo-priv.gpg

# Create signed repository
sudo dpkg-scanpackages /opt/local/repo/debian /dev/null | \
  gpg --clearsign --default-key <key-id> \
  --output /opt/local/repo/debian/Release.gpg

# Generate Release file with signature
gpg --yes --default-key <key-id> --sign --publish-domain local \
  --output /opt/local/repo/debian/Release \
  /opt/local/repo/debian/Release.gpg

# Update apt configuration to trust the repository
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/local.list
deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/local-repo.gpg] file:/opt/local/repo/debian stable main
EOF

# Update package lists
sudo apt-get update

docs.title: Yum Synchronization
docs.text:
# Mirror repository to another location
sudo reposync --repoid=local-repo --newest-only --download_path /opt/backup/yum/

# or use createmirror
sudo createmirror /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo /opt/backup/yum/

# Synchronize with remote repository (if network available)
sudo rsync -avz /opt/local/repo/yum/ user@remote-host:/opt/remote/repo/yum/

docs.title: Debian Synchronization
docs.text:
# Mirror repository structure
sudo rsync -avz /opt/local/repo/debian/ user@remote-host:/opt/remote/repo/debian/

# or use apt-mirror
sudo apt-mirror /etc/apt/mirror.conf

# Synchronize package lists
sudo rsync -avz /opt/local/repo/debian/Release* user@remote-host:/opt/remote/repo/debian/

docs.title: Yum Client Configuration
docs.text:
# Enable the local repository
sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo file:///etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo

# Disable all other repositories and use only local
sudo yum-config-manager --disable '*'
sudo yum-config-manager --enable local-repo

# List available packages from local repository
yum list available --disabled='*' --enabled=local-repo

# Install package from local repository
sudo yum install package-name

docs.title: Debian Client Configuration
docs.text:
# Enable the local repository
sudo apt-get update

# Pin the local repository priority
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/apt/preferences.d/local-pin
Package: *
Pin: release o=Local Offline Debian Repository
Pin-Priority: 900
EOF

# Install package from local repository
sudo apt-get install package-name

docs.title: Package Dependency Resolution in Air-Gapped Environments
Yum Dependency Resolution
docs.text:
# Install package with all dependencies from local repository
sudo yum localinstall /opt/local/repo/yum/package-name.rpm

# Solve dependencies without installing
sudo yum deplist package-name --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-repo

# Resolve and download missing dependencies
sudo yum-builddep -y /opt/local/repo/yum/package-name.spec

# Manual dependency resolution
# 1. List package dependencies
rpm -qpR /opt/local/repo/yum/package-name.rpm

# 2. Install missing dependencies recursively
sudo yum localinstall --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-repo \
  $(rpm -qpR /opt/local/repo/yum/package-name.rpm | tr '\n' ' ')

docs.title: Debian Dependency Resolution
docs.text:
# Install package with dependencies from local repository
sudo apt-get install ./package-name.deb

# Resolve build dependencies
sudo apt-get build-dep package-name

# Check unresolved dependencies
dpkg -s package-name | grep -E "^(Depends|Status):"

# Manual dependency resolution with dpkg
# 1. Download all dependencies first
apt-get --download-only install package-name

# 2. Install downloaded debs in correct order
sudo dpkg -i /var/cache/apt/archives/*.deb

# 2. Fix any remaining issues
sudo apt-get -f install

docs.title: Air-Gapped Dependency Extraction
docs.text:
# Extract dependencies from offline media
# Yum: repo-create with --downloadonly option
sudo yum install --downloadonly --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-repo \
  -d /opt/downloads package-name

# Debian: apt-get with --print-uris to list all debs
apt-get --print-uris install package-name | grep "'" | cut -d"'" -f2 | \
  xargs -I{} wget -P /opt/downloads {}

# Create consolidated repository from downloaded packages
# Yum
sudo createrepo_c /opt/downloads/yum

# Debian
sudo dpkg-scanpackages /opt/downloads/debian /dev/null | gzip > /opt/downloads/debian/Packages.gz

docs.title: Dependency Conflict Resolution
docs.text:
# Yum: show what would be installed and why
sudo yum check-update --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-repo
sudo yum depsolve --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-repo \
  package-name

# Debian: show dependency conflicts
apt-cache show package-name | grep -E "^(Depends|Version):"
sudo dpkg -C  # check for broken state

# Force install with --force-depends (use with caution)
sudo yum localinstall --force --nodeps /opt/local/repo/yum/package-name.rpm
sudo dpkg --force-depends -i /opt/local/repo/debian/package-name.deb

docs.title: Verifying Installed Package Dependencies
docs.text:
# Yum
rpm -q --requires package-name
rpm -q --whatprovides $(rpm -q --requires package-name | grep 'library-name' | cut -d' ' -f1)

# Debian
dpkg -l package-name
apt-cache depends package-name

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document offline upgrade procedure: upgrade Kubespray release, Kubernetes version, images, OS packages without internet.

Cross-references offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, kubespray/multi-version-support.md, lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md.

docs.title: B. Upgrade phases
docs.text: Phase Action Downtime 1. Inventory new artifacts Download new images/packages to internal mirror None 2. Validate artifacts Verify signatures, checksums, SBOMs None 3. Upgrade etcd Rolling etcd upgrade one member at a time Minimal 4. Upgrade control plane Rolling kube-apiserver/scheduler/controller-manager upgrade Minimal 5. Upgrade workers Drain, upgrade, uncordon one node at a time Per node 6. Upgrade CNI Rolling Cilium upgrade Minimal 7. Upgrade addons Ingress, metrics-server, etc. Minimal

docs.title: C. Offline artifact inventory
docs.text:
Before upgrading, inventory all artifacts:

# List images required by new Kubespray release
cat inventory/<cluster>/group_vars/k8s_cluster/k8s-cluster.yml | grep image

# Verify images exist in internal registry
skopeo inspect docker://registry.internal/k8s.gcr.io/kube-apiserver:v1.36.5

docs.text:
1. Pull new Kubespray release to internal Git mirror
  2. Pull new images to internal registry
  3. Pull new OS packages to internal mirror
  4. Update artifact-matrix.md with new versions

docs.title: Phase 2: Validate artifacts
docs.text:

  2. Verify SBOMs with Trivy
  3. Verify OS package checksums
  4. Validate artifact-matrix.md consistency

docs.text:

  2. Upgrade etcd binaries on one member
  3. Verify etcd health
  4. Repeat for remaining members

docs.title: Phase 4: Upgrade control plane

1. Run kubespray upgrade playbook on control-plane nodes
  2. Verify kubectl get nodes shows all Ready
  3. Verify API server health

docs.text:
1. Cordon worker node
  2. Drain pods to other nodes
  3. Upgrade kubelet and container runtime
  4. Uncordon node
  5. Repeat for remaining workers

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
End-to-end test procedure for offline upgrade validation in air-gapped environments. Verifies that Kubernetes clusters can be upgraded without internet access, using only pre-mirrored artifacts from internal registries and mirrors.

Cross-references `offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md`, `offline-artifacts/offline-upgrade-procedure.md`, `offline-artifacts/offline-artifact-architecture.md`, `security/image-provenance.md`, and `lifecycle/upgrades/kubernetes.md`.

docs.title: B. Test prerequisites
docs.text:
• Air-gapped environment with internal artifact mirror (Harbor/Nexus) populated per offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md

  • Verified offline artifacts: images, Helm charts, OS packages, binaries — all signed and checksummed per offline-artifacts/signature-verification.md

  • Kubespray release tagged and mirrored to internal Git

  • kubectl configured against the target cluster

  • etcd snapshot verified per kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-restore.md

docs.title: Test 1: Artifact availability validation
docs.text:
1. Confirm all required artifacts are present in the internal mirror:
# Validate Kubernetes components

crictl pull harbor.internal/platform/kubernetes/kube-apiserver:v1.36.5



# Validate Kubespray roles

ansible-galaxy collection list | grep kubernetes.core



# Validate CNI plugin

ls /opt/cni/bin/cilium *
  1. Verify artifact signatures and SBOMs per offline-artifacts/signature-verification.md:
# Cosign image verification

cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.internal/:<tag>



# SBOM verification

cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub --sbom sbom.json registry.internal/:<tag>
  1. Confirm OS package checksums:
sha256sum -c <checksum-file>

docs.title: Test 2: Offline upgrade playbook execution
docs.text:
1. Run the Kubespray offline upgrade playbook:
# From the mirrored Kubespray repository

ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster> upgrade.yml \

  --extra-vars "kubernetes_version=v1.36.5 kubespray_version=v2.27.0"

  1. Monitor upgrade phases per offline-artifacts/offline-upgrade-procedure.md:

  2. Phase 1: Inventory new artifacts ✓

  3. Phase 2: Validate artifacts ✓

  4. Phase 3: Upgrade etcd (rolling, one member at a time)

  5. Phase 4: Upgrade control plane (rolling kube-apiserver/scheduler/controller-manager)

  6. Phase 5: Upgrade workers (drain, upgrade kubelet/container runtime, uncordon)

  7. Phase 6: Upgrade CNI (rolling Cilium upgrade)

  8. Phase 7: Upgrade addons (ingress, metrics-server, etc.)

docs.title: Test 3: Post-upgrade validation
docs.text:
1. Verify cluster nodes are Ready:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
  1. Verify API server health:
kubectl get componentstatuses
  1. Verify workloads are scheduling:
kubectl get pods -A -o wide
  1. Verify CNI connectivity:
cilium status
  1. Verify ingress functionality:
kubectl get ingress -A

docs.title: Test 4: Rollback validation (failure scenario)
docs.text:
1. etcd rollback:
# Restore from verified snapshot

kubectl patch etcd <name> -p '{"spec":{"backupPlanName":"<snapshot-name>"}}'
  1. Control plane rollback:
# Revert to previous Kubespray version

ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster> upgrade.yml \

  --extra-vars "kubernetes_version=v1.36.4 kubespray_version=v2.26.0"
  1. Worker rollback:
# Revert kubelet and container runtime to previous version

docs.title: D. Test success criteria
docs.text:
• [ ] All required artifacts are present and verified in the internal mirror

  • [ ] All artifact signatures and SBOMs verify successfully

  • [ ] Upgrade playbook executes without errors

  • [ ] All cluster nodes reach Ready state post-upgrade

  • [ ] API server and component health checks pass

  • [ ] CNI connectivity is functional

  • [ ] Ingress/load balancing is operational

  • [ ] Rollback procedures verified (documented, not necessarily executed)

  • [ ] Zero downtime or documented minimal downtime per phase

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Generate Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for container images and filesystem artifacts using Syft and Trivy. This procedure covers SBOM creation, verification, storage, and distribution for offline environments.

docs.title: Syft SBOM Generation
docs.text:
# SBOM for directory of staged artifacts
syft dir:./staging -o cyclonedx-json > staging/SBOM.json

# SBOM for OCI image
syft oci://registry.internal/app:tag -o cyclonedx-json > staging/SBOM-image.json

docs.title: Trivy SBOM and Vulnerability Scan
docs.text:
# SBOM from Syft output combined with Trivy vulnerability scanning
trivy fs --scanners vuln --format json ./staging > staging/trivy-fs.json

# Trivy image scan with SBOM inclusion
trivy image --input ./staging/oci/owner-repo.tar --format json --sbs SBOM.json > staging/trivy-image.json

docs.title: SBOM Verification
docs.text:
# Validate SBOM JSON schema
python3 -c "
import json
with open('staging/SBOM.json') as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)
assert 'bom' in sbom or 'components' in sbom, 'Invalid SBOM structure'
print('SBOM schema validated')
"

# Cross-check SBOM components against known good list
syft dir:./staging -o cyclonedx-json | jq -r '.components[].name' > /tmp/sbom-components.txt
sort /tmp/sbom-components.txt -u > /tmp/sbom-components-sorted.txt

docs.title: SBOM Integrity
docs.text:
# Checksum verification
sha256sum staging/SBOM.json > staging/SBOM.checksum
sha256sum -c staging/SBOM.checksum

# Cosign signature verification (if SBOM is signed)
cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub --sbom staging/SBOM.json registry.internal/app:tag

docs.title: Trivy Scan Validation
docs.text:
# Verify trivy scan results are not empty (indicates DB fetch failure)
if [ ! -s staging/trivy-fs.json ]; then
    echo "Trivy scan produced no results - check DB availability"
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: SBOM Artifact Storage
docs.text:
# Store SBOM in internal artifact repository
mv staging/SBOM.json /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# Store Trivy vulnerability report
mv staging/trivy-fs.json /opt/artifacts/vuln-reports/app-name-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# Keep SBOM alongside related artifacts
cp staging/SBOM.json /opt/artifacts/staging-archives/

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
/opt/artifacts/
├── sboms/
│   ├── app-name-20240115.json
│   └── app-name-20240122.json
├── vuln-reports/
│   ├── app-name-20240115.json
│   └── app-name-20240122.json
└── staging-archives/
    └── (complete staging directories for rollback)

docs.title: Immutable Storage
docs.text:
# Write-once, reference-only after verification
chmod 444 /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-*.json
chmod 444 /opt/artifacts/vuln-reports/app-name-*.json

docs.title: Internal Distribution
docs.text:
# Publish SBOM to internal artifact registry
curl --upload-file /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json \
    https://nexus.internal/repository/sboms/app-name-20240115.json

# Distribute via artifact matrix entry
# See offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md for per-component SBOM records

docs.title: Consumer Access
docs.text:
# Make SBOM available to security tools
ln -s /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json /opt/sbom-current.json

# Expose via internal API endpoint
# Configure Trivy to fetch SBOM from: SBOM_URL=https://nexus.internal/repository/sboms/

docs.title: Downstream Sharing
docs.text:
# Package SBOM for external compliance reporting
cp /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json /tmp/sbom-for-audit.json

# Generate SPDX from CycloneDX
jq -r '.components[] | {ref: .ref, name: .name, type: .type}' \
    /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json > /tmp/sbom-spdx.json

docs.title: Workflow Summary
docs.text:
1. Create: Run syft or trivy to generate SBOM JSON from staged artifacts or OCI images
  2. Verify: Validate SBOM schema, checksum, and signature integrity
  3. Store: Persist SBOM to internal artifact repository with immutable permissions
  4. Distribute: Make SBOM available to security tools, compliance teams, and downstream consumers

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document signature and checksum verification: GPG signatures, SBOM verification, cosign verification, artifact integrity.

Cross-references offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, security/image-provenance.md, security/secret-delivery.md.

docs.title: B. GPG signature verification
docs.text:
OS packages and software artifacts are verified with GPG signatures:

# Import signing key
gpg --import <vendor>-signing-key.asc

# Verify package signature
gpg --verify package.rpm.asc package.rpm

# Verify checksum
sha256sum -c package.sha256

docs.title: C. Cosign verification
docs.text:
Container images are verified with Cosign:

# Verify image signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.internal/:<tag>

# Verify SBOM
cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub --sbom sbom.json registry.internal/:<tag>

docs.title: D. Artifact integrity
docs.text:
All artifacts in the artifact matrix must have verified integrity:

Artifact type Verification method Frequency Container images Cosign signature + SBOM Every pull OS packages GPG signature + SHA256 Every install Helm charts Cosign signature Every install Kubespray release GPG signature + SHA256 Every deploy OS ISOs GPG signature + SHA256 Every download

docs.title: E. Verification failure handling
docs.text:
If verification fails:

  1. Do not deploy/install the artifact
  2. Quarantine the artifact
  3. Notify the security team
  4. Document the failure
  5. Replace with verified artifact from mirror

docs.title: Version Pinning and Synchronization
docs.text: This document describes the offline version pinning strategy for the platform, covering Kubespray/Kubernetes version matrices, container image tags, package versions, repository synchronization schedules, and drift detection.

docs.title: 📋 Kubespray Version Matrix
docs.text:
Kubespray Release Kubernetes (default) Min Kubernetes etcd containerd Helm Cilium Calico Ansible Python release-2.32 1.36.5 v1.34.0 3.6.15 2.3.7 3.22.0 3.22.0 3.31.7 >= 2.19.0, < 2.20.0 3.11 - 3.13 release-2.31 1.35.9 v1.30 3.6.15 2.2.10 3.18.4 3.19.3 3.31.7 >= 2.18.0, < 2.19.0 3.11 - 3.13 release-2.30 1.34.12 v1.30 3.5.34 2.2.10 3.18.4 3.18.6 3.30.7 >= 2.17.3 3.10 - 3.12 release-2.29 1.33.10 v1.30 3.5.29 2.1.6 3.16.4 3.18.4 3.30.7 >= 2.17.3 3.10 - 3.12 release-2.28 1.32.13 v1.30 3.5.29 2.0.7 3.16.4 3.17.9 3.29.7 >= 2.16.4 3.10 - 3.12

Rule: One virtualenv per Kubespray release. The Ansible version differs between releases (2.16.4 to 2.19.0), and a shared virtualenv will break one of them. Each venv installs that release's own requirements.txt.

One inventory per (cluster, release) pair: The group-vars differ between releases (variable names change). A single inventory would accumulate conditional variables for five releases, and every run would carry dead configuration.

docs.title: 🔍 Drift Detection
docs.text: Drift is detected when the actual deployed component version diverges from the pinned version in the artifact matrix. Detection methods:

docs.title: Container Image Drift
docs.text:
# Verify mirrored digest matches matrix
crictl pull harbor.internal/platform/kubernetes/pause:3.9
crictl images | grep pause
# Compare output digest against artifact-matrix.md entry

docs.title: OS Package Drift
docs.text:
# Verify installed version against matrix
rpm -qa | grep oraclelinux
dnf list installed --releasever=9
apt-getInstalled=$(dpkg -l | grep '^ii' | grep ubuntu)

docs.title: Kubespray/Ansible Drift
docs.text:
# Verify ansible version against matrix
ansible --version | grep "ansible "
# Check installed collections
ansible-galaxy collection list | grep kubernetes-core

docs.title: Helm Drift
docs.text:
# Verify helm version
helm version | grep "version"
# Check chart versions against matrix
helm search repo --versions kube-prometheus-stack

docs.title: Drift Detection Workflow
docs.text:
# Step 1: Generate current state report
bash scripts/generate_drift_report.sh > /tmp/drift-report-$(date +%Y%m%d).md

# Step 2: Compare against artifact-matrix.md
python3 scripts/check_drift.py \
  --matrix /workspace/project/github/public-repository/cloud-native-guide-next/offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md \
  --report /tmp/drift-report-$(date +%Y%m%d).md

# Step 3: Output
# - No drift: "All versions match the pinned artifact matrix"
# - Drift detected: List of components with version mismatches
#   - Example: "Kubespray release-2.31: installed ansible 2.19.0, expected >=2.18.0, <2.19.0"
#   - Example: "kube-apiserver: mirrored digest v1.36.5-a1b2c3 does not match matrix v1.36.5-a1b2c3d4e5f6"

docs.title: Drift Categories
docs.text: Category Description Action minor Version is within allowed range (e.g., patch bump) Document and continue patch Version matches exactly No action needed out-of-range Version outside allowed range Update pin or upgrade release missing Artifact not found in internal repo Re-mirror or mark EXEMPT

docs.title: Drift Rollback
docs.text:
When drift is detected:

  1. Container images: Re-pull the pinned digest 

    crictl pull harbor.internal/...@sha256:<digest>

  2. OS packages: Re-install from mirrored repo 

    dnf install ./mirror/ol9-baseos/<package>.rpm -y

  3. Kubespray/Ansible: Re-run with pinned release 

    source /opt/kubespray/venvs/release-2.32/bin/activate
ansible-playbook -i inventory/prod cluster.yml

  4. Helm charts: Re-pull from internal repo 

    helm pull oci://harbor.internal/charts/kube-prometheus-stack --version X.Y.Z
