docs.title: Test definitions
docs.text: Each test below states: procedure, expected result, evidence, pass/fail criterion, and the execution context. The full procedure list lives in requirements/validation-strategy.md; this section is the acceptance gate.

docs.title: Offline operation (phase 2, 8, 9)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context F-01 On a host with all external routes removed, apt-get install <pkg> / dnf install <pkg> Package installs at the mirrored version Command output plus dnf list installed Exit 0 and correct version = pass Linux host, isolated segment F-02 crictl pull harbor.internal/<repo>:<tag> with no external route Image pulled and unpacked Command output plus crictl images Exit 0 = pass Kubernetes node F-03 helm install <chart> --set image.repository=harbor.internal/... Deployed, pods Ready helm output plus pod status All Ready = pass Cluster B-14 Run the full rebuild order in lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md section G in the isolated environment The platform is recreated and passes the tests in this table Runbook log plus test results All referenced tests pass = pass Full environment

docs.title: Availability and recovery (phase 14)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context D-01 Power off one control-plane node; call the API through the VIP continuously API responds throughout Request log during the failure No failed requests = pass Staging or approved window D-02 Stop one etcd member Quorum maintained, etcdctl endpoint health all healthy etcdctl output All healthy = pass Staging D-03 Drain a node running a replicated deployment Pod rescheduled, service continues to serve kubectl events plus a continuous request log Zero failed requests = pass Staging D-04 Remove one OSD Pool rebalances, ceph -s returns to HEALTH_OK ceph -s time series HEALTH_OK within the rebalance window = pass Staging D-06 Stop the active Vault node A new leader is elected within the documented window vault status Leader elected = pass Staging D-07 Stop the Management Cluster Application workloads keep serving; new deploys are blocked Request log plus an Argo CD sync attempt Workloads serve, sync blocked = pass Staging

docs.title: Secrets and security (phase 10)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context S-01 Deploy a workload that reads a secret via the chosen delivery method; grep the Git history The workload gets the value; Git contains no value Pod log plus a git log -p search Value present at runtime, absent from Git = pass Cluster plus GitLab S-02 Rotate the secret in Vault; wait for the renewal interval The workload sees the new value without a redeploy Pod log before and after New value observed = pass Cluster S-03 Reduce a certificate's lifetime in the CA policy; wait for the renewal cycle The certificate is re-issued with the new validity cert-manager logs plus openssl x509 New certificate issued = pass Cluster C-11 Stop Keycloak; log in with the emergency account; run sudo -n true The login succeeds and sudo works Session log Success = pass Any node C-05 Push an image with a known CRITICAL CVE The pipeline fails at the scan stage Pipeline log Pipeline failed = pass GitLab CI

docs.title: GitOps and pipeline (phase 13)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context P-01 Open an MR with an invalid manifest Stage 5 fails, the job is blocked Pipeline log Failure at stage 5 = pass GitLab P-02 Run the Ansible baseline twice The second run reports 0 changed Playbook recap 0 changed = pass Automation server P-03 Merge a change to an application repo Argo CD syncs and the app becomes Healthy argocd app get Synced and Healthy = pass Cluster P-04 Manually change a live resource The drift job reports it Drift report Drift reported = pass GitLab scheduled job

docs.title: GPU and AI (phase 12)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context G-01 Schedule a pod requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1; run nvidia-smi The pod runs and sees exactly one GPU Pod log Correct GPU = pass GPU cluster G-02 On a MIG-configured GPU, request more memory than the profile allows The allocation fails; the workload cannot touch memory outside its slice kubectl events plus the failing pod log Hard limit enforced = pass GPU cluster G-03 Start vLLM with a mirrored model; send a completion request; run the benchmark A valid completion; the benchmark reports throughput, TTFT, ITL Response plus the benchmark report Valid response = pass GPU cluster G-04 curl http://<gpu-node>:9400/metrics; check the Prometheus target Metrics present; the target is UP curl output plus the target status Present and UP = pass GPU node

docs.title: Observability (phase 11)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context M-01 Trigger a test alert (for example by stopping an exporter) The notification arrives at the receiver Receiver inbox plus the Alertmanager record Notification received = pass Management cluster M-02 Print a timestamped line in a pod; search for it in the backend The line is searchable Backend query result Found within 5 minutes = pass Cluster M-03 Print a string that looks like a credential The string is not retrievable from the backend Backend query returning nothing Absent = pass Cluster

docs.title: Backup and restore (phase 14)
docs.text: Test Procedure Expected Evidence Pass/fail Context E-03 Snapshot a PVC, restore to a new PVC, compare file checksums The checksums match Checksum comparison Identical = pass Cluster B-13 Restore the whole cluster from a Velero backup into a new cluster The workloads return with their data Velero restore log plus application checks Restored = pass Staging D-13 Upgrade the cluster one minor version The upgrade completes and the applications still work Upgrade log plus post-check results No data loss = pass Staging

docs.title: Gate
docs.text: Production go-live requires: 1. Every test in the relevant phase marked PASSED with evidence. 2. Every failure either fixed, or recorded as an accepted risk with a named owner and a review date in requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md. 3. The offline set (F-01, F-02, F-03, B-11, B-14) passed in the production environment, not only in staging. 4. A handover walkthrough completed with the operations team.

docs.title: Deliverable 10 — Implementation Roadmap
docs.text:
Dependency-aware. Each phase lists prerequisites, deliverables, acceptance criteria, risks, effort range, rollback.

Effort is engineering days for one engineer, excluding hardware lead time and network/change-window waits.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Requirements and architecture
docs.text: Prerequisites None Deliverables requirements/requirements-and-assumptions.md, architecture/*, decisions/ADR-0001..0025, initial compatibility/version-matrix.md Acceptance Every unresolved decision D-01..D-14 has a recorded decision; every version claim has a source URL + check date; failure-domain table reviewed against site topology Risks Decisions deferred without owner -> rebuild churn later Effort 8-15 d Rollback Documentation only; no runtime impact

docs.title: Phase 2 — Offline artifact infrastructure
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 1 version baseline; Harbor + Nexus deployed (VM or bare metal); internal CA for TLS Deliverables offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md (populated), staging-and-import.md, repo/registry config, client configuration runbooks Acceptance Every artifact in the matrix imports into the internal system; a clean node can install packages, pull images, and deploy a Helm chart with no internet; skopeo inspect and apt-get update succeed using internal sources only Risks RK-01 missing transitive dependency -> blocked mid-deploy. Mitigation: staged full dry run on a throwaway cluster before production Effort 15-25 d Rollback Repositories are additive; no production dependency until Phase 7

docs.title: Phase 3 — Foundational infrastructure
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 2 registries reachable; network segments allocated Deliverables DNS (CoreDNS + forwarders), NTP (chrony), PKI (internal CA), identity (Keycloak), load balancer (keepalived/haproxy), SSH/sudo baselines, firewall rules from the matrix Acceptance DNS resolves forward and reverse; clock skew < 100 ms across nodes; CA cert distributed and trusted; Keycloak issues tokens; LB VIP fails over between nodes; firewall matrix implemented and evidenced by nmap/ss from allowed and denied hosts Risks Network misconfiguration is hard to diagnose later; keep a firewall-rules-generation.md mapping Effort 10-18 d Rollback Standalone services; no cluster dependency

docs.title: Phase 4 — Automation
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 3 identity + Vault hosts; GitLab installed Deliverables Automation Management Server (Ansible + AWX), GitLab runner, Vault (standalone, 3 nodes), inventories, site-<env> overlays, CI pipeline templates Acceptance ansible all -m ping from AWX succeeds; a GitLab MR triggers lint -> ansible syntax -> helm lint -> policy -> scan and blocks on failure; Vault seals/unseals with offline shares; AWX job audit log retrievable; Vault backup snapshot created and verified Risks RK-02 automation SPOF -> second standby node + documented rebuild Effort 12-20 d Rollback Ansible/GitLab are not yet load-bearing for runtime workloads

docs.title: Phase 5 — OS preparation
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 4 automation + inventories; internal package repos configured Deliverables operating-systems/oracle-linux/*, operating-systems/ubuntu/*: repo config, sysctl, security baselines, local accounts and break-glass access, TLS trust, monitoring/logging agents Acceptance Provisioned host from bare metal to a hardened, monitored node with one Ansible run; ansible all -m setup idempotent (0 changed on second run); break-glass local account works with the directory unreachable; auditd/journald shipping verified; package install works with no internet Risks SELinux/AppArmor blocking container runtime; AppArmor profile mismatch on Ubuntu; documented per-distro Effort 12-20 d Rollback Re-run playbook; hosts rebuildable from PXE/ISO + Ansible

docs.title: Phase 6 — Storage foundation
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 5 hardened OS on storage nodes; storage VLAN; Phase 2 repos for Ceph packages/images Deliverables storage/ceph/* (cephadm path), storage/rook-ceph/* (in-cluster path), CRUSH map, capacity worksheet, monitoring, recovery procedures Acceptance ceph -s reports HEALTH_OK; 3 MON quorum survives one MON loss; OSD failure triggers automatic rebalance; RBD + CephFS + RGW (if selected) functional test passes; Ceph exporter feeds Prometheus; capacity worksheet reviewed with real numbers Risks RK-04 failure domain collapse -> CRUSH host/root mapping; a single-host test pool is not production Effort 15-25 d Rollback ceph orch decommission; no K8s dependency yet

docs.title: Phase 7 — Kubernetes deployment
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 6 storage (or at least node prep), Phase 4 automation, Phase 2 images mirrored Deliverables kubespray/ inventories + group vars (version-pinned), kubernetes/control-plane/*, offline image override config Acceptance kubectl get nodes shows 3 control-plane Ready; etcd 3/3 healthy; control-plane node loss does not interrupt API access via VIP; a worker can be removed and re-added by Kubespray; no imagePullBackOff with internet disabled; kubectl get pods -A all Running/Completed Risks RK-05 Kubespray variable drift -> pin release, keep inventory/VERSION file, diff vars on upgrade Effort 12-20 d Rollback kubespray reset on the node; cluster rebuild from inventory

docs.title: Phase 8 — Cluster services
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 7 cluster healthy Deliverables Cilium CNI + Hubble, MetalLB IPAddressPool + L2Advertisement, NGINX Ingress + Gateway API, Rook-Ceph CSI + StorageClasses, ExternalDNS, cert-manager Acceptance Pod-to-pod and pod-to-service connectivity across nodes; NetworkPolicy enforced (allowed and denied test); type: LoadBalancer service gets a VIP and is reachable; Ingress routes HTTP and TLS terminates correctly; PVC binds and mounts, and expands online; CSI snapshot and restore works Risks MTU mismatch between overlay and underlay -> measured MTU documented; cert issuance fails offline -> internal CA configured Effort 15-25 d Rollback Helm uninstall per component; StorageClass deletion destroys data -> back up first

docs.title: Phase 9 — Management cluster
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 7 done; Phase 3 identity; Phase 4 Vault Deliverables Rancher on dedicated 3-node cluster, cluster registration, Keycloak realm + OIDC clients, Argo CD with SSO, Velero on both clusters, platform dashboards Acceptance Rancher registers the Application Cluster and can read its nodes; Keycloak login works for Rancher and Argo CD; Argo CD syncs a test app from GitLab; Velero backup completes and a restore into a fresh namespace succeeds; Rancher and Argo CD survive Management Cluster restart Risks OIDC claim/group mapping mismatch -> groups tested explicitly Effort 15-25 d Rollback Uninstall; clusters continue running independently

docs.title: Phase 10 — Secrets and security
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 4 Vault; Phase 9 Argo CD; Phase 7 clusters Deliverables secrets-management/vault/* policies, auth methods, PKI, Kubernetes integration; security/ Gatekeeper constraints, Kyverno policies, Pod Security Standards, Falco ruleset, Trivy/Cosign pipeline integration, CIS baseline scripts Acceptance App reads a secret through the chosen delivery method and it is not in Git; rotation updates the delivered value within the documented interval; Gatekeeper rejects a privileged pod in audit mode then in enforce mode; Falco raises a test alert; Trivy blocks a CRITICAL image in the pipeline; Cosign verification passes for signed images and fails for unsigned Risks Policy over-blocking -> deploy in audit mode first, review violations, then enforce Effort 15-25 d Rollback Gatekeeper failurePolicy: Ignore / uninstall; Vault policies adjustable without restart

docs.title: Phase 11 — Monitoring and logging
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 7/8 clusters; Phase 9 Management Cluster Deliverables monitoring/ Prometheus Operator stack, Alertmanager routes, Grafana dashboards, recording rules, Thanos (if selected); logging/ Fluent Bit, Loki/OpenSearch, retention policy, redaction rules Acceptance Prometheus scrapes node, kube, etcd, CNI, CSI, Ceph, Argo CD, Vault, GitLab, Harbor, GPU targets; a test alert fires end-to-end to the receiver; a pod's logs are searchable within 5 minutes; a deliberately injected secret string is not found in the log backend; dashboards render for each domain Risks RK-10 log volume -> sampling, retention, cardinality limits Effort 12-20 d Rollback Scale down/disable; no data plane impact

docs.title: Phase 12 — GPU and AI infrastructure
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 7/8 clusters; Phase 2 GPU artifacts mirrored; GPU node hardware ready Deliverables gpu-ai/* drivers, GPU Operator, device plugin, scheduling labels/taints, sharing matrix applied, inference deployment, model mirror procedure, monitoring dashboards Acceptance kubectl get nodes -l nvidia.com/gpu.present=true shows Ready; a GPU pod runs nvidia-smi and sees the correct GPU; MIG partition is visible as a separate resource and memory is hard-isolated (test: allocate beyond the profile and observe failure); time-slicing pod shares the GPU with no memory isolation (documented); vLLM serves a mirrored model and returns a completion; DCGM metrics visible in Prometheus; two concurrent tenants do not OOM each other under MIG Risks RK-06 version mismatch -> use the driver/toolkit/operator matrix; operator upgrade briefly disrupts GPU pods -> drain window Effort 15-25 d Rollback Remove taint, drain node, roll back operator to pinned version

docs.title: Phase 13 — GitOps and CI/CD
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 9 Argo CD; Phase 10 policies; Phase 11 dashboards Deliverables automation/gitlab-ci/ full pipeline with all 14 stages, protected branches, approval gates, App-of-apps, drift detection job Acceptance A deliberately broken manifest is rejected at stage 5; a secret in a commit is rejected at stage 7; production job requires 2 approvals and runs from a protected tag; drift job reports a real manual drift without auto-fixing it; post-deploy health check fails the pipeline when a pod is unhealthy Risks Pipeline over-blocking -> per-stage bypass documented and audited Effort 12-20 d Rollback Revert to previous pipeline config; Argo CD self-heal unaffected

docs.title: Phase 14 — Lifecycle and recovery
docs.text: Prerequisites Phases 7-13 complete Deliverables lifecycle/upgrades/* per component, lifecycle/backup/*, lifecycle/disaster-recovery/* runbooks, troubleshooting/* Acceptance A K8s minor-version upgrade completes on a staging copy of the cluster with no data loss; a full cluster restore from Velero into a new cluster works; a single-node rebuild from Ansible + Kubespray completes unattended; a complete-environment rebuild procedure is exercised in the offline environment with no internet; RTO/RPO measured against the declared targets Risks Upgrade path may be one-way for some components -> irreversible steps flagged in each upgrade doc Effort 20-30 d Rollback Per-component; some upgrades are irreversible and documented as such

docs.title: Phase 15 — Acceptance and handover
docs.text: Prerequisites Phase 14 done Deliverables tests/acceptance/ executed test suite with evidence, requirements/acceptance-criteria.md, runbooks published, known limitations recorded, ownership matrix Acceptance Every acceptance test in requirements/acceptance-criteria.md executed with recorded evidence and a pass/fail verdict; failures either fixed or recorded as accepted risk with owner; handover walkthrough with the operations team completed Risks Untested claims -> only executed tests are marked passed Effort 10-18 d Rollback n/a (documentation and sign-off)

docs.title: Performance and capacity planning
docs.text: Guidance is separated into what is measured and proven versus what is workload-dependent. Every recommendation states the prerequisite, the impact, and how to undo it.

docs.title: Linux kernel
docs.text:
Setting Value Why Risk net.ipv4.ip_forward 1 Required for routing None net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables 1 Required for pod networking with bridged CNI Traps bridged traffic through iptables fs.inotify.max_user_instances 8192 Node agents watch many files Memory per watch fs.inotify.max_user_watches 524288 Same Memory fs.file-max 1048576 File descriptor ceiling None vm.max_map_count 262144 Required by Elasticsearch and OpenSearch Memory vm.swappiness 1 Kubernetes nodes should not swap A swap-heavy workload will OOM instead net.core.somaxconn 32768 Listen backlog Memory per socket net.ipv4.tcp_keepalive_* 600/30/10 Detect dead peers faster None

Baseline and rollback: the values live in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kubernetes.conf, applied by Ansible. Rollback is to delete the file and sysctl --system.

Measured, not guessed: any sysctl change is benchmarked before and after, with the same workload, and the numbers are recorded in the change record.

docs.title: CPU and memory
docs.text:
• Every container declares requests and limits. Requests drive scheduling; limits bound the blast radius.
  • CPU limits throttling is a symptom of an incorrect limit, not a fix for contention.
  • Memory limits equal the application's actual peak plus headroom. Too low causes OOM kills; too high allows one pod to starve a node.
  • QoS classes: Guaranteed (requests == limits for CPU and memory) for critical system components; Burstable for applications; BestEffort for nothing.
  • Do not set a CPU limit on latency-sensitive services without measuring the throttling.

docs.title: NUMA
docs.text:
• One GPU per NUMA node on H100/H200 SXM systems (the vendor topology).
  • Pin GPU workloads with nvidia.com/gpu plus a topology-aware scheduler (Volcano, or a topology manager policy).
  • Verify with nvidia-smi topo -m and lscpu -e.
  • Impact: a workload that crosses NUMA boundaries pays a memory-bandwidth penalty.

docs.title: Disk and filesystem
docs.text:
Media Use Notes NVMe etcd, Ceph journal, OSD DB, model cache, Prometheus Local, not shared SSD Ceph data (hot), container logs HDD Ceph data (cold), backup, archive
  • XFS with ftype=1 for any filesystem under an overlay2 container runtime.
  • noatime on data filesystems: a measurable reduction in write amplification.
  • Separate the journal from the data device on Ceph.
  • Use fio for a baseline before any storage change. Record the queue depth and the block size; the numbers are meaningless without them.

docs.title: Network throughput and latency
docs.text:
• Measure the fabric before sizing storage. A 3x replicated pool consumes roughly 2x the client write bandwidth on the replication path.
  • iperf3 between OSD hosts establishes the real ceiling.
  • MTU: with VXLAN, pod MTU = physical MTU - 50. With native routing, pod MTU = physical MTU.
  • Bonding and LACP need the switch configured for the same mode; a mismatched hash policy causes poor distribution.
  • RDMA/RoCE for multi-node model parallelism. Without it, inter-node tensor parallelism collapses.

docs.title: Container runtime
docs.text:
• containerd 2.x, SystemdCgroup = true.
  • The runtime's log configuration controls disk growth: max-size and max-file on the containerd log driver.
  • Registry mirror latency is on the critical path of every pod start. Keep the registry local to the cluster.

docs.title: Kubernetes scheduling
docs.text:
• Spread constraints for the control plane and for storage nodes.
  • Pod anti-affinity for replicas of the same service, so a node loss does not take all of them.
  • Topology spread constraints across zones where the site has them.
  • Priority classes: system-node-critical for the platform, a defined priority for applications.
  • Draining a node with a pod that has no matching toleration or a long grace period takes longer than expected. Test the drain time.

docs.title: Resource requests and limits
docs.text:
• Requests drive the scheduler's decision. An application with no requests is scheduled first-come-first-served and lands on the fullest node.
  • A CPU request above the real usage wastes capacity; below it causes the scheduler to overcommit.
  • Memory requests are the hard reservation. Set them from the measured peak.

docs.title: Autoscaling
docs.text:
Controller Use Caution HPA Stateless services on a CPU or request-rate metric Scale-up lag; the metric must reflect saturation VPA Memory-heavy services, in recommendation mode Do not use with an HPA on the same metric KEDA Event-driven and queue-driven scaling The queue metric must be real Cluster autoscaler Node count Needs a working node template and a working CNI on new nodes

For GPU inference, scale on queue depth, not on GPU utilization: a batched server shows high utilization while requests are still queuing.

docs.title: CNI and service mesh
docs.text:
• Cilium with kube-proxy replacement removes the iptables bottleneck. Measure the improvement before and after.
  • Hubble adds flow observability with modest overhead.
  • A service mesh adds a sidecar tax: roughly 10-30 MB per pod. Measure it before adopting (ADR-0009).

docs.title: Ceph
docs.text:
See storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md for the capacity worksheet. Performance-relevant settings:

Setting Guidance osd_pool_default_size 3 for production osd_pool_default_size with EC 4+2 for capacity-bound, read-mostly data mon_osd_min_in_size / max_in_size 1 / 2 during a degraded period only, as a temporary measure osd_max_backfills 1 for predictable IO during recovery, higher for faster rebuild osd_recovery_sleep 0 for faster rebuild at the cost of foreground IO BlueStore allocator bluestore_allocator on NVMe osd_memory_target Percentage of RAM for the OSD process cache; tune against the observed working set

These are workload-dependent. Every change is benchmarked with fio against the same pool before and after.

docs.title: Prometheus and logging
docs.text:
• Prometheus: cardinality is the cost driver. Fix the label set before adding retention.
  • Use recording rules for the expensive queries that dashboards run.
  • Remote write to long-term storage rather than a longer local retention, when the object store is cheaper.
  • Loki: label count per stream is the cost driver. Do not index the log content.
  • OpenSearch: JVM heap and the merge policy dominate. Size the heap at half the container memory and no more.

docs.title: etcd
docs.text:
• etcd latency is disk latency. Use a dedicated local NVMe, never a shared filesystem.
  • Monitor etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds. The p99 above 25 ms means the disk is the bottleneck.
  • --max-txn-ops and the client-side rate limiters protect etcd from a burst.
  • Compaction and defragmentation during business hours cause write latency spikes. Schedule them.

docs.title: GPU inference
docs.text:
See gpu-ai/inference/llm-serving.md for the serving configuration and gpu-ai/drivers/compatibility-matrix.md for the driver matrix.

  • --gpu-memory-utilization controls how much VRAM the engine claims. Higher means more KV cache and more concurrency, but less headroom for fragmentation.
  • --max-model-len is the context window. It scales the KV cache linearly with the sequence length, so an oversized value silently reduces concurrency.
  • Continuous batching is why vLLM outperforms a naive implementation at high concurrency.
  • Quantization (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8) reduces VRAM and increases throughput, at a documented accuracy cost. Measure the accuracy impact for the specific model before adopting it in production.
  • Prefix caching removes repeated prefill cost for shared system prompts.
  • The model load time is the scale-up latency. Keep minReplicaCount high enough to cover the steady-state load.

docs.title: Benchmarking discipline
docs.text:
A benchmark result without metadata is not a result. Record:

Field Example Software versions vLLM 0.32.0, CUDA 13.x, driver 595.71.05 Model and revision org/model@sha256:... Quantization AWQ INT4 Hardware 4x H100 80GB SXM5, NVSwitch Parallelism tensor-parallel 4 Engine settings max-model-len 8192, gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 Workload 200 prompts, 512 in / 512 out, concurrency 32 Seed 42 Results throughput, TTFT p50/p95/p99, ITL p50/p95/p99

Re-run the identical benchmark before and after every change. A claim of improvement without a re-run is not evidence.

docs.title: Platform standards
docs.text: Consolidated standards across the stack. Each item is marked Mandatory, Strongly recommended, or Optional/workload-dependent.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
Object Pattern Example Kubernetes namespace <team>-<domain> payments-core Application (Argo CD) <team>-<component> payments-api Helm release <component> argocd, cilium Hostname <role><index> k8s-cp-1, k8s-gpu-2, ceph-st-3 GitLab project <domain>-<artifact> platform-obs-monitoring, apps-payments Git branch main, release/<version>, hotfix/<ticket> GitLab environment <env> staging, production Ansible group role name from the topology control-plane, gpu-node Ceph pool <purpose> replicapool, cephfs_metadata Vault path <domain>/<team>/<name> secret/apps/payments/db Grafana dashboard folder <domain> storage, gpu-ai

Rules: lowercase, hyphen-separated, no underscores in Kubernetes names, no version in the name.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
• Internal zone for all platform endpoints (*.internal).
  • Every externally-reachable service gets a DNS record managed by ExternalDNS, never a hard-coded IP in Git.
  • Split-horizon where the DMZ and the internal zone need different answers for the same name.
  • Forwarders to the internal resolver only. No public resolvers.
  • TTL: 60 seconds for service records, 3600 for platform records.
  • Reverse DNS for every node address.

docs.title: IP addressing
docs.text:
Segment Range (PROVISIONAL) Management 10.10.0.0/24 Control plane 10.20.0.0/24 Pod 10.30.0.0/16, 10.31.0.0/16 Service 10.32.0.0/16, 10.33.0.0/16 Storage (public / cluster) 10.40.0.0/24 / 10.41.0.0/24 GPU 10.50.0.0/24 DMZ 10.60.0.0/24 MetalLB pool 10.61.0.10-10.61.0.30

Rules: - One address plan per site, in Git, versioned. - No overlap between segments. - The pod CIDR is never routed to the internet. - Reserved ranges (RFC 1918 space not used, and the shared address space) are documented and excluded.

docs.title: VLAN and network separation
docs.text: Segment VLAN Isolation Management dedicated Full access to the automation, registry, identity, and secrets services Control plane dedicated Reachable from management and from the control-plane segment only Pod / service dedicated Not routable to the internet Storage dedicated Only the storage hosts and the clients that mount volumes GPU dedicated Plus the RDMA fabric where present DMZ dedicated Only the load balancer and reverse proxy

docs.title: Version pinning
docs.text:
• Every artifact has an exact version. No latest, no floating Git reference.
  • Container images deployed by digest wherever the consumer supports it.
  • A version bump is an MR that updates the version matrix, the artifact matrix, and the component guide together.
  • Upgrades follow lifecycle/upgrades/upgrade-procedures.md.

docs.title: Secrets handling
docs.text:
• Vault is the only place a secret value lives.
  • Secrets never enter Git, container images, pipeline artifacts, ordinary logs, or values files.
  • Kubernetes Secrets hold a synchronized copy where the delivery method requires it; that copy is a separate access boundary and is audited.
  • Every secret has an owner, a rotation interval, and a documented revocation path.
  • Break-glass credentials are held offline and tested quarterly.

docs.title: Certificate management
docs.text:
• One internal CA, rooted in Vault PKI, with the root key offline.
  • cert-manager issues and renews every in-cluster certificate.
  • leaf lifetime: 90 days. Renewal at 30 days remaining.
  • Expiry alerting at 14 days (warning) and 7 days (page).
  • Root CA rotation is a multi-step runbook, not a one-line operation.

docs.title: RBAC and least privilege
docs.text:
• Humans authenticate through Keycloak (OIDC). No shared accounts, except the documented break-glass.
  • RBAC is namespace-scoped for application teams; cluster-admin is held by two named operators.
  • Service accounts are per-application, never shared.
  • pods/exec and pods/portforward are restricted by RBAC, because they are equivalent to a shell on the node.
  • Vault policies are path-scoped per application and per namespace.
  • Quarterly review of cluster-role bindings and of the Argo CD project permissions.

docs.title: Firewall policy
docs.text:
• Default deny inbound. Explicit allow rules generated from the network matrix.
  • One firewall implementation per host. Never two.
  • The matrix is the source of truth; the ruleset is generated from it.
  • Every rule carries a purpose in the matrix.

docs.title: Image provenance
docs.text:
• Images are built in CI, scanned, SBOM-generated, signed with Cosign, and pushed to Harbor.
  • Production deploys by digest.
  • Signature verification is enforced in CI and (where the policy engine supports it) at admission.
  • Harbor projects are per-team, with retention and immutability tags enabled.
  • The vulnerability database is refreshed monthly in the connected staging environment and mirrored offline.

docs.title: Backup retention
docs.text: Target Frequency Retention etcd snapshot Daily 30 days, 1 copy offline Velero backup Daily full, plus pre-change 30 days, 1 copy offline Vault raft snapshot Daily 30 days, plus offline escrow of the unseal material GitLab Daily 30 days, plus monthly full Harbor and Nexus Daily 30 days Keycloak Daily 30 days OS and Ansible configuration Every change (Git) Indefinite (Git history) AI model artifacts On change (immutable) Indefinite

docs.title: Change management
docs.text: Change class Approval Window Documentation 1 reviewer Any Application deployment 1 reviewer Any Add-on or policy change 2 reviewers Any OS baseline or Ansible role 2 reviewers Change window Kubernetes upgrade 2 + platform lead Change window Storage or Ceph change 2 + storage owner Change window Network or firewall change 2 + network owner Change window Secrets or PKI change 2, SecOps only Change window Emergency change 1 + post-hoc review Any, retroactive review within 24 h

docs.title: Monitoring and alerting
docs.text:
• Every component exposes metrics. A component that cannot be scraped is an accepted risk with a written justification.
  • Alerts are actionable: every alert has a runbook link and a named owner.
  • Cluster-level inhibition so one node failure does not produce hundreds of pages.
  • Silence is itself an alert: a Prometheus that cannot scrape a target produces a "no data" alert.
  • Paging only on symptoms users feel (availability, latency, data loss risk). Everything else is a ticket.

docs.title: Logging and auditing
docs.text:
• All node, control-plane, application, security, and CI logs reach the central backend.
  • Redaction happens in the collector, before forwarding.
  • Audit logs are retained separately and longer than application logs.
  • Audit logs are shipped off-host immediately.
  • Kubernetes audit level is Metadata; RequestResponse on secrets requires a documented decision.

docs.title: Resource sizing and capacity thresholds
docs.text: Threshold Action Node CPU > 70% sustained 1 h Review requests; add capacity Node memory > 75% sustained Review limits; add capacity Pod memory > 90% of its limit Fix the request/limit or the application Ceph pool > 70% used Plan expansion Ceph pool > 80% used Expand now Prometheus disk > 70% Reduce retention or expand Log backend disk > 70% Reduce retention or expand MetalLB pool > 80% assigned Extend the pool Model cache disk > 80% Prune old revisions

docs.title: Maintenance windows
docs.text:
• OS patching: monthly, in a defined window, one node at a time.
  • Kubernetes minor upgrades: quarterly, staging first.
  • Certificate renewal: automatic, with an expiry report weekly.
  • Vulnerability database refresh: monthly.
  • Restore drill: quarterly for one application, annually for the full environment.
  • DR exercise: annually.
  • ADR review: annually, or when a decision's assumptions change.

docs.title: Incident response
docs.text:
1. Detect (alert or report).
  2. Triage: impact, scope, and whether the blast radius matches the failure-domain analysis.
  3. Mitigate: restore service first, root cause second.
  4. Communicate: who is affected and what is blocked.
  5. Recover: verify with the acceptance tests for the affected component.
  6. Review: within 5 working days, produce a blameless review and update the runbook, the matrix, and the ADR if needed.

Rules: the break-glass path is used when the normal path is unavailable, not only when it is convenient. Every break-glass use is reviewed.

docs.title: Documentation and runbooks
docs.text:
• Every component has a guide following the template in requirements/component-guide-template.md.
  • Every troubleshooting scenario has a runbook with the seven required sections.
  • Every alert links to a runbook.
  • Every ADR has a status and a review date.
  • Documentation lives in the same Git repository as the code it describes, and a change to one updates the other.

docs.title: Configuration drift
docs.text:
• Nightly drift job compares the live state with Git.
  • Drift is reported, never silently fixed — except by the designated owner of that object (Argo CD for declared state, Ansible for node state).
  • A drift report older than 24 hours is an incident.
  • The drift report names the object, the owner, and the expected value.

docs.title: Disaster recovery testing
docs.text:
• Quarterly: restore one application from a Velero backup into a scratch namespace.
  • Annually: rebuild the entire environment from the documented order, offline, and pass the acceptance tests.
  • Annually: restore Vault from a snapshot and unseal with the offline shares.
  • Every drill records the measured RTO and compares it to the declared target.
  • A drill that fails is a finding, not a formality.

docs.title: Canonical Test Registry
docs.text: Repository: DavoudTeimouri/cloud-native-guide (Repository 1 — canonical technical source of truth) Status: Authoritative single source of truth for all test IDs. Generated from: Reconciliation of requirements/acceptance-criteria.md (48 IDs) and requirements/validation-strategy.md (73 IDs). Total distinct test IDs: 86 (after resolving the B-12 ID collision).

docs.title: 1. Status model
docs.text:
Status Meaning NOT RUN Execution has not started; no specific blocker established. BLOCKED A required infrastructure component or prerequisite is unavailable. PASS Executed with evidence stored in tests/acceptance/<test-id>/. FAIL Executed and failed; evidence stored. N/A Not applicable; requires documented justification.

Rule: a test is PASS only when executed with evidence. Current status distribution: 7 NOT RUN (A-01, A-02, A-05, A-06, A-07, A-08, C-08 — executable from the docs repo with no infrastructure blocker), 79 BLOCKED (require cluster, Vault, Ceph, GPU, internal registry, or isolated segment that are not provisioned in this documentation repo), 0 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 N/A. No test is marked PASS or FAIL without execution evidence.

docs.title: 2. Evidence structure
docs.text:
Every executed test stores evidence under:

tests/acceptance/<TEST-ID>/
  procedure.md    # exact commands used
  result.md       # observed output, timestamped
  verdict.md      # PASS/FAIL, tester, date
  environment.md  # tool versions, cluster state, deploy profile
  logs/           # command output, screenshots, scan reports (sanitized: no secrets)

No placeholder or fake evidence may be committed. The directory tests/acceptance/ exists but contains only this README; per-test evidence directories are created only when a test is executed.

docs.title: 10. Recommended next task for CI implementation
docs.text:
1. Create tests/acceptance/run.sh — a suite runner that accepts --suite <integration|smoke|offline|security|...> and --env <staging|production>, executes the corresponding acceptance tests from the canonical registry, and writes evidence to tests/acceptance/<test-id>/.
  2. Wire tests/acceptance/run.sh into automation/gitlab-ci/pipeline.md stages (integration tests and postcheck health) replacing the dangling references.
  3. Add a CI gate job that runs python3 tests/test_repo_tools.py plus static validation (yamllint, markdownlint, kubeconform, trivy, gitleaks, cosign).
  4. Provision a staging cluster to begin executing acceptance tests; mark PASS/FAIL with evidence per test.
  5. Update test_repo_tools.py acceptance-criteria check when the first test is marked PASS (it currently asserts all are NOT RUN).

Stop — awaiting review before any commit or push.

docs.title: 11. Validation Method Assessment
docs.text:
Execution status (NOT RUN / BLOCKED / PASS / FAIL / N/A) is independent of validation method. A new Validation Method column has been added to every registry row with values: Static, Offline, Integration, Infrastructure, Manual.

  • Static: validated from repository docs/files only, no cluster or infrastructure. Executable now from this docs repo.
  • Offline: requires an air-gapped/isolated segment with internal repos/registry, but no live cluster. Blocked until the offline environment is provisioned.
  • Integration: requires a running component (GitLab CI, Argo CD, Ansible automation server) but not necessarily a full cluster. Blocked until that component is provisioned.
  • Infrastructure: requires a live cluster, Vault, Ceph, GPU, or full environment. Blocked until infrastructure is provisioned.
  • Manual: requires human-driven steps (e.g. break-glass SSH with IdP stopped).

docs.title: Tests that are infrastructure-blocked but have independent static/offline validation
docs.text:
These tests carry Execution Status: BLOCKED (infrastructure not provisioned) but expose a Validation Method: Static or Offline path that can be executed independently once the prerequisite artifact is available, without marking the full test PASS:

Test Validation Method Independent static/offline step Why full test stays BLOCKED A-03 Infrastructure helm show chart <chart> to read appVersion statically "vs deployed version" needs a live cluster C-06 Offline cosign verify with offline trust root against a local image Needs signed + unsigned images to compare C-08 Static gitleaks/trufflehog over full Git history Already NOT RUN (executable now) — no blocker F-01..F-06, F-08 Offline Procedure validation against internal repo/registry config Needs internal yum/apt repo, Harbor registry, isolated segment

Rule: a test is marked PASS only when its complete procedure (including any static pre-check) is executed with evidence stored under tests/acceptance/<test-id>/. Partial static validation does not justify marking a test PASS.

docs.title: Deliverable 12 — Validation Strategy
docs.text:
Seven test families. Every test states: procedure, expected result, evidence artifact, pass/fail criterion, execution context.

Status column is authoritative: a test is PASSED only if it was executed and evidence is stored. Not-run tests read NOT RUN.

This file is the acceptance gate: it lists every acceptance-test ID with its phase, owner, validation method, and current status. All IDs, statuses, and cross-references are generated from or synchronized with requirements/test-registry.md.

Total acceptance-test IDs: 86 (families A–G, M, P, S; all currently NOT RUN).

docs.title: Execution rules
docs.text:
1. A test is PASSED only when executed and evidence exists. Never mark a test passed from documentation.
  2. Run destructive tests (node loss, cluster loss) only in staging or in an approved maintenance window, with the operator present.
  3. Record the exact version of every tool in the evidence.
  4. Re-run the whole suite after any upgrade that touches a tested component.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Document Vault's Kubernetes auth method configuration for in-cluster workload identity. This governs how Kubernetes service accounts map to Vault roles and obtain short-lived tokens.

docs.title: Kubernetes Auth Method
docs.text:
Enable the Kubernetes auth method:

vault auth enable kubernetes

Configure the Kubernetes auth method with the cluster's CA certificate and API server URL. The following parameters are required:

Parameter Description kubernetes_host URL of the Kubernetes API server (e.g. https://kubernetes.default.svc) kubernetes_ca_cert CA certificate for TLS verification of the API server kubernetes_service_account_token Path to the service account token (optional, for bootstrap) token_review_jwt JWT for token review requests to the API server

docs.title: Auth Role
docs.text:
Create a Kubernetes auth role that binds a service account to a Vault policy. The role defines which service accounts can authenticate and what permissions they receive.

# Write a policy first (if not already created)
vault policy write readonly policy/readonly.hcl

# Create the auth role binding a service account to the policy
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/platform \
  bound_service_account_names=platform-app \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=platform \
  policies=readonly \
  ttl=24h \
  audience=vault

docs.title: Role parameters
docs.text: Parameter Required Description bound_service_account_names yes Comma-separated list of service account names that can authenticate bound_service_account_namespaces yes Comma-separated list of namespaces where the above SAs reside policies yes Comma-separated list of Vault policies to assign ttl no Maximum token time-to-live; defaults to system max max_ttl no Maximum allowed TTL; cannot exceed system max audience no Audience claim to validate in token requests

docs.title: Example: Restricted role with short TTL
docs.text:
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/api-reader \
  bound_service_account_names=api-reader \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=production,staging \
  policies=api-reader \
  ttl=10m \
  max_ttl=15m

docs.title: Service Account
docs.text: Workloads authenticate to Vault by presenting a Kubernetes service account token. The token is exchanged via the Kubernetes TokenReview API for a Vault token.

docs.title: Creating the service account
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: api-reader
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    # Optional: configure token lifetime
    vault.hashicorp.com/role: api-reader

docs.title: Token review mechanism
docs.text:
When a workload presents a service account token, Vault's Kubernetes auth method performs a TokenReview against the Kubernetes API server:

  1. The workload mounts its service account token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  2. The application calls vault token create or uses the Vault Agent Injector/CSI driver
  3. Vault sends a TokenReview request to the Kubernetes API server: 
    {
  "apiVersion": "authentication.k8s.io/v1",
  "kind": "TokenReview",
  "spec": {
    "token": "<presented-token>"
  }
}
  4. Kubernetes validates the token and returns:
  5. status.authenticated: true/false
  6. status.user.username: the service account name (<namespace>/<name>)
  7. status.user.uid: the service account UID
  8. status.user.groups: the service account groups

The token review is the core mechanism that ties Kubernetes identity to Vault access. Without a valid token review, no Vault token is issued.

docs.title: Verifying token review is functional
docs.text:
# Check the Kubernetes API server's token review endpoint
kubectl get apiservers.authorization.k8s.io

# Example TokenReview request
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -
apiVersion: authentication.k8s.io/v1
kind: TokenReview
spec:
  token: <service-account-token>
EOF

docs.title: Workload Identity (Kubernetes 1.24+)
docs.text: For clusters running Kubernetes 1.24+, projected service account tokens can be used. These tokens are automatically managed and have shorter lifetimes, reducing the risk of token theft.

docs.title: Projected token configuration
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: api-reader
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: api-reader
    # Project the token into the container volume
    volumes:
      - name: sa-token
        projected:
          sources:
            - serviceAccountToken:
                name: api-reader
                mountPath: /var/run/sa

The projected token is automatically refreshed by the Kubelet and presented to Vault's Kubernetes auth method via the TokenReview API.

docs.title: Cross-references
docs.text:
• secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md — Overall Vault deployment architecture and identity integration
  • secrets-management/vault/access-control.md — Auth methods, roles, policies, and token policies
  • secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md — Secret delivery to workloads via Vault
  • kubernetes/security/security-controls.md — Kubernetes security controls including audit policy for token reviews

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Auth role binds a Kubernetes service account to a Vault policy, controlling what permissions the workload receives
  • Service account is the Kubernetes identity that workloads present via their mounted token
  • Token review is the Kubernetes API mechanism that validates the service account token and passes the identity to Vault
  • All three components (auth role, service account, token review) must be correctly configured for in-cluster workloads to authenticate to Vault without static credentials

docs.title: Kubernetes secret delivery
docs.text: Four methods are supported. Each is used for a different case, and each has a different persistence and access profile.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Method Mechanism Persisted in etcd Refresh App reload Complexity Use when Vault Agent Injector Sidecar writes a file, syncs on renewal No (file only) Agent renews and rewrites App re-reads the file Med The app reads a file Vault Agent templates Agent renders a template to a file No Same Same Med Config templating from many secrets Secrets Store CSI Driver Mounts a secret as a read-only file No Driver refreshes the mount App re-reads Med The app wants a volume mount External Secrets Operator Syncs Vault into a K8s Secret Yes ESO refreshes on interval App restart/reload Low The app needs a native K8s Secret Direct app -> Vault App calls the Vault API No App handles it App-native Varies The app already integrates K8s native Secret Plain etcd secret Yes Manual Yes Low Non-sensitive data only

Explicit statement: External Secrets Operator does not remove the etcd exposure. It centralizes the source of truth and the rotation, but the synchronized value still lands in etcd and is readable by anyone with RBAC on that Secret in that namespace. The mitigation is namespace isolation, RBAC, and etcd encryption at rest — not the operator itself.

docs.title: Method 1 — Vault Agent Injector
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: app-vault-auth
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: harbor.internal/apps/app@sha256:...
          env:
            - name: VAULT_ADDR
              value: http://vault.vault.svc:8200
          volumeMounts:
            - name: secrets
              mountPath: /var/run/secrets/vault
      annotations:
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-app-db: "app-db"
        vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-template-app-db: |
          {{- with secret "secret/apps/app/db" -}}
          DB_PASSWORD={{ .Data.data.password }}
          {{- end }}
        vault.hashicorp.com/role: "app"
        vault.hashicorp.com/auth-path: "kubernetes"
        vault.hashicorp.com/service-account: "app-vault-auth"

The pod runs as the app's service account, so the injector uses that token for the Vault Kubernetes auth. The Vault role bound to the service account determines what the pod can read.

Refresh: the agent renews the lease and rewrites the file. The application must re-read the file. Applications that read the file once at startup will use the old value until restarted. This is the single most common cause of "rotation did not work".

docs.title: Method 2 — External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault-backend
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: "https://vault.internal:8200"
      path: "secret"
      version: "v2"
      caProvider:
        type: ConfigMap
        name: vault-ca
        key: ca.crt
        namespace: external-secrets
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: kubernetes
          role: external-secrets
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: external-secrets-vault
            namespace: external-secrets

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-db
  namespace: payments
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: vault-backend
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: app-db
    creationPolicy: Owner
    template:
      type: Opaque
      data:
        password: "{{ .password }}"
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: apps/payments/db
        property: password

Refresh: refreshInterval controls how often ESO re-reads Vault. The change reaches the K8s Secret within that interval, but the application still needs to reload.

Rotation test: change the value in Vault, wait for refreshInterval, then confirm the K8s Secret changed and the application picked it up. If the application does not reload, use a reloader-style sidecar or a rolling restart triggered by the secret's resourceVersion hash in the pod spec.

docs.title: Method 3 — Secrets Store CSI Driver
docs.text:
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: vault-provider
  namespace: payments
spec:
  provider: vault
  parameters:
    vaultAddress: "https://vault.internal:8200"
    roleName: "app"
    objects: |
      - objectName: "db-password"
        secretPath: "secret/apps/payments/db"
        secretKey: "password"

volumes:
  - name: secrets
    csi:
      driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
      readOnly: true
      volumeAttributes:
        secretProviderClass: vault-provider

The value is mounted as a file and is not stored in etcd. The driver refreshes the mount on the lease renewal interval.

docs.title: Method 4 — Direct application access
docs.text:
# Example: the app authenticates to Vault itself
import hvac

client = hvac.Client(url=os.environ["VAULT_ADDR"])
client.auth.kubernetes.login(role="app", jwt=open("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token").read())
secret = client.secrets.kv.v2.read_secret_version(path="secret/apps/payments/db", mount_point="secret")
password = secret["data"]["data"]["password"]

Use this when the application already has a Vault SDK integration. It gives the finest control over renewal and caching, at the cost of application work.

docs.title: Kubernetes auth in Vault
docs.text:
# Enable the method
vault auth enable kubernetes

vault write auth/kubernetes/config \
  kubernetes_host="https://kubernetes.default.svc:6443" \
  kubernetes_ca_cert=@ca.crt \
  token_reviewer_jwt=@reviewer.jwt \
  issuer="https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local"

The token reviewer JWT must be a long-lived ServiceAccount token in the Vault namespace, with system:auth-delegator bound. The issuer must match the token's issuer claim.

# Role binding
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/app \
  bound_service_account_names=app-vault-auth \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=payments \
  policies=app-payments \
  ttl=1h

# Policy
vault policy write app-payments - <<EOF
path "secret/apps/payments/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF

Scope policies to the namespace. A role that can read secret/apps/* from any namespace defeats the namespace isolation the External Secrets Operator created.

docs.title: etcd encryption at rest
docs.text:
Because some delivery methods persist into etcd, enable encryption at rest:

# On every control-plane node, in /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: <base64 32-byte key>
      - identity: {}

Then in the Kubespray group vars:

encryption_provider: aescbc

The key must come from Vault, not from a file in the repository. In this platform the key is written to the node by Ansible from a Vault lookup during cluster deployment, and backed up in the Vault snapshot set.

docs.title: Choosing per component
docs.text: Component Method Reason Application runtime secrets External Secrets Operator Applications expect native K8s Secrets; lowest application effort Application config files Vault Agent Injector File-based, no etcd persistence Database credentials Vault DB engine + External Secrets or Agent Dynamic credentials with a lease Argo CD repository credentials Argo CD repo secret, value from ESO Argo CD reads its own secret CI/CD credentials GitLab protected variables or Vault OIDC Not a Kubernetes concern TLS certificates cert-manager + Vault PKI Renewal is the requirement Ansible credentials Vault lookup at execution time Never in the inventory Node-level secrets Ansible from Vault Written to disk with 0600

docs.title: Rotation verification
docs.text:
Rotation is only complete when the consumer has the new value. Test it:

# 1. Change the value in Vault
vault kv put secret/apps/payments/db password=NEWVALUE

# 2. Wait for the refresh interval, then check the K8s Secret
kubectl -n payments get secret app-db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# 3. Confirm the application observed it
kubectl -n payments logs deploy/app --tail=20

A secret that changed in Vault but not in the application is a failed rotation, and the credential is now in two places with an unknown value.

docs.title: Internal CA and PKI
docs.text:
Two PKI systems coexist and must not be confused:

PKI Issues Owner Rotation Kubernetes internal PKI API server, kubelet, front-proxy, etcd certificates Kubespray Kubespray certificate workflow Platform PKI Ingress, service, and client certificates Vault PKI + cert-manager cert-manager renewal; root rotation by runbook

Source of the split: secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md §8.7.

docs.title: Chain of trust
docs.text:
Offline root CA (Vault PKI root, key offline)
└── Intermediate CA (Vault PKI, online, auto-renewed)
    └── Leaf certificates (cert-manager, Kubernetes TLS Secrets)
  • The root key is generated once, kept offline, and backed up separately from the platform. It is never present on a cluster node.
  • The intermediate is the only CA that signs day-to-day. Compromise of the intermediate is recoverable by revoking it and issuing a new one from the root.
  • Leaf certificates are short-lived and renewed by cert-manager.

docs.title: Components and pins
docs.text: Component Pin Note cert-manager v1.21.2 (chart v1.21.2) compatibility/version-matrix.md cert-manager (Kubespray-managed) 1.15.3 — not adopted Older than the standalone chart Vault v2.2.0, chart 0.34.1 compatibility/version-matrix.md

docs.title: Bootstrap order
docs.text:
1. Build the offline root CA (once per estate). Store the key offline; record the custodian and the storage location outside Git.
  2. Deploy Vault and configure the PKI secrets engine with the root, then generate the intermediate (secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md).
  3. Deploy cert-manager with a ClusterIssuer pointing at the Vault intermediate.
  4. Issue a test certificate and confirm the chain before any ingress depends on it.
  5. Only then configure ingress hosts (network-matrix/external-load-balancer.md).

docs.title: Operating rules
docs.text:
• No private key is committed to Git or stored in a Kubernetes Secret by hand; cert-manager writes TLS Secrets.
  • The Vault PKI role constrains allowed domains and maximum TTL. A request outside the allowed domains must fail.
  • Certificate expiry is alerted at 30, 14, and 7 days. An expired ingress certificate is a platform outage for every host behind it.
  • The root CA is used only to sign intermediates. Any other use is an incident.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
kubectl get clusterissuer
kubectl get certificate -A
kubectl describe certificate -n <namespace> <name>
openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text: Failure Effect Recovery Intermediate expired cert-manager cannot issue or renew; existing leaf certificates stay valid until expiry Re-issue the intermediate from the root Root key lost No new intermediate can be issued; the chain cannot be extended Rebuild the PKI and re-issue every certificate — treat as a full certificate replacement cert-manager unavailable Renewals stop; certificates expire on schedule Restore cert-manager; existing certificates are unaffected until expiry Vault sealed Issuance stops Unseal per secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md

find /etc/kubernetes/pki -name '*.crt' -exec sh -c 'echo "{}:"; openssl x509 -in "{}" -noout -enddate -dates' \;

# Check ingress certificate expiry

docs.text:

  • kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Certificate expiry — Control plane context
