docs.title: Root CA rotation runbook
docs.text:
Rotation replaces the root that signs the platform intermediate. It is downtime-sensitive and cannot be done in one step: certificates already issued remain valid until they expire, so the old and new chains coexist during the transition.

Prerequisite reading: secrets-management/pki/index.md, secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md §8.7.

docs.title: When to rotate
docs.text:
• Scheduled rotation per the estate's cryptographic policy.
  • Suspected or confirmed root key compromise (then rotate immediately, and treat every issued certificate as untrusted).
  • Change of custody or storage medium for the root key.

docs.title: Order of operations
docs.text:
1. Prepare. Generate the new root key and self-signed root certificate offline. Record the custodian, storage location, and serial number. Do not touch the running intermediate yet.
  2. Distribute trust. Add the new root certificate to every trust store that validates platform certificates — nodes, ingress clients, and any external system that pins the chain. Both roots are trusted at this point.
  3. Issue the new intermediate. From the new root, issue an intermediate and import it into Vault's PKI engine alongside the old one.
  4. Switch issuance. Point the cert-manager ClusterIssuer at the new intermediate. New certificates now chain to the new root; existing ones still chain to the old.
  5. Wait for leaf expiry. Keep the old intermediate and old root trusted until the longest-lived certificate issued under the old chain has expired. Do not revoke the old intermediate before this point, or every unexpired certificate becomes invalid at once.
  6. Retire. Revoke the old intermediate, remove the old root from trust stores, and archive the old root key according to the retention policy.

Steps 2 and 5 are the long poles. Skipping step 2 breaks every client that has not yet learned the new root; skipping step 5 causes an outage when the old intermediate is revoked.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Issuer now points at the new intermediate
kubectl get clusterissuer -o yaml | grep -A3 vault

# Newly issued certificate chains to the new root
kubectl get certificate -A
openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates

# Old root still trusted during the transition (expected until step 6)
openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt <leaf>.pem

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Before step 6, rollback is a configuration change: point the ClusterIssuer back at the old intermediate. After step 6, rollback requires re-trusting the old root and re-issuing under the old intermediate — treat it as a new rotation, not a revert.

docs.title: Record keeping
docs.text: Record in the change ticket: old and new root serials, intermediate serials, the date each trust store was updated, the expiry date of the last certificate issued under the old chain, and the date the old root was removed from trust.

docs.title: Vault recovery
docs.text: The recovery path must work when the cluster, the identity provider, and the network are all in a bad state. This procedure is written for that case.

docs.title: Preconditions
docs.text:
Item Where it lives Who holds it Vault raft snapshot Object storage (Ceph RGW bucket vault-backup/) and offline media SRE + a second custodian Unseal key shares Offline, split between custodians 3+ custodians, quorum of 3 Root token Offline, separate from the shares Security lead Configuration backup (vault config directory) Encrypted offline archive SRE CA material Vault PKI, backed up offline SecOps

If any of these is missing, the backup is not a backup. Verify the procedure quarterly.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
# On a Vault node
vault operator raft snapshot save -name=backup-$(date +%F)
vault operator raft snapshot status -name=backup-$(date +%F)

# Copy to object storage
aws --endpoint-url https://rgw.internal s3 cp \
  backup-$(date +%F).snapshot s3://vault-backup/snapshots/

# Copy to offline media (physically separate, later)

Also back up the Vault server configuration:

tar czf vault-config-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc/vault.d /etc/systemd/system/vault.service

docs.title: Restore onto new hosts
docs.text:
1. Install the same Vault binary version on the new hosts. Verify with vault version.
  2. Restore the configuration archive and set the file ownership to the vault user, mode 0640 for /etc/vault.d.
  3. Initialize the new cluster's storage:
# On the first new node, with the storage backend configured but not initialized
vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3

This prints the unseal key shares and the root token. Do not store them in a ticket, a chat message, or a Git repository. Print them, record them offline, and destroy the terminal output.

  1. Join the remaining nodes:
vault operator raft join -node-id=<node-id>
  1. Unseal with the quorum of shares:
vault operator unseal <key-share-1>
vault operator unseal <key-share-2>
vault operator unseal <key-share-3>
  1. Verify leadership and health:
vault status
# expect: initialized, unsealed, HA enabled, leader = true
  1. Restore the raft snapshot (this replaces the freshly initialized data):
# Stop Vault on all nodes first
vault operator raft snapshot restore backup-2026-10-17.snapshot

Restoring a snapshot into a freshly initialized cluster and then unsealing works. Restoring into a cluster that already has data requires the documented snapshot_force_restore procedure — read the Vault documentation for the pinned version before using it.

  1. Re-authenticate with the root token from the offline escrow:
vault login
  1. Verify the data:
vault secrets list
vault auth list
vault policy list
vault kv list secret/
  1. Restart the remaining nodes and confirm HA:
systemctl start vault
vault status

docs.title: Recovery of a single failed node
docs.text:
# On the failed node
systemctl stop vault
rm -rf /etc/vault.d/raft
# Re-join from a healthy node
vault operator raft join -node-id=<node-id>

docs.title: Recovery when the seal status cannot be cleared
docs.text:
If a quorum of the original shares is unavailable, the cluster cannot be unsealed with them. The options, in order of preference:

  1. Use the root token with vault operator generate-root to generate a new set of shares. This requires a quorum of existing shares, so it does not help if the shares are lost.
  2. Restore from the raft snapshot (the path above). This loses everything since the snapshot.
  3. Accept the loss of the secrets and re-issue them. This is why some secrets have an external source of truth (the directory, the GitLab registry, the OS configuration) and why a rotation plan exists.

There is no fourth option. A sealed Vault with lost shares is unrecoverable. That is the reason for offline custody of the shares and the reason for the break-glass procedure.

docs.title: Post-recovery verification
docs.text:
# Auth methods work
vault auth list

# Dynamic secret engines issue credentials
vault read database/creds/<role>

# PKI issues certificates
vault write pki/issue/<role> common_name=test.internal ttl=1h

# The Kubernetes auth method can reach the API server
vault write auth/kubernetes/login role=<role> jwt=<token>

# Audit device is active
vault audit list

Then re-run the acceptance tests for secrets: S-01 (delivery), S-02 (rotation), S-03 (certificate renewal), and D-06 (failover).

docs.title: Order of recovery in a total-loss scenario
docs.text:
1. Network, DNS, NTP
2. OS baseline via Ansible
3. Internal CA
4. Artifact repositories (Harbor, Nexus)
5. GitLab
6. Keycloak
7. VAULT          <- before the cluster
8. Automation server / AWX
9. Ceph
10. Kubernetes cluster
11. Management Cluster + Rancher
12. Argo CD + add-ons
13. GPU workers
14. Applications

Vault comes before Kubernetes on purpose. The cluster's secrets must exist before the cluster that consumes them, and a cluster loss must not be able to take the secrets with it.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
• Least privilege: every role grants only the minimum permissions needed
  • Namespace isolation: roles are scoped to specific namespaces by default
  • Explicit allow: default deny — every permission must be explicitly granted
  • Role aggregation: combine related permissions into fewer roles to reduce combinatorial complexity

docs.title: Recommended Role Set
docs.text:
# admin — full control within a namespace (emergency use only)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: admin
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]
  resources: ["*"]
  verbs: ["*"]

# view — read-only access for auditors and monitoring
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: view
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "replicasets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["batch"]
  resources: ["cronjobs"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

# edit — read-write for application teams (no resource creation)
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: edit
  namespace: production
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["events"]
  verbs: ["create"]

docs.title: ClusterRole Design (cluster-wide)
docs.text:
# cluster-admin — only for cluster operations, never assigned to users
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: cluster-admin
rules:
- apiGroups: ["*"]
  resources: ["*"]
  verbs: ["*"]
  resourceNames: [""]  # empty resourceNames = all resources, but restricted by subject

# certificate-approver — approve/rotate PKI certificates
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: certificate-approver
rules:
- apiGroups: ["certificates.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["certificatesigningrequests/approval", "certificatesigningrequests/signing"]
  verbs: ["get", "create", "update"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  resourceNames: ["ca-key-pair"]  # specific secret name

# ingress-controller — manage ingress resources
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: ingress-controller
rules:
- apiGroups: [" networking.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["ingresses"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["services", "endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Vault access control: auth methods, roles, policies, token policies, seal/unseal process.

Cross-references secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md, secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md, kubernetes/security/security-controls.md.

docs.title: B. Auth methods
docs.text: Auth method Use case Configuration Kubernetes Workload identity vault auth enable kubernetes GitHub Human operator vault auth enable github LDAP Enterprise directory vault auth enable ldap Token Service-to-service Built-in

docs.title: C. Roles and policies
docs.text:
Policies are HCL-based and attached to roles:

# policy/readonly.hcl
path "secret/data/platform/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "secret/data/secrets/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

# Write policy
vault policy write readonly policy/readonly.hcl

# Create role with policy
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/platform \
  bound_service_account_names=platform-app \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=platform \
  policies=readonly \
  ttl=24h

docs.title: D. Token policies
docs.text:
Tokens are short-lived with least privilege:

# Create token with TTL
vault token create -policy=readonly -ttl=1h

# Revoke token
vault token revoke <token-id>

docs.title: E. Seal/unseal process
docs.text:
Vault starts sealed. Unseal requires 3 of 5 shares:

# Unseal with one share
vault operator unseal <share-1>

# Check seal status
vault status

# Seal Vault
vault operator seal

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:
• secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md — Vault deployment architecture
  • secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md — Secret delivery to workloads
  • kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §Vault — Vault in security context

docs.title: Deployment Modes
docs.text:
Mode Description Use Case Dedicated Linux hosts (3-node) Standalone Vault processes on separate VMs/hosts, each running Vault agent in Raft mode. Independent of Kubernetes lifecycle; unseal path does not depend on the cluster. Recommended production mode — no circular dependency between cluster and secrets. Inside Management Cluster Vault deployed as a Deployment/StatefulSet within the management Kubernetes cluster. HA via built-in Raft storage. Cheaper, Helm-managed, but cluster loss = secret loss; unseal may require the cluster available. Kubernetes on a separate small cluster Vault runs on a dedicated small K8s cluster. Middle ground if host count is constrained; still couples secrets to K8s lifecycle.

Decision: Deploy Vault on 3 dedicated Linux hosts outside the Management Cluster (ADR-0025). This eliminates circular dependencies and makes the unseal path independent of cluster availability.

docs.title: Topology (3-node Raft)
docs.text:
vault-a (active) ── raft ── vault-b (standby) ── raft ── vault-c (standby)
      │
      └─ File storage backend + periodic snapshot to S3 (Ceph RGW) or offline media
  • One active node, two standby nodes in Raft group.
  • Storage backend: integrated Raft (default) with snapshots exported to object storage for disaster recovery.
  • TLS on port 8200 for all client communication.

docs.title: Storage Backends
docs.text: Backend Characteristics Recommendation Integrated Raft Built-in consensus storage; 3-node cluster provides HA. Snapshots exported to object storage. Default and recommended for most deployments. File system Simple start-up; not HA. Use only for dev/testing. ❌ Production Consul External KV store for Vault secrets; requires separate Consul cluster. Use only if integrating with existing Consul. S3-compatible (Ceph RGW) Periodic snapshot replication to object storage. Enables offline recovery. ✅ Recommended for DR snapshot storage.

docs.title: Snapshot Strategy
docs.text:
• Automated snapshots: vault operator raft snapshot save triggered hourly via cron.
  • Retention: Keep 7 daily + 4 weekly + 6 monthly snapshots offline.
  • Offline storage: Snapshots copied to S3 (Ceph RGW) or removable media; not in the same region as running nodes.
  • Verification: vault operator snapshot-verify after each snapshot.

docs.title: 3-node Raft Quorum
docs.text:
• Minimum of 3 nodes required for quorum (N nodes, quorum = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1).
  • Node roles: one active, remaining standbys.
  • Standby election: if active node fails, a standby is promoted within ~30 seconds.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
• Server certificate signed by internal CA.
  • Client certificate pinning for automated integrations.
  • Port 8200 (HTTPS) for API traffic; port 8201 (HTTPS) for telemetry.

docs.title: Resource Minimums
docs.text: Component CPU Memory Storage Each Vault node 2 vCPU 4 GB 10 GB (root) + snapshot storage Snapshot host (optional) 2 vCPU 4 GB 100 GB (object storage cache)

docs.title: Resource Limits
docs.text:
• Set memory limits to prevent OOM kills on noisy neighbors.
  • CPU limits proportional to request count; enable maxrequests per-token to throttle burst.

docs.title: Unseal Strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Description Key Management Shamir's Secret Sharing (3 of 5) 5 key shares generated; any 3 can unseal. Shares held by separate custodians. Offline; documented in secrets-management/vault/recovery/. Auto-unseal KMS Vault auto-unseals using cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS). Keys stored in KMS; no plaintext keys on disk. Hybrid Shamir shares as fallback; auto-unseal primary. Both paths documented; tested quarterly.

Break-glass unseal: Shamir key shares (3 of 5) held offline by separate custodians; or a KMS auto-unseal device if available. Both are documented in secrets-management/vault/recovery/.

docs.title: Unseal Rotation
docs.text:
• Rotate unseal keys annually or after any suspected compromise.
  • Regenerate shares; redistribute to custodians.
  • Test rotation in staging before production.

docs.title: Core Formula
docs.text:
nodes = 3 (minimum for Raft quorum)
cpu_per_node = max(2, ceil(requests_per_second * 0.5)) vCPU
mem_per_node = max(4 GB, requests_per_second * 1 GB) + overhead
snapshot_storage = 100 GB per node (object storage cache)

docs.title: Example sizing
docs.text: Load (auth ops/sec) Nodes CPU per node Memory per node Snapshot storage < 10 3 2 vCPU 4 GB 100 GB 10–50 3 4 vCPU 8 GB 200 GB 50–200 5 6 vCPU 12 GB 300 GB > 200 7+ 8+ vCPU 16+ GB 500 GB+

docs.title: Sizing Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] 3+ nodes for Raft quorum
  • [ ] CPU: 2 vCPU minimum per node, scale with auth ops/sec
  • [ ] Memory: 4 GB minimum per node, scale with auth ops/sec
  • [ ] Storage: 10 GB root + 100 GB snapshot cache per node
  • [ ] TLS certificates provisioned and renewed automatically
  • [ ] Snapshot cron job configured and verified offline
  • [ ] Unseal strategy (Shamir or KMS) documented and tested
  • [ ] Audit logging shipped to centralized platform
  • [ ] Monitoring alerts for: seal status, leadership changes, storage usage, auth failures, snapshot freshness

docs.title: Identity Integration
docs.text:
Consumer Auth Method Notes Human admins OIDC via Keycloak Group → Vault role mapping Ansible automation server AppRole or JWT Prefer JWT/OIDC if identity flow allows GitLab CI jobs OIDC (GitLab ID token) → Vault JWT auth Fallback = AppRole with short TTL Argo CD Kubernetes auth (SA token) Vault's own K8s auth; alternate = External Secrets Operator Applications (in-cluster) K8s auth (SA token) Least-privilege per app SA Workload identity (K8s 1.24+ projected tokens) Vault K8s auth Short-lived, no static SA secret

Key point: Directory integration is application-level and never automatic. Each service gets its own explicit OIDC or LDAP procedure — see identity/directory-integration.md.

docs.title: Secret Categories and Storage
docs.text: Category Vault path (example) Delivery Rotation Linux/root creds secret/infra/linux/* Ansible fetch at runtime 90d SSH keys secret/infra/ssh/* Ansible + Vault SSH agent signing 90d / on use Kubespray bootstrap creds secret/infra/kubespray/* Ansible vault lookup 90d K8s app secrets secret/apps/<ns>/* External Secrets Operator → K8s Secret 30d DB creds database/creds/<role> Dynamic (Vault DB engine) 24h lease Ceph keys secret/infra/ceph/* Ansible → Ceph 180d GitLab CI creds secret/ci/* GitLab CI masked variables or OIDC 30d Harbor/Nexus auth secret/registry/* Ansible, containerd registries.conf 90d Argo CD repo creds secret/gitops/* Argo CD repo creds via API (not in Git) 90d Monitoring creds secret/observability/* External Secrets 90d Keycloak client secrets secret/identity/* Ansible / External Secrets 90d TLS certs + keys pki/issue/<role> cert-manager via Vault PKI 30d, auto-renew GPU service creds secret/ai/* External Secrets 90d Model API keys secret/ai/models/* External Secrets 90d Backup encryption keys secret/backup/* Ansible, Velero 180d Root CA private key pki/root/ca (offline storage recommended) Offline only long, rotate by re-issue

docs.title: Dynamic Secrets and Rotation
docs.text:
• Database credentials: Vault DB engine issues username/password with TTL (default 24h). Application must re-read the credential on renewal. Vault has no control over apps that cache credentials forever — verify per application.
  • SSH certificates: Vault SSH signer issues short-lived certs; host/user trust against a CA. Requires sshd TrustedUserCAKeys configuration.
  • PKI: Vault PKI issues and renews certs; cert-manager consumes it. Root CA private key stored offline; intermediate held in Vault.
  • Cloud/registry: where the upstream supports dynamic tokens, use them; otherwise rotate static tokens on a schedule.
  • Revocation: revoke leases, remove policies, rotate the underlying credential. For static credentials, rotation is an external automation action (Ansible job) — not transparent to the application.
  • After compromise: revoke lease, rotate the credential at the source, re-deploy dependents, verify the new value is in use.

docs.title: Secret Delivery to Kubernetes — Comparison
docs.text:
Method Mechanism Persisted in etcd Rotation behavior App reload needed Complexity Notes Vault Agent Injector Sidecar writes file, syncs on renewal Only if app uses K8s Secret; agent uses memory/file Agent renews and rewrites file App must re-read file or SIGHUP Med Best for file-based apps Vault Agent templates (no injector) DaemonSet/Deployment writes templated file No Same Same Med Good for static config Secrets Store CSI Driver Mounts secret as file via CSI No (unless synced) Driver refreshes on renew App must re-read Med Needs Vault CSI provider External Secrets Operator Syncs Vault → K8s Secret Yes ESO refreshes on interval App must restart or reload Low Operator-agnostic; adds etcd exposure Direct app → Vault API App authenticates and reads No App handles renewal App-native Varies No extra infra; more app work K8s native Secret Plain etcd secret Yes Manual Yes Low Baseline only; no dynamic

Explicit statement: External Secrets Operator does not eliminate the etcd persistence risk. It centralizes the source of truth and rotation, but the synchronized value still lands in etcd and is readable by anyone with RBAC on that Secret in that namespace. Mitigation: namespace-scoped RBAC, separate namespaces per team, encrypt etcd at rest with a KMS-backed key, restrict get secrets audit logging.

docs.title: PKI
docs.text:
Element Owner Location Root CA (offline) Vault PKI root Encrypted Vault entry + offline backup; ideally on separate host/media Intermediate CA Vault PKI intermediate Vault only, auto-expiry renewal policy Server certs (ingress, services) cert-manager Kubernetes TLS Secrets Client certs (Vault auth, mesh) cert-manager or Vault Depends K8s internal PKI (apiserver, kubelet) Kubespray /etc/kubernetes/pki per node, rotated by Kubespray workflow

Root CA rotation: issue new intermediate from root, switch issuance, wait for leaf expiry, revoke old intermediate. This is a multi-step, downtime-sensitive process — not a one-line operation. Document the runbook in secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
• Vault backup: snapshot storage + vault operator raft snapshot save; store offline.
  • Unseal: Shamir shares offline, or auto-unseal KMS.
  • Restore runbook: secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md.
  • Recovery order: Vault first (unseal), then identity (Keycloak), then Management Cluster, then Application Clusters. Argo CD may re-sync applications once Vault is back.
  • Kubernetes backup (Velero): does not include Vault's data unless Vault runs in-cluster and its storage is included. Our model keeps Vault outside the cluster, so Vault backup is a separate, mandatory procedure.

docs.title: Monitoring and audit
docs.text:
Monitored: seal status, cluster leadership, replication health, storage usage, request latency and error rate, auth failures, lease/token expiry, certificate expiry, audit device health, backup freshness, rotation failures.

Audit: file or syslog device shipped to the logging platform. Audit logs must never contain secret values — Vault's audit log contains request/response metadata; HMAC-request-response mode is available to further protect values.

Never log: secret values, tokens, private keys, request payloads containing credentials.

Document version: 1.0 — reviewed quarterly. See compatibility/version-matrix.md for license check dates and version tracking.

docs.title: Audit Device Enablement
docs.text: Vault's audit devices are the mechanism through which all request and response data is logged. An audit device must be configured and enabled before any other Vault operations are recorded.

docs.title: Enable an Audit Device
docs.text:
# File-based audit device
audit "file" {
  path = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  mode = "0640"
}

# Socket-based audit device
audit "socket" {
  path = "/var/run/audit.sock"
  mode = "0640"
}

# Syslog-based audit device
audit "syslog" {
  mode = "0640"
  facility = "local0"
  tag = "vault-audit"
}

Enable the device via the CLI after writing the configuration:

vault audit enable file path=/var/log/vault/audit.log
vault audit enable socket path=/var/run/audit.sock
vault audit enable syslog

docs.title: Verify Audit Device is Active
docs.text:
vault audit list

Expected output includes the enabled device(s), e.g.:

Output: file            path=/var/log/vault/audit.log mode=0640
      socket            path=/var/run/audit.sock mode=0640
      syslog            mode=0640 facility=local0 tag=vault-audit

docs.title: Audit Log Storage
docs.text: Vault supports three primary audit log storage mechanisms, each suited to different deployment patterns:

docs.title: File Storage
docs.text:
• Path: Configured via the path parameter in the audit device definition
  • Format: JSON Lines (one JSON object per line) by default
  • Permissions: Set via the mode parameter (octal, e.g., 0640)
  • Best practice: Write to a dedicated, regularly rotated volume or partition
  • Example HCL:
audit "file" {
  path = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  mode = "0640"
}

docs.title: Socket Storage
docs.text:
• Path: Unix domain socket path via the path parameter
  • Format: JSON Lines, piped to a consumer process
  • Use case: Real-time streaming to log shippers (Filebeat, Fluentd, etc.)
  • Example HCL:
audit "socket" {
  path = "/var/run/audit.sock"
  mode = "0640"
}

docs.title: Syslog Storage
docs.text:
• Format: Syslog RFC 5424 over UDP/TCP
  • Facility: Configurable via the facility parameter (e.g., local0 through local7)
  • Tag: Identifies the source via the tag parameter
  • Use case: Integration with syslog-ng, rsyslog, or centralized log platforms
  • Example HCL:
audit "syslog" {
  mode = "0640"
  facility = "local0"
  tag = "vault-audit"
}

docs.title: Log Formatting
docs.text:
Vault audit logs are structured as JSON objects, one per line. Each log entry contains the following standard fields:

Field Description time ISO 8601 timestamp of the request type Request type (request, response, error) role Vault role used for the request (if applicable) token Token ID used (masked in logs by default) request_id Unique identifier for the request operation API operation invoked path API path accessed request The original request payload (sanitized based on sensitivity) response The response from Vault

docs.title: Custom Formatting with Go Templating
docs.text:
Vault supports custom log formatting via Go templating in the audit device configuration:

audit "file" {
  path    = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  template = "{{.Time}} {{.Operation}} {{.Path}}"
}

Available template fields are documented in the Vault source and include all standard log fields plus any custom fields added via response wrapping.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: Audit log retention is critical for compliance and forensic analysis. Retention strategy depends on the storage mechanism:

docs.title: File-Based Retention
docs.text:
• Rotation: Use logrotate or external log rotation system
  • Retention period: Configurable via logrotate daily/weekly/monthly cycles + maxage
  • Example logrotate configuration:
/var/log/vault/audit.log {
  daily
  rotate 90
  compress
  delaycompress
  missingok
  notifempty
  create 0640 vault vault
  postrotate
    systemctl reload rsyslog >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  endscript
}

This config retains 90 days of compressed audit logs.

docs.title: Syslog/Rsyslog Retention
docs.text:
• Configuration: /etc/rsyslog.d/vault.conf with $ActionFileDefaultTemplate and $ActionFileRetentionLimit
  • Retention: Configured per the organization's compliance requirements (typically 1-7 years)
  • Best practice: Ship logs to immutable storage before local deletion

docs.title: Immutable Retention with Object Lock
docs.text:
For compliance requirements (e.g., SOX, HIPAA, GDPR):

# Archive audit logs to S3 with Object Lock
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "org-audit-logs"
    key            = "vault/audit/${terraform.workspace}.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    encrypt        = true
    acl            = "private"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-state-lock"
    region         = "us-east-1"
  }
}

# S3 bucket policy with Object Lock
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ComplianceRetention",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:PutObjectRetention",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::org-audit-logs/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "s3:x-amz-object-lock-mode": "COMPLIANCE",
          "s3:x-amz-object-lock-retain-until-date": "2025-11-26T00:00:00Z"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This ensures audit logs cannot be deleted or modified for the retention period.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text: Audit log rotation prevents unbounded growth and maintains log usability.

docs.title: File Log Rotation
docs.text: Managed externally via logrotate (as shown above) or through the log shipping agent's built-in rotation.

docs.title: Socket Log Rotation
docs.text:
• The socket consumer (Filebeat/Metricd) should be configured with its own rotation
  • Ensure the socket path is cleaned up on rotation restart
  • Use copytruncate mode if the consumer cannot handle log replacement gracefully

docs.title: Syslog Rotation
docs.text:
• Configured via rsyslog $ActionRotateEvery and $ActionRotateMaxFiles
  • Ensure Vault's syslog process receives SIGHUP after rotation to reopen files

docs.title: Rotation Verification
docs.text:
# Check last rotation timestamp
ls -la /var/log/vault/audit.log*
# Verify log file is not growing unboundedly
watch -n 60 ls -lh /var/log/vault/audit.log

docs.title: Integration with External SIEM Systems
docs.text: Vault audit logs can be forwarded to external SIEM platforms (Splunk, Elasticsearch, Sentinel, QRadar, etc.) via several methods:

docs.title: Filebeat/Metricbeat Integration
docs.text:
# filebeat.yml
filebeat.inputs:
- type: log
  enabled: true
  paths:
    - /var/log/vault/audit.log
  json.keys_under_root: true
  json.add_error_key: true
  json.message_key: message

output.logstash:
  hosts: ["logstash.example.com:5044"]
  ssl.certificate: "/path/to/cert.crt"
  ssl.key: "/path/to/key.key"

outputelasticsearch:
  hosts: ["es.example.com:9200"]
  index: "vault-audit-%{+yyyy.MM.dd}"

docs.title: Syslog Forwarding
docs.text:
# Vault syslog configuration
audit "syslog" {
  mode    = "0640"
  facility = "local0"
  tag     = "vault-audit"
  # Additional syslib parameters can be added here
}

Configure the syslog daemon to forward local0 to the SIEM:

# rsyslog.d/vault.conf
local0.info     @@192.168.1.100:514
local0.warning  @@192.168.1.100:514
local0.err      @@192.168.1.100:514

docs.title: Direct TCP/UDP JSON Forwarding
docs.text:
# Custom template for JSON forwarding
audit "file" {
  path    = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  template = "{{.Time}}\\n"
}

Ship the file directly via Logstash, Fluentd, or custom scripts:

# Example Logstash pipeline
input {
  file {
    path => "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
    start_position => "beginning"
    sincedb_path => "/var/lib/logstash/sinldb/vault-audit"
  }
}
filter {
  json {
    source => "message"
  }
}
output {
  elasticsearch {
    hosts => ["es.example.com:9200"]
    index => "vault-audit-${+yyyy.MM.dd}"
  }
}

docs.title: HMAC-Verified Forwarding
docs.text:
For integrity validation during SIEM ingestion, compute an HMAC-SHA256 digest over each log entry and include it as a verified field:

audit_entry_hmac = hmac_sha256(key, json_encode(entry))

The HMAC key must be shared out-of-band between Vault and the SIEM ingestion pipeline.

docs.title: Audit Hash Format and HMAC Verification
Hash Format
docs.text: Each audit log entry includes a SHA-256 hash of the raw JSON line, computed over the canonical form before any forwarding modifications. This allows recipients to verify log integrity.

docs.title: HMAC Verification Procedure
docs.text:
1. Key establishment: Share an HMAC key between Vault and the SIEM pipeline via a secure channel (e.g., AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault transit, out-of-band exchange)
  2. Per-entry HMAC: For each audit log line, compute:
import hmac
import hashlib
import json

# Raw line from audit log
raw_line = '{"time":"2024-01-15T10:30:00Z","type":"request","operation":"read","path":"secret/data/app"}'

# Shared key (32 bytes minimum, base64-encoded)
key = base64.b64decode(" shared-hmac-key-base64-value==")

# Compute HMAC-SHA256
hmac_digest = hmac.new(key, raw_line.encode("utf-8"), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

print(f"hmac: {hmac_digest}")
# Output: hmac: 3a7d4e9f...

  1. Verification at SIEM: The SIEM pipeline recomputes the HMAC over the received raw line and compares against the embedded hmac field. A mismatch indicates tampering or corruption.

  2. Include HMAC in log entry (via custom template):

audit "file" {
  path    = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  template = "{{.Time}}\" hmac=\"{{hmac .Data}}\\n"
}

The {{hmac .Data}} function computes HMAC-SHA256 over the structured data. The key must be configured globally or per-audit device.

  1. Verification at rest: When archiving audit logs to immutable storage (S3 with Object Lock), also store the HMAC digest in a separate manifest file, enabling post-hoc integrity checks:
# Generate manifest
cd /archive/vault-audit
for f in *.log; do
  h=$(hmac-sha256 -k "$SHARED_KEY" "$f")
  echo "$h  $f" >> SHA256SUMS
done

docs.title: Audit Entry Structure with HMAC
docs.text:
A complete audit log entry with embedded HMAC:

{
  "time": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "type": "request",
  "role": "root",
  "token": "va_token_PxYZABc123",
  "request_id": "12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012",
  "operation": "read",
  "path": "secret/data/app",
  "request": {
    "client_token": "va_token_PxYZABc123",
    "display": "true"
  },
  "response": {
    "auth": null,
    "data": null,
    "wrap_info": null,
    "errors": null
  },
  "hmac": "3a7d4e9f8c2d1e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a"
}

The hmac field is computed over the canonical JSON representation of the entry (excluding the hmac field itself to avoid circular dependency).

docs.title: Configuration Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Audit device enabled (file, socket, or syslog) with vault audit enable
  • [ ] mode set to restrict file permissions (0640 minimum)
  • [ ] Retention policy defined (logrotate, rsyslog, or Immutable S3 Object Lock)
  • [ ] Rotation schedule configured (daily/weekly via logrotate)
  • [ ] SIEM integration configured (Filebeat, rsyslog, or direct TCP/UDP)
  • [ ] HMAC key distributed and configured for integrity verification
  • [ ] Custom log template includes hmac field if integrity verification required
  • [ ] Quarterly audit review scheduled to validate log completeness and accuracy
  • [ ] Archive protocol documented (S3 bucket with Object Lock COMPLIANCE mode, 365-day minimum)

docs.title: Raft Storage
docs.text:
HashiCorp Vault uses integrated Raft storage for high availability. The default deployment consists of 5 nodes forming a Raft quorum (3 of 5), where each node stores a full copy of the Raft log and state.

Node roles: - Active node: Handles all client requests and log replication - Standby nodes: Remaining nodes that replicate the Raft log but may or may not serve client requests depending on configuration

Quorum operations: - Write operations require majority agreement (3 of 5) across the Raft cluster - Read operations can be served by any node once the Raft state is committed - Snapshots are taken periodically and stored externally (e.g., S3, Ceph RGW)

Failure handling: - If the active node fails, one standby automatically becomes the new active node - The remaining nodes continue replication without interruption - Manual intervention is only needed if multiple nodes fail simultaneously exceeding the quorum threshold

docs.title: Auto-Unseal
docs.text:
Auto-unseal eliminates the need for manual unseal share provisioning by automating the unseal process through cloud KMS services.

Configuration types: - KMS auto-unseal: Integration with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or GCP KMS - Vault sends encrypted unseal keys to the KMS service - KMS returns the decrypted key material to Vault on startup - Configured via the auto-unseal block in the Vault configuration

  • Device auto-unseal: Hardware security modules (HSMs) or cloud-native device attestation
  • Vault uses sealed content from the HSM to auto-unseal on startup
  • Common in air-gapped environments with on-premise HSMs

Unseal key management: - Shamir's Secret Sharing: 3 of 5 shares required for manual unseal - Auto-unseal KMS: No shares needed; KMS provides the unseal key automatically - Periodic key rotation recommended for compliance

Standby nodes are configured via the ui and cluster_name settings in the Vault configuration. The active node is elected automatically through Raft, and standby nodes seamlessly take over client traffic without manual intervention.

docs.title: Standby Nodes
docs.text:
Vault HA architecture uses an active-passive model with standby nodes that provide both high availability and load distribution.

Active-Passive topology: - 1 active node: Accepts all client requests and processes leases - N-1 standby nodes: Replicate the Raft log and take over if the active node fails (in a 5-node cluster, 4 standbys)

Standby node behavior: - Standby nodes do not serve client requests under normal operation (unless configured for performance standby) - They maintain Raft state synchronization with the active node - In case of active node failure, the cluster automatically elects a new active from the standbys - State transfer is seamless; no manual intervention required for failover

Performance consideration: - Standard standby nodes reduce read load on the active node by serving stale-read queries if performance_standby is enabled - They provide redundancy without additional compute cost during normal operation - Monitoring replication lag is critical to ensuring smooth failover

docs.title: Performance Standby
docs.text:
Performance standby is a deployment pattern where standby nodes are tuned for specific workload characteristics rather than pure HA readiness.

Use cases: - Read-heavy workloads: Standby nodes can serve read-only queries, distributing read traffic - Disaster recovery: One standby can be positioned in a separate geographic region - Maintenance windows: Standby nodes can be taken offline for updates while the active node continues serving

Configuration: - Performance standbys are configured with the same Raft storage backend - They can be tuned for specific performance characteristics (CPU, memory, I/O) - Network latency between nodes should be minimized for fast failover - Metrics to monitor: Raft election latency, replication lag, CPU utilization, disk I/O

Monitoring and alerts: - Raft state health: leader, follower states, election timing - Replication lag between nodes - Seal status across all nodes - Node resource utilization (CPU, memory, disk) - Unseal progress and seal/unseal latency

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault — product decision
docs.text: Check date: 2026-10-17. The project standard is HashiCorp Vault. This file records why, which edition, what it costs, and what to do about the license.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: HashiCorp Vault is the platform standard for secrets management and PKI. OpenBao remains the documented fallback if legal rejects the license (see the licensing section), but the primary design, the runbooks, and the integrations all target HashiCorp Vault.

docs.title: Why HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
The requirement set from the master prompt §15:

Requirement Vault OpenBao SOPS / Sealed Secrets Dynamic database credentials with leases Yes (DB secrets engine) Yes No Short-lived tokens with renewal and revocation Yes Yes No SSH certificate signing Yes (SSH secrets engine) Yes No Internal PKI with issuance and rotation Yes (PKI secrets engine) Yes No Kubernetes auth method (service account tokens) Yes Yes No Audit devices with request/response logging Yes Yes No HA with quorum (Raft integrated storage) Yes Yes No Air-gapped install Yes Yes Yes Air-gapped secret injection into workloads Yes (Agent, injector, CSI) Yes (Agent, injector, CSI) Partial Enterprise-grade support contract Yes (HashiCorp) Community only No Official commercial product with a support SLA Yes No No

The deciding factors are the dynamic secrets engine, the PKI engine, and the support path. The first two are impossible with the Git-encrypted tools, and the third is a procurement question that SOPS and OpenBao cannot answer.

docs.title: Edition selection
docs.text:
Capability Vault Community (BSL) Vault Enterprise HCP Vault (hosted) Core secrets engines (KV, database, PKI, SSH, transit) Yes Yes Yes Integrated Raft storage Yes Yes Yes HA (multi-node) Yes Yes Yes (hosted) Auto-unseal (KMS, cloud) Yes Yes Yes Audit devices Yes Yes Yes Namespaces (multi-tenancy) No Yes Yes Replication No Yes Yes Performance (standalone, secondary, batch) No Yes Yes Sentinel policy-as-code No Yes No HSM / FIPS boundary support Community only Yes n/a Support contract Community Yes Yes Runs in an air-gapped environment Yes Yes No

Decision: Vault Community (self-hosted), because the platform is air-gapped and HCP Vault is a hosted service.

Two consequences to accept explicitly:

  1. Namespaces are not available. Multi-tenancy is provided by separate Vault deployments or by strict policy path separation, not by namespaces. Since Vault already runs outside the cluster on dedicated hosts (ADR-0016), running one Vault instance per trust boundary (platform, AI) is the natural way to get isolation without the Enterprise feature.
  2. Replication is not available. The disaster-recovery copy is a raft snapshot to object storage plus an offline escrow of the unseal material, not a live secondary cluster. The DR procedure in secrets-management/recovery/restore.md is written for exactly that.

Move to Vault Enterprise if the organisation needs namespaces, live replication, Sentinel, or a support SLA. The deployment model does not change: the same host topology, the same Raft storage, the same unseal procedure. Only the binary, the license file, and the feature set change.

docs.title: Licensing — what to verify and with whom
docs.text:
Fact Verified Source HashiCorp changed from MPL 2.0 to BSL 1.1 on 2023-08-10 Yes https://www.hashicorp.com/en/blog/hashicorp-adopts-business-source-license Vault 1.15.0 and later are BSL 1.1 Yes https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/blob/main/LICENSE The licensor of record is IBM Yes Same LICENSE file: "The Licensed Work is (c) 2024 IBM Corp." Internal production use is permitted Yes The Additional Use Grant permits production use that is not a "competitive offering"; "Hosting or using the Work for internal purposes within an organization is not considered a competitive offering" Each version converts to MPL 2.0 four years after its first public distribution Yes Same LICENSE file: Change Date HashiCorp's own guidance The license FAQ is the reference for edge cases https://www.hashicorp.com/license-faq

What the organization must confirm with legal before adopting:

  1. That the intended use is internal production use and not a competitive offering.
  2. Whether any part of the platform is offered to third parties (for example a managed platform sold to customers) — that would be a competitive offering and would require a commercial license.
  3. Whether the organization prefers to avoid BUSL for policy reasons, in which case OpenBao is the fallback.
  4. The commercial cost of Vault Enterprise if the Enterprise features are required.

Record the legal decision and its date in compatibility/version-matrix.md next to the Vault row, and in the ADR.

docs.title: Why the design is not hostage to the license
docs.text:
Every Vault-dependent component is designed to be portable to OpenBao:

Component Vault-specific Portable Deployment (3 hosts, Raft, TLS, offline unseal) No Yes Policies and roles (path-based) No Yes Kubernetes auth method No Yes PKI engine layout (root offline, intermediate in Vault) No Yes External Secrets Operator with a Vault provider The provider is Vault-specific The operator is vendor-neutral; a different provider is a values change Vault Agent and injector Vault-specific OpenBao provides equivalent components Backup (raft snapshot + unseal escrow) No Yes

The only genuinely Vault-specific pieces are the Consul integration and any Vault Enterprise-only feature. Neither is used in the base design.

docs.title: Version baseline
docs.text:
Item Version Status Vault Community v2.2.0 VERIFIED, https://github.com/hashicorp/vault/releases/tag/v2.2.0 Vault Helm chart 0.34.1 (app 2.0.4) VERIFIED, https://helm.releases.hashicorp.com/index.yaml vault-k8s (injector, agent) v1.7.6 VERIFIED, https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-k8s/releases OpenBao (fallback) v2.7.1 VERIFIED, https://github.com/openbao/openbao/releases

The Helm chart is the pin, not the binary: the chart's appVersion defines the Vault binary version that is deployed. Confirm the two match before an upgrade.

docs.title: What the platform uses Vault for
docs.text: Use Engine / method Notes Linux and SSH credentials KV + SSH secrets engine Short-lived, retrieved by Ansible at execution time Application secrets KV, via External Secrets Operator or the injector Never in Git Database credentials Database secrets engine Dynamic, 24h lease, renewable Internal PKI (root offline, intermediate online) PKI secrets engine cert-manager consumes the intermediate Kubernetes service identity Kubernetes auth method Short-lived projected service account tokens CI authentication JWT auth (GitLab OIDC) or AppRole JWT preferred; AppRole is the fallback Human access OIDC via Keycloak Group to policy mapping Backup encryption keys Transit secrets engine Or a KMS outside the cluster

docs.title: Operational rules for HashiCorp Vault
docs.text:
1. Vault runs on dedicated hosts outside every Kubernetes cluster (ADR-0016, ADR-0025).
  2. Unseal material is held offline, split across custodians, and tested quarterly.
  3. The root token is never used for routine access. It lives in offline escrow.
  4. Policies are path-scoped per application and per namespace. A policy that can read secret/apps/* defeats namespace isolation.
  5. Every use of the break-glass path is reviewed.
  6. Audit devices are enabled and shipped off-host. Audit logs never contain secret values.
  7. A raft snapshot is taken daily and verified; the unseal escrow is backed up separately.
  8. Vault availability is monitored, and an alert fires on seal status, leader, replication health, lease expiry, and certificate expiry.

docs.title: Deprecation and replacement plan
docs.text: Trigger Action Legal rejects BUSL Migrate to OpenBao. The deployment topology, policies, and runbooks carry over. Plan as a rebuild, not a binary swap: the data formats are compatible, but the unseal procedure and the audit device configuration must be re-verified A critical CVE in Vault Upgrade to the patched version. Vault's upgrade path is in-place; the raft snapshot is taken first Vault Community lacks a required Enterprise feature Buy Vault Enterprise. Same deployment, license file added, features enabled HCP Vault becomes acceptable (network access restored) Re-evaluate. In an air-gapped site this is not applicable The platform moves to a different secrets model entirely Re-evaluate the whole ADR-0016 decision. The external integration points (External Secrets Operator, the injector, the Ansible lookup) are the parts that must be replaced

docs.title: Quick checklist for the adoption decision
docs.text:
• [ ] Legal has reviewed BSL 1.1 and confirmed internal use is permitted, and has recorded the decision and the date.
  • [ ] The organization's requirement for Enterprise features (namespaces, replication, Sentinel, support) is confirmed.
  • [ ] The offline install path for the pinned version is mirrored and pull-verified.
  • [ ] The unseal procedure is written, tested, and the custodians are named.
  • [ ] The audit device is configured and its log is shipped off-host.
  • [ ] The snapshot and restore procedure has been executed at least once, with the measured RTO recorded.
  • [ ] The OpenBao fallback is documented in secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md with the list of Vault-specific components.

docs.title: Deliverable — Vault Kubernetes Auth Method
docs.text: Path: secrets-management/vault/k8s-auth-and-secret-delivery.md

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: HashiCorp Vault's Kubernetes auth method provides short-lived, dynamic tokens to pods running inside a Kubernetes cluster. Unlike static AppRole secrets, the Kubernetes auth method uses the cluster's service account token volume projection to obtain an JWT, which Vault validates against the Kubernetes API server's Certificate Signing Request (CSR) / token review API. This eliminates long-lived credentials from the threat model and enables per-pod, per-namespace token revocation.

docs.title: 1. Auth Role Configuration
docs.text:
An auth role is the named mapping between a Kubernetes service account and a Vault policy. Each role defines:

  • The service account(s) that may authenticate
  • The bound audience (aud) claim
  • The bound service account name (optional, for exact match)
  • The TTL and max TTL for the resulting Vault token
  • The associated Vault policy

docs.title: Example: dev-readonly auth role
docs.text:
resource "vault_kubernetes_role" "dev_readonly" {
  name = "dev-readonly"

  # The Kubernetes service account that may authenticate
  bound_service_account_name = "dev-readonly"

  # The JWT audience claim — must match what the KSA token projects
  bound audience = "vault"

  # Service accounts in any namespace that match the name
  user_claim = "kubernetes.io/serviceaccount.name"

  # TTL for the dynamically issued Vault token
  ttl = "1h"
  max_ttl = "24h"

  # Associated Vault policy name
  policy = "dev-readonly"
}

Key points:

  • bound_service_account_name enforces exact match; omit to allow any SA with the same name in any namespace.
  • user_claim controls which JWT claim maps to the identity; kubernetes.io/serviceaccount.name is standard.
  • ttl and max_ttl bound the token lifetime — short TTLs reduce the blast radius if a token is compromised.
  • The role name is arbitrary but must be referenced by in-cluster clients.

docs.title: 2. Service Account Binding
docs.text: For a pod to authenticate to Vault via the Kubernetes auth method, its container must run under a Kubernetes Service Account that is bound to the auth role.

docs.title: Steps:
docs.text:
1. Create the Service Account in the target namespace:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: dev-readonly
  namespace: production

  1. Annotate workloads to use that service account (or set serviceAccountName in the controller specification).

  2. Verify the token is projected into the pod:

$ cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjE4azEyNTY ...
  1. Test authentication using the Vault CLI:
$ VAULT_ADDR=http://vault.example.com:8200 vault write -method=kubernetes role=dev-readonly token
Success! Data returned: token=...

Best practice: Use distinct service accounts per environment (dev/staging/prod) and per workload criticality. Avoid a single shared SA across namespaces unless intentionally designing for broad access.

docs.title: 3. Secret Injection
docs.text: Once authenticated, the pod can retrieve secrets from Vault. There are three primary patterns:

docs.title: 3.1 Injector (init-container) Pattern
docs.text:
An init-container calls vault kv get (or the Vault Agent sidecar) and writes secrets into a K8s Secret or environment variables.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app-with-injector
spec:
  serviceAccountName: dev-readonly
  initContainers:
    - name: inject-secrets
      image: hashicorp/vault:1.16
      command: ["sh", "-c", "vault kv get secret/app-config | jq -r '.data.data | to_entries[] | \"\(.key)=\(.value)\"' > /etc/secrets/env && env -i env")
      volumeMounts:
        - name: etc-secrets
          mountPath: /etc/secrets
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: app-config

docs.title: 3.2 Sidecar Pattern (Vault Agent Injector)
docs.text:
The Vault Agent Injector (admission controller) automatically injects a sidecar container that runs vault agent with a configured template. The sidecar fetches secrets and refreshes them lease-bound.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: app-with-sidecar
spec:
  serviceAccountName: dev-readonly
  vault:
    injector:
      enabled: true
      # Configuration injected by the Helm chart / admission webhook
    sidecar:
      containerName: vault
      image: hashicorp/vault:1.16
      resources:
        limits: 100m 200Mi
      env:
        - name: VAULT_ADDR
          value: "http://vault:8200"
      # Template renders secrets as files or env vars
      volumeMounts:
        - name: vault-secret
          mountPath: /vault/secrets
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:latest
      volumeMounts:
        - name: vault-secret
          mountPath: /etc/app/secrets
  volumes:
    - name: vault-secret
      emptyDir: {}

Result: The app container reads secrets from /etc/app/secrets — files auto-updated by the sidecar as leases renew.

docs.title: 3.3 External Secrets Operator (ESO)
docs.text:
ESO bridges Vault to K8s native Secrets. It synchronizes Vault KV paths into K8s Secret objects, which applications consume normally.

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: app-config-secret
spec:
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: Vault
    name: vault-secret-store
    namespace: vault
  target:
    name: app-config
  data:
    - secretPath: secret/infra/app/config
      literalPath: ""

Advantage: No application code changes; standard K8s Secret workflows apply. Trade-off: One layer of abstraction; ESO must be configured with the correct Vault auth method.

docs.title: 4. Sidecar Injection Details
docs.text:
The Vault Agent sidecar performs these functions:

  1. Authenticate using the projected KSA token via the Kubernetes auth method.
  2. Fetch secrets from the configured Vault KV path.
  3. Render templates — either write secret data as files or export as environment variables.
  4. Refresh leases periodically before expiry, using the same auth token (no re-login needed while the token is valid).
  5. Rotate on TTL approach — as the Vault token TTL nears expiry, the sidecar re-authenticates with the KSA token to obtain a fresh token.

docs.title: Sidecar resource template example:
docs.text:
# Template: renders secret data as file content
{{- $path := "secret/infra/app/config" -}}
{{- $secret := kv $path -}}
{{- range $key, $value := .data.data -}}
{{- $key | trimSuffix \".\" }}: {{ $value | quote }}
{{- end }}

This template, combined with the sidecar's volume mount, produces a file like /vault/secrets/config that the application reads.

docs.title: 5. Secret Delivery Patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Use Case Advantages Considerations Init-container injector One-time setup, CI/CD pipelines, ephemeral jobs No persistent sidecar; simple for short-lived workloads Secrets written at pod start only; not auto-refreshed Vault Agent sidecar Long-running services needing auto-rotation Transparent refresh; lease-aware; file or env output Requires admission controller or Helm; adds a sidecar resource External Secrets Operator Standard K8s Secret consumers, multi-cluster Uses native K8s Secret API; no app code changes ESO component adds another control plane; sync latency Volume projection Config as files, not env vars Secrets appear as regular files; apps read FILE env vars pointing to mount paths Requires app to read files instead of env; mount propagation delays

Recommended default: Use the Vault Agent sidecar for long-running workloads (deployments, stateful sets) and ESO for stateless services or migrations. Reserve init-container injection for CI/CD and batch jobs.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Fix Error response from daemon: failed to setup child process Vault Agent sidecar can't reach K8s API server Ensure the pod's SA has aggregate-cluster-admin-reader or equivalent; check RBAC authentication failure: cannot parse token SA token not projected or wrong bound_service_account_name Verify serviceAccountName on the workload; inspect the projected token Secrets not refreshing Vault token TTL expired; sidecar re-auth failed Check Vault Agent logs; ensure KSA token is still valid and not revoked 403 for permission denied Vault policy doesn't allow the role's path Attach the correct Vault policy to the auth role; verify policy field

docs.text:

  • Vault Agent Injector Helm chart: https://github.com/hashicorp/vault-helm/tree/main/charts/vault

  • Kubernetes Service Account token volumes: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-service-account/

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Vault's PKI secrets engine provides a certificate authority (CA) capable of signing X.509 certificates. This document covers the full lifecycle: root and intermediate CA configuration, certificate issuance, revocation, CRL distribution, role management, and rotation procedures.

docs.title: Root CA Configuration
docs.text: The root CA is the trust anchor. The root CA private key must never leave offline storage. Intermediate CAs derive trust from the root and handle day-to-day certificate issuance.

docs.title: Initial Root CA Setup
docs.text:
# Enable PKI secrets engine at path 'pki'
vault secrets enable pki

# Configure root CA with 10-year validity
vault write pki/root/generate/internal \
  common_name="cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=87600h \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096

# Root CA is now live; immediately disable automatic issuance
vault write pki/roles/root-ca \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=true \
  max_ttl=87600h

docs.title: Root CA Export and Offline Storage
docs.text:
# Export the root CA certificate
vault read -field=certificate pki/root/cert > root-ca.crt

# Export the root CA private key (PEM, encrypted)
vault read -field=private_key pki/root/key > root-ca-key.enc

# Store root-ca-key.enc in offline hardware security module or encrypted vault secret
# Store root-ca.crt in a secure offline location (e.g., air-gapped HSM, encrypted USB)

docs.title: Root Key Rotation
docs.text:
Root key rotation is a multi-step, downtime-sensitive process:

  1. Generate a new root CA using vault write pki/root/generate/internal
  2. Issue a new intermediate CA from the new root
  3. Update all intermediate CA roles to point to the new intermediate
  4. Wait for all existing certificates to expire before decommissioning the old root
  5. Revoke the old intermediate and rotate it out

Document the runbook in secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md.

docs.title: Intermediate CA Configuration
docs.text: Intermediate CAs sign end-entity certificates and serve as the operational CA. They can be strict (only sign roles explicitly assigned) or permissive (sign any certificate within the role's path).

docs.title: Enable Intermediate CA
docs.text:
# Generate a new intermediate CA signed by the root
vault write pki/intermediate/generate/internal \
  common_name="cloud-native-guide Intermediate CA" \
  ttl=87600h \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096

docs.title: Intermediate CA Registration with Root
docs.text:
# Download the root CA certificate for CSR signing
vault read -field=certificate pki/root/cert > root-ca.crt

# Register the intermediate CA with the root
vault write pki/intermediate/set-signed \
  signing_cert=@root-ca.crt \
  csr=pki_intermediate_csr.csr

docs.title: Intermediate CA Roles
docs.text:
Define roles that map certificate fields to paths where certificates are stored.

# Strict role: only signs certificates with exact SAN matching
vault write pki/roles/server-api \
  domains="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=8760h \
  max_ttl=87600h \
  allow_subdomains=false \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=true \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096 \
  path_length=0 \
  sans="DNS:api.cloud-native-guide.internal"

# Permissive wildcard role for internal services
vault write pki/roles/internal-service \
  domains="*.internal.cloud-native-guide" \
  ttl=72h \
  max_ttl=8760h \
  allow_subdomains=true \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=true \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=2048 \
  path_length=1

docs.title: CRL Distribution Point
docs.text:
Configure where the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) is published:

# Enable CRL generation
vault write pki/crl/set \
  crl_distribution_points="http://pki.crl.cloud-native-guide.internal/crl.pem"

# Set CRL expiry (default is 24h; adjust per policy)
vault write pki/crl/set \
  expiry="24h"

docs.title: Issue a Certificate
docs.text:
# Issue a certificate for the server-api role
vault write pki/issue server-api \
  common_name="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  alt_names="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=8760h

docs.title: Certificate Output
docs.text:
The above command returns:

{
  "request": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----
",
  "certificate": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
",
  "serial_number": "196604",
  "ca_chain": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
"
}

docs.title: Revoke a Certificate
docs.text:
# Revoke a specific certificate by serial number
vault write pki/revoke serial="196604"

# Revoke all certificates matching a pattern
vault write pki/revoke prefix="0x1234"

docs.title: Revocation List (CRL)
docs.text:
After revocation, the CRL must be refreshed:

# Force CRL regeneration
vault write pki/crl/set

# Verify the CRL includes the revoked serial
vault read pki/crl

docs.title: List All Roles
docs.text: vault list pki/roles/

docs.title: Read Role Configuration
docs.text: vault read pki/roles/server-api

docs.title: Update Role
docs.text:
# Add a new SAN
vault write pki/roles/server-api \
  altnames="DNS:api2.cloud-native-guide.internal"

# Change TTL
vault write pki/roles/server-api ttl=48h

docs.title: Delete Role
docs.text: vault delete pki/roles/deprecated-role

docs.title: Role Best Practices
docs.text: Practice Recommendation client_flag Set to false unless client auth is needed server_flag Set to true for server TLS certificates allow_subdomains false for exact matching; true for wildcards key_bits Minimum 4096 for root; 2048 acceptable for intermediates path_length Limit chain depth; 0 for end-entity, 1 for one intermediate ttl Align with application rotation cadence (hours to days)

docs.title: Automated Rotation (cert-manager Integration)
docs.text:
When using cert-manager with the Vault PKI issuer:

apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Issuer
metadata:
  name: vault-pki
  namespace: cert-manager
spec:
  vault:
    server: "https://vault.cloud-native-guide.internal:8200"
    path: "pki/issue/server-api"
    secretName: vault-tls-secret
    ttl: "8760h"
    maxTTL: "87600h"
    clientCertificateFile: "/certs/client.root.ca.crt"
    clientKeyFile: "/certs/client.root.ca.key"

docs.title: Manual Rotation
docs.text:
1. Issue new certificate from the same or updated role
  2. Deploy the new certificate to the target service
  3. Update service configuration to use the new cert
  4. Revoke the old certificate once the new one is confirmed valid
  5. Wait for certificate expiry before cleaning up old roles/CRL entries

docs.title: Rotation Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] New certificate issued with correct SANs and expiry
  • [ ] Certificate deployed and service validated
  • [ ] Old certificate revoked via vault write pki/revoke
  • [ ] CRL regenerated and published
  • [ ] All clients updated to use new certificate
  • [ ] Old certificate removed from trust stores
  • [ ] Rotation documented and dated

docs.title: Rotation Schedules
docs.text: Component Recommended Rotation Trigger Root CA private key Annually or after compromise Security incident, key expiration Intermediate CA certificate Every 1–2 years Expiry, policy change Service server certificates Per application cycle or 30–90 days Expiry, compliance CRL Every 24 hours (configurable) Automatic Vault PKI roles As needed when service topology changes Topology change, role deprecation

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix "no valid certificate found" SAN mismatch or role misconfiguration Verify domains and altnames in role; check common_name CRL not updating CRL expiry too long or publication path inaccessible Reduce CRL expiry; verify web server serving CRL Certificate revocation not taking effect Client caching old CRL Reduce CRL cache time; force CRL reload "max path length exceeded" path_length set too high in role Lower path_length; restructure CA hierarchy Intermediate CA not signing Intermediate not registered with root Run vault write pki/intermediate/set-signed

docs.title: Debug Commands
docs.text:
# Check current CRL
vault read pki/crl

# List all active roles
vault list pki/roles/

# Show role details
vault read pki/roles/<role-name>

# Check active certifications
vault list pki/certs/

docs.title: Root CA Creation
docs.text: The root CA is the trust anchor of the entire PKI hierarchy. The root CA private key must never leave offline storage — it should be generated in an air-gapped environment and stored in an HSM or encrypted offline vault secret.

docs.title: Initial Root CA Setup (online, in Vault)
docs.text:
# Enable PKI secrets engine at path 'pki'
vault secrets enable pki

# Configure root CA with 10-year validity (adjust per cryptographic policy)
vault write pki/root/generate/internal \
  common_name="cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=87600h \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096

# Root CA is now live; immediately disable automatic issuance
# by creating a role that does not automatically sign certificates
vault write pki/roles/root-ca \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=false \
  max_ttl=87600h

docs.title: Root CA Export and Offline Storage
docs.text:
# Export the root CA certificate (PEM format)
vault read -field=certificate pki/root/cert > root-ca.crt

# Export the root CA private key (PEM, encrypted — password set separately)
vault read -field=private_key pki/root/key > root-ca-key.enc

# Store root-ca-key.enc in offline hardware security module or encrypted vault secret
# Store root-ca.crt in a secure offline location (e.g., air-gapped HSM, encrypted USB)

# Verify the exported key matches what Vault holds
openssl rsa -in root-ca-key.enc -check -noout 2>&1

docs.title: Root Key Rotation Prerequisites
docs.text: See secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md for the full rotation runbook. The root key rotation process is multi-step and downtime-sensitive — do not attempt it without reading that document first.

docs.title: Intermediate CA Hierarchy
docs.text: Intermediate CAs sign end-entity certificates and serve as the operational CA. They can be strict (only sign roles explicitly assigned) or permissive (sign any certificate within the role's path).

docs.title: Enable Intermediate CA (signed by root)
docs.text:
# Generate a new intermediate CA signed by the root
vault write pki/intermediate/generate/internal \
  common_name="cloud-native-guide Intermediate CA" \
  ttl=87600h \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096

docs.title: Intermediate CA Registration with Root
docs.text:
# Download the root CA certificate for CSR signing
vault read -field=certificate pki/root/cert > root-ca.crt

# Register the intermediate CA with the root
vault write pki/intermediate/set-signed \
  signing_cert=@root-ca.crt \
  csr=pki_intermediate_csr.csr

docs.title: Intermediate CA Roles
docs.text:
Define roles that map certificate fields to paths where certificates are stored.

# Strict role: only signs certificates with exact SAN matching
vault write pki/roles/server-api \
  domains="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=8760h \
  max_ttl=87600h \
  allow_subdomains=false \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=true \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=4096 \
  path_length=0 \
  sans="DNS:api.cloud-native-guide.internal"

# Permissive wildcard role for internal services
vault write pki/roles/internal-service \
  domains="*.internal.cloud-native-guide" \
  ttl=72h \
  max_ttl=8760h \
  allow_subdomains=true \
  client_flag=false \
  server_flag=true \
  key_type=rsa \
  key_bits=2048 \
  path_length=1

docs.title: CRL Distribution Point
docs.text:
Configure where the Certificate Revocation List (CRL) is published:

# Enable CRL generation
vault write pki/crl/set \
  crl_distribution_points="http://pki.crl.cloud-native-guide.internal/crl.pem"

# Set CRL expiry (default is 24h; adjust per policy)
vault write pki/crl/set \
  expiry="24h"

docs.title: Certificate Issuance
docs.text:
# Issue a certificate for the server-api role
vault write pki/issue server-api \
  common_name="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  alt_names="api.cloud-native-guide.internal" \
  ttl=8760h

docs.title: Certificate Output
docs.text:
The above command returns JSON with the certificate, request, serial number, and CA chain:

{
  "request": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE REQUEST-----
",
  "certificate": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
",
  "serial_number": "196604",
  "ca_chain": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----
"
}

docs.title: Issuance Restrictions by Role
docs.text: Practice Recommendation client_flag Set to false unless client auth is needed server_flag Set to true for server TLS certificates allow_subdomains false for exact matching; true for wildcards key_bits Minimum 4096 for root; 2048 acceptable for intermediates path_length Limit chain depth; 0 for end-entity, 1 for one intermediate ttl Align with application rotation cadence (hours to days)

docs.title: Revoke a Specific Certificate
docs.text:
# Revoke a specific certificate by serial number
vault write pki/revoke serial="196604"

docs.title: Revoke All Certificates Matching a Pattern
docs.text:
# Revoke all certificates matching a serial prefix
vault write pki/revoke prefix="0x1234"

docs.title: Refresh CRL After Revocation
docs.text:
After revocation, the CRL must be refreshed so all clients pick up the change:

# Force CRL regeneration
vault write pki/crl/set

# Verify the CRL includes the revoked serial
vault read pki/crl

docs.title: Revocation Best Practices
docs.text:
• Revoke certificates only when compromise is confirmed or access must be immediately terminated
  • After revoking, always refresh the CRL and verify it propagates
  • Clients may cache CRLs — reduce CRL cache TTL or force a CRL reload
  • Do not revoke the old intermediate before all leaves under it have expired (see root CA rotation runbook)

docs.title: Root CA Rotation Procedures
docs.text: Root key rotation is a multi-step, downtime-sensitive process. See secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md for the complete runbook.

docs.title: High-Level Rotation Flow
docs.text:
1. Prepare. Generate the new root key and self-signed root certificate offline. Record the custodian, storage location, and serial number. Do not touch the running intermediate yet.

  2. Distribute trust. Add the new root certificate to every trust store that validates platform certificates — nodes, ingress clients, and any external system that pins the chain. Both roots are trusted at this point.

  3. Issue the new intermediate. From the new root, issue an intermediate and import it into Vault's PKI engine alongside the old one.

  4. Switch issuance. Point the cert-manager ClusterIssuer at the new intermediate. New certificates now chain to the new root; existing ones still chain to the old.

  5. Wait for leaf expiry. Keep the old intermediate and old root trusted until the longest-lived certificate issued under the old chain has expired. Do not revoke the old intermediate before this point, or every unexpired certificate becomes invalid at once.

  6. Retire. Revoke the old intermediate, remove the old root from trust stores, and archive the old root key according to the retention policy.

docs.title: Critical: Steps 2 and 5 are the long poles
docs.text:
• Skipping step 2 breaks every client that has not yet learned the new root
  • Skipping step 5 causes an outage when the old intermediate is revoked

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Issuer now points at the new intermediate
kubectl get clusterissuer -o yaml | grep -A3 vault

# Newly issued certificate chains to the new root
kubectl get certificate -A

# Validate the full chain
openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates

# Old root still trusted during the transition (expected until step 6)
openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt <leaf>.pem

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
• Before step 6: Rollback is a configuration change — point the ClusterIssuer back at the old intermediate.
  • After step 6: Rollback requires re-trusting the old root and re-issuing under the old intermediate — treat it as a new rotation, not a revert.

docs.title: Record Keeping
docs.text: Record in the change ticket: - Old and new root serials - Intermediate serials - The date each trust store was updated - The expiry date of the last certificate issued under the old chain - The date the old root was removed from trust stores
