docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Vault policy management: policy creation, policy assignment, token policies, API method restrictions, path-based access control, and policy auditing.

Cross-references secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md, secrets-management/vault/access-control.md, secrets-management/vault/secret-rotation.md, kubernetes/security/security-controls.md.

docs.title: B. Policy creation
docs.text:
Policies are HCL-based and define what capabilities a principal has at which paths.

# policy/readonly.hcl
path "secret/data/platform/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

path "secret/data/secrets/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

# policy/admin.hcl
path "sys/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/seal/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/mounts/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/config/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/audit/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/auth/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

path "sys/cubbyhole/*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

docs.title: C. Policy assignment
docs.text:
Policies are attached to named roles via auth methods. A role maps a principal (e.g., a Kubernetes service account) to a policy.

# Write policies
vault policy write readonly policy/readonly.hcl
vault policy write admin policy/admin.hcl

# Create a Kubernetes auth role with policy assignment
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/platform-app \
  bound_service_account_names=platform-app \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=platform \
  policies=readonly \
  ttl=24h

# Create an admin role
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/admin-app \
  bound_service_account_names=admin-app \
  bound_service_account_namespaces=admin \
  policies=admin \
  ttl=1h

Token policies can also be specified at token creation time.

# Create token with specific policy and TTL
vault token create -policy=readonly -ttl=1h -max-ttl=24h

# Create token with multiple policies
vault token create -policy=readonly -policy=admin -ttl=1h

docs.title: D. Token policies
docs.text:
Tokens carry policies that define their capabilities. Token policies control:

  • TTL and max TTL: How long the token is valid
  • Num uses: Number of times the token can be used
  • Display name: Human-readable token name
  • Policy: Attached policies that grant capabilities
  • No wrap: Whether the token can be wrapped
  • Period: Renewal period for the token

Token accessor and review:

# Review current token's policies and TTL
vault token lookup -self

# Revoke a token
vault token revoke <token-id>

# Revoke all tokens for a specific policy
vault token revoke -policy=readonly

docs.title: E. API method restrictions
docs.text:
Policy capabilities map to Vault API methods. The principle of least privilege applies: grant only the methods needed for the principal's function.

Capability API Methods read GET, HEAD create POST update PUT, POST delete DELETE list LIST sudo Full access (bypasses policy)

Example restricting to read-only access at specific paths:

path "secret/data/*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}

# Deny specific paths even at higher levels
path "secret/data/credentials/*" {
  capabilities = []
}

docs.title: F. Path-based access control
docs.text:
Path-based access control is the primary mechanism for restricting Vault access. Patterns support:

  • Exact match: secret/data/db-passwords
  • Wildcard: secret/data/* matches all data under secret/data/
  • Recursive wildcard: secret/** matches all paths recursively
  • Negation: Empty capabilities [] denies access

Best practices for path-based access control:

  1. Start least-privilege: Begin with [] (no access) and only add needed capabilities
  2. Use specific paths: secret/data/platform/* rather than secret/data/*
  3. Separate environments: secret/data/prod/*, secret/data/staging/*, secret/data/dev/*
  4. Audit-sensitive paths: Restrict sys/ and auth/ paths to operational roles only

Example: Environment-separated policies

# Policy for production
path "secret/data/prod/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

path "secret/data/prod/*" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
  # Limited update scope
}

# Policy for staging
path "secret/data/staging/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list", "update"]
}

# Policy for development
path "secret/data/dev/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list", "create", "update", "delete"]
}

docs.title: G. Policy auditing
docs.text:
Audit policies track who accessed what, when, and from where. Enable audit devices and define audit policies to control logging.

# List existing audit devices
vault audit list

# Enable audit device (file example)
vault audit enable file filePath=/var/log/vault/audit.log

# Enable audit device (syslog example)
vault audit enable syslog address="syslog://localhost:514"

# Write audit policy that logs all methods
audit "file" {
  file_path = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  # Log all requests
  style = "log"
}

Audit log best practices:

  • Ship audit logs to immutable, centralized storage
  • Retain audit logs per compliance requirements (1-7 years minimum)
  • Never log secret values — metadata only
  • Use HMAC-request-response mode for additional value protection
  • Configure alerting on: failed auth, policy changes, unexpected path access, privilege escalation

Example audit policy logging all requests:

# audit/logging.hcl
path "*" {
  capabilities = ["create", "read", "update", "delete", "list"]
}

docs.title: Rotation Schedule
docs.text:
Secret Category Path Pattern Rotation Frequency Method Database credentials database/creds/* Every 24 hours (dynamic TTL) Vault DB engine auto-issues with lease; application must re-read on renewal SSH certificates secret/infra/ssh/* Every 90 days or on use Vault SSH signer issues short-lived certs; host trusts against CA PKI certificates pki/issue/* 30 days, auto-renew via cert-manager Vault PKI issues/renews certs; cert-manager consumes Cloud/registry static tokens secret/registry/* Every 90 days Rotate via automation; upstream may support dynamic tokens Application secrets secret/apps/* Every 30 days External Secrets Operator sync; re-read or restart required Monitoring credentials secret/observability/* Every 90 days External Secrets rotation on interval Keycloak client secrets secret/identity/* Every 90 days Ansible or External Secrets rotation Backup encryption keys secret/backup/* Every 180 days Ansible / Velero rotation Linux/root credentials secret/infra/linux/* Every 90 days Ansible fetch at runtime SSH keys secret/infra/ssh/* Every 90 days / on use Ansible + Vault SSH agent signing Kubespray bootstrap creds secret/infra/kubespray/* Every 90 days Ansible vault lookup Argo CD repo creds secret/gitops/* Every 90 days Argo CD repo API (not stored in Git) GPU service creds secret/ai/* Every 90 days External Secrets Model API keys secret/ai/models/* Every 90 days External Secrets Ceph keys secret/infra/ceph/* Every 180 days Ansible -> Ceph Root CA private key pki/root/ca Long duration; rotate by re-issue Offline only; multi-step process — document runbook in secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md

General TTL defaults: Unless otherwise specified, all Vault dynamic secrets use a 24-hour default TTL with a 75% renewal window. Static credentials rotated on schedule use the frequencies above.

docs.title: Automated Rotation Workflow
docs.text:
The automated rotation pipeline is triggered by Vault's native TTL/expiry mechanism and validated by CI/CD checks. Steps:

  1. Lease expiry — Vault dynamic secrets expire according to their configured TTL. The application or external system must renew or fetch a new secret.

  2. External Secrets Operator (ESO) sync — For static secrets managed by ESO, the sync interval (default 5m) detects the changed secret value and updates the Kubernetes Secret. If the secret has a short TTL, configure ESO's refreshInterval to match.

  3. Ansible automation — For secret categories managed by Ansible (Linux creds, SSH keys, Ceph keys, backup keys), run the rotation playbook:

ansible-playbook -i inventory.yaml rotate-secrets.yml \
  --extra-vault "vault_address=https://vault.example.com:8200" \
  --extra-vault-token "$VAULT_TOKEN"

The playbook performs: - Reads the current secret from Vault - Generates a new value at the source (DB, KMS, certificate authority) - Writes the new secret to Vault (vault kv put) - Updates dependent configurations (K8s Secrets, config files) - Commits changes to the appropriate repo (if applicable)

  1. CI/CD gate — Every PR that modifies secret paths must pass:
  2. checkov — infrastructure policy check for any IaC changes
  3. gitleaks — secret detection to prevent new credentials from being committed

  4. trivy — container image vulnerability scan if the rotation involves container images

  5. Health validation — After rotation, a smoke test verifies the dependent service can read the new secret without errors. If the service requires a restart or SIGHUP, the rotation pipeline blocks until the restart completes.

  6. Rollback — If the new secret fails validation within the 24-hour window, revert to the previous value:

# Restore previous secret version
vault kv put secret/infra/linux/app-key @previous_version
# Or restore from backup
ansible-playbook -i inventory.yaml restore-secrets.yml

docs.title: Manual Rotation Steps
docs.text: Manual rotation is required when automated rotation is unavailable (static credentials, upstream services without dynamic support, or after compromise).

docs.title: General Manual Rotation Flow
docs.text:
1. Pre-rotation preparation
  2. Document the current secret value and its usage
  3. Identify all consumers of the secret
  4. Schedule a maintenance window

  5. Ensure rollback procedure is ready

  6. Generate new credential

  7. For database credentials: use vault read -field=password database/creds/<role> and rotate at the source (e.g., RDS master password reset)
  8. For API keys: generate a new key from the upstream provider (AWS IAM user, GCP service account, etc.)

  9. For SSH keys: generate a new key pair and replace the CA-signed certificate

  10. Write new secret to Vault 

    # Example: rotating a static credential
vault kv put secret/infra/linux/app-key value=new-credential value=old-credential  # keep old as version label

Or for dynamic secrets: 

vault lease renew database/creds/myapp  # renew or extend TTL

  1. Update consumers
  2. Kubernetes Secrets — if managed by ESO, the sync will pick up the change. Otherwise, update the Secret manually: 
    kubectl delete secret <secret-name> && kubectl create secret generic <secret-name> --from-literal=key=new-credential
  3. Application config — if the app reads from a file or environment, update the source and restart/reload the pod

  4. Ansible/automation — update the inventory/group_vars to reference the new path/key

  5. Post-rotation verification

  6. Verify the new secret works: vault read secret/infra/linux/app-key
  7. Confirm no downtime: application logs show successful authentication with new credential

  8. Run the health smoke test from the CI/CD pipeline

  9. Cleanup

  10. Revoke the old Vault lease: vault lease revoke database/creds/myapp
  11. Remove old version labels from the secret if using versioned storage
  12. Update documentation with rotation date and operator

docs.title: Audit Logging Requirements
docs.text:
All secret rotation events must be captured in Vault's audit log and shipped to the centralized logging platform. The following fields must be structured and retained for minimum 365 days (compliance mode):

Field Example Requirement rotation_date 2024-02-15T14:30:00Z Mandatory secret_path secret/infra/linux/app-key Mandatory secret_category linux-credentials Mandatory rotated_by automation or operator or manual Mandatory rotation_method ttl-expiry, manual-rotation, post-compromise Mandatory old_lease_id vaultokv/2 Mandatory for dynamic secrets new_lease_id vaultokv/3 Mandatory for dynamic secrets trigger scheduled, expiry, compromise, admin-request Mandatory status success, failed Mandatory error_message (if failed) Conditional consumers_updated k8s-secret/frontend, k8s-secret/backend Recommended rollback_performed true/false Recommended

Audit log configuration — Ensure Vault has an audit device configured (file or syslog) with the following minimum settings in hcl.hcl or via vault audit:

audit "file" {
  path = "/var/log/vault/audit.log"
  mode = "0640"
}

Shipping to centralized platform — The audit log file must be tailed by Filebeat/Metricbeat and shipped to the SIEM/logging platform. Configure rotation of the audit log itself so it does not fill the disk.

Immutable retention — The S3 bucket storing archived audit logs (if applicable) must have Object Lock in COMPLIANCE mode with 365-day retention, matching the compliance requirement.

Quarterly audit review — Security team reviews a random sample of rotation events each quarter to verify: - All required fields are present - No secret values appear in the audit log (metadata only) - Rotation frequencies match the schedule - Failed rotations are investigated and resolved

docs.title: Automated Rotation
docs.text:
Automated rotation uses Vault's rotation feature with custom scripts:

# Rotate a secret automatically
vault write -field=value secret/rotation/trigger \
  secret_name=prod/db-credentials \
  rotation_interval=2592000  # 30 days in seconds

Automated rotation workflow: 1. Pre-rotation check: Validate secret health, check dependent services 2. Generate new credentials: Create new secret via provider API 3. Update consumers: Write new secret to Vault, update dependent configs 4. Rotate in Vault: vault rotate command updates the secret version 5. Post-rotation validation: Verify new credentials work, deprecate old ones 6. Cleanup: Remove old version after retention period

docs.title: Supported Rotation Types
docs.text:
• Database credentials: Rotate via native database authentication APIs
  • API keys: Generate new key, update routing, depracate old
  • Service tokens: Rotate HMAC keys, update service configs
  • SSH keys: Generate key pair, update authorized_keys, rotate old

docs.title: Manual Rotation
docs.text:
Manual rotation for emergencies or automated failures:

# Step 1: Generate new credentials
# (via provider console, API, or kms command)

# Step 2: Store in Vault
vault kv put secret/prod/db-credentials \
  username=new_user \
  password=new_password \
  rotation_allowed=true

# Step 3: Update dependent services
# (restart pods, update configs, notify teams)

# Step 4: Mark old secret as deprecated
vault kv metadata touch secret/prod/db-credentials \
  --deletion-after=2592000

# Step 5: Remove after verification period
vault kv delete secret/prod/db-credentials

Manual rotation checklist: - [ ] New credentials generated and tested - [ ] All consumers updated before old secret invalidation - [ ] Team notified of rotation - [ ] Old secret marked for deletion with retention window - [ ] Audit log verified for complete chain of custody

docs.title: Audit Logging
docs.text:
All rotation actions are logged to Vault's audit devices:

{
  "time": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "type": "rotation",
  "actor": "team-db",
  "action": "automated_rotation",
  "secret": "prod/db-credentials",
  "version": "2",
  "status": "success",
  "details": "Rotated from v1 to v2, 0 consumers failed"
}

docs.title: Audit Device Configuration
docs.text:
# Audit device config for rotation logging
audit "file" {
  path    = "/var/log/vault/audit.json"
  type    = "json"
  format  = "logfmt"
}

docs.title: Required Audit Fields
docs.text:
• actor: Who initiated the rotation (user or automation)
  • action: Type of rotation (automated, manual, emergency)
  • secret: Fully qualified secret path
  • version: Secret version before/after rotation
  • status: success/failed
  • details: Contextual information (duration, errors, affected services)

docs.title: Log Retention
docs.text:
• Minimum 90 days rotation history
  • Immutable storage for compliance audits
  • Searchable by secret path, actor, and date range
  • Exported to SIEM for correlation with access events

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Vault unseal recovery mechanisms: Shamir's Secret Sharing, auto-unseal with KMS, recovery key management, emergency unseal procedures, and unseal key rotation. This is step 1 of the recovery order defined in lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — all other components depend on Vault for secrets.

Cross-references: secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md, secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md, secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md.

docs.title: 1. Shamir's Secret Sharing (manual unseal)
docs.text:
Vault uses Shamir's Secret Sharing to split the master key into N shares, requiring M-of-N shares to reconstruct the key and unseal Vault.

  • Parameters: Typically 5 shares with 3-of-5 threshold (3 shares required to unseal)
  • Share storage: Shares are stored offline by separate custodians — hardware security modules, physical safes, or trusted individuals
  • No single point of failure: Any 3 of the 5 shares can unseal Vault, but no 2 shares reveal any information about the master key
  • Cryptographic security: Each share is a point on the polynomial; 2 shares define a line, but 3+ shares are needed to determine the constant term (the master key)
# Unseal Vault with a single share
vault operator unseal <share-value>

# Example: Unseal all 3 required shares
vault operator unseal share-1
vault operator unseal share-2
vault operator unseal share-3

docs.title: 2. Auto-unseal with KMS
docs.text:
Auto-unseal delegates unseal key management to a cloud KMS, eliminating manual share handling.

  • AWS KMS: Configured via vault operator init and vault operator unseal with KMS ARNs
  • Azure Key Vault: Integration via vault operator unseal with Azure Key URI
  • Google Cloud KMS: Integration via vault operator unseal with Cloud KMS key reference
  • Benefits: No offline share storage required; unseal happens automatically on restart; integrates with IAM for access control
  • Considerations: KMS must remain available; loss of KMS access = loss of Vault availability; ensure redundancy of KMS keys across regions
# Initialize Vault with auto-unseal (AWS KMS example)
vault operator init \
  -key-shares=5 \
  -key-threshold=3 \
  -root-token-ttl=1h \
  -unseal-kms-arn arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/abc123

docs.title: Key share storage
docs.text: Method Description Risk Offline physical Printed shares in sealed envelopes, stored in separate locations Theft, physical loss HSM-protected Shares encrypted and stored in Hardware Security Modules HSM compromise, single point Cloud KMS Shares encrypted under KMS keys; KMS auto-unseal KMS outage, IAM misconfiguration Split knowledge Multiple custodians, each holds one share; no single person has enough Custody disputes, accessibility

docs.title: Rotating unseal keys
docs.text:
Rotate unseal keys when: - A custodian departs and their share is suspected compromised - M-of-N threshold changes (e.g., 3-of-5 → 4-of-6) - KMS key rotation policy requires it - Security incident involving share storage

Rotation procedure:

  1. Add new shares: Use vault operator init with new shares or vault operator unseal to add additional shares
  2. Remove old shares: Once new shares are verified, securely erase old shares from storage
  3. Verify: Confirm Vault starts and remains unsealed with the new key material
  4. Document: Update this file and the key custody log with rotation date and custodian changes
# Add a new unseal share (requires existing quorum)
vault operator unseal <new-share-value>

# After all new shares are added and verified, remove old shares
# securely erase old share storage media

docs.title: Standard emergency unseal
docs.text:
When Vault restarts and auto-unseal is unavailable:

  1. Locate share storage: Retrieve 3 of 5 stored shares from custodians
  2. Unseal each Vault node: Run vault operator unseal <share> on each pod
  3. Verify status: vault status should show Sealed: false
  4. Restore access: Users can authenticate; secrets are readable

docs.title: Partial unseal (node-specific)
docs.text:
If only some nodes are sealed (e.g., after a rolling restart):

# On each unsealed pod, provide shares until unsealed
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <share-1>
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-1 -- vault operator unseal <share-2>
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-2 -- vault operator unseal <share-3>

docs.title: Emergency access without unseal (break-glass)
docs.text:
In extreme scenarios where all shares are unavailable but the Raft snapshot exists:

  1. Restore from snapshot: Use vault operator raft snapshot restore (requires Vault stopped)
  2. Re-initialize: If snapshot is also lost, re-initialize Vault with new shares (destroys existing data)
  3. Restore data from backup: Apply application-level data backups after Vault is running

Never bypass the unseal process — doing so exposes the master key and compromises all stored secrets.

docs.title: E. Unseal key rotation
docs.text: Rotate unseal key material when the security of existing shares is compromised or when changing the M-of-N threshold.

docs.title: Rotation procedure (3-of-5 → 3-of-5, new shares)
docs.text:
1. Bring existing Vault online: Ensure Vault is running and unsealed with current shares
  2. Add new share shares: Each custodian generates a new share; add via vault operator unseal <new-share>
  3. Remove old shares: Once 3+ new shares are confirmed, securely erase old shares
  4. Verify: vault status should remain unsealed; test secret access
  5. Update documentation: Record rotation date, old shares decommissioned, new custodians
# Add share 4 (while 3-of-5 is already active)
vault operator unseal <share-4>

# Add share 5
vault operator unseal <share-5>

# Now remove share 1 (securely erase it)
# ... securely delete share-1 from all storage locations

# Verify Vault still works
vault status

docs.title: Rotation procedure (threshold change: 3-of-5 → 4-of-6)
docs.text:
1. Add shares incrementally: Add share 6 first, then share 5, while keeping 3-of-5 active
  2. Raise threshold: After 4-of-6 is configured, update Vault's internal threshold
  3. Remove old shares: Securely erase shares 1-3 once new quorum is verified
  4. Full verification: Run disaster recovery drill to confirm the new threshold works

docs.title: Automated rotation with KMS
docs.text:
When using auto-unseal with KMS, key rotation is handled by the KMS service. To rotate:

  1. Create new KMS key: aws kms create-key --description "Vault auto-unseal key rotation"
  2. Update KMS reference: Configure Vault to use the new key (may require re-initialization)
  3. Re-initialize if needed: Some KMS integrations require vault operator init after key rotation
  4. Verify: Confirm auto-unseal works with the new key

docs.title: Deliverable 8 — Secrets Management Architecture
docs.text: Product decision and licence position: secrets-management/vault/hashicorp-vault-decision.md. HashiCorp Vault is the platform standard. OpenBao is the documented fallback if legal rejects the BSL.

docs.title: 8.1 Candidate comparison
docs.text:
Criterion HashiCorp Vault OpenBao SOPS + age Sealed Secrets License BUSL since 1.15 (source-available, not OSI open source) MPL 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Dynamic secrets Yes (DB, SSH, PKI, cloud) Yes (core set) No No Leases/TTL/revocation Yes Yes No No HA storage Integrated Raft Integrated Raft n/a n/a Kubernetes auth Yes Yes n/a n/a Secret injection Agent, injector, CSI Agent, injector, CSI kubectl decrypt controller Audit log Yes Yes No No Air-gap install Yes Yes Yes Yes Ecosystem breadth Largest Smaller, no Vault Enterprise-only features n/a n/a Ops burden Medium Medium Low Low Verdict Adopted (license review required) Fallback Bootstrap static only Bootstrap static only

Selection: HashiCorp Vault as primary because dynamic credentials, PKI, and leases are hard requirements in the master prompt (§15.4) and SOPS/Sealed Secrets cannot satisfy them. OpenBao is the documented fallback if the BUSL license is rejected by legal — the deployment model, policies, and integrations are designed to be portable; the only Vault-specific pieces are the Consul/Consul-template integration and any Vault Enterprise features.

License note: the Vault license changed with the 1.15 release. Confirm the current terms from the official HashiCorp licensing page before adopting, and record the check date in compatibility/version-matrix.md. Do not assume a version's license from memory.

docs.title: 8.2 Deployment model (provisional)
docs.text:
Decision: Vault runs on dedicated Linux hosts outside the Management Cluster.

Option Pros Cons Verdict Dedicated Linux hosts (3) Independent of K8s failure; unseal path independent of cluster; no circular dependency 3 more hosts; manual HA config Adopted Inside Management Cluster Cheaper; Helm-managed Cluster loss = secret loss; unseal may need the cluster; admission issues on startup Rejected (ADR-0025) Kubernetes on a separate small cluster Middle ground Still couples secrets to K8s Alternative if host count is constrained

Topology: 3 Vault nodes, integrated storage (Raft), TLS on 8200, one-way replication for DR.

vault-a (active) ── raft ── vault-b (standby) ── raft ── vault-c (standby)
      │
      └─ File storage backend + periodic snapshot to S3 (Ceph RGW) or offline media

Break-glass unseal: Shamir key shares (3 of 5) held offline by separate custodians; or a KMS auto-unseal device if available. Both are documented in secrets-management/vault/recovery/.

docs.title: 8.3 Identity integration
docs.text:
Consumer Auth method Notes Human admins OIDC via Keycloak Group -> Vault role mapping Ansible (automation server) AppRole or JWT AppRole with CI-like workflow; prefer JWT/OIDC if the identity flow allows GitLab CI jobs OIDC (GitLab ID token) -> Vault JWT auth Edition/compat must be verified; fallback = AppRole with short TTL Argo CD Kubernetes auth (service account token) Vault's own Kubernetes auth method; alternate = External Secrets Operator with Vault provider Applications (in-cluster) Kubernetes auth (SA token) Least-privilege per app SA Workload identity (K8s 1.24+ projected tokens) Vault Kubernetes auth Short-lived, no static SA secret Ceph RGW / RBD Ceph-native auth keys (separate from Vault) Ceph keys stored in Vault, distributed to Ceph at deploy time

Key point: directory integration is application-level and never automatic. Vault, Kubernetes and every other service gets its own explicit OIDC or LDAP procedure — see identity/directory-integration.md.

docs.title: 8.4 Secret categories and storage
docs.text: Category Vault path (example) Delivery Rotation Linux/root creds secret/infra/linux/* Ansible fetch at runtime 90d SSH keys secret/infra/ssh/* Ansible + Vault SSH agent signing 90d / on use Kubespray bootstrap creds secret/infra/kubespray/* Ansible vault lookup 90d K8s app secrets secret/apps/<ns>/* External Secrets Operator -> K8s Secret 30d DB creds database/creds/<role> Dynamic (Vault DB engine) 24h lease Ceph keys secret/infra/ceph/* Ansible -> Ceph 180d GitLab CI creds secret/ci/* GitLab CI masked variables or OIDC 30d Harbor/Nexus auth secret/registry/* Ansible, containerd registries.conf 90d Argo CD repo creds secret/gitops/* Argo CD repo creds via API (not in Git) 90d Monitoring creds secret/observability/* External Secrets 90d Keycloak client secrets secret/identity/* Ansible / External Secrets 90d TLS certs + keys pki/issue/<role> cert-manager via Vault PKI 30d, auto-renew GPU service creds secret/ai/* External Secrets 90d Model API keys secret/ai/models/* External Secrets 90d Backup encryption keys secret/backup/* Ansible, Velero 180d Root CA private key pki/root/ca (offline storage recommended) Offline only long, rotate by re-issue

docs.title: 8.5 Dynamic secrets and rotation
docs.text:
• Database credentials: Vault DB engine issues username/password with TTL (default 24h). Application must re-read the credential on renewal. Vault has no control over apps that cache credentials forever — this must be verified per application.
  • SSH certificates: Vault SSH signer issues short-lived certs; host/user trust against a CA. Requires sshd TrustedUserCAKeys configuration.
  • PKI: Vault PKI issues and renews certs; cert-manager consumes it. Root CA private key stored offline; intermediate held in Vault.
  • Cloud/registry: where the upstream supports dynamic tokens, use them; otherwise rotate static tokens on a schedule.
  • Revocation: revoke leases, remove policies, rotate the underlying credential. For static credentials, rotation is an external automation action (Ansible job) — it is not transparent to the application.
  • After compromise: revoke lease, rotate the credential at the source, re-deploy dependents, verify the new value is in use.

docs.title: 8.6 Secret delivery to Kubernetes — comparison
docs.text:
Method Mechanism Persisted in etcd Rotation behavior App reload needed Complexity Notes Vault Agent Injector Sidecar writes file, syncs on renewal Only if app uses K8s Secret; agent uses memory/file Agent renews and rewrites file App must re-read file or SIGHUP Med Best for file-based apps Vault Agent templates (no injector) DaemonSet/Deployment writes templated file No Same Same Med Good for static config Secrets Store CSI Driver Mounts secret as file via CSI No (unless synced) Driver refreshes on renew App must re-read Med Needs Vault CSI provider External Secrets Operator Syncs Vault -> K8s Secret Yes ESO refreshes on interval App must restart or reload Low Operator-agnostic; adds etcd exposure Direct app -> Vault API App authenticates and reads No App handles renewal App-native Varies No extra infra; more app work K8s native Secret Plain etcd secret Yes Manual Yes Low Baseline only; no dynamic

Explicit statement: External Secrets Operator does not eliminate the etcd persistence risk. It centralizes the source of truth and rotation, but the synchronized value still lands in etcd and is readable by anyone with RBAC on that Secret in that namespace. Mitigation: namespace-scoped RBAC, separate namespaces per team, encrypt etcd at rest, enable etcd encryption at rest with a KMS-backed key, restrict get secrets audit logging.

docs.title: 8.7 PKI
docs.text:
Element Owner Location Root CA (offline) Vault PKI root Encrypted Vault entry + offline backup; ideally on separate host/media Intermediate CA Vault PKI intermediate Vault only, auto-expiry renewal policy Server certs (ingress, services) cert-manager Kubernetes TLS Secrets Client certs (Vault auth, mesh) cert-manager or Vault Depends K8s internal PKI (apiserver, kubelet) Kubespray /etc/kubernetes/pki per node, rotated by Kubespray workflow

Root CA rotation: issue new intermediate from root, switch issuance, wait for leaf expiry, revoke old intermediate. This is a multi-step, downtime-sensitive process — not a one-line operation. Document the runbook in secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md.

docs.title: 8.8 Recovery
docs.text:
• Vault backup: snapshot storage + vault operator raft snapshot save; store offline.
  • Unseal: Shamir shares offline, or auto-unseal KMS.
  • Restore runbook: secrets-management/vault/recovery/restore.md.
  • Recovery order: Vault first (unseal), then identity (Keycloak), then Management Cluster, then Application Clusters. Argo CD may re-sync applications once Vault is back.
  • A Kubernetes backup (Velero) does not include Vault's data unless Vault runs in-cluster and its storage is included. Our model keeps Vault outside the cluster, so Vault backup is a separate, mandatory procedure.

docs.title: 8.9 Monitoring and audit
docs.text:
Monitored: seal status, cluster leadership, replication health, storage usage, request latency and error rate, auth failures, lease/token expiry, certificate expiry, audit device health, backup freshness, rotation failures.

Audit: file or syslog device shipped to the logging platform. Audit logs must never contain secret values — Vault's audit log contains request/response metadata; HMAC-request-response mode is available to further protect values.

Never log: secret values, tokens, private keys, request payloads containing credentials.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Recovery procedure for HashiCorp Vault: unseal, restore from raft snapshot, and confirm read access to secrets.

This is step 1 of the recovery order defined in lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — it runs before every other recovery step because all other components depend on Vault for secrets.

docs.title: B. Prerequisites
docs.text: Prerequisite Source Vault raft snapshot available lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §Vault Unseal keys (3 of 5 shares) Offline storage, key holders Vault TLS certificate valid secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md

docs.title: 1. Start Vault
docs.text:
# If Vault is not running, start it
kubectl -n vault rollout restart sts/vault
kubectl -n vault rollout status sts/vault

docs.title: 2. Unseal Vault
docs.text:
Vault starts sealed. Provide 3 of 5 unseal shares:

# On each Vault pod, or via vault operator
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <share-1>
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <share-2>
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-0 -- vault operator unseal <share-3>

Or use the Vault operator's automatic unseal if configured with KMS/auto-unseal.

docs.title: 3. Restore from raft snapshot
docs.text:
# Copy snapshot to a Vault pod
kubectl -n vault cp /path/to/snapshot.snap vault-0:/tmp/snapshot.snap

# Restore (Vault must be stopped first for raft restore)
kubectl -n vault rollout pause sts/vault
kubectl -n vault exec -it vault-0 -- vault operator raft snapshot restore /tmp/snapshot.snap
kubectl -n vault rollout resume sts/vault

Note: Raft snapshot restore requires Vault to be stopped. Schedule this during a maintenance window.

docs.title: 4. Verify read access
docs.text:
# Authenticate
vault login -method=kubernetes role=platform

# Verify a known secret path
vault kv get secret/platform/database

# Verify AppRole auth works for applications
vault write auth/approle/login role_id=<role_id> secret_id=<secret_id>

docs.title: D. Verification
docs.text:
# Vault is unsealed
vault status | grep "Sealed.*false"

# Secrets are readable
vault kv list secret/platform/

# Applications can authenticate
vault token lookup <app-token>

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document audit logging for Kubernetes: audit policy levels, log destination, retention, analysis, alerting on audit failures.

Cross-references kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §Audit, kubernetes/control-plane/index.md, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md.

docs.title: B. Kubernetes audit policy
docs.text:
The API server audit policy controls what is logged. Metadata level is the default:

apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages:
  - RequestReceived
rules:
  # Log nothing for system components watching endpoints
  - level: None
    users: ["system:kube-proxy", "system:node:agent"]
    verbs: ["watch"]
    resources: ["endpoints", "services", "endpointslices"]
  # Log nothing for garbage collector
  - level: None
    users: ["system:serviceaccount:kube-system:generic-garbage-collector"]
    verbs: ["get"]
    resources: [""]
  # Log request/response for secrets (sensitive)
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets"]
  # Log metadata for other core resources
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "configmaps"]
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: "authentication.k8s.io"
        resources: ["tokenreviews"]
  # Default: log nothing

docs.title: C. Audit log destination
docs.text:
Audit logs must be written to a local file, shipped off-host quickly, and kept out of the cluster's own failure domain:

# kube-apiserver audit configuration
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuditConfiguration
logPath: /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
logMaxAge: 30
logMaxBackup: 10
logMaxSize: 100
policyFile: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml

docs.title: D. Retention
docs.text: Log type Retention Storage API server audit 30 days Local + off-host Vault audit 90 days Local + off-host Ceph audit 30 days Local + off-host

docs.title: E. Analysis
docs.text:
Audit logs should be shipped to a central logging system (Loki/Elasticsearch) for analysis and alerting:

# Example: search audit logs for unauthorized access
grep "Unauthorized" /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | tail -50

# Example: search for secret access
grep "secrets" /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | grep "verb=get" | tail -50

docs.title: F. Alerting on audit failures
docs.text:
Alert when the audit pipeline fails (not just on audit log content):

  • Audit log pipeline failure
  • Audit disk usage > 85%
  • Failed authentication attempts spike
  • Unauthorized access attempts

docs.text:

docs.title: Host security baseline (CIS)
docs.text: The host baseline is the CIS benchmark for the distribution in use, run in audit mode first and then remediated, with every accepted deviation recorded here. Controls that require cluster context are in kubernetes/security/security-controls.md; host build steps are in operating-systems/host-configuration.md.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
1. Install the CIS tooling from the internal repository (no public download).
  2. Run in audit mode and save the report as the baseline artifact.
  3. Remediate, re-run, and record the score.
  4. Record each accepted deviation below with its reason and compensating control.
# Oracle Linux
dnf install -y aqua-sec-cis        # or the CIS-CAT tarball from the internal repo

# Ubuntu
apt install -y cis

Both packages may be absent from the mirror; in that case use the CIS-CAT tarball from offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md. A missing scanner is not a reason to skip the baseline.

docs.title: Baseline by profile
docs.text: Profile Target Notes Control-plane node CIS Level 1 Server + Level 2 where it does not break etcd or the API server Level 2 kernel and audit settings are compatible with stacked etcd Worker node CIS Level 1 Server Container runtime needs explicit SELinux/AppArmor policy, not a disabled profile Storage node CIS Level 1 Server Same baseline as workers; Ceph daemons need no exemption beyond the data disks Edge node CIS Level 1 Server, minimal image set Only the dataplane ports are opened inbound Automation server CIS Level 1 Server Holds SSH access to the estate; treat as a tier-0 host

docs.title: Accepted deviations
docs.text:
Control Deviation Reason Compensating control Password authentication Enabled for the local break-glass account on the console Recovery path when the network or directory is unavailable Account is local, locked in normal operation, credentials stored offline; every use is logged and reviewed SSH root login Disabled (PermitRootLogin no) — not a deviation, recorded because it is commonly relaxed — sudo with an audited account USB storage Blocked on production hosts Prevents data exfiltration and unplanned boot media Firmware-level boot order; physical access controls SELinux/AppArmor Enforcing on all hosts Container runtimes need custom policy, not permissive mode Policies maintained in the security Ansible role

Add new deviations only with an owner, a review date, and a compensating control. A deviation without those three fields is not accepted; it is an open finding.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
# Score, saved as the baseline artifact
cis audit --profile level1-server --report /var/log/cis-baseline-$(date +%F).json

# Spot checks that must agree with the baseline
getenforce                     # Oracle Linux: Enforcing
aa-status                      # Ubuntu: profiles enforced
sshd -T | grep -E 'permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication'
systemctl is-enabled firewalld auditd

docs.text:

  • Host build: operating-systems/host-configuration.md
  • Break-glass design: decisions/ADR-0015-identity-integration-layer.md
  • Backlog item: requirements/component-guide-backlog.md item 37

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document image provenance: image signing, cosign verification, SBOM, vulnerability scanning, Trivy integration.

Cross-references security/host-baseline.md §Container security, offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, security/secret-delivery.md.

docs.title: B. Image signing with Cosign
docs.text:
Images are signed with Cosign at build time and verified at deployment:

# Sign an image
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

# Verify a signature
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

# Verify SBOM attachment
cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

docs.title: C. SBOM generation
docs.text:
Every container image in the artifact matrix must have an SBOM:

# Generate SBOM with Trivy
trivy image --format spdx --output sbom.spdx.json registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

# Verify SBOM
cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub --sbom sbom.spdx.json registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

docs.title: D. Vulnerability scanning
docs.text:
Images are scanned before deployment:

# Scan image
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

# Scan running container
trivy config container registry.internal/<image>:<tag>

Critical/high vulnerabilities block deployment until fixed or accepted with a documented exception.

docs.title: E. Image pull policy
docs.text: All images use IfNotPresent or Never in offline mode. Latest tag is never used.

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:

  • offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md — Image matrix
  • security/secret-delivery.md — Secret delivery to workloads
  • compatibility/version-matrix.md — Version pins

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document the cosign key lifecycle, signing pipeline, and verification at deployment. Cross-references security/image-provenance.md §Image signing, offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, and compatibility/version-matrix.md.

docs.title: B. cosign key generation
docs.text:
Generate a keypair offline and store the private key in a secrets manager. The public key is distributed to all verifiers.

# Generate ed25519 keypair (recommended for short keys, fast ops)
cosign key generate --key-type ed25519

# Output
# PUBLIC_KEY: cosign.pub   (share this)
# PRIVATE_KEY: cosign.key  (keep offline, encrypt, or store in SSM/Azure Key Vault/GCP Secret Manager)

Never commit the private key to version control. Use short-lived rotation and automate key rollover via CI pipeline parameters.

docs.title: C. signing pipeline
docs.text:
Sign images at build time as part of the CI/CD pipeline. The pipeline must have the private key available via a secrets manager (not checked in).

# Example: GitHub Actions step — sign after build and push
- name: Sign image with cosign
  run: |
    cosign sign --key cosign.pub ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ env.TAG }}

Pipeline requirements: - Private key fetched from secrets manager at runtime (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, or GCP Secret Manager) - Key access logged and audited - Signing step runs after container image push - Soft fail disabled — pipeline stops on signing failure

docs.title: D. verification at deployment
docs.text:
Verify signatures before any deployment step. This is a gate — images without valid signatures are rejected.

# Verify image signature at deployment
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.internal/${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ env.TAG }}

# Verify SBOM attachment
cosign verify sbom --key cosign.pub --sbom sbom.json registry.internal/${{ env.IMAGE }}:${{ env.TAG }}

Deployment gate: The CI pipeline must call cosign verify as a pre-deploy step. Failure blocks the entire deployment.

docs.title: E. Key rotation
docs.text:
Rotate cosign keys quarterly or after any suspected compromise. Old public keys remain in the verification registry until all workloads are updated.

# Generate new keypair
cosign key generate --key-type ed25519 --out keybundle.json

# Publish new public key to registry annotation
cosign sign --key keybundle.json registry.internal/image:tag

# Update deployment configs to reference new public key
# Deprecate old key after grace period

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Pod Security Standards (PSS) implementation for the platform: restricted/baseline/privileged profiles per namespace, admission enforcement, and exceptions process.

Cross-references kubernetes/security/security-controls.md §Pod Security Standards, kubernetes/networking/network-policy-examples.md, kubernetes/control-plane/index.md §Security.

docs.title: B. Pod Security Standards profiles
docs.text: Profile Description Use case privileged Unrestricted, widest range of permissions System workloads (CNI, storage, monitoring agents) baseline Minimally restrictive, prevents known privilege escalations Most applications restricted Heavily restricted, follows pod security best practices General workloads, default

docs.title: C. Namespace-level enforcement
docs.text:
Apply PSS at the namespace level via labels:

# Cluster-wide defaults
kubectl label --overwrite ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label --overwrite ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest
kubectl label --overwrite ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
kubectl label --overwrite ns default pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted

kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-system pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged
kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-system pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest
kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-public pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged
kubectl label --overwrite ns kube-public pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# Application namespaces use restricted by default
kubectl label --overwrite ns <app-namespace> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label --overwrite ns <app-namespace> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

The kube-system and kube-public namespaces stay at privileged because CNI and control-plane components require it. Every other namespace is restricted.

docs.title: D. Enforce with admission policy
docs.text:
The PSS label is only an audit signal by itself. Enforce with an admission controller (OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno):

# OPA Gatekeeper constraint template
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sPSPPrivilegedContainer
metadata:
  name: block-privileged
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    excludedNamespaces: ["kube-system", "gatekeeper-system"]
  parameters:
    exemptNamespaces: ["kube-system", "gatekeeper-system"]

# Kyverno ClusterPolicy
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-non-root
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: require-run-as-non-root
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must run as non-root"
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - (securityContext):
                  runAsNonRoot: true

docs.title: E. Restricted profile requirements
docs.text:
The restricted profile means:

  • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  • runAsNonRoot: true
  • seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault or Localhost
  • capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]
  • No hostPath, no hostNetwork, no hostPID, no hostIPC
  • No privileged: true containers

docs.title: F. Exceptions process
docs.text:
Workloads needing less than restricted run in their own namespace with the correct label — not with a cluster-wide exemption:

# Create namespace for workloads needing baseline
kubectl create ns <baseline-ns>
kubectl label ns <baseline-ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
kubectl label ns <baseline-ns> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

All exceptions require: 1. Documented reason 2. Compensating control 3. Owner assignment 4. Review date

docs.title: G. Validation
docs.text:
# Check PSS labels on all namespaces
kubectl get ns --show-labels | grep pod-security

# Test that privileged pods are denied in restricted namespaces
kubectl run test-privileged --image=busybox --restart=Never --privileged -n <restricted-ns> --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Check admission controller enforcement
kubectl get gatekeeperconstraints  # or kyverno policies

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document automated SBOM generation, storage, and vulnerability correlation for container images and filesystem artifacts. Cross-references security/host-baseline.md §Container security, offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md, security/image-provenance.md.

docs.title: Syft SBOM Generation
docs.text:
# SBOM for directory of staged artifacts
syft dir:./staging -o cyclonedx-json > staging/SBOM.json

# SBOM for OCI image
syft oci://registry.internal/app:tag -o cyclonedx-json > staging/SBOM-image.json

docs.title: Trivy SBOM and Vulnerability Scan
docs.text:
# SBOM from Syft output combined with Trivy vulnerability scanning
trivy fs --scanners vuln --format json ./staging > staging/trivy-fs.json

# Trivy image scan with SBOM inclusion
trivy image --input ./staging/oci/owner-repo.tar --format json --sbs SBOM.json > staging/trivy-image.json

docs.title: SBOM Verification
docs.text:
# Validate SBOM JSON schema
python3 -c "
import json
with open('staging/SBOM.json') as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)
assert 'bom' in sbom or 'components' in sbom, 'Invalid SBOM structure'
print('SBOM schema validated')
"

# Cross-check SBOM components against known good list
syft dir:./staging -o cyclonedx-json | jq -r '.components[].name' > /tmp/sbom-components.txt
sort /tmp/sbom-components.txt -u > /tmp/sbom-components-sorted.txt

docs.title: SBOM Artifact Storage
docs.text:
# Store SBOM in internal artifact repository
mv staging/SBOM.json /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# Store Trivy vulnerability report
mv staging/trivy-fs.json /opt/artifacts/vuln-reports/app-name-$(date +%Y%m%d).json

# Keep SBOM alongside related artifacts
cp staging/SBOM.json /opt/artifacts/staging-archives/

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
/opt/artifacts/
├── sboms/
│   ├── app-name-20240115.json
│   └── app-name-20240122.json
├── vuln-reports/
│   ├── app-name-20240115.json
│   └── app-name-20240122.json
└── staging-archives/
    └── (complete staging directories for rollback)

docs.title: Immutable Storage
docs.text:
# Write-once, reference-only after verification
chmod 444 /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-*.json
chmod 444 /opt/artifacts/vuln-reports/app-name-*.json

docs.title: Trivy Scan Validation
docs.text:
# Verify trivy scan results are not empty (indicates DB fetch failure)
if [ ! -s staging/trivy-fs.json ]; then
    echo "Trivy scan produced no results - check DB availability"
    exit 1
fi

docs.title: SBOM-Vulnerability Linkage
docs.text:
# Associate SBOM with vulnerability report by timestamp and component hash
SBOM_HASH=$(sha256sum /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json | cut -d' ' -f1)
VULN_REPORT=$(ls /opt/artifacts/vuln-reports/app-name-20240115.json)
jq -r --arg hash "$SBOM_HASH" '. vulnerabilities[] | select(.sbom_hash == $hash)' "$VULN_REPORT" > /tmp/correlated-vulns.json

docs.title: Upstream Consumption
docs.text:
# Make SBOM available to security tools
ln -s /opt/artifacts/sboms/app-name-20240115.json /opt/sbom-current.json

# Expose via internal API endpoint
# Configure Trivy to fetch SBOM from: SBOM_URL=https://nexus.internal/repository/sboms/

docs.title: E. Workflow Summary
docs.text:
1. Create: Run syft or trivy to generate SBOM JSON from staged artifacts or OCI images
  2. Verify: Validate SBOM schema, checksum, and signature integrity
  3. Store: Persist SBOM to internal artifact repository with immutable permissions
  4. Correlate: Link SBOM components with vulnerability reports for downstream consumption
  5. Distribute: Make SBOM available to security teams, compliance teams, and downstream consumers

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document secret rotation procedures for HashiCorp Vault: PKI certificate rotation, Kubernetes secret rotation, application secret rotation, and etcd encryption key rotation.

Cross-references secrets-management/vault/vault-architecture.md, secrets-management/pki/root-ca-rotation.md, secrets-management/kubernetes-integration/secret-delivery.md, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §Vault.

docs.title: 1. Rotate intermediate CA
docs.text:
# Generate new intermediate CA
vault write -format=json pki_int/intermediate/set-signed \
  certificate=@new_intermediate.crt \
  ca_chain=@new_ca_chain.crt

# Update the role to use the new CA
vault write pki/roles/<role-name> \
  allowed_domains=<domain> \
  allow_subdomains=true \
  max_ttl="72h"

# Verify new certificates are issued with the new CA
vault write pki/issue/<role-name> common_name=test.<domain>

docs.title: 2. Rotate leaf certificates
docs.text:
Certificates issued by Vault PKI have short TTLs (typically 24-72h). Rotation is automatic on renewal:

# Renew a certificate before expiry
vault write pki/issue/<role-name> common_name=<name>

# Revoke a compromised certificate
vault write pki/revoke serial_number=<serial>

docs.title: 3. Verification
docs.text:
# Check CA expiry
vault read pki_int/cert/ca

# Check CRL
vault read pki/crl/pem

docs.title: 1. Rotate secrets via External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
If using External Secrets Operator with Vault:

# Update the secret in Vault
vault kv put secret/<path> key=<new-value>

# External Secrets Operator automatically syncs to Kubernetes
kubectl get secret <k8s-secret> -o yaml | grep data:

docs.title: 2. Rotate service account tokens
docs.text:
Service account tokens are automatically rotated by Kubernetes. Verify:

kubectl get serviceaccount <sa> -o yaml
kubectl describe serviceaccount <sa>

docs.title: 3. Verify rotation
docs.text:
# Check secret age
kubectl get secret <secret> --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Verify secret content matches Vault
vault kv get secret/<path>

docs.title: 1. Application reads secrets at startup
docs.text:
Applications should read secrets from Vault at startup and cache them in memory. Rotation requires restart:

# Rollout restart to pick up new secrets
kubectl rollout restart deployment/<app>

# Verify new secret is in use
kubectl exec <pod> -- <app-command> --verify-secret

docs.title: 2. Dynamic secrets
docs.text:
Vault dynamic secrets (e.g., database credentials) are short-lived and automatically expire:

# Check lease
vault lease lookup <lease-id>

# Revoke lease early if compromised
vault lease revoke <lease-id>

docs.title: 1. Rotate etcd encryption keys
docs.text:
# Create new encryption config
cat > /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml << 'EOF'
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
apiVersion: apiserver.k8s.io/v1
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: new-key-<date>
              key: <new-base64-key>
            - name: old-key-<date>
              key: <old-base64-key>
      - identity: {}
EOF

# Apply new config to kube-apiserver
kubectl apply -f /etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml

# Re-encrypt all secrets
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | \
  kubectl apply -f -

docs.title: 2. Verify
docs.text:
# Check encryption config is active
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

# Verify secrets are encrypted in etcd
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/ --prefix --keys-only --write-out=table

docs.title: E. Rotation schedule
docs.text: Secret type Rotation frequency Method Vault PKI intermediate CA Every 1-2 years Manual via Vault CLI Leaf certificates 24-72h (TTL-based) Automatic renewal Kubernetes secrets As needed External Secrets Operator sync Service account tokens Automatic Kubernetes controller Application secrets 90 days Application restart etcd encryption keys Every 90 days Manual re-encryption Vault unseal keys Every 365 days Key ceremony

docs.title: Service mesh evaluation
docs.text: Decision: no mesh at v1. See ADR-0009. This file records the evaluation and the threshold for revisiting it. If the threshold is met, the deployment procedure is service-mesh/istio/istio-deployment.md (Istio 1.31.3, sidecar or ambient, staged mTLS, revision-based upgrades).

docs.title: What a mesh actually provides
docs.text: Capability What it does Native Kubernetes equivalent Service identity A cryptographic identity per workload, not per IP None. NetworkPolicy works on IP/label selectors mTLS Automatic encryption and mutual authentication between services None natively (service mesh is the standard answer) L7 traffic management Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, outlier detection, mirroring, traffic splitting Ingress handles north-south only Authorization policy Per-method, per-path authorization between services NetworkPolicy is L3/L4 Telemetry Per-request latency, status, and dependency graph Application-level instrumentation only Ingress/egress gateway Controlled entry and exit points with policy Ingress + Gateway API + NetworkPolicy + egress NetworkPolicy

docs.title: Istio
docs.text: Aspect Assessment Feature breadth Largest. Ambient mode removes the sidecar but not the control plane mTLS STRICT mode with automatic certificate rotation via the CA. Well proven Traffic management VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, Telemetry, AuthorizationPolicy — comprehensive Resource overhead Sidecar: roughly 10-30 MB memory and a small CPU share per pod. Ambient (ztunnel): a node-level proxy, lower per-pod cost but new operational model Artifact footprint offline Large: istiod, ingress/egress gateways, ztunnel, CNI plugin, plus the Envoy images the sidecars pull. Every image must be mirrored Version compatibility Istio supports a defined window of Kubernetes versions. Checking that window is mandatory per upgrade Upgrade complexity High. The recommended path is a canary control plane, then namespaces in order. An Istio upgrade that skips the canary has caused outages Operational cost A new control plane, a new failure domain, a new CRD set, and a config model that is powerful enough to break traffic silently

docs.title: Linkerd
docs.text: Aspect Assessment Feature breadth Smaller than Istio. mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting, and a strong observability story mTLS Automatic, per-pod identity Resource overhead linkerd-proxy sidecar, roughly 10-20 MB per pod Artifact footprint offline Much smaller than Istio: proxy, controller, injector, plus the linkerd-cni Version compatibility Broad Kubernetes support Upgrade complexity Lower than Istio, but still requires a proxy restart per workload Operational cost Lower than Istio. Fewer CRDs, smaller surface

docs.title: Cilium's native capabilities (no separate mesh)
docs.text:
Capability Cilium equivalent mTLS Cilium mutual authentication with SPIFFE identities, using certificates from cert-manager or an internal CA L7 policy CiliumNetworkPolicy L7 rules for HTTP and DNS Load balancing kube-proxy replacement with eBPF service handling Observability Hubble: per-flow visibility, DNS logs, and a UI Service identity Cilium is not a service mesh with an identity control plane in the Istio sense. Its identity model is node and workload certificate based

The important caveat: Cilium gives encryption, L7 policy, and observability. It does not give Istio-level traffic management (retries, circuit breaking, traffic splitting, outlier detection) as a first-class platform feature.

docs.title: Decision criteria — the threshold to adopt a mesh
docs.text:
Adopt only when all three hold:

  1. >= 30 services need mutual TLS between them.
  2. Cross-team traffic policy is required (team A must be able to call team B's /orders but not /admin, enforced by the platform rather than by the calling code).
  3. >= 2 Application Clusters are in production, because the mesh's value is in a consistent cross-cluster identity and policy model.

If a mesh is adopted, Istio is the first candidate. Linkerd is the lighter alternative if the requirement set stays within mTLS plus retries and the artifact footprint in an offline environment is the binding constraint.

docs.title: Benefits (what we would get)
docs.text:
• Workload identity that survives IP changes, container restarts, and node replacement.
  • Encryption of service-to-service traffic by default, without application changes.
  • Platform-enforced authorization between teams, independent of the application code.
  • Retry, timeout, and circuit-breaking defaults that remove a class of application bugs.
  • A dependency graph and per-request latency without instrumenting each service.

docs.title: Costs (what we would take on)
docs.text:
• A control plane to operate, secure, back up, and upgrade.
  • A large offline artifact set to mirror and keep current.
  • A second CPU and memory tax on every pod.
  • A new failure mode: a bad DestinationRule or an overloaded control plane can blackhole traffic cluster-wide.
  • Meaningfully longer upgrade cycles, with a mandatory canary phase.
  • A new troubleshooting skill set for the operations team.
  • A large increase in the configuration surface that GitOps must manage.

docs.title: Acceptance criteria if a mesh is adopted
docs.text:
1. mTLS is in STRICT mode across all namespaces, with exceptions explicitly listed.
  2. A network partition between the control plane and a workload does not break existing service-to-service traffic.
  3. A mesh configuration error in one namespace does not affect another namespace.
  4. The mesh upgrade procedure has been executed on a staging copy of a production cluster, including the canary phase.
  5. Every mesh artifact is mirrored offline and pull-verified.
  6. The added per-pod resource overhead is measured and accepted: kubectl top pods before and after.
  7. Hubble or the equivalent is integrated with the existing observability stack.
  8. A documented rollback: removing the mesh returns the platform to native networking without application changes.

docs.title: Interim measures
docs.text:
Until the threshold is met:

  • Cilium network policies (L3/L4 and, where needed, L7) enforce what a mesh would enforce at the network level.
  • Cilium mutual authentication provides workload-to-workload TLS where encryption is required, without a full mesh.
  • Retry, timeout, and circuit-breaking defaults live in the application libraries and in the ingress configuration, owned by the application team.
  • Service identity for platform components is handled by Vault-issued short-lived credentials, not by mesh identity.

docs.title: Offline footprint estimate
docs.text:
Before adopting, count the exact images to mirror. For Istio with the ambient data plane, the set includes: istiod, istio-proxy (or ztunnel), the ingress and egress gateway images, the istio-cni plugin, and the base images the gateway uses. For the sidecar model, every workload also pulls the proxyv2 image, which must be present on every node or the pod stays in ContainerCreating.

The sidecar model's offline implication is the deciding factor for many air-gapped estates: the proxy image must be pullable by every node, and any node that cannot reach the registry will hold pods in ContainerCreating indefinitely.

docs.title: Istio deployment
docs.text:
Istio is not part of the v1 baseline. ADR-0009 sets the threshold for adopting a mesh, and service-mesh/evaluation.md records the evaluation. This document is the deployment procedure for the case where that threshold is met — either because per-workload mTLS and L7 authorization are required by a compliance obligation, or because traffic splitting and retries are needed between services that cannot implement them themselves.

Pinned version: 1.31.3 (compatibility/version-matrix.md).

docs.title: Decide the dataplane mode first
docs.text:
Mode How it works Cost When to choose it Sidecar (default) An Envoy container per pod, injected by the webhook ~10–30 MB and a small CPU share per pod; every pod restart on upgrade Per-workload policy, VirtualService features, teams already familiar with it Ambient A per-node ztunnel for L4 mTLS, plus optional per-namespace waypoint proxies for L7 No sidecar; one DaemonSet per node; L7 only where a waypoint exists New deployments, large pod counts, mTLS as the main requirement

Ambient is the better default for a new adoption. It changes the failure domain: a ztunnel problem affects every pod on that node, not one workload.

Whichever mode is chosen, the control plane (istiod) is the same, and it is a new failure domain: if istiod is unavailable, existing mTLS connections keep working but new pods cannot get certificates.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Kubernetes is inside Istio 1.31's supported version window. Check the support matrix for the exact minor range before the upgrade, not after.
  2. Gateway API CRDs are installed at the version the pinned Istio release expects. The platform already installs them for the ingress portfolio; do not install a second, older copy.
  3. The CNI is compatible. With Cilium, ambient mode requires the CNI chaining configuration, and the Cilium kube-proxy replacement must be reconciled with Istio's traffic redirection.
  4. Every image is mirrored into Harbor. There is no pull from the internet at deploy time.
  5. A certificate authority decision is made: Istio's self-signed CA, or an external CA backed by Vault. The self-signed CA is per-cluster and dies with the cluster; the Vault-backed CA survives a rebuild and is the choice for a production cluster that must be recoverable.

docs.title: Mirror the images
docs.text:
Run this in the connected staging environment, then import the bundle into the air-gapped one.

istioctl manifest generate -f istio-operator.yaml -o /tmp/istio-rendered
# Every image the install and the dataplane need:
grep -rhoE 'image: *[^ ]+' /tmp/istio-rendered | awk '{print $2}' | sort -u \
  > /tmp/istio-images.txt
# Mirror each entry to the internal registry, keeping the tag and digest.

The list includes istiod, proxyv2 (sidecar), install-cni, ztunnel (ambient), the gateway images, and the pilot-agent. Re-run the extraction after every version change: the set changes between releases, and a missing image fails at pod start, not at install time.

docs.title: Option A — istioctl (single cluster, imperative)
docs.text:
istioctl install -f istio-operator.yaml --verify
kubectl -n istio-system get pods

docs.title: Option B — Helm, managed by Argo CD (the platform default when a mesh is adopted)
docs.text:
helm upgrade --install istio-base   oci://{{registry}}/istio/base   -n istio-system --version 1.31.3
helm upgrade --install istiod       oci://{{registry}}/istio/istiod -n istio-system --version 1.31.3 -f istiod-values.yaml
# ambient only:
helm upgrade --install istio-cni    oci://{{registry}}/istio/cni    -n istio-system --version 1.31.3 -f cni-values.yaml
helm upgrade --install ztunnel      oci://{{registry}}/istio/ztunnel -n istio-system --version 1.31.3 -f ztunnel-values.yaml

Helm is preferred here because it makes the mesh a GitOps object like everything else. The IstioOperator path is kept for the initial bring-up and for istioctl diagnostics.

docs.title: Enable mTLS in stages
docs.text:
Never start at STRICT on the whole mesh. The order that works:

  1. Install with permissive mTLS (the default). Verify traffic flows.
  2. Apply PeerAuthentication with STRICT to one non-critical namespace.
  3. Watch the mesh metrics for rejected connections for a full business cycle.
  4. Move namespace by namespace. Leave kube-system and any namespace running a third-party controller that cannot present a certificate for last, or exclude it explicitly.
kubectl apply -f peer-authentication.yaml
istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>   # confirms the effective policy

The generated peer-authentication.yaml also carries a default-deny AuthorizationPolicy and an allow rule scoped to one namespace. Apply the deny rule only after the allow rules are in place.

docs.title: Traffic entry
docs.text:
Two controllers must not claim the same GatewayClass. The platform's Gateway API portfolio (kubernetes/ingress/multi-controller-plan.md) already has NGINX Gateway Fabric and Envoy Gateway as candidates. When Istio is adopted:

  • North–south edge: keep the edge load balancer, then a single ingress path. Either the existing NGINX Gateway Fabric terminates and forwards to the mesh, or Istio's own gateway terminates and the NGINX layer is removed from that path. Pick one, record it in the ADR, and do not run both in front of the same hostname.
  • East–west: VirtualService / DestinationRule for sidecar mode; HTTPRoute attached to a waypoint for ambient mode. Do not mix the two models in one namespace.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Istio's telemetry feeds the existing Prometheus stack. No second metrics pipeline.

istioctl analyze -A                     # configuration errors before they break traffic
kubectl -n istio-system get pods
# Dashboards: Istio's own Grafana dashboards, imported into the platform Grafana.

Kiali is optional and adds a second UI with its own RBAC. Do not install it without a named owner.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Istio supports canary upgrades with revisions, and that is the only supported path that keeps a rollback available.

# 1. Install the new control plane alongside the old one.
istioctl install --revision=1-32-0 -f istio-operator.yaml
# 2. Move one namespace at a time.
kubectl label namespace <ns> istio.io/rev=1-32-0 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n <ns>
# 3. Verify, then move the next namespace.
# 4. Remove the old revision when nothing references it.
istioctl uninstall --revision=1-31-3

Rules:

  • One minor at a time. Istio does not support skipping minors.
  • Control plane before dataplane, always.
  • Rollback exists only while the old revision is installed. Moving the namespace label back is the rollback. Once the old revision is removed, the only path is forward.
  • Downgrade is not supported.
  • The revision name is derived from the version (1-32-0 for 1.32.0); keep the naming rule in the upgrade record so the label and the installed revision cannot drift.

docs.title: Capacity and failure
docs.text: Item Value istiod 2 replicas minimum, PodDisruptionBudget, requests 500m CPU / 2 GiB for a medium cluster Sidecar per pod requests 100m CPU / 128 MiB; limits 1 CPU / 512 MiB ztunnel per node requests 200m CPU / 128 MiB Control-plane outage Existing connections continue; new pods cannot obtain certificates istiod loss mTLS and policy stay enforced by the dataplane; config changes stop applying Certificate expiry Managed by Istio's CA. With an external Vault CA, the Vault PKI is a hard dependency

docs.title: Validation before handover
docs.text:
istioctl version
istioctl analyze -A
kubectl -n istio-system get pods
# mTLS actually on:
istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n <ns> | grep -i 'mTLS'
# Policy is enforced, not just present: connect from a pod that should be denied.
kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://<service>.<ns>:8080/

A mesh that is installed but not enforcing STRICT mTLS, or whose AuthorizationPolicy was never tested with a negative case, is not adopted — it is a second control plane with no benefit.

docs.title: Removal
docs.text:
Removing a mesh is a migration, not an uninstall:

  1. Set every namespace back to permissive, verify, then remove the policies.
  2. Remove the waypoints or sidecars (label change, rolling restart).
  3. Uninstall the control plane and the CRDs last.
  4. Re-verify that NetworkPolicy still gives the isolation the mesh was providing. In most cases it does not, which is why the decision to adopt was made in the first place.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document storage migration patterns: PVC migration between StorageClasses, pool migration, and data evacuation. Cross-references storage/storageclass-design.md, storage/pvc-lifecycle.md, storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md, storage/rook-ceph/rook-ceph.md.

docs.title: B. PVC Migration Between StorageClasses
docs.text: Migrating a PVC from one StorageClass to another requires data copy, not just a label change. The safest approach is online copy using kubectl cp or a CSI migration tool.

docs.title: 1. Create the target PVC in the new StorageClass
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc-new
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ceph-rbd-fast
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi

docs.title: 2. Copy data from the old PVC to the new PVC
docs.text:
# Get the pod name that owns the old PVC
POD_NAME=$(kubectl get pods -l app=myapp -o name | head -1)

# Copy data out of the old PVC and into the new one
kubectl cp ${POD_NAME}:/data ./
kubectl cp ./ ${POD_NAME}:/data

docs.title: 3. Update the application to use the new PVC
docs.text: Either: - Recreate the pod with the new PVC selector - Update the Deployment to reference app-pvc-new - Swap PVC names in the volume definition

docs.title: 4. Delete the old PVC (after confirming data is accessible in the new PVC)
docs.text:
kubectl delete pvc app-pvc-old

Important: The PV from the old PVC remains in the cluster (reclaimPolicy determines if it's deleted or retained). Monitor PV reclamation.

Alternative: RBD migration (Ceph RBD-specific)

For Ceph RBD volumes, you can migrate using rbd migrate:

# On a host with ceph-cli installed
rbd migrate <pool>/<image> <target-pool>/<image> --flags incremental

docs.title: C. Pool Migration
docs.text: Pool migration moves data between Ceph pools (e.g., from a HDD pool to an SSD pool, or from a replicated pool to an erasure-coded pool). This is an online operation via ceph osd pool move.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the source and target pools
docs.text:
Ensure the target pool exists and has sufficient capacity:

# Create target pool (replicated, size 3)
ceph osd pool create target-pool 64 64 replicated
ceph osd pool application enable target-pool rbd

# Or create erasure-coded pool
ceph osd pool create target-pool 64 64 erasure

docs.title: 2. Start the pool migration
docs.text:
# Move all PGs from source-pool to target-pool
ceph osd pool move source-pool target-pool --max 64

The --max flag sets the maximum number of PGs to move per iteration. Monitor progress:

# Check migration status
ceph osd pool migrate source-pool

# When the report shows 0/0, migration is complete
ceph osd pool stats source-pool target-pool

docs.title: 3. Verify migration completed
docs.text:
# Confirm source pool is empty
ceph osd pool pgmap source-pool | grep -c "active+clean"

# Confirm target pool has all data
ceph osd pool pgmap target-pool | grep -c "active+clean"

docs.title: 4. Delete the source pool (after verification)
docs.text:
ceph osd pool delete source-pool source-pool --yes-i-really-delete

Important: Pool migration rebalances data across OSDs. Monitor ceph -s for HEALTH_WARN about backfill or undersized PGs during the migration window.

docs.title: D. Data Evacuation
docs.text: Data evacuation moves data off a specific OSD or node (e.g., for hardware maintenance). This uses ceph osd drain with strategic PG movement.

docs.title: 1. Mark the OSD for evacuation
docs.text:
# Allow new PGs to be placed elsewhere before draining
ceph osd set noout

# Optionally, reduce the PG count on the target OSD
ceph osd out <osd-id>

docs.title: 2. Move PGs off the OSD
docs.text:
# Begin moving PGs off the OSD
ceph osd rebalance

# Monitor rebalance progress
ceph osd pool rebalance <pool-name>

# Or use pagrab to manually grab specific PGs
ceph osd pagrab -n <pg-id>

docs.title: 3. Verify data is relocated
docs.text:
# Check OSD usage before and after
ceph osd df <osd-id>  # before
ceph osd df <osd-id>  # after — size should decrease

# Confirm PGs are no longer on this OSD
ceph osd dump | grep <osd-id>

docs.title: 4. Remove the OSD from the cluster
docs.text:
# After data is confirmed moved, shut down the OSD
systemctl stop ceph-osd@<osd-id>
systemctl disable ceph-osd@<osd-id>

# Remove the OSD from the Ceph map
ceph osd pool remove <pool> <osd-id> --yes-i-really-delete

# If replacing the disk, wipe and re-add the device
wipefs -a /dev/<device>
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd <host> --data-devices /dev/<device>

Important: Always ceph osd set noout before and ceph osd set noout after evacuation to prevent cluster rebalancing from counteracting your moves. Monitor ceph -s for HEALTH_OK before proceeding with hardware changes.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document PVC lifecycle: provisioning, binding, mounting, resizing, snapshotting, deletion, migration.

Cross-references storage/storageclass-design.md, storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md, storage/rook-ceph/rook-ceph.md.

docs.title: B. PVC lifecycle states
docs.text: State Description Next action Pending PVC created, waiting for PV StorageClass provisioning Bound PVC bound to PV Pod can mount Available PV available but unbound Waiting for PVC Released PVC deleted, PV released Reclaim or delete Failed Provisioning failed Investigate error

docs.title: C. Provisioning and binding
docs.text:
# PVC example
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ceph-rbd-standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi

Binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer defers binding until a pod uses the PVC.

docs.title: D. Mounting
docs.text:
# Pod referencing PVC
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: app-pvc

docs.title: E. Resizing
docs.text:
# Expand PVC
kubectl patch pvc app-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"100Gi"}}}}'

# Verify expansion
kubectl get pvc app-pvc

File system resize happens automatically when the pod restarts.

docs.title: F. Snapshotting
docs.text:
# VolumeSnapshot example
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: app-pvc-snapshot
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ceph-rbd-snapshot
