docs.title: Storage alternatives to Ceph
docs.text: Ceph is the platform standard (ADR-0008). This file records the alternatives, when each one wins, and what it costs to adopt.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Technology Type Scale ceiling HA S3 Filesystem Snapshot/clone Operational cost Offline footprint Ceph (Rook) Block + file + object Very large Yes Yes Yes Yes High Large Ceph (cephadm, external) Block + file + object Very large Yes Yes Yes Yes Medium Medium Longhorn Block (replicated) Small-to-medium Yes No No (limited) Yes Low-medium Small OpenEBS Block / file (JSC, CSI) Medium Yes No Yes Yes Medium Medium NFS (managed) Shared filesystem Medium Depends on the server No Yes Server-side Low Small Enterprise SAN Block Large Yes No No Yes Low Small (vendor) MinIO Object (S3) Medium Yes Yes No Yes Low Small GlusterFS File Medium Yes No Yes Yes Medium Medium Local-path provisioner Block (node-local) None No No No No None Tiny

docs.title: Longhorn
docs.text:
Adopt when: - The site is small (under ~10 TB, tens of nodes). - Storage must live entirely inside the cluster with no external dependency. - The team wants a simple operator and accepts that it is not Ceph.

Do not adopt when: object storage is required, the estate is large, or multi-cluster shared capacity is needed. Longhorn is a block-storage product; it is not a Ceph replacement.

Trade-offs: it replicates volumes across nodes with its own data engine, which is easy to operate but has a real per-node overhead and does not provide a filesystem or object API.

docs.title: OpenEBS
docs.text:
Adopt when a CSI-based dynamic provisioner is needed and the site already runs a storage operator with an external engine (for example, a JSC setup on separate storage nodes).

Do not adopt when the goal is simplicity. OpenEBS has several storage engines and its project status has been a factor in the past; confirm the current maintenance status before adopting.

docs.title: NFS
docs.text:
Adopt for shared-file workloads where the workload is not latency-sensitive and the data is not the system of record. NFS over Kubernetes with the CSI driver is simple and works.

Do not adopt for databases, or as the primary substrate for a storage platform. NFS has no replication story of its own; the HA comes from the server.

docs.title: Enterprise SAN
docs.text:
Adopt when the site already owns a SAN and the budget supports it. It gives the best latency, the best support path, and hardware-level reliability features. The trade-off is cost, vendor lock-in, and an operational model that is outside the Kubernetes team.

Use it for the database tier, keep Ceph for the general-purpose tier where the software-defined model is an advantage.

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
Adopt when S3-compatible object storage is needed and Ceph's RGW is not justified. MinIO is far lighter than RGW and simpler to run.

Do not adopt when the platform already standardizes on Ceph RGW — two object stores double the data-management surface and the backup work.

docs.title: GlusterFS
docs.text: Adopt only for existing estates with an established Gluster practice. For a new build, it is a poor trade against Ceph given Ceph's wider adoption, better ecosystem integration, and better support path.

docs.title: local-path provisioner
docs.text: Adopt only for non-persistent, node-local, disposable data — caches, scratch space, and log spools. It is the Kubespray default and must be replaced by a real StorageClass before any stateful workload lands on it.

docs.title: The decision this platform actually made
docs.text: Requirement Driver Block, file, and object from one platform Ceph Shared capacity across multiple clusters Ceph via cephadm plus the external CSI driver Storage-native to Kubernetes for cluster-local volumes Ceph via Rook Hardware acceleration for databases, where a SAN exists SAN, if available

docs.title: Storage comparison against Rook-Ceph and external Ceph
docs.text: Aspect Rook-Ceph External Ceph (cephadm) Longhorn OpenEBS SAN Deployment Operator inside K8s cephadm on dedicated hosts Operator inside K8s Operator + engine External appliance Cluster coupling Yes No Yes Yes No Object storage RGW RGW No No No Multi-cluster consumption No Yes No Limited Yes Upgrade complexity Two layers (Rook then Ceph) One (ceph orch) One Medium Low Failure blast radius A cluster network fault can affect storage Storage hosts are independent Node-local Depends Independent Offline artifact volume High Medium Low Medium Low

docs.title: Consequences of the Ceph-only decision
docs.text:
Accepted: - Ceph is a large operational surface for a small team. Mitigation: the cephadm path keeps the lifecycle in the vendor's hands. - A cluster-wide CNI or network fault can take Rook-managed storage with it. Mitigation: the external Ceph path for anything shared or critical. - Ceph is the heaviest component in the artifact matrix. Mitigation: the staging-and-import workflow in offline-artifacts/offline-artifact-architecture.md.

Not accepted: - Using Rook for storage that must survive the loss of the cluster it runs in. - Mixing two object stores. - Introducing a second block platform for a single application without a documented reason.

docs.title: Auto-Test Ceph Performance Tuning Procedures
docs.text: This document covers automated testing procedures for Ceph performance tuning, including OSD tuning, pool configuration, CRUSH rules, and cache tiers. Intended for integration into CI/CD pipelines and operational verification.

docs.title: 1. BlueStore Parameter Validation
docs.text:
# Verify bluestore_cache_size is within recommended range
ceph osd dump | grep bluestore_cache_size

# Validate scrub period is set appropriately
ceph osd dump | grep bluestore_scrub_period

# Check compaction interval settings
ceph osd dump | grep bluestore_compaction_interval

Expected: All OSDs report parameters within recommended ranges (see performance-tuning.md for defaults).

docs.title: 2. OSD Process Sizing Validation
docs.text:
# Check OSD count and per-host distribution
ceph osd dump | grep "osd.\|host"

# Verify no OSD RAM oversubscription
# One OSD daemon per data disk; each reserves ~4 GiB cache plus DB/WAL working set
# Host with 8 OSDs needs ~32 GiB for OSD processes alone

Expected: OSD count matches hardware; per-host RAM utilization below 75%.

docs.title: 3. OSD Startup Flag Tests
docs.text:
# Set priority for interactive workloads
ceph osd set_priority <osd-id> 1.0

# Throttle OSD disk I/O (bytes per second per OSD)
ceph osd max_bytes_per_sec <osd-id> <bytes>

# Throttle OSD operation rate (ops per second per OSD)
ceph osd max_ops_per_sec <osd-id> <ops>

Expected: Throttle values do not reduce observed throughput below baseline; priority changes take effect without restart.

docs.title: 1. PG Count Calculation Validation
docs.text:
# Calculate recommended PG count per pool
# total_pgs = (num_osd × 100) / pool_replica_count
# Round up to nearest power of 2 per pool

# Example: 9 OSDs, 3-replica pool
echo "scale=0; (9 * 100) / 3" | bc
# → 300 → round to 512

# Validate with ceph pg calc
ceph pg calc

Expected: PG count is a power of 2 and matches ceph pg calc output.

docs.title: 2. Pool Parameter Setting Tests
docs.text:
# Create pool with tuned settings
ceph osd pool create <pool-name> <pg-num> <pgp-num> replicated

# Set maximum size to prevent unbounded growth
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> max_size <n>

# Verify size <= max_size
ceph osd pool get <pool-name> | grep -E "size|max_size"

Expected: size ≤ max_size; pool operates within quotas.

docs.title: 3. Pool Monitoring Signal Tests
docs.text:
# Monitor pool bytes used
ceph osd pool stats <pool-name> | grep bytes_used

# Check PG degradation
ceph pg stat | grep decommission

# Monitor OSD operation rate
ceph osd stat | grep ops

Expected: ceph_pool_bytes_used within normal range; ceph_pg_degraded = 0; ceph_osd_op ops/sec within baseline.

docs.title: 1. CRUSH Ruleset Validation
docs.text:
# List existing rulesets
ceph osd crush rule ls

# Show default host ruleset
ceph osd crush rule dump host

# Verify custom ruleset is assigned to pool
ceph osd pool get <pool-name> | grep crush_rule

Expected: Rulesets exist; pool uses intended ruleset; no misplacement from rule changes.

docs.title: 2. CRUSH Reweight and Rebalance Tests
docs.text:
# Reweight a CRUSH bucket
ceph osd crush reweight <bucket> <new-weight>

# Run rebalance after rule change
ceph osd rebalance

# Verify PG distribution is correct
ceph osd tree | grep -E "pg|root"

Expected: PGs redistribute correctly; no data distribution anomalies after reweighting.

docs.title: 3. Misplacement Detection Tests
docs.text:
# Check for misplaced objects
ceph osd misplaced_pg sum

# Check for crushed (misconfigured) PGs
ceph osd crushed map

Expected: ceph osd misplaced_pg sum = 0; ceph osd crushed map shows no entries.

docs.title: 1. BlueStore Cache Hit Ratio Tests
docs.text:
# Check cache read hit ratio per OSD
ceph osd stat

# Verify read hit ratio > 0.9
# (Collect via Prometheus: ceph_osd_cache_read_hit_ratio)

Expected: Cache read hit ratio > 0.9 across OSDs; if < 0.7, investigate cache size.

docs.title: 2. Write-Back Cache Tests
docs.text:
# Enable write-back for OSD with BBU
ceph osd set slow_key <osd-id>  # disables sync write until cache is flushed

# Configure cache tier retention
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> write_cache_size <size>

Expected: Write-back enabled without data loss; cache size within OSD memory limits.

docs.title: 1. Full Performance Test Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# Auto-test: Ceph performance tuning validation

set -e

echo "=== Ceph Performance Auto-Test ==="

# Pre-check: cluster health
if [ "$(ceph health -q)" != "HEALTH_OK" ]; then
    echo "FAIL: Cluster not HEALTH_OK"
    exit 1
fi

# Check OSD status
OSD_COUNT=$(ceph osd stat | grep -oP 'osd.\d+' | wc -l)
echo "OSD count: $OSD_COUNT"

# Validate PG count per pool
for pool in $(ceph osd pool ls); do
    PGs=$(ceph osd pool get $pool pgp | grep -oP '\d+')
    echo "Pool $pool PGP: $PGs"
done

# Check CRUSH ruleset misplacement
MISPLACED=$(ceph osd misplaced_pg sum)
if [ "$MISPLACED" -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "FAIL: $MISPLACED misplaced PGs"
    exit 1
fi

# Check cache hit ratios (via Prometheus if available)
if command -v prometheus-cli &>/dev/null; then
    RATIO=$(prometheus-cli "ceph_osd_cache_read_hit_ratio" | awk '{print $2}')
    if (( $(echo "$RATIO < 0.7" | bc -l) )); then
        echo "FAIL: Cache hit ratio $RATIO < 0.7"
        exit 1
    fi
fi

echo "=== All auto-tests passed ==="

docs.title: Snapshot Strategies
docs.text:
Ceph provides cluster‑aware snapshots that capture the state of a pool or the whole cluster at a point in time. Snapshots are copy‑on‑write, inexpensive to create, and can be used as the foundation for backups, rollbacks, or disaster‑recovery drills.

Aspect Recommendation Scope Snap individual pools (ceph osd pool snapshot <pool> <name>) or the entire cluster (ceph snapshot create <name>). Frequency Align with your RPO. For critical workloads, create snapshots every 5‑15 minutes; for less critical, hourly or daily. Retention Use a lifecycle script that retains the last N snapshots and prunes older ones (ceph osd pool snapshot <pool> rm <name>). Automation Deploy a cron job or operator that snapshots pools, pushes the snapshot metadata to an external object store (e.g., Ceph RGW) for long‑term retention. Verification After each snapshot, run ceph osd snapshot ls <pool> <name> and confirm the size_max and size_used values are as expected.

docs.title: Example: Automated weekly snapshot script (bash)
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
POOLS="data metadata logs"
for POOL in $POOLS; do
  NAME="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
  ceph osd pool snapshot "$POOL" "$NAME"
  # Optional: upload to RGW for off‑cluster retention
  # rclone copy ceph://$POOL/. s3://backups/ceph/$POOL/$NAME \
    --include "*.json" --fast-list
done

docs.title: OSD Replacement
docs.text:
When an OSD fails or reaches end‑of‑life, Ceph’s self‑healing mechanism replaces it with minimal disruption.

  1. Mark the OSD out – ceph osd out <osd_id> (or use the dashboard/CRUSH map edit).
  2. Remove the OSD – ceph osd purge <osd_id> --yw (the --yw flag waits for the OSD to become inactive).
  3. Add the new OSD – physically install, enable, and join it to the cluster (ceph osd create <id> then ceph osd crush add‑osd <new_id> <host> <device>).
  4. Re‑balance – Ceph will automatically re‑assign placement groups; monitor with ceph pg stat and ceph pg <pg_id> query.
  5. Verify health – ceph health detail should show no PEMBALANCE or UNAVAIL warnings after the re‑balance completes.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] OSD is marked out and drained.
  • [ ] New OSD appears in ceph osd tree.
  • [ ] PGs are re‑distributed evenly (ceph pg stat shows balanced).
  • [ ] No recoveries or activating PGs remain after 2× the normal PG activation time.

docs.title: Pool Recovery
docs.text: Recovering a pool may be needed after accidental deletion, corruption, or a catastrophic OSD loss. Ceph’s pool recovery leverages existing PG data and, if needed, snapshots.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Identify the missing pool – ceph osd pool ls.
  2. Create an empty pool with the same type – ceph osd pool create <pool> <pg_num> <type> (e.g., replicated or erasure_coded).
  3. Restore from snapshot (if available) – 
    ceph osd pool snapshot <pool> <name>
rbd export‑snapshot <pool>/<obj> <snapshot> <dest>   # for RBD pools
    Or use ceph osd pool set <pool> snapshot <name> restore to point the new pool at the snapshot’s data.
  4. Verify data integrity – run ceph tell pool/<pool> injectfiles or compare checksums.
  5. Re‑balance – ensure the pool’s PGs are fully recovered (ceph pg stat shows active+clean).

docs.title: When snapshots are not available
docs.text:
• Use CRUSH map adjustments to recover from an OSD failure; Ceph will rebuild from remaining replicas.
  • For erasure‑coded pools, Ceff can rebuild using XOR parity; monitor ceph osd pool meta <pool> for erasure_code_profile.

docs.title: Disaster Recovery (DR) Procedures
docs.text: DR in Ceph typically means recovering from a full site loss or a prolonged cluster outage. The primary mechanisms are cross‑cluster replication and snapshot‑based restoration.

docs.title: 1. Cross‑cluster RGW replication (recommended for RPO ≤ 1 min)
docs.text:
• Configure Ceph RGW bucket replication to a remote cluster (ceph rbd mirror pool target or RGW replication rules).
  • Periodically verify the remote replica (ceph rbd mirror status <pool>/<obj>).
  • Failover procedure:
  • Promote the remote cluster as the primary (ceph rbd mirror promote <pool>/<obj>).
  • Update DNS / endpoint to point to the restored cluster.
  • Re‑establish replication in the opposite direction once the original site is repaired.

docs.title: 2. Snapshot‑based restoration (RPO depends on snapshot frequency)
docs.text:
• Ensure a recent snapshot exists (ceph osd pool snapshot ls <pool>).
  • Create a new pool from the snapshot: 
    ceph osd pool clone <pool>@<name> <new_pool>
  • Migrate applications to use <new_pool>.
  • Verify application data and application‑level consistency (database dumps, log checks, etc.).

docs.title: 3. Full cluster restart after loss
docs.text:
• Re‑install failed nodes, add new OSDs, and allow the cluster to recover (ceph health → HEALTH_OK).
  • Once the cluster is healthy, restore any missing pools from the most recent cross‑cluster snapshot or external backup.

docs.title: DR Run‑book checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Snapshot taken < RPO ago.
  • [ ] Remote replica verified healthy.
  • [ ] Failover test performed in a staging environment.
  • [ ] DNS / client config updated and validated.
  • [ ] Post‑failover data consistency checks passed.
  • [ ] Original cluster re‑integrated and re‑synced.

docs.title: Validation Steps
docs.text:
Regular validation ensures that snapshots, OSD replacements, and DR procedures actually work. Include these checks in your SRE routine.

Validation Command / Action Expected Outcome Snapshot list ceph osd pool snapshot <pool> ls Lists all snapshots with timestamps; no errors. Snapshot integrity ceph osd snapshot ls <pool> <name> --format json JSON includes size_used, size_max; values match pool usage. OSD health ceph health detail No INACTIVE, UNDER‑REPLICATED, or PEMBALANCING warnings. PG consistency ceph pg stat All PGs active+clean, recovery count = 0. Pool recreation from snapshot ceph osd pool clone <pool>@<name> <new_pool> then rbd ls <new_pool> New pool contains the same objects as the snapshot. RGW replication status ceph rbd mirror status <pool>/<obj> (or RGW ceph rgw replication ls) Remote mirror is synced or up‑to‑date. DR drill – promote remote Promote remote cluster, switch client endpoint, run application smoke test Application functions without data loss; RPO/RTO met. Checksum verification (optional) ceph osd calc check <pool> <object> Matches stored checksum; no silent corruption.

docs.title: Automated validation pipeline (example cron)
docs.text:
0 * * * * /usr/local/bin/ceph-snapshot-validate.sh >> /var/log/ceph/validate.log 2>&1
0 3 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/ceph-dr-drill.sh >> /var/log/ceph/dr-drill.log 2>&1

The scripts should exit non‑zero and send an alert (e.g., PagerDuty, Slack) if any check fails, ensuring that a broken backup or unrehearsed failover is caught long before an incident.

This document is intended to be kept under version control alongside the rest of the cloud‑native guide. Update it whenever Ceph version, topology, or RPO/RTO targets change.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Documented backup and recovery process for the Ceph cluster managed by Rook.

docs.title: RPO and RTO
docs.text:
• RPO: <= 1 minute — continuous WAL archiving enables point-in-time recovery.
  • RTO: <= 30 minutes — measured from failure detection to cluster HEALTH_OK with data restored.

docs.title: Backup Strategy
docs.text:
• Continuous WAL/binlog archiving to a durable store.
  • Periodic base backups (physical) for fast full restore.
  • Cross-region copy for disaster recovery.

docs.title: Restore Verification
docs.text:
• Automated scheduled restore tests against a throwaway instance.
  • Measured RTO recorded; alert if restore fails or exceeds the RTO budget.
  • Integrity checks (row counts, checksums, smoke query set) performed after restore.

docs.title: Ceph storage (cephadm path)
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Ceph deployed by cephadm on dedicated Linux hosts, consumed by Kubernetes through the external CSI driver, and optionally exposed as S3 via RGW.

        K8s cluster                    Ceph cluster (dedicated hosts)
  +-------------------+           +-----------------------------------+
  | CSI driver pod   |---------->| MON x3 (10.40.0.x:6789)            |
  | (external)       |           | MGR x2 (active/standby)              |
  +-------------------+           | OSD x N (10.40.0.x:6800-7568)      |
                                  | MDS x N (CephFS, optional)         |
                                  | RGW x N (S3, optional)              |
                                  +-----------------------------------+

Two supported deployment models exist in this platform: this one (cephadm on dedicated hosts) and Rook-Ceph inside the cluster (storage/rook-ceph/). cephadm runs every Ceph daemon as a container under one container engine — Docker or Podman, picked per cluster and never mixed — and orchestrates placement, upgrades, and recovery across the dedicated hosts.

This document is a full, ordered instruction set for the cephadm path:

  1. Prepare servers for each role
  2. Prepare air-gap repositories/registries
  3. Deployment type: Docker, Podman, then Cephadm bootstrap
  4. Assign roles to nodes (and all roles to one server when co-locating)
  5. Check services and apply best practices
  6. Define OSDs
  7. Define pools (Kubernetes and non-Kubernetes) and other
  8. Prepare monitoring daemons

docs.title: B. Step 1 — Prepare servers for each role
docs.text: Do this on every Ceph host before any cephadm command. Ceph assumes a clean, tuned host; it does not fix the OS for you.

docs.title: 1.1 Host roles and counts
docs.text:
Role Minimum hosts Placement rule Failure tolerance MON 3 Separate hosts, separate racks if available 1 host (odd count only; 2 is worse than 1; 4 tolerates the same as 3) MGR 2 Separate hosts from MON when possible 1 host (one active, one standby) OSD ≥ 3 One OSD daemon per data disk; ≥ 3 hosts for a 3-replica pool 1 host MDS 2 Active + standby; required only for CephFS 1 host RGW 2 Behind the edge load balancer; stateless 1 host Crash/exporter all hosts Co-located —

Never put MON on the same host as the only OSD of a pool, and never let the DB/WAL device be shared with the OS.

docs.title: Which roles can be hosted together
docs.text:
Co-location is a deliberate trade-off: fewer hosts, higher blast radius. The safest default is one role type per host. Co-locate only when the site cannot spare the hosts.

Allowed co-location: - MON + MGR may share a host (never all three MONs on one host). - OSD + RGW may share a host; RGW is stateless. - MDS + MGR may share a host. - MON + OSD on the same host only with ≥ 3 hosts; losing one host loses a monitor and a third of the data at once.

Never co-locate the only MON store with the OSD DB device.

docs.title: Minimum requirements: VM vs physical
docs.text: Concern Physical (bare metal) Virtual machine Ceph OSD Recommended; direct disk access, predictable latency Acceptable with raw/SCSI-passthrough disks; never a shared virtual disk MON / MGR / OSD Local SSD for MON store and OSD DB/WAL Local SSD + dedicated vCPUs; never shared storage Failure domain Physical host Host + hypervisor + storage array Disk passthrough N/A (native) Required for Ceph OSD data disks; shared virtual disks break replication

docs.title: Requirements calculations
docs.text:
State the assumptions; do not use a single formula.

Replicated (3x) usable capacity:

usable_raw = Σ(disk_size_available) × (1 - reserved_fraction)
usable_3x  = usable_raw / 3

reserved_fraction is typically 0.05–0.10 (filesystem, WAL, DB). Working target: 70% of usable — keep 25–30% of raw capacity free so a failed OSD can be replaced and rebalanced without filling the pool.

Erasure coding (k+m):

usable_ec = raw × (k / (k + m))

A 4+2 pool gives ~67% usable. EC saves space but read-decode on recovery is slow; not recommended for write-heavy databases.

IOPS: derived from disk type and queue depth.

Network: a 3x pool writes 2 copies to the network per 1 GB of client write. A 10 GbE link supports roughly 1.25 GB/s of client write throughput before saturation.

Compute resources (vCPU and RAM): Ceph is not CPU-heavy; the drivers are network, decompression, and per-OSD memory. Size from the role count and daemon count per host, not from disk capacity.

Role vCPU grows when RAM grows when Starting point MON Client request rate (kubectl, CSI, RGW, admin) and MON count in quorum MON count and mon store size 2 vCPU, 8 GiB MGR Enabled modules (prometheus, dashboard, orchestration) and scrape targets Dashboard state and cached metrics 2 vCPU, 8 GiB OSD Number of OSD daemons on the host and rebuild/rebalance activity OSD daemon count (cache per daemon) and BlueStore DB/WAL cache 1 vCPU per OSD daemon (min 4), 4 GiB per OSD daemon (min 16 GiB) MDS CephFS clients and metadata operation rate CephFS filesystems and metadata cache 4 vCPU, 16 GiB RGW S3 request rate and concurrent connections RGW instance count and object cache 4 vCPU, 8 GiB

Key principle: Disk capacity does NOT drive CPU or RAM. A 10 TB disk with 1 OSD needs the same RAM as a 1 TB disk with 1 OSD. RAM scales with the number of daemons, not with how full the disks are. CPU scales with request/rebuild activity, not with capacity.

Memory per OSD daemon: each OSD daemon reserves roughly 4 GiB for its cache plus the BlueStore DB/WAL working set. A host with 8 OSDs needs ~32 GiB for OSD processes alone, plus OS overhead. Do not size RAM from disk capacity — size from the OSD count per host.

vCPU oversubscription: Ceph tolerates CPU oversubscription better than memory oversubscription. If hosts are RAM-bound, reduce OSDs per host before reducing vCPU.

Placement groups (PGs): PGs are the unit Ceph uses to distribute objects across OSDs. Too few PGs = uneven distribution and hot spots; too many PGs = CPU and memory pressure on every MON and OSD.

Rule of thumb (approximate, tune from ceph pg calc): - total_pgs = (num_osd × 100) / pool_replica_count - Round up to the nearest power of 2 per pool.

Example: 9 OSDs across 3 hosts, 3-replica pool → (9 × 100) / 3 = 300 → round to 512 PGs. A small 3-host site needs only ~512–1024 PGs total across all pools. Adding pools without reducing PG count per pool multiplies PG count and increases MON/OSD memory.

Check PG health: 

cephadm shell -- ceph pg stat
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool ls detail
cephadm shell -- ceph osd df
active+clean with undersized or degraded means PGs are not yet placed; stuck unclean means a failure is in progress.

OS and application reservation: Always reserve resources for the operating system and non-Ceph applications on every host, before allocating the rest to Ceph daemons:

Reservation vCPU RAM Purpose Operating system 1 2 GiB Kernel, systemd, journald, SSH, cron Container engine (Docker/Podman) 0.5 1 GiB Engine daemon, container metadata, image layers Monitoring agent (node_exporter / prometheus scrape) 0.25 0.5 GiB Host metrics collection Cephadm / orchestrator overhead 0.25 0.5 GiB cephadm container management on the host Break-glass / admin tools 0 0.5 GiB cephadm shell, diagnostics, logs Total reserve per host 2 vCPU 4.5 GiB Reserve on every Ceph host before Ceph daemons

Correctly sized example — 3-host site, replicated 3x (separated roles, no MON+OSD co-location):

Host Roles vCPU RAM Disk ceph-mon-1 MON 2 8 GiB 100 GiB SSD ceph-mon-2 MON 2 8 GiB 100 GiB SSD ceph-mon-3 MON + MGR 4 16 GiB 100 GiB SSD ceph-osd-1 OSD x3 7 28 GiB 100 GiB SSD + 3 data disks + 1 NVMe DB/WAL ceph-osd-2 OSD x3 7 28 GiB 100 GiB SSD + 3 data disks + 1 NVMe DB/WAL ceph-osd-3 OSD x3 7 28 GiB 100 GiB SSD + 3 data disks + 1 NVMe DB/WAL

Total per OSD host = 7 vCPU / 28 GiB for Ceph OSDs, plus 2 vCPU / 4.5 GiB OS + agent reservation. This layout satisfies the 3-replica pool (9 OSDs across 3 OSD hosts) and keeps MONs off OSD hosts.

docs.title: 1.2 OS and kernel — mandatory or best practice?
docs.text:
Mandatory: OS (Oracle Linux 8/9 or Ubuntu 22.04/24.04) and XFS with ftype=1 for BlueStore. Ceph does not install or fix the OS.

Best practice: Kernel 5.4+ (OL9) / 5.15 (Ubuntu 24.04), dedicated NVMe for OSD DB/WAL, chrony for NTP. Confirm the exact kernel floor against the Ceph release notes for the pinned version.

Required kernel modules (mandatory for networking and RBD):

modprobe br_netfilter
modprobe nf_conntrack
modprobe rbd

cat > /etc/modules-load.d/ceph.conf <<'EOF'
br_netfilter
nf_conntrack
rbd
EOF

How to check:

cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
lsmod | grep -E 'br_netfilter|nf_conntrack|rbd'
getenforce || aa-status --enabled   # SELinux / AppArmor

Impact if not applied: - Missing br_netfilter / nf_conntrack: bridged container traffic and Ceph replication traffic can be dropped or misrouted by netfilter; daemons may appear down. - Missing rbd: RBD block devices cannot be mapped; the external CSI driver cannot attach volumes. - No XFS ftype=1: BlueStore refuses the device; OSD creation fails. - Wrong kernel: Ceph daemons may crash or refuse to start on unsupported kernels.

docs.title: 1.3 Time and name resolution
docs.text:
All Ceph hosts must agree on time; monitor quorum depends on timestamp agreement. A drifting clock can drop a monitor from quorum.

NTP (internal only; air-gapped site):

chronyc sources -v
chronyc tracking

Use at least two internal NTP sources; a third on a different switch is recommended.

Name resolution: every Ceph host must resolve every other Ceph host by name:

getent hosts ceph-mon-1 ceph-mon-2 ceph-mon-3 ceph-osd-1

No DNS environment: If there is no DNS server, use /etc/hosts on every Ceph host and keep it identical everywhere:

cat >> /etc/hosts <<'EOF'
10.40.0.11  ceph-mon-1
10.40.0.12  ceph-mon-2
10.40.0.13  ceph-mon-3
10.40.0.14  ceph-osd-1
10.40.0.15  ceph-osd-2
10.40.0.16  ceph-osd-3
EOF

Name resolution failures prevent cephadm from adding hosts and daemons from forming quorum.

docs.title: 1.4 Disks and filesystems (node preparation)
docs.text:
One OSD daemon per data disk. Each data disk must be a dedicated device — never a shared virtual disk, never a partition shared with the OS. XFS with ftype=1 is required by BlueStore.

# List candidate data devices
lsblk -d -o NAME,SIZE,TYPE,ROTA,MODEL

# Destructive: wipes stale filesystems/signatures from data devices only
wipefs -a /dev/sdb
wipefs -a /dev/sdc

Do not format the device yourself — cephadm formats and manages OSD disks via BlueStore. This step only clears stale signatures so device detection is clean.

Reserve a separate NVMe device per host for the OSD BlueStore DB/WAL when data devices are HDD or SATA SSD. Do not share the DB/WAL device with the OS or with another OSD's data disk.

How many OSDs per host: - One OSD daemon per data disk. - Minimum 3 OSD hosts (one OSD each) for a 3-replica pool. - More OSDs per host = more throughput and more rebuild load per host failure. Balance rebuild time against host count.

docs.title: 1.5 Network
docs.text:
Two NICs/VLANs (recommended): one public (client/MON/RGW traffic, 10.40.0.0/24) and one cluster/replication (replication/OSD traffic, 10.41.0.0/24). Replication traffic is the driver; 10 GbE is the minimum for production. Separating them keeps Ceph replication from competing with client and management traffic.

One network: If the site has only one network, put MON and OSD traffic on the same subnet/VLAN. Ceph still works, but replication traffic competes with client traffic on the same link. Mitigations: - Size the link for the combined load (replication is roughly 2× the client write volume for a 3x pool). - Use separate IP ranges within the same VLAN so firewall rules can still distinguish MON vs OSD traffic. - Prefer 10 GbE or faster; 1 GbE is not suitable for production Ceph.

Verify reachability between every pair of hosts:

ping -c 3 10.40.0.12

docs.title: 1.6 SSH access
docs.text:
The bootstrap host must reach every other Ceph host over SSH without a password prompt, because cephadm installs the engine and daemons on remote hosts itself.

Service user: SSH as a non-root deploy user (e.g. cephadm) with passwordless sudo is preferred over direct root login. cephadm elevates via sudo when needed. This user is a local account on each Ceph host — not a directory account.

# From the bootstrap host, as the deploy user
ssh cephadm@ceph-osd-2 'hostname'
ssh cephadm@ceph-osd-3 'sudo hostname'

Ensure the deploy user can run sudo without a password on each Ceph host:

# On each Ceph host
echo "cephadm ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/cephadm

Install the same SSH public key (break-glass key) for the deploy user on every Ceph host so the bootstrap host can connect without a password:

# From the bootstrap host
ssh-copy-id cephadm@ceph-osd-2
ssh-copy-id cephadm@ceph-osd-3

AD authentication: Hosts must NOT be joined to Active Directory/LDAP (ADR-0015). Identity is application-layer only; nodes keep local accounts plus an offline break-glass key. Do not rely on AD/Kerberos for the SSH access cephadm uses — use local key-based authentication.

Verify:

ssh cephadm@ceph-osd-2 'sudo cephadm --version'

docs.title: C. Step 2 — Prepare air-gap registry/repository
docs.text:
cephadm pulls Ceph container images at bootstrap and whenever it deploys or upgrades a daemon. In an air-gapped site there is no internet, so the images must already live in your internal registry and every host must pull from it.

Terminology: - Registry = the server/manager that stores images (Harbor, Nexus, or a self-hosted OCI registry). - Repository = a named collection of images inside a registry (e.g. ceph/ceph, ceph/ceph-osd). - Repositories = plural, multiple collections.

Pick one registry manager per site and do not mix them. Supported options:

Registry manager Best for Notes Harbor (platform default) Image + OCI chart registry with projects, robot accounts, vulnerability scanning Already referenced throughout this platform as harbor.internal; has a web GUI for managing projects and robot accounts Nexus Single manager for images and OS packages (yum/apt) plus docker repos Good when one tool must own both artifacts and packages; has a web GUI for repositories Self-hosted OCI registry (suggested alternative) Smaller air-gap sites that only need image mirroring Single binary, filesystem storage, OCI-compatible; lighter than Harbor/Nexus; minimal or no GUI

The engine-side configuration (Docker daemon.json, Podman registries.conf) is in section D, per deployment method. This section covers the registry side: what to mirror and where, using either the CLI or the web GUI.

docs.title: C.2.0 Addresses to proxy / mirror
docs.text:
Configure your internal registry/repository manager to proxy or mirror these addresses. Every Ceph host must reach only the internal addresses; nothing on the Ceph hosts may reach the public internet.

What Public source (proxy from) Internal address (configure hosts to) Notes Ceph container images quay.io/ceph harbor.internal/ceph, nexus.internal:<port>/ceph, or registry.internal:5000/ceph Mirrored with skopeo; tags pinned in compatibility/version-matrix.md OS packages (Oracle Linux) yum.oracle.com Internal OL mirror (Nexus yum group or yummirror.internal) dnf repo files point here OS packages (Ubuntu) archive.ubuntu.com, security.ubuntu.com Internal Ubuntu mirror (Nexus apt repo or ubuntumirror.internal) apt sources.list points here Container engine (Docker) download.docker.com Internal mirror or the RPM/DEB already staged Engine installed before bootstrap Container engine (Podman) OS vendor repos Internal OS mirror podman package comes with the OS skopeo OS vendor repos Internal OS mirror skopeo package comes with the OS

Do not configure Ceph hosts to use any public registry directly. Set NO_PROXY=no_proxy to exclude all internal addresses (harbor.internal, nexus.internal, registry.internal, 10.40.0.0/24, 10.41.0.0/24, .internal, localhost, 127.0.0.1) so internal traffic never goes through a proxy.

docs.title: C.2.1 Harbor (platform default)
docs.text:
Mirror Ceph images into Harbor ahead of time from a connected build machine:

# Run on a connected machine, never on an air-gapped host
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18 docker://harbor.internal/ceph/ceph:v18 --dest-tls-verify=false
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v17 docker://harbor.internal/ceph/ceph:v17 --dest-tls-verify=false

What is skopeo? skopeo is a tool for inspecting and copying container images between registries without running a daemon. It copies image layers and metadata directly from one registry to another (e.g. from the public quay.io to your internal Harbor), so you can stage Ceph images on a connected machine and push them into the air-gapped registry. Install it from your internal mirror (dnf install -y skopeo on Oracle Linux, apt install -y skopeo on Ubuntu).

Via Harbor GUI: log in to the Harbor web UI, create a ceph project, push or mirror the Ceph images into it, then create a robot account with pull permission for cephadm to use. Record the exact image tags in compatibility/version-matrix.md so the pinned version propagates through the build.

docs.title: C.2.2 Nexus
docs.text:
Mirror Ceph images into a Nexus docker (group) repository, e.g. nexus.internal:8083 or nexus.internal/repository/ceph/:

# Run on a connected machine, never on an air-gapped host
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18 docker://nexus.internal:8083/ceph/ceph:v18 --dest-tls-verify=false
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v17 docker://nexus.internal:8083/ceph/ceph:v17 --dest-tls-verify=false

Via Nexus GUI: log in to the Nexus web UI, create a docker (group) repository named ceph, mirror the Ceph images into it, then create a service account with pull permission. Record the exact image tags in compatibility/version-matrix.md.

Nexus can also serve OS packages (yum/apt group repos) so the same manager holds both images and packages. When Nexus is the registry, replace harbor.internal with nexus.internal:<port> everywhere below, and point Docker/Podman at the Nexus docker repository.

docs.title: C.2.3 Suggested alternative: self-hosted OCI registry (distribution)
docs.text:
For smaller air-gap sites that only need image mirroring and do not need Harbor's projects/robot accounts or Nexus's package repos, run a minimal OCI-compatible registry (the Docker distribution image) on a filesystem-backed store:

# Run on a connected machine, mirror into the self-hosted registry
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18 docker://registry.internal:5000/ceph/ceph:v18 --dest-tls-verify=false
skopeo copy docker://quay.io/ceph/ceph:v17 docker://registry.internal:5000/ceph/ceph:v17 --dest-tls-verify=false

Run it as a single container or systemd unit backed by a persistent volume. Configure it as insecure (or terminate TLS at the edge load balancer) and point Docker/Podman at registry.internal:5000.

docs.title: D. Step 3 — Deployment type: Docker, Podman, Cephadm
docs.text: cephadm runs every Ceph daemon in a container. It supports Podman (upstream default) and Docker. Pick one engine per cluster and never mix engines inside one cluster — the orchestrator records the engine at bootstrap and reuses it for every daemon. Whichever engine is chosen, it must already be installed, enabled, and pulling from the internal registry before cephadm bootstrap; cephadm will not install the engine.

docs.title: D.1 Engine: Docker
docs.text: Docker must be installed from the internal mirror, pointed at the internal registry, and allowed through the host firewall before cephadm bootstrap. cephadm does not install or configure the engine.

docs.title: D.1.1 Install Docker from the internal mirror
docs.text:
# Oracle Linux (from the internal OL mirror)
dnf install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io

# Ubuntu (from the internal Ubuntu mirror)
apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io

systemctl enable --now docker
docker info | grep -i server-version

docs.title: D.1.2 Configure daemon.json for air-gap
docs.text:
/etc/docker/daemon.json on every Ceph host:

{
  "registry-mirrors": ["https://harbor.internal"],
  "insecure-registries": ["harbor.internal"],
  "live-restore": true,
  "storage-driver": "overlay2",
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "100m",
    "max-file": "3"
  },
  "dns": ["10.10.0.10"],
  "iptables": false,
  "bridge": "none",
  "default-address-pools": [
    { "base": "172.20.0.0/16", "size": 24 }
  ]
}
  • registry-mirrors — pulls are redirected to Harbor so daemon and cephadm never reach quay.io.
  • insecure-registries — Harbor terminates TLS at an internal load balancer; Docker treats it as insecure without this flag and refuses to pull.
  • live-restore — containers keep running if the Docker daemon restarts.
  • iptables: false / bridge: none — the platform manages the network and firewall with nftables/firewalld; Docker must not punch its own holes.
  • dns — internal DNS so containers resolve harbor.internal, ceph-mon-1, etc.
mkdir -p /etc/docker
cat > /etc/docker/daemon.json <<'EOF'
{ ... }
EOF
systemctl restart docker

docs.title: D.1.3 systemd environment drop-in (air-gap)
docs.text:
If the site uses an HTTP proxy for the connected build machine only, exclude it on Ceph hosts and never proxy internal traffic:

mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d
cat > /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/no-proxy.conf <<'EOF'
[Service]
Environment="NO_PROXY=harbor.internal,10.40.0.0/24,10.41.0.0/24,.internal,localhost,127.0.0.1"
Environment="no_proxy=harbor.internal,10.40.0.0/24,10.41.0.0/24,.internal,localhost,127.0.0.1"
EOF
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart docker

docs.title: D.1.4 Firewall rules for Docker (nftables)
docs.text:
Docker daemon traffic to Harbor and between Ceph hosts:

# Allow outbound to the internal registry
ip daddr @harbor_hosts tcp dport 443 accept
# Allow outbound to the internal registry registry API
ip daddr @harbor_hosts tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
# Allow Ceph daemon container traffic on the cluster network
ip saddr @storage_hosts ip daddr @storage_hosts tcp dport { 6789, 6800-7568, 7480 } accept

Do not open Docker's default 2375/tcp (unencrypted Docker API). Verify:

docker info --format '{{ .ServerVersion }}'
curl -sk https://harbor.internal/api/v2.0/systeminfo | head -c 200

When bootstrapping with Docker, pass --docker to cephadm bootstrap and to every subsequent cephadm invocation.

docs.title: D.2 Engine: Podman
docs.text:
Podman is the upstream default for cephadm. It must be installed from the internal mirror, pointed at Harbor, and configured for air-gap before cephadm bootstrap. cephadm does not install or configure the engine.

cephadm runs Ceph daemons as root with privileged host access, so Podman is run rootful on Ceph hosts (not rootless).

docs.title: D.2.1 Install Podman from the internal mirror
docs.text:
# Oracle Linux (from the internal OL mirror)
dnf install -y podman

# Ubuntu (from the internal Ubuntu mirror)
apt install -y podman

systemctl enable --now podman.socket
podman info | grep -i host.version

docs.title: D.2.2 Configure registries.conf for air-gap
docs.text:
/etc/containers/registries.conf on every Ceph host:

[registries.search]
registries = ['harbor.internal']

[registries.insecure]
registries = ['harbor.internal']

[registries.block]
registries = ['docker.io', 'quay.io', 'ghcr.io']
  • registries.search — unqualified image names resolve to Harbor first.
  • registries.insecure — Harbor terminates TLS at an internal load balancer; Podman refuses plain-HTTP registries without this.
  • registries.block — explicit deny-list so nothing accidentally pulls from the public internet.
mkdir -p /etc/containers
cat > /etc/containers/registries.conf <<'EOF'
[registries.search]
registries = ['harbor.internal']

[registries.insecure]
registries = ['harbor.internal']

[registries.block]
registries = ['docker.io', 'quay.io', 'ghcr.io']
EOF

docs.title: D.2.3 Configure containers.conf for air-gap
docs.text:
/etc/containers/containers.conf on every Ceph host:

[containers]
dns = ["10.10.0.10"]

[storage]
driver = "overlay2"

[containers]
log_driver = "k8s-file"
log_opts = {
  "max-size": "100m",
  "max-file": "3"
}
  • dns — internal DNS so containers resolve harbor.internal and Ceph host names.
  • log_driver / log_opts — bounded container logs so a churning Ceph daemon cannot fill the root filesystem.
cat > /etc/containers/containers.conf <<'EOF'
[containers]
dns = ["10.10.0.10"]

[storage]
driver = "overlay2"

[containers]
log_driver = "k8s-file"
log_opts = {
  "max-size": "100m",
  "max-file": "3"
}
EOF

docs.title: D.2.4 systemd environment drop-in (air-gap)
docs.text:
If the site uses an HTTP proxy for the connected build machine only, exclude it on Ceph hosts:

mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/podman.socket.d
cat > /etc/systemd/system/podman.socket.d/no-proxy.conf <<'EOF'
[Socket]
Environment="NO_PROXY=harbor.internal,10.40.0.0/24,10.41.0.0/24,.internal,localhost,127.0.0.1"
Environment="no_proxy=harbor.internal,10.40.0.0/24,10.41.0.0/24,.internal,localhost,127.0.0.1"
EOF
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart podman.socket

docs.title: D.2.5 Firewall rules for Podman (nftables)
docs.text:
Podman daemon and Ceph daemon container traffic:

# Allow outbound to the internal registry
ip daddr @harbor_hosts tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
# Allow Ceph daemon container traffic on the cluster network
ip saddr @storage_hosts ip daddr @storage_hosts tcp dport { 6789, 6800-7568, 7480 } accept

Do not expose the Podman API socket over TCP. Verify:

podman info --format '{{ .Host.Version }}'
curl -sk https://harbor.internal/api/v2.0/systeminfo | head -c 200

When bootstrapping with Podman, omit --docker (Podman is the default).

docs.title: D.3 Cephadm bootstrap
docs.text:
Run on the first storage node only (the initial MON host). This creates the cluster, the first MON, the MGR, and writes /etc/ceph/ceph.conf and /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring.

# Install cephadm on the first node (from the internal mirror)
dnf install -y cephadm   # OL
# apt install -y cephadm   # Ubuntu

# Bootstrap. Pass --docker only when Docker is the engine; omit for Podman.
cephadm --docker bootstrap \
  --mon-ip 10.40.0.11 \
  --cluster-network 10.41.0.0/24 \
  --registry harbor.internal \
  --log-to-file

# Verify the bootstrap host is healthy
cephadm shell -- ceph -s
cephadm shell -- ceph orch ps

--registry harbor.internal tells cephadm to pull daemon images from your internal registry. Without it, cephadm reaches for quay.io, which fails in an air-gapped site.

Copy the cluster config to the other hosts so they can join:

scp /etc/ceph/ceph.conf /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring root@10.40.0.12:/etc/ceph/
scp /etc/ceph/ceph.conf /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring root@10.40.0.13:/etc/ceph/

docs.title: E. Step 4 — Assign roles to nodes (and all roles to one server when co-locating)
E.1 Add hosts
docs.text:
Run from the bootstrap host (or any host with cephadm shell access). Ensure the engine is installed on each new host first; cephadm does not install it.

cephadm shell -- ceph orch host add ceph-mon-2 10.40.0.12
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host add ceph-mon-3 10.40.0.13
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host add ceph-osd-1 10.40.0.14
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host add ceph-osd-2 10.40.0.15
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host add ceph-osd-3 10.40.0.16

cephadm shell -- ceph orch host ls

docs.title: E.2 Label hosts by role
docs.text:
Labels are the contract between the node inventory and the service spec:

cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mon-1 mon
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mon-2 mon
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mon-3 mon
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mgr-1 mgr
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mgr-2 mgr
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-osd-1 osd
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-osd-2 osd
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-osd-3 osd
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mds-1 mds
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-mds-2 mds
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-rgw-1 rgw
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-rgw-2 rgw

docs.title: E.3 Assign all roles to one server (co-location)
docs.text:
Small sites cannot spare ten hosts. Co-location is a deliberate trade-off: fewer hosts, higher blast radius.

Allowed co-location: - MON + MGR may share a host (never all three MONs on one host). - OSD + RGW may share a host (RGW is stateless). - MDS + MGR may share a host. - MON + OSD on the same host only with ≥ 3 hosts; losing one host loses a monitor and a third of the data at once.

Never co-locate the only MON store with the OSD DB device.

To assign all roles to one server, apply all labels to that single host and use explicit host placement via labels (E.2). The generated platform layout uses separated hosts by default; co-location is a manual edit and the operator owns that decision.

Example — all roles on one host (lab/small site only):

cephadm shell -- ceph orch host label add ceph-all-1 mon,mgr,osd,mds,rgw

docs.title: F. Step 5 — Check services and apply best practices
F.1 Check services after bootstrap
docs.text:
# Cluster health
cephadm shell -- ceph -s
cephadm shell -- ceph health detail

# Daemon placement and state
cephadm shell -- ceph orch ps
cephadm shell -- ceph orch host ls

# Monitor quorum
cephadm shell -- ceph mon stat
cephadm shell -- ceph mon dump

# MGR status (active/standby)
cephadm shell -- ceph mgr services

Expect HEALTH_OK before you create OSDs or pools. HEALTH_WARN about missing daemons is normal until placement is applied; HEALTH_ERR is not.

docs.title: F.2 Best practices (mandatory)
docs.text:
• One OSD per device; data and journal/DB on separate devices.
  • CRUSH failure domains at host level, rack level when the site has racks.
  • ≥ 3 hosts for any replicated pool that must survive host loss.
  • Keep 25–30% of raw capacity free for rebalance.
  • Back up the monmap, OSD map, and the data; the monmap is what makes a cluster rebuildable.
  • Use a restricted cephx user for the CSI driver, not client.admin.
  • Never mix Docker and Podman in one cluster.

Strongly recommended: - Separate physical network for Ceph cluster (replication) traffic. - NVMe journal/DB device on HDD-backed pools. - Page on HEALTH_WARN, not only on HEALTH_ERR. - Test an OSD replacement under load before production.

docs.title: G. Step 6 — Define OSDs
docs.text:
List devices, then create OSDs. Create OSDs by label so a host replacement keeps working.

# List available devices on all hosts
cephadm shell -- ceph orch device ls

# Create OSDs across all hosts (uses all available data devices)
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd --all-available-devices

# Or, explicit per-host with DB on a separate NVMe device
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd ceph-osd-1 \
  --data-devices /dev/sdb,/dev/sdc \
  --db-devices /dev/nvme1n1

Verify:

cephadm shell -- ceph osd tree
cephadm shell -- ceph osd stat
cephadm shell -- ceph osd df

Each OSD daemon owns one data disk. ceph osd tree must show every OSD up and in.

docs.title: H. Step 7 — Define pools (Kubernetes and non-Kubernetes)
docs.text: Pools are where data lives. Choose replicated for low-latency/block workloads and erasure coding (EC) for capacity; never EC for write-heavy databases.

docs.title: H.1 Replicated pool for Kubernetes (RBD / CSI)
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create kube-rbd 64 64
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool application enable kube-rbd rbd

# Restricted user for the CSI driver (not client.admin)
cephadm shell -- ceph auth get-or-create client.csi-k8s \
  mon 'allow r' \
  osd 'allow class-read object_prefix rbd_children, allow rwx pool=kube-rbd'

The external CSI driver (cephcsi) consumes this pool and is deployed separately in the cluster; it uses ceph.conf and a restricted keyring, injected from Vault via External Secrets — never inline.

Kubernetes StorageClass:

apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ceph-external-rbd
provisioner: rbd.csi.ceph.com
parameters:
  clusterID: <fsid-from-`ceph fsid`>
  pool: kube-rbd
  imageFeatures: layering
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name: ceph-csi-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-namespace: ceph-csi
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-name: ceph-csi-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-namespace: ceph-csi
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-name: ceph-csi-node
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-namespace: ceph-csi
reclaimPolicy: Delete
allowVolumeExpansion: true
volumeBindingMode: Immediate

docs.title: H.2 Erasure-coded pool for non-Kubernetes bulk data
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool create ec-pool 64 64 erasure
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool application enable ec-pool rgw

EC usable = raw × (k / (k+m)). A 4+2 pool gives ~67% usable. EC saves space but read-decode on recovery is slow; not recommended for write-heavy databases.

docs.title: H.3 CephFS (non-Kubernetes or shared filesystem)
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph mgr module enable cephfs --force
cephadm shell -- ceph fs new cephfs cephfs_metadata cephfs_data
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mds --placement="2 ceph-mds-1 ceph-mds-2"

docs.title: H.4 RGW (S3 object)
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph mgr module enable rgw --force
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply rgw rgw \
  --placement="2 ceph-rgw-1 ceph-rgw-2" \
  --spec '{"rgw_frontend_port": 8080}'

Place RGW behind the edge load balancer (network-matrix/external-load-balancer.md), never expose it directly to clients.

docs.title: H.5 RBD images (non-Kubernetes use)
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- rbd create --pool kube-rbd --size 100 --image-type thick vm-disk-1
cephadm shell -- rbd info vm-disk-1
cephadm shell -- rbd ls kube-rbd

docs.title: I. Step 8 — Prepare monitoring daemons
docs.text:
The Ceph manager exposes Prometheus metrics directly; no separate exporter is needed on every host.

# Enable Prometheus metrics from the MGR
cephadm shell -- ceph mgr module enable prometheus
cephadm shell -- ceph prometheus self-managed

Key metrics to alert on: ceph_health_status, ceph_osd_up, ceph_pg_degraded, ceph_pg_incomplete, ceph_pool_bytes_used, ceph_osd_commit_latency_ms, ceph_mon_quorum_status.

Enable the dashboard (optional UI):

cephadm shell -- ceph mgr module enable dashboard
cephadm shell -- ceph dashboard ac-user-create admin [REDACTED] administrator

Dashboard + alerting rules are wired into the platform Prometheus in monitoring/prometheus.md. Scrape the MGR metrics endpoint (:9283) from the management network.

Verify monitoring:

cephadm shell -- ceph mgr services
curl -s http://<mgr-host>:9283/metrics | grep ceph_health_status

docs.title: OSD failure
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph orch device ls
cephadm shell -- ceph osd tree
# Replace the failed disk on the host, then:
cephadm shell -- ceph orch device ls
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd <host> --replace <osd-id>

Watch ceph -s until pg_degraded clears and backfill completes.

docs.title: MON loss
docs.text:
With 3 MONs, losing 1 keeps quorum; losing 2 does not.

cephadm shell -- ceph mon dump
cephadm shell -- ceph mon remove <removed-mon-id>
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mon --placement="3 ceph-mon-1 ceph-mon-2 ceph-mon-3"

docs.title: Quorum loss (all MONs down)
docs.text: Requires the monmap and OSD map from backup; see lifecycle/backup/. Back up ceph mon dump and the OSD map alongside the data — without the monmap the cluster is not rebuildable.

docs.title: K. What this document intentionally does not cover
docs.text:
• Disk partitioning and layout (per-site, manual).
  • Joining hosts to Active Directory/LDAP — intentional per ADR-0015; identity is application-layer only.
  • Rebooting after kernel args (operator decides when).
  • The in-cluster Rook-Ceph model — that is storage/rook-ceph/rook-ceph.md.

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: CRUSH Ruleset Design
docs.text: CRUSH (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing) is Ceph's algorithm for mapping object data to OSDs without a centralized metadata store. The ruleset defines how data is replicated or erasure-coded across the cluster, how device classes influence placement, and how bucket types organize the hierarchy.

docs.title: Ruleset Overview
docs.text:
• Default ruleset: Ceph clusters ship with a built-in ruleset (usually ruleset 0) that provides simple uniform replication across all OSDs.
  • Custom rulesets: Production clusters should define dedicated rulesets (e.g., ruleset 1, 2) to enforce device-class-aware placement, rack/zone awareness, and erasure-code profiles.
  • Ruleset identification: Each ruleset is referenced by an integer ID. Pools declare their ruleset at creation (ceph osd pool ruleset <pool> <id>) and it cannot be changed without recreating the pool.

docs.title: CRUSH Rule Grammar
docs.text:
A CRUSH rule consists of:

Component Description id Unique integer identifier for the rule. type Bucket type (host, rack, row, pdu, room, datacenter, zone, region, root). Determines the scope of the rule. min, max Minimum and maximum number of OSDs involved in the placement. For replication, min is the number of replicas; for erasure coding, it relates to data + parity chunks. step Placement step (take, choose, choose-last). Controls how CRUSH selects OSDs within the bucket hierarchy. class Device class filter (hdd, ssd, nvme, pmem). Restricts placement to OSDs of the specified class. type_name Named type reference, linking to a previously defined rule or a device class. index Ordered list of bucket names or IDs that CRUSH iterates during placement.

docs.title: Rule Design Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Always associate rules with device classes so that, e.g., SSD-only pools place data on SSDs and HDD pools on HDDs.
  2. Use separate rulesets for different workloads: replication‑heavy pools, erasure‑coded analytics pools, and gateway pools should each have their own rule to avoid cross‑contamination.
  3. Respect rack/zone topology: Include rack and zone bucket types in rules to prevent losing all replicas in a single physical failure domain.
  4. Set appropriate min/max: For 3‑way replication, min=3, max=3. For erasure coding with 2 data + 2 parity chunks, set min=4, max=4 (or let CRUSH compute the chunk count from the profile).
  5. Document the ruleset ID in cluster runbooks so that operators know which rule a pool uses and can troubleshoot placement anomalies.

docs.title: Replica Rules (Replication)
docs.text: Replication rules ensure that each object exists on N distinct OSDs, spreading across failure domains.

docs.title: Example: 3‑Way Replication with Device-Class Awareness and Zone Spread
docs.text:
rule replica {
    step choose
    size 3
    type osd
    class ssd
    index_rule (type host min 3 max 3 step choose class ssd) # inline illustration
}

In practice, a Ceph CRUSH command to create such a rule looks like:

ceph osd crush rule create-replica \
    1 \
    "replica-ssd" \
    host \
    min 3 \
    max 3 \
    step choose \
    type osd \
    class ssd

Result: Objects in pools using ruleset 1 will be placed on 3 OSDs that all belong to the ssd device class. CRUSH will automatically spread the 3 OSDs across distinct host buckets (i.e., different physical hosts) because the default CRUSH map groups OSDs under host buckets.

docs.title: Replication Bucket Types Commonly Used
docs.text: Bucket Type Purpose host Physical server; CRUSH ensures replicas land on different hosts. rack Rack-level failure domain; useful when multiple hosts share a power source or network switch. row Row-level domain within a datacenter (less common). datacenter Geographic region; used for cross‑datacenter replication. region Wide‑area region; for multi‑region clusters.

docs.title: Tuning Replication Rules
docs.text:
• Add until/choose‑first steps if you need to enforce that the first N choices respect a particular constraint (e.g., avoid placing two replicas on the same rack).
  • Use index_rule to compose complex rules from simpler ones (e.g., “choose 3 hosts, then within each host choose 1 OSD”).
  • Test with ceph osd crush rule dump <rule_name> and verify that size matches the desired replica count and that class and type filters are applied as expected.
  • Avoid step take in most replication rules; choose or choose-last gives CRUSH freedom to spread replicas across the hierarchy, whereas take tends to cluster them under the first matching branch.

docs.title: Erasure Code Rules (Erasure Coding)
docs.text: Erasure‑coding rules define how data is striped across OSDs with parity chunks for fault tolerance. They are more complex than replication rules because CRUSH must stripe data and compute parity while respecting device classes and failure domains.

docs.title: Example: 2‑Data‑2‑Parity (RS 4+2) Erasure Coding on SSDs
docs.text:
ceph osd crush rule create-erasure-code \
    2 \
    "ec-2p-ssd" \
    host \
    min 4 \
    max 4 \
    step choose \
    type osd \
    class ssd

Result: Objects in pools using ruleset 2 will be striped across 4 OSDs, each holding a different data or parity chunk. The total storage efficiency is 4 / 6 = 66.7 % (2 data + 2 parity). The cluster can tolerate the loss of any 2 OSDs without data loss.

docs.title: Erasure Code Bucket Types and Considerations
docs.text: Bucket Type Purpose in EC Rules host Ensures parity and data chunks land on different hosts. rack Prevents losing all chunks in a single rack failure. region For multi‑region EC profiles; may use a separate ruleset with cross‑region OSD selection. root The top‑level bucket; the rule’s root directive maps to the cluster root.

docs.title: EC Rule Tuning Tips
docs.text:
• Match the size (min/max) to the erasure‑code profile: A 4+2 profile (6 chunks) requires min=6, max=6. The profile is set separately (ceph osd erasure code profile set <profile> <k> <m>) and referenced by the pool; the CRUSH rule’s size must agree.
  • Always include a class filter so that EC chunks are placed on the intended device class. Mixing SSD and HDD chunks in the same EC pool is possible but requires careful rule design and is generally not recommended.
  • Use step choose for even distribution across the hierarchy. step take can be used for “filled‑last” placement (e.g., always fill the lowest‑indexed OSDs first), but this can lead to uneven utilization.
  • Verify with ceph osd erasure code profile get <profile> and then ceph osd crush rule dump <rule_name> to confirm that the rule’s parameters align with the profile’s k and m values.
  • Test failure scenarios: Remove an OSD with ceph osd out <id> and confirm that the cluster enters HEALTH_WARN during recovery but no data is lost; the EC profile should rebuild parity from remaining chunks.

docs.title: Device Classes
docs.text: Device classes allow CRUSH to distinguish OSDs by their storage medium (SSD, HDD, NVMe, Intel Optane/pmem, etc.). Using classes in CRUSH rules ensures that pools respect the intended performance and capacity characteristics.

docs.title: Defining and Assigning Device Classes
docs.text:
1. Create the class (if not already present): 
    ceph osd device class add /dev/nvme0n1 nvme
ceph osd device class add /dev/sda1 hdd
  2. Assign the class to all OSDs of that type (batch example): 
    ceph osd crush reweight type hdd 1.0
    Actually, class assignment is done per‑OSD; you can view current classes: 
    ceph osd dump | grep class
  3. Use the class in rules: 
    ceph osd crush rule create-replica 3 my-replica-rule host min 3 max 3 step choose class ssd

docs.title: Common Device Classes
docs.text: Class Typical Use Case hdd Capacity‑oriented, cost‑effective storage for backups, archives, and less latency‑sensitive workloads. ssd General‑purpose SSD, good for databases, caches, and mixed workloads. nvme High‑performance NVMe, used for low‑latency databases, hot caches, and performance‑critical pools. pmem Persistent memory, combines memory‑speed access with data persistence; used for WAL‑heavy workloads or crash‑safe databases. cpu (rare) OSDs that are actually CPU‑bound accelerators (e.g., GPUs used as storage targets in specialized setups).

docs.title: Best Practices for Device‑Class Rules
docs.text:
• Never mix classes within a single pool’s rule unless you have a specific, documented reason (e.g., a tiered storage pool where hot data goes to SSD and cold data to HDD via separate sub‑pools). Even then, prefer using separate pools with separate rules.
  • Label OSDs at provisioning and verify the assignment after any OSD re‑balancing or cluster re‑install; a missed class label leads to mis‑placement and performance anomalies.
  • Document the class‑to‑purpose mapping in your cluster runbook so that operators can quickly determine which OSDs a given pool will use.
  • Use ceph osd device class list to audit all OSDs and their classes periodically.

docs.title: Bucket Types
docs.text: Bucket types define the hierarchy that CRUSH uses to track failure domains and scope placement decisions. A well‑structured bucket hierarchy is essential for both replication and erasure‑coding rules to spread data across the right failure domains.

docs.title: Standard Bucket Hierarchy
docs.text:
root
├── region
│   ├── datacenter1
│   │   ├── rack1
│   │   │   ├── host1
│   │   │   │   ├── osd.0
│   │   │   ├── host2
│   │   │   │   ├── osd.1
│   │   │   └── ...
│   └── datacenter2
│       └── ...
├── region2
│   └── ...

docs.title: Bucket Type Cheat‑Sheet
docs.text: Bucket Type Typical Label Depth in Hierarchy Role in CRUSH root root 0 Top of the CRUSH map; all other buckets are descendants. region region‑us‑east‑1, region‑eu‑central‑1 1 Geographic region; used for cross‑region replication and EC rules that span sites. datacenter dc‑atl, dc‑sjc 2 Individual data center; used to isolate failures within a city/region. rack rack‑01, rack‑12 3 Rack or cabinet level; prevents all replicas from landing in the same rack. host ceph‑node‑01, ceph‑node‑02 4 Physical server; the most common level for ensuring replicas are on different hosts. osd osd.0, osd.1, … 5 Individual OSD device; the granularity at which CRUSH actually places data. pdu (optional) pdu‑a, pdu‑b 5a Power distribution unit; useful for rack‑level power redundancy modeling. row (optional) row‑A, row‑B 6 Row within a datacenter; less commonly used but helpful for large facilities.

docs.title: Creating and Managing Buckets
docs.text:
Buckets are typically created as part of the initial Ceph deployment via ceph osd crush add-bucket, but they can be added or renamed later:

# Add a new region bucket under root
ceph osd crush add-bucket region-us-east-1 root=root

# Add a rack under that region
ceph osd crush add-bucket rack-01 region=region-us-east-1

# Add hosts under the rack
ceph osd crush add-bucket host1 rack=rack-01

# Add OSDs under each host (example)
ceph osd crush add osd.0 host=host1
ceph osd crush add osd.1 host=host1

docs.title: Bucket Type Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always have at least region, datacenter, rack, and host levels in your CRUSH map for proper failure-domain awareness.
  2. Keep the hierarchy shallow; deep hierarchies can increase CRUSH computation time and make it harder to reason about placement.
  3. Naming consistency: Use a consistent naming scheme (e.g., region-<name>, datacenter-<name>, rack-<number>, host-<name>) so that automation and documentation stay synchronized.
  4. Document the full hierarchy in your runbook; when a new site is added, the CRUSH map must be updated and the change validated.
  5. Use ceph osd crush tree to visualize the current hierarchy and verify that new buckets are attached at the correct level.

docs.title: Adding a New CRUSH Rule
docs.text:
1. Determine the ruleset ID you want to use. Check existing rulesets: 
    ceph osd crush rule list
  2. Create the rule using the appropriate create-replica or create-erasure-code command. Example for a 3‑replica SSD pool: 
    ceph osd crush rule create-replica 1 replica-ssd-3 \
    host min 3 max 3 step choose class ssd
  3. Assign the rule to a pool: 
    ceph osd pool set <pool> ruleset 1
  4. Verify the rule: 
    ceph osd crush rule dump replica-ssd-3
  5. Test placement by putting an object in the pool and checking which OSDs it lands on: 
    rados -p <pool> put test-object <file>
ceph osd map <pool> test-object

docs.title: Modifying an Existing Rule
docs.text:
• CRUSH rules are immutable once created; to change a rule, you must create a new rule with a different ID and reassign the pool. Old rules can be left dormant or deleted after confirming no pools reference them.
  • To change replica count: Create a new rule with the desired size and migrate the pool to the new ruleset. During migration, data is gradually re‑balanced.
  • To change device class: Same as above — new rule, pool reassignment, verify placement, then optionally remove the old rule.

docs.title: Removing a CRUSH Rule
docs.text:
1. Ensure no pools reference the rule: 
    ceph osd pool ruleset <pool>   # check current ruleset
  2. Migrate pools away to another ruleset if needed.
  3. Remove the rule: 
    ceph osd crush rule remove <rule-name>
  4. Clean up: Optionally run ceph osd crush rule list to confirm the rule is gone.

docs.title: Tuning for Performance and Balance
docs.text: Tuning Lever Effect When to Adjust step choose vs step take choose spreads placement more evenly; take fills first‑matching branch. Default to choose. Use take only for specialized "fill‑last" scenarios. min/max size Controls the number of OSDs involved. Set min/max to the desired replica count or EC chunk count. class filter Restricts placement to a device class. Always specify a class for performance‑tiered pools. index_rule Composes sub‑rules. Use when you need compound constraints (e.g., "3 hosts, each from a different rack"). type osd vs type host Determines whether the rule operates at the OSD or host level. Replication rules typically use type osd with class filtering; CRUSH internally spreads across hosts based on the bucket hierarchy.

docs.title: Validation Checklist After Rule Changes
docs.text:
• [ ] ceph osd crush rule dump <name> shows the expected step, size, class, and type.
  • [ ] ceph osd pool stats <pool> reflects the new ruleset and shows correct size (replica count or EC chunk count).
  • [ ] ceph pg stat after placing a test object shows the correct number of OSDs and that they span different host buckets.
  • [ ] ceph osd tree visually confirms that the selected OSDs are in distinct failure domains (different hosts, racks, etc.).
  • [ ] No CRUSH map parse errors in ceph -s output.
  • [ ] Run a short‑term load test or object placement test to ensure no unexpected hotspots appear on specific OSDs.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls and Fixes
docs.text: Pitfall Symptom Fix Forgot to assign device class to OSDs OSDs of the wrong class are selected, or CRUSH falls back to the default ruleset. Re‑assign classes: ceph osd device class add <device> <class> and re‑verify with ceph osd dump. Rule min/max mismatch with pool profile Pool creation fails or objects are placed with wrong redundancy. Align min/max in the rule with the pool’s min_size/max_size and EC profile’s k/m. Missing rack or host level in bucket hierarchy All replicas end up on the same physical rack, defeating fault tolerance. Add the missing bucket level and re‑balance: ceph osd crush rebalance. Using step take for replication Data concentrates on the first few OSDs, causing uneven utilization. Switch to step choose for even distribution. Cross‑region pool using a single‑region ruleset Writes are localized to one region, violating data‑distribution policies. Create a separate ruleset that includes region bucket types and references it for cross‑region pools.

docs.title: Automated Rule Auditing (Optional)
docs.text:
You can write a small script that parses ceph osd crush rule list and ceph osd dump, cross‑checks device classes, and reports any rules that: - Reference a class that no OSDs have. - Have min/max larger than the number of OSDs in the cluster. - Lack a step directive (defaults to choose, but explicit is preferred).

Example skeleton:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
RULES=$(ceph osd crush rule list)
for rule in $RULES; do
  echo "=== Rule: $rule ==="
  ceph osd crush rule dump "$rule"
  # Add custom checks here
done

Schedule this as a cron job or integrate it into your cluster health monitoring pipeline.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Documented automated failover process for the Ceph cluster managed by Rook.

docs.title: Failover Topology
docs.text:
• Primary: The write-active OSD node.
  • Sync Replicas: Replicas that acknowledge writes before ACK to the app (quorum-based, no data loss on failover).
  • Async Replicas: Read-scaling only; NOT a failover target when lagging.
  • Cross-Region Replica: DR target; survives a full region loss.

docs.title: Automated Failover
docs.text:
• Health checks + consensus decide the primary is gone (avoid split-brain via quorum/fencing).
  • Promote the MOST CURRENT sync replica (never a lagging async one).
  • Repoint the app through a stable endpoint (VIP / service discovery / proxy).
  • Fence the old primary so it can't accept writes and split-brain.

docs.title: Drill Requirements
docs.text:
• Failover drilled on a schedule until it is a non-event.
  • Record measured RTO; verify no data loss or split-brain after drill.
  • Document runbook from what actually happened during the drill.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text:
Document Ceph failure recovery procedures: MON loss, OSD loss, MGR loss, pool corruption, PG recovery, rebalancing.

Cross-references storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md §Recovery, lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md §Storage cluster degraded, lifecycle/backup/backup-and-dr.md §Ceph.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: ceph health shows HEALTH_WARN with "mon" warnings. MON quorum lost if fewer than majority of MONs are available.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check MON status
ceph mon stat

# Check quorum status
ceph quorum_status

# If MON is down but data is intact, restart it
cephadm shell -- ceph mon enable <mon-name>

# If MON data is corrupted, deploy a new MON
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mon <new-host>

# Verify quorum restored
ceph quorum_status
ceph health

Rule: Never remove all MONs simultaneously. Always maintain quorum (majority of MONs available).

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: ceph osd stat shows down OSDs. PGs show degraded or undersized state.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check OSD status
ceph osd stat
ceph osd tree

# Check PG status
ceph pg stat

# If OSD is temporarily down, restart it
cephadm shell -- ceph orch restart osd.<osd-id>

# If OSD is permanently lost, mark it destroyed and replace
ceph osd destroy <osd-id> --yes-i-really-mean-it
ceph osd purge <osd-id> --yes-i-really-mean-it

# Deploy new OSD
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd <new-host:device>

# Verify recovery
ceph osd stat
ceph pg stat  # All PGs should be active+clean

Rule: Never destroy more OSDs than the pool can tolerate. A 3-replica pool can lose 2 OSDs; a 2-replica pool can lose 1.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: ceph mgr stat shows no active MGR. Dashboard and metrics unavailable.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check MGR status
ceph mgr stat

# If MGR is down, failover to standby
ceph mgr fail <active-mgr>

# If no standby, deploy a new MGR
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mgr <new-host>

# Verify
ceph mgr stat
ceph health

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: ceph pg stat shows PGs in inconsistent or undersized state. Data may be inaccessible.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check PG status
ceph pg stat
ceph pg dump pgs | grep -v active+clean

# For inconsistent PGs, mark them as clean (data loss possible)
ceph pg repair <pg-id>

# For undersized PGs, wait for recovery or add more OSDs
ceph pg set <pool-name> size <new-size>

# Verify
ceph pg stat  # All PGs should be active+clean

Rule: ceph pg repair can cause data loss. Only use after verifying the data on other replicas is correct.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: PGs are in recovering or rebalancing state. Cluster performance degraded.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check recovery status
ceph recovery status

# Check rebalancing status
ceph osd rebalance status

# Wait for recovery to complete (automatic)
# Monitor progress:
watch ceph pg stat

# If recovery is stuck, check for down OSDs
ceph osd stat

Rule: Do not add or remove OSDs during recovery/rebalancing. Wait for the cluster to reach active+clean state.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: ceph health shows HEALTH_ERR with "OSDFULL". Writes are blocked.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
# Check capacity
ceph df

# If near full, add more OSDs or delete unnecessary data
ceph osd df

# If a pool is full, increase its quota or delete old snapshots
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> size <new-size>

# Verify
ceph health
ceph df

Rule: Keep cluster capacity below 85% to avoid OSDFULL.

docs.title: Kubernetes PVC Lifecycle with Rook-Ceph
docs.text: Documentation of Rook-Ceph Kubernetes integration: StorageClass configuration, PVC lifecycle, snapshot/restore, volume expansion, and troubleshooting PVC binding issues.

docs.title: StorageClass Configuration
docs.text:
Rook-Ceph creates default StorageClasses when the operator is deployed. The primary StorageClasses are:

  • ceph-rbd-standard — RBD (RADOS Block Device) for block volumes.
  • cephfs-standard — CephFS for file-system volumes.
  • cephfs-csi-standard — CSI plugin for CephFS (newer deployments).

docs.title: Example StorageClass (RBD)
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
provisioner: rook/ceph
parameters:
  cluster: rook-ceph
  pool: rbd
  user: admin
  userId: admin
  fsType: ext4
  volumeBindingMode: Immediate

See [storage/storageclass-design.md] for overarching StorageClass design guidelines.

docs.title: PVC Lifecycle States
docs.text:
State Description Next action Pending PVC created, waiting for PV StorageClass provisioning Bound PVC bound to PV Pod can mount the volume Available PV available but unbound Waiting for a PVC to bind Released PVC deleted, PV released Reclaim or delete the PV Failed Provisioning failed Investigate error messages

Cross-reference: PVC Lifecycle in storage/pvc-lifecycle.md.

docs.title: Provisioning and Binding
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: ceph-rbd-standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi

Binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer defers binding until a pod uses the PVC.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: app-pvc

docs.title: VolumeSnapshot
docs.text:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: app-pvc-snapshot
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ceph-rbd-snapshot
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: app-pvc

docs.title: Restoring from a Snapshot
docs.text:
1. Create a PVC from the snapshot:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-pvc-restored
spec:
  storageClassName: ceph-rbd-standard
  dataSource:
    name: app-pvc-snapshot
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  1. Mount the restored PVC in a pod.

Cross-reference: VolumeSnapshot classes are defined in [storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md].

docs.title: Volume Expansion
docs.text:
Rook-Ceph supports online PVC expansion. After increasing the PVC request, the underlying Ceph OSD pool is resized and the file system is grown on pod restart.

# Patch the PVC to request more storage
kubectl patch pvc app-pvc -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"100Gi"}}}}'

# Verify the PVC size
kubectl get pvc app-pvc

File system resize happens automatically when the pod restarts, or you can manually resize inside the pod (e.g., resize2fs /dev/...).

docs.title: Troubleshooting PVC Binding Issues
docs.text: Symptom Likely Cause Resolution PVC stays Pending No available PV, wrong storageClassName Check StorageClass provisioner, ensure Ceph cluster is healthy, pool exists. PVC Pending with FailedBinding Insufficient resources, cluster not ready Verify Rook-Ceph operator is running, OSDs are healthy, pool has quota. PVC binds but I/O errors Wrong fsType or mount options Check PV capacity and fsType match the actual filesystem. PVC Pending VolumeExpansion not allowed Expansion feature gate disabled Enable allowVolumeExpansion: true in the StorageClass.

docs.title: Commands for diagnosis
docs.text:
# Describe the PVC to see events
kubectl describe pvc app-pvc

# Describe the underlying PV
kubectl describe pv <pv-name>

# Check Rook-Ceph cluster health
kubectl -n rook-ceph get cluster rook-ceph -o yaml

# Check storage class parameters
kubectl get storageclass ceph-rbd-standard -o yaml

For deeper debugging, consult [storage/ceph/failure-recovery.md] and the Rook-Ceph documentation.
