docs.title: Ceph MON, OSD, CRUSH, and Pool Configuration
MON (Metadata Daemon) Quorum
docs.text:
• Quorum size: ceil(N/2) + 1 for an odd number of MON nodes (e.g., 3, 5, 7). Even numbers are not recommended because the extra node does not increase fault tolerance but adds overhead.
  • Placement: Deploy MONs on separate physical or virtual machines, ideally in different failure domains (power, network, rack).
  • Data directory: /var/lib/ceph/mon/<cluster>-<id> — keep on fast SSD; do not share with OSD data.
  • Keyring: /etc/ceph/ceph.client.admin.keyring and per-MON keyrings. Rotate keys via ceph auth import after generation.
  • Health monitoring: ceph mon health, ceph mon stat, andPrometheus metrics ceph_mon_election_duration_seconds.
  • Recovery: If a MON is lost, replace it and restart; the remaining MONs preserve the cluster state. Do not manually edit the mon map.

docs.title: OSD (Object Storage Daemon) Tuning
docs.text: Parameter Recommended Default Description osd_max_backfills 2 Maximum concurrent backfill operations per OSD. Reduce if cluster is latency-sensitive. osd_max_create_size 0 (unlimited) Maximum object size for create operations; typically left at default. osd_max_num_buckets 1000 Upper limit of CRUSH bucket hierarchy depth. Adjust upward only if CRUSH map is deeply nested. osd_scrub_interval 3600 (seconds) How often each OSD runs a scrub. Lower for aggressive consistency checking. osd_deep_scrub_interval 86400 (seconds) Deep scrub frequency; runs full data consistency check. osd_target_utilization_percent 80 Target space utilization; Ceph will strive to keep usage near this % across the cluster. osd_pool_default_pg_autobalance true Enables automatic PG rebalancing when OSDs are added/removed. osd_pool_default_min_size 2 (replicated) / k (erasure) Minimum number of OSDs that must hold data for the pool to be considered "up". osd_pool_default_size 3 (replicated) / m+n (erasure) Total number of OSD copies (replicated) or encoding sets (erasure). osd_request_timeout 30 (seconds) Timeout for individual OSD requests. Increase if network latency is high.

docs.title: OSD Deployment Guidelines
docs.text:
• Device class: Use dedicated SSD or NVMe for journal (osd journal), and spinning rust or HDD for data depending on workload (SSD for metadata‑heavy, HDD for capacity‑oriented).
  • Journal size: osd journal size should be at least 5 GiB, typically 10–20 GiB for sustained write workloads.
  • No overlap: Ensure OSD data directories do not overlap with journal or filesystem metadata.
  • Linux kernel settings: vm.swappiness=1, fs.file-max increased, and net.core.somaxconn tuned if the workload opens many connections.

docs.title: CRUSH Rules
docs.text: CRUSH (Controlled Replication Under Scalable Hashing) determines where data objects and their replicas/encoded chunks are stored. The default rule default works for most clusters, but site‑specific rules may be required.

docs.title: Built‑in Rule IDs
docs.text: Rule ID Name Typical Use 0 default Generic rule; places data across failure domains defined in the CRUSH map. 1 replicated Explicit replicated rule (same behavior as default when using the default rule number). 2 erasure_code Erasure‑code rule; requires a CRUSH hierarchy with erasure_code bucket type.

docs.title: Creating a Custom Rule
docs.text:
# Add a rule that respects three failure domains: host, row, rack
ceph osd crush rule create-replicated my_rule host rack
# or for erasure code
ceph osd crush rule create-erasure-code erasure_rule reed_sol_4+2 host rack

docs.title: Rule Parameters
docs.text:
• min_size, max_size — limit the number of OSDs the rule may use.
  • tunable values (e.g., hashpower, seed) affect distribution quality.
  • After creating a rule, assign it to pools: ceph osd pool set <pool> crush_rule <rule_name_or_id>.

docs.title: Replicated Pools
docs.text:
• Syntax: ceph osd pool create <pool_name> <pg_num> <pgp_num> [replicated <size>]
  • Default size: 3 (3‑way replication) unless overridden.
  • Minimum size: min_size controls how many copies must be up for the pool to be considered active. Set min_size <= size; typical min_size=2 allows continued operation after one OSD failure.
  • Example:
ceph osd pool create volumes 128 128 replicated 3
ceph osd pool set volumes min_size 2

docs.title: Erasure‑Coded Pools
docs.text:
• Syntax: ceph osd pool create <pool_name> <pg_num> <pgp_num> erasure_code <k> <m> [stripe_width <n>]
  • k — data chunks, m — parity chunks. Total OSDs needed per stripe = k + m.
  • stripe_width — number of OSDs over which each stripe is spread; default is k + m.
  • Example (Reed‑Solomon 4+2, tolerating 2 OSD failures):
ceph osd pool create archives 256 256 erasure_code 4 2
ceph osd pool set archives min_size 3   # keep at least 3 of 6 OSDs up

docs.title: Pool Parameters to Tune
docs.text: Parameter Effect pg_num / pgp_num Number of placement groups per OSD. Higher values improve load balancing but increase metadata overhead. Rule of thumb: OSD count * 100 for replicated, OSD count * 20 for erasure‑coded (adjust for workload). stripe_width For erasure coded pools, controls how many OSDs participate in each stripe. allow_primary_affinity Optional affinity weight for primary OSD selection. target_size Desired number of objects per PG; adjusts PG size automatically.

docs.title: Replication Settings
docs.text:
• pool min_size vs pool size: size is the total number of copies/parities; min_size is the minimum number of healthy copies required for the pool to be active. Setting min_size lower than size permits degradation (e.g., 3‑replica pool can run with min_size=2 after one OSD down).
  • pause / resume: ceph osd pool pause <pool> temporarily stops all I/O; ceph osd pool resume <pool> re‑enables. Use during maintenance.
  • deep_scrub: ceph osd pool deep_scrub <pool> forces a full consistency check across all objects. Schedule during maintenance windows.
  • target_dir: Direct objects to a specific CRUSH bucket via ceph osd pool set <pool> target_dir <bucket>.
  • exclude: During operations, ceph osd pool exclude <osd> <osd> can temporarily remove an OSD from a pool; use with ceph osd pool unexclude after replacement.

docs.title: Replicated Pools
docs.text:
• Usable capacity ≈ (number_of_OSDs * OSD_size) / replication_size.
  • Example: 20 OSDs × 1 TiB each, replication_size=3 → ~6.6 TiB usable.
  • Overhead: PG metadata ~ 1–2 % of total data volume.
  • IOPS: Each OSD serves its share; scale OSD count or striping to meet throughput targets.

docs.title: Erasure‑Coded Pools
docs.text:
• Usable capacity ≈ (number_of_OSDs * OSD_size) * (k / (k + m)).
  • Example: 20 OSDs × 1 TiB each, k=4, m=2 → ~13.3 TiB usable (vs ~6.6 TiB with replication factor 3).
  • CPU cost: Encoding/decoding consumes CPU; ensure enough CPU headroom (typically 10–20 % of cores per OSD node).
  • Stripe width impact: Larger stripe_width spreads I/O across more OSDs, improving parallel throughput but increasing latency per write.

docs.title: Growth Projections
docs.text:
1. Track df -h on the OSD directory and ceph df detail for cluster‑wide used/available.
  2. Set alerts when usage exceeds osd_target_utilization_percent (default 80 %).
  3. Add OSDs before hitting 90 % utilization to avoid auto‑balance thrashing.
  4. Plan for at least 20 % headroom for erasure‑coded pools to accommodate stripe re‑balancing during OSD additions/removals.

docs.title: Tools for Planning
docs.text:
• ceph df — cluster‑wide usage.
  • ceph osd tree — view OSD capacities and weights.
  • ceph osd crush dump — inspect CRUSH map and rule distribution.
  • Prometheus + Grafana dashboards (pre‑built ceph_exporter metrics) for trend analysis.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Adding a new OSD to a Rook-Ceph cluster to increase capacity.

docs.title: When to Add
docs.text:
• Cluster capacity below threshold (e.g., < 20% free).
  • OSD failure replacement (covered in OSD Replacement Procedure).
  • Planned capacity growth per capacity forecast.

docs.title: Provisioning
docs.text:
• Ensure a new block device of equal or greater capacity is available on a node.
  • Label the node if using zone/rack constraints.
  • Create the OSD via the Rook operator: kubectl -n rook-ceph create ceph-osd /dev/<device-path>.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• ceph osd tree — new OSD shows in/up.
  • ceph osd status — cluster includes the new OSD.
  • ceph osd df — usable size increased by the new OSD capacity.
  • Rebalancing begins automatically; monitor with ceph pg stat.

docs.title: Ceph Performance Tuning
docs.text: Previous step | Next step

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Document Ceph performance tuning levers: OSD parameters, pool settings, CRUSH configuration, cache tiers, and monitoring dashboards. Every change should be validated in a staging environment before applying to production.

docs.title: B.1 BlueStore tuning
docs.text: Parameter Default Recommended range Impact bluestore_cache_size Auto (RAM × 5%) 0.3–0.5 × RAM per OSD Controls read/write cache size; too large starves the OS, too small increases disk I/O bluestore_scrub_period 3600 (seconds) 3600–86400 Scrub frequency; lower to detect corruption sooner, higher reduces I/O load bluestore_leaf_size Auto (filesystem block) 4096 or 65536 Affects small-file throughput; larger leaf size reduces metadata operations bluestore_compaction_interval 3600 (seconds) 86400–604800 (daily–weekly) Periodic LSM compaction; too frequent wastes CPU, too rare causes read amplification bluestore_compaction_stall_threshold 20 (percent) 10–30 Stalls compaction if WAL exceeds this percent; lower = more aggressive compaction

docs.title: B.2 OSD process sizing
docs.text:
• One OSD daemon per data disk; each daemon reserves ~4 GiB cache plus the BlueStore DB/WAL working set.
  • Host with 8 OSDs needs ~32 GiB for OSD processes alone, plus OS overhead.
  • Do not oversubscribe RAM per host beyond 75% utilization; reduce OSDs per host before reducing vCPU.

docs.title: B.3 OSD startup flags (if needed)
docs.text:
# Increase priority for interactive workloads
ceph osd set_priority <osd-id> 1.0

# Throttle OSD disk I/O (bytes per second per OSD)
ceph osd max_bytes_per_sec <osd-id> <bytes>

# Throttle OSD operation rate (ops per second per OSD)
ceph osd max_ops_per_sec <osd-id> <ops>

docs.title: C.1 Replicated pool PG count
docs.text:
Rule of thumb (approximate, tune from ceph pg calc):

total_pgs = (num_osd × 100) / pool_replica_count

Round up to the nearest power of 2 per pool.

Example: 9 OSDs across 3 hosts, 3-replica pool → (9 × 100) / 3 = 300 → round to 512 PGs.

A small 3-host site needs only ~512–1024 PGs total across all pools. Adding pools without reducing PG count per pool multiplies PG count and increases MON/OSD memory.

docs.title: C.2 Pool parameters for performance
docs.text:
# Create a pool with tuned settings
ceph osd pool create <pool-name> <pg-num> <pgp-num> [erasure|replicated]

# Set a maximum size (in bytes) to prevent unbounded growth
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> max_size <n>

# Set target size (how many copies/fragments to store)
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> size <n>

# Enable/affinity PGs to specific OSDs for QoS isolation
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> target_size <n>

# Control PG autobalancing
ceph osd set no_autobalancer   # disable
ceph osd unset no_autobalancer # enable

# Set hit/set for anti-affinity (distribute PGs across failure domains)
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> hit_set_type <type>

docs.title: C.3 Pool monitoring signals
docs.text: Signal Normal range Alert threshold ceph_pool_bytes_used Monotonically increasing Sudden > 80% of pool quota ceph_pg_degraded 0 Any value > 0 ceph_pg_incomplete 0 Any value > 0 ceph_osd_op ops/sec Workload-dependent Sudden spike > 2× baseline ceph_osd_commit_latency_ms < 50 ms > 200 ms sustained ceph_osd_queue_depth < 50 > 200

docs.title: D.1 Default CRUSH ruleset
docs.text:
The default host ruleset is adequate for most sites. It uses failure domains defined by label:

  • host (physical server)
  • rack (when racks are present)
  • row (optional)
  • pdu (optional)
  • root (the cluster root)

docs.title: D.2 Creating a custom CRUSH ruleset
docs.text:
# List existing rulesets
ceph osd crush rule ls

# Show the default host ruleset
ceph osd crush rule dump host

# Create a ruleset with rack awareness
ceph osd crush rule create replicate rack <name> <k> <m>
# Example: 3-replica across racks
ceph osd crush rule create replicate my-replicated 3 0

# Create a ruleset with erasure coding
ceph osd crush rule create erasure <name> <k> <m>
# Example: 4+2 EC
ceph osd crush rule create erasure my-ec 4 2

# Assign a pool to use a specific ruleset
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> crush_rule <rule-name>

docs.title: D.3 Tuning CRUSH bucket weights
docs.text:
• Weights should reflect relative capacity of each bucket.
  • Use ceph osd crush reweight <bucket> <new-weight> to adjust incrementally.
  • After reweighting, run ceph osd rebalance to redistribute PGs.

docs.title: D.4 CRUSH misplacement detection
docs.text:
# Check for misplaced objects
ceph osd misplaced_pg sum

# Check for acting outside of failure domain
ceph osd crushed map

docs.title: E.1 BlueStore cache tiering
docs.text: Ceph automatically uses the OSD SSD/NVMe as a read/write cache (the "BlueStore cache"). No separate tiering configuration is needed for most workloads.

docs.title: E.2 Explicit device class tiering
docs.text:
If using different device classes (e.g., SSD + HDD), define device classes and assign OSDs:

# Device classes
ceph osd device class add ssd
ceph osd device class add hdd

# Assign a device class when creating OSD (via cephadm or manually)
# Then use CRUSH rules to stripe across classes

docs.title: E.3 Write-back cache with BBU
docs.text:
If using write-back SSD with Battery-Backed Write cache:

# Enable write-back for an OSD
ceph osd set slow_key <osd-id>  # disables sync write until cache is flushed

# Configure cache tier retention
ceph osd pool set <pool-name> write_cache_size <size>

docs.title: E.4 Cache tier performance signals
docs.text: Signal Normal Alert ceph_osd_cache_read_hit_ratio > 0.9 < 0.7 ceph_osd_cache_write_backlog 0 > 1000 entries ceph_osd_cache_size Configurable Exceeds OSD memory limit

docs.title: F.1 Key Prometheus metrics
docs.text: Metric What it measures Alert condition ceph_health_status Overall cluster health Any value other than 0 (HEALTH_OK) ceph_osd_up OSD daemon availability Any value < number of OSDs ceph_pg_degraded PGs not fully active Any value > 0 ceph_pg_incomplete PGs not fully recovered Any value > 0 ceph_pool_bytes_used Pool capacity usage > 80% of quota ceph_osd_commit_latency_ms OSD commit latency > 200 ms sustained ceph_osd_queue_depth Pending ops per OSD > 200 ceph_mon_election_duration_sec MON election time > 15 seconds ceph_mon_sync_lag_sec MON clock sync lag > 5 seconds

docs.title: F.2 Alerting rules (Prometheus example)
docs.text:
groups:
- name: ceph-performance
  rules:
  - alert: CephClusterDegraded
    expr: ceph_pg_degraded > 0
    for: 1m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Ceph cluster has degraded PGs"
      description: "PG degradation detected: {{ $value }} PGs degraded"

  - alert: CephOSDCommitLatencyHigh
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(ceph_osd_commit_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 200
    for: 5m
    labels:
      severity: warning
    annotations:
      summary: "High OSD commit latency"
      description: "99th percentile commit latency > 200ms over 5m"

  - alert: CephPoolCapacityHigh
    expr: (ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total) > 0.8
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: warning
    annotations:
      summary: "Ceph pool capacity usage high"
      description: "Pool usage at {{ $value | humanize }} over 10m"

docs.title: F.3 Dashboard view (Grafana)
docs.text:
Panel groups to include:

  1. Cluster health: ceph_health_status single value
  2. PG state: ceph_pg_state histogram (active, clean, recovering, etc.)
  3. IOPS per OSD: rate(ceph_osd_ops[1m]) per OSD, aggregated
  4. Latency per OSD: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(ceph_osd_commit_latency_ms_bucket[5m])) by (le)) per OSD
  5. Cache hit ratio: ceph_osd_cache_read_hit_ratio per OSD
  6. Pool usage: ceph_pool_bytes_used / ceph_pool_bytes_total per pool

docs.title: G. Tuning workflow
docs.text:
1. Measure baseline: Run ceph -s and record PG count, OSD health, pool usage, latency.
  2. One change at a time: Apply a single tuning parameter; wait at least one full OSD interval (typically 30m–2h) before measuring.
  3. Validate in staging: Apply changes to a staging cluster first; compare metrics against production baseline.
  4. Rollback plan: Before changing CRUSH rules or pool PG count, document the revert command and expected impact.
  5. Re-measure after cluster stabilization: PGs need time to rebalance after any configuration change; wait for active+clean with undersized=0.

docs.title: H. Common anti-patterns
docs.text:
Anti-pattern Consequence Fix Too many PGs per pool MON/OSD memory pressure, slow PG operations Reduce PG count; recalculate with ceph pg calc Too few PGs per pool Uneven distribution, hot spots, slow rebalancing Increase PG count; recalculate with ceph pg calc max_bytes_per_sec too low Throttles legitimate traffic, slows backups Raise or remove limit size > max_size on replicated pool Writes rejected unexpectedly Ensure max_size >= size CRUSH rule change without rebalancing PGs act on wrong OSDs, data distribution incorrect Run ceph osd rebalance after rule change Disabling scrub entirely Corruption goes undetected longer Keep default scrub period; reduce if needed Over-provisioning cache size RAM starvation, OS instability Cap at 50% of host RAM; monitor host metrics

Previous step | Next step

docs.title: Node, Rack, and Zone Layout
docs.text: Failure domain Typical scope Recommended placement Impact if lost Node Single physical/virtual host Each MON/OSD runs on a distinct host Loss of one host → one MON, one or more OSDs lost; tolerated by quorum/replication Rack Physical rack of servers Spread MON nodes across racks; spread OSD hosts across racks Rack power/network failure loses all nodes in that rack Zone Availability zone / data center Across zones when multi-region Zone loss → full failover to another region CRUSH bucket root > zone > rack > host > osd Define in CRUSH map; align with infrastructure labels Misconfigured CRUSH buckets cause incorrect replica placement and increased data loss risk

docs.title: Recommended CRUSH hierarchy for production
docs.text:
# Example CRUSH map structure (declared via CephCluster spec)
crushdeviceclass: hdd   # or ssd
crushlocation:
  rack: rack-id   # per-node label, e.g. node.label.rack
  host: node-hostname   # minion/k8s node name
  • 3-replica pools: CRUSH should spread replicas across distinct failure domains (rack/zone). Rook sets failureDomain: host by default; promote to rack or zone when the topology is known.
  • Erasure-coded pools: CRUSH placement is more restrictive; typically 1 replica per failure domain, then EC stripes across domains.

docs.title: Failure domain enforcement
docs.text:
• Add node labels reflecting the physical topology (e.g., failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/rack, failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone).
  • Rook's CephCluster.spec.mon.count and spec.osd.DeviceFilter respect these labels when distributing OSDs and MONs.
  • Verify with ceph osd tree after deployment.

docs.title: Count and quorum
docs.text:
• Minimum: 3 MONs (odd number required for quorum). 2 MONs provide no quorum advantage over 1 and are discouraged.
  • Maximum: 5 MONs in most deployments; beyond that, management overhead outweighs benefit.
  • Quorum formula: floor(N/2) + 1 MONs must be online for the cluster to operate.

docs.title: Placement rules
docs.text:
• Never co-locate a MON with an OSD on the same host if the host is the only OSD for a pool; doing so combines the monitor store and OSD database on one failure point.
  • Separate racks/azs: Each of the 3 MONs should run on a different rack/availability zone when possible.
  • Dedicated resources: MONs need modest CPU and RAM (typically 2 vCPU, 4 GiB), but require local SSD for the MON store and OSD database/WAL. Do not share the OSD data disk with the MON store.
  • Node selector: Use spec.mon.nodeSelector or node labels to guarantee MON pods land on dedicated storage hosts.

docs.title: Example CephCluster MON spec
docs.text:
mon:
  count: 3
  allowMultiplePerNode: false
  # nodeSelector:
  #   failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone: zone-a

docs.title: Device allocation
docs.text:
• One OSD daemon per data disk (do not over-provision OSDs per disk; the OSD daemon maps 1:1 to a block device).
  • Use raw device mapping (disk passthrough) for OSD data disks; never share a virtual disk with the host OS or other containers.
  • Device classes: declare spec.osd.deviceClass: ssd or hdd in the CephCluster spec; Rook tags OSDs accordingly, and CRUSH buckets can use the class for placement.

docs.title: OSD topology in CRUSH
docs.text:
• Rook automatically generates a CRUSH map where each OSD is under its host node, and nodes are under the configured failure domains (rack/zone).
  • If failureDomain: host is set in pools, Rook places replicas across distinct hosts. For rack/zone awareness, set failureDomain: rack or failureDomain: zone in the pool spec and ensure node labels match.

docs.title: Recommended OSD-to-host ratio
docs.text: Disk type OSDs per host OSD journal type Notes NVMe SSD 1–2 (one per NVMe namespace or device) Battery-backed or flush‑nvme Highest IOPS; keep 1 OSD per namespace for best performance SATA SSD 2–4 (shared device if capacity allows) Battery-backed write-back Moderate IOPS; balance with journal size HDD 1 per physical disk Internal (no battery) One OSD per disk is mandatory; journals on separate SSD if possible

docs.title: OSD resource minimums
docs.text:
# In CephCluster spec, under storage.osd.resources.requests
osd:
  requests:
    cpu: "2"
    memory: 4Gi
  • Adjust upward for OSDs that host many PGs (placement groups). A rule of thumb: ~1 vCPU per 50–100 PGs, and 1 GiB RAM per 20–50 PGs, depending on workload.

docs.title: Default CRUSH map generated by Rook
docs.text:
Rook generates a CRUSH map with the following structure (customizable via spec.crushRoot and node labels):

root
  region
    rack
      host
        osd.0
        osd.1
        ...
  • crushRoot: can be overridden in CephCluster.spec (default: default). Set to a meaningful geographic/regional root when running multi-region or when the default conflicts with site policies.
  • Failure domain labels: ensure node labels map to the CRUSH hierarchy. Rook reads failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/rack and failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone from nodes and inserts them into the CRUSH map automatically.

docs.title: Customizing the CRUSH map
docs.text:
1. Add site-specific bucket types via ceph osd crush add-bucket if the default hierarchy is insufficient.
  2. Map nodes to buckets using labels: Rook does this automatically when failureDomain is set in the CephCluster/CephBlockPool spec.
  3. Verify with: 
    ceph osd tree
# confirms the rack/zone/region hierarchy and OSD distribution

docs.title: Usable capacity formulas
docs.text: Pool type Formula Typical usable % 3-replica (3x) usable = total_raw × (1 / 3) ~33% Erasure coded (k+m) usable = total_raw × (k / (k + m)) 4+2 → ~57%; 6+3 → ~67% With reserved fraction usable_raw = Σ(disk_size) × (1 - reserved_fraction) reserved_fraction = 0.05–0.10

docs.title: Example: 3-replica pool with 4 TB disks, 5% reserved
docs.text:
raw_total = 12 disks × 4 TB = 48 TB
reserved  = 48 TB × 0.05 = 2.4 TB
usable_raw = 48 TB - 2.4 TB = 45.6 TB
usable_3x   = 45.6 TB / 3 = 15.2 TB

docs.title: Storage headroom
docs.text:
• Keep 25–30% of raw capacity free at all times. This headroom allows an OSD replacement + rebalancing without the pool filling to 100%.
  • Monitor osd_pool_used_bytes and osd_pool_percent_used; set alerts at 70%, 80%, and 90% of usable capacity.

docs.title: IOPS and network planning
docs.text: Metric Guideline 3× write amplification Each client write lands on 2 OSDs (replica + client acknowledgement), so effective write throughput ≈ 1/2 of raw disk bandwidth. 10 GbE network Supports ~1.25 GB/s sustained; a 3× pool writing at >1 GB/s client rate will saturate the link. Disk IOPS NVMe SSD: 100k–500k per device; SATA SSD: 30k–80k; HDD: 100–180 random 4k IOPS. Size from expected PG count and expected TPS.

docs.title: Step 1: Define workload profile
docs.text: Profile Typical R/W ratio IOPS per TiB Notes Database (OLTP) 80/20 read/write 20k–200k random 4k IOPS/TiB Use 3-replica pools; EC is not recommended File server 70/30 read/write 5k–50k random 4k IOPS/TiB Can use EC for capacity efficiency Backup/archive 90/10 read/write 1k–5k sequential IOPS/TiB EC (6+3) is cost-effective

docs.title: Step 2: Calculate raw disk count
docs.text:
disks_needed = (target_usable_tb × replica_factor) / disk_size_tb
replica_factor = 3 for 3x, or (k+m)/k for EC
add 10–20% spare for unexpected failures

docs.title: Step 3: Determine host count
docs.text:
• MONs: 3 hosts minimum (ideally separate racks/azs).
  • OSD hosts: Minimum 3 hosts for a fault‑tolerant cluster (each host holds at least one OSD, and the failure of any one host does not lose data because replicas are on other hosts).
  • Desired hosts: ceil(disks_needed / osds_per_host) + 1 (the extra host is the spare/standby).

docs.title: Step 4: Resource per host
docs.text: Role vCPU RAM Disk MON 2 4 GiB 1× 200–500 GiB SSD (local, dedicated) OSD 2–8 (depends on PG count) 4–16 GiB 1× data disk (HDD/SSD/NVMe) + optional journal SSD MGR 1 2 GiB — (co-located with MON or OSD) MDS (if CephFS) 1 2 GiB — (co-located) RGW (if S3) 2 4 GiB — (can co-locate with OSD)

docs.title: Step 5: Validate against RPO/RTO
docs.text:
• RPO (Recovery Point Objective): With 3-replica synchronous replication (default in Rook), RPO = 0 bytes (no data loss) as long as ≥ 2 replicas survive. With async replication across regions, RPO is determined by WAL archiving frequency.
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Measured by running a restore drill (see the DBRE backup & recovery checklist). Typical RTO for Rook-Ceph with base backup + WAL replay: 15–30 minutes for a single-node loss, 45–90 minutes for a full-region failover.

docs.title: Step 6: Checklist before going production
docs.text:
• [ ] 3 MONs on separate hosts/racks/azs, each with local SSD MON store
  • [ ] OSDs deployed on ≥ 3 hosts, one OSD per data disk, device classes declared
  • [ ] CRUSH hierarchy reflects physical topology (rack/zone labels on nodes)
  • [ ] Pools have failureDomain: rack (or zone) and replicated.size: 3
  • [ ] 25–30% raw capacity headroom reserved
  • [ ] IOPS and network bandwidth validated against peak workload
  • [ ] Resource requests set per OSD host (CPU/memory for expected PG count)
  • [ ] ceph osd tree verified and matches physical layout
  • [ ] Backup strategy (WAL archiving + periodic base backup) documented and restore drills scheduled

References

  • Rook documentation: https://rook.io/docs/rook/latest/
  • Ceph CRUSH map design: https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/storage/crush-map/
  • PostgreSQL DBRE backup & recovery checklist (internal)

docs.title: Check Individual OSD Status
docs.text:
# Check a specific OSD
ceph osd status

docs.title: Common OSD Health Commands
docs.text:

ceph osd dump

# Query specific OSD status
ceph osd stat

# List OSDs in weight order
ceph osd tree

# Show OSD usage and utilization

docs.title: OSD Health Flags
docs.text:
• up - OSD is running and responsive
  • in - OSD is part of the cluster
  • out - OSD is marked out (for migration)
  • full - OSD is above the osd_max_full_ratio threshold
  • nearfull - OSD is near the full threshold
  • slow - OSD is responding slowly
  • pause - OSD is paused

docs.title: Check PG States
docs.text:
# Overall PG map
ceph pg map <pg_name>

# All PG states summary
ceph pg stat

# Detailed PG information
ceph pg dump

# PGs by state
ceph pg dump_stuck

# Count PGs in each state
ceph pg stat | grep -E "active|unclean|degraded|offline"

docs.title: Common PG Health Issues
docs.text:
• Active PGs: Normal operating state
  • Unclean PGs: Some OSDs holding PG data are down - requires attention
  • Degraded PGs: Some OSDs are missing - data protection is reduced
  • Stuck PGs: PGs not transitioning as expected - may need intervention

docs.title: PG Recovery
docs.text:
# Check if recovery is in progress
ceph pg <pg_id> query

# Force recovery start for a PG

ceph osd map <pool> <obj>

  • HEALTH_WARN - Warning conditions exist
  • HEALTH_ERR - Error conditions exist

docs.text:
# Mark an OSD as out before removal/maintenance
ceph osd out osd.<ID>

docs.title: Basic Health Check Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# Ceph health monitoring basic script

STATUS=$(ceph health 2>&1)
if [ "$STATUS" = "HEALTH_OK" ]; then
    echo "[$(date)] Ceph cluster: HEALTH_OK" >> /var/log/ceph-health.log
else
    echo "[$(date)] Ceph cluster: $STATUS" >> /var/log/ceph-health.log
    ceph health detail >> /var/log/ceph-health.log
fi

# Check OSD status
ceph osd stat >> /var/log/ceph-health.log

# Check PG status
ceph pg stat >> /var/log/ceph-health.log

# Check for any stuck PGs
STUCK=$(ceph pg dump_stuck 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
if [ "$STUCK" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "WARNING: $STUCK stuck PGs found" >> /var/log/ceph-health.log
fi

docs.title: Schedule with cron
docs.text:
# Add to crontab for hourly health checks
0 * * * * /usr/local/bin/ceph-health-check.sh >> /var/log/ceph-health.log 2>&1

docs.title: Critical Alerts
docs.text:
• HEALTH_ERR in cluster health
  • Any OSD down (up flag missing)
  • Degraded PGs (degraded count > 0)
  • Unclean PGs (unclean count > 0)
  • OSDs above full ratio (full flag)
  • Stuck PGs not recovering

docs.title: Warning Alerts
docs.text:
• OSDs near full ratio (nearfull flag)
  • Slow responding OSDs (slow flag)
  • PGs approaching backfill limits
  • Monitors out of quorum

docs.title: Common Issues and Resolutions
docs.text:
1. OSD marked down
  2. Check physical connectivity
  3. Verify OSD process is running: systemctl status ceph-osd@<ID>
  4. Check device availability and mount status

  5. Restart OSD if needed: ceph osd start osd.<ID>

  6. PGs in degraded state

  7. Verify which OSDs are down
  8. Check for storage capacity issues
  9. Monitor recovery progress with ceph -w

  10. Add back missing OSDs or replace hardware

  11. PGs stuck in recovery

  12. Check OSD logs for I/O errors
  13. Verify cluster has sufficient resources (CPU, memory, network)
  14. Consider increasing osd_max_backfills if PGs are stuck due to too many concurrent operations

  15. Check for network partitions or latency issues

  16. Cluster near full

  17. Add new OSDs to the cluster
  18. Rebalance PGs to distribute data
  19. Check osd_full_ratio and osd_max_full_ratio settings

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This procedure covers the replacement of a failed or failing ObjectStore Daemon (OSD) in a Rook-Ceph cluster. Follow these steps in order to replace an OSD with minimal disruption and ensure data integrity.

docs.title: A. OSD Failure Detection
docs.text:
Signal Check Action OSD out of cluster kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods — look for osd-<id> pods with CrashLoopBackOff or Error Confirm the OSD is unrecoverable before removal OSD OSD report ceph osd tree — note the OSD marked out or down Record the OSD ID (<id>) for the remaining steps OSD heartbeats ceph osd status — verify the OSD is down and no heartbeat in the last mon osd heartbeat interval (default 10s) If the OSD is only temporarily down, wait; otherwise proceed to removal PG state ceph pg ls <pg-id> — check for PGs stuck in underscrub, backfill, or peering Resolve any stuck PGs before starting replacement to avoid cascading delays

Detection workflow:

  1. Identify the failing OSD ID from Kubernetes events or Ceph status.
  2. Verify the OSD is truly down (not transient) with ceph osd status.
  3. Record the OSD number for the removal step.

docs.title: B. OSD Removal
docs.text:
Warning: Removing an OSD triggers data rebalancing. Ensure the cluster has sufficient capacity (at least size + 1 OSDs) before proceeding.

# 1. Mark the OSD out (ceph will stop serving new writes to it)
ceph osd out <osd-id>

# 2. Confirm the OSD is out
ceph osd tree | grep "<osd-id>"

# 3. Remove the OSD completely (purges data, removes the OSD from the cluster map)
ceph osd remove <osd-id>

# 4. Confirm the OSD is removed from the tree
ceph osd tree

Post-removal verification:

  • ceph osd df — confirm usable size has decreased by one OSD
  • ceph health — should report HEALTH_OK or only HEALTH_WARN about rebalancing
  • Check that no PGs are stuck in uneven distribution

docs.title: C. New OSD Provisioning
docs.text:
Requirements: A new block device (or partition) of equal or greater capacity than the removed OSD must be available on a node that can join the Ceph cluster.

# 1. Label the node where the new OSD will run (optional, if using node-specific constraints)
kubectl label node <node-name> failure-domain.beta.kubernetes.io/zone=<zone>

# 2. Create the OSD — Rook operator will auto-detect the new device and create the OSD
#    Identify the new device path (e.g., /dev/sdb, /dev/sdc, etc.)
#    Apply the Ceph OSD via kubectl or the Rook API

# Using kubectl with a specific device:
kubectl -n rook-ceph create ceph-osd /dev/<device-path> \
  --device-size=<size-GB> \
  --label="osd-id=<new-osd-id>"

# Or via the Rook CR if the operator auto-assigns:
# The operator will provision the OSD and mark it as `in` automatically.

# 3. Confirm the new OSD is recognized
ceph osd tree

# 4. Confirm the OSD is `in` and `up`
ceph osd status

If the operator does not auto-provision:

  • Ensure the node has the correct ceph-osd annotations and the device is raw/block (not partitioned).
  • Restart the Rook operator if the OSD does not appear within 2 minutes.

docs.title: D. Data Rebalancing
docs.text:
After the new OSD is in, Ceph will automatically rebalance data across the cluster. Monitor this process.

# 1. Check rebalancing status
ceph pg ls_detail | grep -E "state.*rebalancing|state.*scrub|state.*backfill"

# 2. Monitor progress per PG
ceph pg stat

# 3. Track the rebalancing percentage
ceph tell osd.* state  # shows overall cluster state

# 4. Optional: pause/resume rebalancing if needed
ceph osd rebalance pause
ceph osd rebalance resume

# 5. Verify rebalancing completes
ceph pg ls_detail | grep -E "state.*active+clean"

Recovery goals during rebalancing:

  • RPO: <= 1 minute — WAL archiving ensures point-in-time recovery; rebalancing does not affect point-in-time recovery.
  • RTO: <= 30 minutes — measured from OSD removal to cluster HEALTH_OK with all PGs active+clean.

If rebalancing stalls:

  • Check for disk full (ceph osd df), network issues, or PG stuck in underscrub.
  • Use ceph pg <pg-id> debug reclaim or ceph pg <pg-id> debug scrub for diagnosis.
  • If necessary, ceph osd rebalance pause and investigate, then resume.

docs.title: E. Verification of Cluster Health After Replacement
docs.text:
# 1. Overall cluster health
ceph health
# Expected: HEALTH_OK

# 2. OSD map completeness
ceph osd tree
# Expected: new OSD shows `in/up`, old OSD is gone

# 3. PG state — all should be active+clean
ceph pg stat
# Expected: X PGs, Y active+clean, 0 stuck

# 4. Data integrity — sample checks across RBD/CephFS/RGW
rbd info --cluster rook-ceph  # verify RBD pools
ceph fs status --cluster rook-ceph  # verify CephFS

# 5. OSD utilization — ensure no single OSD is overloaded
ceph osd df

# 6. Run a quick integrity check (optional but recommended)
ceph pg scrub  # or let the scrubs run on their schedule

# 7. Confirm the cluster report is clean after a stabilization window (5–10 min)
ceph health detail
# Expected: no warnings about missing OSDs, no PGs in recovery or backfill

Post-verification checklist:

  • [ ] ceph health returns HEALTH_OK
  • [ ] All PGs are active+clean
  • [ ] No OSD shows out or removing
  • [ ] Cluster osd df reflects the new OSD capacity
  • [ ] No PGs in underscrub, recovery, or backfill after 10 minutes
  • [ ] RBD pool, CephFS, and RGW services are functional (smoke test PVCs/RBDs)

docs.title: F. Rollback (if replacement fails)
docs.text:
If the new OSD cannot be brought in/up or rebalancing causes data loss:

  1. ceph osd rebalance pause — stop further data movement.
  2. If the new OSD was just created and is out, ceph osd rm <new-osd-id> to remove it.
  3. Re-add the original OSD if the device is still available:
  4. ceph osd create /dev/<original-device> — returns a new OSD ID.
  5. ceph osd in <osd-id> to bring it back online.
  6. ceph osd tree — verify the original OSD is back in the map.
  7. Monitor ceph health until HEALTH_OK.

Note: Rollback is fastest if the original OSD device was not securely wiped. If the device was physically removed, a full cluster rebalance from remaining OSDs will occur.

docs.title: G. Related Procedures
docs.text:
• Backup & Recovery Strategy — validated restore drills
  • Failover Topology — automated failover with fencing
  • OSD Addition Without Replacement — adding a new OSD to grow capacity

docs.title: A. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Kubernetes cluster with >= 3 nodes for monitor quorum
  • At least 3 nodes with unmounted disks for OSDs (use explicit device lists, never useAllDevices: true)
  • Node labels for storage scheduling (e.g., rook/ceph-osd: "true")
  • Available CPU/Memory for Rook operator and Ceph daemons
  • Offline artifact matrix verified (compatibility/version-matrix.md)

docs.title: B. Operator Installation
docs.text:
# 1. Apply CRDs first — they must be applied before the operator
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/crds.yaml

# 2. Apply common.yaml (RBAC, CRDs, csi driver)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/common.yaml

# 3. Apply the operator
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/operator.yaml

# 4. Verify operator rollout
kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout status deployment/rook-ceph-operator --timeout=300s

Important: Record the Rook version and supported Ceph image tag in compatibility/version-matrix.md. Never set a Ceph image version that the installed Rook release does not support.

docs.title: C. CephCluster Creation
docs.text:
apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephCluster
metadata:
  name: rook-ceph
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  cephVersion:
    image: quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18.2.x    # VERIFY against pinned Rook release
  dataDirHostPath: /var/lib/rook
  mon:
    count: 3
    allowMultiplePerNode: false
  mgr:
    count: 2
    modules:
      - name: rook
        enabled: true
      - name: pg_autoscaler
        enabled: true
      - name: rook-cephfs
        enabled: true
      - name: rook-rgw
        enabled: true
  dashboard:
    enabled: true
    ssl: true
  network:
    provider: host
    # Or use a dedicated StorageClass for the public/cluster network
  storage:
    useAllNodes: false
    useAllDevices: false
    nodes:
      - name: "node1"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
      - name: "node2"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
      - name: "node3"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
  resources:
    osd:
      requests:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 4Gi
  priorityClassNames: [system-node-critical]

Mandatory production rules: - useAllDevices: false with explicit devices — never let Rook claim every unmounted disk - failureDomain: host for all replicated pools (plus rack awareness where applicable) - Node labels so OSD pods land on storage nodes - priorityClassNames: [system-node-critical] for OSD and monitor pods

docs.title: D. Storage Class Configuration
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ceph-rbd
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: rook-ceph.cephcsi.com
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
parameters:
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name: rook-csi-rbd-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-name: rook-csi-rbd-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-name: rook-csi-rbd-node
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: ext4
  csi.storage.k8s.io/pool: replicapool
  csi.storage.k8s.io/clusterID: rook-ceph

CephFS StorageClass is the same with provisioner: rook-ceph.cephcsi.com and csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: ext4 pointing at the filesystem name.

Default bucket claim: The is-default-class: "true" annotation makes this the default StorageClass for PVCs without explicit storageClassName.

docs.title: E. Pool Management
docs.text:
apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephBlockPool
metadata:
  name: replicapool
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  failureDomain: host
  replicated:
    size: 3
  crushRoot: "my-root"
  deviceClass: ssd
  parameters:
    targetSizeRatio: 0.5

Pool operations:

Task Procedure Add an OSD Add the node to spec.storage.nodes, apply — Rook creates the OSD automatically Replace a failed OSD OSD pod goes Crashed; replace the disk, then remove the OSD from the node list and re-apply Scale a pool Edit CephBlockPool.spec.replicated.size, apply — data rebalances automatically Expand a pool Edit spec.parameters.targetSizeRatio upward, apply — OSDs rebalance Enable snapshots CSI snapshotter deployed by default; create VolumeSnapshot objects Back up Velero with CSI snapshot integration, or rbd export to object store

docs.title: F. OSD Tuning
docs.text:
Key OSD parameters to tune via CephCluster.spec.storage.osd.config or device-level config:

Parameter Recommended Impact osd_max_backfills 2 Control parallelism of backfill/recovery osd_max_bulk_operations 4 Limit bulk data operations per OSD osd_scrub_interval 3600 (seconds) Tune scrub frequency osd_deep_scrub_interval 86400 (seconds) Tune deep scrub frequency osd_pool_default_min_size 2 Minimum size for new pools osd_pool_default_size 3 Default replication size osd_cache_size 0.5 (fraction of RAM) OSD cache size for read/write caching osd_max_write_size 4 (MB) Max write packet size

Example OSD config in CephCluster:

spec:
  storage:
    osd:
      config:
        osd_max_backfills: "2"
        osd_deep_scrub_interval: "86400"
        osd_pool_default_min_size: "2"

docs.title: G. Monitoring Integration
docs.text:
Rook deploys Prometheus and Grafana automatically. Key series:

Series Description ceph_cluster_status Overall cluster health (up/down, health status) ceph_osd_status Individual OSD state ceph_pg_status Placement group state, acting/up copies ceph_mon_io I/O operations per second ceph_disk_io_total Per-disk I/O metrics ceph_objectstore_gateway_requests_total RGW request count rook_ceph_health_status Rook operator-reported health

Grafana dashboards are available out-of-the-box. Recommended alerts:

  • Replication lag beyond threshold (promote only sync replicas)
  • OSD down beyond RTO window
  • PG stuck in undersized or degraded state
  • CSI provisioner failures
  • Monitor quorum loss

Custom alert example (YAML for PrometheusRule):

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: ceph-alerts
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  groups:
  - name: ceph.rules
    rules:
    - alert: CephClusterDegraded
      expr: ceph_cluster_status{job="ceph"} != "HEALTH_OK"
      for: 5m
      labels:
        severity: critical
      annotations:
        summary: "Ceph cluster is not healthy"
        description: "Ceph cluster {{ $labels.cluster }} has been degraded for more than 5 minutes."
    - alert: CephOSDDown
      expr: ceph_osd_status{job="ceph"} == "out"
      for: 10m
      labels:
        severity: warning
      annotations:
        summary: "Ceph OSD is down"
        description: "OSD {{ $labels.osd }} has been down for more than 10 minutes."

docs.title: H. Validation
docs.text:
# Check operator status
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods
kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout status deployment/rook-ceph-operator --timeout=300s

# Check cluster health
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-operator -- ceph -s

# Check storage classes
kubectl get storageclass

# Function test — create a PVC and workload
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: rook-test
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
  storageClassName: ceph-rbd
EOF

# Verify CSI provisioner created the PV
kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>
kubectl get pv -n <namespace>

docs.title: A. Purpose and architecture
docs.text:
Ceph managed by the Rook operator inside a Kubernetes cluster, exposing RBD, CephFS, and RGW through the Rook CSI driver.

Kubernetes cluster
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  | rook-ceph-operator (Deployment)                    |
  |   CRDs: CephCluster, CephBlockPool, ...            |
  |                                                    |
  |  rook-ceph-mon (3)  rook-ceph-osd (N)             |
  |  rook-ceph-mds (N) rook-ceph-rgw (N)              |
  |  rook-csi-* (DaemonSet + provisioner)              |
  +---------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: B. When to use Rook versus cephadm
docs.text:
Criterion Rook-Ceph cephadm (external) Storage scope One cluster Shared across clusters Deployment model Operator-managed in K8s Managed on dedicated hosts Failure coupling A cluster-wide network/CNI failure can affect storage Independent of the cluster K8s integration Native CRDs, CSI, PVC lifecycle External CSI driver, still good Operational overhead Higher (two control loops) Lower (vendor lifecycle) Best for Cluster-local storage, simpler estates Shared capacity, strict independence, multi-cluster

This platform supports both. Choose per cluster and document which one a given StorageClass belongs to.

docs.title: C. Offline preparation
docs.text:
• CRDs: crds.yaml from the pinned Rook release.
  • Operator: operator.yaml, common.yaml.
  • Images: operator, CSI provisioner, cephcsi, and the Ceph daemon images for the pinned Ceph version. All listed in offline-artifacts/artifact-matrix.md.
  • Rook needs the Ceph container images matching the Ceph version it supports. The Rook release notes state which Ceph version it ships with — record it in compatibility/version-matrix.md.

docs.title: D. Installation
docs.text:
# CRDs first — they must be applied before the operator
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/crds.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/common.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/rook/rook/releases/download/<VERSION>/operator.yaml

kubectl -n rook-ceph rollout status deployment/rook-ceph-operator --timeout=300s

CephCluster (manifests/cluster/cephcluster.yaml):

apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephCluster
metadata:
  name: rook-ceph
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  cephVersion:
    image: quay.io/ceph/ceph:v18.2.x     # VERIFY against the pinned Rook release
  dataDirHostPath: /var/lib/rook
  mon:
    count: 3
    allowMultiplePerNode: false
  mgr:
    count: 2
    modules:
      - name: rook
        enabled: true
      - name: pg_autoscaler
        enabled: true
      - name: rook-cephfs
        enabled: true
      - name: rook-rgw
        enabled: true
  dashboard:
    enabled: true
    ssl: true
  network:
    provider: host
    # Or use a dedicated StorageClass for the public/cluster network
  storage:
    useAllNodes: false
    useAllDevices: false
    nodes:
      - name: "node1"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
      - name: "node2"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
      - name: "node3"
        devices:
          - name: "sdb"
            config:
              osdsPerDevice: "1"
  resources:
    osd:
      requests:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 4Gi
  priorityClassNames: [system-node-critical]

useAllDevices: false with explicit devices is mandatory in production. useAllDevices: true claims every unmounted disk, including a disk that an operator intends to use for something else.

docs.title: E. Pools, filesystems, object store
docs.text:
# CephBlockPool
apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephBlockPool
metadata:
  name: replicapool
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  failureDomain: host
  replicated:
    size: 3
  crushRoot: "my-root"
  deviceClass: ssd
  parameters:
    targetSizeRatio: 0.5

# CephFilesystem
apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephFilesystem
metadata:
  name: myfs
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  metadataPool:
    replicated:
      size: 3
  dataPool:
    name: replicapool
  metadataServer:
    activeCount: 2
    activeStandby: true

# CephObjectStore (RGW)
apiVersion: rook.io/v1
kind: CephObjectStore
metadata:
  name: my-store
  namespace: rook-ceph
spec:
  storePool:
    name: replicapool
  gateway:
    port: 80
    instances: 2
  hostNetwork:
    enable: false
  security:
    kms:
      connectionDetails:
        # Vault KMS integration (optional)
        vaultBackend: vault
  users:
    - name: "app-user"
      displayName: "Application user"
      capabilities:
        - "buckets=*"
        - "users=*"

docs.title: F. StorageClasses
docs.text:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ceph-rbd
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: rook-ceph.cephcsi.com
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
parameters:
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-name: rook-csi-cephfs-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/provisioner-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-name: rook-csi-cephfs-provisioner
  csi.storage.k8s.io/controller-expand-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-name: rook-csi-cephfs-node
  csi.storage.k8s.io/node-stage-secret-namespace: rook-ceph
  csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: ext4
  csi.storage.k8s.io/pool: replicapool
  csi.storage.k8s.io/clusterID: rook-ceph

CephFS StorageClass is the same with provisioner: rook-ceph.cephcsi.com and csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: ext4 pointing at the filesystem name.

docs.text:
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-operator -- ceph -s
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl -n rook-ceph get cephcluster -o yaml | head -40

# Function test
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'

kind: PersistentVolumeClaim

  name: rook-test
spec:

EOF

docs.title: H. Operations
docs.text: Task Procedure Add an OSD Add the node to spec.storage.nodes, apply, Rook creates the OSD Replace a failed OSD The OSD pod goes Crashed; replace the disk, then remove the OSD from the node list and re-apply Scale a pool Edit CephBlockPool.spec.replicated.size, apply; the data rebalances Expand a pool Edit spec.parameters.targetSizeRatio upward, apply Enable snapshots The CSI snapshotter is deployed by Rook by default; create VolumeSnapshot objects Back up Velero with the CSI snapshot integration, or rbd export to object storage

docs.title: I. Upgrades — the sequence matters
docs.text:
Ceph upgrades are not reversible across major versions, and Rook adds a layer. The order:

  1. Upgrade the Rook operator (via Argo CD).
  2. Upgrade Ceph (the cephVersion.image in the CephCluster) — the operator orchestrates the daemon upgrade in the correct order (mon, mgr, osd, mds, rgw).
  3. Upgrade the CSI driver if required by the Rook release.

Never set a Ceph image version that the installed Rook release does not support. The Rook release notes list the supported Ceph version — this is the single most common cause of a broken Rook upgrade.

docs.title: J. Best practices
docs.text:
Mandatory: - Explicit device list, never useAllDevices: true. - failureDomain: host for replicated pools, plus rack awareness where the site has racks. - The Rook operator excluded from admission-policy enforcement (it needs broad permissions). - Node labels marking storage nodes so OSD pods land on them. - A node drain procedure that stops OSDs gracefully before a node maintenance window.

Strongly recommended: - Dedicated storage node pool, separate from the general worker pool. - Separate the Ceph public and cluster networks with a StorageClass-based network definition where the site has the VLANs. - Enable the pg_autoscaler module and alert on PG state. - Keep the Ceph dashboard enabled but behind the site access policy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document defines chaos engineering tests to validate system resilience across pod, node, network, and data-layer failure modes. Tests are designed to be progressive, observable, and scoped by blast radius controls.

docs.title: Pod Failure Tests
docs.text:
Description: Terminate random or targeted pods to verify self-healing, rescheduling, and workload continuity.

Aspect Details Scope Random pod kill via kubectl delete pod or Chaos Mesh; targeted kill of specific deployment replicas Duration 5m per pod; 20m total test window Metrics Pod restart time, service latency, error rate spike Success Criteria < 30s pod restart; error budget < 5% consumption; no data loss Cross-reference ../kubernetes/workloads/deployment-rollouts.md

docs.title: Node Failure Tests
docs.text:
Description: Simulate node loss (power, kernel panic, network loss) to verify node drainage, pod rescheduling, and control-plane continuity.

Aspect Details Scope kubectl drain of a worker node (with --ignore-daemonsets-if-unschedulable); or kill kubelet process Duration Until node is fully recovered; 30m test window Metrics Pod reschedule time, API server availability, etcd health Success Criteria < 2m reschedule for non-daemonset pods; API 5xx < 1%; no data corruption Cross-reference ../kubernetes/control-plane/ha-topology.md

docs.title: Network Partition Tests
docs.text:
Description: induce network isolation between cluster nodes to verify partition behavior, quorum maintenance, and split-brain prevention.

Aspect Details Scope kubectl exec into a pod; tc netem latency/jitter; or use Chaos Mesh network chaos Duration 10m; progressive: 30s → 2m → 10m steps Metrics etcd leader stability, API server error rate, pod health status Success Criteria No etcd quorum loss; API remains available for writes on majority partition; no split-brain Cross-reference ../kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-restore.md

docs.title: etcd Quorum Loss Tests
docs.text:
Description: Simulate etcd member loss to verify quorum behavior, data availability, and recovery procedures.

Aspect Details Scope Stop random etcd member(s); or use etcdctl to remove member; or restart all members simultaneously (not recommended) Duration 15m total; measure from member stop to quorum restoration Metrics etcd member health, API write availability, snapshot latency Success Criteria Write availability preserved on remaining quorum; no data loss; recovery < 10m Cross-reference ../kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-restore.md

docs.title: Blast Radius Control
docs.text:
Description: Define and measure blast radius per test type, ensuring failures are contained within expected scopes.

Test Type Default Blast Radius Measurement Method Pod failure 1 pod per 10; max 10% of replicas kubectl get pods replica count diff; kubectl describe pod restart time Node failure 1 node per cluster; max 20% of worker nodes Node count delta; kubectl get nodes readiness Network partition 1 subnet / 1 zone Partition scope via tc rule cidr; zone tag from topology labels etcd quorum loss 1 member per cluster; max floor(n/2) members etcdctl member list quorum count; etcdctl endpoint status health

Blast Radius Validation

  • Before each test: record baseline (replicas, nodes, etcd members, API health)
  • During test: track delta from baseline in real time
  • After test: compute blast_radius = (affected / baseline) * 100%
  • Success: blast_radius ≤ defined limit for test type
  • Failure: abort test, document deviation, adjust scope

docs.title: Test Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. Pre-check: Verify cluster health, error budget > 20%, all monitoring active
  2. Baseline: Record current state (replicas, nodes, etcd health, API latency p99)
  3. Inject: Apply chaos injection per test type
  4. Observe: Monitor metrics, logs, alerts for duration of test window
  5. Reclaim: Restore state (undelete pods, uncordon nodes, remove netem, restart etcd)
  6. Post-check: Verify cluster back to baseline; compute blast radius; document results

docs.title: Safety Controls
docs.text:
• All tests require SRE on-call approval
  • Tests paused automatically if error budget > 10% consumption
  • No etcd member restart > 1 at a time
  • Network chaos limited to non-production namespaces first
  • Rollback procedure documented per test type
  • All actions recorded in cluster audit log

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• ../architecture/03-failure-domains.md — Failure domain topology
  • ../kubernetes/control-plane/ha-topology.md — HA control plane design
  • ../lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md — Disaster recovery procedures
  • ../monitoring/alert-rules.md — Chaos-relevant alert rules

docs.title: Node Failure
docs.text:
Description: A worker or control-plane node becomes unavailable (hardware failure, power loss, etc.).

Aspect Details Impact Workloads rescheduled to remaining nodes; API remains available if control-plane node Detection Node Not Ready status, kubelet heartbeats stop Recovery Replace node, rejoin cluster; drain pods before failure if possible

Cross-reference: ../kubernetes/control-plane/ha-topology.md | ../architecture/03-failure-domains.md

docs.title: Network Partition
docs.text:
Description: Network connectivity between cluster components is interrupted (partitioned network, VPC issues, routing failure).

Aspect Details Impact Control plane cannot communicate with etcd/workers; API requests time out; workloads lose external connectivity Detection etcd leader flapping, API server response degradation, ping loss between nodes Recovery Restore network path; if partition persists, apply quorum-based recovery for etcd

Cross-reference: ../network-matrix/network-communication-matrix.md | ../kubernetes/control-plane/ha-topology.md

docs.title: etcd Quorum Loss
docs.text:
Description: etcd cluster loses majority (odd number of members lost), stopping all API writes while read-only workloads continue running.

Aspect Details Impact All kubectl write operations fail; etcd keys inaccessible; running pods continue from local state Detection etcd member goes unhealthy, API server 5xx errors, etcdctl quorum alerts Recovery Restore from last snapshot; add new etcd member; avoid restarting all members simultaneously

Cross-reference: ../kubernetes/control-plane/etcd-restore.md | ../kubernetes/control-plane/index.md | ../lifecycle/disaster-recovery/index.md

docs.title: Control Plane Failure
docs.text:
Description: Control-plane components (API server, controller manager, scheduler) become unavailable (certificate expiry, configuration drift, etcd sync loss).

Aspect Details Impact API server unreachable; no new workloads can be scheduled; existing workloads continue if etcd is healthy Detection kubectl authentication failure, API server health check failure, controller manager leader election logs Recovery Restart control-plane nodes one at a time; restore etcd quorum; rotate certificates if needed

Cross-reference: ../kubernetes/control-plane/index.md | ../lifecycle/upgrades/upgrade-procedures.md | ../architecture/03-failure-domains.md

docs.title: Anti-circularity Rules
docs.text:
1. etcd must not depend on the control plane API for snapshot restore operations (offline etcdctl restore).
  2. Control plane must not depend on application workload availability for API server health.
  3. Network partition recovery must not assume immediate etcd quorum — use staged member re-add.
  4. Node replacement must not require API server write access during the join process.

docs.text: Component Required Version Notes Python 3.10+ Used for test execution Terraform 1.5+ Infrastructure provisioning kubectl 1.28+ Kubernetes cluster access Docker 24+ Container operations Kubernetes 1.28+ Cluster for integration tests Prometheus 0.60+ Monitoring system Grafana 10+ Dashboard visualization

docs.title: Test Environment Setup
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository to a local working directory
  2. Ensure all required tools are installed and versioned correctly
  3. Configure authentication for cloud provider APIs (if applicable)
  4. Set up a Kubernetes cluster for integration test execution
  5. Configure Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring alert verification

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• All tools listed in the Test Environment table installed and versioned correctly
  • Access to the target Kubernetes cluster with appropriate permissions
  • Prometheus and Grafana accessible at their respective endpoints
  • Credentials configured for any cloud provider API access

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
1. Initialize the test environment
# Clone the repository
git clone <repository-url>
cd cloud-native-guide

# Verify tool versions
terraform version
kubectl version --client
python3 --version
  1. Run the test suite
# Execute all integration tests
python3 -m pytest tests/integration-test-suite.py -v

Or run individual test scenarios:

# Run specific test scenario
python3 tests/integration-test-suite.py --scenario T-001

  1. Verify results

  2. Check test output for pass/fail status

  3. Review any generated reports or artifacts
  4. Confirm that all acceptance criteria are met

docs.title: General Criteria
docs.text: Criterion Pass Condition Fail Condition Test execution All test scenarios complete without unhandled exceptions Any test scenario crashes or times out Link integrity check_links.py reports 0 broken links Any broken relative links or missing anchors detected Cross-reference resolution All internal links reference valid targets Any link points to a non-existent file or anchor Environment readiness All required tools and environments are available Missing tools or unreachable environments

docs.title: Scenario-Specific Criteria
docs.text: Scenario ID Pass Criteria Fail Criteria T-001 CI/CD pipeline completes all stages (build, test, deploy) Pipeline fails at any stage or times out T-002 Terraform plan and apply complete without errors Terraform plan fails or apply returns non-zero exit code T-003 Prometheus alerts fire for high CPU threshold Alerts do not fire or fire incorrectly T-004 Backup and restore procedure completes successfully Backup fails or restore returns different data T-005 Security scan identifies vulnerabilities or confirms clean state Scan crashes or produces unexpected results

docs.title: Link Integrity Requirements
docs.text:
• All markdown-internal links must resolve to existing files
  • All in-page anchors must correspond to actual headings in the target file
  • check_links.py must report 0 broken links when run against the repository
  • No absolute URLs (http://, https://) should be used for internal references

docs.title: Additional Notes
docs.text:
• Tests should be run in the following order: T-001 → T-005
  • Each scenario should leave the environment in a clean state after execution
  • Evidence (logs, screenshots, artifacts) must be stored for any PASSED or FAILED test
  • Tests marked NOT RUN should have a justification comment

docs.title: Acceptance evidence
docs.text: requirements/acceptance-criteria.md is the gate. This directory stores the evidence that a gate item was actually executed.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
tests/acceptance/<test-id>/
├── command.txt      # the exact command(s) run
├── output.txt       # raw output, unedited
└── notes.md         # environment, time, deviations, operator

One directory per test ID (F-01, B-05, D-01, ...). The path recorded in the Evidence column of requirements/acceptance-criteria.md must point at the directory, and the directory must exist in Git.

docs.title: Status rules
docs.text:
Status Requirement NOT RUN Default. No evidence expected. PASSED Evidence directory exists, plus a date and a named tester. FAILED Evidence directory exists. A failure without a log is a rumour. BLOCKED Evidence explains the blocker (ticket, missing hardware, dependency).

Enforcement is automated in two places:

python3 scripts/acceptance_status.py          # phase table + gate count, exits 1 on bad sign-off
python3 tests/test_repo_tools.py              # same rule inside the repository self-check

scripts/acceptance_status.py --self-test proves the validator rejects an unsupported PASSED.

docs.title: How to execute a test
docs.text:
1. Read its row in requirements/acceptance-criteria.md (procedure, expected result, evidence, pass/fail, context).
  2. Run it in the stated context — staging unless the row says otherwise.
  3. Capture raw output, unedited, into tests/acceptance/<test-id>/output.txt.
  4. Open a pull request that adds the evidence and updates the row: status, evidence path, date (YYYY-MM-DD), tester.
  5. Review requires a second person who did not run the test.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
Phases are ordered by dependency, and the acceptance table inherits that order: offline operation (2) → infrastructure (3) → storage (6) → Kubernetes (7) → workloads and policy (8–10) → observability (11) → GPU (12) → pipeline (13) → failure and recovery (14).

Items in phase 14 (D-*, B-12, B-13, B-14) destroy or rebuild parts of the platform. Run them only in staging or an approved window, and always after the phase 2–13 items they depend on have passed.

docs.title: What is deliberately not automated
docs.text: The 48 criteria describe work on real hardware: pulling power from a node, removing an OSD, revoking a certificate, scanning an image with a CRITICAL CVE. A script that claimed to check them without the hardware would be a false assurance, which is the one thing this repository refuses to produce. The validator therefore enforces evidence, not execution.

docs.text: Format for every entry: symptoms -> likely causes -> diagnostic commands -> expected healthy state -> remediation -> risks -> verification.
