docs.title: Universal first-response sequence
docs.text:
Run this before any component-specific procedure. It eliminates most misdiagnoses.

# 1. Is the problem in my session or in the system?
date; timedatectl            # skew?
dig +short <target>          # name resolution?

# 2. Is the target reachable at all?
ping -c 3 <target-ip>        # layer 3
nc -zv <target> <port>       # layer 4
curl -vk https://<target>    # layer 5/7

# 3. Is the service actually running?
systemctl status <unit> --no-pager
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -30

# 4. Is it the cluster, or the workload?
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl describe node <node>

docs.title: Universal rules
docs.text:
1. Root cause before remediation. Restarting a component hides the symptom and loses the evidence. Collect the evidence first.
  2. One change at a time. Each change is a new hypothesis.
  3. Check the version matrix. Most "impossible" failures are a version incompatibility.
  4. Check the network matrix. Most "the service is down" reports are a firewall rule.
  5. Preserve the evidence. Copy logs before restarting anything.
  6. Never run a destructive command without explicit authorization.
  7. Record the resolution in the relevant runbook, with the command that actually fixed it.

docs.title: Diagnostic commands by layer
docs.text: Layer Command Healthy state Name resolution dig +short <name> The expected IP Reverse dig -x <ip> The expected hostname Time chronyc tracking Leap status normal, offset < 100 ms Reachability ping -c3 <ip> 0% loss Port nc -zv <ip> <port> Connection succeeded TLS openssl s_client -connect <ip>:443 -servername <name> Verify return code 0, correct chain Service systemctl is-active <unit> active Container kubectl get pod -o wide Running, 0 restarts Events kubectl describe pod No recent warnings Logs kubectl logs <pod> --previous The previous container's output (for crash loops) Cluster kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' All checks ok Storage kubectl get pvc Bound Admission kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations Expected configs present

docs.title: When to escalate
docs.text: Escalate to a second engineer when: - The evidence contradicts the runbook (the runbook is then wrong and must be corrected). - A destructive action is required and the authorization is ambiguous. - The failure spans two components and the boundary is unclear. - The same symptom returns after a documented remediation.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• All pod creation rejected ("admission webhook denied the request")
  • ValidatingWebhookConfiguration pointing to wrong service
  • MutatingWebhookConfiguration modifying resources unexpectedly
  • Webhook certificate expired
  • Webhook service unreachable

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• Webhook configuration points to deleted/changed service
  • Webhook backend pod crash-looping
  • Webhook TLS certificate expired
  • Webhook rejects all resources (too broad rules)
  • NamespaceSelector excludes required namespaces

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check webhook configurations
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration

# Check webhook service
kubectl get svc -l app=<webhook-app>
kubectl get pods -l app=<webhook-app>

# Check webhook logs
kubectl logs -l app=<webhook-app> -n <webhook-ns>

# Check webhook certificate
kubectl get secret <webhook-cert-secret> -o yaml

# Test webhook directly
kubectl create -f <test-resource.yaml> --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
  kubectl apply -f - --validate=false

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• Webhook configurations: valid, pointing to existing services
  • Webhook backend pods: Running
  • Webhook TLS certificate: valid
  • kubectl create --dry-run succeeds for allowed resources

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Fix webhook service reference (service name, namespace, path)
  • Restart webhook backend: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<webhook-app>
  • Rotate webhook TLS certificate
  • Narrow webhook rules (exclude system namespaces)
  • Fix NamespaceSelector to include required namespaces

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting webhook configuration can allow unrestricted resource creation
  • Wrong webhook rules can block all cluster operations
  • Certificate rotation can cause brief webhook failures

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: bash kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration -o yaml kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration -o yaml kubectl create -f <test-resource.yaml> --dry-run=client

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• ansible-playbook fails with "unreachable" on targets
  • Module not found or "No module named ansible"
  • Playbook fails with syntax error
  • Variable not defined error
  • Permission denied on remote hosts

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• SSH key not deployed to target hosts
  • Wrong inventory path or host groups
  • Ansible version mismatch with Kubespray release
  • Python not installed on target hosts
  • Sudo/become not configured correctly

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Test connectivity
ansible -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini all -m ping

# Check Ansible version
ansible --version

# Check Python on targets
ansible -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini all -m raw -a "python3 --version"

# Debug variables
ansible -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini <host> -m debug -a "var=ansible_host"

# Check become/sudo
ansible -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini all -m raw -a "whoami" --become

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• All hosts respond to ansible -m ping with "pong"
  • Ansible version matches Kubespray release requirements (>=2.19.0, <2.20.0)
  • Python 3.11-3.13 installed on all targets
  • ansible --become shows root on targets
  • Inventory variables resolve correctly

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Deploy SSH keys to target hosts
  • Fix inventory file (hosts, groups, variables)
  • Install correct Ansible version in virtualenv per Kubespray release
  • Install Python 3 on target hosts
  • Configure passwordless sudo for Ansible user

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Wrong inventory can cause changes to wrong hosts
  • Running playbooks without --check can make unintended changes
  • Mixing Ansible versions across Kubespray releases causes unpredictable failures

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: bash ansible -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini all -m ping ansible-playbook -i inventory/<cluster>/hosts.ini site.yml --check --diff ansible --version | head -3

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• kubectl commands fail with "connection refused" or "timeout"
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns failures
  • API server pod crash-looping
  • Authentication/authorization failures
  • Admission webhooks rejecting all requests

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• API server static pod not created by kubelet
  • etcd unreachable from API server
  • Certificate expired or wrong
  • Admission webhook configuration pointing to wrong service
  • etcd quorum lost

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Is API server running?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-apiserver

# Is etcd reachable?
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check API server certificate
kubectl get -n kube-system secret <apiserver-cert-secret> -o yaml

# Check admission webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration

# Test authentication
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• API server pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all checks ok
  • kubectl auth whoami returns authenticated user
  • etcd endpoint health: all endpoints healthy

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart API server: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix etcd connectivity (see etcd troubleshooting)
  • Rotate expired API server certificates
  • Fix admission webhook service references
  • Restore etcd quorum (see etcd troubleshooting)

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting API server pod makes cluster temporarily unreachable
  • Fixing admission webhooks can block all cluster operations if done wrong
  • Certificate rotation can break existing client connections

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: bash kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' kubectl auth whoami kubectl get nodes kubectl get pods -A | head -5

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• An application is stuck OutOfSync.
  • ComparisonError on an application.
  • A sync fails with a webhook or admission error.
  • argocd app sync reports "the application has not been modified".
  • The repo-server cannot fetch from the internal GitLab.
  • An image is pulled from the wrong registry.
  • Secrets are not populated in the target namespace.

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text: Cause Discriminator The Git repo has a change the cluster does not argocd app diff <app> shows the difference The repo-server cannot reach GitLab The application shows ComparisonError The CA is not trusted by the repo-server The repo-server log shows an x509 error The Git branch or path does not exist argocd app get <app> shows the error An admission controller rejects the resource The sync error names the webhook The image name points to the upstream registry The pod fails with ImagePullBackOff The ExternalSecret has not synced kubectl get externalsecret -A shows SecretSyncedError The application is paused argocd app get <app> shows paused Sync waves are blocking argocd app get <app> --show-operation

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Application state
argocd app list
argocd app get <app>
argocd app get <app> --show-operation
argocd app diff <app>
argocd app history <app>

# In-cluster
kubectl -n argocd get applications
kubectl -n argocd describe application <app>
kubectl -n argocd logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-repo-server --tail=100
kubectl -n argocd logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-application-controller --tail=100
kubectl -n argocd logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-server --tail=100

# The target state
kubectl -n <target-ns> get deploy <name> -o yaml
kubectl -n <target-ns> get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

# Secrets
kubectl get externalsecret -A
kubectl describe externalsecret <name> -n <ns>
kubectl -n external-secrets logs deploy/external-secrets --tail=100

# Admission
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
$ argocd app get payments-api
Name:           payments-api
Project:        team-payments
Server:         https://kubernetes.default.svc
Namespace:      payments
Sync Status:    Synced
Health Status:  Healthy

docs.title: ComparisonError
docs.text:
# The repo-server log names the cause
kubectl -n argocd logs -l app.kubernetes.io/name=argocd-repo-server --tail=200 | grep -i error
Error in the log Cause Fix x509: certificate signed by unknown authority The internal CA is not trusted Mount the CA into the repo-server pods and restart Could not resolve host DNS or network path to GitLab Check DNS and the firewall matrix authentication required The repository credential is missing or expired Update the Argo CD repository secret remote: HTTP Basic: Access denied The deploy key or token is invalid Re-issue the credential in GitLab, update the Argo CD secret

The Argo CD repository secret:

# The credential itself lives in Vault; ESO writes it into the argocd namespace
kubectl -n argocd get secret repo-payments -o jsonpath='{.data.url}' | base64 -d
kubectl -n argocd get secret repo-payments -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d

docs.title: Sync fails with an admission error
docs.text:
The error names the webhook and the constraint. Read the constraint:

kubectl get constraints -o yaml          # Gatekeeper
kubectl get clusterpolicy                 # Kyverno
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations -o yaml | grep -A5 failurePolicy

Two distinct problems: 1. The resource genuinely violates a policy. Fix the manifest. 2. The webhook is unavailable. Check the webhook's pods and the failurePolicy. A Fail policy blocks all writes to that namespace when the webhook is down.

docs.title: The image pulls from the upstream registry
docs.text:
argocd app get <app> | grep -i image
kubectl -n <ns> get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}'

Fix the source, not the symptom: - If the Git repo contains upstream image names, add an Argo CD image rewrite rule in argocd-cm, or use a Config Management Plugin. - If the CI pipeline builds the image, the pipeline should write the internal registry path into the manifest. That keeps one source of truth.

docs.title: Secrets not populated
docs.text:
kubectl describe externalsecret <name> -n <ns>
Condition Cause Fix SecretSyncedError ESO cannot read Vault Check the ClusterSecretStore, the Vault role, and the service account SecretSynced but the target Secret is empty A template mismatch Check the target.template and the remoteRef.property The Secret is synced but the app is unchanged The app does not reload Restart the app or use a reloader

docs.title: The application is paused
docs.text:
argocd app set <app> --sync-policy=none     # pause
argocd app set <app> --sync-policy=automated # resume

An application is often paused during an incident so that Argo CD does not revert a hotfix. Resume it after the incident.

docs.title: Sync waves blocking
docs.text:
argocd app get <app> --show-operation

A wave waits for the previous wave's resources to be healthy. A resource with a failing readiness probe blocks every later wave. Find the unhealthy resource in the wave and fix it, or remove the wave annotation.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• argocd app sync --prune with prune: true deletes resources removed from Git. A wrong path in Git can delete a StatefulSet or a PVC holder.
  • Removing a finalizer from an application orphans the resources it manages.
  • argocd app delete --cascade=false leaves the resources in the cluster but removes them from GitOps, which is a drift source.

docs.title: Verification after remediation
docs.text:
argocd app get <app>          # Synced + Healthy
kubectl -n <target-ns> get pods
kubectl -n <target-ns> get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}'

Then re-run acceptance test P-03 (Argo CD syncs an application from Git).

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• etcd snapshot fails
  • Backup not created at expected time
  • Restore fails: "snapshot not found" or "corrupt snapshot"
  • PV backup fails (Velero/rook-ceph)
  • Disaster recovery runbook steps fail

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• etcd not reachable for snapshot
  • Backup storage (S3/NFS) not mounted or unreachable
  • Snapshot corrupted or incomplete
  • Velero not installed or misconfigured
  • Rook-Ceph cluster unhealthy

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check etcd snapshot
ls -la /var/lib/etcd/snapshot/
etcdctl snapshot status <snapshot.db>

# Check backup storage
aws s3 ls s3://<backup-bucket>/
# or
mount | grep <backup-mount>

# Check Velero
kubectl -n velero get pods
kubectl -n velero get backup
kubectl -n velero logs -l app=velero

# Check Rook-Ceph
kubectl -n rook-ceph get pods
kubectl -n rook-ceph get cephcluster
ceph health
ceph osd status

# Check backup schedule
kubectl -n velero get schedule

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• etcd snapshots: recent, valid, not corrupt
  • Backup storage: reachable, writable
  • Velero: Running, backups completing
  • Rook-Ceph: HEALTH_OK
  • Backup schedules: enabled, last backup recent

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Fix etcd connectivity for snapshots
  • Fix backup storage connectivity/credentials
  • Create new etcd snapshot if old one is corrupt
  • Fix Velero configuration: velero backup create <name>
  • Fix Rook-Ceph cluster: replace failed OSDs, rebalance

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Restoring from corrupt snapshot causes data loss
  • Overwriting current data with old backup loses recent changes
  • Deleting old backups removes rollback options

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: bash etcdctl snapshot status <snapshot.db> kubectl -n velero get backup kubectl -n rook-ceph get cephcluster ceph health ls -la /var/lib/etcd/snapshot/

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• ceph -s reports HEALTH_WARN or HEALTH_ERR.
  • A pool is stuck in active+clean or active+remapped+backfilling.
  • A PVC write is slow or times out.
  • An OSD is down.
  • MON quorum is lost.

docs.title: Likely causes and their signatures
docs.text: Message Cause Action 1 pgs degraded A single OSD or host is down; the pool is recovering Replace the OSD. The pool heals itself 1 pgs stuck degraded More failures than the replica count can tolerate Data loss is possible. Stop writes and investigate immediately osd.N down OSD process or host failure Check the host, then the OSD OSD(s) ... have full status of down OSD is marked out but still referenced ceph osd in <id> mon.N (age ...) A monitor is unreachable Check the host and the MON port pgmap_full_percent The pool is near full Add capacity or free space; PGs cannot be created pgs not deep-scrubbed Informational, not an error Schedule deep scrubs no candidates for ... No eligible OSD for the CRUSH placement The CRUSH map or the host count does not satisfy the replica size MON_CLIENT errors from a CSI pod Network path or auth problem Test from the CSI pod's namespace

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# cephadm path
cephadm shell -- ceph -s
cephadm shell -- ceph status
cephadm shell -- ceph health detail
cephadm shell -- ceph osd tree
cephadm shell -- ceph osd df
cephadm shell -- ceph df
cephadm shell -- ceph pg stat
cephadm shell -- ceph pg ls
cephadm shell -- ceph mon dump
cephadm shell -- ceph osd df tree
cephadm shell -- ceph crash ls

# Rook path
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-operator -- ceph -s
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-operator -- ceph health detail
kubectl -n rook-ceph exec deploy/rook-ceph-operator -- ceph osd tree

# Host level
df -h
ceph-volume lvm list
iostat -x 1

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
HEALTH_OK
  services:
    mon: 3 daemons, quorum a,b,c
    mgr: 1 daemon, 1 active
    osd: 12 osds: 12 up, 12 in

docs.title: An OSD is down
docs.text:
# 1. Identify the host and device
cephadm shell -- ceph osd tree
cephadm shell -- ceph orch device ls

# 2. Check the host
ssh osd-2 "systemctl status ceph-osd@<id>; df -h /var/lib/ceph"

# 3. If the disk is gone, replace it and recreate the OSD
#    cephadm path:
cephadm shell -- ceph orch device ls
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply osd osd-2 --replace <osd-id>

#    Rook path: add the device to spec.storage.nodes and apply

The pool backfills automatically. Watch it:

watch -n 10 "cephadm shell -- ceph -s"

docs.title: MON quorum loss
docs.text:
With 3 MONs, losing 1 keeps quorum. Losing 2 does not.

# Identify and remove the dead mon
cephadm shell -- ceph mon dump
cephadm shell -- ceph mon remove <mon-id>
cephadm shell -- ceph orch apply mon --placement="3 host1 host2 host3"

If all 3 MONs are down, the cluster is unrecoverable without the monmap and OSD map backups. That is why those maps are part of the backup set.

docs.title: The pool is full
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph df
cephadm shell -- ceph osd df tree

Free space: 

# Remove old snapshots
cephadm shell -- rbd snap ls <image>
cephadm shell -- rbd snap rm <image> <snapshot>
# Remove unused images
cephadm shell -- rbd ls
cephadm shell -- rbd rm <image>
# Or expand the pool
cephadm shell -- ceph osd pool set <pool> size <new-size>

docs.title: A stuck PG
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph pg <pgid> query
cephadm shell -- ceph pg <pgid> stuck
cephadm shell -- ceph osd find pgid <pgid>

If a PG is stuck because the required OSDs are down, fix the OSDs. Forcing a PG to incomplete loses the consistency guarantee and should be a last resort with explicit authorization:

cephadm shell -- ceph osd rm-pg-upmap-items <pgid>

docs.title: Slow IO
docs.text:
# Per-OSD commit latency
cephadm shell -- ceph osd perf
# Host level
iostat -x 1
# Network between OSDs
iperf3 -c <peer-osd-host>

Common causes: a slow journal device, saturated network on the replication path, or an OSD running on an oversubscribed disk. Check the capacity worksheet in storage/ceph/cephadm-deployment.md against the measured numbers.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• ceph osd pool delete destroys data irreversibly. Never run it to "clear" a pool.
  • ceph osd purge removes an OSD's data. Only after the OSD's data is confirmed replicated elsewhere.
  • Removing an OSD during a rebuild slows the rebuild and can push the pool closer to full.
  • Changing the CRUSH map triggers data movement. Do it in a window, and only when the pool has headroom.

docs.title: Verification after remediation
docs.text:
cephadm shell -- ceph -s          # expect HEALTH_OK
cephadm shell -- ceph osd tree    # expect all OSDs up and in
# Write test
rbd create --pool rbd --size 1 testvol
rbd map testvol && rbd rm testvol

Then re-run acceptance test E-07 (Ceph health sustained for 24 hours) if the incident involved a pool event.

docs.title: A. Purpose and scope
docs.text: Troubleshooting guide for cert-manager certificate issuance failures. Covers certificates stuck in Pending, webhook startup failures, ClusterIssuer configuration errors, and ACME challenge failures. Cross-references service-mesh/evaluation.md and kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md.

docs.title: Symptom: kubectl get certificate shows Ready: False with reason Pending
docs.text:
Possible causes: - Issuer not ready - ACME challenge not reachable (public ACME path only) - Secret not found for issuer TLS key - DNS-01 challenge not configured for internal DNS

Verification: 

kubectl describe certificate <name> -n <ns>
kubectl get issuer -n <ns>
kubectl get clusterissuer

Fix: - Verify issuer is Ready: kubectl get clusterissuer -o yaml - For public ACME: ensure outbound internet connectivity and reachable challenge endpoint - For internal CA/Vault PKI: verify Vault PKI CA is operational - Create the referenced secret if missing

docs.title: Symptom: cert-manager-webhook pod crash-looping
docs.text:
Possible causes: - Webhook needs a certificate from itself (chicken-and-egg on first install) - cert-manager CRDs not installed before webhook starts

Verification: 

kubectl -n cert-manager get pods -l app=webhook
kubectl -n cert-manager logs -l app=webhook -c webhook
kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager

Fix: - Install cert-manager with --set installCRDs=true first, then apply issuers, then enable webhook - Or use the Helm chart which handles ordering automatically

docs.title: Symptom: ClusterIssuer not Ready, certificates reference unknown issuer
docs.text:
Possible causes: - ClusterIssuer not deployed or not Ready - Certificate references wrong issuer name or namespace - ClusterIssuer is namespace-scoped (use Issuer instead)

Verification: 

kubectl get clusterissuer -o yaml
kubectl get issuer -A
kubectl describe certificate <name> -n <ns>

Fix: - Deploy ClusterIssuer before certificates that reference it - Use Issuer for namespace-scoped certificate authority - Verify issuer name matches in certificate spec.issuerRef

docs.title: Symptom: Order or Challenge resources show failure
docs.text:
Possible causes: - DNS-01 challenge: DNS provider credentials missing or wrong - HTTP-01 challenge: ingress not reachable from public internet - TLS-ALPN challenge: port 443 not accessible

Verification: 

kubectl get order -n <ns>
kubectl get challenge -n <ns>
kubectl describe challenge <name> -n <ns>

Fix: - For DNS-01: verify DNS provider secret exists and credentials are valid - For HTTP-01: ensure ingress controller is reachable from public internet - For internal CA/Vault PKI path: skip ACME entirely, use Vault PKI issuer

docs.title: F. Cross-references
docs.text:
• service-mesh/evaluation.md — Service mesh evaluation with cert-manager context
  • kubespray/kubespray-deployment.md — Kubespray deployment with cert-manager integration

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Pods stay ContainerCreating with a network error.
  • Pod-to-pod traffic between nodes fails; same-node traffic works.
  • A NetworkPolicy blocks traffic that should be allowed.
  • DNS resolution from inside a pod fails.
  • The API server is unreachable from a node.

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text: Cause Discriminator CNI agent not ready kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium MTU mismatch between the pod network and the physical network ping -M do -s 1472 across nodes fails, same-node succeeds Missing route for the pod CIDR On the node: ip route get <pod-ip> fails; on a router: no route for the pod CIDR kube-proxy not installed and Cilium's replacement not enabled kubectl -n kube-system get ds kube-proxy absent AND kubeProxyReplacement not set A default-deny NetworkPolicy with no allow rule Traffic fails only for pods in that namespace IPtables/ipvs rules stale Services do not resolve to a backend DNS service unreachable nslookup kubernetes.default from a pod fails

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# CNI status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium -o wide
cilium status --verbose
cilium connectivity test

# Hubble (Cilium observability)
cilium hubble list
cilium hubble observe --namespace default

# Node routes
ip route get <remote-pod-ip>
ip -br addr

# MTU
ping -M do -s 1472 <peer-node-ip>     # 1472 + 28 = 1500
ping -M do -s 1400 <peer-node-ip>     # smaller payload

# Service resolution from a pod
kubectl run nettest --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl run nettest --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- \
  wget -S -O- --timeout=5 http://<service>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local

# Network policies in a namespace
kubectl get networkpolicies -n <ns>
kubectl get ciliumnetworkpolicies -n <ns>
kubectl get cnp -n <ns> -o yaml

# Kube-proxy / service handling
kubectl -n kube-system get ds kube-proxy
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head -30

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• cilium status: KubeProxyReplacement: True when enabled, KVStore: Disabled for the embedded etcd mode, all agents Ready.
  • cilium connectivity test: all probes pass.
  • A pod can resolve kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local and reach the API.
  • ip route get <remote-pod-ip> returns a route on the node.

docs.title: MTU
docs.text:
Set the MTU to the physical network MTU minus the encapsulation overhead, then restart the CNI agent.

# Cilium Helm values
ipam:
  mode: kubernetes
ipv4:
  enabled: true
mtu: 1450        # 1500 - 50 for VXLAN; for native routing use the physical MTU

ip link show cilium_host

docs.title: Missing route
docs.text:
With Cilium in routingMode: native, the node needs a route to the pod CIDR via the other nodes. Either:

  • BGP (bgpControlPlane.enabled: true) and a BGP speaker on the router, or
  • static routes on the router for each node's pod CIDR segment, or
  • encapsulation (VXLAN), which does not need external routes.

The native-routing mode requires the network team to add routes. This is the single most common cause of cross-node pod failures in a native-routing deployment.

docs.title: kube-proxy replacement
docs.text:
kubeProxyReplacement: strict
k8sServiceHost: <apiserver-vip>
k8sServicePort: 6443

k8sServiceHost and k8sServicePort are mandatory when kube-proxy is absent, otherwise the agent cannot reach the API server.

docs.title: A NetworkPolicy blocks the traffic
docs.text:
# Which policies apply to a pod
kubectl get networkpolicies -A -o json | \
  jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector.matchLabels as $l | ...)'

# Cilium policy trace
cilium policy trace <src-pod> <dst-pod> --to-dst-port 443

cilium policy trace is the fastest way to see which policy allows or denies a flow.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
# From a pod
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

# CoreDNS
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50

If CoreDNS is healthy but resolution fails from one namespace, a NetworkPolicy is blocking the DNS egress (UDP 53 to the CoreDNS service). A default-deny egress policy needs an explicit DNS allowance.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Changing the Cilium MTU requires a pod restart on the node; the agent restarts and pods lose their network.
  • Enabling strict kube-proxy replacement is not reversible at runtime without a node drain.
  • Deleting a NetworkPolicy to "fix" connectivity removes a security control. Find the offending rule instead.

docs.title: Verification after remediation
docs.text:
cilium connectivity test
kubectl run nettest --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- \
  wget -q -O- --timeout=5 http://kubernetes.default.svc

Then re-run acceptance test B-09 (network policy enforcement: the allowed flow succeeds and the denied flow still fails).

docs.title: Kubernetes Control Plane Troubleshooting
docs.text: This document covers troubleshooting for all Kubernetes control plane components: API server, etcd, controller-manager, and scheduler. Each section includes symptoms, likely causes, diagnostic commands, expected healthy state, remediation steps, risks, and verification checks.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• kubectl commands fail with "connection refused" or "timeout"
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns failures
  • API server pod crash-looping
  • Authentication/authorization failures
  • Admission webhooks rejecting all requests

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• API server static pod not created by kubelet
  • etcd unreachable from API server
  • Certificate expired or wrong
  • Admission webhook configuration pointing to wrong service
  • etcd quorum lost

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Is API server running?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-apiserver

# Is etcd reachable?
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check API server certificate
kubectl get -n kube-system secret <apiserver-cert-secret> -o yaml

# Check admission webhooks
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration

# Test authentication
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• API server pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' returns all checks ok
  • kubectl auth whoami returns authenticated user
  • etcd endpoint health: all endpoints healthy

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart API server: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix etcd connectivity (see etcd troubleshooting)
  • Rotate expired API server certificates
  • Fix admission webhook service references
  • Restore etcd quorum (see etcd troubleshooting)

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Deleting API server pod makes cluster temporarily unreachable
  • Fixing admission webhooks can block all cluster operations if done wrong
  • Certificate rotation can break existing client connections

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl auth whoami
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A | head -5

docs.title: etcd
docs.text: Please refer to etcd.md for detailed etcd troubleshooting including member health, quorum loss, disk space, clock skew, and snapshot restoration.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Cloud controller manager specific operations fail
  • Node controller stops updating node status
  • Route/load balancer creation fails
  • Statefulset operations stall

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• Controller-manager static pod not running
  • kubeconfig misconfiguration
  • API server unreachable
  • Certificate expiry
  • Resource starvation (CPU/memory)

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check controller-manager pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-controller-manager
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-controller-manager

# Check for errors related to node controller
kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -i "notready\|unschedulable"

# Verify API server access
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check certificate validity
ls -l /etc/kubernetes/pki/controller-manager/

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• Controller-manager pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • Node controller: Nodes transitioning through expected states
  • Cloud resource creation: Operational within SLA
  • API server health: All checks passing

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart controller-manager: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix kubeconfig if misconfigured
  • Rotate expired certificates
  • Increase resource limits if starved
  • Debug specific cloud provider API rate limits

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Restarting controller-manager causes temporary loss of node management operations
  • Certificate rotation can break controller-to-API-server authentication
  • Increasing resource limits may not help if the issue is a memory leak

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'
kubectl get pods -A -l component=kube-controller-manager

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text:
• Pods not scheduled onto available nodes
  • Scheduler pod crash-looping
  • Node affinity/anti-affinity not working
  • Pods stuck in Pending state

docs.title: Likely causes
docs.text:
• Scheduler static pod not running
  • API server unreachable from scheduler
  • Predicate/ priority plugins failing
  • Resource distribution imbalance
  • Node label/node selector mismatch

docs.title: Diagnostic commands
docs.text:
# Check scheduler pod status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-scheduler
kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-scheduler

# Check pending pods and reasons
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Describe a pending pod for detailed reasons
kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> -n <namespace>

# Verify API server access
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# Check scheduler policy config
ls -l /etc/kubernetes/scheduler/

docs.title: Expected healthy state
docs.text:
• Scheduler pods: Running, 0 restarts
  • Pending pods: 0 (or expected number from topology spread)
  • All nodes receive pods according to scheduling logic
  • API server health: All checks passing

docs.title: Remediation
docs.text:
• Restart scheduler: delete static pod manifest, kubelet recreates
  • Fix kubeconfig if misconfigured
  • Debug and disable problematic predicates/priorities
  • Rebalance resource distribution across nodes
  • Verify node labels and pod affinity/anti-affinity rules

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Restarting scheduler can cause a brief period of no new pod scheduling
  • Disabling predicates may allow pods to be scheduled on unsuitable nodes
  • Resource rebalancing may take time to propagate

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending | wc -l
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'
kubectl get pods -A -l component=kube-scheduler

docs.title: Cluster health checks
docs.text:
# Overall cluster readiness
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'

# API server health
kubectl get --raw='/healthz'

# etcd health (from a control-plane node)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  endpoint health --cluster

# Node status
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Control-plane component status
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=kube-apiserver,kube-controller-manager,kube-scheduler

docs.title: Logs collection
docs.text:
# All control-plane component logs
for component in kube-apiserver kube-controller-manager kube-scheduler; do
  kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=$component
done

docs.title: etcd specific
docs.text:
# Member list
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/healthcheck-client.key \
  member list -w table

# Endpoint health
